Uniform Title: *Tantracintāmaṇi* Main Title: *Tantracintāmaṇi* with the *Pañjikā* Commentary Author: Navamīsiṃha
Alternative Name: Ādyānanda Manuscript: NGMCP Manuscript No. 4-1665; Reel No. B 131/2 Description:
The first thirty chapters of the *Tantracintāmaṇi* together with its commentary, the *Pañjikā*.
Description by Mark S.G. Dyczkowski:
The author of the *Tantracintāmaṇi* is Navamīsiṃha, who is also known as Ādyānanda. At the beginning of his work, he tells us that...

He was a minister of King Bhūpālendra of Nepal, whom he describes as a pious and learned man. He was likely King Mahendra Malla or Bhūpālendra Malla of Kathmandu, who reigned for approximately five years between 1689 and 1694 CE. Like the *Kulamuktikallolinī*, by the same [author]...

Navamīsiṃha, this too is a massive compendium of passages drawn from a wide range of tantras. In its first chapter, he discusses the creation of the universe and, along with it, the tantras themselves. He maintains that Kālī...
Kṛṣṇa Tārā and Rāma are essentially the same. He presents the mantras and ritual procedures for the worship of the ten Mahāvidyās, which by his time had become a popular group of deities in Nepal.

They were located in North India. He also treats the worship of Śiva and Śakti. Furthermore, he devotes considerable space to an exposition of the worship of Śyāmā. The chapters are termed *prakāśas*. The twentieth—
The fifth chapter is missing from this manuscript. A complete manuscript containing all forty chapters is deposited in the Asiatic Society of Mumbai.
The format of all the colophons is exemplified by that of the first chapter, which is as follows:
*iti śrītantracintāmaṇau sṛṣṭikramanirūpaṇātmakaḥ prathamaprakāśaḥ* (Thus ends the first chapter, consisting of the description of the process of emanation, in the venerable Tantracintāmaṇi).
The titles of the chapters indicate their respective contents. They are as follows:
sṛṣṭikramanirūpaṇa || 1 ||

1. An exposition on the greatness [of the practice], preceded by the necessity of the extraction and worship of the Śrī-Śyāmā and other Vidyās; 2. The determination of the Guru, the disciple, and the Mantra; 3. [The determination of the Mantra].
The determination of the sixteen sacraments, beginning with conception, for practitioners.
The Determination of the Time for Initiation. 6.
The Determination of the Vāstu Sacrifice. || 7 ||
The determination of the Paśupati-kuṇḍa and other sites. 8.
The determination of the ritual procedure for initiation. || 10 ||
The Determination of the Full Empowerment (Pūrṇābhiṣeka-nirṇaya) || 11 ||
The Determination of Conduct, Beginning with the Giving of Honoraria (Dakṣiṇā). 12.
The determination of the sequence beginning with Mahānīla. || 13 ||
The Determination of Cultivation. 14.
The determination of the morning duties and so forth. 15.
The determination of the procedures beginning from the entry into the worship pavilion up to the completion of the network of ritual placements (*nyāsa*) for the common daily worship.
The determination of the rites from the worship of the Tāraka-mantra up to the final dismissal within the common daily worship.

In the Kaula and Vāma traditions, regarding the common daily worship (nityārcanā), this is the determination [of the procedure] beginning with the origin of that path and ending with the installation of the Śrīpātra and other vessels. 18.
In the general daily worship of the Nityās during the Kaula and Vāma traditions, there is the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and the consumption of the Kula substances.
The determination of the distinctions among the *sāttvika* and other types of worship, such as the offering of food and so forth. (20)
The Determination of the Daily Worship of Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā. 21.
The determination of the hymns, armor-chants, and so forth for the daily worship of Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā. 22.
The determination of the rites for Mahākāla and others, as well as for Amitāyus and Antaka. || 23 ||
The determination of the daily worship common to the three divisions of Tārā. || 24 ||
25. Missing from this manuscript or erroneously numbered: *Śrīvidyānityārcananirṇaya*. 26.
The Determination of the Daily Worship of the Vidyās of Tripurabhairavī, Mahālakṣmī, Mātaṅgī, Bhuvaneśī, Dhūmāvatī, and Vagalāmukhī. || 27 ||
The determination of the worship of the entire common wheel. || 28 ||
The determination of the concluding consecration (pratiṣṭhānta) preceded by the ritual of the yantra and so forth. || 29 ||
The determination of the installation of various types of rosaries and so forth. || 30 ||

Country of publication: India.
Oṃ, salutation to Śrī Kālikā.
She by whom this creation, consisting of the *kula* and *akula*, has been brought about in its true nature.
The elements, the five flavors, the radiant [deities], and the four Vedas respectively. || 1 ||

Salutations to her whose essence is the syllable *Bhūḥ*, who is eternally accompanied by the ocean within the circle of the world, the bestower of accomplishment upon practitioners, and she of stainless and renowned fame.
I bow to the lotus-feet of the Guru, who is intent on bestowing the supreme knowledge; to the divine stream [of gurus] beginning with Prabhūti; to Vighneśa and Laṃbodara;
to Paśupati, the author of the compositions of the Tantras; and to Guhyeśvarī and Kalikā.
To the Yoginī Vajrā and others, who are most highly praised by Brahmā, Upendra, and Mahendra;

O King, you are the ninth minister of the sovereign of Nepal, the crest-jewel of all the lords of the earth, a treasury of learning whose character is defined by poetry, who is devoted to various acts of charity, asceticism, and vows, and who is a lord of kings and ruler of the land.
Having determined the sequence, he now elaborates the Śrītantracintāmaṇi together with those of pure intellect.
If, with the thought of brevity in this work, you were to keep the secret concealed, then my status as a scholar would appear as mere foolishness.
Therefore, O Mother Goddess, since the disclosure of secrets is certain in this world, please perform the pacification of the fault of its public revelation.
Therefore, you wise ones, whose minds are fixed on the ultimate truth, who desire supreme accomplishment, and who are eager to know the entire secret doctrine of each respective deity—
please behold this my work, composed by me.
Therefore, you should understand that this is considered easy to practice because it has been examined through various manuals.
The names of those whose words regarding mantras have been made manifest in this treatise, as well as the account of the origin of the tantra, are stated once again.
The preeminence of the Āgamas, the creation and its origin, and the sequence thereof;
the identity of Kālikā and Kṛṣṇa, and of Tārā and Rāma.
The determination of the ten sciences is the worship of the forms of Śiva and Śakti;
the fact that Śyāmā is the root of all was stated in the first illuminator (Prakāśa).
The characteristics of the left and right [paths] according to the sequence of the extraction of mantras (mantroddhāra),
as well as the determination of the path within one's own tradition (svāmnāya) regarding the Vidyā, are each distinct.
Among the *makāras*, the fourth is the *āvaśyaka* (the necessary), which depends upon its basis;
without a guru, one has no authority over that *tantra* or *mantra*—this is the definition.
In the second chapter, the praise of initiation (dīkṣā) was proclaimed,
as well as the equality of the venerable Guru with Śiva and the determination of the characteristics of a Guru.
Without a guru, there is no instruction; for women, it is from their own male leader.
Regarding the characteristics and non-characteristics of the disciple, the determination of these two rests upon the oral tradition (āmnāya).
There should be a discernment between what is to be abandoned and what is not; for them, there is another instruction:
women and Śūdras have no entitlement to Vedic mantras and the like.

Birth and the mind should be given [as gifts] to the Brahmins and others; the discernment of what is to be given should also be imparted. Their established status, however, is to be understood from the third chapter of the *Prakāśa*.
In the fourth light, there are exactly sixteen consecrations for the practitioner;
therein, in the one called "Bestowing of Names," the drawing of the wheels is performed.
Sixteen consecrations for mantras have been taught;
their bestowal upon the Lord of the Center is revealed in the fifth [chapter].

The determination of the month and so forth is proclaimed in the sixth chapter; furthermore, the procedure for initiation, the acquisition of wealth and other matters, and the ritual circumambulation of the earth are described therein.
At the outset of the ritual procedure for the Vāstuyāga, its origin is proclaimed;
likewise, its maṇḍala as prescribed in the scriptures and the determination regarding the deity therein are declared.
The *vali-mantras* for the deities of the *vāstu-maṇḍala* as described in the Tantras have been explained in the seventh chapter; now, in this eighth [chapter], they are being declared.
The consecration of the pavilion, the characteristics of the sacrificial pits and other features,
and the sowing of sprouts are declared in the ninth illuminating chapter.
The procedure for inviting the Guru, the auspicious and inauspicious nature of the tooth-stick,
the dream, the procedure for the formal request, and the discernment regarding the abiding of the fire.
First, there is the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), followed by the installation of the fire;
then, since the rites such as initiation (dīkṣā) have not yet been performed, the gathering of forest materials for its constituent parts follows thereafter.
There is a distinction in the bestowal of mantras between the Left and Right paths;
they provide instruction regarding Kula women and teach the different types of initiation.
The procedure for worship, the determination of mantras obtained in dreams,
and the abandonment of the preceptor, the deity, and the *manu*— these are the ten illuminations.
The conducts (ācāra) are declared to be tenfold, beginning with Mahānīla and so forth, in due order;
[they are taught] in the Trayodaśaprakāśaka concerning the Śyāmā and other Vidyās.

In the fourteenth chapter, there is a discernment of what is fit and unfit for the worship of the divine heroes (*divyavīras*) and the bound souls (*paśus*), as well as their internal dispositions (*bhāvas*).

Worship is proclaimed to be divided according to the distinctions of *sāttvika* and the other [guṇas]; each distinct rite bestows liberation. Following that is the procedure for the morning duties (*prātaḥkṛtya*).
The ritual procedure for Ajayā, various types of ablutions as prescribed by tradition,
the wearing of sacred ash (vibhūti), the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), and sandalwood paste are to be performed in successive order.
The extraction of the *gāyatrī* mantras shines forth in [this work] consisting of [the specified] number of verses;
it includes the praise of worship, the installation of the door-deities, and the expulsion of obstructing spirits.

The purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the Mātṛkā-nyāsa and others, the enumeration of the Kalās, the inner worship, the rites, and the procedure for placing the arghya and other offerings in the illuminator [of the lamp].
The materials for drawing diagrams (yantras), the determination of the ritual seats (pīṭhas),
and the origin and characteristics of the Śālagrāma stone.
Hari, Īśa, the Daughter of the Mountain, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, and the guardians of the directions and planets—
their distinctions have been correctly explained individually according to their differences.

The mudrās for all the ritual services, along with their individual characteristics and so forth; then the procedure for the daily fire offering (nityahoma), the bali offering to the spirits, and the concluding rite (ārātrika).
The *karamālā* is taught as divided according to the [specific] deities;
everything beginning with the *brahmārpaṇa* [mantra] is in the seventeenth chapter.

The origin of the Kula path, the fivefold purity, and the ritual procedure; then the purification of power (śakti) according to the Kaula and other traditions, along with their specific distinctions and definitive conclusions.
The classification of material gifts, their origin, the ritual of cooking,
the proper determination regarding meat and other substances, and the secondary alternatives for the prescribed methods.
The internal distinction consists of the refinement and the sequential description;
in the exposition of the number of vessels, there is the determination of the Mānasa-iṣṭi and so forth.
Furthermore, [the text describes] the purification, the characteristics, and the ritual procedure for the great vessel (mahāpātra),
as well as the placement of the venerable vessel (śrīpātra) and so forth, the libation (tarpaṇa), and the purification of the principles (tattva).
The offering (bali) to Vaṭuka and others exists in the eighteenth [chapter], the Prakāśaka;
as do the ritual services for worship, the mantras, the kula-substances, and their consumption.
In this nineteenth chapter,
the rules for the evening meal and so forth have been revealed, as well as the procedure for recording one's daily duties.
The lineage of Śiva, the nocturnal ritual, and the definitive determination of the eternal distinction have been written in the twentieth chapter, which is approved by all.
The sequence of worship for Śyāmā is in the twenty-first [chapter] and so forth;
the proper writing of hymns and other such works is in the twentieth [chapter].
Furthermore, the extraction of the mantras for Mahākāla and the other Nityās is revealed in this twenty-third chapter.
The sequence of Tārā worship is indeed in the twenty-first [chapter],
while the worship of Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā is in the twenty-fifth.
The sequence of Śrīvidyā is correctly [expounded] in the twenty-sixth chapter:
Bhairavī, Mahālakṣmī, Mātaṅgī, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Dhūmāvatī and Vagalā— the worship of these [deities] individually has been set forth in this twenty-seventh chapter.
First is the worship of the wheel (*cakrapūjā*), then the preliminary rites and the characteristics of the ritual materials;
therein follows the two-fold sacrifice and the distinct characteristics of the messengers (*dūtās*).
Then follows the ritual of the sacrifice to the female messengers (dūtīyāga) according to the sequence of the ten sciences;
this practice of the wheel (cakrācāra), consisting of twenty-eight [verses] and more, has been revealed here.
The arrangement of the yantras, beginning with the *prastāra*, proceeds sequentially on the right and left;
thus, twenty-one types of installations (*pratiṣṭhā*) have been described in the *Prakāśaka*.
The garland is of two kinds, mobile and immobile, according to the different traditions of the deities;
the specific power of each is said to arise from its origin, such as that of the rudrākṣa.
The determination of the great fruits resulting from piercing with the great conch and other [piercing instruments],
as well as the distinctions regarding threading and so forth, and likewise the various types of consecrations and other rites.
The Mahāmālā, its emanation, and the two primary types of refinement (saṃskāra) are described;
the awakening of that [mālā] is taught in the Triṃśatprakāśaka.
p.
2b) Then follow the timing of the practice, the ancillary limbs of the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa),
the procedure for Vighnarāja, the Vidyā-mantra, and the definitive determination of the specific oral tradition (āmnāya).
The determination of the number of recitations and other details for the ten vidyās in their respective order;
the specific abodes of the deities that bestow all siddhis.
The origin of the pīṭhas, the procedure for the acquisition of the kṣetra,
the thorough knowledge of the kūrmacakra, and then the rite of consecration (abhiṣeka).
Then follows the consideration of what should and should not be done, the method of forming the mental resolve (saṃkalpa),
the statement regarding the time for recitation (japa), and the secret concerning impurity (sūtaka).
The determination of the time of awakening is made through the distinction between mantra and vidyā;
when there is a distinction between those two, there follows the crest-mantra (śikhā-mantra) and the consciousness of the mantra.
The procedure for the *kullukā* of the ten *vidyās* has been declared in sequence;
thereafter follows the exposition of *nirvāṇa* according to the distinctions of the *setu*, such as the Brahmin and others.

There is no distinction between the piercing of the curse and its extraction; there is no difference between the removal of the curse and the purification of the mind; and there is no particular difference between the heart of the mantra and the determination of its meaning.
This [work] illuminates twenty-one aspects, including the commencement and divisions of *japa*, the re-performance of the *vīra* initiation, and the hymns and other liturgical texts of Śiva.
The means for the accomplishment of mantras, the rites of the corpse-accomplishment (*citāsādhana*),
the various types of hero-accomplishment (*vīrasādhana*), and the distinct [practices] regarding the Vidyā-mantra.
The measure of the number of recitations is thirty-two pairs in the *Prakāśaka*;
[this section also contains] the determination of the time and other factors for occasional rites (*naimittika*), as well as the distinction between *Kula* and *Akula*.
Appropriation is said to be twofold, distinguished as external and internal;
[this section covers] the origin of the *damanaka* offering and the ritual procedure for the *damanaka* offering.
The origin of the Pavitrāropaṇa, the ritual procedure for the Pavitrāropaṇa,
the types of knots, their distinctions, and the deities— these are elucidated in the thirty-third chapter.
The ritual for the autumnal festival is in the thirty-fourth chapter;
the "Discrimination regarding the Offering of Animals" is the determination of the various types of sacrificial animals and so forth.
The time for the gratification of the deities, the examination of the characteristics of the sacrificial animal,
the sprinkling of the men, the characteristics of the sword, and the determination of the vessels.
The thirty-five types of auspicious and inauspicious food offerings,
and the determination of the characteristics of the maidens in the ritual of their worship.
The conventions regarding auspicious and inauspicious times and so forth, the illumination of the thirty seasons,
the general rules for rites performed for specific desires, and the determination of the sequence of the six ritual acts.
The miscellaneous discourse on these includes the description of seats and other requisites,
the various methods of stringing mantras, and the determination of rosaries, sacrificial pits, and so forth.
The measurement of the sacrificial substances is explained in thirty-seven ways;
furthermore, the application of the ten Vidyās is set forth individually and in sequence.
Subsequently, in the thirty-eighth chapter, there is the procedure for expiation (prāyaścitta),
as well as the description of the characteristics of the yantras in sequence, while beholding the imperial seal (sāmrājya-mudrikā).
In the *Prakāśaka*, there are forty *dhāraṇās* for the practitioners of mantra;
in each of these, the description of the visualization (*dhyāna*) and so forth of the letters of the Mother-mantra is provided.
The various divisions of mantras for the ten vidyās have been proclaimed in sequence;
there are forty mantras for the various ritual applications in this illuminating work.
Kumārī, Yoginī, Kālī, Vārāhī, Kubjikā, Parā,
Nārāyaṇī, Muṇḍamālā, Cāmuṇḍā, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Gautamī, Samasūtrāmaṇi, Vijayamālinī,
Līlāvatī, Guhyasiddhi, Mālinī, and Parameśvarī.
Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍikā, Śambhū, Nityā, Kātyāyanī,
Phetkārī, Bhairavī, Bhūtasiddhi, and likewise Siddheśvarī.
Meru, Nīla, Mataṅga, Śaktisaṃgama,
Bhairavī, Sāṃkhyāyana, the one called Kiraṇa, Gandharva, and Bhūtabhairava.
Vīrārdana, Vīrabhadra, Rudra, Kālāgnirudra,
Siddhisārasvata, Hāhārāva, and Manthānabhairava.
Siddheśvara, Viśvasāra, and likewise Vauddhāyana;
Māheśvara, Mahāhāra, Kālāgni, and also Mṛḍānī.
Therefore, the individual meanings of the word "tantra" for these [deities] should be known:
Siddhanātha, Mahākāla, and Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Surendra, Brahmagorakṣā, Śaṃpāyana,
Nandikeśvara, Vāyavya, Vārāhī, and Śāmbhavī.
Sanatkumāra, Śrīkaṇṭha, Agastya, Tattvasāraka,
and Vasiṣṭha— these are the names of their respective Saṃhitās.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Siddha, Devī, Umā, Candra, and Śakti—
from these [eight] their union (yāmala) is to be known as the one designated by the name "Eight" (aṣṭasaṃjñaka).
The Kulavīra-mantra-bhāva-cūḍāmaṇi was proclaimed by Hayagrīva to Nārada and from Mahākapila.
Then there are the *Pañcarātra*, the goddesses, the *Śaiva-linga-āgamas*,
and the renowned *Kumārikalpa*, *Vijayākalpa*, *Kālīkalpa*, and *Tārākalpa*.
The Mātṛ-mantras, the various forms of knowledge, the secret Kulas, and the Kulas themselves—
from these words, the ocean is proclaimed.
The secret sequence of Kullolinī and Śrīmatkāla is to be known as the northern state; it is proclaimed as the Caṇḍī-pīṭha.
The Nityāhnikamātilaka, the Uḍḍīśa preceded by the Kula,
the Svāyaṃbhuvatantra, the Somaśambhu, and likewise the Piṅgalāmata.
The six-lineages, the Great Jewel, and the two Lords of the Nine Jewels— the Kāmadhenu doctrine and that known as the one born of the Kumbha family.
The Kālikrama, the Matsyasūkta, the Udayākara-paddhati,
the Yoginīhṛdaya, and the Kālīhṛdaya.
The *Triśaktiratnaka*, the *Somabhujaṅga*, the *Vali*,
the *Kulāvatāraka*, the *Padyavārāhī*, and that which begins with *Hara*.
The *Gaurīsaṃvādaka* is to be known, as well as the *Samākarṇika-mātṛkā*,
the *Tūrṇāyāga*, the *Lalita*, and that which is proclaimed as the *Svacchanda*.
The Kulaprakāśaka, the Kulāmṛtapradīpikā,
the work known as the Navadurgākalpa, and the Kulamūlāvatāraka.
The *Tantrarāja* and *Kāmākhyā* are known from the word; the *Pañcāsikā* is likewise remembered.
From among these texts, the *Kularatnadyotaka* shall [be extracted].
The words are written down as something to be brought together, but they are not actually performed.
The drops of nectar from flowers such as the *jātī*, *kadaṃba*, *karavīra*, and *kuśeśaya* are well known.
What is that which the honey-bees bring and accumulate, which the gods take for the performance of divine rites?
The Goddess said:
Save us, save us, O Great God, you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge!
We are deluded by egoism, claiming "We are lords."
O Śiva, how is Mahākāla to be known, and how may liberation come to be? O God, how many kinds of liberation are there, which is the most excellent, and what is the means for its attainment?
If there is compassion for us from the Goddess, as well as for Viṣṇu and the gods;
The illustrious Lord said:
By its power, everything is known from the words of the Vedas;
indeed, it was composed by Śaṅkara after extracting the essence from the gods.
The Goddess is proclaimed as the Āgama because it is superior to the Vedas;
it has come from the mouths of Śiva and gone into the mouth of the Daughter of the Mountain.
Because it destroys the three impurities, it is therefore called Āgama;
now listen as the origin and enumeration of the Āgamas are being told.
When Brahmā was born at eight and a half years of age, the deities were present;
then, by the power of knowledge, the Great Principle (Mahat) was born as the ego (ahaṃkāra).
Then, in that Kali age, people will be devoted only to their genitals and bellies;
they will not respect the Vedas and other scriptures, following instead false traditions.
In every land and in every city, people indulge in eating, drinking, and sexual pleasure;
no one regards Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśa, or Narasiṃha.
Thinking that the entire world is empowered by Śakti, they perform the worship of Bhaga;
at that time, O Grandfather, I was devoured by them in the form of a Vaṭuka.
"O Brahmā, let dharma be commanded so that we may indeed cross over.
Then Brahmā said: "It has issued from my upward-turned mouth."
The Āgama is the fifth Veda, the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it was first proclaimed by me to Pitāmaha at the onset of the Kali age.
"You must say to Brahmā, 'Sadāśiva is the creator. Then, when addressed by the Grandfather (Brahmā), you should say, 'I am both the creator and the protector.'"
And you consider another scripture to have arisen from my upward-facing mouth;
thus, through their devotion to such conduct, they shall go to the state of death.
"You shall experience the misery arising from food, drink, and women.
Having heard these words of Brahmā, [he acted] indeed for the sake of establishing righteousness.
Then, his three eyes becoming bloodshot with rage upon seeing the Creator’s contempt, he [struck] with a sharp claw.
When the head of the Dhātṛ was struck down upon the surface of the earth by the finger of his hand,
the fifth Veda emerged from its mouth and entered my body with ease.
Therefore, I am the author of the Āgamas, the creator of the Vedas, and the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Indeed, fifty great padmas of verses are said to constitute the Āgama text.
In that regard, O Great Goddess, all the mantras are well-established:
thirty nikharvas, six vṛndas, ninety arbudas, and [ninety-nine] koṭis.
"O Maheśānī, the mantras have been declared; where indeed does the Āgama reside?
Listen to that, O Maheśānī, if I am dear to you."
The great [lotus] consists of fifty petals; twenty-six are situated on the earth, fourteen are situated in heaven, and ten have their range in the netherworlds (pātāla).
Thus, O Lord of Gods, the Āgama has been narrated by me in due order;
for all scriptures are within the Āgama, and all deities are within the Āgama.
In the Āgama all merit is found; what is not obtained in the Āgama?
The Āgama is the entirety of knowledge; all sciences are established therein.
Now follows the sequence of emanation.
For the sake of accomplishing the mantra scriptures,
Pārvatī manifests as the beginningless Vidyā Kālī, the supreme one known by the name Mahātārā.
The Vidyā of the six Śambhaveśvarīs is to be expressed as the supreme power (parākalā) that transcends all;
having reached the great dissolution, she is the mistress of ten million cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
Having unified the body composed of Śiva and Śakti, she remains eternally present;
while Bhava and the other [deities], though possessing ten million faces, are Brahmās in the form of spirits (pretas).
Dancing and singing in that cremation ground,
Pārvatī, absorbed in meditation, remained there having attained the very nature of the protection of consciousness.
The infinity of the Māheśvaras exists, as does the multiplicity of Viṣṇus;
however, O sweet-spoken one, there is simply no counting of Śakra and the others.

Now, [the ritual] of Dhūmāvatī.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the supreme mantra of Dhūmāvatī:
"Dhūṃ Dhūṃ Dhūmāvatī Svāhā"; this eight-syllabled mantra has been proclaimed.
Now, [the ritual] of Bagalā.
Having uttered *tāram* and *māyā*, one should say *bagalāmukhī*;
after that, [the words] *sarvaduṣṭānāṃ*, then *vācam*, *mukham*, and the word *padam*.
The word "staṃbhaya" (paralyze), then "jihvāṃ kīlaya" (nail the tongue),
followed by "buddhiṃ vināśaya hrīṃ oṃ svāhā"— this consists of thirty-six syllables.
Thus, the ten Vidyās have been proclaimed according to the division of time;
now I shall explain, according to the rule, the procedure for the goddess known as Dakṣiṇā.
In the Kṛta age, the path taught in the Śrutis prevails; in the Tretā, it is the discourse of the Smṛtis;
in the Dvāpara, it is that spoken in the Purāṇas; and in the Kali age, it arises from the speech of the Aṅgas.
Brāhmaṇas born in the Kali age who perform the duties of Śūdras are impure; for them, accomplishment comes through the path of traditional lineage (āgama), not by the Vedic way.
In the Kali age, a wise person should worship the gods according to the injunctions declared in the Āgamas;
for the gods do not become pleased in the Kali age by any other method.
Worship is said to be threefold, but among them, the sāttvika is the most excellent;
in it, mental worship and recitation (japa) are considered the most primary.
The southern path is characterized by passion (rājasa); for those of that disposition and others, worship of the image with external offerings such as flowers and the like is especially recommended.
The worship of the Tāmasa [deity] is said to consist of offering oblations (bali) at the sacred seats (pīṭha) and other locations;
that is the primary [form] of the Vāmamārga, which is praised when one has abandoned caste distinctions.
This supreme system of the Left and Right has been fully proclaimed;
O Goddess, conduct is of two kinds, distinguished as Left and Right.
Devoid of the five seals and so forth, it is known as the Right Conduct (dakṣiṇācāra). [The five are:
liquor, meat, fish, the seal, and sexual union.
In the syllable *maka*, the Kaula should worship the Goddess with the five [elements] in the womb;
the worship of the drink from the left hand is proclaimed as the sequence of the gates.
Because of the practice of drawing [the substance] from the right hand, because of the satisfaction [offered] by the left hand,
and because of the worship performed with the right hand, one is called a Kaula.
Because worship is performed with the right hand alone, it is called "Dakṣiṇā.
This form of service is said to be twofold, distinguished by whether it is motivated by desire or free from desire.
The seed of liberation belongs to one free from desire, while the seed of worldly existence belongs to one with desire;
the southern path is considered superior, but the northern path is regarded as even more excellent.
He who understands the Vāma [Tantra] is indeed the supreme guru;
I know it in its entirety, while Sanaka and the others know it minus one quarter.
Vasiṣṭha and the others know half [of it], Śakra and the others know a quarter;
the masters of calculation know a sixth part, and other people know a sixteenth part.
Millions fall here and are born in the wombs of worms;
those who recognize that path are liberated—of this there is no doubt.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa indeed taught the left-hand path (vāmamārga) to Phālgunī;
reflect upon that which was seen by me and described to the sages.

Whether he be a Cāṇḍāla, a Turuṣka, a killer of a Brahmin, or a wandering mendicant; whether he be a learned Vedic scholar or one following the path of darkness—he is a worthy recipient for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Indeed, the left and right paths are prescribed in the rites of Kālī and Tārā;
in the rite of Chinnamastā, the left path is used, while Vagalā follows both the left and right paths.
Sundarī and Vāmā are divine and established on the left path, while Mātaṅgī is established on the right path; Bālāvidyā is both left and right, as is Dakṣavidyā.
Kevalā, Bhuvanā, Lakṣmī, and Dhūmā proceed along the southern path;
Sumukhī is satisfied with the left, and Vaṭuka belongs to both the left and the right.
Bhairavī resides in the yoga of the left, while Bagalā belongs to both the left and the right;
in the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya) they are the right and the left, and in the Southern and the Divine-Left [traditions] they are likewise.
Kaula and Dakṣa are in the west, while Kaula and Vāma are likewise in the north;
O Maheśānī, the two Divyas are above, and Vāma alone is in the netherworld (pātāla).
If Īśā and all other Vidyās, as well as Kāminī, the mistress of Yoga, are accomplished through the left-hand path (vāmamārga), they grant success; otherwise, they never bestow success at any time.
Through the union of the left and the right, she is devoted to both modes of conduct (ubhayācāra),
as well as to the Śaiva, Śākta, Gāṇapatya, Saura, and Svāyaṃbhuvā traditions.
In the Cāndra, Cīna, Pāñcarātra, Vaiṣṇava, Vaidika,
and Vāma systems, there will arise in the Kali age those born of the twice-born castes.
Likewise, O Goddess of the Gods, if one does not perform the *vāma* [practice] even on the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), his success will not be achieved; he is proclaimed to be my enemy.
In the Kula scriptures, the Vāma path is declared to be superior to all others;
even therein, Kālikā and Tārā are remembered as being most beloved in ritual practice.
O Maheśānī, in the Kāpālika tradition, this is the reason for the Left-hand Path (vāmamārga);
by means of the method of the Left-hand Path, everything is accomplished, and not otherwise.
Without the left-hand path (vāmamārga), the goddesses and deities do not grant accomplishment;
however, as declared in the Northern Tradition (uttarāmnāya), the gods are pleased by the five [mūdrās].
If even a single ritual element is deficient, they curse your means of accomplishment;
for the deities of the Western Tradition, the drinking of wine is both performed and completed.
They desire the fourfold [set of meats], and without them they utter curses;
the meat of the deities mentioned in the ancient tradition (pūrvāmnāya) is both prepared and unprepared.
They consider that triad of essential rites to be indispensable; otherwise, they regard those gods mentioned in the Ūrdhvāmnāya as being like fish—whether prepared or unprepared.
Except for the two Āvaśyakas, they lie down before him;
however, those four are prohibited for the deities of the Dakṣiṇāmnāya.
For even without the ascending [vowels], they indeed bring success to the practitioner;
the Kaulika [mantra] is formed from the *kūrca* syllable, while the Vedic rite is not so designated.
The Vedic rite is performed from the *kūrca* (the seat of grass), while the Kaulika rite is not designated by that;
because they are contradictory, both would be ruined, so one should practice them along a single path.
When one who follows the left path enters the right, he is afflicted by the gods at the end of the obstacle and does not attain success.
When the path of the right enters the left, O gods,
then they cause that left-walker to perish from both worlds and devour him.
Therefore, having understood the path of one's own family, one should perform worship;
whether a tantra has been heard by chance, or through deception, or even by force.
O Lord, if one recites a verse prompted by another that causes harm,
one should not look upon the scripture, nor practice it, nor even recite it.
Those who recite mantras after merely looking at them written in a book do not see [the truth], nor should they teach it, nor perform it, nor accomplish it.
The sin of those [who do not perform initiation] is proclaimed to be equal to the murder of a Brahmin;
therefore, one should always diligently undergo the Tantric initiation.
Now, therefore, I shall first explain initiation (dīkṣā) in detail:
through it, higher knowledge (jñāna) and realized wisdom (vijñāna) are bestowed, and the heaps of sins are destroyed.
Therefore, it is called *dīkṣā*, and it has been obtained from the mouth of the true guru;
now, O practitioners, listen to the fault of mortals who have not received initiation.
His food is equal to excrement, and likewise his water is equal to urine;
so too is a Śrāddha performed for one who is uninitiated, or a Śrāddha in which the performer himself is uninitiated.
Having taken hold of their fathers, they fall indeed into a most terrible hell,
without a doubt, for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Even if one who is endowed with devotion should worship with thousands of riches,
nevertheless, the gods will certainly not accept the offerings of one who is uninitiated.
Since all ritual action is in vain for him, he is therefore an uninitiated animal;
thus, upon seeing one who is uninitiated, one should not accomplish any purposeful task.
At the time of receiving initiation, however, the heap of sins departs;
intent upon that [initiation], he goes outside, joined with the state of nirvāṇa.
At that time, one becomes oneself worthy of the arghya offering for the gods and ancestors;
otherwise, whatever rite is performed is like an oblation poured into ashes.
In all stages of life, they declare that initiation is a constant duty;
for one who lacks the Lord's mantra, there is no protector on earth.
Likewise, for one devoid of initiation (dīkṣā), there is no mastery over this world or the next,
neither through austerities, recitations, fire-offerings, nor by various other means of accomplishment.
However, for one devoid of initiation, no ritual action ever succeeds,
even for the twice-born who are purified by the Mantras in their own duties, such as Vedic study and the like.
Just as there is no entitlement for one who has not undergone the initiation (*upanayana*) and other rites,
so too there is none for those who have not been initiated in the matter of mantras, the worship of deities, and the like.
Therefore, one should not perform [rites] having consecrated oneself with mantras without [proper] authority;
the entire world has initiation as its root, and initiation is the root of supreme austerity.
Having taken initiation, one may dwell anywhere while reciting [the mantra] on level ground;
however, one who dies without initiation shall go to the Raurava hell.
Therefore, it is called *dīkṣā* by the teachers who are knowers of the Tantras;
for as long as *dīkṣā*, which bestows the fruits of the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*), has not been attained.
Initiation brings about all accomplishments and bestows all prosperity;
it grants intuition, the correct pronunciation of vowels and consonants, luster, and the maintenance of nourishment.
Delusion, paralysis, attraction, killing, and expulsion;
subjugation, skill in poetry, and intellect endowed with retention.
It provides crossing over the ocean, coolness against fire, victory in battle,
freedom from fear in the forest, and likewise removes grief and suffering.
To those who grant the four goals of life— dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa— there is no doubt;
likewise, they bestow various types of vidyās upon many tens of millions of beings.
One [mantra] obtained from the mouth of the Guru initiates all accomplishments;
having obtained it through the Guru's instruction, one should perform recitation, worship, and so forth.
Thereafter, one who is always permeated by that state should accomplish all of that.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Majesty [of the Śyāmā-vidyā] Preceded by the Necessity of the Extraction and Worship of the Śrī-Śyāmā-vidyā," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*.
O beloved, how can He be worshipped— He who is Śiva, all-pervading, subtle, beyond the mind, partless, immutable, having the form of space, unborn, and infinite?
For this very reason, Śiva, having directly assumed the form of the Guru,
wanders this earth out of compassion for the miserable, accompanied by the Goddess.
Adorned with human skin, he is himself the supreme Śiva manifest;
with Atri as his eye, he is Śiva manifest, and with four arms, he is Acyuta.
O beloved, the Śrī Guru is said to be Brahmā with four faces;
yet to those of sinful deeds in this world, the Śrī Guru appears as an ordinary man.
And Śiva is seen directly by men of meritorious deeds,
as the supreme reality, the venerable Guru, standing before their very eyes.
Those of little fortune do not see him, just as the blind do not see the risen sun;
Guru Sadāśiva is truly manifest before them—of this there is no doubt.
If Śiva himself is not the Guru, who else can bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation?
Pārvatī is the consort of both the Lord Sadāśiva and the venerable Guru.
There is no difference between the two; he who makes a distinction is a sinner. Just as "ghaṭa," "kalaśa," and "kuṃbha" are expressive of one and the same meaning.
In this way, the deity, the mantra, and the guru are said to have one and the same purpose;
there is no object equal to the guru, nor is there a deity comparable to Śaṅkara.
There is no yoga higher than Kaula, and no knowledge equal to Kālikā;
the letter *ga* is the attainment of gnosis, and the letter *a* is its illuminator.
The Guru is traditionally taught that the syllable *ukāra* bestows identity with Śiva;
for even those who have studied the Nigamas along with the six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*), O Dear One, [attain this through it].
Scriptures such as the Āgamas and other treatises cannot yield knowledge without a guru;
therefore, that man who, having carefully examined a guru, worships him for the sake of Śiva [attains success].
They declare that clear knowledge of Yoga belongs to him; of this there is no doubt.
For who in this cycle of existence is a savior for living beings other than the true Guru?
How can a false guru protect another when he himself is ruined?
In the Kali age, gurus seek wealth while disciples seek spiritual accomplishments.
Therefore, the failure of both [the deity and the disciple] is a deception of the deities;
rather, the disciple and the guru, endowed with devotion and faith, must possess all the complete characteristics.
Every path at that time bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Now, therefore, follows the characteristics of the teacher.
Therefore, I shall first explain the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple:
O Supreme Goddess, the venerable Guru is of pure appearance and captivating.
Endowed with all the primary marks, beautified by all the secondary limbs,
he knows the reality of the meaning of all scriptures and is conversant with the ritual procedures of all mantras.
The world has the form of a delusion, yet it is pleasant to behold like a god; it is fair-faced, easily accessible, clear, and veiled by the gestures and appearances of its signs.
Inward-turned yet possessing outward vision, he is omniscient and knows time and place;
he is perfected through command, knows the three periods of time, and is capable of both restraint and grace.
One who has reached the depths of the Vedas and Vedanta, who is devoted to compassion for all living beings,
whose movement of the senses is self-governed, and who is capable of conquering the six internal enemies.
In this regard, he who is profound in discernment, who distinguishes between worthy and unworthy recipients,
who is stainless, eternally contented, free from dualities, and possessed of constant power— is truly a *gaṇī*.
Affectionate toward his true devotees, steadfast, compassionate, and one whose speech is preceded by a smile;
dear to his followers, bestowing joy upon all, and a teacher of his disciples.
The wise man who is devoted to his chosen deity and eager to worship the Goddess is not censured in these rites— whether daily, occasional, or for specific desires.
Free from attachment, aversion, fear, anger, hypocrisy, and egoism;
content with whatever is obtained by chance; and discerning between virtues and faults.
One who is unable to manage his wife’s property, addicted to evil company and vices, lacking in vigor,
harmful, partial, and unwise;
One who knows mantras yet sells wealth, learning, yantras, tantras, and the like;
one who is free from intention and free from conceptual construction, having determined the ultimate truth, is truly righteous.
One who regards censure and praise as equal, who is silent, indifferent, self-restrained,
pure in mind, compassionate, and has mastered the Vedas— such a person is a Brāhmaṇa.
Now, concerning the family preceptor.
One who is of noble birth is proclaimed to be qualified for all branches of knowledge.
In this matter, he alone is the master of all mantras, and no other.
Akula is said to be Śiva, while Kula is proclaimed to be Śakti;
he who is skilled in the contemplation of both Kula and Akula is the beloved Kaulika.

He who becomes joyful upon seeing those devoted to the lineage, those who follow the conduct of the lineage, those who possess the knowledge of the lineage, and those who observe the vows of the lineage— he, the Kaulika, is dear to me.
By accepting those three principles, one who knows the reality of the meaning of the root mantra and is devoted to the deity and the guru shall become a Kaulika through that initiation.
He is always devoted to the family tradition, an exponent of the Kula scriptures,
tranquil, self-controlled, all-knowing, and free from greed and delusion.
Always renouncing anger and delusion, he is dispassionate and honored by heroes;
having abandoned all supports, he is intent on the worship of women.
Thus, O beloved, the illustrious Guru has been described as endowed with these characteristics:
he is neither too young nor too old, nor is he lame or emaciated.
Neither with redundant limbs nor deficient limbs, neither bald nor with protruding teeth;
one who is grateful, eloquent, brave, established in learning, and has reached the further shore.
One who has practiced the science of architecture (vāstu-vidyā), who is discerning in the extraction of structural defects (śalya-uddhāra),
who knows the sequence of ritual procedures (kriyā-anukrama), and who is discerning in the tantras of mudrās;
He is the illuminator of the practices of one's own knowledge and the duties of austerity;
he is the illuminator of the duties of caste and stage of life, as well as of knowledge and austerity.
He who is well-perfected in the sixfold ritual, who is a giver and an enjoyer rather than a beggar—he alone is a Kaulika teacher; any other is a mere hypocrite of the Kula.

He who correctly understands the state of the *piṇḍa*, as well as form (*rūpa*), that which transcends form, and the stainless (*nirañjana*), is a true Guru and leads [the disciple] to the supreme state.
O Dear One, he who understands the threefold nature of the fetter, the pillar, the initiation by piercing, and the seizing of the bound soul— he is declared to be a Guru.
O lady of excellent hips, he who knows the secret meaning and the ritual prescriptions regarding the Paśus, the Pāśas, and the Paśupāśa is proclaimed as the Guru.
Compassion, doubt, fear, shame, and disgust as the fifth;
lineage, conduct, and likewise power—these eight are proclaimed to be the bonds (pāśas).
One bound by fetters is called a bound soul (paśu); one freed from fetters is Maheśvara.
Therefore, he who removes the fetters is called a Guru; no other is so described.
O beloved, he who knows the fruits of the soul's movement from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) within the seven lotus-petals— he alone is the Guru, and no other.
Now, the characteristics of a false teacher.
A family blemish.
One who eats excessively, procrastinates, is greedy for sense objects and the like,
delights in fallacious reasoning, is wicked, is a mere talker, and reviles his guru.
One who has hair growing on the nose or eyebrows, one who is censured, one who is merely exhausted,
one with black teeth, one with dark lips, one who is foul-smelling, and one who breathes heavily [are to be avoided].
One who possesses wicked characteristics, even if he himself is a lord,
being addicted to accepting gifts from the land of Vaṅga, brings about the destruction of the teacher's prosperity.
One who is sonless, one whose sons have died, a *kuṇḍa*, as well as a dwarf,
one with deformed nails, one with long teeth, one conquered by women, and one with an extra limb.
One who is deficient in limbs, deceitful, diseased, suffering from skin disease, or hunchbacked—
only he who is free from these defects is a teacher worthy of being a disciple’s vessel.
One should not take a preceptor whose name is the same as one's own, nor a wife whose name is the same as that of one's mother.
Now, there is a distinction of the Guru based on the distinction of place.
A learned man born in the land of Kumārī, situated in the midst of the Himalayas and abounding in white and black deer, is worthy of the status of an Ācārya.
The preceptors from Aṅga, Madhyadeśa, Kaurukṣetra, Acalaṭaja, Antarvedī, Pratiṣṭhāna, and Āvantya are the most excellent.
The Rāḍha, Varendra, Indrakāsta, Āgaura, Rāmāgadha, as well as those born from the Aṅgaja lineage— these seven are remembered as the Madhyama [Sāmagas].
The Āndhras, Kāliṅgas, Karṇāṭas, Mahārāṣṭras,
Ṭhakvas, Vīrajas, Āḍas, Viḍas, and Pauṇḍras— these eight are considered base gurus.
The Kāmarūpas, Campākas, Pālotthas,
Saindhavas, Vāṅgas, Gāndhāras, and Paulingas— these seven are the lowest of the low.
The Kāñcīs, Kauśalas, Kāsthakāvelās, Kaukaṇas, Bhujas,
Saurāṣṭras, and Devarāṣṭras— these eight were severely censured.

The best [type] grants all desires without exception; the middling [type] is that which has caused prosperity to perish; the lowest is that which has been destroyed by inauspiciousness; one who is noble and pure incurs no fault.
They consist of four lines and three divisions, adorned with the six categories of meaning;
they are joined with the lineages and spheres of activity, and possess characteristics consistent with the commitments and so forth.

Those who know the *avyasaṃhitā*, which is complete with dreams and established in initiation (*dīkṣā*), should be recognized as practitioners of right conduct (*ācāra*); others are merely worldlings who practice hypocrisy.
But that man who knows the Self as distinct from all material substances—
even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks— is undoubtedly a Guru.
The initiation of a father, of one who has already been initiated, of forest-dwellers,
or of those in the secluded stage of life, destroys the longevity and wealth of the son.
If one performs the initiation of the ancestors (pitṛ-dīkṣā) either through negligence or due to ignorance,
one should then perform an expiation and undergo the initiation once again.
Those who have abandoned the sacred fires, those devoid of ritual acts, as well as those without wives or possessions—
even such forest-dwellers are merely [members of] castes, since they belong to a lower stage of life.
Therefore, they have no entitlement to initiation other than that of Maheśvarī;
for even if one who has taken the initiation of a *yati* should ever become deluded, [the former initiation remains].
The expiation is either one cow or a three-night vow;
having performed that expiation, one should undergo initiation once again.
O beloved, if one should obtain the perfected vidyā solely by the power of fortune,
then one may indeed receive initiation from that very deity, abandoning all consideration of a guru.
In the bestowing of one's own chosen lore, however, one should not entertain thoughts of [the disciple being] a guru;
among those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, it is the Kṣatriya who is capable of showing such favor.
O high-minded one, a Vaiśya should always show favor toward such a Śūdra of his own caste by means of that [same duty].
The *anugraha* and *abhiṣeka* initiations should always be performed for a Śūdra, whether he belongs to the lowest caste, is of noble birth, or is even renowned.

One who desires auspiciousness should not perform this rite in one's own country or elsewhere while it is already being performed by someone else; for wherever such a conflict occurs, there is a reversal of results.
Indeed, there would be a loss of urine for him; therefore, one should act according to what is declared in the scriptures.
Only such a person as this should be made the guru, and not otherwise.

A field-tiller of Śūdra birth should not initiate one who is of inverse caste (prātilomya). Nor should one initiate an Ācārya, a maternal uncle, an officiating priest (ṛtvij), a paternal uncle, a father-in-law, or a king.
Thus, the six gurus have been declared here by those expert in mantra;
however, the mantra of one's father and likewise that of one's maternal grandfather would be devoid of power [if used].
The mantra of the father becomes powerless against a younger brother who has taken the side of the enemy; indeed, it is corrupted by the Śaiva-Śākta [mantras].
When the right path is devoid of potency for one's father, maternal grandfather,
or a householder brother, he becomes potent through the left path.
A husband should not initiate his wife; a father should not initiate his daughter;
likewise, a brother should not initiate his son, nor should he initiate his own brother.
For women, initiation is declared to be auspicious; it is remembered as possessing eight qualities:
being virtuous, of good conduct, devoted to the guru, and having her senses subdued.
She who knows the true meaning of all mantras, is virtuous, devoted to worship,
and worthy of her guru— she indeed should be a widow, free from [other] husbands.
Indeed, the initiation of the Śāmbhavī tradition should be bestowed upon women with truthfulness;
the auspicious initiation received through the lineage of goddesses is considered the highest for women.
Listen with reverence to the supreme distinction regarding the lineage of goddesses:
that which is taught in the lineage of goddesses has been transmitted through the succession of generations.
For women, initiation (dīkṣā) is supreme; the goddess Dīkṣā is considered auspicious. Initiation obtained through that lineage is regarded as bestowing spiritual perfection (siddhi).
From him, a lineage of initiation for men has arisen;
hear now the primary rule, O Great Goddess, which is prescribed for women.
The person (puruṣa) is to be known as the rule (niyama), never in women;
O Dear One, how could there be initiation in the Śākta [tradition] when it is accompanied by such dualistic conceptualization?
If she is to be given by the presence of the Guru, then she is considered a sister;
if she is indeed to be given by oneself, then she is proclaimed a maiden.
If she were to be made to give [the offering] by someone else, then she would have strayed from the path;
for many kinds of paths have been proclaimed by me, O Goddess, in the mantra scriptures.
O Śaṅkara, tell me what should be done with the mind when it is in distress for that purpose;
[it is said that] initiation should be received from one who is the most excellent within one's own tradition.
O Great Goddess, what has been declared as auspicious in the absence [of other options], listen to that with respect:
on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, when the moon is conjoined with the Sarasa [constellation].
Having written the mantra on a palm leaf, one should perform the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras);
through the application of these ten rites, the mantra will become perfected.
On that day, having prepared milk-rice (pāyasa) in the presence of Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
one should offer the milk-rice and other items, and worship Śaṅkara with bilva fruits.
Having thus recited the vācamanīya mantra one thousand and eight times,
one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) for the Goddess according to the method prescribed by her respective mantra.
If there is no capacity for recitation, then what is prescribed?
Either the water for sipping (ācamanīya) is offered through the son, or that son is indeed the preceptor himself.
O beloved, when the mantra is received in this manner, success indeed occurs;
now listen to another method of initiation.
At an auspicious moment and on an auspicious day, by a river flowing toward the ocean,
having first observed the ancient tradition, one should draw the orb of the glorious Sun.
Having fully worshipped Sūrya together with his limbs (aṅgas) and retinue (āvaraṇas), O beloved of my life,
one should write the mantra beginning with the *tāra* (oṃ) and ending with *phaṭ*, and have it recited in his presence.
Whether it be the recitation of the sacred words one hundred and eight times or the mental repetition of the syllables,
by worshipping the Sun and Jupiter therein, one shall become a master of all accomplishments.
This has been declared as the supreme [path] for the Paśus, but not the supreme [path] for the Vīras, O Beloved;
rather, the Master should perform initiation for the Vīras who belong to the Kaula tradition.
In the Kālikāgama, however, there is no fault in the bestowal of initiation upon one's husband;
for Śiva first bestowed that auspicious initiation upon Gaurī.
And she was either a daughter or a wife; likewise here too, Pārvatī was not called a daughter, but is celebrated as the wife of Vīra.
Now, the characteristics of a disciple.
O Mistress of the Family, he is a true disciple, endowed with all auspicious marks,
possessed of the practice of meditative absorption, and gifted with virtuous qualities and conduct.
He was one of pure body, worthy of worship, righteous, and pure-minded;
firm in his vows, of virtuous conduct, and endowed with pure devotion.
Grateful and fearful of evil, esteemed by the virtuous and the noble,
possessing faith and a disposition for generosity, he is devoted to the welfare of all living beings.
Endowed with trustworthiness and humility, free from stinginess regarding wealth,
capable of accomplishing the impossible, heroic, and possessed of strength and splendor.
One who is compliant, engaged in appropriate action, vigilant, discerning,
who grasps the meaning upon being told once, and who is clever and rich in intelligence.
One who is equal toward the floor and the lap, free from agitation, without a servant,
acting with deliberation, steadfast, and devoid of mental poverty.
He is skilled in all undertakings, steadfast, and helpful to all;
he is pleasant-faced when censuring others for minor faults, but turns his face away from what is dear.
One who has conquered the senses, is well-contented, knows the mantras, observes celibacy,
has abandoned excessive fickleness, and is free from ill-will and anxiety.
One who is always eager for the meditation, praise, and stories of the guru,
devoted to the guru as the deity, yet eager to worship women;
O Goddess, [I praise] the protector who possesses all knowledge, who extols the fame of the guru,
who recognizes the authority of the guru’s words, and who is devoted to the service of the guru.
O leader of the family, [one should look for] one who follows the mind, acts with foresight,
and is free from shame, pride, arrogance, and the like in the presence of the guru.
One who is indifferent toward the property of the Guru, who desires the Guru’s favor,
who is devoted to the meditation on forms and so forth, and who proceeds along the path to liberation.
The Guru should accept as a disciple one who is endowed with such characteristics as these.
Now, the characteristics of a wicked disciple.
One who is wicked, an evildoer, corrupt, devoid of virtues, deformed,
a disciple of another, a heretic, a rogue, and one who considers himself a scholar.
One with deficient, excessive, or deformed limbs, possessed of missing parts,
as well as one who is lame, deaf, filthy, or afflicted by disease.
He was impure, foul-mouthed, and possessed a form assumed at will;
he was wickedly clever, ill-behaved, poorly dressed, and had a terrifying gaze.
One who is possessed by sleep and laziness, afflicted by sloth and vices such as gambling,
and whose body is always concealed behind doors, walls, or other coverings.
One who is prone to slander, base, devoid of faith and devotion, boastful, stubborn, a mere messenger, fickle, and deceitful— [such a person is not fit].
One who is devoid of purity regarding wealth and wife, who disregards prohibitions and injunctions,
who reveals secrets, and who destroys the purpose of divine rites.
One who behaves like a cat or a crow, intent on seeking out vulnerabilities,
deceitful, ungrateful, and one who gives evasive answers.
One who betrays trust, a hater of the gods, an evildoer, one who is untrustworthy, one who is blameworthy, and one who desires success through illicit means— [these should be avoided].
O Goddess, one who has killed an assassin, one who is censured, a false witness, a beggar everywhere, and one who approaches the wives of all men— these are declared to be the most despicable.
One who is possessed by falsehood, or one who is capable of speaking excessively about village affairs and the like,
who indulges in evil thoughts and fallacious reasoning, and who is fond of quarreling;
One should know that he who acts fruitlessly and causes distraction, who is deluded yet speaks kindly in one's presence,
who utters words of abuse, and who praises others with his speech [is a fool].
Virtues [do not dwell] in one who is patient and of a tolerant mind, nor in one possessed by anger,
nor in a Cārvāka, nor in a friend of the wicked, nor in one censured by all the world.
One who is slanderous, who torments others, who causes fear to all living beings,
who speaks words that cause affliction, who betrays friends, and who deceives his own brothers.
O Goddess, the tongue and the genitals are supreme thieves, behaving like beasts;
they cause hatred without cause, laughter, suffering, and the creation of wheels and other such things.
One who causes excessive laughter, one who mocks with delight, a lustful person, one who is utterly shameless, one of false and wicked conduct, and a slanderer.
It is joined with envy, intoxication, jealousy, hypocrisy, and egoism;
it is characterized by malice, slander, harshness, unkindness, and the infliction of anger.
One who is lacking in fortitude, corrupted, hateful, incapable, devoid of a body,
insolent in mind, deluded, and whose heart is crushed by anxiety.
O beloved, [one should avoid] one whose greed has fallen away, who is wretched, discontented, a performer of all kinds of sacrifices,
a glutton, deceitful, a deceiver, and crooked.
Devoid of devotion, faith, compassion, peace, and righteous conduct,
it causes laughter among mothers, fathers, gurus, the wise, and the great.

O Kuleśvarī, [one who is] loathsome regarding family property and such, who is conceited about serving the guru, who is corrupt with women, who has fallen from his commitments, and who is oppressed by the guru— [such a one is not to be accepted].
A teacher should abandon a disciple who is possessed of such defects as these.
The Goddess said:
O God, a mantra given by an unaccomplished guru to a disciple, or a guru who is himself unaccomplished,
will never be effective even when another accomplished mantra is used.
O Lord of Gods, when a disciple belonging to one lineage serves a deity belonging to a different lineage, what kind of accomplishment (*siddhi*) is attained there? Please tell me that.
Ishvara said:
The Guru belongs to the Dakṣiṇa-āmnāya and is initiated in all the āmnāyas;
likewise, he is a follower of the Ūrdhva-āmnāya among others, and a follower of the Pūrva-āmnāya among yet others.
Of the two, however, the follower of the Western Tradition (paścimāmnāyī) is superior, while the follower of the Lower Tradition (adhara) is inferior.
By means of the Lower Tradition alone, one may attain spiritual authority (gurutva) pertaining to the next world in certain cases.
A devoted lay follower who, at the proper time, stands upright shall attain union (sāyujya) with the deity;
likewise, the former attains similarity of form (sārūpya), while the latter attains excellence.
Proximity [to the higher realms] and association with the world above are the fruits pertaining to this life;
furthermore, through the renunciation of greed, one provides assistance that brings about future results even on the lower path.
When a guru who has attained perfection in another mantra bestows that mantra [upon a disciple],
the disciple’s accomplishment arises through practicing it exactly as prescribed.
Out of compassion, the supreme Guru bestowed the perfected mantra upon him;
even without recitation and without worship, all spiritual accomplishments rested in his hands.
If both the teacher and the disciple, out of delusion, give or receive instruction without examining one another's lineage, they shall indeed attain the state of a piśāca.
If, out of affection or even greed, he should accept [a disciple] or initiate him,
the deity will inflict a curse upon that guru and that disciple.
Therefore, one should never accept such a disciple under any circumstances;
if one accepts him out of delusion, the teacher becomes tainted by that person's sins.
Just as a wife’s sin affects her husband and a minister’s sin affects the king,
so too does the sin committed by a disciple generally affect the teacher as well.
One should examine the teacher and the disciple through both knowledge and compassion for one year, or half of that, or half of that again, or even half of that.

One should perform the highest and intermediate rites for living beings through supreme actions; and for those who have offered their life-force or material wealth, one should act with equal-mindedness through gifts and other such means.
By words that pierce the vital spots, by deceptions, by the actions of a teacher,
by partialities, by indifference, and by many other such means, [he assails others] again and again.
Whether being drawn away or even oppressed by the practice of sitting upon the vulva (yoniṣāda), one should always reflect: "The Guru is showing compassion. One should always contemplate this.

O beloved, whether in the remembrance of the glorious Guru, or in his glorification, or in taking delight in him, or in serving him according to the prescribed path, or in sending him on errands, or in seeking him out;
By remembering the bliss, the supreme, and the transformations of the eyes and other senses,
there shall be union with those three, as well as the sovereign accomplishment of mantra.
And having understood the capacity for awakening, one should become a disciple and not otherwise;
the logic that applies to the beginning, middle, and end has been established by Śakti.
O Goddess, disciples are proclaimed to be of three kinds: inferior, middling, and superior.
O Goddess, those who speak for the sake of initiation must first possess devotion.
Furthermore, those whose state has been lost are said to be "fit for initiation";
having received initiation and the observances, they remain devoid of knowledge and realization.
Therefore, those whose vigor has been destroyed are said to be "intermediately fit.
One who is devoid of devotion at the beginning may or may not possess devotion in the middle.
And in the end, there shall be devotion; they become worthy at the conclusion by performing service to the teacher through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
One who is pure in disposition, possesses great enthusiasm, and is an awakened disciple is thus remembered.
Such a person is to be instructed by the king; he is a son, one who reverses the cycle of existence, and likewise a giver of wealth.
Knowledge is obtained from a teacher through service, or at the proper time through wealth, or else through knowledge;
a fourth means does not exist.

Having constantly examined, through body, speech, and mind, [the suitability of] that which is to be accepted along with its requisites— up to the limit of three, two, or one [vessels]— the first [type of person] is one whose mind is restrained.
Within just one year, they will come to know each other’s status as either teacher or disciple; there is no other way—this is the certain conclusion.
A disciple who, having received a mantra from a true guru, should abandon it,
becomes certainly liable for penance as one who has forsaken his guru.
If by chance this knowledge is obtained from an animal by men of noble birth,
they should then obtain the knowledge again by approaching a Kaulika twice-born man.
Whoever learns the lore of the animal, for him there will certainly be physical suffering or even affliction for his kinsmen; of this there is no doubt.
Having taken refuge in a true guru—
one who is endowed with auspicious marks and who cuts through doubt— one should receive the consecrated mantra.
O Goddess, having obtained one who bestows knowledge, one should not resort to a heavy [ignorant] teacher;
for by obtaining an ignorant teacher, one falls into doubt and undergoes the sixfold transformation.
Having gone between the disciple and the preceptor, one is not defiled by their faults;
for there are many preceptors who are experts in evil mantras and medicines.
One who knows the mantras taught in the Nigamas, Agamas, and Shastras is rare on this earth;
a fool cannot rescue another fool, nor can one who lacks knowledge uplift a fool.
A boat indeed carries stone across, but stone does not carry stone across;
just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from flower to flower.
Likewise, one who is greedy for knowledge should be made to wither away; he may go to another guru, for Śūdras have no authority over mantras, as this is a supreme rule.
In the absence of mantras, one may recite everything without using mantras;
however, one should not impart the collections of mantras to a Śūdra.
There would be as many instances of Brahman-murder [as there were grains]; therefore, one should perform the consecration for it.
One should offer that which is Tantric, free from cries of "Hā! Hā! and accompanied by the sound "Yaṭ-ca."

Worship should be performed even by women and Śūdras according to the path taught in their own scriptures; and they should perform it using Sanskrit according to the method prescribed in those scriptures.
Indeed, for a Śūdra, there is no entitlement to recite the Goddess’s [mantra];
O Pārvatī, the Praṇava mentioned in the Tantras and the Vahnijāyā (Svāhā) belong to the Goddess.
O Goddess, O beloved, the recitation and retention [of this] must be performed constantly;
O Maheśānī, whoever—be they a Śūdra or a woman—should chant that which is declared in the Purāṇas.
He is always cooked in that terrible [hell] for as long as fourteen Indras [reign].
Even a Śūdra should never utter the Praṇava or the Vahni-jāyā (the consort of Fire).
By the utterance of the Praṇava, by performing fire-sacrifices (homa), by worshipping the Śālagrāma stone,
and by having sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Śūdra shall fall into the state of a Cāṇḍāla.
O beloved, the Purāṇas state that for a Śūdra, the utterance of the Praṇava is equal [to other rites];
therefore, that which is prescribed in the Tantras should be performed with effort by those of the Śūdra caste.
By the power of the Great Vidyā, a Śūdra may attain the status of a Vaiśya;
O Maheśānī, those of the Śūdra caste should take up [the mantra] beginning with the Praṇava.
O Supreme Goddess, this reality concerning initiation is to be kept strictly secret;
it concerns Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those born of the Paulastya lineage.
The five types of men are proclaimed according to their defects in reverse order:
the seed-syllable *māyā* (hrīṃ) belongs to the Brāhmaṇa, while the seed-syllable *śrī* (śrīṃ) is remembered as belonging to the Kṣatriya.
The Vaiśya is indeed the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja), while the Śūdra is said to be Vāgbhava;
having abandoned these four seed-syllables, the mantra is designated as Paulastya.
The four seed-syllables belong to the Brāhmaṇas; the three seed-syllables to the Kṣatriyas;
the two seed-syllables to the Vaiśyas; and the single seed-syllable to the Śūdras.
One of lower caste or lineage may bestow a mantra upon one of higher caste;
likewise, Umā and Maheśvara, as well as Dakṣiṇāmūrti and Aghoraka [may do so].
Then Hayagrīva and Vārāha, followed by the eight-syllable mantra;
likewise Vāsudeva preceded by the Praṇava, and Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
It should be given to those of the three [higher] castes, and never to one of another caste;
[namely] the Pāśupata, the Nārasiṃha, and likewise the Sudarśana.
It should be given to those of two castes and never to others at any time;
this applies to whatever fire-mantras there may be, as well as to the sun-mantras.
The Tārā and other compassionate mantras should be given to those of the three castes;
likewise, the Ānuṣṭubh Śakti-mantras and that of Vindhyanivāsinī.
Nīlasarasvatī should be depicted first in the primary color;
likewise Mātaṅgī, Ugratārā, Kālikā, and Śyāmarā.
Chinnamastā and Vālā should be given in all types of paintings;
likewise Tārā and others, Gaṇeśa, and the one known as Haridrā.
They should be given as offerings to those of the three castes, especially to the protectors of the city;
[namely] the Praṇava, Māyā, Lakṣmī, Vāgbhava, and another seed-syllable.
This should be given joined with this seed-syllable at the beginning of the coloring;
for a Kṣatriya as well, Māyā, Lakṣmī, and Vāgbhava should be given.
Lakṣmī and Vāgbhava are indeed said to belong to the Vaiśya caste;
and another seed-syllable, Vāgbhava, is proclaimed for the Śūdras.
The heart-mantra and so forth, beginning with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*, are praised for the Śaṅkaras;
a single offering as prescribed in the Kalpa should be given to the Brahmin Vindhyavāsinī.
The [mantras] of the Goddess are called Pāśupata for the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya;
those of Saudarśana and Nārasiṃha belong to Kārtavīrya and not to anyone else.
The Ghoraka mantra of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the eight-syllabled Hayagrīva, and likewise the Mumāmāheśvara should be given to those of all three castes.
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, the Goddess Tārā, Varāhaka,
the rays of Agni and Sūrya, Tārā and the others, and the lords of the Gaṇas.
They should be bestowed upon all castes: Kālikā, Śyāmā, Chinnamastā, Bālā, Mātaṅginī, and Ugratārikā.
O twice-born, among the *yoginīs* and *yakṣiṇīs*, those such as Traipurāvadukā and the Śāvaras and Pulastyas are not to be recited during one's birth.
Many paths have been proclaimed by the wise in the science of mantra;
having relied upon the doctrine of one's own guru, one should perform what is auspicious, and not otherwise.
Furthermore, when a mantra is being recited, if one is intent upon other practices and is devoid of the traditional lineage, it becomes possessed of all defects.
Thus, O Goddess, have I described to you the characteristics of both the teacher and the disciple.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Determination of the Guru, the Disciple, and the Mantra," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*.
The Goddess said:
Hundreds of people here are established on the paths of the divine systems;
yet nowhere is perfection or prosperity seen—what will happen in the next world?
If karma is indeed paramount, what is the use of propitiating the deity? If propitiating the deity were truly effective, why would practitioners remain in suffering?
In this matter of my doubt, what is the accomplishment through the cakras and the measures? And how should the consecration be performed for practitioners? Tell me that.
Īśvara said:
One should perform three rites while in the womb, ten upon being born, and then three more;
thus the sacraments (saṃskāras) are recorded as sixteen.
Likewise, the preceptor should perform the three rites with the mantra for the twice-born;
thereafter, the disciple should perform the three rites again with the perfected mantra.
Six purificatory rites for birth are prescribed even for women and Śūdras;
likewise, sixteen purificatory rites involving mantras are proclaimed for them as well.
Indeed, among the Cāṇḍālas and others, there are exactly four such mantras;
for the Yavanas and others, there are three, and in their respective mantras, O Father, there are three.
Listen to how they are to be employed according to the distinction between the left and the right:
one should arrange liquor in the place of clarified butter on the left for the purpose of the fire-oblation and other rites.
Whatever meat may be found among the edible [animals], it is traditionally held that one should avoid it from the first to the eleventh;
likewise, sexual intercourse, ritual gestures (mudrās), and those who perform such acts are forbidden for one practicing celibacy (brahmacarya).
Now follows the sacramental rite of conception (garbhādhāna).
First, the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) should be performed according to the procedure prescribed in one's own ritual manual;
then, one should perform the sacrifice to the female messengers (dūtī-yāga) on the right or on the left.
One should satisfy this [deity] with mantras, as one does Gaṅgā, and likewise the womb from the sacred site;
upon that, one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (nyāsa) on the limbs of the deity.
One should contemplate all the nyāsas within one's own body as Bhairavī;
having become Bhairava himself, one should perform the act of union.
Seated upon a seat facing the east and placing the penis into the vulva, one should recite this mantra five thousand times; thus, one obtains a son according to one's desire.
"Lakṣmī and Prāṇeśvarī—protect me! There is no word beyond these syllables.
Of her [Lakṣmī], there is Soma; of him [Soma], Garbha of the Sun should abide in the water of the earth.
Now follows the sacramental rite known as Puṃsavana.
Then the second sacrament, called Puṃsavana, should be performed;
the wise man should perform the Puṃsavana in the third month.
In the third month, on a day prescribed by the Vedas, one should perform [the rite] according to the method taught in one's own ritual manual.
There, in place of the Vedic fire-offering, one should offer oblations to one's own deity within the causal [mandala] by means of four offerings.
In that case, for the deities of the Vāmamārga, there are two [seals] each for the gods and the human beings, and one for the women; the remainder is declared to be as previously stated.
He is the sacred ford, he is the sacrificial animal, he is the vessel; at night, he is the terrifying offering.
Now follows the sacramental rite known as Sīmantonnayana.
Now, the third sacrament known as Sīmantonnayana is proclaimed;
it should be performed in the fourth, sixth, or eighth month, which are considered excellent, middling, and inferior respectively.
On a day prescribed by the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra), according to the method taught in his own Kalpa,
he should have the Vāmī deity’s mantra well written on the parting of the hair (sīmanta).
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon one's limbs, which removes the affliction of birth-pains;
thereafter, out of fear of the curse of the deities, one should not approach that wife.
Whether performed out of desire, delusion, at an improper time,
according to a different rite, or by another person, such a *sīmantonnayana* brings misfortune to oneself.
Now follows the sacramental rite known as the birth-ceremony (jātakarman).
Then, O Brahmin, one should perform for a woman or even a Śūdra the fourth sacrament called Jātakarman, according to the procedure prescribed in their own respective Kalpas.
Upon the birth of a daughter for Brahmins, or upon the birth of a son for a Śūdra,
one should perform the rite silently, preceded by the remembrance of Viṣṇu.
One who follows the left-hand path (vāmācārī) should not perform the rite for generating intelligence;
rather, he should write with a pen made of gold for the sake of the causal [attainment].
One should satisfy the deity with the root-mantra at the region of the palate, as well as the mantra of the nectars; thereafter, one should perform the subsequent rite like Dakṣa.
Now follows the sacrament known as the naming ceremony (nāmadheya).
Now, the rite named the fifth consecration (pañcama-saṃskāra), which is for the elevation of both [the deceased and the living],
is prescribed for all at the end of the period of impurity (sūtaka) on an auspicious day.
One should commence the naming ceremony according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Kalpa;
those sixteen wheels of the Mothers which are enjoined in the Tantras [should be employed].

One should perform the naming ceremony after due deliberation; if the naming is performed, it becomes fruitful. However, if the naming is not performed here, even if the guru is of such a nature, [the result will be otherwise].
