One should perform the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka); that is now described as being "with seed" (sabīja), for by such qualities the accomplishment of brahmins is fully realized.
Now, the wheel of constellations.
I shall now proclaim the Tārā-cakra for the sake of mantra-attainment by children: A Ā are the two [seeds] of Hayagrīva; I Ū Ū are the three fires of the fire-oblation.
The vowels *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ* belong to Carā; *e* belongs to Mṛga and Śiva-bha (Ārdrā);
*ai* belongs to Punarvasu; and *o* and *au* belong to Puṣya, Karā (Pūrvaphalgunī), Sarpa-bha (Āśleṣā), and Khaga (Hasta).
Pitṛ, vagha, and aṅgha are considered to be in Bhāgya; Āryaman, iccha, and aja are in Hastā; i, ga, ja, ṭa, ṭha, and u are in Āṣāḍhā; while ḍa, u, dvi, īśa, bha, e, ḍha, and śa are in Svātī.
Likewise, when it is in Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, or Mūla;
when it is in Pūrvāṣāḍhā, the syllable *na*; and in Śatabhiṣaj, the syllable *va*.
Maḥ is in Dhaniṣṭhā; ya-ra-la-śa are in Śatabhiṣaj;
va-śau are in Pūrvabhādrapadā; and ṣa-sa-ha-asyu-rū-pa are at the end [of Uttarabhādrapadā].
From the asterisms corresponding to the mantra syllables *laṃ*, *kṣaṃ*, *aṃ*, and *aṃ* belonging to Aśvinī,
Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, and Rohiṇī, the results for the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) are determined by repeating three times the asterism of the first letter of their name.

Loss of position, association with the virtuous, great friendship, and death—these occur simultaneously; one incurs mental anguish and verbal censure, yet from the practitioner comes the accomplishment of one's goals.
The casting of enemies by many [planets] brings misfortune, while the casting of them by [benefics] brings the end of calamity;
having understood these results of the *tārācakra*, one should act accordingly.
Now, the gaṇacakra.
Having understood through the *mātṛkās* spoken by Tāra the [compatibility] of the practitioner and the object of practice—
whether they be female or male, or even when separated— one should deliberate upon them without regard for the *gaṇacakra*.
The host of men is known to be steadfast, free from the depths of fear, fierce, and formidable;
they strike down enemies and the like, and do not abandon their horses, chariots, and infantry.
The gods, horses, and rākṣasas belong to the practitioner and the one to be accomplished; the fruit for humans and gods is swift, while for those who are contrary, the fruit comes with difficulty.
If a human and a Daitya oppose one another, there will be death;
if a Deva and a Dānava oppose one another, their battle will be fruitless.
Now, the zodiacal wheel.
In the mantras of the planets and their satellites, one should examine the zodiacal wheel:
[the sequence] is four, three, two, two, six, five, and six.
Then, from the position of the letters of the name consisting of six syllables, there are six groups;
wherever the first letter occurs, this is the result that shall be there.
The Sun is a beloved servant and a nourisher; it causes disease, yet bestows sons and is auspicious.
It brings happiness from women, produces wind-disorders, grants good fortune, and effects the accomplishment of one's tasks.
This *rāśimātrikā* is said to be both a bringer of gain and a cause of misfortune;
for women, Śūdras, and those of inverse-caste (patiloma), worship is performed with the mantras of their names.

The previously mentioned signs, beginning with Aries and Pisces, correspond respectively to the twice-born classes starting with the Brahmin; their respective colors are to be understood accordingly, and this is especially so regarding the Vedic [tradition].
Now, the wheel of the five elements.
One should explain that on the Kaulika path, there is accomplishment (siddhi), ritual action (kṛtyā), and the elemental (bhautika);
one should deposit five and four [syllables] as far as fire, earth, water, and space.
Two vowels each should be written on the base; then again, the vowels beginning with *e*, as well as the six groups beginning with *ka*, and *ṣa-kṣa-lā-sa-ha-tha*.
The mantra, consisting of the letters of the mantra, should be written repeatedly alongside the name;
therefore, the mantra should be written again so that it becomes simultaneous with the hand-form.

One should perform the mantra-sādhana when the *iṣṭa* (desired), *adhika* (excessive), or *kalpaka* (suitable) *kaṣṭa* (obstacles) are present; otherwise, *bhūtas*, *vetālas*, and *piśācas* cause harm to the person.
There is friendship between earth and water, and even between wind and fire;
likewise, there is a commonality between fire and prosperity, as well as between water and wind.
The wheel of the enemy is the reverse of this, and the elemental wheel is likewise in the reverse order.
16b) Now, the wheel of the forest-dweller.
I shall here describe the wheel of the Siddhas and others, by knowing which one brings about [the attainment of] names;
on the path of southern worship, one's own mantra is one's own deity.
Likewise, upon the twelve-spoked wheel, one should rotate the six peak-syllables;
one should write the letters from the beginning to the end, starting from the east as far as the northeast.
Starting from the syllable of one's own name up to the mantra syllables ending in *phaṭ*,
one should repeatedly determine whether it is *siddha*, *sādhya*, *susiddha*, or *ari*.
A *siddha* [mantra] succeeds in due time; a *susiddha* succeeds either quickly or not at all; but a *ripu* [mantra], from the very moment it is grasped, cuts away one's very root.
Now, the accomplished wheel of the enemies.
Now I shall explain the perfected Mātṛkā for the practice of Mahāvidyā;
it should be understood according to the fundamental sequence, wherein there are sixteen squares.

One should properly arrange the Mātṛkās in sequence upon those wooden planks: Ka, Ḍī, Sāṃ, Ka, Ḍva, Ddhi, Sūrya (12), Diś (10), Ṣaṭ (6), Aṣṭa (8), and Dayā (3). These correspond to Taurus and the others.
In that [diagram], squares for the five-limbed lunar days and the Viśvedevas are proclaimed;
first, one should know the Siddha and others in the four groups located in the intermediate directions.
Furthermore, having counted the squares equal to that position according to the teacher’s instruction, [the mantra] becomes perfected through recitation;
it is perfected by twice the number of recitations when accompanied by the offering of *sārddhya*.
The *Siddha* [yoga] brings success; the *Susiddha*, attainment; the *Siddhāri* destroys those born of one's lineage.
The *Sādhya* brings about accomplishment through effort; the *Sādhyāsādhya* causes suffering.
Through worship, the *sādhya* becomes well-accomplished (*susiddha*), while the *sādhya-ari* (enemy of the sādhya) seizes one's own wife.
Through recitation (*japa*) exceeding that of the *siddha*, the *susiddha* becomes a *siddha* for one who is devoted to the extensive recitation and worship.

If the planet is excessively swift, it is twice as effective; a well-accomplished [planet] destroys a well-accomplished enemy, while an accomplished enemy destroys the son. An enemy [planet] situated in the seventh house destroys the daughter.
An *ari* (enemy) planet is "well-accomplished" (*susiddha*) when it destroys its protector; an *arghari* (neutral) planet is one that removes the practitioner's [benefit].
In this context, a planet is known by its established name as "asleep" (*prasupta*) when it awakens [to bestow results].
Now, he states another method.
Whatever name may be well-known, or whatever birth-name he may have, or that which was given by the preceptor through the casting of flower petals upon the castes; [that name should be used].
Having separated its phonemes according to their specific classes and distinctions,
one should then begin the purification of the mantra's syllables in that very same manner.
The *bindu* and the double *bindu* are to be meditated upon as arising at the tip of the tongue;
they are obtained through combined pronunciation and consist of additional syllables.
Having subtracted four parts from the hundred thousand syllables of the mantra,
one should purify each of the letters of the name together with the letters of the mantra.
Consonants are to be purified by consonants together with vowels, and likewise vowels by vowels;
the first [category] is to be purified by the first, and the second by the second.
Alternatively, if the syllables in a mantra or even in a name should be uneven,
then one should begin with that mantra and continue until it becomes even.
O fair-faced one, that which is the first wound of those two, in which there are three lines,
bestows all perfections in a very short time.

If the mantra is born with the *sādhya* at the end and so forth, it is accomplished only with great difficulty; however, if it is well-established at the beginning and the end, it bestows the prosperity of all desires.

If a mantra has an enemy at its beginning or at its end, it will succeed when meditated upon with double the effort; however, if it is an enemy at the beginning and a friend at the end, it succeeds even more quickly.
If the Siddha mantra at the beginning is well-established as the established conclusion, it is accomplished through recitation as prescribed;
however, if the enemy mantra at the end is established first, it must be abandoned by the best of practitioners.
The *sādhya* and other categories are accomplished through the recitation of mantras according to the three qualities (*triguṇa*);
first, the *sādhya* is accomplished by means of the well-established doctrine (*susiddhānta*) and the prescribed path.
The "well-accomplished" (susiddha) and so forth, ending with the "to-be-accomplished" (sādhya), depend on a fourfold [classification];
likewise, the "well-accomplished" and so forth, ending with the "enemy" (śatru), are proclaimed as the "to-be-accomplished."
Āghārin and Antasiddhāri— these too, when abandoned during the three ritual acts—
at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end— are perfected and bestow auspicious fruits.
The self-existent Lord has declared in the Tantra that one who is indifferent toward all that is to be accomplished is "indifferent" (udāsīna);
such a person, having attained perfection in the three locations, shall accomplish all goals.
If an enemy resides in all three positions, death from the mantra is certain;
if it ends with a pair of "Siddha" and "Sādhya," it is declared by the wise to be useless.
The *siddha* and other [categories] are well-established in the final doctrine as the means for accomplishing all purposes;
however, the *siddha* and others ending in the pair of enemies are proclaimed to be destroyers.
When the enemy is in the middle [house], the Siddha [planet] is at the end;
for him, the accomplishment of his task occurs with great difficulty, and the fruit is indeed very small.
If there is an enemy in the end, it is neutral in the first and middling; and if it is in the pair, it is to be won over.
If the work is delayed, it will be praised at the very end;
when the first and last [stages] are to be accomplished, success arises in the middle.
When the first of those two is accomplished, the middle one becomes the object to be accomplished.
Indeed, both the goal to be accomplished and its attainment are achieved through an abundance of recitation;
likewise, success against an enemy and the state of being well-accomplished shall come to pass.
It should be known that this brings about the total destruction of the practitioner; there is no doubt.
The object to be accomplished must be separated by a *siddha* or else by a *susiddha*.
"This mantra is accomplished quickly," said Īśāna himself;
"an enemy is neutralized by one who has attained accomplishment, and even more so by one who has attained perfect accomplishment."
That [mantra] shall not become an enemy, but rather it is accomplished with difficulty;
likewise, even if it is well-accomplished (susiddha), it becomes merely "to be accomplished" (sādhya) when interrupted by another sādhya.
Having observed such characteristics from afar, one should avoid them;
a mantra corrupted by an enemy must never be imparted.
In all these defects, having first cast away either illusion or desire, one should bestow prosperity for the sake of liberation from those defects.
Now, the six-petaled wheel of the Mātṛkās.
In the case of a mantra consisting of seed-syllables (bīja), the Mātṛkā [mantra] should be understood as having six petals;
there, one should fashion an auspicious six-petaled lotus.
In that regard, among the other Mātṛkās, excluding those that are *kūṭa* (consonant clusters) or *ṣaṇḍha* (vowels),
one should investigate starting from the first letter of one's own name.
Prosperity, poverty, fortitude, conflict with kinsmen,
danger, and total ruin— these occur in sequence according to the position of the first letter of one's name within the grid.
For this purpose, I shall certainly [practice] so that the accomplishment of the mantra may be attained.
Now, the wheel of debtors and creditors.
In that [system], the matrices of the destruction of wealth (dhanāśamātṛkā) are formed by six, three, two, one, six, and four;
the numbers are written as fire (3), sky (0), brother (2), and brow (1), while the vowels are eleven.
The syllables *ta*, *tta*, *re*, *kā*, *ca*, *ṭha*, *tkat*, *ka*, *le*, *khyā*, *va*, *rṇa*, *ha*, *roṃ*, and *mikā* should be written;
below that, the oceans [are placed] in positions of two, two, seven, three, six, three, seven, and five.
The fifty-six numbers for the practitioner's desire-mantras have been previously stated,
separately for each of the mantra-syllables distinguished by vowels and consonants.
Likewise, the numerical calculation (aṅkayoga) based on the name of the practitioner should be performed;
both the number eight (nāga) and the remainder (śeṣa) should be established until the mantra reaches its conclusion.
If there is an excess, it should be given by the practitioner using the mantra;
if the mantra should be deficient, then the wise one should recite the mantra.
One should recite the mantra even when it is equal, and one should recite it when it is greater than that debt;
one should know that death occurs when it is zero, therefore one should avoid zero.
Even if one undertakes that same number [of rites], one will not accomplish even those things that ought to be accomplished;
likewise, those who are deficient due to planetary conjunctions or have fallen from their initiatory vows [will fail].
One should perform the *puraścaryā* again for the sake of rekindling the mantra,
when the practitioner is known to be a debtor because the number of recitations is still insufficient.
When one performs as many repetitions as are required to exceed [the prescribed number],
then those acts known as *puraścaraṇa* will bring about equality [with the deity].
By performing the *puraścaryā* again, he will then become an achiever of his purpose;
but when a single task has been completed, he falls back into dullness once more.
Furthermore, by performing that vajra once more, it becomes capable of accomplishing a single task;
this reality-mantra has been revealed in all tantras, yet remains concealed.
Thus has been explained in sequence the clearing of debts and assets;
having ascertained both debt and asset, Maheśvarī shall not grant [the name].
Otherwise, O Supreme Goddess, when a name is bestowed, the fruit does not correspond to that name; yet the practitioner does not fall from his state.
In the Kali age, due to the fault of the gods, one does not recognize one's own face before oneself;
having understood all this, the Guru bestowed the command of the Name.
Having learned that from the mouth of one's guru, one should perform my ritual action;
for the Vaiṣṇavas, purity of disposition is essential, while for Śiva, it is purity of the vessel.
In the Traipura systems, the purification of the zodiac signs (*rāśiśuddhi*) is remembered as being [performed] by Gopā and Eka-damara;
one should investigate the *Kulākula* [tradition] regarding Pratyaṅgirā and Siddhilakṣmī.
The wheel of Tārā is prescribed for Kālikā and Tārā;
herein, one should not consider any other wheel for those mantras that are most desired.
In the case of Kālikā, Tārā, Kullukā, and Trikaṇṭaka,
as well as in the Ekākṣara-kūṭa and the five-syllabled Śiva-mantra;
[This applies] to that very Viṣṇu’s six-syllable [mantra], as well as his eight-syllable [mantra],
and to those of Nṛsiṃha, Arka, Varāha, Prāsāda, and Praṇava.
One should not examine the *siddha* status and so forth of mantras whose syllables are joined together,
such as the eight-syllable *haṃsa* mantra and likewise the five-syllable mantra.
One should not examine the success (siddhi) and other qualities of a neuter mantra;
likewise, this does not apply to a single-syllable mantra, a *kūṭa* mantra, a garland mantra (*mālāmantra*), or a three-seed mantra.
One need not purify mantras obtained in a dream, those received from a woman, or those belonging to the Siddhas and similar classes.
Mantras consisting of more than twenty syllables are proclaimed as *mālāmantras*.
Now follows the sacramental rite of the first feeding with solid food (annaprāśana).
The *annaprāśana* sacrament is the sixth rite common to all people;
it is performed according to the procedures prescribed in one's own ritual manual (*kalpa*), with the name-mantras of the Śūdras and others included.
In that [practice], the Pitṛs are to be worshipped; in the Vāmamārga, however, it is the Bhairavas.
At the conclusion of the worship of one’s own chosen deity and the Cakra, [one should offer] what remains of one's own [portion].
He should bestow that sacred ford and that supreme [gift], and he should utter the root mantra;
for one who has performed the ritual in this manner, no minor misfortune shall arise.
Now follows the consecration of the thief-demon.
Now, O Parvati, listen to the seventh sacrament, O Cauraksha;
this is prescribed for all as the destroyer of the sins committed in childhood.
For Buddhists and for those who wear topknots,
as well as for women, this [rite] should be performed by means of installation upon the crest-lock for the increase of good fortune and health.
The locks of hair on the left side, which are equal to the seed-syllables of the mantra, should be worn;
having cast them into a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), one should scatter them on the ground, especially these locks on the left.
Now follows the sacramental rite known as the binding of the girdle (mauñjībaṃdha).
Now I shall describe the eighth sacrament, the tying of the girdle (mauñjībandha);
leading [the boy] into the presence of the Guru is known as that initiation (upanayana).
One should perform that for the sake of spiritual luster according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Kalpa;
first, the family initiation (kuladīkṣā) must be performed by twice-born practitioners of the left-hand path (vāmācāra).

But that initiation which comes later is to be considered superior; it becomes effective immediately. Furthermore, initiation from a lesser deity is for those who are small, while that from a great deity is likewise for the great.
When the mantra of a minor deity has been mastered, even insignificant beings become self-subdued;
one should accept initiation from them and perform the preparatory rite (puraścaryā).
One should never perform ritual applications for one's own sake;
nor should one cause even a good disciple or a good son to grant the initiation without having been formally requested.
If one should give a perfected mantra out of greed, fear, or lust,
success arises for the disciple, but a curse arises for the guru.
In whichever deity's praise [is recited] and in whatever place,
his excellence on that particular path shall be like that of a sovereign king in his own kingdom.
O Pārvatī, one hundred and eight tantras have been proclaimed by me;
whichever [tantra] was asked about by anyone, its preeminence has been described therein.
I shall speak without partiality, according to the true meaning in the Merutantra:
among all [traditions], the Vedic is the best, and the Smārta is traditionally held to be inferior to that.
Then, there too, are the Saṃhitās, the oceans, the Yāmalas,
the Saṅgamas, the Tantras, and the Uḍḍīśas in Tāḍava.
The *indrajāla*, the *kacchapuṭa*, the *avaudha*, the *jaina*, and the *śāvara* should be known as diminished in sequence; let them be summarized according to their respective fitness.
One born in a low position will surely be raised very high;
all people perform their duties according to their own conduct for the sake of their kin and others.
This has been declared as the Paśumata; now I shall speak of the other two, Kaula and Vāmaya.
Among all, the Vaidika is the best, and the Vaiṣṇava is superior even to the Vaidika.

The Vaiṣṇava is the best among the [devotees of] Aghora; the Gāṇapatya is superior to that; the Saura is the most excellent; the Śaiva is even more excellent than the Saura; and the Śākta is considered supreme above the Śaiva.
The Dakṣiṇa is superior to the Śākta, while the Vāma is indeed superior to the Dakṣiṇa;
the Vīra is more excellent than the Vāma, and the Kaula-avadhūta is superior to the Vīra.
Beyond Kaula is Kaulāvadhūta; indeed, there is nothing higher than Kaula.
Now follows the sacramental rite known as the Prājāpatya-vrata.
One should know the ninth sacrament as the Prājāpatya, called the Vrata;
it is performed according to the path prescribed in its own ritual manual, being either Vedic or Tantric.
In the consecration of this vow, the mantra of Gāṇapati is prescribed;
those beginning with Vakratuṇḍa are for the right-hand path (dakṣiṇa), while those beginning with Ucchiṣṭa are for the left-hand path (vāmaka).
Now follows the sacrament known as the Saumyavrata.

O gentle one, one should perform the tenth rite, the Vedic vow (vrata), according to the procedure prescribed in its own ritual manual; however, a follower of Tantra should perform it in that same place according to the Tantric method.
One should take up the Bhairava mantra from the Vāmaka tradition known as Vaduka,
or from whichever division of Kālabhairava belongs to the Dakṣiṇa tradition.
Since Bhairava is the destroyer of the fetters of those who have performed the preliminary rites (puraścaryā),
the Svarṇākarṣaṇabhairava [mantra] should be adopted by practitioners who are destitute.
Now follows the consecration known as the Āgneya.
The practitioner of Tantra, remaining vigilant, should perform the eleventh consecration called Āgneya at that location according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya texts.
O dear one, at the outset, one should receive from the mouth of the guru the mantras of the deities,
as well as the instructions regarding the rites beginning with worship and ending with the concluding mantras, along with the rules concerning the ritual substances.
Now follows the consecration known as *devākhya*.
And the twelfth refinement (saṃskāra) is called Vaiśvadeva-vrata;
in that state, there should be initiation (dīkṣā) into one's desired mantra according to the Tantra.
Now follows the sacramental rite known as Godāna.
The thirteenth sacrament is proclaimed as the Godāna;
in its place, the practitioner of Tantra should perform the rite that liberates one from all sins.
Seated upon a pure spot, having placed before him either a mirror or water in a jar,
he should then make his request with truthful words.

Desiring the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for the destruction of my sins and for liberation, I perform my recitation (*japa*) during the afternoon; may the deities be pleased and act as witnesses.
O deities, as long as sins remain within my body, so do earth, water, fire, ether, air, the sun, the moon, and the stars.
And just as a reflection is seen in a mirror, in turbid water, in a stain, or within purified mercury, so too is it perceived.
Having become pure and composed of consciousness, one should contemplate the personification of sin (pāpapūruṣa) situated in the right side of the abdomen,
black in color and the size of a thumb.
The head is joined with the murder of a Brahmin; the arms with the theft of gold;
the heart with the drinking of liquor; and the hips with violating the teacher’s bed.
That pair, joined with evil, which causes the hair to stand on end,
bearing swords and shields, wicked, face-downward, and most unbearable—
Having reflected thus, one should perform the recitation (japa) while contemplating;
at the conclusion of the recitation, one should again look upon the sinful person being offered.
When all reflections are clearly seen in a mirror and such objects,
then one's sin has departed and the preliminary rites have been accomplished.
Now follows the sacramental rite known as *samāvartana*.
The fourteenth sacrament is called *samāvartana*;
in its place, Tantric practitioners should perform the *puraścaryā*.
Having first performed the abbreviated worship on the day,
the Kaulika should perform the recitation until evening, and likewise the worship of the circle at night.
Accompanied by the Śaktis and endowed with the five M’s (pañcamakāra) and so forth, one thus attains perfection; not otherwise, even through ten million recitations.
Now follows the sacramental rite known as marriage.
Marriage is prescribed as the fifteenth for all;
however, the marriage of a widow never occurs during the Picchala period.
Freed from all sins, she shall indeed go to the abode of Viṣṇu;
however, a twice-born woman who is not a Brāhmaṇa may likewise take another man as her husband.
Now follows the sacramental rite known as Pitṛmedha.
The sixteenth [chapter], known as the Pitṛmedha, follows the path prescribed by one's own Gṛhya-sūtra;
therein, the Vedic and Tantric rites are performed, and at the place of the deity, one's own chosen deity is worshipped.
Having set it aside, he should proceed with faith toward the Brahmins who walk the path of immortality;
or else, in their absence, he should follow the path of the patron of the sacrifice.

One should perform the *āmaśrāddha* (funeral rite with raw food), but the *pārvaṇa-paitṛka* (ancestral rite for the ancestors) should be performed with cooked meat. Furthermore, in the *kāula* tradition and likewise during the worship of the *cakra*, the twice-born who possess the requisite capacity should be fed.
One should avoid *tulasī* there; one should worship with *bhṛṅgarāja*.
There should be cooked food of *kaulika* substances and sacrificial cakes (*piṇḍa*) sprinkled with blood.
The supreme practitioner, consecrated by these sixteen purificatory rites (saṃskāra),
is then to be known as one liberated while living (jīvanmukta); such is his capacity for the worship of the deity.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Sixteen Saṃskāras for Practitioners, beginning with Garbhādhāna," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Now follows the mantra for the sixteen purificatory rites (*ṣoḍaśasaṃskāra*).
Now, I shall here describe sixteen consecrations established by mantra,
by performing which mantras are liberated from curses ordained by fate.
Now, first of all, regarding all mantras: elsewhere, they remain dormant;
however, when recited at the time of awakening, the mantra becomes awakened.
Alternatively, having joined together those letters beginning with *ja*, provided with the nasal bindu (*m*),
and again provided with the visarga (*ḥ*), he should recite them followed by the letter *kṣa* alone.
If [the mantra] thus instructed by recitation is awakened, it bestows swift accomplishment.
Now, O Pārvatī, hear about the awakening of mantras that possess enclosures (sāvaraṇa).
Having brought a bell-metal vessel purified with ashes and other substances,
one should recite [the mantra] eight hundred times during the night of the Sun.
One should strike a bell-metal vessel with a staff made of khadira wood and say:
"O Bhava-mantra, you must speak while I am awake; now, in the fourth state."
During the watch of the night, one should offer the bali-oblation to Kālī; for Bhairava, one should offer that which is produced by mantras;
and among other deities, one should offer a cock and a bursting coconut.
Now, in response to the inquiry as to how all mantras are empowered, he states their seed-syllable:
When the ancient gods were utterly deluded by liquor,
the Blessed One Madhusūdana then spoke.
"Who among you is worthy of worship? Who is the most excellent? Let him be declared.
Then the gods, like madmen, each cried out, "I am the best!"
"Is it Viṣṇu, that Blessed One, who is deluding them by means of his own māyā? Thus he spoke, whose words were capable of both censuring and bestowing grace.
"Whether he be the foremost among the gods, the first,
or even another," having heard these words of Viṣṇu, that mutual curse was pronounced.
Therefore, O Goddess, the forms of the mantras [are purified] by means of consecrations;
for without the release from the curse, what person could attain perfection?
The Goddess said:
By whom and how was the curse given? What is the fruit when it is recited while under a curse? And how may they attain freedom from the curse and success? Tell me this.
Śiva said:
That mantra in which the letter *vāyu* (ya) is established at the beginning, middle, and end;
which consists of four [syllables] or more, or even a single seed-syllable (*bīja*), wherein there is a manifold convergence.
And he who, in the month of Kārttika, has his [name] inscribed by someone else with a sword that severs mantras, his wife and his desires are likewise severed.
The pair of seed-syllables *bhūḥ* may occur at the beginning, the middle, or the end;
or, according to another method, the first [part] is threefold, the middle is twofold, and then the last is twofold.
Due to the curse of Śakra, Rudra and his consort were deprived of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; nevertheless,
they became mantras that are practiced even on the paths of passion and patience.
Wherever one of the seeds *hrīṃ*, *moṃ*, *phreṃ*, or *śrīṃ* is not seen,
or where there is the syllable *hraṃ*, that mantra has been rendered powerless by the gods.
If such a mantra is recited [with these flaws], it destroys the power of the practitioner;
for one who is powerless and perverse, death ensues—of this there is no doubt.
The syllable *hrīṃ* is not seen at the beginning, nor *klīṃ* in the middle, nor indeed *kroṃ* at the end;
this mantra has become turned away from its goal due to the curse of Sūrya.
If one resorts to a mantra with an averted face, the deity will be averted;
even if the task is accomplished by chance, one remains averse to the world.
Just as no dwelling is seen in the beginning, at the end, or in the middle,
so too the ritual procedure (vidhi), the mantras, and the hosts of gods and teachers remain established.
If one becomes deaf while reciting a mantra, forgetfulness arises for him;
he certainly becomes deaf—this was spoken by Mahākāla.
The letter *ha* is the seed-syllable of the Sun, while *sa* is known as the seed-syllable of the Moon;
the letter *ra* is declared to be the seed-syllable of Fire—these three constitute my eyes.
If even one [of these] is absent from the five-syllable mantra,
then by my curse he shall be blind and a source of suffering, grief, and fear.
That mantra consists of *hsauṃ*, *vāhaṃ*, *savātha*, *hauṃ*,
or else *aiṃ*, *phreṃ*, *hrūṃ*, or *namo* and *hrīṃ*, neither at the beginning, nor in the middle, nor at the end.
O Pārvatī, when the eye is pinned by a curse, as it was by King Rājadeva,
a mantra that has been recited but remains pinned does not attain success.
If there is the syllable *e* in the middle, or *kolaka*, or both *phaṭ* and *voṃ*,
or two *phaṭ*s, or three *vāṃ*s, by that the mantra is paralyzed.
By this terrible curse, even what is accomplished becomes auspicious;
never indeed will there be suffering, though for the most part it will be abundant.
However, if at the beginning of a mantra there are seven syllables in sequence,
joined with either the letter *ra* or the letter *ya*, that is indeed a *manu*.
If consumed by the elements of wind and fire, it will cause distress to the practitioner;
therefore, the best of practitioners should consecrate the goddess for the sake of accomplishment.
It is perceived as being separated by two, three, six, or eight syllables; when the *phaṭ* sound is thus interspersed, it is so designated.
Terrified by the curse of Nārasiṃha, he shall always cause the practitioner to tremble in his dreams and other states; indeed, no success is ever seen anywhere.
If the syllable *oṃ*, *vā*, *haṃ*, or the letter *sa* occurs at the beginning, that mantra is terrified;
due to the curse of Brahmā, it becomes devoid of success and brings extreme suffering.
When the four [syllables] are combined at the beginning, middle, and end, that mantra is impure;
due to the curse of Māyā, it causes impurity.
If the syllable *hūṃ* is placed at the beginning, or the pair of *phaṭ*s at the end or in the middle of the mantra,
then even if [the mantra] has been rendered ineffective by the curse of Rudra, it will accomplish the intended goal despite being suppressed.
If there are two *tāra*s at the beginning and *vaṣaṭ* at the end, or if *mādale* is present,
the child, pierced by a curse, will engage in quarrels and strife.
That three-syllabled mantra which is devoid of the letters *ha* and *sa* is said to be in a state of deep sleep due to the curse of Siṃha; it destroys the desired fruits [of its recitation].
That [mantra] which begins with eighteen syllables and is preceded by five *phaṭ*s was born from the curse of Cāmuṇḍā; it is intoxicated with pride and not auspicious.
In the center and at the end are the syllables *phaṭ*; by means of this *Kālikā*, one brings about a curse.
It causes fainting, and it especially brings about the fainting of the left-hand practitioner (*vāmī*).
Thus, at the end, he uttered the fivefold *phaṭ* syllable;
however, his virility was destroyed by Rambhā’s curse, and he was rendered impotent.
Where there are four *phaṭ* syllables, including those at the beginning, middle, and end, it is deficient by eighteen syllables; due to the curse of Bhairava, it brings about ruin.
The nineteen-leaved [mantra], conjoined with the syllables *hrīṃ*, *kroṃ*, *māṃ*, and *kāra*,
shall destroy the cause of desire by means of desire, having already destroyed the curse of Kāma.
The seven-syllabled mantra is known as a child (manu), the eight-syllabled as a youth (kumāra);
the sixteen-syllabled is a young adult (taruṇa), while the one with more syllables is mature (prauḍha) and the colorless (vivarṇaka) is the void (vyoma).
Where there are three hundred and ten *kalās*, four *vedas*, and eight *varṇas*,
these always produce sufferings at once through time.
The nine-syllable mantra of Cāmuṇḍā, joined with the syllable Oṃ, is a curse-mantra:
"O sword, cut the practitioner with your blade; of this there is no doubt."
That mantra which lacks "namaḥ" at the end, or "svāhā," or which lacks "vaṣaṭ," "vauṣaṭ," "hūṃ," or "phaṭ" in its middle, is not [complete].
The practitioner of this world-system who is cursed as "seedless" (nirbīja) shall suffer the destruction of his lineage within three years from the time he begins his service.
He in whose [mantra] there are the sounds "phaṭ phaṭ" at the beginning, middle, and end,
is devoid of success through the curse of Kaumārī and does not bring about accomplishment.
That ten-syllable mantra of Gaṇeśa,
when recited slowly due to a curse, shall cause one to become a fool in birth after birth.
When there is a conjunction of initial consonants with a single vowel, that is known as a *kūṭa*;
from such a *kūṭa*, loss occurs due to the curse of Mātaṅgī.
Due to the curse of the son of Aśvinī, he shall be deprived of his two-colored subjects;
he shall destroy the power of the practitioner and annihilate the king's army.
Born with four colors due to the curse of Sarpāli, he became squint-eyed;
even after reciting the Kekara mantra, he could not see with his eyes.
The six-syllable mantra became deprived of its seed-syllable due to the curse of Rāvaṇa;
there is no increase of one's lineage from its recitation, otherwise there is indeed no happiness for women.
Due to the curse of Dhūmāvatī and the appearance of twenty-one suns,
the mind of the practitioner becomes smoky and agitated.
Twenty, twenty-one, and thirty syllables belong to Tārā;
when this [mantra] is embraced by the seven [vowels], there is no death for one who recites it for seven [days].
The twenty-two-syllable mantra of Sarasvatī,
when deluded by her curse, causes the practitioner to become overwhelmed by addictions such as gambling and other vices.
That which consists of twenty-four syllables or twenty-seven syllables causes poverty through the curse of Rājamātaṅgī when she is afflicted by hunger.
Due to the curse of the Kaulikas, the twenty-three groups of three Rudra-syllables became arrogant mantras; by the recitation of those, a person becomes like a Vedic scholar.
Consisting of twenty-six, twenty-nine, thirty, and thirty-six syllables, he was deprived of his limbs due to the curse of Pūṣan; yet he was not one whose form was subject to desire.
A mantra of twenty-eight or thirty-one syllables, due to the curse of Nandīśa, becomes exceedingly cruel;
it brings about the destruction of the practitioner's goal, and the practitioner himself perishes.
The thirty-eight syllable mantra [is subject] to the curse of the Mātṛkās;
if one recites it while excessively enraged, there will be the destruction of one's own self for one's own sake.
Starting from forty up to sixty-three syllables, due to the curse of Mālikāśāpā, she was ashamed; those are his practitioners of shame.
Those mantras consisting of sixty-five syllables are pacifying in nature;
however, due to the curse of Kāma, there is no fruit from the exertion of reciting them.
From sixty-six up to ninety-nine, however, for Mars,
there are eight of its own [signs] which, through a curse, have become such practitioners of the ritual (sādhaka).
"Dhāti-dhṛti-dhātri-dhṛti-kvaṃ-kayugma, two gokaras,
and three hundred syllables— therein [the mantra] was sworn by Acchinnamastā."
May you be devoid of affection yet terrifying to practitioners;
when recited by desireless ascetics, you destroy attachment to worldly existence.
Starting from four hundred up to one thousand syllables,
those that are excessively long are excluded from rites for nourishment and the like due to the curse of the sacrifice.
There are more than a thousand mantras belonging to Daṇḍapāṇi;
by his curse, those afflicted by the name Daṇḍaka shall encounter suffering through their recitation.
Due to the curse of Bhārgava, more than two thousand mantras were split into seven parts; they are remembered as the "Siddhikhaṇḍakas" (the sections that grant accomplishment).
But when, O gods, I heard something else from the sages as they were chanting their prayers,
and yet no success was attained, then a most terrible curse was pronounced.
Because the deities have become despondent due to the lack of success, the Guru should provide encouragement; therefore, he should perform the purification of that mantra.
I shall explain that method; listen, O you along with the asuras!
The Guru, seated in the Siddhāsana, should firmly press the space between the anus and the genitals.
Pressing the left heel against [the perineum], one should place the right foot upon it,
with the two ankles pressing against each other at the junction.
It should be performed in such a way that [the breath] flows; then, having firmly pressed the base of the *liṅga* with the right heel, one should sit with the body steady.
Then the Guru, contracting the anus, should cause the wind known as *apāna* to rise;
thereafter, he should properly restrain the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
With one-pointed mind, one should bring about the union of the apāna and prāṇa breaths at the mūlādhāra,
which is the true nature of Kuṇḍalinī within the Supreme Self.
There, the true guru should contemplate his own mantra which has become defective;
then, he should [analyze] the syllables of that mantra one by one in their proper sequence.
One should cause [the breath] to enter the mūlādhāra by way of the suṣumṇā path,
and then into the svādhiṣṭhāna cakra, and then into the maṇipūra and anāhata cakras.
One should cause it to enter, piercing again and again the pure wheel of consciousness (ājñācakra).
Having thus led it to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), one should place it there from the lunar mandala.
One should clearly visualize [the breath] emerging and sprinkling the mantras of the deceased;
then, by way of the *suṣumṇā*, one should cause it to reach the *ājñā-cakra*.
In the Viśuddha, the Āhata, and the Maṇipūra cakra,
as well as in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, one should then cause [the breath] to enter the Mūlādhāra through its various divisions.
Then, having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantra upon the ṛṣi and other components, one should recite the mantra;
once it is freed from the aforementioned curse, one should subsequently instruct that person in it.
Due to the paucity of merit and the abundance of sin, the sinful person in the Kali age obtains but a small fruit from a blessing, while the fruit born of full sin is great.
Now, for the purpose of destroying verbal curses and so forth, this is being stated.
Now follow the purificatory rites for mantras, beginning with their birth.
On a seat made of śrīparṇī, sandalwood, or mango wood,
one should draw the pañcabhautika [maṇḍala] using musk, saffron, and lotuses.
One should invoke there the goddess Sarasvatī, known as Mātṛkā;
having performed worship according to the prescribed rite, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times.
Having recited the Mātṛkā, one should [extract] from its midst the mantra desired by oneself,
consisting of vowels, consonants, bindus, and syllables joined with visargas.

Having extracted each [syllable] individually and then unified them according to the instructions of the Guru, one should produce the mantra thus grasped; this is declared to be "saṃjanana" (the generation).
Having placed the *praṇava* at the beginning and end, one should recite the *praṇavāntaritā* mantra one hundred and eight times; this [mantra] consisting of syllables is indeed the life-force.
One should write the mantra on a palm leaf with yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma),
and strike it one hundred times for each syllable with sandalwood water.
Uttering this seed-syllable of Vāyu is called "striking" (tāḍana).
Śāvara mantras that have become blunted become effectors of success when they are struck.
Having drawn [the diagram] upon the previously mentioned seat according to the number of syllables of its mantra, one should then take karavīra flowers while reciting [the mantra].
One should offer oblations with those flowers one hundred times for each syllable while reciting the seed-syllable of fire;
this is called "awakening."
As before, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus on the pedestal with those same materials;
in its pericarp, one should draw a single bud of *mālatī*.
For each individual syllable of the mantra, one should take as many aśvattha leaves as there are syllables in that mantra, while reciting the mantra in this manner.
One should consecrate him with the mantra "I consecrate this one; obeisance," using various fragrant substances, sprouts, and whatever syllable [is appropriate].
This consecration is known to consist of one hundred and eight [repetitions];
just as water purifies people, so does this consecration bring about the purification of mantras for men.
The Jyotirmantra should be meditated upon within the fire-mandala at the mūlādhāra; one should then consecrate that mantra and visualize it thus ascending upwards.

The impurity known as *āṇava* is considered innate (*sāhajika*), while that called *kārmaṇa* is adventitious (*āgaṃtu*). That which is termed *yogika* and *māyika* resides within one's own mantra; thus, the threefold impurity is described.
One should contemplate each [syllable] as being completely consumed by the Jyotir-mantra;
thus, one should contemplate that one's own mantra has become pure.
The Jyotirmantra is considered to be the two-syllabled "Hauṃ" at the beginning of the Veda;
one should also perform its application for the sake of purification.
As before, one should inscribe the mantra upon the pedestal using substances such as saffron;
or [one may write it] on a vessel of copper or other metal with camphor or white water.
Having consecrated pure water one hundred and eight times with the written mantra,
he should [sprinkle] it with drops of water from *kuśa* grass using that same mantra.
One should sprinkle [the mantra] syllable by syllable; this is considered to be its nourishment (āpyāyana).
For those who have been exhausted by the preparatory rite (puraścaryā), this is like a formal graduation ceremony (samāvartana).
One should inscribe the mantra within a copper vessel using musk and other substances,
and in another vessel, one should place water scented with camphor and other fragrances.
Having taken [the water] with the arghya vessel while reciting this mantra, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with "I satisfy [you], obeisance" (tarpayāmi namaḥ). Thus is the libation.
One should recite the mantra preceded by *oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ* one hundred and eight times;
this should be used for the kindling (*dīpana*) of the mantra, as it is desired for all mantras.
The concealment and non-disclosure of the mantra being recited—
these ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) have been proclaimed in all tantras as secrets.
Thus, eleven consecrations have been declared, as well as five others;
for each mantra, the recitation, the fire-oblation, and the libation will now be described.

The cleansing and the feeding of the twice-born constitute the sixteenth; thus have been declared the sixteen purificatory rites (saṃskāras) of the mantra, which liberate one from the curses of the gods and other afflictions.
I shall now declare the time for initiation; listen to that, O fair-faced one.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Sixteen Saṃskāras, beginning with the Vigil (jāgaraṇa), of Mantras," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Now, the results for the months.
The Lord said:
In Caitra, there shall be initiation for the sake of suffering; in Vaiśākha, an accumulation of jewels;
death occurs in Jyeṣṭha; and in Āṣāḍha, there is the destruction of kinsmen.
Prosperity will surely come in Śrāvaṇa, while there will be a decline in Bhādrapada;
furthermore, there will be the destruction of subjects in Āśvina, and indeed nothing but inauspiciousness.
In the month of Kārttika there shall be knowledge, and in Mārgaśīrṣa there will indeed be the glory of the path to happiness;
in Pauṣa there is the loss of knowledge, while in Māgha there is the increase of intelligence.
In the month of Phālguna, there shall be the accomplishment of all goals; one should avoid the intercalary month (malamāsa).
Now listen to the specific distinctions regarding those [months] that are prohibited, according to their differences.
The sixth day of the month of Bhādrapada, likewise the fourteenth of Āśvina,
the ninth of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, and the third of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight in Pauṣa, the fourth of the bright fortnight in Māgha,
the ninth of the bright fortnight in Phālguna, and the thirteenth known as Kāma in Caitra.
In Vaiśākha there is indeed the Akṣaya-tithi, in Jyeṣṭha the Daśaharā-tithi,
in Āṣāḍha the bright fifth day (Śukla-pañcamī), and in Śrāvaṇa the bright fifth day.
On these divine festival days (parvan), one obtains the fruit of ten million sacred fords (tīrtha).
Even during censured times, initiation (dīkṣā) is said to be auspicious on these festival days.
Now, the results for the fortnights.
The Śukla [path] bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, while the Kṛṣṇa is traditionally held to bestow only liberation;
for those who follow the Vāmācāra, the Śukla is not honored, nor even the Kṛṣṇa, which is considered mediocre.
For the sake of perfect accomplishment, the destruction of the intellect resulting from the failure to pay the tenth part [of one's gains] should be understood to occur gradually.
Those who do not worship Gaurī, the Mantrikas, the Mothers, and Gaṇeśa shall become miserable.
All mantras will indeed be successful, and never fail;
there shall be prosperity, swift accomplishment, the eradication of ignorance, and the destruction of suffering.
The destruction of dullness and impurity occurs, and the fruit becomes entirely full;
for men, O Hari, neither white nor black [lines] are auspicious or inauspicious.
There shall be success for all mantras, yet there is great danger for those who are not devotees of Śiva.
Success departs especially [for them], and there is loss of sons when one acts contrary to the Pitṛs.
The new moon on a Monday, the fourteenth day on a Tuesday,
and the seventh day on a Sunday are equal to hundreds of solar eclipses.
Now, the results according to the day of the week.
On Sunday there will be wealth; on Monday, indeed, there will be peace;
on Tuesday, it destroys longevity; therefore, one should avoid initiation on that day.
From Mercury one attains beauty; from Jupiter, the food of knowledge; from Venus, one attains good fortune—and [from the others,] *śo* * * * * * (##?).
Now, the results of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-phala*).
In sequence, there is the fruit of initiation, equanimity, as well as calamity,
mental anguish, the happiness of loved ones, worldly pleasure, and the accomplishments of the mantra.
The accomplishment of fierce mantras, the successes of the Śakti mantra,
all mantras become effective, and the successes of the serpent mantra [are attained].
There is destruction, royal punishment, mastery, and all supernatural powers;
through the perfection of Rudra as the presiding deity, there is swift attainment of auspicious wisdom.
Friendship with the gods, the cessation of all desires, quarrels, and great fear; prosperity, disease, success through recitation, agitation, torment, and lordship [result from these].
The fruit of all accomplishments is attained gradually through the right or the left;
however, in the fourth [direction], there is a fall downward when [the breath] is scorched, embraced, or fumigated.
When the zodiacal sign is facing downward and is auspicious, and especially when the moon is pure,
one should employ the strength of the lunar mansions (tārābala) during the dark fortnight, while contemplating one's own name and so forth.
Now, the fruit of yoga.
And the yogas are Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, Śobhana, Śubha,
Śukarmā, Dhṛti, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Siddhi, and Harṣaṇa.
Varīyān, Śiva, Siddha, Brahmā, and Indra as the sixteenth;
the results of the conjunctions (yogas) beginning with Viṣkambha shall correspond to their respective names.
The fruits of all yogas, beginning with Ānanda, are complete everywhere;
however, they say that auspicious instruments are especially required for initiation (dīkṣā).
Now, the results of the instruments.
Vava, vālava, kaulava, taitila, and vaṇija—
these Karaṇas are auspicious in all the Tantras, O Bhāvinī.
One should especially avoid Śakuni and the other Viṣṭis;
by abandoning Viṣṭi, success will quickly be attained in the best of Karaṇas.
All success is achieved in Viṣṭi and Puccha; in the Sthira yogas, however, there shall be stability.
Now, the results of the ascendant (lagnaphala).
Now, regarding the results of the ascendant (lagna): there will be wealth from the gods, grain, and prosperity;
or else there may be death, loss, and the destruction of one's cattle.
Sovereignty, or a deity, spiritual accomplishment, loss, or the destruction of intelligence;
the acquisition of jewels and the like, fortune, wealth, grain, and various attainments.
Full accomplishment, majesty, loss, destruction of wisdom,
the birth of a son, success in mantra, cattle, and abundant wealth.
There is constant suffering as well as loss; the union is auspicious for the Vāmita [Vāmana] school, but it is contrary for the Vāgins and Yavanas, though it is auspicious in many ways.
Now, the fruit according to time.
According to the nature of things, the time for union that bestows a kingdom occurs at dawn;
at midday there shall be all success, and in the evening it would be mediocre.
The night is prohibited for the imparting of mantras by the best of preceptors;
however, it is auspicious when occurring in fixed zodiac signs (sthirarāśi), provided all movable [degrees] are avoided.
A stable ascendant is auspicious for the Viṣṇu-mantra, while a moving ascendant is auspicious for the Śiva-mantra;
an ascendant situated in its own nature (dvisvabhāva) is praised for the Śakti-mantra.
The Moon situated in the third, eleventh, sixth, or tenth house is auspicious;
the Moon at birth is also declared auspicious, provided it is not the birth-star (janmanakṣatra).
In the bright fortnight, the Moon is auspicious even when conjoined with those planets that are pure in their direct motion, provided it occurs on the second, fifth, or ninth lunar day.
Even if the moon is situated in a neutral sign, it shall bestow auspiciousness;
on a day when the five limbs [of the horoscope] are pure, one should perform the Svādya rite of the moon and the sun.
The consecration of mantras is recommended during the rising of Jupiter and Venus;
even if Jupiter is setting or has become old, provided he is not eclipsed by the Sun or other planets.
At that time, no fault exists during the periods of Aries, Scorpio, and Leo; nor is there a fault during times of non-study, earthquakes, or the roaring of clouds at twilight, O Bhairava.
One should avoid initiation on a day when a meteor falls,
as well as on one's birth asterism, during a solar transit, at the equinoxes, or at the solstices.
On other occasions involving the accumulation of merit, during lunar and solar eclipses,
on the five festival days (parvan), on the anniversaries of the beginning of the Yugas, and on days such as Vyatīpāta.

In this matter, initiation is declared to be auspicious; there is no need for deliberation here, for the purification of the month, lunar day, weekday, and so forth has indeed already been prescribed.
In that regard, the initiation into the mantra (mantra-dīkṣā) should be understood as paramount by the best of practitioners;
the initiation into the vidyā is not so, nor is there any need for purification based on lunar days, months, and the like.
Whenever there is a desire, at that very time initiation [should be performed] according to the command of the Guru;
no restriction regarding time and so forth is prescribed for those seeking prosperity.
All these [actions], though censurable, are praised when they lead to liberation.
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the birth of a disciple, or during the transit of the sun into Capricorn (makara-saṃkrānti).
And at the time of the Guru's compassion, the constellation and other signs shine forth; therefore, [this is the time] for initiation.

During a lunar eclipse, a solar eclipse, the day of the sun's entry into a new sign (saṅkrānti), the day of the sun's turning back (ayana), and on the two festival days (parvan), one performing a mantra-initiation need not purify the month, the lunar mansion, and so forth.
During the sun's transit into a zodiac sign and likewise during a solar eclipse,
one should never consider any matter such as the ascendant or other astrological factors.
Especially on the Mahāṣṭamī, for the sake of attaining wealth and the fulfillment of one's aims.
At the time of a solar eclipse, however, nothing else need be sought;
there is no occasion equal to the time of a solar eclipse.
In that regard, whatever is performed there shall all yield infinite fruit;
on the occasion of a solar eclipse, there is no need for the calculation of months, lunar days, weekdays, and so forth.
At that time, among men, one should give what is desired and receive it from the guru;
then the mantra becomes effective without effort, and not otherwise.
Those desiring the accomplishment of mantras should perform this with every effort;
it is equal to a thousand lunar eclipses and even a solar eclipse.
Therefore, an eclipse occurring on its own day is said to be a hundred thousand times more efficacious;
among those, a solar eclipse is praised, but a lunar eclipse is never so.
During a lunar eclipse there is poverty, whereas during a solar eclipse there is total prosperity;
the solar eclipse is declared to be Śiva, and that called the lunar is indeed Śakti.
During a solar eclipse, one should not perform the initiation of power (śaktidīkṣā) or the initiation of the bound soul (paśudīkṣā);
during a lunar eclipse, one should not perform the Vaiṣṇava initiation (viṣṇudīkṣā) or the Pañcarātra initiation.
Initiation during an eclipse of the moon or sun is considered auspicious among all initiations;
initiation for Śakti during a lunar eclipse is the most excellent of all initiations.

One should not observe restrictions regarding the nine planets, lunar days, constellations, days, months, and so forth; nor should one perform calculations of yogas or karaṇas, nor engage in such deliberation.
O Goddess, initiation performed by the wise during the period beginning from the first day (Bodha) up to the ninth lunar day (Navamī) bestows all desired fruits.
During the awakening of Durgā, one should not observe restrictions regarding the proper or improper time;
for there, the eighth day is called Aśoka and the ninth day is likewise called Rāmā.
On the anniversary of the beginning of a Yuga, on one's birthday, on the day of marriage,
and likewise during the two equinoxes and the two solstices, one should not deliberate upon anything at all [regarding the suitability of time].
During the solstices, the equinoxes, and likewise on the anniversaries of the Yugas,
as well as during eclipses, there is no consideration of the specific time for a great pilgrimage site.
Near a Tulasī plant, at the root of a Bilva tree, likewise at the foot of a Dhātrī tree,
in the presence of the Anādi-deva, in a great sacred field (mahākṣetra), or in a cowshed;
Regarding the Goddess, there is no fixed determination of time even on the day of worship;
listen now to the special occasion for initiation apart from the lunar date (tithi).
When the rare opportunity to meet a true guru has once arisen,
and when one has obtained his permission, that initiation is the great treasure.
Whether in a village or a forest, in a field by day or by night,
when the Guru is seen or heard, or at a sacred site (siddhakṣetra), it is most auspicious.
When the Guru says "Come," then initiation occurs by divine providence;
whenever there is a desire, then initiation occurs in accordance with the Guru's command.

Neither the lunar day, nor vows, nor fire-offerings, nor ritual bathing, nor recitation, nor any formal rite is the cause for initiation; rather, it is one’s own desire when a true guru has been found.
If the Guru, out of compassion, bestows [initiation] upon his disciples,
then the ascertainment of the auspicious moment (lagna) and other such factors need not be considered in any way whatsoever.
On that day when all the lunar days, all the planets, all the constellations, and the zodiac signs are well-disposed, the Guru brings about all happiness.
At the holy pilgrimage site of Kurukṣetra, at the four divine seats (pīṭhas),
at Prayāga, Śrīgiri, and Kāśī, one need not distinguish between the auspicious and inauspicious times.

Initiation is declared by Śiva to be auspicious during the two equinoxes, on Sundays, during the Ardhodaya, and likewise during the Mahodaya; indeed, the defect of the Lion [zodiacal sign] is not considered in these cases.
He shone at Gayā, in the field of Bhāskara, on Mount Candra,
at Catvara, at Mataṅga, and likewise in the hermitages of the maidens.
"Therefore, O Pārvatī, one should not receive initiation at those sacred sites.
Thus, O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Gods, I have described to you the proper time for initiation.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Time for Initiation," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*.
The Śrī Devī said:
How does initiation occur in the Vāma path, and how does it occur in the Dakṣiṇa?
What is essential therein, and for whom? Tell me this definitive conclusion.
The Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the fivefold procedure for initiation, which is concealed in all the tantras and is the most excellent of the best for kings.
For those who are exceedingly wealthy, it is said to be the best; for ordinary people, it is middling;
for Brahmins, it is said to be small; and for ascetics, it is even smaller.
Therefore, I shall first explain to you that which is the most supreme among the supreme,
by knowing which the domain of the various categories, beginning with the "supreme," is understood.
Therein I shall describe the initiation (dīkṣā), preceded by the ritual sacrifice to the site (vāstuyāga);
therein, one who is expert in the knowledge of the site (vāstu) should examine the ground.
24b) Therein, first is the examination of the site:
a place suitable for floating, a deep lake with a long-lasting reservoir of water.
The fire-sanctuary of the Agnihotris is renowned as a place of merit.
O Pārvatī, these places— whether they be the abodes of the twice-born who observe vows or one's own hermitage— are highly praised for the performance of initiation.
The banks of great rivers, the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, and likewise the praiseworthy holy fords (tīrthas), sacred fields (kṣetras), and hermitages (āśramas).
All the forests, as well as all the mountains,
including Mount Nila and the secondary peaks, and even the abodes of the deities.
Now, those [places] that are prohibited:
one should not perform initiation in a thicket, in a dense forest,
at the junction of two boundaries, in a great wilderness, or in a place frequented by predatory beasts.
Ground that is cracked, pierced by stakes, or overgrown with anthills should be avoided from afar;
it takes away the life and wealth of the builder.
A cracked [vessel] causes death; one that is difficult to fill brings about poverty;
one with a thorn in it constantly gives rise to affliction; and one that is uneven increases enemies.
A house sloping toward the northeast (Īśakoṇa) certainly brings prosperity to the owner;
one sloping toward the east increases wealth, while one sloping toward the north is a bestower of boons.
Ground that slopes toward the south always brings fear of death;
and that ground which slopes toward the direction of Nirṛti causes the destruction of the household.
The earth known as Varuṇaplavā is said to cause the loss of wealth;
likewise, the earth known as Vātaplavā constantly causes agitation.
On the first plot of ground, the wise man should cause an examination to be made:
the ground belonging to a Brāhmaṇa is covered with Kuśa grass, while that of a Kṣatriya is filled with Śara reeds.
The Vaiśyas are like thickets of Kuśa and Kāśa grass; the Śūdras are like thickets of all kinds of grass.
From the Brāhmaṇa onwards, their complexions are like the Kunda flower, the moon, cow dung, and a swarm of bees.
A Brāhmaṇī brings about the accomplishment of all goals; likewise, a Kṣatriyā bestows sovereignty;
a Vaiśyā produces wealth and grain; but a Śūdrā is censured.
Having smelled the scent of the earth, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) perceived both the auspicious and inauspicious;
he encountered various fragrances, including those of great sorrow and the smell of raw flesh.
If it has a pungent odor, the patient will suffer from disease; if it smells like excrement, it is fruitless;
if it has a mild odor, he shall be free from illness; and if it is foul-smelling, one should anticipate fear.
Success comes from the scent of nagagandha; sudhā and vaṇija are auspicious; likewise, the scents of kṣāra and nāśa bring about destruction, while the scent of upāni brings good fortune.
Furthermore, I shall describe the taste associated with the auspicious and the inauspicious:
sourness brings obstacles, whereas the astringent ground indeed leads to freedom from disease.

Even by means of salt, which is a great destroyer of taste, one's own enemy—the sense of relish—is specifically perceived once it has attained its flavor through that [salt]. It is his minister who is thus described.
One should take possession of the ground as far as the site extends;
one should clear away thorns and the like, and remove husks, charcoal, and other such debris.
Where there are pebbles, a human being experiences distress;
likewise, from charcoal come diseases, and from iron, exhaustion.
Fear of the king arises from wood that has been burnt and the like;
sorrow arises from grass; and through bricks, one becomes stable.
If it is pervaded by the Vetasa-avaṃdha, death shall occur; through Vaṃśa, imprisonment is obtained;
through Viṣṭi, one encounters bondage; and through Śūnyabhāṇḍa, emptiness.
One should know that a quarrel arises from leather; from a rag comes the loss of wealth;
and from bones, death occurs on earth—this is known through the bones.
That man who finds clay and glossy leaves shall obtain his share;
where sand is found, there one should know that great happiness exists.
A stone of great fortune becomes crystal and devoid of splendor;
by means of a gem there is the destruction of disease, and by means of gold one becomes wealthy.
I shall now declare the auspicious and inauspicious results arising from specific notes in the *svara*:
with the *uraga* [note], the ground becomes unstable; with the *maṇḍūka*, there is the arrival of wealth.
If *pippalīkā* occurs, there will be grief; if *mukhaka*, one’s grain will increase. If *chuchuṃdarī* occurs, there is great destruction; through *kaumya*, one becomes wealthy.
By means of a cricket one falls into illness; by a moth, great danger;
by a *hidiṅgikā* insect, great terror; and by a scorpion, certain death.
A house-lizard brings great accomplishment, and a chameleon destroys fear;
in this way, such creatures bestow auspiciousness through their auspicious presence.
One should know that for living beings, especially, impurity arises from impure things;
however, in rites such as the construction of one's desired sacrificial pits and the like, the ground is purified by digging.
While digging, as long as water is not reached, the fault of the thorn remains;
but where the water is far off and stable, it is impossible to dig at all.
It should be made five cubits in length for the pacification of the defects caused by splinters;
free from bones, insects, charcoal, impurities, and the like, it brings about auspiciousness.
Otherwise, having discarded that clay,
one should fill it with auspicious clay from outside the village, [specifically] that belonging to each respective caste, such as Brahmins and others.
Then, having extracted the splinter, one should fill it so that it is perfectly level;
if this is not done, the practitioner shall obtain no fruit whatsoever.
Thus, the sequence for extracting the thorns has been briefly explained by me;
having thus purified the ground, the worship of the site (vāstuprapūjana) should be performed for the sake of the ritual work.
It is declared to be of two kinds: that pertaining to the Smṛti and that pertaining to the Tantra;
and the site (vāstu) is likewise proclaimed to be of two types according to the distinction between mobile and immobile.
Regarding houses, palaces, wells, pavilions, and water,
as well as other tasks such as ritual applications, fire oblations, and the like.
In a conflict that must be undertaken, there may arise great calamities.
Now follows the origin of the Vāstupuruṣa.
In ancient times, there was a certain very powerful Asura named Vāstu;
by him the three worlds were conquered, as were the fifty-three deities.
Because they were born face-to-face in battle, they were thus oppressed;
having been defeated again and again in combat, he alone remained as the lord of creatures (prajāpati).
At the end of a thousand divine years, the gods came for refuge to Viṣṇu, me, and Pārvatī; this was also heard by Devendra.
Desirous of fighting, he rushed forward, urged on by Antarada;
he engaged in combat with him for five years like a wrestler.
Then the Daitya, intoxicated with pride and deluded by Viṣṇu’s Māyā, being pleased, spoke these words: "Choose, choose!"
Neither by Indra nor by Kubera was such a battle performed that brings me satisfaction;
indeed, it was fought by you alone, even with your matted hair and accompanied by your army.
This has been accomplished by Viṣṇu, who is aided by me and bears half of Pārvatī’s body;
therefore, I, the Supreme Lord of the three worlds, have attained satisfaction.
"There is nothing whatsoever that I cannot give, even including all three of us.
Having heard these words of his, Śiva’s brow was moved.
Hari said: "O most fortunate lord of Daityas, there is no one equal to you.
Then Romā spoke these three true words: "May that be so."
"Even Śiva is one with Pārvatī; indeed, there is no other. Or rather, [he is] in the three. Then Viṣṇu signaled to the Daitya.
"Tell us that means by which death may come quickly; for we know this to be a ruse of Viṣṇu. Having understood this, the lord of the Daityas replied.
One must certainly go to the mouth of Death along with all beings;
nevertheless, he who strives for the sake of his own vow lives.
However, when the service was performed by Śaya alone for one less [night],
he showed him the way, and his body fell down.
And at that time, O Lord, a voice from the sky, bodiless and most excellent, spoke:
"O Lord of the Daityas, do not grieve; there shall be for you a birth upon the earth."
Dissolve yourself right there for the sake of my satisfaction; now hear a boon:
those castes who, for their own enjoyment, shall build a new house—
There, apart from your festival, the female servants such as Kālakarṇī and others, as well as those headed by Vināyaka, are afflicted by various miseries.
"Your servants shall cause them affliction," thus was the command of Rāmeśvarī.
Having heard this, he too descended to the surface of the earth.
Then he entered [the city] which had been filled with stones by the gods,
those gods who, having been defeated in battle, were intent on emerging once more.
Above that, however, they strive to establish fifty-three abodes;
fire is ordained for the head, and water is situated in the mouth.
Pṛthvīdhara and Urvyamā, stationed at the base,
should always be worshipped by the wise as they hold their bows against the chest.
The two sons of Aditi, Jayanta and Vijaya,
who are the lords of serpents stationed upon his shoulders, should be worshipped with great effort.
Likewise, Satya, Roga, and the others— five external and five internal—
are situated together in the left hand, along with Rudra, Īśvara, and Ajayakṣman.
Savitṛ, belonging to Savitṛ, likewise stationed himself in the right hand;
then Mitra and Varuṇa were established within the belly.
Pūṣan and Pāpayakṣman are located at the wrists of the hands;
likewise, Asura and Śeṣa are situated on the left side.
Likewise, on the right side is Vitatha, accompanied by Gṛhakṣata;
both Uccāra and Mṛga should be known as being on the two shanks, along with Gandharva and Puṣpaka.
In the two shanks are Bhṛṅgin and Sugrīva; in the two knees are the two doorkeepers; in the penis is Mṛga; likewise, Jaya and Śakra are in the feet, and the Pitṛs are in the same place.
And Brahmā is in the middle of the feet; he is worshipped in the heart. Therefore, one should certainly worship him there according to one's desire.
Hearing that procedure, the gods, via the left and right paths,
purify the auspicious ground and should draw ten lines.
By means of that [measurement], one should construct the eight-cubit Vāstu mandala, beginning with the downward, upward, and transverse lines; it shall not be larger than that.
The wheel consists of eighty-one squares; therein are the Vedic deities.
One should worship Brahmā first in the nine central compartments, beginning with the son [Viṣṇu].
One should place Apavatsa in the northeast, Prāṇa in the food-triangle,
Savitṛ in the southeast, and Vivasvat among the rays.
Indra is in the southwestern quarter; Mitra is situated in the three western directions;
Rājayakṣman is in the northwest; and Sumeru is in the three northern directions.
In the medical squares, the deities are located from the northeast corner of the Vaiśya square:
Agni (Fire) in the two upper corners, Varuṇa (Water) in the two lower corners, and Aditi is said to be in the center.
These five deities are to be known in succession from the right-hand path:
Jayanta, Indra, Sūrya, Satya, and Bhṛṅga are located in the southeast corner.
Likewise, Antariksha, Vata, Pushan, and Savitra—these four gods are from the northeast; thereafter, in the south, are five.
In the pair [of directions], there are Krama and Vitatha; in the four-square [section] situated in the southwest (Nairṛtī), there are Bṛhatkṣata, Yama, Gandharva, and Bhṛṅgarāja.
From Īśāna come Jayanta and Nṛpa; likewise, Vāruṇa and Aja from the Pitṛs.
After that, in the west, are Vikaṭa, Pañcamukha, Ugrīva, and Puṣpadantaka.
Varuṇa and the remaining gods are in the northwest; you indeed rule in the northeast. Rudra, Pāpayakṣman, and Roga are in the five [directions] of the north.
Saravyu, Bhallāṭa, Soma, Bhuja, and likewise Aditi—
these forty-five deities are worshipped with devotion.
Having filled the squares for the aforementioned deities with five [syllables],
one should erase the central nine squares among those squares and fill them [with the remaining syllables].
Having further smeared those six [squares] in all four directions with white powder, one should fill them completely with red powder.
One should arrange the remaining parts here according to their proper places;
then, having filled the center with various [elements], one should fully complete Brahmā therein.
One should offer oblations to them with chariot-remnants, such as milk-rice;
one should worship all of them with sweet milk-rice mixed with other sweets.
One who possesses self-conceit regarding those various materials should worship for the pacification of faults;
whether in stone or in an image, one should perform the ritual for Vāstoṣpati.
Having performed the invocation and worship of that [deity] with the Vedic mantra,
and having performed the worship of the others with their respective name-mantras, one should complete the rite.
Now, in the Tantric path, one should likewise [draw] on a sixty-four-square grid two lines at the corners and determine the Brahma-lines in the middle.
In the four squares starting from the east, in pairs of squares,
[one should place] Āryaka, Vivasvat, Mitra, and the other, Mahīdhara.
In the two half-cells of the corner, one should place the mantras of Śaivya: *sāvitraḥ*, *savitāśakraḥ*, *indutidrudratarjayau*, and *ayāyavatsakau*.
Every seizing spirit being summoned— the Bhañjaka, the Pilipicchaka,
the Carakī, and the Vidārī— [and] the Pūtanā [are located] in the two directions from the east.
Īśāna, Artha, Parjanya, Jayanta, Śakra, Bhāskara,
Saṃvya, Vṛṣa, and Antarīkṣa are likewise situated in the eastern quarter of the grid.
Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Gṛharakṣaka,
Gandharva, and Bhṛṅgarāja— these are the deities situated in the southern direction.
Nairṛti, as well as Dauvārika, Sugrīvaka, Varuṇa, Puṣpadanta, and the Asura along with the two known as Rogaka.
Then, in the west or the north, Vāyu and the Nāga are the principal deities;
following that are those named Soma, Bhallāṭa, and Argala, as well as Aditi and Diti in the north.
The station of Brahmā is with red colors; the cardinal directions are yellow, and the intermediate directions are marked with white.
Then the cardinal directions are green, and the intermediate directions are black.
A reddish enclosure should be made so that the mandala becomes beautiful;
the forms of all the aforementioned deities are now described.
One should worship him who has eight eyes, seated upon a lotus in the center, holding a rosary and a boon-granting gesture in his right hands, and a staff and a water-pot in his left hands.
All four-armed deities are established within the body of Vāstu.

Now, the meditation on Vāstu: one should visualize Vāstu as having the form of an Asura, with his hands drawn back and lying supine; during worship, one should meditate upon him as having the face of the Earth, situated within the dwelling and so forth.
With the knees at the northeast (Īśāna), the elbows at the southeast (Agni) and northwest (Vāyu),
one should prostrate with the feet at the southwest (Raudrī) and place the head and hands in añjali at the heart (Hṛdaya).
With palms joined in reverence, holding a sword and shield raised aloft,
they gaze intently at Brahmā, facing his very countenance.
When they are situated in their respective places, it is declared to be the common [arrangement].
Marīci is white in color, and Vivasvat is of a single color.
Mitra is like refined gold, while Bhūdhara is black in color;
Savitṛ has the luster of sapphire blue, and Sāvitra has a body like smoke.
Indra has the luster of the color of dawn, and Indrajaya is likewise white;
Rudra resembles coral, and Rudrajaya is yellow.
Āpa is white as cow’s milk; Āpavatsa has the luster of lightning;
Īśāna is white as milk; Parjanya is like the color of collyrium.
Jayanta resembles a common person, while Mahendra possesses stainless luster;
Āditya is red in color, and Satyaka is variegated in hue.
Vṛṣa has the luster of a bandhūka flower; Antarīkṣaka has the luster of a kunda flower;
Agni has the luster of the rising sun; and Pūṣan resembles one smeared with liquid lac.
Vitatha is like a rainbow; Gṛhakṣata is the color of lightning;
Yama resembles a cloud; and Gandharva is like a ruby.
Bhṛṅgarāja is like a cloud, resembling a bee;
Nirṛti has eyes like fire and is yellow; he is known as Dauvārika.
Sugrīva, Nīlakaṇṭhābha, Candrābha, Puṣpadantaka,
Varuṇa who has the luster of crystal, and Avaroma, who is hairless from the waist down.
The remaining [serpents] are like blue lotuses; Roga is like Indra-nīla (sapphire);
Vāyu is the color of black collyrium; and Nāga is like a conch shell or the moon.
Mukhya is like a pearl; Bhallāṭa is like a white lotus;
Soma is like crystal; and Argala has the luster of a red lotus.
Diti is remembered as white as a jasmine flower or the moon, while Aditi is tawny;
Carakī resembles a conch shell, and Vidārī has the luster of fire.
Pūtanā holds a frost-blossom, Meghābhā holds a pilapicchaka, and [the others hold] a sword, a noose, a vessel, a small knife, and likewise a razor.
Those of terrifying form are proclaimed as the attendants of Tārākṣa;
Skanda and the other planets are white, red, yellow, and black.
Holding a vajra, a spear, a sword, and a noose, and appearing distorted,
these terrifying ones are declared to be the grahas, such as Skanda and the others.
One should likewise perform the fire-oblation (homa) and other rites, offering oblations with their respective materials—
rice, mung beans, barley, honey, clarified butter, and milk— in successive order.
One should offer oblations one hundred and eight times, or twenty-one times each, with those respective substances and likewise with milk-rice (pāyasa) accompanied by the mantras.
And one should offer them an oblation consisting of milk-rice mixed with various side dishes,
combined with sugar, milk, plantains, cakes, and other such items.
The practitioner should first worship Valivadāya,
