and then [worship] that which is provided with food and other offerings, adorned with black gram cakes and the like.
O Brahman, accept this offering and destroy the defects of the site;
it is accompanied by fragrance and other substances, along with sugar, cakes, and milk-rice.
O noble one named Āryaka, accept this and destroy every defect;
O Lord worshipped with sandalwood and other offerings, adorned with camphor and agallochum!
O Vivasvat, please accept this; destroy all defects, O Lord, along with this milk-rice mixed with jaggery and well-endowed with flowers and other offerings.
Accept this pleasing bali offering and grant me peace from my friends;
it consists of black gram rice with meat, combined with perfumes and milk.
"Accept this sovereignty over the earth and destroy all defects.
Having thus worshipped in the center, one should offer the *bali* to Īśāna and the other deities.
O Savitṛ, accept these flowers and other offerings, kusha grass, sugar, and white clarified butter; grant us peace quickly.
O Lord Sūrya, accept this offering of flour-cake with molasses, adorned with red perfumes and other ornaments; quickly destroy all obstacles.
O Lord Śakra, accept this pleasing offering consisting of cooling food, flowers, and saffron and other such substances; salutations to you!
O Indra, accept this delightful oblation—rice mixed with clarified butter and adorned with garments, perfumes, and other offerings; homage be to you, O progenitor.
O Lord Rudra, who is dear to the heart, accept this offering consisting of cooked and uncooked meat, along with cloth, flowers, and other items; I bow to you.
Accept this bali offering, which is level, cooked with ghee, and endowed with fragrant flowers and other ingredients; O Rudra, victory and well-being to you, salutations unto you!
Combined with milk and sugar-candy, adorned with flowers and other offerings—
accept this pleasing bali and grant me peace from calamities.
Accept this offering, O Vatsa, well-prepared with curd, sugar, and perfumes; destroy this obstacle.
Accept this offering of black gram rice with clarified butter, combined with red sandalwood and other perfumes;
protect us from all sides and destroy all obstacles.
Accept this offering (bali) consisting of flowers and other items for a month, accompanied by the monthly meal; O Skanda, destroy the obstacles that cause harm.
O Aryaman, accept this [offering] of one's own flesh mixed with flour-cakes and accompanied by cooked meat and water; destroy all obstacles.
O Jambhaka, accept this food of blood and flesh, accompanied by the fragrance of fish and incense; protect us and destroy all obstacles.
O Pilipiccha, accept this meat provided with goat's ears, along with garments, perfumes, and other offerings; protect us and destroy all obstacles.
This meat, prepared with clarified butter and endowed with garments, perfumes, and other offerings—
accept this, O Cāraṇa, and destroy this obstacle to our protection.
O Vidārī, take this red flower, together with red garments and other offerings;
accept this and destroy the Brahmin who harms us.
O Pūtana, accept this [offering] which is joined with bile, blood, and bone, and adorned with the scent of blood and other things; protect [the child] and destroy all obstacles.
O Lord, remover of the defects of the site (vāstu), accept this bali offering, which is accompanied by ghee, unbroken rice, flowers, garments, perfumes, and other ornaments.
O King of Gods, accept this pleasing offering consisting of blue lotuses joined with milk-rice and accompanied by garments and other gifts; salutations to you!
O son of Tṛṣṇu, accept this five-cubit long, bright yellow banner adorned with a conch and other ornaments; take this pleasing offering; salutations to you!
O King of Gods, accept this pleasing bali-offering—rice porridge filled with ghee and adorned with the five [sensory objects]; homage be to you!
O King of Clouds, accept this pleasing offering consisting of cooked rice mixed with red flowers and endowed with red perfumes and other such offerings; salutations to you!
O Satya, accept this canopy, which has the luster of smoke-colored [saffron], beautifully adorned with perfumes and other offerings, and joined with red [garments]; salutations to you.
This meat, indeed honored with garments, perfumes, and other offerings, is presented;
accept this bull-offering and destroy the defects of the site.
O Śārdūla, accept this tiger-flesh well-joined with offerings and the like; take this pleasing bali and grant me peace from the sky-demon.
O Seven-tongued One, accept this gold, flour-cake, and cloth along with perfumes and other offerings, accompanied by clarified butter; salutations to you!
O Lord Pūṣan, accept this pleasing offering consisting of milk mixed with parched grain and accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and other articles; salutations to you.
O Vitatha, accept this offering of meat-rice accompanied by perfumes and garlands, adorned with garments and other ornaments; destroy the defects of the site.
O King Yama, accept this bali offering consisting of cooked rice mixed with fish and meat, adorned with perfumes, flowers, and other ornaments; grant me peace.
Accept this cooked meat, rice, fresh butter, garments, and other ornaments;
accept this which brings delight, protect the house—homage be to you!
O Gandharva, accept this offering (bali) endowed with various fragrances and accompanied by red incense and other substances; destroy all defects.
Take this crow-like tongue situated upon the bean-eater;
take this king of bees as an offering, and grant me peace.
Thus, [O] Mṛgadeva, accept this pleasing bali-offering, consisting of sesame, ghee, and water, joined with perfumes, flowers, and so forth; homage be to you!
O King of the Rakshasas, accept this offering with joy—this sugar-sweetened morsel adorned with cloth, perfumes, and other ornaments; homage be to you!
Accept this pleasing bali offering, provided with sandalwood, pieces of aguru, garments, perfumes, and so forth; homage to you, O Gatekeeper!
O Lord, O Sugrīva, please accept this milk-rice mixed with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; grant me peace.
O God of Water, accept this pleasing offering of milk prepared with barley-gruel and served upon the meal; salutations to you.
O Puṣpadanta, accept this black-gram rice situated on Kuśa grass and joined with ghee, fragrance, and other offerings; destroy the defects of the site.
O Disease, accept this offering (bali), prepared with honey, ground flour, perfumes, and other ingredients, and adorned with beauty; destroy all my ailments and defects.
O you who ride upon a deer, accept this pleasing offering of ghee and sweetmeats, adorned with Vedic mantras and the like; salutations to you.
But this kṛśara-rice, prepared with the scent of milk and other ingredients, is for me;
O Lord of Pātāla, accept this and quickly destroy my obstacles.
Accept this offering consisting of cooked rice such as coconut and the like, together with yellow garments and other items; O Lord, destroy the primary defects of the site.
May Soma accept this offering, endowed with the fragrance of curd and other substances and accompanied by yellow flowers, and may he destroy all defects.
O Bhallātaka, salutations to you! Accept this pleasing offering of rice mixed with clarified butter and accompanied by fragrant flowers.
O you who are named Argala, accept this delightful offering of black gram cooked with ghee, adorned with perfumes, flowers, and other ornaments; homage be to you!
O Mother of the Gods, accept this pleasing offering consisting of a vessel mixed with honey and endowed with cloth, incense, and other gifts; salutations to you!
O Mother of the Daityas, accept this [offering] combined with milk and sugar-candy, adorned with various forms of worship; destroy all defects.
Whatever gods or deities dwell in heaven, the netherworld, or among mortals,
may they accept this pleasing offering and, being satisfied, return to their own abodes.
May the Mothers, the Bhūtas, the Vetālas, and others who desire the offering, as well as the attendants of Viṣṇu, accept this bali.
Having offered the bali-oblation to the ancestors and the guardians of the field according to one's desire,
one should worship with kuśa grass, flowers, and so forth, in the absence of the prescribed path.
The ritual for the remainder of the site-consecration (*vāstuśeṣa*), which brings about all protection and prosperity and bestows delight upon the spirits (*bhūta*),
is here proclaimed as the *diśābali* (offering to the quarters).

The offering to the quarters (diśāṃ bali) is to be understood as that which is performed by addressing all the spirits of the assembly of the world-protectors (dikpāla) by their names, beginning with worship and ending with the ritual dismissal (visarjana).
Having combined curd, water, turmeric, and sesame oil with parched grain flour,
he should offer an oblation of sugarcane in each direction as he proceeds toward the northeast.
Furthermore, that [power] belongs to the gods, to the radiant ones, to the pretas, and even to the rākṣasas;
it belongs to the goddesses, to the nets, to the vital breaths, and to the constellations.
One should offer those aforementioned oblations to the lords of the sciences (vidyādhipas),
and to their retinues and powers (śaktis) as designated by the term "with vehicle" (savāhana).

Then, having joined [the mantra] with "and to all his attendants," and further with "to the spirits" (bhūtebhyaḥ) in succession, one should cast the bali offering in the eastern direction and so forth.
For those here who desire protection from enemies, piśācas, vetālas, and rākṣasas,
this specific offering of the regions (deśāṃvali) bestows the abundance of all prosperity.
The goddess, having performed various divine rites with an excellent minister,
spread throughout the region by means of the offering of a great *bali*.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Kuchāla with the Astra-mantra;
and once it has been dug up, one should cause even the laborers to be given their wages and other offerings.
One should avoid earth from a place where limbs have been amputated, and likewise one should avoid that which is impure; having immediately extracted clay from the ground, one should worship it.
Two-armed and with a golden body, he is equal to Brahmā, the sustainer of the world;
Viśvakarman holds a mace, the gesture of teaching (jñānamudrā), and a rosary of beads.
O Viśvakarman, you who pervade the universe and are the creator of the world’s manifestation;
here, you hold a pickaxe in your hand—O Viśvakarman, salutations to you!
Break open the eighty-one squares; you whose nature is the activity of Viśva, now perform the digging with the mantra as if it were a spade.
Resorting to an auspicious moment (bhadramuhūrta), the site (vāstu) is excavated within its grid;
in the work of digging the ground, the golden spade takes on the form [of the deity].
Salutations always to Viśvakarman, the weapon, and to the form of Vāstu;
even by those who cause harm with spades or by hundreds of millions of insects.
May the goddess Earth forgive me for the purpose of establishing Viṣṇu; I shall now describe, in due order, the auspicious and inauspicious characteristics of sites.
In the armpit region there is always auspiciousness for one like me everywhere;
however, on the head there would be death, and on the chest, the lot of suffering.
One should know that there is danger from thieves in the hand, the destruction of cattle by a serpent,
travel to a foreign land through the two knees, and fruitlessness through the two feet.
Thus, the site and field are described as being on the left and right;
the practitioner of mantra should skillfully perform that which is auspicious and established in the state of Puṣan.
Having become composed and equanimous, one should dig where the site has been excavated.
Now follows the mantra for dismissal.
Then the Goddess should dismiss the deities who have been worshipped at the site;
for all the hosts of gods, having received this earthly offering, [depart].
O Goddess, this protection of the Vāstuyāga has been described for the sake of accomplishing one's desired wishes and for the purpose of returning once more.
It removes all sins and fulfills all desires;
such is the Vāstuka of the Asuras according to its specific arrangement.
In the eighty-one squares, the northeast and southwest corners form the mandala;
with the head in the northeast and the tail likewise [in the southwest], that site-plan (vāstu) takes the shape of a mandala.
Having worshipped the deities in the [respective] compartments, one should worship Brahmā in the center;
starting from the month of Bhādrapada, for every month, three [deities] each.
And the practice of *digānāmiśamādini* is prescribed;
having known the transition [of the sun] into Virgo and the other signs, O serpents, the sequence of the *digānas* is established.
In Kārttika, the asterism Āśvinī occurs at the beginning of the zodiac signs Libra and Gemini;
in this same sequence, it proceeds through Mārgaśīrṣa and Pauṣa.
He made the month of Māgha consist of Sagittarius, Capricorn, and Aquarius;
and Phālguna and Caitra consisted of Pisces, Aries, and Taurus.
Having understood the sequence ending with Vaiśākha, or the sequence beginning from Paścima and so forth,
[one should know] Karkaṭa in Mithuna, Siṃha in Jyeṣṭha and Āṣāḍha, and [the next] in Śrāvaṇa.
Thus, having awakened to this sequence, there is the transition of the Tathāgatas;
the three months are the commencement, and the four directions are the progression.
He sleeps on his left side; he has two arms and nine hoods;
his limbs extend over one and a quarter *koṣṭhas*; such is the Nāga-vāstu.
The wise man should skillfully cause a pit to be dug at the front of the left neck;
thus are the sites of the serpent determined, especially for water-related works.
Alternatively, once the house has been constructed, one should commence the ritual worship of the site (vāstupūjā);
in the south-western corner of the house, one should prepare an auspicious square-shaped diagram.
Having made the ground level and a ledge one span high,
measuring one cubit in width and length, the wise man should draw [the mandala] there.
The wise man should cause [the grid] to be drawn upon eighty-one squares on pure ground;
then, as before, he should worship the deities of the site (vāstu) with their respective mantras.
Thus, when the sun has entered Leo, on the full moon day each year,
whoever performs the Vāstu-pūjā in his own home or in pavilions, [attains the fruit].
There will be untimely death, disease, and afflictions from spirits, ghosts, and the like;
no suffering from snakes, mutual quarrels, or other inauspicious events.
Possessing abundance of sons, grandsons, wealth, health, cattle, and female slaves, he remains free from disease, victorious, and renowned; he lives for a long time in that house.
Everywhere in the royal palaces, as well as in the residence of the queen, in the houses of the ministers, counselors, and generals, and likewise throughout the city;
The preceptor should perform this every year for the sake of accomplishment;
otherwise, as stated, there will certainly be suffering through results contrary to what was taught.
For the Bhairavas, the Kṣetrapālas, and especially for the Yoginīs,
the bali offering should be performed with those following the left-hand path (vāmācāra), using either buffaloes or cocks.
When propitiated with offerings on the left, the deities become hungry;
they desire the bali offering, and if that is lacking, it destroys the practitioner.
Those who are intoxicated by liquor and meat, though urged by him [the Buddha], may occasionally desire what is auspicious; therefore, they are avoided by the virtuous.
Since their worship is performed near the place where they are slain,
it may or may not bring auspicious results, just as it is taught in the scriptures and observed in the world.
As long as people do not eat liquor and meat, they will not be greedy;
once they have eaten it, their minds will be fixed upon it—where then is recitation, and where are the deities?

He who, through the renunciation of liquor, meat, and so forth, and through the diligent practice of that [path], appears identical in form [to the perfected ones], is a *siddha*; any other, however, is a sinner.
Having examined them in this manner, one should associate even with those who have attained perfection;
however, another who merely associates with such a person is counted as a fifth [type of practitioner] due to that association.
In the form of Time, the song of reckoning was sung before the ordinance of the Gītā-gāthās:
"Through lack of fortitude, the bull [Dharma] perishes in me; through craving, the two [the self and the world] perish."
"The discourse on the elements shall perish in three ways, but total destruction comes from the left.
Having reflected thus, O gods, one's own duty leads to the highest good.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Vāstu Sacrifice," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Having thus performed the rite for pacifying the site (vāstu-śānti) for the sake of discerning what is beneficial and what is harmful,
one should then proceed with the measurement of the day on the leveled ground.
Having taken the thread, the hook, and the peg during the night,
the tube is joined at both ends for the purpose of piercing the fixed star.
Between those two, which run from south to north, one should draw a circle centered on the middle point;
then, within the circle, one should draw a line using a pair of compasses.
One should draw a bow, and from that, another bow;
thus, there are six bows there, and a six-petaled lotus is formed.
Having made three [lines] from north to south and having drawn them through the middle of the squares,
that long line which is thus formed shall be designated as the east-west line.
A thread extending halfway across the two bows situated in the south-west and north-east, as well as those above, shall run from the northeast (Īśānī) to the southwest (Rākṣasī).
In the same way, for the other two [directions], the southern line would become the northern one;
for the lines situated at the intermediate points are indeed equal in their circular form.
Having brought them outside as desired, one should bury stakes there;
a firm thread is fastened upon the heads of the four stakes.
When the measurement from the ear to the corner is equal, it shall be a pure square;
having first worshipped Gaṇeśa, the wise man should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
Then, one should construct an auspicious pavilion with five archways;
for the initiation into the Kula, one should make the pavilion twenty cubits in size.
Just as there is the union of wine, meat, and women,
so too in the Vāmamārga Siddhānta is the pavilion (maṇḍapa) consisting of eighteen parts.
Because the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) there are few, even in the case of the "excessive" fivefold [rite], it is performed with a large collection of Vedic materials;
however, in the nine-pit rite, there are sixteen [officiants].
In the case of a small sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) should have Indra’s hand (one cubit) on the west with a small set of materials,
but Sūrya’s hand (two cubits) on the east with an extensive set of materials.
In the case of those of little means, it should be ten cubits; for Vaiśyas, it should always be nine cubits; for Śūdras, it should be seven cubits, and for Śaṅkaras, five.
The measurement of pavilions, which is concealed in all the tantras, has been declared;
various types of cubits have also been mentioned—now hear their determination.
In whatever country and at whatever time he was born, and according to the measure of barley grains used there,
the finger-breadth (aṅgula) of the twice-born shall consist of eighteen such grains.
For Śūdras, however, it is with those of equal status; likewise for those born of mixed castes (saṃkara) and so forth, it is with those of similar tastes.
For non-Vedic Brāhmaṇas and others, it is with those possessing this same number [of qualities].

Where the agent himself is present, there the means of knowledge is direct; otherwise, it is from another source. Having performed the ritual, [he should place] the middle finger in the middle of the right hand.
The distance between two joints is declared to be one long measure (mātrā) of a finger;
this is the height of the image, while the construction of the temple is to be made according to [the same] proportions.
The measurement for altars, pedestals, palanquins, chariots, and so forth, is determined by that [forefinger] alone;
a fist is formed by the remaining fingers, excluding the thumb.
One should divide [the space] into four parts; one part shall be a fist-length (muṣṭāṅgula).

The implements for the fire-oblation (homa), such as the sruk and sruva ladles, as well as the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the leveled ground (sthaṇḍila), and the altar (vedikā), [are to be placed there].
One should fashion the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) from muñja grass using a fist-width and finger-width measurement;
having divided any given human height into ten parts once again.

Having thus divided [the circumference] into twelve parts, one should fashion a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) for those who perform sacrifices; furthermore, one should know its measurement in finger-breadths as obtained from the body.
By these twenty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas), a cubit (hasta) is formed; furthermore, by this [cubit], the limbs of the image and its proper measurements should be determined.
For both men and women, one should perform this rite, whether in secret or openly;
at ten million oblations (koṭi-homa), it bestows fourteen cubits of prosperity and wealth.
Otherwise, for the *rakṣahoma* (sacrifice to the demons), the pavilion should be twelve cubits square;
having divided it into nine sections, the altar is located in the central portion.
The pillars, however, are situated outside at the corners of the altar-platform at the base of the pavilion;
one should place the fifth [pillar] on the ground according to the thread-measure for their thickness.
One should fashion the shape of a water-pot (kalaśa) on the summit;
the altar (vedi) should be equal in length and height to one-tenth of that, with joints arising from nine compartments.
One should properly place pillars that are one-third the length of the pavilion;
likewise, there should be twelve such pillars on the ground, and one should provide a pinnacle (kūṭa) from a portion of the fifty-fifth part.
One should fashion the pinnacle (kūṭa) situated upon the central pillar as being made of clay and resembling a bull;
twelve rings should be placed outside, above the outer pillars.
In the ritual of Dakṣa-dīkṣā, one should have a lotus-like peak constructed;
in the Vāma-dīkṣā it should have three edges, and in the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice it should be conch-white.
An altar that is square with four corners bestows all fruits;
for the consecration of tanks and similar works, it should resemble the leaf of a lotus.
For kings, there should be the Sarvatobhadra [mandala] during the consecration of the four auspicious ones;
for a wedding, the goddess Śrīdharā, endowed with twenty weapons.
In initiation according to the left-hand path (vāmamārga), the altar (vedikā) should be protected by the weapons-mantra (astra) and others;
the pillars should be placed upon it, being free from wounds and straight.
One should place wooden pieces of a single species as supports for the vidyā-stambha,
and then cover it again with coconut leaves and *vaśaka* mats.
Just as the wind, rain, and so forth may arise from the house, so it is with this.
One should construct four doors for the pavilion in the directions previously established;
the threshold (dehalī) shall indeed measure five parts, and there, the door-posts (kapāṭa) and lintels (vaśākhā) shall be twice as high.
This door is on the left path; in the excellent southern pavilion, one should construct a beautiful threshold measuring two cubits and eight finger-breadths.
Standing at the door, one should place two wooden planks on both sides of the doorway, nine finger-breadths in height from the vitasti-measure, according to the best, middle, or lowest dimensions.
The two bases of the pavilion should be, in order of length, two and a half cubits,
two and a quarter cubits, two cubits, and five parts [of a cubit] upon the ground.
One should bury the fire with the verse "agnim īḷe" in the two side-pits using wood of the same species, making them equal in width and depth.
One should drive stakes into the two uneven corners of the square;
then, according to the ritual procedure itself, one should bind a garland of *darbha* grass at the eastern gate.
Thus, at the southern gate, one should place a garland made from the *plakṣa* wood-box at that gate with the mantra "iṣe tvā," and likewise bind it as previously described.
One should make this [staff] from udumbara wood for the western door;
however, in a Vedic sacrifice, it should be made of plakṣa wood with the mantra beginning with "agneḥ".
In the same manner as before, one should likewise fashion [an image] made of the vaṭa tree;
with the mantra "śanno devī," one should install it from the door on the northern side.
Having made a hole in the middle of the wooden beams situated above and across them, one should fashion a pure enclosure of the same kind as the archway within that chamber.
In the Śaiva sacrifice, the trident— whether superior, middling, or inferior—
is one *viśveśa-gongula* in length and one-fourth of that in width.
In the twelfth part dedicated to Viṣṇu, one who is a Vaiṣṇava, even if he be a Saura, should place the conch, discus, mace,
and lotus in sequence starting from the east.
The central prong is straight, while those on the two sides are slightly curved;
thus is the trident of Gaṇapati, while the [tridents] of Śiva and the others are considered to be like those of Śiva.
Then, in front of that, there should be a pavilion ten cubits high above the ground and two cubits wide at its base; it should be covered with bamboo poles and draped with clean cloth.
The banner should be one cubit wide and five cubits long;
thereupon, one should draw the deity of the mantra, together with his weapons and his vehicle.
Having installed the banner, which is equipped with bells and chowries and adorned with the colors of the deities, one should subsequently arrange it toward the ten directions.
The banners of the lords of the directions shall also be half the measure of the main flag;
they should be of their respective colors and offered in their respective directions with the specific mantras prescribed in the Vedas.
One should bring the yellow-colored [deity] from the eastern direction with the mantra "Trātāram indram";
from the southeast, the tawny-colored [deity] with "Tvaṃ no agne"; and from the west with the mantra "Varuṇa".
The fragrant path in the south was created by Manu and is black in color;
at its end, O Asu, there is a smoke-colored one in the southwest, also created by Manu.
The white-colored [line] in the western direction should be with the mantra "tattvā yāmi brahmaṇā";
and that in the northwestern direction should be yellow with the mantra "ā no miyūdhibhiḥ."

On the Saumya (north) [direction], there is the banner of Candravarṇikā with the mantra "vayaḥ somavrata"; and on the Īśāna (northeast), there is the banner of Ativiśvetā with the mantra "tam īśānam".
Between Īśāna and the East, one should place Śeṣa, who possesses a red banner; and between the West and Nairṛta, one should place Vidhi, who also possesses a red banner.
On the path of the left (vāmamārga), even a Vedic mantra is considered equal to a thunderbolt strike;
for Brahmins, the path of the left leads only to hell.

In the absence of specific mantras, one should recite the hundred names beginning with *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namas*; however, on the path of the right-hand way (*dakṣiṇamārga*), they are recited with *praṇava*, while on the left-hand way (*vāmamārga*), they are devoid of *praṇava*.
One should construct a pavilion with an exceedingly white canopy;
one should adorn it with flower garlands and the like, and encircle it.
Having encircled the pillar with a long garland made from mango and *aśvattha* leaves arranged in a continuous sequence, one should construct an altar in the center.
With unbaked bricks measuring one cubit in width, the mass [of the foundation] for the pavilion should be [constructed];
in the spaces marked by the Rudra-parts, it is established with pillars.
Or, having observed his pride to be elevated by [the possession of] horses,
the pavilion was constructed so that he might experience the full immersion [of devotion] through the completeness of ritual materials and other requisites.
A homa of ten thousand oblations should be performed upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
the pit (kuṇḍa) is prescribed to be one cubit in measure for those up to ten thousand repetitions.
One should increase the measurement by one cubit for every ten hundred thousand oblations;
it is taught that for Vedic altars, the measure reaches ten cubits at ten million oblations.
The offering (homa) of liquor, meat, and so forth is prescribed specifically in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
When the number of oblations reaches fifty, the pit should be made with a fist-sized opening at the level of the forearm.
When [the number] is one hundred, it should be equal to one hundred cubits;
when it is one thousand, it should be one cubit; and for ten thousand, it is considered to be two cubits.

A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring four cubits is prescribed for one hundred thousand oblations, six-petalled for one million, and eight-cubit wide for ten million oblations; these are established by those who know the left-hand path (vāma).
In the procedure for a single pit, however, a square one is prescribed;
this especially applies to Brāhmaṇas, and it is also used for the purpose of paralyzing (staṃbhana) when directed toward the east.
In the ninefold division, however, the portion belonging to Agni is shaped like a vulva;
for the sake of enjoyment or for the sake of sons, it is also [treated] like a square by means of the cord.
Alternatively, for all rites of the Vaiśyas, it should be like a half-moon;
for others, it is declared that four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are desired for the rite of killing.
A triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the southwest is known to cause the destruction of enemies;
it is especially recommended for those who perform acts of inciting hatred and for Śūdras.
The circular (vṛtta) shape is the primary one for all Kṣatriyas in rites of pacification (śāntikarma);
however, that same [shape] performed in the west grants success to Buddhists and Āryas.
A hexagon causes eradication and is especially effective for acts of destruction;
one should construct it in the northwest, particularly for those of mixed caste.
In the north, for rites of nourishment, the lotus bestows rain as well as contentment;
it is considered to bring joy to others through its application in all ritual practices.
An eight-cornered [diagram] is prescribed in the northeast for the sake of granting liberation;
through it, one shall obtain release from prison, as well as from disease and anxiety.
This is the sequence for the rite of eight sacrificial pits; however, in the case of nine pits, the ninth shall be square, located between the eastern and northeastern directions.
In the arrangement of five sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), all five may be situated in the northeast;
however, in the arrangement of equal-sized pits, there should be no excavation or altar outside [the central area].
Another five-cornered [pit] is for the destruction of malevolent magic;
likewise, another seven-cornered one is for the removal of obstacles arising from the sacrificial fire-pit.
Now, first, the procedure for the square fire-pit (kuṇḍa) is described:
the excellent pit is provided with a navel and a womb, and possesses three ridges.
For Śūdras, however, there should be two girdles, while for Śaṅkaras, there should be one girdle;
indeed, the depth of the excavation should be exactly equal to the width of the pit.
Once the desired pit has been prepared here,
one should make it square and even, with well-proportioned corners, provided one possesses the skill of craftsmanship.
For a one-cubit ear, the arms are two cubits;
for a two-cubit ear, the measurement of the arms is three cubits.
In the case of a [stūpa] measuring four cubits and so forth, the neck should likewise be level with the ground everywhere;
its outer moldings (mekhalā) should be made equal to one part of the Jina.
It should be twelve finger-breadths in width and four finger-breadths in height;
above that, the others should be longer, measuring eight finger-breadths in length and four in thickness.
It should be four finger-breadths in height and as much in width; above that,
the *yoni* should be twelve finger-breadths in length and reduced by one-third in its breadth.
It is one finger-breadth high and likewise enters within;
it is joined with two pot-like bases and is considered to be like the leaf of an *aśvattha* tree.
The middle [band] is joined with a girdle of the thumb's width, while the external support is patience;
on the western side of the womb, there is an external triple girdle.

The pedestal should be square, with a width equal to one-sixth of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and likewise its length and height; one should then draw a palm-tree shape (tāla) from the center of that.
Then, in the middle of the *yoni*, a circle is drawn with a measurement equal to one-sixth of the *kuṇḍa*;
this is declared to be the *yoni* of the *kuṇḍas* other than those facing east and southeast, which faces north.
One should avoid the remaining [angles] facing east and the kuṇḍayoni;
however, one should fashion the keṃdra situated in the middle of the kuṇḍa with a karkaṭaka.

The subsequent [circle] should be equal to one-sixth of the span of the extended [radius], which is equivalent to the portion of the sun's rays; however, the previous circle shall be the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
On the tip of the pericarp, there are eight petals within the outer circle;
thus, the navel should be six finger-breadths high, as it is said to be four [finger-breadths] and five [in diameter].
The one-fifth part of the desired square is called the *bhaga*.
One should extend the central line by five and a quarter parts.
Then, one should construct a square divided into four parts in the east;
from the center, one should draw a diagonal line toward the two points situated in the west.
One should drop a thread from the tip of that [mark] toward the exterior directions in the shape of a half-bow; at that time, it will likewise form two horse-heads (hayas) up to the end of the mark.

The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should resemble the leaf of the Aśvattha tree and face north; here, the lines of measurement should be drawn facing east, and the altar should be shaped like a womb with beautiful girdles.
The wise one, an expert in the system, should divide the square field into ten parts and omit one part each at the bottom and at the top.
One should drop the bowstring in front and then bend it back from that measure;
thus this beautiful pit (kuṇḍa), resembling a half-moon, shall come into being.
In this case, one [digit] from the south-facing [number] is for that purpose, and another for its killing;
the north-facing [number] is for something else, while the womb is directed toward the western direction.
The tip should be made on the eastern arm; all three [lines] should be equal in length.
In all the Tantras, it is taught that there is a space between them, whereas the petals are without interval.
In a one-cubit [structure], there are twelve arms starting from one cubit;
in a two-cubit [structure], three times two; and in a three-cubit [structure], five times three and six earths.

In a circle of three cubits, the Moon [is the first]; in one of five cubits, the remaining signs; in one of six cubits, the planets; and in one of eight cubits, the constellations. In one of nine cubits, the forms [of the deities]; and in one of four cubits, the oceans.
The earth was fashioned by the eight hands of Viśvakarman through the application of yoga;
these [beings] possess ten hands and arms, and they know the Vedas, the Dhṛtis, and the pairs [of meters].
The semi-diameter of a square [altar] increased by its own eighteenth part;
a circle drawn from that point with a compass is here called a circular *kuṇḍa*.
One should draw a circle, as beautiful as possible, with a radius equal to half the diagonal of a square increased by one-eighth of that diagonal.
One should also perform this with a compass (karkaṭaka).
Having marked six points there according to that same *karkaṭa*-measure as before,
and having assigned the arms [of the triangle] therein, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is thus hexagonal.
Having made a division into twenty-four parts of the desired square,
one should [mark] from its center with a compass according to the solar orbit.
One should again draw a circle with a radius equal to one and a half lunar-day parts;
then, one should cast eight threads at the cardinal and intermediate directions and their intervening spaces.
Then, from the northeast point of the inner circle, the thread at the tip of the cord should be led along the line to the top of the eastern thread on the outer circle.
Then, from the top of the inner circle on the southern line, one should draw that [line] to the petal;
in this manner, the eight petals are formed.
The pericarp (karṇikā) is that which is formed by a circle measuring one and a half parts;
then, the filaments (keśarāṇi) are formed by a circle measuring six parts and one and a half.
O Vyāsa, one should carve the six petals, the pericarp, and the filaments,
and arrange them according to the method taught by the Guru, so that they take the form of a lotus.
One should fashion it in the shape of a lotus together with a neck-band and a girdle;
it should be made beautiful with [ornaments] such that it is perfectly square.
Now, for a desired square, the diagonal increased by its own twelfth part is used;
with that very length, one should draw a circle and mark points in the eight directions.
One should place [the lines] in sequence and provide arms above that;
it becomes an eight-sided (*aṣṭāsra*) pit, and likewise its neck and girdle (*mekhalā*).
For the desired square, [the side] increased by one-seventh of its own semi-diagonal;
from that semi-diagonal, it [the square] arises. Therein, however, there are five marks.
The lines should be laid out in equal proportions;
with the form of a bowstring and the omission of the arc, the pit (kuṇḍa) becomes five-cornered.
One should take half the diameter of the desired square, add a fifth part of that, and rotate it; by means of that, one should mark out a circle with seven divisions.
These are known as *kuṇḍas* for both Tantric and Smārta rites;
they are said in the Śruti to be "not excessive" (*anādhika*) and "without necks" (*akaṇṭha*), and are designated as "of non-womb origin" (*viyoni*).
The preceptor’s pit is the ninth, square-shaped on the altar;
however, in the case of an inability [to construct all nine], there are four pits in the cardinal directions according to the Tantra.
If one is unable to do that, one should construct only a single square;
or, for worship according to one's capacity, a single Yoni-shaped pit on the north side.
If a sacrificial pit possesses the fault of being uneven or its measurement is deficient or excessive,
then this must be properly examined by one desiring auspiciousness before it is constructed.
If the pit is too deep, there will be disease; if it is too shallow, there is loss of cattle and wealth.
In the case of a circular pit (cakrakuṇḍa), there is suffering; if the boundary line (mekhalā) is broken, death occurs.
In the absence of a girdle (mekhalā), there is grief as well as an excessive loss of wealth;
a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) made without a proper womb (yoni) is said to cause the destruction of one's wife.
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) that is devoid of its neck is said to cause the destruction of one's offspring;
likewise, a pit that lacks ornamentation and has frayed boundary lines (mekhalā) is defective.
Exorcism performed on a crystal leads to the destruction of the patron;
if there is an excess of threads, it causes heartache, and if it is devoid of threads, it results in poverty.
If there is no fire in the hearth, there is disease; if there is a crack in the hearth, there is infamy;
and even if the hearth is as described, if portents arise, the result is as follows.
The five girdles should measure six, four, three, two, and one [finger-breadths] respectively;
this applies whether there is a difference in dharma or a difference in caste between the preceptor and the sacrificer.
The two girdles are considered to be one-sixth and one-eighth [of the height] respectively,
in the Kaulika, Vāmamārga, Buddhist, Jaina, and Śavara traditions.
The characteristics of the sacrificial pits have been declared; next, the characteristics of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles shall be described.
One should fashion the *sruva* according to the method that will be explained in the course of the ritual application.
One may have it fashioned from *kālaskara* wood, or from *āmalakī*, or even from *śākharadira*;
or one may have it made of gold, silver, copper, or even iron.

The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles should be made of metal and not of brass or lead; they may also be made of sacrificial wood (*yajñadāru*) or according to the specifications of the *Tantras*, as approved by skilled artisans.
On a leaf of a tree such as the *brahmavṛkṣa*, which is unblemished, elevated in its center, and broad;
or on a leaf of the *dhīparṇī*, *siṃsapā*, *akṣī*, or *kṣīra* trees—the Guru [should perform the rite] upon one of these.
Having taken [the cord], one should divide it by thirty-six cubits;
with twenty parts there shall be the staff, and with eight [parts] the Vedic [altar].
The neck is measured as one part, and the mouth is considered to be seven parts;
the width of the pedestal (vedī) is proclaimed to be three parts of the neck.
In this regard, the throat should be level;
one should fashion the opening at the mouth according to the measure of the little finger, for the purpose of the exit of the clarified butter.
In the center of the altar, a pericarp should be fashioned with one part;
then, surrounding it with one part, one should fashion a pit on all sides.
Its circumference is declared to be divided into three parts;
outside of half a part, one should arrange the petals all around using one part.
The girdle (mekhalā) should be at the front altar (mukhavedī), measured from the center of the nave;
at the base and tip of the staff (daṇḍa), there should be two jars (kuṃbha), each measuring three and two finger-breadths (aṅgula) respectively.
The pair of staffs (daṇḍīyuga) shall consist of one-eighth parts; this is declared to be the girth (anāha) of the staff.
The back portion shall consist of six parts, and it should be shaped like a tortoise (kūrma).
One should draw the mantra on the back of the face of either a swan, an elephant, or a boar; this is declared to be the characteristic of a fine needle.
The *sruk* and *sruva* ladles for all Saumya rites should be made of gold;
these two should be made of iron for rites such as *stambhana*.
In the absence of that, the oblation is offered with two leaves of the *palāśa* tree;
a flawless and beautiful *palāśa* leaf is considered suitable for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
Or one should perform the rite of oblation using a small leaf of the *aśvattha* tree when the ritual is concise.
Now, the characteristics of the *sruva* ladle:
one should fashion the *sruva* from twenty-four parts of the *sruk* ladle;
its handle measurement is declared to be twenty-two parts.
With four parts, the head is drawn out with armor;
with two parts, the neck is bent, and in one part, it has the shape of a deer's foot.
The gaṇḍī should be at the base and tip of the staff and adorned with bracelets;
thus has the procedure for the sruva ladle been declared in this scripture known as the Mantra[-tantra].
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Pit for Animals and Others," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Now follows the ritual of offering the seed-sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa).
During the installation, the initiation, the ceremonial bath, and likewise during festivals;
for the purpose of pacification during consecration, marriage, and the tying of the sacred thread.
In all auspicious rites, one should perform the ritual offering of the *kūra*; and for installations and similar ceremonies, it should be done on the seventh or ninth day prior to the main event.
On the fifth, the third, or immediately,
the preceptor, together with the Brahmins, shall perform the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-ghoṣaṇa*) and the offering of the sprouts of speech (*vācāṃkura*).
This rite of sowing the seed, which grants all desires, must be performed;
in the northern part of the pavilion, one should construct a hall extending from east to west.
The experts should construct that pavilion extending from east to west and from north to south;
it is prescribed for the northern initiation.
On ground smeared with cow dung, one should worship on the right and left [sides] with sesame and rice,
and indeed with sesame and the liquid of *vijayā*.
There, five lines should be drawn, each five cubits long; likewise, five long Rudra-lines should be drawn at intervals of one span (vitasti).
There should be forty-four squares; with twenty-four squares, there shall be a pathway for the Brāhmaṇas, which one should fill with red powders.
Afterwards, the group of four squares is declared to be the abode of Brahmā;
one should fill it starting from the southeast square and ending in the northeast.
One should fill two squares and the pathway with yellow, red, white, black, and blue powders according to the path of emanation, and likewise fill [the remaining area] with red powder alone.
In front of that, however, the four squares should be known as the station of Viṣṇu;
it is to be filled with dust as before, and in front of that there is also a pathway (vīthikā).
That which is called the "four-square" (koṣṭhacatuṣka) is declared to be the location of the door;
it should be filled with reddish colors as before, and all the lines [should be drawn].
The four *pālikās*, dedicated to Viṣṇu as their deity, should be made in the shape of hand-drums (*āḍamaruka*), measuring one cubit in width, height, and length.
Adorned with dūrvā grass, mango sprouts, and aśvattha leaves, and wrapped with a thread, one should place Viṣṇu in the four corners of the site.
One should install those five-faced Vairavyas made of wood, sixteen finger-breadths in height, width, and length, facing the directions.
In the Brahma-position, fresh leaves and other items are joined with threads as previously described;
they say there are three kinds of vessels for the rite of offering the *kuru* fruit.
The *pālikās*, the five-faced [liṅgas], and the four shallow bowls (*śarāvas*) are said in sequence by those who know all truths to be of the nature of Hari, Brahmā, and Śiva.
Among these, the height of the jewel [stūpa] is sixteen, twelve,
and eight finger-breadths respectively; those auspicious [structures] should be encircled with a thread.
Having washed those places where rice has been placed,
the preceptor should deposit [the vessels] starting from the west upon fragrant *darbha* grass and flowers.
The circumference of the rim is said to be sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
its neck-opening should be eight finger-breadths wide.
The width of the footstool (padepīṭha) is declared to be six aṅgulas;
its height is four aṅgulas, and its joint should be one aṅgula.
The navel should be at the junction of those [sections], and the pedestal should be half a square;
this five-faced *ghaṭikā* indeed grants all desires.
They say that there are five faces, each four finger-breadths in width:
four in the four directions and one above, according to the rule.
The width of the *ghaṭikā* is said to be twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*);
some teachers state that it is said to be sixteen finger-breadths.
Some teachers say that the mouth of the śarāva is remembered as being sixteen aṅgulas long and twelve aṅgulas wide.
Its base is said to be four finger-breadths in width;
it may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay.
One should place four hundred Śiva-vessels among them,
arranging them individually within the four [corners] from the southeast (vahni) to the northeast (īśāna).
One should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva in those vessels previously mentioned;
one should honor them in earthen bowls with sandalwood paste and flowers.
One should fill the vessels with clay, sand, and dried cow-dung, and place Viṣṇu in the *pālikās* and Brahmā in the *ghaṭikās*.
And after Brahmā and the others have worshipped the spade on another day,
accompanied by song and dance, and attended by elephants and horses;
Then some mounted on elephants, while others mounted on horses;
having gone to the bank of a pond or a river, or to a flower in the forest—
There, having strewn a pure portion of ground with *darbha* grass or with cloth,
and having sprinkled it with water from the *arghya* vessel while recollecting the respective mantra;
Having invoked the Earth with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers;
then, with the *kuddālī* mantra, one should take up the earth from the ground using a spade.
Having taken it with the Vāmadeva mantra, one should pour it into a bronze vessel;
having cleansed the mud from the heart [of the image] and covered it with a cloth, one should preserve it.
Then, having performed a circumambulation of the city or the residence with the sounds of all auspicious instruments, the preceptor should lead [the image] to the pavilion.
A wise person should perform this rite during the daytime and not at night;
thereafter, one should sow ten seeds in a vessel made of gold or other precious materials.
The practitioner of mantra should then recite the seed-syllable *vaṃ* and wash [the image] with milk.
These are the grains: priyaṅgu, guñjā, māṣa, tila, śarṣapa, and śālī.
Muñja grass, āḍhakī, suriṣya, or khalva-māṣa beans are prescribed;
these should be consecrated with the root mantra, preceded by the five sounds.
Preceded by auspicious customs and the benedictory words of the twice-born,
the preceptor, with a disciplined mind, offers oblations into the three fires.
Facing either east or west,
one should sow all the seeds with their primary roots first, starting from the *pālikā* vessels and proceeding in due order.
Soma is the lord of seeds;
therefore, one should offer [the oblation] at night, because he is radiant at night for the sake of the seeds and the deities.
Therefore, the preceptor should sow the seeds only at night:
*skanda* in *priyaṅgu*, *niṣpāva* in wind, and *kulattha* in fire.
One should worship Nirṛti in the Āḍhakī plant, Soma in the Muṅga bean, Svadhi in the sesame seed, Prajāpati in the Śāli rice grain, and Ananta in the mustard seed.

One should worship Indra during the dark fortnight (Śyāma-māsa), and Varuṇa during the month of Māgha; however, O Daughter of the Mountain, one should always worship the son of Soma (Soma) for at least one day.
When the day of the formal acceptance (adhivāsa) has arrived, the preceptor should perform the ritual dismissal of Soma with the mantras:
"To Tryambaka, to Śarva, to Śaṅkara, and to Śiva."
"Salutations again and again to the eternal one, the foremost in all the worlds.
Having scattered [the offering] with this mantra, [mixed] with turmeric powder—
The preceptor should cause water to rain down upon them, sprinkling them with water every day;
having removed the turmeric, he should cover them with cloths.
One should cast the offering (bali) for the three types of vessels into the directions starting from the east,
using the syllable Om at the beginning, followed by the names of the Mothers and the Lords of Night (Rātrīśas).
The spirits, ancestors, yakṣas, nāgas, Brahmā, Śiva,
and Hari— [all these] have properly entered the three vessels by means of the path instructed by the guru.
For nine days, one should offer the bali-oblation intended for each respective deity;
one should also present the bali at both twilights and at midnight.
On the first day, rice, sesame seeds, parched grain,
and roasted flour mixed with turmeric powder— this is considered the offering for the spirits (bhūtas).
Thus, on the second day, [offerings] of sesame and rice are for the ancestors;
on the third day, parched grain flour mixed with barley and curd is for the yakṣas.
One should joyfully offer parched grain flour soaked in coconut water as a gift to the Nāgas, and present an offering of flowers and unbroken rice to Brahmā on the fifth day.
On the sixth day, rice mixed with non-putrid substances is recommended for Śiva;
on the seventh day, one should offer rice cooked with jaggery to Viṣṇu.
The offering of boiled rice (*odana*) is prescribed for Viṣṇu alone on the eighth day and subsequent days;
however, on the ninth day, rice mixed with sesame (*kṛśarānna*) is especially recommended for Viṣṇu.
On the left-hand path (vāmamārga), one should offer oblations to that mantra in the four directions;
however, at the station of Brahmā, liquor is the oblation for the Vetāla and the ram.
In the place of Viṣṇu, Bhairavī should be present, and a goat is considered her sacrificial offering (bali).
But Bhairava, in the place of Śiva, desires a buffalo as his offering.
Gauḍī, Mādhvī, and Yaṣṭī are considered to be the types of liquor there, in that order.
Wine, meat, and offerings mixed with wine are prescribed as oblations for the spirits (bhūtas).
To the ancestors, an offering of meat with liquor; to the yakṣas, a cock and honey;
to the nāgas, a frog and a lizard-offering; these are the offerings on the left-hand path.
When nine days have passed in this manner, one should examine [the sprouts];
one should never look at the sprouts when they have already grown.
Either the preceptor himself or his disciple, by his command, should enter;
for the sake of the prosperity of the sacrificer, he should examine the sprouts.
Has its emergence occurred correctly, or what has been lost in the middle?
If the emergence is perfectly complete, there is success; if it is sluggish, one will encounter obstacles.
If another fruit is eaten by insects or makes a sound, it portends total destruction; likewise, those that are smoke-colored, incomplete, or have fallen to the level of animals [are inauspicious].
One should avoid those that are dark, humpbacked, and inauspicious;
a black cloud brings about drought, while one with the appearance of smoke likewise causes strife.
There will be incomplete births and deaths, famine, and a land filled with dark-skinned people;
in the Tiryag-jāti there will be disease, and in the Kubja there will be fear of enemies.
If one is born into an inauspicious family, one should perform a peace-offering (śāntihoma);
one should offer oblations with the root mantra (mūlamantra) together with those who embody the form of the Guru.
With the Aghora-weapon and the Astra-weapon, one hundred or even a thousand times,
[he should strike] those which have previously grown properly, being tender and white.

Success is to be known through *priyaṅgu* flowers; through *śyāmāka* grains, there will be happiness from women; through sesame seeds, there is delight among those worthy of worship; and with mustard seeds, there is malevolent sorcery (*abhicāra*).
If there is a preponderance of *śāli* rice, there will be honor from all; if there is *mudga* or *māṣa*, there will be compassion.
If there is *āḍhakī*, *niṣpāva*, or *kṣetra* in the field or the house, there will be four-footed livestock.
Through the *khalva* [planets], there is the accomplishment of virtuous deeds; through the *māsa* [planets], there is peace from enemies.
Through all the planets risen in the left [hemisphere], there is success; otherwise, there is a fall.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Offering of Sprouts," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Now, out of a desire for the welfare of practitioners, I shall describe the procedure for initiation (dīkṣā),
since without it the fruit of all mantras cannot be obtained.
It is taught to be fourfold, according to the divisions beginning with Kriyāvatī:
Kriyāvatī, Varṇamayī, Kalātmā, and Aveśamayī.
Among those, the ritualistic initiation (kriyāvatī-dīkṣā) is not described here at length.
On the day prior to the conferral of initiation, having performed the morning duties, [the following should be done].

Having adorned one's own body, one should perform worship in one's own home according to the ritual procedure for Gaṇeśa; thereafter, one should have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha-vācana) recited.
Having offered libations to the Nāndīmukha ancestors accompanied by the five musical instruments, and having prepared the materials as prescribed, he should proceed toward the house of the preceptor.
The selection of the preceptor and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), as well as the ritual preparations, are ten cubits from here;
these [seats] made of *śrīparṇī* wood are one cubit in height and measure.
They are twenty-seven blades of *darbha* grass, each eight finger-breadths in height and equal in size, with their tips bound together by a knot.
The characteristics for all sacrifices have been fully proclaimed regarding the seats;
for the purpose of water for the feet, there should be copper jars filled with pleasantly warm water.
Conch shells, filled with water, fragrance, and flowers for the offering of *arghya*,
along with water-pots of fine copper filled with water for the ritual sipping (*ācamana*).
Along with those, there should be bronze vessels filled with curds and other items for the sake of honeyed cooked offerings,
as well as costly garments and fine ornaments such as finger-rings.
One should collect peacock-feather umbrellas and turbans;
there, one should also fetch sandals adorned with leather ornaments.
Having performed this, one obtains a fruit equal to the honor paid at a great sacrifice;
the honoring of other Brahmins with the madhuparka is thus prescribed.
One who is possessed of great devotion should give double that amount to the preceptor with sincere devotion;
for where the worship of the teacher is performed together with other twice-born brahmins, [the merit is manifold].
In that [case], the fruit of the sacrifice is very small, just as the yield of the earth is meager during a drought;
likewise, having gone to the teacher’s house and bowed to the teacher’s sandals—

Having provided the materials for the formal offering and having made the formal resolve, that best of the twice-born should choose a guru by reciting: "For the purpose of receiving such-and-such mantra."

"Because of his status as a guru, he is worthy of being addressed with respect; therefore, I choose him. Having said this, the disciple should choose [the teacher], and then the teacher should say, "I am chosen."
The disciple should say, "Perform the service for the guru as is appropriate," and having uttered,
"I shall do so," he should then call out to the guru alone.
One should select eight Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
as well as those who worship the deity of that [sacrifice], or alternatively, when acting through a single officiating priest (ṛtvij).
Then four sacrificial pits are prescribed, and four officiating priests are appointed;
thereafter, the preceptor, accompanied by his disciple, should proceed to the sacrificial hall.
Having sat down at its door, the Guru himself should then begin the examination with a tooth-stick produced from a milk-tree or similar source.
Alternatively, one should give a tooth-stick made from a mango tree measuring twelve finger-breadths in length to the disciple, having consecrated it with the root mantra.
Having cleansed his teeth, he should stand before a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit;
then the Guru should cause him to cast [the flower] and examine him.
Regarding that which is situated in the cardinal directions, this is the result starting from the east:
prosperity, heartache, destruction of kinsmen, and likewise death.
Sorrow, agitation, happiness, and the attainment of knowledge are the results in successive order;
if it falls upon an inauspicious place, one should perform an expiation.
Either one thousand and eight, or one hundred and twenty,
[recitations] should be performed with their names enclosed by the weapon-mantra (astra) and suffixed with *svāhā*.
One should offer oblations with clarified butter alone, reciting the mantra "Doṣā jahīhi jahīhi," which concludes with the name [of the deity], in the case of a bad dream as well.
The tooth-stick should be given again; if it is defective, it should be fourfold [in length].
If it is defective even for the third time, that deity must not be accepted.
On the left-hand path, even once, [the practice] may destroy both the teacher and the disciple.
Now he speaks of the examination of dreams:
"Thereafter, one should perform the examination of dreams; its procedure is stated [as follows]:
for those of the Vedika, the Dakṣiṇa, the Vaiṣṇava, and the Vāma [traditions]."
While awake, he should recite three times these mantras dedicated to the divine Mother;
eating but once during the day and sleeping on his right side, he should examine his dreams according to the instructions.
Having relied upon the dream-mantra, one should sleep with the head toward the east;
likewise, householders should be protected by sleeping on beds of *darbha* grass with their heads facing east.
With his heart [focused], he should cause the disciple to dwell [in the preliminary rite] on a bed of pure ashes, with his head toward the south,
on the southern side of the deity.
On a clean bed spread with an unwashed coverlet and strewn with *darbha* grass, he, being pure,
should lie down at night with his head toward the east, reciting mantras and meditating on Śiva.
The Guru, having tied the thread to the crest-lock with a silken cord,
should wrap it around [the disciple] with a new cloth and cover him with the armor-mantra.

Having drawn three lines all around with ashes, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds consecrated by the recitation of the Astra-mantra, one should offer oblations to the guardians of the directions outside of that area.
Having performed the worship of the Guru’s feet, fasting and with senses subdued, he should go to a bed of *darbha* grass at night; having seen a dream, he should report it.
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, wielder of the trident, whose vehicle is the bull:
please now explain the auspicious and inauspicious [signs] in the dream of one who has fallen asleep.
At the end of the night, he sees a dream, whether auspicious or inauspicious:
"Oṃ! To Viṣṇu, the sovereign lord of all the worlds, who possesses a heart [of compassion]..."
Salutation to Viśva, the one of universal form, the lord of dreams;
this is the mantra for the Manava of the dream state, [to be recited by one] who has fasted and subdued his senses.
Having gone to a bed of darbha grass at night, he should see a dream exactly as it will be;
having eaten, he should lie down on a very pure bed upon the surface of the earth.
Rising at midnight, having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should remember the Lord and worship Him with the fivefold offerings.
Contemplating the identity of Śiva and the deity, one should mutter this:
"Obeisance to the one born from the lotus, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul."
Salutation to Vāma, who possesses all forms and is the lord of dreams;
may you always relate to me in my dreams every undertaking in its entirety.
A dream occurring in the first watch [of the night] will bear fruit within one year;
one arising in the second watch, in six months; and one from the third watch, in three months.
If, however, within only four months at the time of dawn,
there is quickly a web of anxiety and illness accompanied by long sighs, that fruit does not exist at all.
From a predominance of wind (vāta), there occurs sleep preceded by rashness and leaping;
from the paternal element, there arises fire, heat, yellow and red colors, as well as anger and the like.
One who has been afflicted by Vāta should be made to lie down on a bed and so forth that is directed [toward the wind];
in the morning, there is aching of the limbs from Vāta, while from Pitta there is burning in the eyes.
Out of delusion (kapha), one constantly pursues two by two; why not pursue all three?
Or one may worship one's own guru as a deity, or a maiden who is gracious.
The Gaṅgā, the Gaṅgā, Bhāratī, Bhānu, the wearer of the linga, the Īśvara-linga,
the parasol, the umbrella, the chariot, the lamp, the temple, the lotus, and the river.
An elephant, a bull, a garland, the ocean, a tree laden with fruit,
a mountain, a blazing fire, and divine liquor— these I beheld in my dream.
From the planet [Saturn], one obtains the sun, the sun-gem, and various ornaments;
as well as a lion-throne, a celestial chariot, a banner, and royal consecration.
White sandalwood, garments, śāli rice, saffron, honey, parched grain, white mustard seeds, women, new vessels, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
A horse, fruits, prepared food, curds, a courtesan, milk, musical instruments, a blue jay, a peacock, a noble family, and clay.
An elephant, a single animal, a flower, a virtuous person, a word, sugarcane,
collyrium, a full pitcher, a mirror, a fish, clarified butter, and yellow pigment.
The *Śaṃvara*, the *Udanahīna*, weapons, banners,
Bhāradvāja, kings, the sound of the Vedas, and singing;
Having seen these in a dream— the whip, auspicious songs, and the goad which is dear to the heart— the practitioner shall attain success.
There is no suffering from the affliction of disease, and one shall attain ordinary happiness;
when, during auspicious rites, one sees a woman in dreams.
The river Sindhu, desiring [to reach] the crossing, underwent wandering;
likewise, there was the rising of the sun and the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
Ascending a palace, a temple, a bull, a mountain, or fire;
eating curd-rice and consuming cooked meat.
Anointing with worms and excrement, sprinkling with blood,
chewing betel, drinking liquor, and [eating] curd, milk, and sandalwood.

A fierce, clear ray of light is a sign of the accomplishment of one's purpose; likewise, a woman who is dark-complexioned, wearing fine garments, and anointed with black perfumes and unguents [is a favorable omen].
If she embraces him in a dream during the final watch of the night,
he will suffer from disease through a red woman, and grief through one who is reddish-brown.
Whatever [is done] by a woman who is divided, quarrelsome, addicted to killing, and fickle— [if she is] wearing white garments, with white garlands and unguents.
In his dreams, the goddess Śrī Sarvatomukhī embraces him—
whether he is on a seat, in a bed, in a vehicle, in water, in a boat, or in a house.
If he awakens while it is blazing, his fortune will be all-pervading;
if the bite of a white serpent occurs on his right hand.
Within ten days there will be gain; one who is ill is freed from disease;
or else, one may be bound by fetters or the noose of the arms, or a son shall be born.
By drinking milk, his status increases, yet there is a loss of wealth;
by drinking liquor and blood, a Brāhmaṇa may obtain knowledge, while another obtains great wealth.

Upon seeing curd, there shall be joy; with wheat, the arrival of wealth; one should know that with *siddhārthaka* (white mustard seeds), there is the attainment of desired knowledge and likewise profit.
The acquisition of curd brings wealth; from the acquisition of ghee, certain victory follows.
From sitting upon ghee comes the distress of losing wealth, whereas eating curd brings victory.
Upon seeing the worship of the *liṅga* and other [deities], one shall achieve victory in worldly affairs;
furthermore, he who eats ghee and milk-rice in the midst of a lake or similar body of water [shall likewise succeed].
One should know that a king who possesses a steady lotus-mark on his palm is a lord of the earth;
likewise, cows, ancestors, Brahmins, and kings are all bearers of divine signs.
Whatever he says to a man in a dream will happen exactly so;
likewise, he who should encircle a village or a city with weapons.
In a village there shall be a kingdom of circles, and in a city one shall become a sovereign;
there shall also be the swallowing of the moon, stars, and sun, as well as thorough searching.
The swallowing of the earth by the wise, the act of slaying enemies,
victory in marriages and gambling, and likewise victory over foes.
Milk may be drawn from a mare, a buffalo, a lioness, a cow, or an elephant;
likewise, a favor from a preceptor, from the best of Brahmins, or from gods, Siddhas, and others, is auspicious.
Bathing, royal consecration, the death resulting from the severing of one's own head,
crossing over waters at sacred fords (tīrtha), and likewise the swallowing of poison;
The birth of cattle, horses, or mares; fire, and likewise a mirage;
embracing another's wife, and weeping when she is not obtained.
Anointing with *viṣṭā* (feces), beholding the *kunda*, *jātī*, *vakuḷa*, and *kṣeśa* flowers,
and being bound in fetters during the clash of flashing lightning— these bring victory.
The acquisition of cattle, mortals, and wild animals, as well as mastery over them; the appearance of a crest, the wearing of white garments, and the application of flowers and sandalwood paste.
When one sees food in a vessel made of jewels, palm leaves, gold, or other such materials, then it should be known that success has become established for the practitioner.
For those distressed by their affairs, there is the accomplishment of their business; for those burdened by debt, the arrival of wealth.
A barren woman [gives birth], and armor, frost, fire, snakes, salt, charcoal, and fuel [become effective].

One who is a parasite, a eunuch, a madman, one who has not bathed, one with matted hair, or one afflicted by disease; likewise, a mendicant, one smeared with oil, or one tormented by hunger [should not be approached].
A person with disheveled hair, skin or blood smeared all over,
a lizard, a sneeze, a fight between two cats, cotton, a pregnant woman, and a menstruating woman [are inauspicious omens].
A jujube fruit and buttermilk were found by the one clad in ochre robes in a muddy pit at the house of Kali; likewise, the blood of a goat and other animals was found in the dwelling of Lulapa.
A blind man, a hunchback, one of foul speech, a deaf person, one with a lame foot, one with a protruding belly, one who vomits, a pot-bellied woman, a washerwoman, and a woman in soiled garments.
If these are seen, no purpose will be achieved, and one will meet with death;
likewise, if an Ashoka, a Karavira, or even a Palasha tree is in bloom.
Even in a dream, having seen water, a man may experience grief;
likewise, there is entry into another form and travel toward the southern direction.
Bathing in mud is an immersion that brings about the destruction of one's sons and wife;
it is auspicious only when performed by Kṛṣṇa, excluding cows, elephants, and the twice-born Brahmins.
One who wears red perfumes and garments, is adorned with garlands, has black sacrificial offerings,
or rides upon a donkey, a camel, or a buffalo, shall not live for three months.
Whether he falls into a chasm, or his house collapses, or his door is not provided [with a bolt],
he who does not rise from that state— his life ends there.
He who sees in a dream excrement, urine, feces, a continuous lineage, birth, death, or semen, has a lifespan of only ten months.
He is beaten by deformed black men with uplifted weapons, and he is also struck with stones; his death is certain, there is no doubt.
He who sets out toward the southern direction mounted upon a buffalo, a camel, or a donkey, smeared with those [substances], and shaven-headed, will undoubtedly meet his death.
One may see the collapse of palaces and houses, as well as the falling of the moon and sun;
there shall also be the downfall of those in positions of authority over mountains and trees.
Furthermore, there is the wasting away of one's own limbs and being overcome by disease;
likewise, the sweeping of the house and its smearing with cow dung or even with clay.
Having arrived at the river Tīrthānadī and put on another garment on its bank,
a sick person shall be freed from disease, while for one who is healthy, a loss occurs.
Male-named deer and birds, a female monkey, a sow, a female rat, a female mongoose, a female chuchuka, a female palli, a female cuckoo, and a female jackal— these are auspicious.
The animals and birds bearing female names— such as the śrīkaṇṭha, ayābhara, ururu, chikara, pippala, and bhāsa— are auspicious on the right side, as are the crow, the hyena, and the dog.

If sick people are seen, there will be the destruction of disease; if practitioners are seen, there will be success. For one who is healthy, there is gain from exertion; however, it is not auspicious due to a change of direction.
Now, regarding suffering and its pacification:
having fasted for three nights and subsisted on sacrificial food (haviṣya),
the domestic priest shall burn one hundred fuel-sticks that are smeared with ghee and accompanied by milk.
A Śūdra, having bathed with palāśa leaves while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra and eating sacrificial food (haviṣya),
should offer a lamp at the house of a Brāhmaṇa, in the temple of Viṣṇu, or in a shrine of Śiva.
Having seen such an auspicious dream, one should accept it with the approval of the mantra;
otherwise, if it is accepted [without this], there will surely be loss, or one should contemplate another deity.
Now, regarding the reporting of the dream:
the disciple, being pure and having sipped water for purification, with flowers in hand and a joyful heart, should bow his head to the supreme guru and report the dream to him.

If one suddenly sees during the day something that was either seen in a dream or perceived directly before the eyes— an object that causes wonder or great joy— that should not be told to anyone except the Guru.
If a dream results in fruitlessness due to sleep, the dream must be spoken of; otherwise, it need not be. Having reflected thus, the preceptor should then perform the worship.
Having fixed the mind there and having prepared the general offering (sāmānyārghya),
one should sprinkle [the area] with the offering water and perform the worship of the door.
Then the preceptor, by means of divine vision, shall gradually dispel the obstacles situated in the intermediate space with water consecrated by mantras.
Having diligently driven away the kings with three blows of his heels,
slightly contracting his body and touching a branch extending to the left;
Having dismissed the Brahmins, he should give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) while reciting the *Vanavada* hymn;
then he should worship Brahmā as the presiding lord in the southwestern direction (nairṛtī).
When the places where [the materials] were kept have been sprinkled with water fit for libations and with cow’s urine,
one should then perform the purification of the four doors through the rites beginning with inspection (vīkṣaṇa).
Having inspected it with the root mantra, one should then sprinkle it with the Astra-mantra;
one should perform the striking with the Mantra and protect it with the Kavaca-mantra.
Fumigated with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor, and strewn with parched grain;
for the sake of accomplishing the rite, [he should offer] barley, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, ashes, unbroken rice, and kuśa grass.
The practitioner should scatter parched grain mixed with sesame seeds within the pavilion, for these indeed ward off obstacles;
then, with a handful of darbha grass, the practitioner should sweep them away while reciting the Astra-mantra.
One should cause those [images] to rest on the Īśāna side of the Vardhanī vessel for the sake of the seat;
then, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited and having diligently gratified the Brahmins.
Thereafter, one should draw the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala upon the altar;
now I shall explain that, which one should employ in tantric rites.
Having summoned the group of kings, one should prepare square grids;
there, in the center, one should erase six groups of squares and write [the names] therein.
Having set aside one-twelfth of the length on the outside from the center,
one should then duly fashion three equal circles in the middle according to the prescribed rule.
With the second circle drawn through the center of the pericarp, one marks the filaments;
with the inner circle, the petals; and the petal-extensions from the abandoned portion.
Having placed [the lotus] upon the tips of the filaments, one should place half-moons on the sides;
then, at their front, one should arrange the feet in the corners using three squares.
The remaining parts of the pedestal (pīṭha) and the body [of the temple] should be arranged in two rows beyond that;
having cleared the area, one should form a pathway (vīthī) in the four directions and in the center.
Successively, with two and four squares at each of the four gates,
and with three and one square respectively on both sides of each gate.
From this, the *śobhās* (ornaments) are formed by three squares on one side;
then, one should fashion the *upaśobhās* with six squares and the corners (*koṇas*) [with the remaining squares].
The white powder of rice should be used for the height and width;
the boundary lines and the petals should be made with a finger's breadth.
One should fill the pedestals, the body-parts, and the four doors;
the petals should not be filled with black, nor indeed with red.
The door-ornaments and the feet of the pedestal should be filled with safflower powder, which is reddish; however, according to the definitive rule, they may be made in all colors.
The powder of turmeric should be yellow;
the interior of the pedestal and the pericarp [should be yellow], as well as the secondary ornaments, O Brahmin women, and the interior of the pedestal should be black.
One should fill the joints and the *kalpavallī* stalks with green powder made from *vilva* leaves,
and the filaments with yellow-red [powder].
In the center of the fourfold street, one should fill it with wish-fulfilling creepers (kalpavallī),
which are heart-pleasing and adorned with the forms of leaves, roots, and fruits.
The skillful Guru should conquer her with powders of various colors;
with black-colored powder, he should then draw three outer lines at the corners.
One should decorate it in sequence with white, reddish-brown, and black powders;
this is declared to be the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala, which grants all desired results in all tantras.
You shall describe the Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala for the divine classes;
seek it there in the south, consisting of squares arranged in groups of three.
Just as before, however, in the center of that, there should be an auspicious lotus with thirty-six [petals];
