the pedestal (pīṭha) should consist of a single row, and the door and the ornamentation (śobhā) should be as previously described.
The corners should be colored with six squares as before;
the pedestal feet, the enclosures, and the lotus and so forth are considered to be as previously described.
In the left-hand path (vāmamārga), the mandala should consist of squares leaping over the apūpas;
there should be a lotus in the center with four [squares], or else a pathway outside of it.
It should be joined with a *kalpavallī* (wish-fulfilling creeper), and the lotus should indeed be as described previously;
one should proceed with four lotuses in the four directions using four squares.
In the intermediate directions, there should be four [lotuses] numbering four each;
in the center of the four lotus-paths, there is a figure resembling a svastika.
That [maṇḍala] arises within four squares, and in all four intermediate directions as well;
one should fill it with powders that are white, yellow, red, and blue.
One should visualize the svastikas as blue and red, as before;
for this mandala that has arisen is a most beautiful nine-petaled lotus.
One should fasten it upon the altar, adorned with fruits and flowers;
then, he should sit upon a seat on the altar facing the east.
The silent sage, with a mature lotus-like countenance, upright body, and conquered senses—
the lord of preceptors— having arranged the articles for worship, [proceeded].
One should place an auspicious water-pot on the right and on the left side,
filled with fragrant water for the purpose of washing the hands.
Afterward, having placed the vessel down, the knower of mantras should then light auspicious lamps;
he should also place a fan, a bud, an umbrella, and chowries in the various directions.
One should consecrate all of those according to the procedure to be described hereafter;
then, having performed the purification of the hands, one should perform the three claps (*tāla*).
With a focused mind, the practitioner should perform the binding of the directions using the Śara-mantra;
he should then protect that light which has arisen from it on all sides.

Then, having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), the preceptor, with a restrained mind, should perform the stabilization of the vital breaths (prāṇasthāpana) and thereafter carry out the ritual placement (nyāsa) and other rites.
Then the preceptor should place the Ṛṣi upon the head; he should place the Chandas within the mouth; and having placed the Deity at the heart, he should place the Mūlamantra [of the disciple].
The practitioner of mantra should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of six limbs or five limbs according to the prescribed rule;
for this mantra, the placement of five limbs is ordained, with the eyes being its [sixth] limb.
One should not even conceive of the limbs of the mantra for one who is devoid of the [mantric] limbs;
rather, one should perform the various other ritual placements (nyāsa) according to the path taught in their respective tantras.
One who knows the mantras should conceive of the seat of yoga within one's own body;
then, upon that seat which is identical with the body, one should meditate upon the deity of the mantra.
Then, having displayed the mudrās, one should place the supreme arghya;
thereafter, one should place the prokṣaṇī vessel filled with water on the right.
There, the knower of mantras should place the self-purification upon conch shells, and then, to the north of that,
the water for washing the feet, the water for sipping, and the honey-mixture.
Then, with a concentrated mind, the practitioner, using water from the root-vessel and water from the sprinkling-vessel,
should sprinkle himself, the mandala, and all other ritual implements and materials.
The best of preceptors, a knower of mantras, should sprinkle the place with perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
and having worshipped the Yoga-pīṭha according to the method of ritual placement (nyāsa).
Then, at the end of the *pīṭha*, one should worship the chosen deity there;
thereafter, becoming one with the deity, one should perform the five [offerings] ending with flowers.

One should worship [the deity] in the head, the heart, the foundation (ādhāra), the throat (varaṇa), and all the limbs with sandalwood paste and other offerings, excluding the food offering (naivedya).
One should complete all this with every ritual service (upacāra) according to the path instructed by the guru;
one should perform it all using the water from the sprinkling-vessel (prokṣaṇī).
Having set aside the water for drinking and the water for sprinkling, and having filled them as before,
the Guru should worship the mandala with services such as sandalwood paste and other offerings.
One should first worship the pericarp with śāli rice, then with taṇḍula rice;
one should place darbha grass upon these, and then a tuft of grass (kūrcaka) together with unbroken grains (akṣata).
Twenty-seven long blades of kuśa grass, with their roots cut, are placed at the tip in the form of a brahmagranthi; this is here called the *kūrca*.
One should worship the foundational powers, beginning with Ādhāra-śakti and ending with the mantra of the pedestal (pīṭha-mantra).
Therein, one should place a pitcher made of gold or other materials, free from any cracks or defects.
A golden vessel is twelve finger-breadths [in height], a silver one sixteen,
and an earthen or copper jar is prescribed to be thirty-six finger-breadths.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; if [the rite] is performed, one obtains the fruitlessness [of the effort].
It is wrapped on all sides externally with a thread consisting of three strands.
The supreme preceptor, reciting the mantra continuously according to the prescribed rite, should place [the vessel] in the center, thoroughly perfumed with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.
Having placed the nine gems into the pitcher, one should then place a tuft of grass (kūrca) upon it,
together with sandalwood paste from the eastern direction and accompanied by unbroken grains of rice (akṣata).
Blue flower-gems, lapis lazuli, coral, and likewise pearl; then emerald, diamond, hessonite, and ruby.
The nine gems have been proclaimed by the masters through their mastery of the tantras;
while mentally reciting the Mātṛkā mantra in sequence from 'kṣa' to 'a', one should [perform the rite].
At the end, the best of practitioners should recite the root mantra, contemplate his own oneness [with the deity], and meditate upon the non-difference between the jar and its pedestal.
Immediately thereafter, one should fill [the vessel] with decoctions of fifty medicinal herbs;
these varṇa-herbs are those fifty-one.
Sandalwood, as well as that called red sandalwood, and likewise aguru;
camphor, uśīra, kuṣṭha, vālaka, and also keśara.
Kaḥkolaka, jātiphala, jaṭāmāṃsī, murā,
granthika, rocanā, jātīputra, pippalī, and bilva.
Pṛśniparṇī, Citraka, and abundant Lavaṅgaka,
as well as Karkola, Guñjā, Udusvaraka, and Kāśmarī.
Padmaka wood, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, the crest of a peacock, as well as Plakṣa, Agnimantha, Muñja grass, and Kuśa grass; again [these are used].
Pāṣāṇabheda, Kṛṣṇa, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Rohiṇa, Śyonāka, Bṛhatī, Pāṭalā, and Mukhakarṇikā.
Tulasī, Śikharī, Indravallī, and the king named Bhṛṅga; then Aparājitā and Tālamūlī, with palms joined in reverence.
Dūrvā grass, the one called Śrīdevikanyā, Bhāratha, Bhadramustaka,
and Lavaṅgarahita— these constitute the number fifty.
One should bathe [the deity] with milk, or with decoctions produced from the *brahmabhūrja* and *vikaṅkata* trees,
or with a *prastha* measure of fragrant paste, or with auspicious white waters.
Having filled the conch with water such as decoctions and the like,
one should stir the eight fragrances (gandhāṣṭaka) appropriate for that particular deity within it.
Through the combination of the eight fragrances and by the power of the preceptor,
the wise know that collyrium endowed with potency will indeed be produced in the jar.
First, one should worship the ten digits related to Fire:
Dhūmārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, and Visphuliṅginī.
One should worship the beautiful and well-formed tawny cow for the sake of carrying the *havya* and *kavya* offerings;
thereafter, one should worship the sixteenfold solar *kalās*.
Tāpinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumṇā,
Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā.
Thereafter, the best of gurus should worship the sixteen lunar digits (kalās):
Amṛtā, Ānandā, Pūṣā, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Rati, and Dhṛti.
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā, and Pūrṇāmṛtā— these are the digits (kalās) born of herself who bestow splendor.

Having brought together and established the fifty parts (kalās) born from the divisions, which are joined with the moon (the letter *i*), one should worship them in the sequence as they have been praised.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, Ṛddhi, Dīpikā,
Recikā, Mocikā, Pārā, Sūkṣmā, Sūkṣmāmṛtā, and likewise [the others].
She is the nourisher of knowledge, the pervasive one, whose form is space;
she is infinite, the creative power, prosperity, memory, intelligence, and radiance.
Lakṣmī, Dyuti, Sthirāsthiti, Siddhi, Jarāpālinī,
Kṣānti, Īśvaryā, Rati, Kāmāvaradā, and Ahlādinī.
Joy, Long, Fierce, Terrible, Fear, Sleep, Torpor, Hunger,
Wrathful, Action, Eructation, Death— these are yellow, white, and red.
One should worship Asitā and Anantā in the middle of each [section] with the mantra "ha oṃ saḥ śuciṣad" and "prati viṣṇustave."

The wise one [should perform worship] with the *triyaṃvaka*, the *gāyatrī*, and likewise the *viṣṇuryoni* mantras, for the purpose of worshipping the kalās arising from the five divisions of the *tāra*.
Having invoked the ten Kalās beginning with Sṛṣṭi and having caused them to become present,
one should worship them after reciting the verse beginning with "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat."
Having performed the stabilization of the vital breaths (prāṇasaṃsthāpana), one who knows the ritual procedure should worship those digits (kalās),
such as Jarā and the others, Tīkṣṇā and the others, and Pītā and the others.
The wise one should also worship Nivṛtti and the others according to the stated method;
the letter *a* and the letter *u* are proclaimed, and the letter *m* is named Bindu.
Śakti, Śānta, Hyami, and the seven Dhruva varieties are thus proclaimed;
these last two varieties are indeed declared to be distinct from one another.
Then, one should strike the tender sprouts of mango trees growing near an *aśvattha* tree with the creeper of *indravāruṇī*, while reciting this mantra.
And one should meditate upon that vessel as being a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) atop the flask;
it is filled with rice and accompanied by a coconut fruit.
For this is indeed the fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree; one should place it with this intention.
Then, one should wrap the jar in a pair of silk cloths.
This is proclaimed as the installation of the principal pitcher;
now, in the directions beginning with the east, in the vicinity of the archways (toraṇas).
One may construct mandalas according to one's desire, including eight-petaled lotuses;
above those, one should arrange heaps of rice at each door.
One should worship the full jar placed there with offerings;
first Dhruva, then Dhara on the right, Vākpati behind, and Uttara on the left.
Then, one should properly place the jars in the southeast and the other directions starting from Agni,
and worship Vighneśa, Amṛta, Durjaya, Siddhārthaka, and Maṅgala.
Furthermore, one should worship Indra and the other guardians of the world (lokapālas) in order within the directions starting from the east, both upon the mandalas and likewise upon the jars.
Airāvata, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Kumuda,
Añjana, Puṣpadanta, Sārvabhauma, and Supratīka were at their head.
Then the Guru, having gone to his own altar, should sit upon his seat;
the most excellent Guru, having meditated upon the form [of the deity] therein by means of the root mantra.
Having invoked his chosen deity into that image,
the practitioner of mantras, recollecting the root mantra, should worship it properly according to the sequence of the nādis.
Having caused the consciousness to emerge and exit through the tip of the nose,
the Guru [places it] in his joined palms (añjali) within a lotus of the Mātṛkās, accompanied by light and flowers.
Having raised [the deity] up to the top of the head, one should then invoke it into that [image].
Thereafter, one should perform the rites of installation (saṃsthāpana), presence (sannidhāna), and confinement (sannirodha).
Then there is the manifestation [of the deity], followed by the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa;
thereafter the veiling (vaiguṇṭhana) should be performed, and after that, the transformation into nectar (amṛtīkaraṇa).
One should perform the act of perfection (paramīkaraṇa) sequentially with each respective mudrā; thereafter, one should duly arrange the ritual services (upacāra) in their proper order.
One should arrange the ritual services beginning with the seat and ending with flowers,
as well as the limbs and enclosures prescribed in the specific injunctions for their respective mantras.
Having performed the worship of all the world-protectors and their weapons,
one should indeed perform the worship with incense, lamps, and food offerings.
Having performed the offering, one should then sequentially place vessels containing coral sprouts all around the mandala while reciting the mantra.
Having prepared an excellent sacrificial mound on the southern side of the altar and having established and consecrated the fire, one should commence the Vaiśvadeva rite.
Then, according to the prescribed rule, one should worship the deity there with perfumes and other offerings;
having first offered oblations there with the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*.
One should offer oblations with the root mantra using milk-rice and ghee;
afterwards, one should again offer twenty-five oblations with the *avyāhṛti* mantras.
Having worshipped [the deity] with sandalwood paste and other offerings, one should join [the deity] to the pedestal-form (pīṭhamūrti).
Having dismissed the fire, one should offer an oblation (bali) with the remaining milk-rice (pāyasa).
Then, having offered sandalwood paste and other substances along with flowers and unbroken rice (akṣata) to the attendants,
the wise practitioner should rise and cleanse that place where the food offering (naivedya) was placed.
Then one should worship again with the five services and present:
libation, the fan, the umbrella, the fly-whisk, and mouth-perfume.
The practitioner, with a concentrated mind, should recite the root mantra one thousand times;
then, having offered that recitation to the deity, he should dedicate it for the sake of prosperity.
In the northeastern direction, where the *vikira* has been placed previously,
one should prepare a golden vessel filled with water and adorned with cloth.
One should install and worship here the weapon-deity (Astradevatā) of terrible form,
facing west, holding a shield and a sword, and seated upon a lion.
Standing there and having worshipped him, one should then take hold of him and circumambulate him clockwise, uttering the words: "May the world-protectors be favorable."
O God, the command of the deity is not satisfied by mere garlands or water;
therefore, one should establish it in its proper place and then worship it with merit and sacred mantras.
Having sat down again, the best of those who know mantras should duly perform the installation of the fire in the prescribed sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) with perfumes and other offerings.
Now follows the consecration of the fire.
The sages said: "Where is the fire and where are the gods? How are the deities offered oblations in the fire?"
O gods, tell me why those who have attained that state suddenly become indistinguishable from one another.
Īśvara said: Neither in heaven, nor in sacred fords, nor in medicinal herbs, nor in the stars do the Ṛṣis and deities reside; for mantras alone are indeed the deities.
The gods assumed those various forms in order to bestow the fruits [of practice] upon practitioners;
however, their primary nature consists solely of mantras and nothing else.
What does the fire burn that has been offered into it with those mantras?
The presiding deity (graha) gathers that merit, just as the channels collect the sap produced from the food.
Just as a flawless channel carries the light essence of food,
so too does a planet suitable for the gods carry its portion of excellence toward the divine.
The Sun shines with splendor, the Arka tree flourishes, and the Nandī creeper increases in excellence;
it nourishes the Vedic mantras and utterly destroys all enemies.
Therefore, in the three [houses], the [aspect] of Mercury produces the play of the intellect;
likewise, in those same three, that of Venus bestows great nourishment upon women.
Then, in the three *śanas*, one should destroy the accumulation of mantras;
then, in the three [following], it nourishes all mantras of the Moon.
Therefore, when the breath is in another [channel] other than the three channels of Saturn, it causes destruction;
hence, the channel of Jupiter during the three periods swiftly bestows the accomplishment of mantras.
Then, in the three [periods], the Rāhu-nāḍī is not present in the other [categories] such as the Sat-paiśāca;
however, the Ketu-nāḍī remains in the three [periods] of the Sad-bhūta, which removes the mantras of the gods.
From the conjunction of the lunar day (tithi) and the weekday (vāsara), the fire of digestion (hutāśana) arises from the remainder of the Kṛta [yuga];
when the eye is in the sky at Kaukutala, it is manifest in its own form within the fire.
If situated in the sky, it kills the practitioner; on the earth, it takes away wealth.
Fire, when present in its own form, bestows only auspicious results directly before one's eyes.
In rites that are obligatory or occasional, such as the fire-oblation to Durgā and others, one should not engage in deliberation;
rather, a follower of the Vedic path should perform the installation of the fire according to the ritual manual.
The practitioner of Tantra should perform eighteen purifications of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
he should inspect it with the root mantra and sprinkle it with water while reciting the weapon mantra (astra-mantra).
One should strike the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) three times with kuśa grass while reciting the Astra-mantra;
thereafter, it is prescribed that one should protect the pit with the Kavaca-mantra.
The digging of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be done with the Astra-mantra according to the measurement of finger-breadths;
one should then extract that earth with the thumb and ring finger while reciting the mantra.
Furthermore, one should fill it with pure clay while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛdayāṇu);
then, one should level it with the weapon-mantra (astra) and sprinkle it with the armor-mantra (kavaca).

One should pound it with wood and other materials while reciting that mantra until it becomes firm; then, one should sweep the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with kuśa grass while reciting the Kavaca mantra.
One should not perform the smearing with cow-dung using the Kavaca mantra;
rather, one should contemplate the fires, the sun, and the digits of the moon within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) by means of the Kavaca mantra.

One should wrap [the cord] around each girdle three times with a triple-stranded thread, using the armor mantra (varmamantra); thereafter, one should perform the worship of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
With "Tāraḥ" (Oṃ) and "Āsanam tena saḥ" (the seat for him),
one should perform the entire worship using variations such as "Eṣo 'rghyaḥ" (this is the water offering) and so forth.
One should perform the worship of the navel and the girdles in this manner;
thereafter, one should contemplate that sacrificial pit as being made firm like a diamond by means of the Astra-mantra.
Then, for the sake of extinguishing the flames and wind of the fire, one should create four paths in the four directions of the sacrificial pit using kuśa grass and the heart-mantra.

One should perform the rite for impure beings, such as *bhūtas* and *pretas*, whose gaze has fallen upon the walls of the sacrificial pit, using uncut *kuśa* grass over which mantras have been recited.
These consecrations for eradication have been declared to be equal in number to the *dhṛti* [forty-nine];
by this procedure, there shall also be the eradication of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

In the left-hand homa, however, there are only the first four purificatory rites (saṃskāras). One should now draw three lines from the southeast to the northwest, with their tips pointing toward the east.
And it is traditionally taught that for lines with their tips facing east, the presiding deities are Deva, Viliśa, and Vāsava;
for lines with their tips facing north, they are Brahmā, Sūrya, and Aida, respectively.
One should draw a hexagon upon a triangle with a blade of *darbha* grass according to the mantra, following the left-hand path; then one should draw a triangle within that triangle.
There, the worship of Viṣṇu, Śiva, Indra, and the others is performed;
however, in the Vāmamārga, the worship of the chosen deity takes place within a triangle.
Having gazed [upon it], one should worship the Yoga-pīṭha with the Praṇava;
I shall now fully explain its ritual procedure: one should contemplate the Maṇḍūka at its base.
Above that, one should contemplate Kālāgnirudra joined with Śakti;
above that, one should contemplate the Tortoise (Kūrma), and upon its back, the Earth (Vasundharā).
There, Śvetadvīpa is to be meditated upon, beautifully encircled by an ocean of nectar,
[and filled with] mandāra, pārijāta, saṃtāna, and haricandana trees.
One should likewise contemplate and worship the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) right there;
such a house should be contemplated as a delightful mansion made of jewels.
In the center of that, one should contemplate a golden pedestal and its feet as being dharma and the other goals of human life— namely, dharma, knowledge, and dispassion.
The limbs of the seat (pīṭha) are said to be "sovereignty" (aiśvarya) and so forth;
therein, in the center, is Ananta, and there the lotus has a bulb consisting of bliss (ānandamaya).
Its stalk is said to be severed, its filaments consist of the transformations (vikāra),
its receptacles are the constituents of primordial nature (prakṛti), and its pericarp consists of the fifty phonemes.
Then there is the triad of spheres belonging to the Sun, the Moon, and Fire;
thereafter, in the directions beginning with the East, are sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Furthermore, there is the inner self (antarātman), then the self (ātman), and beyond that the supreme self (paramātman);
then the principle of illusion (māyātattva), and the principle of the nature of knowledge (jñānātmakatattva) is established.
The supreme reality is the reality of knowledge (vidyā-tattva), which is declared to be the seat of yoga (yoga-pīṭha).
On the filaments of that lotus, beginning from the eastern petal and proceeding clockwise, the Lord resides.
One should worship these at the center and the ends:
Jayā, Vijayā, as well as the one named Ajitā, Aparājitā, Nityā, and Vilāsinī.
Then, in that place, one should utter: "To Dogdhī, Madyorā, and likewise Maṅgalā;
Hrīṃ, salutation to the Lotus-seated One who possesses all powers."
Having offered a handful of flowers into the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should worship Bhuvaneśvarī;
one should perform the worship beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the supreme transformation (paramīkaraṇa).
There, one should meditate upon and worship Śiva, intoxicated by passion, and likewise the Goddess in her fertile season, within the Gāṇeśa, Śaiva, and Śākta [mandalas].
Likewise, one should contemplate Lakṣmī as being in her menses within Viṣṇu and Śauri;
one should meditate on the fire born from the union with Nārāyaṇa.
From a forest, from a self-sacrificing brahmin, or from the house of a virtuous elder, she should fetch fire and a young girl who has bathed,
is dressed in clean garments, and has performed her purification.
When an auspicious vessel, such as one made of copper, is covered with another vessel, one should perform the bringing of the fire; or else, one may do so in a new earthen bowl.
One should offer the oblation with the *antreṇa* mantra, having covered the vessel with the *kavaca* mantra;
[one should not offer] into a worn-out shard, a skull, a broken vessel, or likewise into a firebrand.
One should not perform the formal bringing forward of the fire, as it removes disease and wards off fear;
one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyād) from the fire toward the southwest using the Astra-mantra.
The wise practitioner should first establish the portion belonging to the deity before him with the root mantra;
thereafter, he should purify that fire through the consecratory rites, such as inspection and the rest.
Then, one should invoke the light in the form of a lamp-flame,
[effecting] the unification of the digestive fire, the lunar fire, and the terrestrial fire.
Then, having recollected the fire-seed syllable (*agni-bīja*), one should join the consciousness to the chariot;
then, having consecrated it with the *oṃ* syllable and rendered it immortal by means of the *dhenu-mudrā*.
Then, having protected it with an arrow, one should cover it with something;
thereafter, having performed worship, the lord of the village should circumambulate the sacrificial pit.
Then, with his own generative organ facing the well-prepared sacrificial pit,
the preceptor should place it within the womb of the Goddess, while he himself remains with his knees touching the ground.
Having meditated upon it as the seed-syllable of Śiva, one should quickly cast [the oblation] into the fire;
one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) for the God and Goddess with the intention of sexual union.
O Citpiṅgalā, strike, strike! Cook, cook! Burn, burn!
O Omniscient One, grant your command! [This is] the praise of the Victorious One beginning with the syllable *hā*.
Having recited this mantra, one should then kindle the fire;
having made the two hands level at the wrists with the fingers extended.
Having placed the two middle fingers together, one should insert the two thumbs into their midst;
this is that supreme mudrā called Jvālanī, used in the rite of homa.
I praise Agni, the blazing one, the knower of all beings, the consumer of oblations—
the fire of golden hue, kindled and facing in every direction.
With this mantra, one should worship the consumer of oblations (the fire).
One must not blow on the fire with the mouth; for from the mouth, the god was indeed born.
Having silently cast into the fire a fuel-stick of the measure of a span (prādeśa), moistened at both its root and tip with ghee, one should place the deities upon the tongue [of the fire].
The practitioner of mantra should place [the syllables] throughout his own body, beginning from the tongue and extending to the arms,
as well as upon the genitals, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes.
O Teacher, the syllables from *sa* to *ya*, joined with *va* (vahni), *ra* (rāghrīśa), and provided with the *bindu*,
are declared to be the mantras for the seven tongues of fire.
Then, with kuśa grass, or leaves such as those of the *palāśa* tree, or some other purifying object (*pavitra*),
the mantra-practitioner should duly place [the mantras] upon the tongues and body of the Fire-god.
One should place the wheels (cakras) in sequence upon the penis, anus, head, mouth, nose, and eyes;
then on all the limbs, the tongue, and the teeth—these are said to be of threefold nature.
Hiraṇyā, Āgneyī, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, Suprabhā, Bahurūpā,
and Atiraktā— these are the seven tongues of fire.
Padmarāgā, Suvarṇā, and the third, Bhadralohitā; after Lohitā come Śvetā, Dhūminī, and Karālikā.
In rites performed for specific desires, Rajasī and Rasā are ordained for Vahni;
likewise Viśvamūrti and Sphuliṅginī, as well as Dhūmavarṇā and Manojavā.
Lohitā is called Karālā, and Kālī is said to be Tāmasī;
these seven are appointed by their excellent ministers for cruel deeds.
The immortal gods, the ancestors, the gandharvas, the yakṣas, the nāgas, and the piśācas possess auspicious semen and tongues that shine with their own respective names.
The Rākṣasas are declared to be the presiding deities of the seven tongues,
for the sake of accomplishing the respective tasks of the gods and others upon those tongues.
One should perform oblations; those deities, ending with the word *analera* and joined with the syllable *svāhā*, will grant the desired accomplishment.
The minister should again duly assign the limbs of Fire in sequence:
Sahasrārcis, Svasti, Pūrṇa, and likewise Utiṣṭhapuruṣa.
Dhūmavyāpin, Saptajihva, Havyavāha as the third,
Aśvodaraja, Vaiśvānara, and Kaumāratejas.
Viśvamukha and Devamukha—these eight forms are proclaimed;
having sprinkled them with water in a clockwise sequence, one should proceed.
Mekhala, having set aside the eastern [portion], should again spread around [the fire] with four perfectly pure darbha grasses, which have their tips pointing eastward and are held upright.
In a pit with one girdle, one should spread [the grass] below the girdle;
in a pit with two girdles, on the second [girdle]; and in a pit with three girdles, on the middle one.
One should spread sand upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on the site of the dwelling;
and between the altar and the girdle, one should establish the enclosing sticks (paridhi).
Likewise, the wise man should make an opening above the middle girdle from wood produced from the Palāśa,
Kāśmarī, Bilva, and Vikaṅkata trees.
Having taken three fuel-sticks (*paridhi*) made from a single tree, which are not green and are the size of a span,
one should duly perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and strew *kuśa* grass between them.
According to the procedure prescribed for one's own ritual manual, to the east of the direction of Vāyu,
he should place the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the *praṇītā* vessel, and the pair of *prokṣaṇī* vessels.
The first vessel, the enclosing sticks, the handfuls of kuśa grass,
the vessels turned face down, as well as the oblation materials and the sacrificial offering (bali).
Then, one should arrange all the perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and so forth;
having sprinkled them with water using a purifier and having placed them face upwards.
Having filled the pair of *prokṣaṇī* vessels with pure water,
and having offered *kṣata* grass and a sacred thread (*pavitra*), one should place them upon the *ūti*.
In the northern direction, that vessel for the *praṇītā* water is filled by the wise;
then, having placed a little of the *praṇītā* water into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, [one sprinkles] with those waters.
One should sprinkle the collection of materials for the sacrificial means with the root mantra;
one should choose a peaceful Brāhmaṇa who has been initiated into the mantra of the deity.
One should seat him on a seat of kuśa grass to the south of the sacrificial pit, [saying]:
"I, belonging to such-and-such a lineage, [invite] you, who belong to such-and-such a lineage."
"In this oblation which is an ancillary part of the initiation (dīkṣā), I choose you as Brahmā";
having said this, one should honor him with garments, ornaments, and so forth, thereby fulfilling his requirements.
If a Brāhmaṇa is not available, one may also use Kuśa grass;
however, within the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), there should be a vessel adorned with gold and containing a hexagon.
One should contemplate an eight-petalled lotus joined with various filaments, surrounded by four gates, and enclosed within three successive squares.
There, upon that sacrificial seat of Fire,
one should worship the Yoga-pīṭha, beginning with Maṇḍūka and ending with Jñānātman, within the eight petals.
One should worship the yellow, white, red, black, and smoke-colored flames, as well as the spark-emitting fire, from the southeast to the center.
One should worship the entire sacred seat (pīṭha), including Rucirā and Jvālinī;
this twelve-syllable mantra is for the tender-seated one who possesses all powers.
In the worship of all the seats (pīṭhas), the mantra of Vahni is proclaimed;
thereafter, one should meditate upon Hutāśana [Agni] with his excellent svastikas and śaktis.
It is perfectly adorned with arms joined in the gesture of fearlessness,
possessing the color of vermilion, seated upon a lotus, and decorated with golden ornaments.
Having thus meditated upon him who has three eyes, matted locks and a crown, and who is clad in red garlands and garments, one should worship him with ritual offerings using this mantra.
O Vaiśvānara, Jātavedas, red-eyed one, bring [the gods] here;
may I accomplish all rites, preceded by the Praṇava and ending with Svāhā.
This mantra consists of twenty-seven syllables; it is for the worship of Agni.
Then, in the center of the hexagon, there is the meditation upon and worship of the tongues of fire.
Likewise, in the northeast is Jihvā, radiant with flames and holding all-protecting and fear-dispelling gestures;
and Hiraṇyā, golden-hued, who bestows the accomplishment of peace and nourishment.
The golden one, colored like lapis lazuli, located in the east, performs the rite of immobilization (staṃbhanakārya);
for the rite of inciting hatred (vidveṣa), she is red, resembling the color of the sun, and resides in the southeast corner (agnikoṇa).
Those resembling black collyrium in the southwest (nairṛtya) are capable of killing;
those with excellent luster like rubies in the northwest (vāruṇya) bestow wealth.
Extremely red, she is present in the direction of the wind for the purposes of victory, manifestation, and eradication;
Bahurūpā, however, resides in the center of the hexagon, conjoined with the six syllables.
Impartiality brings about the accomplishment of many tasks and also their destruction;
just as the task requires, so the tongue is seen directed toward its own side.
At that time, it takes the form of a flame; however, in the case of failure to achieve success, the opposite occurs.
[This applies] in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and also in the direction in front of the deity.

One should worship the six limbs on the petals, as well as the deities of the directions, Indra and the others, together with their weapons; having worshipped them, one should again sacrifice to the fire.
Then, having turned the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles face downwards, one should heat them;
one should cleanse their tips with the tips of *kuśa* grass, and their middles with the middle parts.
Having cleansed the roots with the roots in three ways, one should heat them;
holding them with the left hand, one should sprinkle them with the waters from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
Again, he should heat those two with the tip of his right hand;
then, having thrown kuśa grass into the fire, [he places] the kuśas upon the heap of kuśas at his own right side.
Having placed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles behind [the fire], one should then perform the consecration of the clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Taking the vessel of clarified butter, one should sprinkle it with the mantra.
Having filled it with ghee and thoroughly consecrated it through the rites of inspection and so forth,
one should place a cow in the northwest, lead her out, and then install the [deities] within those [limbs] while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having indicated the heating, one should then cast two blades of kuśa grass;
it should be placed in the blazing fire within the clarified butter, accompanied by that ghee.

One should perform the purification with two *darbha* blades while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*; having offered clarified butter (*ājya*) while reciting the *varma-mantra* and performed the lustration (*nīrājana*), one should cast the two *darbha* blades into the fire.
This shall be the illumination; then the manifestation is spoken of.
Having shown the *kuśa* grass as blazing in the eye, one should cast it into the heart with the mind.
Having placed clarified butter and embers from the fires before the fire-ignorant person,
the knower of mantras should touch the iron and then perform the leaping over it.
Holding the Astra-mantra and the Mantrāṅkuśa mantras, each measuring a span (prādeśa),
with the thumb and ring finger, one should leap up while holding clarified butter (ghṛta).
Then, one should firmly immerse [the sacrificial post] facing oneself with two blades of kuśa grass;
that immersion in clarified butter is what is called the six purificatory rites (ṣaṭsaṃskāra).
Cow’s ghee is declared to be the best; that produced from a buffalo is middling;
that born from a goat is inferior; while that originating from a sheep and so forth is prohibited.
When ghee purchased in the marketplace is tasted, it should be treated as if it were cow-derived;
then, having placed two blades of kuśa grass into the ghee, each measuring a span (prādeśa).
Having tied the knot, he should contemplate two snakes, one white and one black;
the left side as the *iḍā* and the right as the *piṅgalā*, and then [the central channel] in the middle.
The mantrin should contemplate the Suṣumṇā; then he should perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Now, with the Heart-mantra, he should take up the sacrificial ladle (sruva) from the right side and offer the oblation.
One should offer oblations with "Svāhā" into the right eye of the Fire-god, which is of the nature of Agni;
having taken clarified butter from the left side, one should offer it into the left eye of the Fire-god with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
The renunciation "To Huta and Soma, Svāhā! is accepted everywhere.
Having taken the clarified butter from the center with the Heart-mantra, O Mid-eye one (Agni)!
One should offer the third portion with the mantra "To Agni and Soma, Svāhā," and again take clarified butter from the right side, offering it with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
When the Agni-Sviṣṭakṛt offering has been performed at the mouth of the fire, one should offer oblations with the mantra "svāhā.
Then, one should again offer clarified butter with the Vyāhṛtis accompanied by the Sāvitrī.
The best of preceptors should offer oblations three times with the Agni-mantra;
[these rites] for the fire, beginning with conception (garbhādhāna) and ending with marriage (samudvāha), [are thus completed].
In an auspicious rite, the ritual action should be performed with eight oblations of clarified butter;
having first uttered the Praṇava, one should then pronounce the name of the rite.
"I accomplish [this], svāhā!"—this is the self-performed rite for all rituals.
One should perform the rites of conception (*garbhādhāna*), the male-impelling rite (*puṃsavana*), and the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*).
One should first mentally offer oblations into the fire born from the womb of Vāgīśvarī;
then, having performed the birth-rite (jātakarman), one should carry out the cutting of the umbilical cord.
Then, having performed the birth-rite (sūtaka), one should perform the naming ceremony according to the prescribed rule;
that which serves for his satisfaction in the [mantra] foot should be preceded by his name, with the word "Agni" following it.
The initiation of the thief (cauropanayana), the fire-ritual, the Mahānāmnī vow,
the Great Vow (mahāvrata), the Upaniṣad vow, and the Godāna ceremony as well.
The return home and marriage [are performed] with the Śākta [mantra] preceded by the Vāgbhava;
thereafter, the fire, the ancestors, and likewise the gods and goddesses, and so forth.
Having worshipped and then dismissed [the deities], one should cast fuel-sticks soaked in ghee into the fire at the base and the tip, as before.
Some say that one should offer a *kāma-āhuti* with the seed-syllable and the *rasa-mantra*;
thereafter, one should offer oblations to the limbs (*aṅga*) and likewise to the eight forms (*mūrti*) of the Fire-god.
Then the wise one [should worship] Indra, Agni, and the world-protectors (lokapālas), as well as their weapons,
with a mantra beginning with the syllable "A" and ending with "svāhā."
One should offer the oblation of clarified butter with the mantra "svāhā" while meditating on the deity of the mantra;
having taken the ghee four times with the *sruva* ladle, one should pour it into the *sruc* offering spoon.
Having performed that very rite, the Guru himself, standing, offers oblations into the fire with the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
which is the same as that [previously mentioned] for the fire.
The mantra practitioner [should worship] on the tongue situated in the center of the tree of the garland of flames with the ten variations beginning with *Tārā*, each joined with the preceding one.
One should first offer ten oblations with the *gāṇapatya* mantra of Manu;
one should also offer four oblations with that same mantra used in its entirety.
Then, having properly worshipped the seat of the deity within the fire,
the Guru should there worship his chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) who assumes the form of the fire.

The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations twenty-five times with clarified butter while reciting the *sādhya-mantra*; this is indeed the "unification of the mouth" (*vaktraikīkaraṇa*) within the mouth of the fire.
The knower of the Self should contemplate the oneness of the Self with the fire and the deities;
then, one should offer oblations of clarified butter eleven times with the root mantra.
The evening twilight is likewise declared by the supreme teachers to be dedicated to that [deity];
one should offer one oblation for each [deity], beginning with the limbs and ending with Amṛtī.
Having thus duly consecrated the fire in all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in the directions beginning with the east, one should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) with cow's milk.
Then, as if sprinkling water upon a vessel made of copper or other metals,
one should consecrate with mantras the rice grains produced from the *śāli* paddy.
Chanting the mantra while measuring the duration of the lunar day (tithi) with the span of his fingers,
he should cast the arrow into a washed vessel, covering it up to the mouth.
Then, facing the east, the preceptor— the best of teachers— should cook it with the *hraṃ* mantra and the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), and subsequently sprinkle that heated substance [with water].
Then, one should pour [the remainder] using the ghee situated in the *śruva* ladle with the root mantra;
it should be distributed upon the *kuśa* grass strewn over the ground, which has been consecrated by the *astra* mantra, while reciting "Haṃ."
Having divided [the offering] threefold, one part should be offered to the deity and the other part presented into the fire;
then the preceptor, who knows the mantras, should eat the remainder together with the disciple.

Having recited the prescribed mantra twice over a tooth-stick of the size of a span, he should give it to the disciple; once the cleaning is finished, he should discard it after washing it thoroughly.
Having performed the *ācamana* mantra according to the prescribed rite and having secured this [disciple] with the bonds at the crest-lock (*śikhā*), the practitioner,
together with the disciple, is addressed by the sage on another altar strewn with sacrificial grass (*kuśa*).
The dwelling place of wisdom.
Now, the ritual duties for the day of initiation (dīkṣā): Having risen at dawn, one should again perform the bath, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and so forth;
then the Guru, the disciple, and the officiating priests (ṛtvij) should proceed toward the sacrificial hall (yāgagṛha).
All of them should offer oblations in their respective fire-pits with sesame seeds mixed with ghee;
again, they should perform one thousand and eight oblations with the mantra of the person to be accomplished (sādhya).
One should offer oblations into a fire that is not blazing, nor one that is merely smoldering;
rather, for the successful accomplishment of the rite, one should offer oblations when the fire is fully kindled and flickering.
"He who offers oblations into a fire that emits smoke is a wise man who is blind;
the sacrificer, along with his sons, shall become blind—so says the Śruti."
If a person offers oblations into the fire when it is devoid of ghee or when the embers have been extinguished,
he is born with weak digestion, prone to disease, and impoverished.

If there is an obstruction to the fire due to an illness or a defect in the ear, blindness in the eyes, or a disorder in the nose, there should be a cutting of the sacrificial substance at the head; therefore, the wise man should always perform the oblation within the mouth.
Where there is wood, there is the ear; where there is smoke, the nose;
where there is the flickering flame, the eyes; and where there is ash, that is the head.
Wherever the fire blazes, there the tongues [of flame] are proclaimed;
the preceptor, in the case of perfected homas, should meditate upon Vaiśvānara as being present there.
While lying down during the offerings of clarified butter (ājya-homa) and amidst substances remaining from the sacrificial residue,
[the tongue] resembles gold, vermilion, the rising sun, saffron, and honey.
A fire that is of the same color as gold is proclaimed to be beautiful;
the sound of a kettledrum, a water-cloud, or a lordly elephant brings auspiciousness to the fire.
The Naga resembles the Campaka, Punnāga, Pāṭala, and Yūthikā flowers; he is like the lotus, the Indīvara, and the Kalhāra, and resembles clarified butter and guggulu resin.
The auspicious fragrance of the purifier (fire) has been described by those who know the Vedas;
the flames of the fire, free from trembling, perform circumambulation and possess the luster of umbrellas.
Smoke as white as a jasmine flower or the moon, which issues from the fire, is declared to bring auspiciousness, bestowing prosperity upon the sacrificer and especially upon the kingdom.
A black color appearing on a black ground would destroy the sacrificer;
a white color destroys his kingdom, while one resembling the sky leads to heaven.
A voice that is discordant with one's own natural tone, O Agni, and a sound that causes universal destruction;
likewise, a foul odor from the fire shall indeed bring about suffering.
A smoke with a severed crest or tip causes death and the loss of wealth;
that which resembles the wing of a parrot or has a luster like a pigeon [is likewise inauspicious].
It causes the swift decline of the Raghu dynasty and of cattle;
when such faults exist, the preceptor [should prescribe] an expiation.
One should offer twenty-five oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra;
then, the most excellent knower of mantras should cause the bathed disciple to drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having brought [the deity] from the vessel, one should gaze upon it with divine vision;
one should then project the consciousness from the heart-lotus into that [deity's] own self.
There, the teacher should gradually purify the sixfold path;
purification consists of contemplating the unity of the causes of the named principles (tattvas).
The Guru should externally perform the meditation on the unity of consciousness with those phonemes (varṇas) and digits (kalās), according to the prescribed method for consecrated [substances].

Having worshipped all the officiating priests with sandalwood paste and other offerings, they should then offer oblations into the fire with the root mantra to the aforementioned deity, accompanied by all the surrounding retinues.

With milk mixed with twenty-five parts of clarified butter, one should offer an akṣa-measure with a sruva-ladle; the remaining portions should be offered with a samit-stick and the sruva-ladle, while the rest is offered by hand.
There, one should offer oblations with divine substances or likewise with external substances at a sacred ford;
one should respectfully present the bali offering preceded by perfumes, flowers, and incense.
One should separately state the positions for the lunar mansions, the weekdays, and the zodiac signs, as well as their presiding deities; likewise, one should declare the day and night.
Then, the best of instructors should utter "namas" to all the wandering beings and to all elemental spirits, and then perform the oblation with the Great Utterances (Mahāvyāhṛtis).
The wise one should again offer oblations with clarified butter for the *vṛtti* mantras beginning with the limbs (*aṅga*),
using the mantra known as *brahmārpaṇa*, for the severing of all karmic bonds.
The knower of mantras should offer eight oblations of pure clarified butter;
having offered them, the practitioner of mantra should then pour the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) while reciting the root mantra.
Having invoked Agni with the complete mantra, one should offer a single oblation of clarified butter;
having filled the ladle with ghee, one should place a flower upon it with its face downward.
Having placed the *sruva* ladle upon the *sruc* vessel, one should cause a flower to fall therein;
then, with the left and right hands joined together in the *saṃpuṭa* gesture, as in the remaining rites.
Having gathered [the materials] and stood up, the two [hands] joined together and placed transversely at the navel,
he should offer [the oblation] with the *pūrṇādarvī* mantra and the root mantra, accompanied by wealth (*vasu*).
One should offer three full oblations (pūrṇāhuti) that fulfill all desires;
this is prescribed for a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya), while another may perform the full oblation on his behalf.
With the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ* and ending in *svāhā*,
one who has gone to the left should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) with meat and liquor, and bring it to completion with water from a sacred ford and clarified butter.
A follower of the Vedic path should perform the rite with the root mantra ending in "svāhā," using fruit and clarified butter;
placing his right foot forward, the adept should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
In the Śakti-homa, the knower of mantras, following the left-hand path, should cast his left foot everywhere;
then, having again offered perfumes and other substances with the root mantra.
Having raised the deity from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the preceptor should install it in the water-pot (kalaśa);
there, he should worship it together with its limbs and enclosures according to the prescribed rite.
Then the Guru, having sprinkled the fire with milk— each of the seven vyāhṛtis, the tongues of Agni, and the forms of the limbs— should pray to the fire.
O Agni, O you of great power, bestower of all desires!
Even when another ritual act has arrived, please grant your presence with due respect.
Having thus offered prayers with this mantra, one should also dismiss the fire;
then, having dismissed Brahmā, one should cause him to be presented to the Brāhmaṇa.
This copper vessel, fashioned by Ātreya, measures twenty-two finger-breadths;
it should be filled with rice and accompanied by gold and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One should give a full vessel (pūrṇapātra) to a brāhmaṇa for his satisfaction; this is what has been declared.
Thereafter, one should cast the enclosing sticks (paridhi) into the fire, and not otherwise.
The most excellent preceptor should perform the rite with the obligatory and occasional [mantras];
he then binds the eyes of the disciple with a cloth while reciting the Netra-mantra.
Taking [the flowers] with his hand from the vessel and leading them into the vicinity of the maṇḍala,
he should fill his joined palms with flowers and scatter them.
Preceded by the recitation of the root mantra, the Guru, for the sake of pleasing the deity,
shall cause the disciple to sit with eyes blindfolded upon a bed of kuśa grass.
Then, while instructing the disciple in this mantra, the supreme guru [should say]:
"With the probe of the ointment of knowledge, for one blinded by the darkness of ignorance..."
Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom the eye was opened;
one should withdraw [the deity] and worship it with the rite of internal worship.
Then the disciple should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of that mantra upon his body,
having worshipped the chosen deity residing within the kalaśa with the five articles of offering (pañcopacāra).
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa there according to the path described,
he should then cause the disciple, who has been adorned, to sit within the maṇḍala.

Then the preceptor, together with the trees of the forest and the Brahmins, [performed the rite] for the child who had the celestial tree (Kalpavṛkṣa) placed upon his head like a water-pot, amidst the fivefold sounds.
One should sprinkle the well-established and self-controlled [disciple] with jar-flowers (kalaśapuṣpaka),
in the same manner as he was previously joined with those consisting of nectar.
Then, by means of waters joined with syllables through the very path situated within the jar,
one should consecrate the disciple for the swift attainment of prosperity.
Having first taken up the consecrated water-pot, which has the form of the Astra-mantra,
the supreme preceptor should sprinkle him with its waters for the sake of protection.
Then, the Guru should cause the person who is instructed to place the child upon his left side;
he should then perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the infusion of the deity's form) by means of that very form of the deity.
Having put on two pure and beautiful garments by the command of his guru,
and having sipped water (ācamana) in his presence, he should properly repeat that mantra three times.
A wise man should speak [the mantra] into the right ear of a Brahmin preceded by the offering of water;
however, for others, the discerning one should speak the mantra directly into the ear.
One should recite the Triśūla-vidyā three times with a single utterance into the right ear;
this is the rule for the twice-born, while for women and Śūdras it is done from the left.
The Guru should contemplate the Vidyā as self-luminous and departing;
the disciple should contemplate it as not yet arrived, especially with the thought, "I am not that."
The disciple should recite one hundred and eight times what is instructed by the guru,
or he may recite twenty-eight times, or eight times.
The disciple, contemplating the oneness of the Guru, the Deity, and the Mantra,
the devoted practitioner should repeatedly offer prostrations to the Guru.
Then, being well-restrained in the performance of worship, one should perform either the eight-limbed or the five-limbed prostration with both hands, both feet, the two knees, and likewise the chest.
The eightfold [prostration] is said to consist of the head, the sight, as well as speech and the mind;
the hands, knees, head, and words are also declared [to be its components].
And one should respectfully give ornaments and garments to the officiating priests.
After understanding the dispraise of Īśvara, Nandana, along with the twice-born sages,
should give half of his own wealth to the preceptor for the sake of his own property.
Or, avoiding deceit regarding one's wealth, one should give a tenth part,
such as cattle, land, gold, forests, houses, fields, and so forth.
Without causing distress, one should give food, clothing, and so forth according to one's wealth;
having taken refuge within the enclosure wall, one should satisfy the Guru with diligent effort.
With his mind dependent on that [Lord], impermanent [in worldly concerns], and devoted solely to the contemplation of Him,
the best of practitioners should become adorned with the pollen of His lotus feet.
Then, one should properly feed the Brahmins with various kinds of foods—both those to be licked and those to be sucked—and likewise others; one should also bestow abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Thus has been described the initiation consisting of ritual action,
which bestows prosperity upon kings, merchants, Vaiśyas, Brahmins, and those engaged in worldly occupations.
Now, the distinction among heroes.
Having worshipped the Kula-cakra according to the prescribed rite with the substances of the Kula, one should properly show it to the disciple; this is considered the Kaulika initiation.
Having written this [syllable] representing the existence of the Ṛṣis and so forth within the center of the ground,
and having worshipped it thoroughly with flowers and other offerings, one should then show it to the disciple.
If there is great affection for the disciple, then the Guru should speak it into his ear;
even more so if the disciple is a vessel of devotion toward the Guru.
Then, at the beginning of the forenoon, the best of gurus should give this [mantra] as a mouthful of water;
even if the disciple is free from conceptual thought, he should receive it with a joyful mind.
If it is performed without that [substance], success will not occur and one shall incur the curse of the deity.
One should fill the mouth with the substance of accomplishment (siddhidravya) combined with the five-fold nectar of space (pañcavyomāmṛta).
One should consecrate a dear disciple; this is declared to be the rite known as the "mouthful" (gaṇḍūṣa).
This sequence of initiation has been proclaimed for those who desire success accompanied by worldly enjoyment.
Now, the specific procedure for women of noble family:
having brought a virtuous and highly renowned beloved of a hero,
and having approached a Guru who is devoted to his lineage, one should initiate her with the Kula-initiation.
Her eyes were rolling with the nectar of supreme bliss; she was a virtuous woman of noble birth, her mouth filled with betel and areca nuts, while he was devoted to the words of his guru.
The teacher should write [the mantra] upon the forehead-plate of that [disciple] as if it were his own daughter;
having drawn the wheel of power (śakticakra) with three enclosures, he should then write the Kāmakalā.
In the center of that, having established me marked with the *māla* [symbol] using the *deyamantra*,
one should invoke the Goddess there, hold her, and worship her.
Then, the sage, having repeated the root mantra three times together with the Vedic meters, should whisper it into the ear of that daughter using his left hand.
From this day forward, you, as my daughter, devoted to the worship of the family initiation,
shall bring about a state of aesthetic integration (sāmarasya) according to the prescribed injunctions.
Having thus received permission from the guru, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff out of modesty, [saying]:
"O Lord, protector of the Kula tradition, O Lotus-Lord, protect me, the lotus-woman!"
O you whose wealth is fame, place the shade of your lotus feet upon my head;
like one whose eyes are reddened by betel, he should offer that as a fee to his guru.
Having elevated one's own family (kula) to the status of the supreme, one should perform worship as prescribed;
for if the family does not proceed in the rites such as the worship of the limbs and the enclosures (aṅgāvaraṇa), [the rite is incomplete].

Then, having meditated on the Guru at the crown of the head and having gratified the Kula with the nectar-essence of the Kula, one should meditate on the Kula and recite the mantra that is free from agitation.
Now follows the initiation consisting of phonemes (varṇamayī-dīkṣā). Now listen to the initiation consisting of phonemes, which bestows knowledge;
the nature of the phonemes as being composed of the Puruṣa and Prakṛti has been proclaimed.
And such a [method] for the body has indeed been taught by the masters;
therefore, the best of teachers should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the ten lunar days upon the child’s body.
The supreme teacher, by his own power and through the command of the deity’s self, should withdraw the phonemes situated in their respective locations in the reverse order.
Then the disciple becomes one with the deity, his essence completely absorbed;
thereafter, he should unite the consciousness of the disciple with the Supreme Self.
Having then produced those phonemes, one should place them within the body of the disciple;
and into that [body], one should again place that consciousness according to the order of emanation.
The disciple shall become the very self of the deity, Śiva, whose nature is eternal bliss;
this initiation, consisting of the ocean of knowledge, is said to bestow all perfections.
Now I shall describe the initiation of the Kalās, beginning with Maṇi, which bestows the eight supernatural powers;
it is known as the fivefold Kalā-initiation, and for those skilled in initiation, it is considered the desired threefold Kalā.
The fifty-four *kalās* on the left belong to the Guru who possesses perfected mantras;
they should be received swiftly as they bring about accomplishment, whereas in the opposite case, the result is the reverse.
The wise one should pierce, in due order, the five elements within the body of the disciple— which is composed of the elements— beginning with the *kalās* headed by Nivṛtti.
The kalās known as Nivṛtti are established from the feet up to the knees;
from the knees up to the navel, the kalās called Pratiṣṭhā are situated.
The kalās known as Vidyā are situated from the navel up to the throat;
the kalā known as Śānti is situated from the throat up to the forehead.
The wise one should pierce [the channels] from one location to another in sequence: from the forehead up to the head for the Śāntyatīta-kalās, and likewise for the Saṃhṛti-kalās.
In the Sthāna [initiation], the initiation of the five kalās is prescribed by one’s own command;
O deities, listen now to the method for the initiation of the thirty-eight kalās.
The twelve letters beginning with *ka* are situated in order upon the petals; where the letters beginning with *bha* are in reverse order, there is a digit (*kalā*) in those two places.
The sixteen digits of the Sun and likewise those of the Moon should be meditated upon;
in the place beginning with the letter Ya, the ten digits of Fire should be meditated upon.

Then, having performed the worship of the locations of the phonemes according to the proportions of the phonemes, one should again generate the disciple; this is the procedure for the initiation into the Kalās.
Now, the initiation consisting of piercing (vedhadīkṣā):
In the Kaulika and Vāma paths, the Vedic initiation bestows its fruit;
otherwise, on the Dakṣiṇa path, those other [initiations] would result in a fall from one's status.
I shall describe the initiation consisting of piercing (vedha), by which a person abandons shame;
at that very moment, he becomes liberated while living (jīvanmukta) from saṃsāra.
One should meditate upon a four-petaled lotus at the disciple's mūlādhāra;
within its center is a triangle, and in the middle of that is Kuṇḍalinī.
The Goddess, who consists of three revolutions, whose form is like a mass of lightning,
who is identical with Mahādeva himself, and who is the direct embodiment of the mere act of bestowing [boons] upon embodied beings.
The divine goddess, subtler than the subtlest, who pierces the six wheels,
proceeds along the path of the Suṣumṇā toward the abode of Śiva.
One should extract [the letters] from the syllable situated in the *sāntavādi* group into the position of the lotus;
[one should place them] in a six-petalled lotus ending with the seed-syllable (*tantu*), and in a two-petalled [lotus] beginning with the consonant (*vādya*).
Having properly joined [the disciple] at the Svādhiṣṭhāna, the Guru should pierce him;
he should bring those syllables into Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu into that lotus of the navel.
One should oneself pierce the petals of the directions joined with the phonemes beginning with *pha* and ending with *ḍa*;
one should then join those phonemes, from *ru* to *dra*, within the heart-lotus.
The Lord himself should pierce [the mandala] with lotus-leaves inscribed with the letters beginning with *ka* and *ṭha*;
he should then extract those very letters from this *kaṇṭhapadma* (throat-lotus) in that same manner.
Having diligently joined the vowels within a lotus consisting of sixteen petals,
one should then join them in the lotus situated between the eyebrows of Sadāśiva.
Then, having pierced the two petals joined at the eye with his power (śakti), the teacher should lead that divine self up to Paraśiva.

By the power of the teacher’s command, the disciple is burnt away; when that [impurity] is destroyed by knowledge, he falls [into the state of liberation]. Having attained higher realization (vijñāna), he then becomes omniscient.
Sadāśiva shall himself become manifest; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
This auspicious initiation, consisting of piercing (vedha), is said to bestow knowledge.
Now follows the initiation consisting of touch (*sparśamayī-dīkṣā*).
The Guru should meditate upon his own Guru, who is the form of Śiva, with his own hands,
while reciting the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the Mātṛkā-mantra, and other mantras.
Having placed his right hand with compassion upon the head of the disciple, he should thereafter give the instruction; this aforementioned initiation by touch bestows spiritual perfection.
One should cause the mind to rest upon the Guru in the form of Consciousness as Sadāśiva,
while meditating that all mantras born from Him are themselves identical with His nature.
"By the grace of the Guru, I alone am always Sadāśiva"—meditating thus, one should instruct; this is declared to be the initiation of speech (vāgdīkṣā).
Having closed his eyes and meditated upon the deity within the Supreme Self,
the Guru should then gaze with eyes filled with the bliss of that vision.
With a serene mind, he subsequently instructs the disciple;
such is the fruit of initiation bestowed by one who has attained perfection in mantra.
Through merely looking at the guru, through his speech, or even through touch, knowledge arises immediately; this is known as the Śāmbhavī initiation.
Having examined [the disciple] according to the rules for the sake of attaining worldly enjoyment and liberation, the Guru should subsequently impart the mantra; otherwise, one would obtain no fruit.
p. 48a) Now, as for the oral instruction (*upadeśa*):
the great initiation (*mahādīkṣā*), the initiation (*dīkṣā*), and thereafter the oral instruction.
In the Kṛta and other ages, [the dharma] was to be practiced; in the Kali age, it is to be taught.
The mere recitation of a mantra at a sacred ford during an eclipse of the moon or sun, in a field of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra), or in a temple of Śiva, is called "instruction" (upadeśa).
Now, the instruction of the Kaulikas:
Having first performed the array of ritual placements (*nyāsajāla*), and having established the conch-vessel and other implements, one should worship the Goddess, immersed in the five *makāras*.
Having placed that causal principle (kāraṇa) at the beginning of the mouth [of the mantra], one should subsequently utter the vidyā.
O Maheśānī, this Kaulika instruction has thus been declared.
If one should give by an improper method, or he who receives by an improper method—
whether giving or receiving— there will be a curse upon the family.
Both teacher and disciple should examine one another thoroughly;
for he who either receives or gives instruction that is contrary to the scriptures [is at fault].
Both of them shall experience twenty-one terrible hells—
that foolish-minded person who imparts instruction without having performed the purificatory rites.
And those mantras perish like seeds of śāli rice sown in sandy soil;
the knowledge of an unworthy mantra never endures.
Therefore, one should speak only after careful examination; otherwise, it would be fruitless.
This knowledge is taught only to a true disciple who is devoted.
The practitioner of the vow constantly attains that [result], just as ghee is obtained from cow's milk;
however, if one should initiate an unworthy person out of desire for wealth, fear, greed, or other such motives, [the result is lost].
One incurs the curse of the deity, and what has been performed becomes distorted;
now he describes the sequence for the worship of the mantra obtained in a dream.
O Great Goddess, the mantras of the dream are indeed established in three ways:
the wheel in Pātāla, the wheel of Bhuvarāṭ, and the wheel of Svargatāṇḍava.
In heaven, O Goddess, there is the second [city] called Tripura;
first is Virāṭ, and then, O Goddess, Śivatāṇḍava itself.
The third is called Tripura; there, the dream-mantras are situated in three ways.
Those who have reached their end right there are within the scope of the Virāṭ-cakra.
O Great Goddess, ending with the weapon-mantras (astra), they fall within the scope of Śiva’s Tandava;
situated in the center of the Tripura-cakra, they become like fire and desire.
These mantras, O Goddess of gods, have become accessible on earth through eagerness; indeed, they were taught by Śiva via the path of dreams.
But listen now with diligence, O Goddess, to their characteristics;
listen now to the characteristics of the mantras of the Pātālacakra.
O Pārvatī, listen to the description of collyrium, the protection of the pill, the command, the accomplishment, as well as the Śiva-tāṇḍava and the circle.
The accomplishment of the sword-demon (khaḍgavetāla) and the entry into another's body,
as well as the power to move through all things moving and stationary, and likewise the eightfold [attainments] beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
O Pārvatī, listen to the characteristics of the Tripurā-cakra and its mantras;
within the mandala of the Tripurā-cakra, there is no hardship for one’s heart’s desire.
Having become a lord of the sixty siddhis on earth, in heaven,
and on the ground, what indeed should be performed there, and what kind of maṇḍala should exist there?
O Śiva, O Mahādeva, where the seer, the meter, and so forth, as well as the meditation, the seat, the ritual placement (nyāsa), and so on, have not been stated, how can those [elements] exist there?
For the mantra obtained in a dream, Śiva is declared to be the Ṛṣi;
Gāyatrī is the metre, and the deity is proclaimed to be the nature of consciousness (Cidrūpa).
The seed-syllable begins with *ka*, the vowels are the power (*śakti*), and the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is considered the pin (*kīlaka*).
The seat (*pīṭha*) is the seat of the Mother-letters (*mātṛkāpīṭha*); meditation and the rest are as described for the Mother-letters.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) by reciting the root mantra six times.
O Great Goddess, Dakṣamūrti is the supreme lineage obtained in a dream.
One should worship Dakṣiṇāmūrti as the Guru, O Maheśvarī;
his Guru is Viṣṇu, and his Guru is the four-faced Brahmā.
Thus, Śaṅkara has been declared as that Guru; this is considered the lineage of Gurus (gurukrama).
By what means could there be a warding off of the defect of birth-impurity (sūtaka) for one who has [attained] this?
Tell me that, O Mahādeva: one should draw an auspicious eight-petalled lotus;
having placed a water-pot in its center, one should indeed place [the deity] there in reverse order.
Having written the mantra itself with saffron on a banyan leaf,
one should place a water-pot in front and then instill the vital breaths (prāṇas) of the Guru.

O Goddess, the prevention of birth-impurity (sūtaka) resulting from receiving [the mantra] from the presence of a guru is said to render the mantra dead, even without the performance of the preliminary rite (puraskriyā).
Therefore, one should perform the preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) for the pacification of death and birth impurities;
for that mantra which is endowed with consciousness is a true mantra that bestows success.
O Goddess, there is the consciousness of the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), the consciousness of the guru,
the consciousness of the yantra, and likewise the consciousness of the mantra.
Salutation to the consciousness of the Guru, and salutation to the [individual] consciousness; salutation to the triad of consciousnesses.
He who is devoid of this triad of consciousness, even if accompanied by mantras, is certainly not a bestower of success.
If no specific preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*) is prescribed, one should perform a recitation (*japa*) of ten thousand times;
for mantras up to twenty-two syllables, ten thousand recitations are proclaimed.

Thereafter, O Maheśānī, the Great Goddess [performed] a thousand [offerings] to Gajāntaka; according to the ritual procedure, this is considered to be performed from the three parts [of the body] obtained in the dream.

Recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), and feeding Brahmins— this triad is considered the duty of Brahmins. Now, the sequential abandonment of a teacher who is undiscriminating and so forth, of an enemy-mantra, and of a deity that yields undesirable results, as well as [the abandonment] of what is obtained through dreams and the like, is described.
The Śrī Devī said: O Blessed One, O God, Lord of Gods, if mantras are given by a wise teacher out of greed, one suffers misery because of that.
Then what should be done by a god so that happiness arises,
and by which happiness may be obtained both in this world and in the next?
Īśvara said:
O Goddess, in the Kali age, gurus are generally possessed by greed, while disciples are seekers of pleasure; therefore, that [union] is never attained by either of them.
Generally, the grasping of mantras results only in suffering;
therefore, I shall fully explain that which has been concealed in all the tantras.

Distraction results from defects in the mantra; being tormented by the faults of the guru [results from defects in the disciple]; mental anguish and physical illness result from defects in the deity. Therefore, one should avoid that [defective deity].
I shall describe the procedure for the renunciation of mantras, by which liberation is attained;
having recognized a learned Brāhmaṇa who is thoroughly proficient in the tantras.
Having gone to his house in the morning, one should report one's own suffering;
thereafter, he should perform the supreme rite of renouncing the mantra.
Having become pure and composed, on an auspicious day,
the preceptor should commence the excellent rite for the destruction of all suffering.
There, having first entered the temple, the wise one should sequentially perform the rite of initiation; he should place the water-pot in the pavilion and fill it with auspicious waters.
Having invoked the chosen deity there by reciting the mantra in reverse order,
and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and worship, one should worship the attendant deities (āvaraṇas).
Having thus worshipped the deity of the mantra along with its protective covering,
the practitioner should offer a thousand oblations of cow's ghee using the mantra in reverse order.
Then, having offered one hundred and eight oblations to the Lord with the mantra "brahmārpaṇam," he should thereafter present the bali offering to the deities.
O Indra, lord of the gods, O Śatamanyu, husband of Śacī, come from the cardinal and intermediate directions, from below and above, with barley-meals and milk-rice!
Salutations to you; accept this offering of flowers, incense, and so forth.
Come here, O Lord, by your splendor, O bestower of strength like the fire that carries the oblation.
Accept these flowers, lamps, and other offerings presented as a bali; O Lord of the Pretas, depart from this place where people gather in joy.
Having accepted this offering and portion, be well-pleased and grant me boons.
Homage to you, O Lord of the Rākṣasas; you, Nirṛti, have come here.
Accept this offering, worship, and so forth, presented by me with devotion;
O Lord of the Western Quarter, Lord of Waters, homage be to you!
Accepting this worship offered with devotion, may you attain happiness;
O Prabhajana, protector of life, come here along with your retinue.
"Accept with respect this offering (bali) presented by me according to the prescribed rite;
O Kubera and Lord of the Stars (Soma), you two best of gods, understand this!"
May you both, being pleased by offerings of flowers, incense, and the like, become the bestowers of boons upon me;
for you alone, O Blessed One, Lord of all sciences, are indeed the Sovereign.
Honored with flowers, incense, and other offerings, be pleased for the sake of the prosperity of existence; O Brahmā, Lord of all worlds, come to this worship!
Seize all obstacles and turn them back; homage be to you!
Come, O unmanifest bestower of boons, leader of Viṣṇu and of the universe.
"Worshipped with supreme devotion, may you become the bestower of happiness upon me;
thereafter, one should worship the mantra-deity along with his retinue."
Then, with the mantra recited in reverse order and accompanied by offerings of flowers and incense,
the wise one should pray to the deity of the mantra who has been thus worshipped.
This mantra, which brings about suffering, was undertaken by me with a wavering mind that failed to consider its suitability and other factors; therefore, remove its defect.
May my evil be destroyed and may eternal welfare prevail;
may auspiciousness spread for me, as well as purifying devotion.
Having thus offered this prayer, one should write the mantra and yantra in reverse order with pure camphor and sandalwood paste, and then perform worship.
Having placed [the vessel] upon the *kalaśa* with supreme devotion,
one should bind that *yantra* to one's own head and [sprinkle] it with the water from the jar.
One should again fill it completely with water from the pitcher purified by mantras;
having cast the mantra into its midst, one should then fill it once more.
He should cast that pitcher into the water of a river or into another pure reservoir,
and then the brahmin should satisfy [the recipient] according to his ability.
For one who has performed this rite, which is difficult to obtain, the afflictions of the mind perish without a doubt; gradually, clarity of consciousness arises.
Thus endowed, that family is born and grows progressively.
Having spoken thus, the renunciation of the human is described, as well as the renunciation of the Guru.
On whichever lunar day (tithi) a mantra belongs to a particular deity, the observer of the vow should perform that rite on that day;
he should then make a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) regarding the abandonment of the guru, preceded by the acknowledgment of the fault.
And having reflected upon another Guru, whether a human or even a deity,
who is thoroughly purified by the *rāśikūṭa* from among the eight deities;
In that regard, one should have a single guru; in the absence of a predecessor, one may follow a lineage. At the beginning, however, are Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Sūrya, Candra, and Hutāśana.

The deity of the mantra-enclosure, the deity of the lineage, the Lord of the family, and the deity of the locality—these are for the sake of the eightfold [perfection]; or else, a man endowed with auspicious marks [is suitable].
Having worshipped the pair of gurus, one should bow to the two gurus;
one should worship the substance prescribed in the tradition of the deity by its name.
In the right [hand], at the tips of the handfuls of three-leaved Palāśa leaves,
and upon the upward path, he places Kuśa grass blades measuring a span (prādeśa).
A jar full of water in the east, one full of milk in the west, and one full of liquor in the north; these are declared to be the materials for the *āprāya* rite.
Thinking thus— that the consciousness [of the previous] guru has entered into the new guru— one should contemplate the mantra obtained from him.
Having recited the mantra one thousand and eight times,
