one should conclude it with offerings pleasing to the deity, equal in number to the syllables of the mantra.

One should feed Brahmins capable of propitiating the deities with material offerings; in their absence, one should feed those learned in the Vedas, for they are composed of the essence of the Veda through their mantras.
Or one should feed those who have entered that tradition; in its absence, however, one should feed others.
Thus has the renunciation of the Guru been declared, hidden in all the Tantras.
How can one who is himself unaccomplished deliver his disciple?
I shall now declare the abandonment of the deity, which is concealed in all the tantras.
Having performed his daily obligatory rites, he should perform worship to the deity;
thereafter, he should make the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), preceded by the renunciation of the cow and other preliminary acts.
Whether in the absence or in the presence of the guru, one should pray to the deity.
O Lord of the three worlds, Sovereign of the universe, Great Lord,
you whose wondrous peace is inconceivable within the belly of ten million cosmic eggs;
since you, the primordial being, have been meditated upon by me of feeble intellect, [I offer] this hundred-fold apology for my transgressions.
Forgive me for this.
O You who are the very form of the Sun, Moon, Fire, Śiva, Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, Śakti, Nārāyaṇa, and the Mountain;
meditated upon by me in the region of Śivāli and worshipped by me—O Blessed One, forgive these hundred offenses of mine.
Neither the Vedas, nor the sages, nor even Sarasvatī herself know you as I do, according to the instructions of my own dull-witted teacher;
yet, having meditated upon you in such a manner, I have committed this offense and have now reaped this suffering, O You who grant relief to those who seek refuge.
I perform meditation with my mind, yet I do not contemplate this infinite [reality] consisting of the syllables of mantra;
for the Vedas proclaim that your form is [this very reality], and that perfection and victory do not arise from external acts such as ritual worship.
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods, one should prostrate once more like a staff;
then, one should offer everything, including the purification with mantras and so forth, to the Guru.
In the absence of that [recipient], one should cause it to be given to a worshiper who is devoted to Him;
furthermore, in all cases, one should perform double the number of recitations (japa) for their benefit.
And as before, one should feed the Brahmins and satisfy the preceptor and others;
thus has the renunciation for the deity been explained by me to you.
O Maheśānī, by reciting the mantra daily during the interval between initiations, one shall not be abandoned even at the end of life; otherwise, by abandoning [the practice], one incurs a curse.

One should perform worship and then recitation; one should always practice recitation with diligence. At the conclusion of worship, one should recite the mantra; one should not recite the mantra alone.
For one who lacks the full consecrations, there are the fivefold offerings of worship.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Procedure for Initiation," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Now he describes the initiation of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka-dīkṣā).
The initiation of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka-dīkṣā) occurs during an eclipse of the moon or sun;
it proceeds through Sundarī, Tāriṇī, and Kālī, and the initiation thus moves through the three [deities].
O Maheśānī, when [the cycle] is gradually complete, Śambhu will gradually come into being;
[this is] the sixfold [system] known as Candrāgnipakṣa, which is intent upon the supreme Nirvāṇa.
Then, O Goddess, through the sixfold origin and the piercing of the wheels (*cakras*),
there arises the realization of one's own wheel-body and the entry into the body of another.
From the knowledge of this, wisdom arises; thus has initiation been described by me to you.
O Maheśvarī, listen first to the Drāviḍa [initiation] as it is being proclaimed.
O Śivā, [the goddesses] are Cakrāgnī, Rasarājñī, and then Mahārājñī;
O Śivā, [then] Mahākāmakalākālī and Guhyakālī.
Guhyakālī is said to be twofold, namely Sakalā and Niṣkalā in sequence;
the ten-faced one is called Sakalā, or she is the creative power (kalā).
She is proclaimed to be threefold— fierce, gentle, and exceedingly cruel—
and she is celebrated through the divisions of Kālī as Niṣkalā, Guhyā, and Saṃśantā.
This alone would become the wisdom of Medhā, taking the form of universal sovereignty;
likewise, [the mantras] of Candra, Agni, the Vedas, and the five syllables, as well as Nīlā, follow in sequence.
Haṃsatārā is Mahānīlā; at its end is Cīnaśāmbhavī.
Kevalā indeed becomes Medhā, who effects the two kinds of Siddhi and Ṛddhi.
The initiation of the divine imperial sacrifice is proclaimed as threefold:
it is of divine form, of celestial form, and of mantra-form, possessing great power.
Containing all forms and existing from all time, she is the great empire attained through meditative wisdom;
indeed, the manifoldness of divisions is described according to the sequence of accomplishment and supernatural power.
The initiation known as Vidyārājyā is prescribed in the ritual of Chinnamastā;
likewise, there are the Candravahnī, Rasā, Raktā, Śyāmā, and the Ṣoḍaśī.
Beyond the sixfold [set] is the seventeenth; that which is unborn is the supreme (parā).
Bestowing the kingdom of the Vidyās and so forth, she is Dīpinī and Mālinī according to the Kullākrama.
O Maheśānī, the supreme sovereignty of Vagalā consists of the moon, the Vedas, Sūkṣma, and Meru; it is the interior of Śivā, devoid of mantra.
The Heart-mantra, the hundred-syllabled mantra, the five-syllabled mantra, and likewise the Kullukā;
by means of the sequential application of the Gāyatrī, one upholds imperial sovereignty and the state of the Supreme Lord.
Endowed with these five and possessing the consciousness of universal sovereignty,
the Śrī Divya Sarvasāmrājya initiation becomes supreme over all.
Even beyond that, O Goddess of Gods, there is no initiation within the sphere of the universe;
nor are there the tenfold divisions of the Vidyās born from the divisions of the Mahāvidyās.
The various branches of Siddhividyā, as well as the great mantras,
O Goddess of Gods, along with their ancillary mantras, the Śāvara, and the Deśaśāvara.
O Goddess, there is Kālaśāvaraka as well as Siddhaśāvara;
likewise, there are the mantras of the threefold vision (tridhādarśana) which arise from the sequence of the sacred tradition (āmnāyakrama).
O Śivā, in the Kali age, from the Ūrdhvāmnāya, there are the Kādi, Hādi, and Kahādi [traditions],
as well as the mantras of the āyatanas and whatever collection of mantras exists.
O Goddess of gods, one shall possess all authority in this ritual of initiation;
one who is endowed with this initiation is Śrī Kālikā herself.
p.
51a) In due order during the watches [of the day], she assumes the nature of the ten Vidyās;
these are the Vidyās known as Kāmakalā and their various divisions, who are the presiding deities of the functions.
Likewise, O Maheśānī, its limb-mantras and other mantras pertaining to its weapons are always present;
there is the Krama-initiation and the five Vidyās according to their excellent divisions.
O Śivā, the limb-mantras, the Gāyatrī, and the Kullukā— these five are declared in the ritual procedure for other vidyās as the most secret of secrets.
O Goddess, if a base practitioner attempts to unite [the disciple] without the gradual initiation (kramadīkṣā),
he becomes impoverished, a great sinner, and a stealer of his own sons.
O Goddess, if a base practitioner should attempt to unite [the disciple] with Śrīvidyā, Kālikā, Tārā, or Parameśvarī without the Krama initiation, [he incurs sin].
He is poor, most terrible, devoid of fortune, and censured;
he is blind, one-eyed, humpbacked, lame, impotent, and afflicted with leprosy.
May he be afflicted by all diseases and overwhelmed by mental anguish;
may he be a stealer of sons, a stealer of wives, a destroyer of daughters, and a ruiner of kingdoms.
Alternatively, the mantra may become agitated and repeatedly cause distress;
one incurs the curse of the deity, and poverty shall always prevail in that person's home.
O Goddess of the gods, by this distinction, one who steals women is always incapacitated;
however, one who is endowed with the Krama initiation certainly becomes a king.
Endowed with great majesty, possessed of all perfections,
victorious, disciplined, virtuous, accomplished, the bestower of accomplishment, and auspicious.
With a joyful soul, the knower of all, the seer who knows the three times, the leader,
the lord of ten million perfections, the hero, the beautiful one, and the enchanter of desire.
The self of bliss, the supreme self, who has conquered that which transcends the qualities,
he is the manifest Lord of the Kings of Kings, equal to Mahākāla in the Kali age.
For one who worships this knowledge, poverty and wretchedness may occasionally arise due to being bereft of a guru,
the abandonment of the Krama, and separation from the oral tradition.
Poverty shall first prevail; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Wherever the house of the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) exists, it is adorned by jewels.
There is a staircase composed of the nine jewels, encompassing all forms of sovereignty; there is a forest of wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa) as well as a forest of pārijāta trees.
Where indeed could there be poverty for one who touches such a rampart?
Therefore, for one devoid of merit, there is poverty at every step.
Having approached a Guru who is endowed with the lineage, the wise one should request the Krama;
otherwise, through delusion regarding the Guru, he shall incur poverty.
Or he may become short-lived, O Goddess; there is no need for deliberation on this point. Having erased the writing of fate, one proceeds from its exhaustion.
In this manner, the Guru should perform the initiation and the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣecana),
without which consecration the practitioner does not attain the state of complete awakening.
One does not attain the status of an Ācārya nor the desired higher state;
therefore, the Guru, having instructed his beloved disciple, should perform the consecration.
Even Śiva, though he is Śiva, remains in the form of a bound soul (paśu) without the full consecration;
likewise, one who lacks the full consecration may seek to unite with Kālī or Tārā.
O Pārvatī, I shall take away his ritual efficacy; such a man becomes deranged, even without having received the full consecration or the duty toward the Guru.
Neither recitation, nor likewise fire-offering,
nor worship is ever complete for a Kaulika who dies while deprived of the Pūrṇābhiṣeka.
O Goddess of gods, one attains the state of a piśāca until the dissolution of the universe; therefore, the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) is prescribed for the ritual of the ten vidyās.
Staying in the previously mentioned pavilion, intent on meditation upon the Guru,
one should perform the rite of sowing the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) and the Vāstuyāga on the day before [the main ceremony].
Having carefully constructed a sacrificial pit according to the prescribed rules with devotion,
and having performed the fire-oblation, one should honor and worship the venerable lineage of gurus with due respect.
On the altar, the preceptor should reverently worship his chosen deity and the three [gurus],
as well as the powers of the gurus (guru-śaktis), honoring them with garments and ornaments.
O Śivā, O Maheśānī, the fourfold lineage of one's own gurus consists of the divine current (divyaugha), the accomplished current (siddhaugha), and the human current (mānavaugha).
Expert in the ritual of consecration,
Pārvatī, preceded by its performance, diligently performed the two types of ablutions as prescribed.
With the application of the five sprouts, as well as dūrvā grass and bilva fruits,
one should reverently sprinkle the disciple with Vedic and Tantric mantras.
O Great Goddess, this alone is remembered as the sequence of the complete initiation (pūrṇadīkṣā);
everything else, O Great Goddess, falls within the scope of the chapter on initiation.
Having constructed a vast and beautiful pavilion,
one should place a jar filled with a khārī of water in the center of the mandala.
Having duly placed other jars, endowed with jewels, cloth, and gold, upon the petals, one should invoke the eight deities therein.
Having worshipped the deities of the limbs and the surrounding enclosures at the center and the ends,
the preceptor should touch the central jar and recite as follows:
Then, with that water, the Guru sprinkles the disciple with the four Vedas along with their auxiliary branches; this is the "Full Consecration" (pūrṇābhiṣecana).
From the Vedas all the Tantras [arose], and from the Tantras likewise the Mantras;
since they were born from that, the disciple is the sole vessel for all mantras.
One may bear the name of an Ācārya, yet the Guru may bestow another name;
he who receives initiation from such a person shall indeed possess spiritual accomplishment (siddhi).
He becomes capable of bestowing all mantras;
all the gods are under his control, and his path is that of the Vedas, characterized by purity.
This very same procedure shall apply to the path of the Tantra known as Dakṣiṇā;
however, there is a distinction therein: the wise one should fetch waters from various sacred fords (tīrthas).
From the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī; from the great ocean, the Sindhu, Godāvarī, Revā, Kāverī, and Pṛthūdaka.
The water of the Mahānadī, the Vedikā, the Kṣiprā, and the Vetravatī [flows] from Puṣkara to the Sarayū and the Carmaṇvatī, which belong to the wife of Mahendra.
Having offered a water-pot at Kurukṣetra, the Gaṅgā, the Pūrṇā, and Lake Mānasa,
one should recite mantras even those belonging to various tantras.
By those waters, they were consecrated;
these mantras of his are for the purpose of ritual application, or likewise for the purpose of giving to others, or in the left-hand path (vāmaka).
Having placed the *tīrtha*-jar in the center, all other water-jars are considered secondary;
whichever deities were invoked by the preceptor into the liquor-jar [are likewise to be honored].
Those mantras, assuming form, bring their presence into his mouth;
his speech itself becomes perfected, and he shall never bow his head to another.
For one whose head has been bowed for such a purpose, death is certain;
this is the case when one who follows the left-hand path becomes an accomplished master (*siddha*).
And the disciple should be free from egoism, always devoted to the deity;
for the sake of the deity, he should have no concern for the three primal sources (the Vedas) nor any mind for worldly enjoyment.
He alone shall be successful in the Vāmamārga; any other is a vessel for hell, impoverished, miserable, and foolish both in this world and the next.
One should perform the ritual of initiation according to one's capacity and as instructed by the Guru,
using a vessel filled with wine and containing a living fish.
Then, one should perform the consecration with a conch or a jar well-filled with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
using sprouts from the family tree (kulavṛkṣa).
This is proclaimed here as the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) in the Kula path;
the Guru should consecrate the disciple and himself bestow a name upon him.
Having first joined the two-syllable or four-syllable name beginning with "Ānandanātha" followed by "Amuka asi," the Guru should cause him to drink [the nectar].
Just as a woman may pass from her father’s lineage to her husband’s lineage,
so too, through the instruction of the Guru, a Kaula may enter another lineage.
Now it is said, O Great Goddess: the supreme lineage of the Kaulas, which is difficult to find in all the tantras, is proclaimed as that of Śambhu.
This initiation, performed by a preceptor according to the prescribed rite, instantly consumes hundreds of thousands of minor sins and tens of millions of major sins.
Just as iron, when pierced by the lord of mercury (rasendreṇa),
attains the state of gold, so too the self, when pierced by initiation (dīkṣā), certainly attains the state of Śiva.
The Śūdra-ness of the Śūdra has vanished, and the Brahmin-ness of the Brahmin has vanished;
when one is perfected through initiation and purificatory rites, no distinction of caste exists.
Just as Mahādeva is said to be established in liṅgas made of wood, stone, metal, clay, or born of other materials, so too are the castes consecrated [in initiation].
Having performed the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), even if one dies anywhere,
that very person shall take the form of a goddess; that deity shall attain blessedness.
For one who is endowed with the full initiation, whatever nectar there may be,
its ritual application becomes fruitful and the deity is well-pleased.
O Śivā, one who is indeed endowed with the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka), having beheld the mantras, should recite them;
at that very moment he attains perfection—no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Even without a guru, one may perform this recitation for the sake of attaining the status of a Lord of Devas and consecration;
having accomplished that along with its divisions, it is fit to grant me success.
On the paths of the Kaula-avadhūtas, one should not go on pilgrimages,
nor should one practice sitting at sacred fords (tīrthāsana), renunciation (saṃnyāsa), or the observance of religious vows.
One should entirely avoid fasting and shaving the head;
therefore, for one who has received the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka), there is no shaving of the head in that case.
O Great Goddess, even if a Cāṇḍāla should be endowed with the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), he would be a Brahman-sage; there is no need for deliberation on this point.

O Pārvatī, even if he is devoid of the *pūrṇābhiṣeka* and is abandoned by the sages, such a person is declared the lowest of Brahmins; whereas one who has received the consecration is the best of the twice-born.
O Goddess of the gods, in whatever land a master of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) shines,
that region attains blessedness extending ten million yojanas in every direction.
There is no disease, nor indeed death, nor fear of enemies anywhere;
Śiva is declared to be of perfect form, he is indeed Śiva himself—of this there is no doubt.
Whose is the body, and whose are pleasure and pain? Who is born, and who dies, O Goddess? Everything is of the nature of Brahman.
O Goddess, at whatever time one may forget the deity of the mantra, that is declared to be death; for [physical] death is not true death.
For those endowed with the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka), there is indeed authority in all respects;
O Śivā, one who is joined with the full initiation may abandon this pair.
The renunciation of "I-ness" and "mine-ness" is the primary characteristic of awakened intellect;
O Great Goddess, that which is first perceived as "I" is said to be the ego (ahaṃkāra).
And "mine" (mama), O Great Goddess, is said to be the second stage;
one who is devoid of egoism (ahaṃtā) and possessiveness (mamatā) becomes endowed with the complete initiation (pūrṇadīkṣā).
By the recitation of the *kullukā* alone, one obtains the fruit of the complete initiation (*pūrṇadīkṣā*).
Because it is the object of worship for the *kula* of the vidyās, it is therefore celebrated as the *kullukā*.
O Śivā, because she devours the defects associated with knowledge (vidyā),
Kullukā is renowned as the supreme destroyer of all defects.
For those who are joined with the *kullukā* and *jaya*, the accomplishment of the *vidyā* will certainly occur.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Full Consecration," in the *Śrī Tantracintāmaṇi*. 11.
Now, devotion to the guru.
This path, which is the family tradition (kulāgama), has been fully revealed by the Guru;
if it is practiced correctly, it shall be the means for accomplishing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Even one endowed with the qualities of a Brahmin is not praised if he lacks devotion;
whereas even a Mleccha, though devoid of qualities, is called a disciple if he possesses devotion.
For one devoid of devotion to the guru, their knowledge, vows,
and lineage are all as useless as the various ornaments adorning a corpse.
O Goddess, just as devotion should be toward Nārāyaṇa, Mahādeva, one’s mother and father, and the king, so too should it be shown toward the preceptor.
A disciple residing in the same village should prostrate to the guru at the three junctions of the day;
even one residing a *krośa* away should bow to the guru every day.
A disciple who travels half a yojana should prostrate on the five festival days (parvan),
starting from one yojana up to twelve yojanas.
Having traveled that distance of many yojanas along the way,
the disciple, though situated in a distant land, should bow to the Guru with devotion upon arriving in his presence.
One should prostrate to the Guru every month for as many *yojanas* as the distance between them;
however, if the disciple is situated very far away, he should go [to the Guru] whenever he so desires.
One should not approach a king, a deity, or a teacher with empty hands;
one should honor them with fruits, flowers, garments, and so forth, according to one's ability.
One should perform penance in the presence of the guru and must not bathe for the sake of personal purification;
one should not transgress the guru’s command, nor should one speak back to him.
One should never utter unpleasant words, nor especially desire or anger, in the presence of one's teacher with an uncovered mouth at any time.
One should respectfully set aside non-duality, the worship of deities, and the emblems of the Guru— such as the sandals and the yogic belt— in the presence of the Guru.
One should not leap over it, nor touch it, nor keep it within sight; likewise, one should not sleep upon it in a reclining posture, nor stretch out one's feet toward it.
One should not stretch one's limbs, break them, or engage in playful gestures in the presence of the guru; one should not step over his shadow, nor walk in front of him.
One should not display one's power in the presence of the guru, nor should one gather disciples;
one should not harbor egoism, nor should one assume a body with auspicious marks.
If one born in the lineage should, through negligence, fail to perform the oath known as "Guru" or the one known as "Śiva," [the following applies].

For that purpose, one should strive with effort to complete it at the end with worship, recitation, and burnt offerings; for if the task is not completed, the oath for which it was undertaken has failed.
One should perform a thousand-fold recitation of the mantra known as Mūla as an expiation for Manu;
one should not give instructions to the Guru, nor should one speak with the intent of bestowing [one's own] life-force.
In addressing or speaking to him, one should say, "Śrīnātha Deva Svāmī.
Likewise, [one should perform] the giving of loans, the giving of material objects, and the buying and selling of goods.
A disciple desiring prosperity should never act in opposition to his gurus;
O Ambikā, he who, while the guru is present, should worship another, [is a transgressor].
One goes to a terrible hell and that worship becomes fruitless;
whatever substance the Guru has a desire for, one should not obtain it [for oneself].
If you should certainly desire it, let it be according to his command;
for he who accepts even a very small amount of a guru’s property that has been given by me [is not at fault].
Having entered the womb of an animal, he will be devoured by carnivorous beasts in the Kali age;
likewise, one who covets the property of his guru and is eager to violate the wife of his guru [shall suffer the same].
He would undoubtedly fall; no atonement exists for him who causes his guru, his station, the tradition, or its dharma to deviate from their source.

That sinner, having committed such an act, must be expelled by the teachers, punished, or even executed. [He is forbidden from using] the sandals, the seat, the garment, the vehicle, the parasol, and the fly-whisks.
Having seen [the Guru], one should pay him homage; one should not employ him for the sake of his own enjoyment.
O Dear One, one should not practice negligence regarding tasks that have been commanded or those that have not yet been stated.
Whatever the Guru may say, whether it be good or bad, that should be carried out without hesitation;
even after committing a hundred murders of Brahmins, one must fulfill the Guru’s command.
Whether in matters of punishment or favor, the Guru is the cause for everyone;
whatever has issued from the mouth of the Guru is called the scripture.
Disobedience of commands, embezzlement of wealth, acting against the teacher's wishes,
and treachery toward the teacher— one who would utter such things is a sinner.
O Goddess, one should not sit upon a seat in the presence of the deity or the Guru;
even if one is distinguished by birth, learning, or wealth, one should joyfully rise from afar upon seeing the Guru.
One should not harbor pride on account of birth, wealth, or other such factors;
one incurs that very sin through speaking falsehoods in the presence of a guru.
Having committed the killing of a cow or a Brahmin,
one shall not incur that sin by performing a single prostration with the staff and circumambulating three times.
But when there is a conjunction with that guru’s own guru, O beloved, one should salute the *praguru* (the great-grand-guru);
then one should bow to the [current] guru, and he too should prevent [further salutation] in the presence of his own guru.
In the presence of his preceptor’s preceptor, a disciple should honor his own guru mentally;
even if the words spoken by the guru are harsh, he should not harbor them in his heart as a curse.
Even if struck by him, one should remember with serene devotion;
one should offer everything suitable for enjoyment to the Guru as objects fit for his use.
Thinking, "This is the remainder of that," one should accept it with joy at his command;
yet, he who disregards the Guru who has bestowed even a single syllable [is lost].
Having undergone a hundred births, he shall attain the state of a Cāṇḍāla;
likewise, one who perceives the Guru as a mere human, or the Sage within the syllables of the mantra.
One who perceives a stone as an image shall go to hell;
the Guru’s wife, his son, and his elder brother are equal to the Guru.
They regard their juniors as themselves and protect them like their own children.
Now he describes the practice of the right-hand path (*dakṣiṇācāra*).
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"In this terrible Kali age, those who are arrogant because they have achieved only slight accomplishments [abound]."
For those future people, how can there be stable accomplishment?
O Treasure of Compassion, please tell me how the practitioner attains liberation— how there is growth from the tip of the lineage onwards, as well as divine grace within that lineage.
Īśvara said:
Through the abandonment of egoism and the avoidance of actions performed for the sake of desire, [one attains liberation].
By practicing one's own dharma, everything arises without effort.
If one is unable to do this, one should at least avoid what is forbidden;
by performing the prescribed duties, one shall attain success extending to one's sons and grandsons.
In that regard, I shall first describe what is prohibited along with the prescribed rules:
[one should not practice] in a temple, in the abode of a guru, in a cremation ground, or at a crossroads.
One should avoid shoes, seats, excrement, urine, and sexual intercourse;
and one should face toward auspicious cattle, a teacher, deities, fire, a treasury, or a book.
One should not be indolent regarding the preliminary rites, nor should one transgress these [rules]:
laziness, intoxication, delusion, curses, backbiting, and strife.

One should avoid envy, malice, pride, and the censuring of others; likewise, one should avoid those who merely bear the marks of an ascetic, those who observe vows for show, and Brahmins who are ignorant of the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the Saṃhitās.

One should not disparage the Purāṇas, the Agamas, the Śāstras, nor the Kalpas; likewise, one should not find fault with the Yuga, the Kuśa grass, the stone, the water-pot, the Bṛhī grain, or the mortar.
The sun, the broom, the staff, the banner, the musical instrument,
the weapon, the water-pot, the chowrie, the parasol, the mirror, and likewise the ornament.
Whatever other objects of enjoyment there may be, whatever excellent materials,
and whatever items in great places or in temples of the deities;
One should not step over objects declared divine by the gods, nor those inhabited by spirits; one should not cross over them, nor should one touch them.
One should never engage in any social gathering that is despised by the world, which spreads according to one's own whims, and whose nature is to cause harm to others.
One should not accept gifts out of a desire for one's own enjoyment;
rather, one should strive to acquire wealth for the sake of honoring the deities and guests.
One should not cross the shadow of the *vibhītaka*, *karañja*, *arka*, or *snuhī* trees,
nor that of pillars, lamps, humans, or other living beings.

One should avoid from afar the touch of water that has been stirred up by the tips of nails or hair, or that has come from bathing-cloths or rags; likewise, one should avoid the touch of donkeys, dogs, and aquatic creatures.
One should not eat the remains of offerings (nirmālya) from the location of the *liṅga*, nor should one step over them;
one should either cast everything into a river or give it to one who has received Śiva-initiation (*śivadīkṣita*).
One should never utter speech that causes distress to the world, that cuts into the vital points [of others], or that causes agitation regarding one's livelihood.
One should never adopt an attire that, though beautiful, brilliant, and even desired by the mind, is loathed by the world.
By practicing with devotion the rules of conduct prescribed in the tantras, which are appropriate for this world and the next, the initiated person attains perfection.
Practitioners should never employ their own mantra for the sake of protecting others' common accomplishments, even in times of great calamity.
Wherever one hears reproach of the Guru arising from his envy,
one must not wear clothes there; out of negligence, one should remember Hari.
One should not dwell in that place where there is censure of Viṣṇu, Śiva, the scripture, the Veda, the Sun, Gaṇeśa, or Bhavānī.
One should not harm another's wife by deed, thought, or word;
he is to be honored with salutations when initiated for the rites of cursing or bestowing grace.
Neither a mantra, nor a mudrā, nor even the samayas should be disclosed by him.
It is proclaimed that three types of actions are to be performed by one who has attained mastery over the mantra.
There are daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites; among these, the daily is explained first.
[One should worship] the deity and the preceptor, the place of the preceptor, the sacred field (kṣetra), and the presiding deities of that field.
One should utter the word "Śrī" before the names of the Siddhas and those consecrated as Siddhas;
one should maintain uprightness, truthfulness, good character, equanimity, and fortitude.
Having prostrated before the sandals of the Guru, one should always perform peaceful activities, acts of compassion, and divine powers, as well as going and coming.
Subsequently, having prostrated before the teacher's house, he should depart with his right foot first,
being free from impurities such as mucus and the like, and having shaved his hair and beard.
One should meditate upon the deity Viṣṇu, who resides within the moon and the sun and stands amidst the rays of light, as the Guru for the bodies of Brahmins and embodied beings.
One must always maintain secrecy regarding the mantra for the sake of its accomplishment;
one should not utter the name of the guru, but should address him as "the Subduer."
Oṃ; first the name of the Guru, followed by the name of the deity, joined with the word "pāda" (feet), and accompanied by palms joined above the head.
O Supreme Goddess, one should give food while reciting the name of Hari as a debt to the guest; this is declared to be the practice of the right-hand path (dakṣiṇācāra).
Now he describes the family tradition (*kulācāra*).
Next, I shall explain the determination of the meaning of the scriptures regarding the path of the family tradition (*kulācāra*):
if one born into a Kaula family is the eldest [son] yet has not been initiated;
If the youngest [brother] has been initiated, he may perform the family worship (kulapūjana).
At the conclusion of the worship, having taken the remnants (śeṣa) and bowed to the eldest, he should offer them.
The younger brother should take his leftovers; this is the settled rule.
When the Guru, an elder, or one worthy of worship has arrived in the midst [of the assembly], he too should be honored.
One should not speak of one's own station; one should perform the remaining rites with his permission.
One should perform the daily worship during the day and the occasional worship at night.
When many have gathered together at the prescribed time for the worship performed for specific desires,
they should bow to their respective gurus and perform the libation (tarpaṇa) according to their own respective traditions.
One should not perform the family worship without the destruction [of obstacles], without bathing, without perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains, and without liquor and meat.
One should not consume intoxicants after eating without performing worship with mantras;
likewise, one should not drink without using a vessel, nor should one offer worship with only one hand.
One should not perform the Śrīcakra ritual alone, nor should one worship using a single vessel; nor should one perform the rite with only one hand, nor should one discharge saliva upon the Cakra.
Having prostrated, one should enter the *cakra*, and having prostrated again, one should depart.
One should never remain upon a seat nor in the *vīrāsana* posture within the *Śrīcakra*.
The sight of the Śrīcakra destroys the sins of men's eyes;
if that [sight] is absent, the pair of eyes of a Kaulika is merely a pair of sores.

One should contemplate all those who follow improper conduct as being of good conduct, situated within the wheel and bearing the power of the balance, perceiving them with the thought that they are Śiva and Gaurī; one should never despise them.
Having gone to the house of the family preceptor, one should with devotion request either nectar or food for the purification of sins; in the absence of that, one should drink water.
The disciple should respectfully accept the vessel offered by the family preceptor according to his own capacity;
having paid homage, he should take it, for otherwise he would go to hell.

One who wears a turban, one wearing a bodice, one who is naked, one with disheveled hair, one who has not bathed, one who has overeaten, one who is quarrelsome, and one who is turned away [from the teacher] have been so described.

This [fault] does not apply to one born in a noble family, nor to one who has undergone the purificatory rites and is twice-born; yet even such a person, though a student of the Vedas, may become destitute through the consumption of the family’s wealth.
By spitting the nectar of yoga, by wandering around a vessel of liquor,
and by drinking through an upward-pointing stalk, one incurs the curse of the deities.
Those who sit upon a single seat, eat from a single vessel,
and drink from a single bowl, always go to hell.
Those who serve the family property when the Guru resides in a single village,
as well as the one born in that family, his son, and the eldest spiritual preceptor of the lineage;
Without permission, that evil-souled one shall go to the Raurava hell;
likewise for the recitation of the Dharmaśāstra and the pursuit of a woman of noble family.

The non-performance of Vedic rites and association with those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) lead to the destruction of desire, wealth, longevity, fame, freedom from greed, knowledge, happiness, and so forth.
One should not engage in verbal dispute even with an enemy in the midst of the assembly;
one should regard the person who speaks as equal to one's father or mother and honor them.
The wise man, having bowed with devotion to the venerable Guru, the Kula scriptures, and whatever places of worship there may be, should recite their names preceded by the word "Śrī."
The lineage transmission, the traditional teachings, the mantras, the conduct, and so forth—all these, when obtained from the family of the Guru, become fruitful; otherwise, they are not.
One should worship the Śrīśāstra daily and cast it out from the house of the bound soul (paśu).

One should enjoy one's own wife as if she were one's own self, and one should avoid all other women as if they were the wives of others; likewise, one should follow the scriptures of one's lineage while avoiding all others.

For the sake of ritual refinement, one should recite Vedic mantras according to tradition, even if they are broken, divided, or have their syllables disordered; by means of these, there shall be stability in this matter.
That practice which is contrary to the Dharmaśāstras is indeed Kaulika;
one should have these fashioned by means of the Cakra, and if they are obtained by chance, one should worship them.
One must never engage in sexual intercourse; having done so, one would fall into hell.
[This applies to] one's mother, the wife of a guru, a sister, and a sister’s daughter.
The wife of a brother, the wife of a hero, a maiden,
one observing a vow, one with missing limbs, one with deformed limbs, one who is blind, one who is affectionate, or one who has been brought together [as a captive].

I heard of an old woman who had once been beautiful, yet she was no longer attractive; whereas there was another, in the prime of youth, well-attired and smiling charmingly, who was truly captivating.
One should worship the dark-complexioned Kaulika lady whose eyes have reddish corners;
however, one should not forcibly approach a Kulayoginī without her consent.
In the center of the wheel, one should become hungry and thus a petitioner for a dwelling;
[one sees] raw meat, a jar of liquor, an intoxicated elephant, and the vision of a perfected being (siddha).
The mango tree, the aśoka tree, a playful girl, a greedy maiden,
a solitary tree, a cremation ground, and even a multitude of women.
And upon seeing a woman dressed in red garments, one should salute her with devotion; likewise, one should salute the elder and younger sons of the Guru’s consort, as well as the family preceptors.
The scriptures that reveal the Kula, the Kula substances, the practitioners of the Kula,
as well as the instigators, the indicators, the reciters, and likewise the observers.

[One should honor] students, teachers, male and female yogis, perfected beings (siddha-puruṣas), virgins, young maidens, those who have not yet experienced sexual intercourse, and even women who are mad.
One should not criticize, nor loathe, nor laugh at, nor honor anyone; one should not speak unpleasantness or untruth to any bad yogi whatsoever.
Even if she is ill-favored, I do not revile a woman of noble family as "black";
for such a name would bring ruin upon devoted wives and heroes alike, regardless of what has been done or left undone.
One should not look at a woman who has fallen from her status, one who is naked, one who is insane, or one whose breasts are exposed;
one should not serve a woman during the day, nor should one gaze upon her private parts.
One should not strike a woman even with a flower, even if she has committed a hundred offenses;
one should not enumerate the faults of women, but rather manifest their virtues alone.
The Kulayoginīs always reside within the Kulavṛkṣa trees;
one should not eat from their leaves, and especially not from the leaves of the Arka tree.
One should not personally perform any harm beneath one's family tree;
having seen it, one should bow with devotion and never cut it down.
Śleṣmātaka, karañja, akṣa, nimba, aśvattha, kadamba,
bilva, vaṭa, udumbara, and viṃcā— these are remembered as the ten [trees].

In the Kaula tradition, one should avoid these five: performing expiatory rites (prāyaścitta), falling from a height (bhṛgoḥ pātaḥ), renunciation (saṃnyāsa), observing ascetic vows (vratadhāraṇa), and going on pilgrimages to sacred sites (tīrthayātrādigamana).
Sin is public for the Kaula, external for the Śaiva, but within the community for the Vaiṣṇava;
however, O Goddess, one should conceal the Kaula [teaching] like the water inside a coconut fruit.
The wise person should reveal the Guru, but guard the mantra with effort;
through revealing it or not revealing it, one's prosperity and lifespan are diminished.
One who has fallen away from all proper conduct should take refuge in the conduct of his own family;
one who has fallen away from the conduct of his family shall go to the Raurava hell.
A true guru should indeed explain the left-hand practice (vāmācāra) to one of noble lineage;
however, if a disciple falls away from that practice, both he and his guru become sinners.
Devoted to the welfare of all beings, observing the conduct of the samaya,
having abandoned impermanent activities, he is intent upon the constant performance of his duties.
One who offers all ritual actions to another deity,
worships with another mantra, or has faith in the worship of another mantra [is at fault].
A woman of noble family who reviles a hero and steals his property will herself likewise become such that the entire world appears as consisting only of women.

One who strives with a disciplined mind should contemplate all things as the form of a young woman: drinks, foods to be chewed, those to be sucked, those to be eaten, those to be licked, the home, and happiness.
Women are the gods, women are the vital breaths, and women indeed are the ornament;
one should always remain devoted to women, otherwise even toward one's own wife.
One should offer to the deities flowers gathered by one's own hands, water held in one's own hands,
and food prepared by one's own hands.
Upon seeing a young woman of noble birth, one should offer salutation with a concentrated mind,
provided that such a sight of a noble family occurs through the power of fortune alone.
At that very time, one should perform mental worship for them—
whether they be young girls, those intoxicated with youth, or beautiful old women.
Having reviled or paid homage to the Greatly Wicked One, one should meditate upon their blows,
their censure, as well as their deceit and unpleasantness.
In no way should one perform any other rite that obstructs success;
just as milk situated on a cowhide should not be drunk by the best of the twice-born.
Likewise, the Kaulikas should not hear the Dharma from the mouth of an animal;
they should drink the substance without ritual purification and engage in sexual union with the emission of semen.
Having killed an animal with one's own hand, one shall go to the Raurava hell;
likewise for the murder of a hero, the drinking of intoxicants in vain, and the theft of a hero’s property.
Sexual intercourse with the wife of a hero and union with her—
this is declared to be a great sin (mahāpātaka) in the Kula scriptures of the Kaulikas.
Listen, my son, to my secret concerning the origin of the conduct of the observance (samayācāra),
devoid of which one does not attain success even through thousands of millions of births.
This man was a follower of the family scriptures and the traditional conduct of his lineage;
noble-minded, he was everywhere devoted to the practice of Vaiṣṇavism.
One should be patient with the censure of others and always intent on doing good;
whether on a mountain, in a forest, or in a solitary, empty pavilion.
If, by chance, one should find oneself at a crossroads, in water, or in a deserted place,
one should meditate for a moment, recite the mantra, bow down, and then proceed as one pleases.
Having seen a vulture, one should unobserved pay homage to Mahākālī;
likewise, having seen a jackal, one should pay homage to Kṣemaṅkarī and Yamadūtikā.
O Kuraṅgī, Śyenī, Bhūkākī, Kṛṣṇamārjārī,
Kṛśodarī, Mahācaṇḍā, Muktakeśī, and Valipriye!
O beloved of Śaṅkara, whose countenance is serene through family tradition,
having seen a corpse situated in a cremation ground, one should circumambulate it while recollecting the mantra.
By bowing with this mantra, the practitioner shall obtain happiness:
"O you of terrible fangs, of terrifying mouth, who utters the sound 'kiṭi'!"
Homage to you, O dweller in the funeral pyre, who resounds with most terrible cries!
[I offer] red cloth, as well as flowers, a king, and a prince.
Seeing elephants, horses, chariots, weapons, shields, and heroic men,
as well as the buffalo and the lord of the clan, [the goddess] Mahiṣamardinī appeared.
Having prostrated before Jayadurgā, one is not smeared by obstacles;
[salutation] to the Goddess Jaya, the Sustainer of the World, and the three deities of Tripura.
O Goddess, bestower of boons upon your devotees, O slayer of Mahiṣa, salutations to you!
Having beheld a vessel of liquor, fish, meat, and a beautiful woman—
And having seen the goddess Bhairavī,
he prostrated and recited the mantra for the destruction of terrible obstacles and for the prosperity of the family tradition.
I bow to the Goddess who grants boons, adorned with a garland of severed heads;
I bow to her, the granter of boons, who is drenched with streams of blood.
O Goddess who removes all obstacles, salutations to you, O beloved of the bestowers of boons!
If, by fate, they do not perform [this] even upon seeing these [images].
If one prioritizes the mantra of power (śakti-mantra), its accomplishment does not arise;
the Vedas, Śāstras, and Purāṇas become as clear as a courtesan’s limbs.
This Śāmbhavī Vidyā is like a protected noblewoman;
the deities accept the Kaulika practice only when it is well-guarded.
They grant the fulfillment of desires when kept secret, but destroy them through disclosure.
[One should conceal] the family flower, the family substance, the family worship, the family lineage, and the recitation.

One who belongs to the lineage (kulamālin) should never, under any circumstances, reveal the Guru, the head of the lineage (kulapati), the lineage itself, the lineage-cycle (kulacakra), or the lineage-meditation (kuladhyāna).
From disclosure comes the loss of accomplishment; from disclosure comes bondage and the like;
from disclosure comes the loss of power; from disclosure comes the harming of the deity.
O Maheśānī, death may occur if [the practice] is revealed; it must never be disclosed. Even if someone should enter here at the time of worship, [it must remain secret].
One should indeed display the Vaiṣṇavī mudrā, as well as the Viṣṇu-nyāsa and the hymn of praise;
at no time should there be a deficiency in the limbs [of the ritual], nor should it ever be manifest [in its imperfections].
One should never perform worship externally, nor should one ever reveal [one's true nature];
internally Śākta, externally Śaiva, with one's wife one is Vaiṣṇava, and in public one is Āmata.
Heroes assuming various forms wander upon the surface of the earth;
thus has the family tradition known as Dakṣiṇa been described to you, O lady of virtuous vows.
One who desires their own welfare should not speak of this to anyone;
thus he states the requirement of discernment regarding the authority for the path of the Left Family.
One should proclaim the manifest Dharma even to the Kaulikas;
by doing so, one shall attain happiness both in this world and in the next.
A Brahmin, having correctly understood his own status as a Brahmin, should enter [the path];
he must not transgress even the Vāmamārga or the Kaula path therein.

One should not perform the customary practices of one's own respective caste, nor accept gifts from them; furthermore, one should avoid censuring the wives of others, wealth, and the Vedas, Śāstras, and so forth.
The non-restraint of the senses and disobedience toward the teacher and the preceptor must be abandoned with one's whole being; one should remain guarded even when not in the presence of the teacher.
He who lacks association with the virtuous, discernment, and steady eyes is blind; how indeed can such a man obtain happiness?
One should abandon like a goat a worldly person who speaks of himself as "I am a knower of Brahman," whose merit is destroyed, and who has fallen away through fear.
Where liquor, meat, the drinking of wine, fish, women,
and wealth are produced in great abundance, there Vāma bestows a favorable course.
But he who, standing on the right-hand path, eats meat and other such things in secret,
goes to a terrible hell and is born as a worm in excrement.
He who eats meat without an offering, drinks liquor without performing worship,
or approaches a woman without the sacrifice of the *dūtī*, even if he is a practitioner of the Left-hand path (*vāmī*), is destined for hell.
If one practices the family dharma without having learned the conduct of the samaya,
both that guru and that disciple shall quickly become objects of contempt for the yoginīs.
The deluded soul, ignorant of the left-hand path (vāmamārga), desires liberation;
he wishes to cross the shoreless expanse from this side to the other by means of his two arms alone.
Those who are devoid of all ritual actions and free from the distinctions of caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama) are,
in the Kaula or Vāma path, the vessels for both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
May all my kinsmen censure me; may my wife, sons, and others abandon me;
may people laugh at me upon seeing me, or may kings inflict punishment upon me.
Even though I am constantly tormented by disease, poverty, suffering, and the like,
whether Lakṣmī remains or departs, I shall not abandon this [truth].
Thus, he whose devotion is firm shall attain success through the Vāmā [path],
and not from gain of wealth, nor from anger, nor from hatred, nor from envy.
One should not abandon the path one has attained out of desire or even out of fear;
one should worship the Goddess every day, for otherwise one would encounter obstacles on this path.
He who is purified by the compassion of the Guru, whose impurities have been shaken off from his body,
and who is devoted to the worship of the Kula— he alone is a true Kaula, and no other.
One who is out of sight does not know what will happen to whom;
indeed, that alone is the supreme vision which yields its fruit directly before one's eyes.
Some say that great men are those who have received the instructions of their gurus;
yet others, having themselves been previously deluded, delude other people.
Having beheld the beloved’s face, one regards wine as a drink and meat as food;
thus do the supreme ones declare this alone to be the best conduct.
O Umā, if a human being were to attain perfection through the drinking of liquor,
then all those devoted to drinking liquor would become perfected beings.
If a meritorious rebirth were to occur merely by eating meat,
then carnivorous animals would attain liberation, for they eat nothing other than meat.
O Goddess, if liberation were to arise through sexual union with a woman, then everyone would be liberated; who then would be born again?
From walking upon the edge of a sword, from clinging to a tiger’s ear,
and from supporting a serpent— it is certain that [the path] of one's family lineage is impossible to follow.
O Goddess of the Gods, drinking [alcohol] in vain is here called *surāpāna* (the drinking of wine).
That should be known as a great sin (*mahāpātaka*), as it is described in the Vedas and other scriptures.
For the Kaulikas, wine that is without feet, without eyes, without hands, and without things to be drunk— namely, liquor and the meat of animals— brings great fruit.
Indeed, there are eleven types of intoxicants that are impure for the twice-born;
however, the twelfth, the liquor of *surā*, is recorded as the most severe for all of them.
Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, and a Vaiśya shall not drink *surā*;
by the mere sight of *surā*, one should gaze at the sun.

Merely by coming into contact with him, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas); if the contact reaches as far as the knees, it is equivalent to a ritual bath; if it reaches the navel, one must fast for a day.
The rule for touching liquor is that one should fast for three nights;
however, for drinking *surā* intentionally, one must enter a blazing [fire].
If her mouth is scorched by that [act], she shall attain purification;
but he who, O Dear One, kills living beings for his own sake without following the prescribed rule, [is not purified].
A person of wicked conduct shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the body of a beast; thereafter, he is born among the animal species.
One who kills a cow or even a twice-born man according to the prescribed rule is not tainted by the sins of slaughter.
The Kaulika is superior to all, as is the follower of the Urdhvāmnāya who has transcended speech;
he who is endowed with devotion and serves my Guru possesses authority.
That very Kaulika alone is worthy of veneration; others are merely drunkards.
Recollection, chanting of his name, beholding him, and likewise saluting him—[these are the means].
And by engaging in conversation [with him], one obtains a fruit greater than that of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
wherever he dwells, O gods, there shall be prosperity and victory.
Having seen such a person, one should bow to him, while others should avoid him from afar.
The Eastern Tradition is of the nature of emanation; the Southern is of the nature of maintenance;
the Western Tradition is dissolution; and the Northern shall be grace.
They know mantra-yoga as the eastern, bhakti-yoga as the southern,
karma-yoga as the western, and likewise jñāna-yoga as the northern.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Practice Beginning with the Dakṣiṇā," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Now, he explains the sequence beginning with Mahānīla, which is the specific and singular cause for the accomplishment of the mantra within each individual vidyā, such as Śyāmā and the others.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the most secret of secrets:
the tenfold knowledge and so forth, and the sequence of the ten physicians of the Lord."
O Lord, this sequence was previously mentioned; tell it now once again.
Śiva said:
Out of devotion, this most secret of secrets is told to you:
according to the Mahānīla-krama, Kālikā is the bestower of accomplishment.
O Goddess Pārvatī, the Mahānīla-krama is proclaimed to be of two kinds: with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala). Listen now to this sequence.
With a sword in hand and hair perpetually disheveled,
his eyes were rolling with the exhilaration of meat and wine, ever triumphant.
How can that man who does not apply a vermilion tilaka on his forehead nor drink the essence of wine in his hand be a worshiper of me?
That man who does not wander about at night nor worship Śakti at night— how can he be my worshiper?
How can that man who does not perform the act of kissing the vulva and likewise the embracing of the power of action (karma-śakti) be considered my worshiper?
Betel, the vulva-circle, a garland of severed heads, the consumption of corpses, vermilion, a sword, and the essence of youth along with the *saṃvid* wine.
Anyone who abandons this [Goddess] and strives to propitiate Kālī will encounter agitation in this world and shall go to hell in the next.
O Goddess, Tāriṇī is certainly not accomplished by means of two or three [lines];
on the pair of breasts, there is a vermilion dot, and on the forehead, the leaf of the self-born sage (the bilva leaf).
Or else, O Maheśvarī, one should apply a triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) made from red sandalwood, and upon that, a drop of collyrium should be placed.
O Goddess, the Mahānīla-krama is proclaimed as the Tilaka;
it is one who sleeps in the cremation ground, eats flesh, and whose mind rejoices in pure consciousness.
Whether seeing, touching, or approaching a woman at any time, one should perform the recitation;
devoted to a courtesan, staying in a cremation ground, and joined with a soft crest-lock (mṛducūḍaka).
O Goddess, having fashioned a rosary from ivory beads with the upper front tooth as the central bead (meru),
one should always recite the mantra while chewing betel.
Dedicated to the heroic practice (vīrasādhana) consisting of the worship of the skull-bowl as a vessel,
adorned with a garland of skulls, he is intent upon the kissing of women.
Śakti is bliss in the pair of eyes, wine in the mouth, a garland in the courtyard of the house,
and a playful power in the lotus of the vulva within the hand of a courtesan.
Having performed the kiss from the source (yonisaṃcumvana), one should perform recitation at all times;
having brought forth power, this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is to be accomplished.
Free from doubt, joyful in soul, devoted to women, and having conquered his senses—
such a man, O Goddess, is considered fit for the Mahānīla-krama.
Garlands made of ivory, elephants, camels, and horses originate from those who are unattached; for them, there is no [distinction of] parts. Listen to that sequence, O Pārvatī.
Having drunk the milk from the yellow cow, with a mind full of existence, consciousness, and bliss,
and having fashioned a crystal rosary, one should perform the recitation (japa) during the period of leisure.
There is no restriction of direction or time, nor any restriction regarding posture and so forth;
there is no restriction of time for the recitation when practicing the Great Mantra.
In whatever mantra good conduct is found, such is the dharma therein;
one should not entertain doubt regarding that, for it leads to either heaven or even liberation.
O Goddess, having assumed the gentle and soft *cūḍaka* or the *śarvavīrāsana*, or likewise the *yonitogāsana*;
O Goddess, there is the seat of Kāmarūpa and the seat of Muratā;
O Goddess, there is the seat of Siṃdūra and the seat of Parvata.
The lake-seat, the lotus-seat, the victory-seat [formed by] sesame flowers,
the moon-disk, the serpentess, and the kissing-seat.
O Goddess, there is the Prayāgāsana, as well as the Mahāprayāgāsana,
the Sparśakhaṭvāsana, and the Yonicumbanāsana.
O Goddess, the seat of touchlessness, or the seat of wind-touch,
the seat of refuge, O Goddess, as well as the seat of the shaven-headed one;
Or else, Śrīmuṇḍamurata or Śrīvīramurata;
the Goddess occupies the five seats (pañcavīrāsana), with Surendra and the others in the directions in order.
The Goddess said: O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear about the supreme Mahācīnakrama.
Śiva said:
O Goddess, the Mahācīnakrama is now being described by me;
through the Mahācīnakrama alone, Tārā bestows her fruits swiftly.
The Brahmacīna, the Divyacīna, the Vīracīna as the third,
the Mahācīna, and the Anikalaścīna— these five types are recognized.
Mahācīna and Krama are proclaimed as the two kinds of Goddess;
they are the Sakala (with parts) and the Niṣkala (without parts), of which the Sakala is within the sphere of the Buddhists.
O Pārvatī, listen to the second [teaching] for the Brāhmaṇas, which is partless;
it is the supreme essence of essences within the three worlds, consisting of two nines.
The Mahācīnakrama goddess is proclaimed to be of two kinds;
therein, O Goddess of the gods, she becomes the vessel of differentiation due to the three qualities (guṇas).
Purification such as bathing is mental; mental recitation is the most excellent;
worship is divine and mental; and the offering of libations and so forth is likewise mental.
The mental observance (mānasa-niyama) has been declared; the mental cleansing of the teeth (mānasa-dantadhāvana) is likewise prescribed.
All of these are auspicious at all times; there is no time when they are inauspicious.
There is no distinction between day and night, nor at twilight or the dead of night;
purity of mind and body is achieved through water, even without [specific] garments.
One should not perform purification here; the mind should move in a state free from conceptual construction.
Here there is no dependence on purity, nor is there any defilement by impurities and the like.
Whoever should thus contemplate this mantra, which grants the fulfillment of all desires,
his speech in the assembly will become composed of both prose and verse.
Merely by the sight of him, even kings lose their luster before the speaker and submit to servitude; what then of other people?
One should always worship the Goddess, even while unwashed and after having eaten;
at midnight, in a pure place, one should cause an offering (bali) to be presented with the mantra.
One must never harbor hatred toward women; rather, one should especially honor them.
Having placed a large conch shell above the place of recitation, one should perform the *japa*.
Whether approaching a woman, touching, or looking at her anywhere— even on the crown of his head—
after eating betel leaf and other edible substances according to his desire;
Having eaten meat, fish, curd, honey, *saṃvid*, liquor,
and the juice of fruits, or having eaten any other remaining kinds of food, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) after consuming edible [substances].
There is no restriction regarding direction or time, nor any restriction regarding staying in one place and so forth;
there is no restriction regarding the time for recitation, nor regarding worship and other offerings such as bali.
In this practice for the accomplishment of the Great Mantra, the rules regarding one's own will have been stated;
[this includes] the Vallāsana posture, the touching of the feet, the body, and so forth, as well as the water.
O Goddess of gods, having anointed oneself with oil and always chewing betel-leaf,
one should wear various ornaments and cleanse the body with clothing.
Thus, O Goddess, one should always perform the bath with one's intention fixed upon that;
this, O Goddess, is the Mahācīnakrama, which constitutes the bath of the Brahmin.
One should not perform purification here; rather, one should practice with a mind free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa).
If one desires fragrance, it may be done with red flowers and red sandalwood.
One may offer auspicious bilva leaves and maruvaka flowers and the like, excluding tulasī;
however, one should carefully avoid the bilva leaf [in certain rites] and diligently avoid the mantra [when using it].
The goddess always causes the hair to grow when it is nourished with oil;
this should especially be done on the eighth and fourteenth days, which are always auspicious days.
O fair-browed one, no unrighteousness exists here; rather, there shall be great merit.
One whose mind is joyful may proceed according to the rule of one's own desire as stated here.
Considering his purpose accomplished, contented and with a disciplined mind,
he should take up the name of Hari and not touch even a leaf of tulasī.
No other thought should be entertained; success will be achieved in a mere day.
Otherwise, there will be no success at all, even with ten million recitations.
Through hundreds of thousands of preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), and through tens of millions of fire-oblations (*homa*) and other rituals,
when one has become absorbed in the Great Conduct (*mahācāra*) and attained the state of Brahman, one indeed becomes dear to the Lord as one free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).
O Goddess, [there should be] two earrings on the pair of eyebrows, and immediately after that, vermilion,
sandalwood paste on the breasts, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and a lotus with its filaments on the garment.
Wearing a garland of shaven heads around the neck and holding a skull-cup in hand,
one who is constantly devoted to such conduct shall follow the Mahācīna-krama.
He who is delightful at all times, who is always served by his devotees,
and who resides within the ears and eyes, is celebrated as Mahāśaṅkha.
O Maheśānī, one should make a garland from fifty gems or from the bones of a cow, a bull, or an elephant; by doing so, one shall become a master of the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhis).
She alone is Tārā, O Maheśānī; no deliberation need be made on this point.
She is Śiva, Śaṅkara, Viśveśa, the eternal savior of the universe.
How could a Brāhmaṇa practice those duties of physicians which are devoid of the Vedas?
Śiva said:
"O virtuous goddess, O highly wise one, O beloved, O dear practitioner!
One should respect that state of being which arises from the exertion of meditating upon it, O beloved."
O Maheśvarī, just as the flesh of a deity is proclaimed to be the primary substance in the ritual of the Śrāddha, yet that very same flesh is forbidden for Brāhmaṇas; so it is with this.
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, by killing animals one becomes an animal; for as many hairs as there are on those animals, so many births shall one undergo.
O Pārvatī, there is no fault in meditating upon it in that manner;
that hand has been described by me—now listen to the Niṣkala, O Pārvatī.
O Śivā, from the wrist down to the hand and from the toes down to the feet, one should wash the face; this is the Cīna posture for the Goddess.
Placing both knees upon the ground, one should bow the head to the earth.
I have indeed described to you the path of China as it is celebrated in the Namaskāra.

O Goddess of the gods, O beloved, having performed the bathing, giving of gifts, and so forth, as well as the worship and other rites, I have [described] the sequence that is the substitute for the previous sequence.
Likewise, there is no bathing for the body, nor is there indeed any scabies;
what is bathing for anyone? One who has not bathed may have already finished his meal.
The entire lotus of the heart is indeed within me; everything is established in me.
The accomplishment of the mantra is known by me; the gods have granted me their favor.
The entire world is of the nature of light, and Tāriṇī assumes that very form;
having contemplated one’s own body as being within that light, one should perform the recitation of the mantra.
Through cultivation, the yogi becomes a great poet who has attained tranquility;
yet for a Brahmin, wine is like liquor made from molasses and ginger juice.
In the absence of that [water], O Goddess, one should perform the worship by mentally conceiving water;
in its absence, one should always remain near the heart with a mind constantly fixed upon it.
Having abandoned the state of duality, one shall become a sovereign lord of all accomplishments;
even Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, and other lords of sages [attained this].
O Śivā, those devoted to Tārā who constantly worship the partless [deity] through the path of sequential practice have been proclaimed by Brahmā, O Maheśānī.
The knowledge of Brahman is the great knowledge, difficult to obtain everywhere in the Kali age;
it is the most secret of secrets and must be guarded against the presence of the uninitiated.
The Goddess said:
Tell me quickly the sequence of the deities in the ritual procedure for Chinnamastā.
Śiva said:
Divya-cīna, in this very sequence, is Chinnamastā, the bestower of boons;
O Maheśānī, of these two sequences, the first has already been revealed.
O Goddess, there is a tilaka mark between her eyebrows consisting of wheel-shaped sandalwood paste;
at its edge, on a leaf of yellow pigment (rocanā), is a triple-crested mark (tripuṇḍra) made with divine colors.
O Dear One, O Śivā, one should cause a drop of cremation-ground ash to be placed in the center of that;
having joined mouth to mouth, one should recite [the mantra] at all times.
Whatever a person performs after having contemplated the Yonicakra,
that he obtains as inexhaustible through the grace of severed ignorance.
O Śivā, for Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, and likewise the Ṣaṭśāmbhavī,
there is no restriction of direction or time, nor indeed any restriction regarding the stages of cosmic manifestation and so forth.
One should perform the recitation everywhere— in the netherworld, in caves, in inaccessible places, on mountains, on the banks of rivers, in the atmosphere, and likewise upon the earth.
This specific distinction has been declared as the purifying power of the Goddess, the essence of reality.
The Goddess said: O Lord, O Master, please tell me the sequence known as the Gandharva.
Śiva said:
O Goddess, the method known as Gandharva, which is beautiful and difficult to find on earth, is now being described;
listen.
O Goddess, between the eyebrows one should apply saffron, and at its edge, Malaya-aguru;
this constitutes the eight-fold fragrance (aṣṭagandha) for the Tripuṇḍra, combined with musk in the center.
Adorned with fragrant white and red flowers,
the man stands with his body marked by svastikas and encircled by a rampart of jewels.
Adorned with various fragrances by the smoke of the eight perfumes,
wearing red garlands and garments, and graced with a necklace of pearls;
Because the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) is performed upon the head, there is no shaving of the hair there;
O Goddess, one should let the hair grow long, adorned with fragrant oil.
O Great Goddess, these [flowers] have arrived together with various fragrant foods fit for kings;
they are already pure, how much more so when heated by fire?
One should always bathe with warm water, or in its absence, with whatever water is available;
one should decorate the house with various paintings until it resembles the surface of a mirror.
Richly adorned with canopies and banners, graced by the resonant sound of bells,
accompanied by the five types of musical instruments, and endowed with various melodies.
Therefore, he was always adorned with fine garments, gold vessels and other ornaments that delight the senses, as well as necklaces, bracelets, and finger-rings.
The sequence known as the Gandharva consists of various sweet foods and many kinds of milk-preparations, combined with diverse enjoyments.
Thus has been briefly declared that which is called Bhairava; now hear the Krama.
Through the yoga of the sequence with one's own flowers, Bhairavī is difficult to attain on earth.
O Goddess, listen now as the Krama known as Svapuṣpa is being told:
[it concerns] a young woman, beautiful and charming, whose very form is the nectar of youth.
The Great Goddess is ever intent on passion and desire, her mind striving for sexual union, and she is joined with mantras and yantras.
Having first abandoned even the naked woman, one should perform the recitation (japa) while naked oneself;
and mutual gazing should also be performed between them.
When the Goddess is without modification, she is fit for accomplishment and not otherwise;
if there is modification or a lack of meditative cultivation, the practitioner perishes in an instant.
O Maheśānī, that pit may be drawn out in an instant;
nevertheless, one must certainly not cause any alteration to one's own body.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, if she too should become subject to transformation, O Goddess,
one should bring forth a flower instantly by means of the mantra while she is in her menses.
O Goddess, by means of the mantra Drāviṇī, one should bring about the destruction of obstacles through forceful vision;
having grasped both [the enemy and the obstacle], Maheśvarī shall achieve victory.
O Goddess, the Śakti and the practitioner (sādhaka) are considered a rare couple;
this is true even with regard to Vagalā, Sundarī, Tārā, Kālī, and others, despite great effort.
This sequence is perfectly suited to one's capacity; no further deliberation is required here.
However, due to the influence of the defects of the Kali age, this yoga will not be possible for women.
Therefore, O Śivā, in the ritual procedure for those bound by bonds (pāśava), the Vāma is now praised;
however, among the Vāmācāras, the Dakṣiṇa alone is indeed primary.
And if one desires swift accomplishment, one should practice the window-yoga (*gavākṣa-yoga*),
where there is a multitude of women, but no river and no ten-fold water.
Where one does not perform ablutions, there one should provide a window;
having beheld it with effort, one should perform recitation continuously.
O beloved, having thoroughly inspected all [the materials] with gold, jewels, and so forth, O Pārvatī, I have thus briefly described the *tilaka*; now listen.
O Śivā, having carefully inscribed the yantra on the palm of the left hand,
O Supreme Goddess, one should apply the remaining paste as a tilaka.
On the forehead, one should apply a drop of musk, and on the son of a sage (the right ear), pure sandalwood;
in the middle of that, a white dot, and the hair and other features should be as before.
O Goddess, in the procedure for the ten sciences, the increase of hair has been described.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the definitive teaching on the sequence of Kamalā.
Śiva said:
O Goddess, first apply vermilion between the two eyebrows; immediately after that, O Queen of the Gods, apply a white *tripuṇḍra*, and in its center, O Śivā, apply saffron.
Having bathed, wearing white garments, adorned with white garlands and unguents,
and enriched by the splendor of white ornaments, one should perform the ritual bath at the three junctions of the day.
The man who eats sacrificial food (haviṣya), sleeps on the ground,
and avoids sweet foods until the next Saturday (the second Bhṛguvāsara) [attains the fruit].
One should always worship the Kumārī in the sequence of increasing days;
starting from the second day of the bright fortnight (Bhṛgu-bhā), one should decrease [the offerings] according to the increase of days.
O Goddess, one should worship daily with the sounds of various musical instruments;
this practice should be performed every day until the sixteenth day.
Furthermore, beginning from that [day] until the end of those days, the Great Goddess should always worship with self-restraint, intent upon the state of the deity.
Circumambulation should be performed according to the sequence of the waning of the digits (kalās),
and lamps should be offered there according to the sequence of the waxing of the digits.
One should always feed the Brahmins according to the sequence of their respective shares;
thus devoted to such conduct, a glorious man becomes one whose very form is Viṣṇu.
One who is self-restrained should always worship all the royal insignia;
he shall undoubtedly become the lord of the fortune of universal sovereignty.
The king shall become a servant to one who has given wealth, even though that wealth remains within his own body.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, O Śiva, I desire to hear the sequence of the path of Brahman.
Śiva said:
One should apply collyrium to the prostitute, a triple-tilaka mark with vermilion,
apply turmeric to the two eyebrows, and employ a white leaf.
And in the center of that, one should always perceive a red drop;
whether eating, sleeping, or at night during sexual union, it should always be present.
O Goddess of the gods, one should not offer a bali-oblation with hands that are soiled by food remnants, nor while oneself is soiled.
Food that is the remnant of the Śakti or the remnant of another may be eaten at all times.
O Maheśānī, one should perform the recitation; indeed, one should carry out the recitation only at night.
Having consumed betel, the betel-leaf itself will cause her to be enchanted.
Having consumed betel-leaf and meat, one should perform the worship;
having carefully smeared the house, one should carry out the sweeping with a broom.
O Goddess, one should mutter [the mantra] with effort; otherwise, success is certainly not attained.
O Mistress of the Gods, when the hands are soiled with food remnants, one's own body is always sprinkled [with water].
One should recite with hands soiled by food remnants; this is proclaimed as the Brahma-path.
O Goddess, I have thus described to you the Brahma-path according to its sequence and its goal.
By this sequential yoga, the sequence becomes the path of accomplishment;
through the power of the accomplished vidyā, she becomes directly manifest as the bestower of boons.
Even Surendra would become a servant to human beings, so what need be said of others?
O auspicious lady, this secret has been told; it must not be disclosed to others, just as one protects one's own womb.
The Goddess said:
Speak the sequence of the venerable Bhuvaneśānī, which is most difficult to obtain.
Śiva said:
By the very sequence of the divine state, the *bhuvana* bestows swift accomplishment.
The letter *ha*, because it is the form of Śiva, and the letter *u*, which destroys sin.
The letter *i* is proclaimed as *māyā* because it can assume any form at will;
O Goddess, this entire universe is enveloped by that *māyā*.
O Goddess, in that [state] where there is no illusion, nothing whatsoever shines;
and nothing devoid of its own light shines as anything at all.
O Goddess, that which is devoid of existence does not manifest anywhere;
it is only when accompanied by the manifestation of that [existence], O Goddess, that the world shines forth.
Without whom, O Great Goddess, the world would be uniform;
thus, O Queen of Gods, one should always have the mind fixed upon that in this sequence.
One shall become a conqueror of the three worlds; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. O Goddess, listen attentively as the tilaka of this [mantra] is now being described.
One should apply a drop of white sandalwood paste between the eyebrows;
at its end should be the Tripuṇḍra made from fragrant resin (gandhasāra) in a divine color.
And because of those red eyes in its center, one becomes a Lord of Siddhis.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, O Śiva, I desire to hear the ritual sequence of Dhūmāvatī.
Śiva said:
O Goddess Pārvatī, listen as the sequence of Dhūmāvatī is told:
O Goddess, there is collyrium between the eyebrows, and within that, a drop of ash.
There should be a triple mark (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead with the ashes of a corpse in between;
he should wear black garments, hold a boon-bestowing gesture, and be adorned with black perfumes.
Endowed with fragrant flowers and seated upon a cremation ground,
the practitioner of mantra perceives the entire world as smoke-colored and composed of smoke.
One should wear a crow-feather garment or hold a black substance;
one should be a celibate student, moderate in diet, free from conceptual construction, and have conquered the senses.
Speaking the truth, pure in conduct, sleeping on the ground upon a bed of kuśa grass,
he should perform ablutions at the three periods of the day, being devoted to the rite of eradication (uccāṭana).
Having made one's own mind like a crow, one should certainly expel the world;
thus becoming intent on this conduct, one should proceed through the sequence of smoke.
The Kākakrama has thus been proclaimed; what else do you wish to hear?
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the determination of the sequence of Vagalā;
for through the sequence of Saubhāgyārcana, Vagalā becomes swiftly manifest.
The practitioner, wearing yellow garments and adorned with yellow ornaments,
