bearing yellow garlands and bestowing boons, is established in a yellow dwelling.
He is said to be devoted to yellow worship, one whose food and garments are yellow,
an enjoyer of yellow substances, and endowed with a yellow seat.
One who performs the oblation with yellow substances, using yellow flowers and endowed with a yellow power,
should apply yellow pigment (rocanā) to the eyebrows and offer saffron and *munipatraka*.
O Śivā, one should apply a triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with turmeric, and in its center, a piece of khadira wood;
O Supreme Goddess, [the devotee] is then perfumed with incense made of yellow sandalwood.
If one has the capacity, however, one should accomplish everything and remain devoted to the path of the gradual stages;
for in the Kali age, creation, maintenance, dissolution, and worship are each threefold.
In Kerala, there is the Sṛṣṭipūjā according to the sequence of the Kaulāgama;
however, in the Gauḍa country, O Kumārakas, the worship follows the path of Sthiti.
O Goddess, this is the procedure for the worship of the Gauḍa country according to the Guptakaulāgama;
O Goddess, it is the Kāmarūpāgama, the ritual of withdrawal, and the sequential worship.
The sage Sāṅkhyāyana likewise taught the Gauḍāgama, as well as the Vāmāgama; listen to them as they abide, O son.
One should seek a Brahmin girl who is beautiful in all her limbs, lovely, adorned with the splendor of every part of her body, recently married, and in her menses.
On the eighth, the fourteenth, or the full moon day,
or on a Tuesday or a Friday at night, one should [worship] the Kumārakas.
One should likewise prepare another person with well-perfumed oil;
having brought them to the same level as the *bhūlikā* (the ritual diagram), one should then spread [the materials] facing north.
Having spread Jātī and Campaka flowers all around upon that,
as well as sandalwood mixed with camphor and musk;
The wise man should perform an anointing of all her limbs with the Lakṣmīsūkta;
he should place that maiden, who has been smeared with sandalwood paste, upon a couch.
With the mantra beginning with "dhruvādyaiḥ," the boy, facing northward,
should perform the rite of pacification for the girl who is facing southward by means of the Śrīsūkta.
Then, having extended her feet, one should perform worship in secret;
having performed the sixfold placement (nyāsa), as well as the two-fold and the fivefold Vagalā-nyāsa.
One should place the goddess Kanyā and the deity, and one should recollect their respective limbs;
one should purify the people and the city with the root mantra.
One should perform the application of musk with the mantra "gandhadvārā," and there,
one should indeed offer a garland of flowers with the root mantra (mūlamantra).
One should offer the purification of the substances and perform the recitation (japa) right there;
this bestows the perfection of ritual application upon men and is the supreme means for attaining mantra-siddhi.
O Goddess, without this sequence, the practice will never succeed anywhere;
therefore, O Lord, one who desires accomplishment on the surface of the earth should apply every effort toward it.
O Goddess, without this sequence known as Saubhāgya, there is no accomplishment even through ten million [other means];
having abandoned the eightfold pride and having abandoned the three defects.
Having renounced the power of the five senses, one should practice the sequence of auspiciousness;
having made pleasure and pain, gain and loss, and victory and defeat equal.
Having established equanimity toward cold and heat, one should practice the sequence of auspiciousness;
for he who performs worship on this earth without knowing the two groups of sixfold [practices] is [unsuccessful].
O Goddess, he would be fallen and go to the Raurava hell,
being devoid of the knowledge of the distinction between the external and the internal.
One should not perform the sequence of yellow [deities], for one would incur the curse of the deities;
having abandoned the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) with the Kalka [mantra], one whose mind is possessed of higher knowledge [should proceed].
Then one should perform the yellow sequence; otherwise, one will certainly fall from grace.
O Śivā, having first attained mastery over the senses, one should perform the yellow sequence.
He who performs this for the sake of his own pleasure shall incur the curse of the deity;
or rather, having understood the specific rule for his own region, he may do so, O Supreme Goddess.
O Goddess, that brahmin who performs worship [in this manner] shall become fallen;
likewise, O auspicious Śivā, he who causes agitation in the mind of a maiden during the sacrifice.
Even one who is like Vācaspati himself would immediately become deranged in mind;
he could neither produce nor utter [such words], for they are impossible for both mind and body.
If a man were to feel passion for his co-wife,
his mother’s wife, or even the wife of his teacher, he would be utterly ruined.
One should worship a washerwoman, a potter’s daughter, or one endowed with initiation, who is accompanied by the world and not surrendered to Sāṃkhya.
Or one should respectfully worship a Puliṃda maiden, a Golakuṇḍāmṛtā,
or the wife of a sage, endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics.
O Śivā, one who is endowed with all auspicious marks should worship Puṣpiṇī according to the prescribed rite; her worship with dūrvā grass is considered equal [to other forms of worship].
And this which was spoken by the sage Mataṅga brings immediate accomplishment;
O Goddess of the Gods, this is the lineage of the Siddhas—for without a guru, there is no accomplishment.
Therefore, O Goddess of Gods, one who fulfills the command of the Guru with every effort becomes a Siddha; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
The Goddess said:
O Great King, O Lord, O God, please tell me the sequence.
Śiva said:
O Great King, O Goddess, the Krama is now being told; listen.
In a variegated pavilion adorned with various and diverse stairways.
It was beautified by palace turrets and adorned with banners;
it was not crowded, yet filled with people, and graced by swans and peacocks.
It was delightful with various wonders, resplendent with elephants and horses,
auspicious on all sides, and adorned with diverse ornaments.
In a place filled with the fragrance of incense, adorned with variegated lamps,
and furnished with a beautiful jeweled lion-throne embellished with gemstone ornaments.
It was beautified by the fragrance of jasmine, *caṃpaka*, *puṇnāga*, and *ketakī* flowers;
it was endowed with camphor, agallochum, musk, yellow pigment, and saffron.
Adorned with fragrant ointments such as *jaṭāmāṃsī* and other perfumes,
accompanied by the resonance of bells, he is always pure in mind.
His heart immersed in bliss, adorned with divine garments,
wearing divine garlands and excellent ornaments, and graced with celestial decorations.
With his mouth full of betel-leaf, he shone like the lord of the gods;
he resounded with the sounds of Vedic vessels, vessels for the manes, and vessels for worldly enjoyments.
It resounded with dances and songs, with twenty-four kinds of musical instruments,
and with the sounds of melodies, ragas, and rhythmic beats.
Adorned with prose and verse in various regional dialects,
and spoken by the best of practitioners wearing diverse and wonderful ornaments.
The sovereign of all royal dynasties, the enchantress of the mountain,
the illustrious Mahārāja Mātaṅgī, who utterly deludes all the gods.
O Goddess Pārvatī, listen as the *tilaka* of that [lineage] is described:
there is a pair on the breasts and between the eyebrows; within that interval lies the essence of the Guru.
O Śivā, O Mahārājñī, I have thus described to you the sequence for the musk-unguent, the triple mark, and the saffron streak in its center.
Or else, O Goddess of the gods, he himself shall become the supreme Gaṇa.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Sequence Beginning with Mahānīla," in the *Śrītantracintāmaṇi*.
Now, the states of the heroic animal (vīrapaśu) are being described.
The Goddess said:
O Mahādeva, Bhairava, listen as the state of the Hero (vīrabhāva) is described:
having become one whose mind is free from dualities, with the body consisting of the digit of desire (kāmakalā) within the heart.
Indeed, the night is always considered the most excellent time for worship;
having established one's own lineage, one should personally assume the form of Bhairava.
And you are the family of Bhairavī; [perform] the detailed nyāsa upon her limbs in the midst of a bed of flowers, joined with hands full of blossoms.
Having written [the mantra] upon a yantra with family materials (kuladravya) strewn with various fragrances, one should worship it, preceded by the ritual installation of the multitude of Śaktis.
Having drawn a hexagon on one's own left side with the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) in its center,
one should place there a water-pot made either of gold or silver.
One should place the jar, which serves as the support for the water-pot, made either of copper or of earth, avoiding any base metal, and scented with fragrant perfumes.
One should fully provide the causal substances according to the distinctions of the *brāhmaṇa* and other castes;
having first inscribed the yantra there, whatever originates from one's own lineage [should be offered].
Having meditated upon one's chosen deity there, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
then, having displayed the *dhenu-yoni* mudrā, one should contemplate that as nectar (*amṛta*).
Upon seeing a corpse brought forth, the hosts of Yoginīs indeed dance;
all the Bhairavas dance, and the Mothers as well.
All the gods, beginning with Indra, dance, longing for the honey;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the others dance, intent on joy.
Having divided the vessel for the *argha* offering into three parts, one part should be given to the Guru,
one part should indeed be given to the *kula*, and with the remaining one part, the propitiation of the deities (*devatarpaṇa*) is performed.
Having drunk the *kula-rasa*, adorned with various garments and ornaments,
if the Guru is not personally present, then one should offer it into water.
Having become one whose nature is bliss, one should worship the Supreme Goddess;
one should worship her according to the specific ritual procedures for each kalpa and with the appropriate effort for each.
Then, having performed the ritual dismissal (visarjana), one should thereafter unite it with one's own lineage;
by drinking that [nectar], the nectar of immortality (amṛta) is consumed.
Upon tasting the juice of that *cakra* fruit, great exhilaration arises within me;
by the mere grasping of its fruit, one descends from the peak of Mount Meru.
Having bathed one's body with nectar by means of the embrace of the creeper (latāliṅga),
and having performed the root-yoga (mūlayoga) there, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times.
In whatever recitation or fire-offering (homa) the specific number is not prescribed, there this calculation is taught: one thousand and eight [repetitions].
Then, having taken the sacrificial substance purified with water, one should perform the libation;
O Lord, having performed the libation, one should proceed with the circumambulation.
Having praised and prostrated, one should then satisfy [the deity] with the flow [of offerings] as prescribed in the Kalpa;
thereafter, having carefully prepared the Kula, one should perform the recitation with diligence.
In that family, reality itself truly abides in its actual nature:
fresh meat, as well as fish, ritual gestures (mudrā), and sexual union.
The worship performed with these very [substances] is proclaimed as the family tradition (kulācāra);
therefore, it should be diligently practiced by those who know the scriptures of that family.
That family which remains steady and virtuous from generation to generation is blessed; it is wise, and it alone truly possesses the character of a noble lineage.
If one goes to a cremation ground on any day whatsoever during the time of Mars,
there the fruit of worship shall be equal to that of seven days of fasting.
When the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight arrives there, one obtains the fruit of worship;
O noble one, no woman should go to that place, for she would undoubtedly become like a beast.
Thinking, "O God, there is none superior to me," he becomes devoted to such thoughts; yet, though a consumer of wealth through intoxication, he remains devoted to his own lineage.
When the practitioner’s gaze is filled with fear, agitation arises within me;
therefore, the excellent hero should be diligent, possessed of his portion, and happy.
Through enjoyment one attains liberation; through enjoyment, the family and the means of accomplishment [are attained].
Having encountered that which is without cause, Maheśvara becomes possessed of agitation.
There is no worship, nor contact with me, nor meditation, nor contemplation;
therefore, having eaten and drunk, one should worship the Supreme Lord.
There is no fault more ruinous than the defect of failing to maintain the proper sequence;
for whatever one says, whatever one causes to be done, and whatever one worships— all that [becomes fruitless].
Having meditated upon all that as the form of the family (kula), the wise one should dwell alone in a solitary place— whether in a cremation ground, on a mountain, or in a forest.
One should dwell joyfully and without attachment in an empty house or on a riverbank;
for heroes, every time is praised as the proper time for recitation.
This must be performed in every land and at every sacred seat, without any doubt;
and the rite of heroic accomplishment (vīrasādhana) must be performed by heroic men.
It should be performed even by the gods, and not by base commoners;
it is certain that the work of a commoner is better than the work of Maya and Śauri.
If the previously mentioned conventions regarding the substances for mantra practice exist,
the hero of great power should prepare the ointment, the pill, and so forth.
There is no distinction between the divine and the heroic; that which constitutes their difference is now described:
[the divine hero] is peaceful, humble, sweet, and endowed with artistic grace and beauty.
But the divine [hero] is generally like a god, his mind exalted by heroism,
adorned with ornaments or even anointed with sandalwood paste.
Whether he conceals his true form, or is naked, or is a Kulabhairava;
whether he is smeared with red sandalwood paste, or a Vaiṣṇava, or even a non-Vaiṣṇava.
He should always remain joyful and contented, whether facing insult or honor;
whether intent on censuring the gods or devoted to their worship.
Delighting in worship yet free from it, established in the Kula and Akula doctrine, and endowed with his own true nature, he should move about upon the earth like a god.
One should perform the preliminary ritual (puraścaryā) of one's own lineage at night and not otherwise;
just as a twice-born man devoid of the Vedas is not truly a twice-born man, so too is a discourse that is not born of the Śruti.
Just as devotion to the gods cannot prevail without devotion to Viṣṇu,
so too liberation becomes a mere object of laughter without the knowledge of Śakti.
Just as one has no entitlement whatsoever to the Tantra without a guru,
so too is a woman devoid of all ritual action when she is without her husband.
O follower of the Kaula path, one who lacks the ritual procedure of the Kula is never qualified for my practice; therefore, be devoted to the inner state (bhāva).
How can one whose family is undisciplined be a worshiper of me?
Therefore, one must act with such effort that the family becomes endowed with discipline.
Since there is neither existence nor non-existence, there can be no authority whatsoever through the lineage of the Lord of Kula;
therefore, a practitioner who is purified of existence becomes a true Kaulika.
I shall explain the state of the sacrificial animal (paśubhāva); listen, O child, with concentrated mind.
Having received the knowledge according to the rule, one who is devoted to that state becomes a sacrificial animal.
First, for the sake of preliminary service, one should diligently practice purification;
one should not eat fish, nor should one even mentally recall a woman.
One should not be covetous of another's property, nor should one enjoy their objects of enjoyment;
whether on the shore of the ocean, on a mountain, in a forest, or in a temple of the gods.
At the root of a bilva tree, in a secluded place, or in a beautiful and holy field,
one should not allow a Śūdra to see [the ritual], and one should diligently abandon crookedness.
The deities, possessing auspicious forms, should be meditated upon by those who are well-composed.
One should perform the worship of the deity at the three junctions of the day, and one should practice recitation at the three junctions of the day.
At night, one should never touch the mantra or the rosary;
nor should one recite the mantra after eating, but remain observant of silence in all ritual acts.
The best of practitioners should never approach a woman during the sacred festival days (parva-kāla);
he should worship by personally bringing flowers, incense, and water.
One should completely avoid sexual intercourse, talk about it, and social gatherings concerning it;
furthermore, one should not approach a woman with longing except during her fertile period.
One who has faith in listening to the Purāṇas and is devoted to the Vedas and the meaning of the Vedas,
O Supreme Lord, that wise man should not eat at night nor consume betel leaf.
Whatever has been instructed by the Guru, all that one should perform with diligence;
likewise, the flower of one's own birth, as well as the causal substance (hetu-dravya) which is Bhairava.
Having touched, mounted, or smelled [a corpse], one becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
one who is devoted to the Goddess should not accept red garments.
In the Viṣṇu-tantras, one should perform the rituals and their observances;
however, one should not engage in conversation concerning heroes nor offer salutations to heroes.
Devoted to dharma, I shall perform the daily ancestral rite (nitya-śrāddha), the twilight worship (saṃdhyā-vandana),
bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha-snāna), and visiting the seats of power (pīṭha-deśa).
O Bhairava, listen now in due order to how the "beast" (paśu) is said to be of three kinds:
one who is uninitiated, devoid of ritual action, and abandoned by mantra and tantra.
The one known as Mahāpaśu is censured by everyone;
the second is proclaimed to be he who, though initiated, is a slanderer.
One who is not devoted to solitude is called a beast;
such a person has no authority for worship, nor ever for the status of a guru.
The one from the East has no authority regarding the coming and going at the place of worship;
indeed, that person from the East must be excluded by all Kaulas from their own country.
O Lord, it is better to commit a sin such as the killing of a Brahmin than to practice the Kula-observance merely by having seen it before. This is the truth.
I tell you the truth, the very truth: that which was seen before is indeed real here;
O Goddess of gods, she is my very self, and he, O Lord, is likewise all-pervading.
Nevertheless, a doubt arises in me at every step regarding that;
better to abandon one's family, better even to harm one's own kin.
Better is the loss of one's own family, better is the destruction of one's own lineage;
better even is the downfall of one's own family through body, mind, or speech.
One should not form an attachment to a beast, for one's own path leads to destruction;
in the family scripture, two things are considered the gravest sins that bring about the ruin of the lineage.
O Lord of the Kula, there is great censure within one's own family due to the practice of another [tradition];
even greater than that, O Great Sin, arises from association with the uninitiated (paśu).
O Kuleśvara, in every respect, both existence and non-existence are manifested therein;
through aversion toward bound souls (paśu), both existence and non-existence arise.
From destiny a hero is born, and from a hero destiny is born;
there is no doubt regarding destiny and heroism—they are said to be equal.
But existence (bhāva) is a mental property; how could it be verbal?
Therefore, existence should not be spoken of [in this context]; only a mere indication has been given.
Just as the sweetness of sugarcane juice is perceived by the tongue, O Lord,
so too are the emotional states (bhāva) and the determinants (vibhāva) contemplated by the mind.
Listen with diligence, O Goddess of Gods, to this most secret of secrets:
[it is attained] without wine, without meat, and without the service of unchaste women.
A mantra does not attain success if it is worshipped according to the sequence of the moon and sun [alone],
nor when the vessel is filled with wine, nor when the mouth is filled by a woman.
What on earth cannot be accomplished by means of Aliṃ, Valiṃvarā, and Rāmā?
This is the truth: without union with a woman, a mantra does not attain success.
One should indeed practice union, but never engage in sexual intercourse;
one should always honor a woman who is firmly resolved upon the divine nature.
Therefore, sexual union must be performed by my practitioners for the sake of the gods;
for I am the sustainer of the worlds and the one who brings about birth as a mother.
In the case of a woman who is a counter-measure against my state of being, I am indeed most certain that sexual intercourse must never be performed with her, as it would cause a mental agitation.
If a wise man, a hero, or even a divine being performs that [act] out of delusion or through ignorance, he shall go to hell due to his lack of understanding.
One should worship the wife of a guru, the wife of a brahmin, and the wife of one's father;
[if one engages in] sexual intercourse with them, the suffering in hell shall be multiplied ten millionfold.
And I, filled with wrath, shall destroy that lord;
for that sinner, there will arise incessant suffering from disease.
Sometimes there is the torment of karma, sometimes the pain in the ears;
sometimes there is indigestion, and sometimes the itch of scabies.
Loss of sight, deafness, lameness, and likewise hunchbackedness,
as well as various other diseases such as leprosy and the like, indeed arise [from this].
The destruction of the eyes, the cutting off of the ears, likewise the cutting off of the nose,
the cutting off of the feet, the cutting off of the hands, and even the cutting off of the head occurs.
Affliction of cattle, affliction from the king, and affliction by fire arise;
through his fault, his family perishes here—of this there is no doubt.
O woman, these faults arising from sexual intercourse have been described to you;
those who are devoid of qualification should refrain from them, while those possessing qualification may engage in them.
Śiva said:
O Goddess, Sovereign of the Universe, my great doubt increases;
by your grace, O Goddess, you ought to speak for me.
The Goddess said:
I alone am the supreme meditation; I alone am the supreme revelation. Nothing whatsoever is perceived that is higher than me; the entire universe is nothing but me.
I alone am the entire universe, and the universe is indeed I, the Lord. O Śiva, a woman who is permeated by my being shall become just like this.
Thus, one who is distinguished by such knowledge becomes an authorized recipient of Śiva;
indeed, he immediately becomes Śiva himself, surpassing even Brahmā and the other great lords among all the gods.

When a child is being born, the mother’s womb and her own organs undergo a transformation through their mutual contact; yet, no such change ever occurs in those two [the father’s seed and the mother’s blood].
Likewise, that practitioner whose mind possesses the requisite qualification shall always be entitled to the sacrifice and other rites together with his female companions.
When she has attained my state, she is indeed myself, having my own nature;
for no change occurs in that woman, since [the Self] is not actually superimposed upon her.
Thus, for that practitioner whose intellect is firm regarding his own office, there is no doubt that his own body shall become the very form of his chosen deity.
Having stabilized the circle of the forest with meditative visualizations, filled with splendors equal in color to that [deity],
the practitioner becomes absorbed in the deity through meditation.
With a restrained mind, one should contemplate the form, color, and other attributes exactly as they are;
when such knowledge has arisen, a person may move about according to his own will.
Thus, for one who has no [other] son of his own, a substitute is prescribed;
it should be performed with a maiden alone, never with one who is menstruating.
Merely by feeding a maiden, or even by feeding a maiden,
or simply by meditating upon a maiden, one shall become a conqueror of the three worlds.
Listen, O Goddess of excellent hips, to this great and wonderful secret:
the supreme practitioner may unite with a woman in her vulva even without performing worship.
He shall be poor for seven births and dwell in hell for ten million kalpas;
[he commits] the murder of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife.
Thus, various faults arise; there is no doubt about this.
Whether he be a hero or even a divine being, one does not go to hell by virtue of one's intellect.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Bhāvas," in the illustrious *Tantracintāmaṇi*. 14.
Now, first of all, he explains the distinction between eternal and other [categories] based on the differentiation of qualities such as *sattva* and the rest.
The Goddess said:
For the wealthy and the middling classes, for the poor and householders,
for those residing in foreign lands, and for those dwelling in prisons and the like.

O ocean of compassion, for those who are engaged in their duties at the beginning of a task, or who are occupied with ritual observances due to birth-impurity and the like, and for those who are left-handed (vāmaka) in both the performance of rites and their natural disposition;
O Lord, tell me how the daily rites may be performed within the secret tradition of the Six Āmnāyas, or describe the daily conduct for those who possess a sense of worldly shame.
Śrī Śiva said:
That which was spoken by Mahākāla and heard by Mahāmāyā—
that most secret of secrets— is concealed in all the tantras.
I shall now proclaim this daily ritual (*āhnika*), the secret of the sacred traditions (*āmnāya*);
listen, all you gods, for it bestows success upon practitioners (*sādhaka*).
In that regard, the eternal is said to be threefold according to the distinction of the three qualities (guṇas);
if it is devoid of [worldly] authority, it is preceded by the knowledge designated as "Māna."
That which is performed by an ascetic with a healthy mind is called pure;
if such a thing is performed by a householder, or even by one who possesses no wealth, it is likewise pure.
Whether one is afflicted by illness, traveling on a journey, or even confined within the hands of a prison guard,
one should perform external worship with devotion, using either that [substance] alone or mixed with it, according to the prescribed rules for external worship.
The mind of a householder is considered to have slipped away due to fear of cold and other such things, from exhaustion, from minor tasks,
or from the command of women and others.
Whatever external worship and so forth is performed by a householder in solitude and with regularity, out of devotion, that is pure and approved as rājasa.
That which is performed for the sake of worship, having generated faith and devotion,
or out of fear of the world or fear of the gods, is mixed with passion (rājasa).
That wealth which was requested from the name of a deity for the purpose of deceiving people, yet was diverted for a different purpose— that is indeed *rājasa*.
Having resorted to the left-hand path and reflected upon the Kaula doctrine,
and through non-hostility toward other doctrines, that which was performed is indeed pure, though characterized by tamas.
Whatever action has been performed out of desire, whether pertaining to this world or the next,
by resorting to the left-hand path (vāmamārga), that is indeed mixed with poison.
That which is consumed out of greed for the tongue, that which is drunk for the sake of sensual pleasure,
or that which is vomited up for the purpose of killing and so forth— that is tamasic.
Through pure sattva there would be liberation; through mixed sattva, heaven;
through diminished sattva, supernatural powers (siddhi); and [through further diminution], the human state and bodily existence.
From pure rājasa [action], heaven (svarga) results; from mixed rājasa, desire (kāma) results;
and from rājasa that flows into the throat (gali), there is happiness even in the animal realm.
From *sāttvika* [action], a person attains birth among the gods; from mixed *tāmasa*, one becomes miserable; and from purely *tāmasa*, one becomes a denizen of hell.
Action is said to be fivefold, bestowing liberation in five ways:
movement, grasping, sacrifice, study, and splendor.

The purification of a temple through sweeping, plastering, and other such rites constitutes the removal of worldly existence; by performing this circumambulation, one attains residence in the same world as the deity.
The gathering of the requisites for worship and the service of devotion constitute the material cause;
that which brings pleasure to the deity bestows the form of the divinity.
That yoga which, preceded by the worship of the sacred seat (pīṭha), consists of the sixteen and other services,
is indestructible for the body of signs (liṅgadeha) and brings about the yoga of time.
Then, the morning rites are performed as follows.
O Maheśānī, I shall describe the supreme benefit for the practitioner during the Brāhma-muhūrta: the contemplation of the Guru while lying upon the bed of Kālikā.
O Maheśānī, one should abandon the night-vow (rātrivāsa) for Sunda;
likewise, O Devī, for Chinnā, one should repeatedly meditate upon the practitioner in union (saṃyogin).
O Goddess of the gods, one should meditate upon Tārā together with the Guru and Śakti;
having meditated upon the Guru, one should properly unite Kuṇḍalinī through yoga.
Having risen at dawn, the practitioner should bow to the Kula-tree,
meditate upon the Kula from the base (mūla) to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), and then remember the Guru.
Then, one should contemplate upon the crown of the head a thousand-petaled lotus, white as camphor and smiling; there, one should meditate on one's own Guru in his true form.
Thus, while the venerable Guru is present, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) with the [mantra] ending in "Īśāna."
Extremely serene, adorned with shimmering ornaments and white sandalwood paste,
[the deity] has hands occupied with the gestures of granting boons, fearlessness, and wisdom, as well as a book.
He is clad in white garments, peaceful, adorned with white flowers,
and embraced by the Śakti Raṇavarṇā who rests upon his left lap.
Clad in red garments and ornaments, or with red sandalwood paste and garlands,
she embraces him with her left hand holding a playful lotus, while [her] right [hand rests] upon him.
One should meditate upon that peaceful face of the illustrious Guru, who is the very form of Śiva,
and upon his pair of lotus feet, from which flows a stream of nectar.
The disciple should thus contemplate his own body as having been consecrated;
he should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, whether through instrumental music or mentally.

He describes the mental worship of the venerable Guru: Having uttered "laṃ haṃ yaṃ raṃ vaṃ" and having recited "I offer [this] to the self of each respective element," one concludes with "namaḥ" in the mental worship.
Having addressed [the deity] as "Obeisance to the Self of Power (Śakti)," one should offer betel-leaf as before;
[this is done] by joining the little finger, the index finger, the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb.
The *sarvāsī* mudrā is traditionally taught as being fivefold in sequence.
Having released [the previous] mudrā, the yogin should display that mudrā when offering betel leaf (*tāmbūla*).
The convention for his names consists of those perfected by praising the Guru;
having thus prostrated with the heart-mantra, one should contemplate his absorption within the heart.
Now, he describes the specific meditation regarding the status of women as gurus.
I meditate upon my venerable Gaurī, who is slightly reddish like the dawn, whose eyes are filled with compassion, who bestows boons and fearlessness, and who is profoundly peaceful.
Her own lord, the Lord of the Hand (Śiva), [beheld] his own left form,
who possessed lotus-like hands and whose eyes were gracefully swinging.
Now, the distinction among heroes is as follows:
Having meditated upon the Mahācīna Guru, one should then remember one's own Guru;
having worshipped him with the five offerings according to the sequence of heroic substances.
Then he spoke to the family preceptor:
The one named Prahlādānandanātha, as well as Sanakānanda,
Kumārānandanātha, and Vasiṣṭhānandanātha.
One should meditate upon the bliss of wrath, the bliss of pleasure, and the bliss of meditation beyond that;
then, one who delights in the bliss of awakening and the bliss of the beautiful should meditate upon the face of the Kula.
Then, their eyes rolled as their hearts were thrilled by the savor of the great nectar.
The members of the Kula lineage are undifferentiated, having pulverized all darkness;
surrounded by Kula disciples, they are intent upon the fullness of the inner organ.
All of them were endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and they were exponents of the meaning of the Kula Tantras.
Now, the meditation on the venerable Guru.
Clad in blue garments and smeared with blue unguents, his body adorned with conch shells and other ornaments, he is joyful and possesses three eyes.
I shall describe the Hero, the treasury of compassion, whose blue Śakti is seated upon the seat of his left side.
Having meditated upon the Hero, the wise one should recite the Vīramālā mantra one thousand and eight times and offer it into the left hand.
Now, he speaks of the Guru-pādukā.
Alternatively, one should extract the Vāgbhava, Māyā, and Lakṣmī-bījas; likewise, [the mantra] called Nandabhairava is *hasakhaphreṃ* followed by *sahakhaphreṃ*.
One should remember the name of the Guru and likewise the name of the Śakti as the Śrīpādukā.
The wise practitioner should recite the mantra ten times, seven times, or even three times;
thereafter, he should offer the recitation into the right hand of the venerable Guru.
Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom that state was revealed— the state which is of the form of an unbroken circle and by which the moving and the unmoving are pervaded.
Salutations to that venerable Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance was opened with the ointment-stick of knowledge.
Then, [the energy] rises from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*.
They call the *ādhāra* the "root-stalk" (*skanda*), located between the anus and the genitals.
Seated upon a soft seat, free from all thoughts,
one should visualize a square, four-gated palace, golden in color and filled with splendor.
In the center of that [triangle] is a circle consisting of will, knowledge, and action;
it resembles ten million suns and is as cool as ten million moons.
Having the form of three concentric circles, adorned with all ornaments,
in its center is a self-manifested liṅga (svayaṃbhuliṅga) with a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Above that is the seed-syllable of Kāma (klīm), with the leader Moon (i) as its digit;
above that is Kuṇḍalī, whose form is like a flame, the very embodiment of Brahman.
Having meditated upon the staff of fire (tejodaṇḍa) within the suṣumṇā, resembling a thousand suns,
and having visualized the root mantra as being of that same nature, enveloped by that radiance.
Having thus contemplated one's own body, one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma);
then, one should perform the ritual assignment of the mantra’s seer (ṛṣi) and other elements using the root mantra.
Then, having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), one should meditate upon the deity in the heart;
having worshipped with mental offerings, one should recite the mantra.
Then, according to one's ability, one should offer the recitation to the deity.
Now he states the specific distinction regarding Śyāmā.
Having meditated upon Kālī as described in the visualization within the lotus of the heart, one should then worship her;
having worshipped her with mental offerings, one should recite the mantra.
Having offered perfumes and other substances, one should mutter the Gāyatrī twenty-eight times or ten times; now hear that Bhairavī as well.
The syllable *kāma* (kḷm), ending with the letter *a* (a) and joined with the right limb (*dakṣiṇāṅga*, i.e., *u*),
then the seed-syllable *kūrca* (huṃ), and then *cāmuṇḍā* joined with *ṅeṃ* (cāmuṇḍāyai).
One should say "dhīmahi" and then "tanno kālī pracodayāt.
This Gāyatrī has been declared by me; it is hidden in all the Tantras.
Without which those arts and sciences can never be perfected.
Now, the procedure for recitation (japa) is described.
The wise one should perform the visualization (saṃkalpa) consisting of the Vīrahaṃsa-avidyā.
Out of a desire for the welfare of [practitioners], I shall describe the practice known as Haṃsa for the sake of mantras.
By the mere knowledge of whom one becomes omniscient on earth—
the Blessed Lady whose essence is the *haṃsa*— the individual soul always conquers.
By the mere remembrance of this, a man becomes liberated while living;
O Goddess of the gods, the two wings of this Haṃsa are the Nigamas and Āgamas.
Likewise, Agni and Soma are the two wings, while Tāra is the head;
the three Bindus are the crest-lock, Nāda is established in the eyes and the mouth.
The pair of feet of Śiva and Śakti, with Kālāgni as their twin attendants on either side—
this is indeed the Supreme Swan (Paramahaṃsa), all-pervading and luminous.
With the sound *ha* one goes out; with the sound *sa*, one enters again.
By the mere awakening to *sayāḥ*, a person becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
By the power of *prāṇāyāma*, one indeed becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).
The seer is Haṃsa, the meter is said to be Gāyatrī with the unmanifest as its beginning.
The deity is the supreme *Aum*; *Haṃsaḥ* is said to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
Together with its power (*śakti*), it is the pin (*kīlaka*); *So'ham* is indeed the *praṇava*, which is the very reality itself.
The *udātta* accent is thus proclaimed as belonging to this *mantra*;
its application is for the sake of liberation, and so a person should always act in this manner.
O Goddess, the heart belongs to the Sun-self, and likewise the head to the Moon-self;
the flame is the stainless light, and the radiance is likewise without appearance, O Beloved.
Having placed the unmanifest (avyakta) upon the two eyes, one should worship Ananta with the weapon-mantra "phaṭ.
Having thus performed the rite of placement (nyāsa), one should offer it to Gaṇeśa and the others.
Sixty breaths constitute one *prāṇa*, and six *prāṇas* are considered one *nāḍikā*.
Sixty *nāḍikās* indeed make up a day and night; this is the number of recitations for the mantra of Japamanu.
A living being should recite daily twenty-one thousand and six hundred times the supreme mantra consisting of the bliss of Brahman.
Its origin is the commencement of recitation, and its death is the offering;
even without formal recitation, it is always present in the state of constant recitation.
When the recitation has been thus completed, one should offer it to Gaṇeśa and the other deities;
six hundred for Gaṇeśa results in six thousand.
Six thousand [prostrations] to the wielder of the mace (Gadāpāṇi), six thousand to the wielder of the Pināka bow (Pinākin),
one thousand to the Self (Ātman), and one thousand to the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
And likewise, this visualization according to the rule consists of a thousand [petals] for the city;
one should contemplate Gaṇeśa, who is red in color, in the four-petaled mūlādhāra.
One should offer six hundred [oblations] into that which is joined with the Vādiveda;
the Svādhiṣṭhāna [cakra] is the color of coral, hexagonal, and possesses the sixfold Vādi mantra.
One should offer [the mantra] joined with the Sāvitrī to Brahman;
it consists of ten syllables beginning with "dalabhā," and possesses the brilliance of a mass of lightning.
I bow to Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa; one should offer six thousand [petals] upon a great blue-shining lotus with twelve petals beginning with the letter 'Ka'.
I bow to Umā and Maheśvara; one should offer six thousand [oblations] into a pure, smoke-colored vessel for the kalās, which is endowed with the vowels.
I salute the two [lotuses] consisting of the power of *prāṇa* and offer a thousand [petals];
one should employ the auspicious and skillful [hands] in the *ājñā*-cakra, which has the luster of lightning.
One should offer a thousand [oblations] into the Supreme Self, the Supreme Power;
having praised and bowed to the Lord, one should request His command with these verses.
One should cause the recitation of the hymn beginning with "śivādikasthala" for one's own desired deity.
O primordial deity, whose nature is the consciousness of the three worlds, O Śrī Śaṅkara, by your command alone,
having risen at dawn for your pleasure, I shall pursue the journey of worldly existence.
O Śaṅkara, God of gods, as I follow the journey of saṃsāra according to your command, I am beset by rivalry, pride, delusion, and negligence; O Lord, do not let these overcome me.
Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods and obtained his permission,
and having requested the earth, one should place the foot together with the breath.
O Goddess whose girdle is the ocean, whose breasts are the mountain ranges, O Consort of Viṣṇu, salutations to you; forgive this touch of my feet.
If one worships the Goddess with devotion without having performed the morning rites,
that worship is fruitless, just like a ritual action devoid of purity.
Now follows the procedure for purification.
Then, from that house, he should go toward the southern or the south-western direction;
at every step he should remember the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), and he should travel far away from the dwellings of the twice-born.
Having looked toward the ground just beyond the range of an arrow from the village,
one should not [perform it] in a cremation ground, nor on a triple-path, nor at a crossroads.
In a cow-pen, on a royal road, in a forest, or likewise in a grove, as well as in a temple,
one must avoid [passing] especially during the time cows are grazing.
Since feces, urine, and the like must be avoided by one born under Kṛttikā,
one should discharge urine at least ten cubits away from a body of water.

If one passes feces or urine while wearing a sacred thread (pavitra) on the ear, then forty times as many [clay washings] are required in a village, and four times as many in a river at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
One should void both urine and feces facing north during the day, and facing south at night; during both twilights, one should act as during the day.
O twice-born ones, whether in shadow or in darkness, by night or by day,
or when there is fear of danger to life, one should perform [the rites] facing in whatever direction is appropriate.
"Arise, O gods, Vṛṣaya, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas! Abandon this place on all sides; this is a spot for the discharge of feces and urine."
Having dismissed the deities with this mantra using clods of earth or blades of grass,
one should effect the removal of impurity there, or having entered together [with them].
One should not look at the tip of the nose nor gaze into the sky;
rather, having properly performed the act of subjugation (*vaśyaka*) and wiped the breath with a wooden stick.
If one wipes the anus with a clod of earth or even with a stone,
purification must be performed again using a quantity of clay equal to an *āmalaka* fruit.
The second and third [lines] are proclaimed to be half and half again of that;
they should be collected from a pure place, free from gravel, stones, and the like.
For a Brāhmaṇa, white clay is prescribed; likewise, red is said for a Kṣatriya;
yellow is prescribed for a Vaiśya, and black for women and Śūdras.
In whatever region a particular water and a particular kind of earth may be found, that very same shall be considered commendable there; by means of them, purification is prescribed.
One application of clay should be made on the penis, seven on the anus, likewise seven on the left hand, seven on both hands together, and three applications of clay on the two feet.

During the voiding of urine, one should apply five applications of clay to the penis with the left hand; for each of the two types of excrement (feces), one should apply one application, or alternatively, one may do so for both feet.
One should perform twelve mouthfuls of gargling after voiding feces; this removes the odor and coating [of the mouth] and is supreme for dispelling mental fatigue.
But upon voiding urine, having performed four sips of water (ācamana), one should then perform three [sips] more;
this is the rule for householders, while for students it is double.
The purification for forest-dwellers is threefold, and for ascetics it is fourfold;
the purification for the night is half that of the day, and this applies to one's own purification at all times.
Half of that is for those engaged in the path of illness, for women, and for Śūdras; half of that again is the purification required for them.
Having performed the cleansing with earth, one should then purify oneself through the recitation of mantras.
For one who is devoid of the practice of purification, all ritual actions are fruitless.
Now follows the procedure for cleaning the teeth.
Then he should collect the tooth-sticks from the prescribed fuel-wood;
these are *apāmārga*, *badarī*, *nirguṇḍī*, *vilva*, and *vāsaka*.
Aśoka, campaka, plakṣa, parṇaja, jambu, dhava, śrīparṇī, arka, nyagrodha, khadira, karañja, kakubha, and so forth.
At the Śīrṣa tree there is valor; at the Vaṭa, radiance; at the Kadamba, victory in battle;
at the Plakṣa, the accomplishment of all goals; and at the Vadari, a sweet voice.
From *khadira* one gains the fragrance of the mouth; from *vailva*, abundant wealth;
from *apāmārga*, fortitude, intelligence, wisdom, splendor, and likewise fame.
Longevity, virtue, as well as prosperity and good fortune arise;
by the Sun, diseases are destroyed and the acquisition of wealth occurs.

Through the *audumbara* flower, there is purity of speech; through the *campaka*, one hears what was not previously seen or heard; and through the *jāti*, *vakula*, and *mandāra* flowers, one does not see [inauspicious] dreams.
All thorny trees are meritorious, while those that exude milky sap bring renown;
one should not use the tooth-cleansing sticks of other species of trees.
He who eats the palāśa, vakula,
kāśa, and mustard plants becomes a caṇḍāla for as long as he does not see a cow.
Whether it be made of crystal, or overgrown, inferior, or devoid of bark;
likewise, one that is half-burnt, fallen from its place on the road, or situated in a cremation ground.
One should carefully remove any thread or the like adhering to it;
it should be twelve finger-breadths long, as thick as the tip of the little finger, and straight.
For Brahmins it is twelve finger-breadths, for Kshatriyas nine finger-breadths,
for Vaishyas eight finger-breadths, and for Shudras six finger-breadths.
The rule for women is said to be a measure of four finger-breadths;
one should take [the substance] with its tip powdered and joined with bark, accompanied by this mantra.
O Lord of the Forest, grant us long life, strength, fame, splendor, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence.
Having sat upon a comfortable seat, facing either the east or the north,
one should consume the prescribed tooth-cleansing twig for the purpose of purifying the mouth.
Having uttered "klīṃ" for Kāmadeva, the beloved of all people,
followed by "namaḥ" at the end— this mantra, consisting of fifteen syllables, is for the purification of the tip [of the tongue].
Having rinsed the tooth-stick, one should discard it in a clean place to the east;
one should always rinse the mouth with the root mantra for the sake of attaining success.
On the sixth days of the fortnights, on the ninth day, on Sundays,
and during lunar and solar eclipses, one should not perform the cleaning of the teeth.
In the absence of a tooth-stick, or on a prohibited lunar day,
one should perform the cleansing of the mouth with twelve mouthfuls of water.
Now, the ritual bath for the successful accomplishment of the acts of worship and fire-offerings is described.
All rituals should be preceded by bathing, and the bath for the deity should take place in the morning, at midday, and in the evening during the recitation of hymns.
Whenever there is mental distress, one should perform a bath at that very moment;
for he who recites the Vidyā while remaining unbathed and having already eaten [incurs a fault].
His knowledge shall be destroyed, and he shall go to the Raurava hell,
O Maheśānī, if one who is impure should perform the recitation of the Vidyā.
O Goddess, his destruction will surely occur; he shall certainly be consumed by the Vidyā.
Now listen, O beloved, to the distinctions of bathing as they have been declared regarding the time for bathing.
Bathing is said to be fivefold, by means of which one becomes identical with the Goddess:
the Vāruṇa, the Nābhasa, and the third is known as the Bhasmaja.
O Goddess, the fourth is Taijasa, and the fifth shall be Daivata;
these are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
These five great beings are established in the five ablutions:
Parā, Avantā, Anītā, Tatparā, and immediately after that, Tadanantara.
The fifth [case-ending] is proclaimed as being beyond the state of consciousness (cit).
Vāruṇa is said to be of two kinds: Vaidika and likewise Tāntrika.
The Vedic bath is declared to be performed according to the rules prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (śākhā);
one should perform the Tantric bath according to the procedure prescribed in one's own respective Tantra.
Having taken earth from a pure place with a ritual stake consecrated by the Astra-mantra,
and having sprinkled it with water using the Astra-mantra, one should go toward the abode of the waters.
There, first, one should wash the water's edge with the water of the weapon-mantra;
then, having divided the clay into two parts, one should take one portion from there.
Having placed cow dung, darbha grass, and consecrated sesame seeds,
one should perform the bath by rubbing [the body] with both clay and cow dung.
Having first bathed with water drawn from outside to become free of impurity,
he should thereafter perform the Vedic ritual bath as well as its ancillary libation (tarpaṇa).
Now, O child, I shall describe to you the bathing ritual that brings prosperity to one's lineage:
my forms are black, red, yellow, white, blue, and various others.
Then, following the procedure for the Tantric bath, one should take earth with the Astra-mantra and consecrate it,
as well as grass and other materials, with the Astra-mantra.
Having removed [the impurity] with the Śikhā-mantra, one should consecrate it three times with the Mūla-mantra;
having smeared [it] from the head down to the feet, one should offer water with the Praṇava.
I bow down to those waters, which are the support of Viṣṇu of incomparable splendor— the source of all beings— and from which they were born, having his very form.
Having manifested [the deity], bound the mudrā, and restrained the vital breath (prāṇa),
one should submerge [oneself] in silence and then rise, standing in water reaching up to the navel.
Having sipped water with the *kuladravya*, he should take a *kulapuṣpa* along with *darbha* grass;
then, as a *kulapātra*, he should take that *darbha* together with sesame seeds and water.
O Goddess of the Gods, the threefold *kuladarbha* has indeed been enjoined by Kālaśantunā; it is described therein, O Mistress of the Kula, as something to be kept secret.
Family *darbha* grasses, which are placed upon the family wheel, grant desired objects at the mouth [of the rite];
three *darbha* blades are prescribed, made of gold, silver, or *kuśa* grass.
In that regard, for the Śākta, two other [substances] are prescribed, while for others, three are considered appropriate:
gold and silver for rites such as recitation and worship.
One should prepare a purifier (pavitra) measuring half a karṣa or one karṣa;
it is said that [the grass] used for the rites of kuśa must be true kuśa, for not all wild grasses are kuśa.
Silver should be worn on the index finger, and gold should be worn on the ring finger;
this very [metal] is declared to be *kuśa*, while *darbha* is produced from the *varuṇa* plant.
Having drawn five *kūrca*s around a circular girdle,
and having inscribed a trident and a skull-cup, it is proclaimed as the *brahmakūrca*.
By the mere holding of this [Darbha grass], one shall obtain the desired result;
Darbha is said to be of three kinds in the tradition of Kālikā.
O auspicious lady, this must be kept secret; it is the great essence of essences:
the skull, the sword, and likewise the five female seeds.
This golden-colored [image], which brings auspiciousness, should be worn on the ring finger;
it represents Tārā of the Kūrcādi-kālika and the Seven Stars (Saptatārā) and so forth.
One should wear the *sarvabījādya* and the *kuladarbha*;
these generate knowledge, prosperity, and fame, bestow peace, and grant all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
O auspicious lady, having taken that which bestows all beauty and demonstrates the perfection of the seed-syllables,
one should perform the ritual bath for the pleasure of the family deity.
Having performed the Tantric ritual resolve (saṃkalpa) preceded by the mention of the month and other details,
he, once the resolve is made, should place the Kula-cakra in the water.
Then, having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra,
and having performed the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa), one should prepare the sacred water (tīrtha) in front.
In a square space of one cubit imagined within that water,
the holy fords from the interior of the cosmic egg are touched by his rays.
"By that truth, O Lord of Gods, O Sun, grant me a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Having thus prayed to the Sun, [he should strike] with the *kroṃ* syllable and the goad-mudrā (*aṅkuśamudrā*).
The goad mudrā is as follows.
Then, forming the right fist with the index finger in the shape of a blade of *kuśa* grass,
this great mudrā called the "Goad" is capable of attracting the three worlds.
Having entered the solar orb, one should cause the sacred fords to flow here:
the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Godāvarī, and the Sarasvatī.
"O Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, take up your residence in these waters!
Having spoken thus, one should unite the sacred fords (tīrthas) with that water.
Then, with the root mantra, one should invoke Śakti at the sacred ford (tīrtha) and,
having meditated upon the orb of the sun, worship it with its specific mantra.

She consists entirely of universal bliss, she is the destroyer of all sins without exception, her splendor is like that of the moon, she possesses three eyes, and she holds a noose and a goad in her two upper hands.
Within, I worship the Śrītīrtha-Śakti, who holds a golden pitcher filled with nectar, a rosary of pearls, and a garment, accompanied by the Gaṅgā, Sindhu, Saridvarā, and other rivers.
hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ hraiṃ hrauṃ hraḥ ||
Thus, [it is] supreme within that which consists entirely of bliss.
The great mantra of Tīrthaśakti is said to consist of twenty-one syllables: *tīrthaśakti*, followed by *hili* twice (*hili-yugam*), and ending with *vahnigehini*.
One should consecrate that water eight times with the *Gaṅgā-mantra*:
"Tāraḥ (Oṃ), namo bhagavati bhūyād ambe tatoṃ vike."
O Ambālikā, O Mahāmālinī, come, come to the path of the Blessed One!
At the root of the entire multitude of holy fords, one should utter the seed-syllable of Māyā-Śrī.
O Gaṅgā, who has ascended the matted locks of Śiva, O Mother Gaṅgā!
This is declared to be the Gaṅgā-vidyā, consisting of fifty-three syllables.
On the left, however, there is a distinction regarding the mantra and meditation of Gaṅgā:
Tāra, "namo bhagavati," Vāgbhava, and two instances of "hilī."
One should utter the mantra "Hili dvayaṃ pañcagaṅge māṃ pāvaya dvitayaṃ svāhā," which consists of the syllables of the Savior (Tāraka) and destroys all sins.
Meditative concentration.

Clad in red garments and red in complexion, she holds in her hands a trident, a jar, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness; she stands upon a tortoise, surrounded by the gods and other beings.

Having stirred that which is frequented by sages with those [mantras] of the same form for the destruction of the world along with its suffering, one should render it nectar-like by means of the atom of Sudhā (Amṛtīkaraṇa) through Bhuvaneśī.
Then, having veiled [the deity] with the Kavaca mantra and protected [her] with the Astra mantra,
the knower of mantras should [worship] the deity there with the root mantra, together with her limbs (aṅga) and her retinue (āvaraṇa).

Having meditated on the water as the Samāvāṣka [mantra], and having visualized the sacred ford (tīrtha) emerging from its two feet, the practitioner of the root mantra should bathe thoroughly with those waters while recollecting it.
Afterwards, one should remember the deity in the heart and sprinkle [water] with the *kuṃbha-mudrā*.
As for the *kumbha-mudrā*: [it is formed] as follows.
Having placed the right thumb upon the left thumb with both hands,
this single fist with space remaining is the mudrā known as the Kumbha.
By means of the three verses preceded by the root mantra, the Tāra, and the seed-syllable,
one who desires to create repeatedly generates the entire universe as pure semen.
May the Waters, the goddesses who are the mothers of all beings, purify me— they who,
existing within all beings, take the form of the impurity of misfortune.
May my own touch purify you, O goddesses, and may you in turn purify me;
whatever misfortune resides in my hair, at my parting, or upon my head—may it be cleansed.
One should offer water to the forehead, the two ears, and the two eyes with the mantra "Āpastambhantu vo namaḥ";
thereafter, one should perform the mental sprinkling three times with the root mantra ending in "svāhā."
Having thus gratified the deity in three ways, one should then depart from the midst of the water,
wearing a pair of washed garments and likewise having rinsed one's hands.
In that case, one should sip water using clay; this is recorded as the rule for bathing. A ritual bath with mantras (mantrasnāna) should be performed during cool places and times.
When there is a lack of water, when in a fortress, when in a state of illness, and in old age;
and whatever must be done in the absence of water, in a fortress, or during the cold season.
O best of Brahmins, O sage, for the sake of swift success in one's journey, one should remain untiring in weighty duties during the night-time when misfortune has arrived.
Having washed one's feet and sipped water with water drawn up [from a vessel],
one should then sit down after purifying the place and the ten directions as before.
Having placed water upon the palm of the hand, one should then proceed with the *prāsas* in sequence;
likewise, the placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*) for the *mātṛkā*s and so forth should be performed at the base (*mūla*) without exception.
One should touch water with these [mantras]; this is the excellent mantra-bath, superior to the water-bath performed by a deity that lacks ritual refinement.

Whatever fruit is obtained by one who has completed his vows from bathing at sacred fords such as Prabhāsa, it should be known that the fruit of the mantra-bath is ten times greater than that, according to certain authorities.
Now follows the mental bath (mānasasnāna).
One should perform mental bathing preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra, through the contemplation of the sacred fords that have been seen.
Now follows the lustration with fire (taijasasnāna).
I shall now fully explain the fiery [nature], by which all accomplishments are attained;
one should indeed contemplate with the intellect the identity of the Guru, the deity, and the mantra.
Having unified the splendor of the Guru, the splendor of the mantra, and likewise that of the deity— this triple consciousness— one should conceive it as the [divine] form.
One should contemplate the deity in the heart, the mantra in the throat, and the guru in the thousand-petaled lotus; thus one should meditate upon the threefold consciousness.
O Maheśānī, one should contemplate that form within one's own body as the most excellent of all one's limbs; this bestows the vision of the Deity.
O Goddess Pārvatī, listen now to that which is described as Taijasa, whose presiding deity is Deva.
Now follows the ritual bath for the deities.
O Goddess, O Śivā, beginning from the Mūlādhāra,
one should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess Virāj as the deity, her face joined with one's own face.
O Goddess, by means of the yoga of placement within one's own body, she possesses all parts;
O Maheśānī, at the location of the door are both the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā.
If one's own body is purified [by meditation], what fruit could there be from the Gaṅgā?
The channel named *iḍā* is situated on the left side, and to its right is the channel named *piṅgalā*.
Between these two, resting against the spinal column, stands the *suṣumṇā*, extending as far as the *brahmaraṃdhra*.
The *iḍā* is renowned as the Gaṅgā, the *suṣumṇā* is the river Yamunā, and the *piṅgalā* is the Sarasvatī; Prayāga is situated within the center of the body.
Without knowledge of the body, what fruit is there for the Goddess in external bathing?
One should contemplate the lineage of gurus in the thousand-petaled lotus and the limbs [of the mantra] between the eyebrows.
O Goddess, one should diligently contemplate all the deities of the enclosures as extending from the base of the throat [to the end]; this, O Goddess, is declared to be the "deity-bath."
By this method of bathing, what [impurity] that resides in the hand is removed;
indeed, all ritual actions preceded by bathing attain purity and perfection.
Therefore, one should first perform a bath according to the capacity of one's body;
thereafter, one should apply the *tilaka* appropriate to one's caste and to the deity.
The vertical *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* mark belongs to the Brāhmaṇa; the triple horizontal *tripuṇḍraka* to the Kṣatriya;
the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) to the Vaiśya; and the circular shape to the Śūdras.
One should apply the *ūrddhvapuṇḍra* with clay and the *tripuṇḍra* with ashes;
the remainder may be made with saffron or musk, or whatever else is cool and according to one's preference.

The vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) belongs to a devotee of Viṣṇu; the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) to a servant of Śiva; the half-moon to a devotee of Gaṇeśa; and the circular mark (vartula) to a devotee of the Goddess.
He who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa should apply a trident of sandalwood upon his forehead, like sacred ash, as the embodiment of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
The vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) should be made with ash, while the horizontal mark (*tiryakpuṇḍra*) should likewise be made with clay;
thus, the *puṇḍra* is called *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*, but the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* does not exist within the *tripuṇḍra*.
It has been declared by sages who have mastered the Vedas that this is equal to the murder of a Brahmin;
it arises from the Rudra-piṇḍa and is accompanied by the delusion of the twice-born.
Those who do not recognize their father are like the sons of prostitutes;
a learned Brāhmaṇa should not transgress the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), even in his mind.
But he who, having heard [the Veda], performs [the rite] would become a renouncer of truth and a priest;
just as a Śūdra has no entitlement to the study of the Veda.
A Brahmin who does not wear the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) has no authority for the worship of Śiva;
likewise, the wearing of sacred ash (vibhūti) must be performed according to both Vedic and Tantric rites.
That weapon was taken from Kapilā by him;
it remained in the sky, neither moist nor hard, neither foul-smelling nor putrid.
If it should fall, one should discard what is above and below and pick it up;
having formed it into a ball, one should cast it into the Śiva-fire while reciting the root mantra.
Having discarded both the under-ripened and the over-ripened [parts], as well as those that are stained or white,
one should take [the remainder], stir it with a cloth, and cast it into a receptacle for ashes.
One should perform the collection of the ashes once the deity has been dismissed;
for when the dismissal is performed, the fierce ashes (caṇḍabhasma) are produced.
O Goddess, O Sovereign of the Gods, the supreme rite of the ashes bestows the blissful realm of Satyaloka;
by means of the ashes, all bonds and all sins are destroyed.
That has been described as *bhasma* by the sages who know the truth;
furthermore, know that it is of two kinds: primary (*mukhya*) and likewise secondary (*gauṇa*).

The supreme Brahman is declared to be the "mouth" (mukha), while the ash is said to be the secondary (gauṇa) Agni; having thus begun with that [ash], the wise man should regard it as that other mouth.
O Ambikā, know that the secondary [means] is of various kinds; it destroys ignorance, is a means for attaining knowledge, and is auspicious, yet it takes away life.
O Śivā, that fire born from the Agnihotra is indeed born from the Virajā oblation;
it is produced from the Aupāsana fire and originates from the Samidh fire.
[The smoke] arising from cooking fires, arising from forest fires,
and arising from the agnihotra sacrifices of all members of the three varṇas.
O daughter of the mountain, one should wear the ash produced from the fire of the *virajā* plant;
it is especially prescribed for householders as that which arises from the sacred domestic fire (*aupāsana*).
The fire produced from the *samit* wood must be maintained by those practicing the life of a student (*brahmacārin*);
for Śūdras, it is the fire born from the ear-cavity, originating from the supreme fire.
For all others as well, that which arises from the fire of the funeral pyre should be maintained;
when the twice-born wish to prepare ashes, they should bring cow dung immediately.
Having placed [the substance] in the vessel with the left hand, one should burn it away with the Ghoramantra;
having lifted it up with the Puruṣamantra, one should purify it with the Īśānamantra.
In this manner, the consecrated ashes [should be applied] with the mantra beginning with "agniriti" and so forth,
and with the Yajurvedic mantra "tadrudrāya," which is known as the Rudra-mantra.
O Dear One, with these four mantras beginning with the Praṇava,
and with the names beginning with the five syllables, [one should worship] on the forehead, the shoulders, and the heart.
One should apply the triple mark on the head with the five-syllabled mantra;
furthermore, the twice-born and others should apply the sacred ash while reciting these names.
Brahmā is to be known on the forehead; Havyavāhana (Agni) in the heart; Pūṣan at the navel; and Rudra in the right arm. Skanda is in the throat.
Āditya is in the middle of the arm, and Śaśin is at the wrist;
Vāmadeva is in the left arm, and Prabhañjana is in the middle of the arm.
The Vasus are at the wrist, and Hari is remembered in the region of the back;
Śambhu is proclaimed to be in the hump of the neck, and the Supreme Self is remembered in the head.
The immersion of yogins is considered to extend from the soles of the feet to the aperture of Brahma;
for householders and ascetics, it specifically extends from the navel upwards.
Now listen as I declare the Tantric view:
a follower of Śakti should wear ashes well-blended with musk and other substances.
O Queen of the Gods, for all others as well, [the rite is performed] with the recited root-mantra or the five-syllabled mantra of Śiva, and not without a mantra.
Now, however, as for the distinction:
Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra for wearing the vibhūti; Tṛṣṭubh is declared to be the meter (chanda), and Rudra is the deity (devatā).
The seed-syllable of the temple, the power of the seed-syllable, the *kūrca*, and the *kīlaka*,
as well as the *kṣetrapāla*, are employed for the purpose of destroying all sins.

Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) beginning with the seer (ṛṣi) and so forth, one should then gaze at [the ashes] with the root mantra; having thus recollected [the deity], one should indeed place the sacred ash (vibhūti) upon the right hand.
Having covered [the vessel] with his left hand in the *kapota* gesture,
he should consecrate it three times with the mantra to be recited hereafter.
One should perform the encirclement with water while reciting the syllable *phaṭ* three times;
having chanted the root mantra five times, one should perform the purification.
Then, having placed the ashes from the right hand into the left hand,
one should stir them with water using the root mantra, O Dear One.
Having drawn a circular mandala, the best of the twice-born should place a hexagon in its center and a triangle within that, with the root-syllable at its core.
Then, covering [the disciple] with his right hand, he should recite this mantra:
"Prāsāda," "Kūrcabīja," "Kṣatrapāla," and likewise "Aṅkuśa."
Having addressed the stage of sovereign power (*vibhūtipada*), which removes all impurities without exception,
and having spoken of [the purification] of mind, speech, and body, I shall state the second [stage] for you to practice.
The mantra is proclaimed as being joined with the *kūrca*, the weapon (*astra*), and the fire-woman (*vahnilalanā*).
In this regard, there is a certain specific rule concerning the wearing of cremation-ground ashes.
One should perform the inspection with the root mantra and carry out the enveloping with the *kūrca* mantra.
The heart-mantra consists of the syllable *Tāra*, the three *medha*s, *Kāma*, *kūrca*, *varma*, and *astra*.
O Goddess, having purified [it] seven times with this mantra,
and then having recited the root mantra ten times, O Sovereign of the Gods.
Having offered [the substance] three or seven times to one's chosen deity,
one should apply a tilaka at the end for the sake of attaining the state of identification with the deity.
A person should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) with ashes while reciting the prescribed mantra;
one should cause the triple mark, which embodies Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, to be made upon the forehead.
The Tripuṇḍra should be made with the middle, ring, and index fingers; it should be neither too small—thereby being invincible—nor too long, for such a mark is imperishable.
A twice-born man should wear the Tripuṇḍra according to the measure of his two eyes;
however, for Brāhmaṇas, the Tripuṇḍra shall be six finger-breadths in measure.
The discharge [of semen] for kings is four finger-breadths; for Vaiśyas, three finger-breadths;
and for Śūdras and women, one finger-breadth.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the presiding deities of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra). Householders should meditate upon the ash-triple-mark combined with water.
Listen to the fruit of merit for him by whom ashes are thus worn at all times, except for women and ascetics, and excluding water.
Multitudes of great sins (mahāpātaka) as well as other minor sins (upapātaka) are indeed destroyed, O Goddess of Gods; this is the truth, the absolute truth, and not otherwise.
What is the use of saying more? The wearing of ashes is the means for attaining liberation, provided that the *vibhūti* which bestows prosperity is worn according to the prescribed rite.
In whatever manner it may be worn, [the sacred ash] reduces a person to ashes;
yet he who, out of delusion, wears the ash and then washes his hands upon the ground [is likewise destroyed].
That mortal shall dwell in the Raurava hell as long as the moon and stars exist,
for as many atoms of ash as there are fallen upon the earth.
A man who first applies sacred ash and then a tilaka with sandalwood paste remains a sinner for as many thousands of years as there are grains [of sand].
In particular, O Dear One, two things are essential for the Śāktas;
therefore, understand according to the rule how one should likewise wear sandalwood paste.
Having placed white sandalwood paste upon the palm of the left hand,
one should then write the root mantra there with the ring finger.
Having taken [the earth], one should cast it upon the ground while reciting the five mantras;
these are said to begin with *Tāra* (Oṃ), end with the *Hṛdaya* (Namaḥ), and also conclude with the dative case ending *-ṅe*.
Knowledge and will are the power of action; the desires are all the Kalottaras.
Having covered [the face] with the palm of the right hand, one should then [proceed].
O Īśvarī, while reciting the mantra that will be described, one should apply the *tilaka*,
not overstepping the horizontal line of ashes according to the prescribed rule.
Having uttered "Māyā, the one who assumes forms at will, the deluder of all people,
the bringer of subjection to all," he should then recite the pair of protective mantras.
The weapon-mantra accompanied by the head-mantra has been proclaimed to you by me;
O Goddess, this application of the forehead mark (tilaka) as taught in the Tantra has thus been declared.

Now, regarding the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā): Having sipped water (ācamana), facing the east and sitting down, one who knows the mantras should then perform the Vedic and Tantric saṃdhyā with a concentrated mind.
One should perform the Tantric twilight ritual (saṃdhyā) and the threefold sipping of water (ācamana) with the root mantra.
He states the number of *saṃdhyās* according to the different systems of knowledge (*vidyā*).
Sundarī should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā-vandana) four times a day:
in the morning, at midday, in the evening, and at midnight.
Pārvatī should diligently recite the fourfold Gāyatrī:
the Prastārā, the Kṛtirūpā, and likewise the one named Upasthānā.
O Goddess, the fourth is proclaimed as Vāñchākalpalatā;
the sixth is Pārāyaṇa in the morning, and that known as Nama at midday.

The recitation of the mantra known as the *cakrasaṃjñaka* at night during the dark of the moon is declared in this *Kālikā* [Tantra] to be performed without the ritual of formal attendance (*upasthāna*).
Due to the sovereignty of Medhā, Dīkṣā, and Ādirājñī, there are four twilight sessions for Kālī;
for Tārā there are three; and for Chinnā, it is of three kinds.
Indeed, there is no distinction among these; he who makes a distinction shall go to hell.
Then, having tied the topknot with the root mantra, one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform the placement of the limbs upon the body preceded by the placement of the hands (karanyāsa),
having consecrated the water in front with the Amṛtīkaraṇa rite and the Dhenu-mudrā.
And having consecrated it seven times with the root mantra,
he should then do so with the letters of the Mātṛkā, from 'a' to 'kṣa', accompanied by the bindu.
The knower of mantras should sprinkle [water] three times upon his head with the root of *kuśa* grass for every syllable,
while meditating on the deity as situated within the orb of the sun.
Having taken up water while reciting the mantras with the seed-syllables representing the elements—
namely *laṃ*, *vaṃ*, *raṃ*, *yaṃ*, and *haṃ*— one should [purify] that which is born of the seven [elements] by means of these.
Having consecrated it thus, one should further consecrate it seven times with the root mantra;
holding that water in the left hand, one should sprinkle it with the drops flowing from it.
Sprinkling with the right hand while reciting the root mantra,
one who follows the left-hand path (vāmācārī) should practice the service through the repeated application of the hands.
Having embraced her with that remaining portion in the form of splendor,
it entered within, purified all the internal impurity, and emerged.
Having remembered this in the right nostril, one should take [the substance] held in the right hand;
having visualized the Dakṣa-stone on the left side, one should cast it with the Astra-mantra.
Having washed his hands and sipped water (ācamana),
the knower of mantras should then offer three arghyas with the root mantra, with the Gāyatrī, and again with the root mantra.
Then, having taken water for the *argha* offering in his joined palms, he should offer it three times with the *Gāyatrī* mantra to the deity residing in the solar disc.
Regarding Tārā, however, there is this distinction:
having placed yellow mustard seeds, flowers, *kulapuṣpa*, water with *kuśa* grass, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) in a copper vessel, one should present the *arghya*.
At the end of the root mantra, from the word "rising sun" (*udyadāditya*), one adds "maṇḍale," then "vartinyai śivacaitanyamayyai svāhā"; that is the mantra for that [offering].
The distinction among persons.
Having placed it within the solar disc, one should offer it to one's chosen deity;
thereafter, one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra according to one's capacity.
A wise person should recite the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times;
even one burdened with great sins should recite it ten times.
Truly, truly, O Great Goddess, one becomes liberated at that very moment;
one should recite the Gāyatrī ten times according to the distinction between those who are capable and those who are incapable.
Having said, "With water, at the end of the root mantra, I satisfy [the name] amuka," one should perform the libation three times using the left hand for that purpose.
One should recite the Gāyatrī of one’s chosen deity twenty-eight times; in its absence, however, one who adheres to the Vedic tradition should recite the Brāhmī Gāyatrī.
The Tantric practitioner should recite the seed-mantra of Śiva; its ritual application is now described:
*Oṃ tanmaheśāya vidmahe vāgviśuddhāyadhīmahi*.
May that auspicious one impel us forward.
Now follows the meditation on Gāyatrī during the forenoon.
One should meditate upon Brāhmī, who resembles the rising sun, holding a book and a rosary in her hands,
wearing a black antelope skin, and seated upon a starry lotus.
At midday.
The goddess is dark-complexioned, four-armed, with hands resplendent with the conch and discus,
holding a mace and a lotus, and has made her abode within the orb of the sun.
In the evening.
In the evening, the wise man should meditate upon the goddess Gāyatrī,
the giver of boons— white-complexioned, holding white objects, and seated upon the bull.
