One should meditate upon the Goddess— three-eyed, bestowing boons, holding a noose, a trident, and a human skull-cup, and situated in the center of the solar disc— and practice her worship.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the dark Gāyatrī.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, the Gāyatrī was previously proclaimed [to you],
as well as its seer and other [limbs], its meditation, and likewise its recitation and worship.
And tell me, O Great God, O Lord, the means of accomplishment.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
I shall speak, O Mahādeva; listen, O beloved of my life!
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the seer (ṛṣi) of that [mantra], and Gāyatrī is its meter (chanda).
For the deities are proclaimed to have the very nature of Śiva and Śakti; O Goddess, listen with devotion as I describe their meditation here.
And in the cremation ground, one should meditate upon the goddess Mahākālī,
naked, with a face made terrible by fangs, and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
In the upper right hand he holds a bow, and likewise arrows in the left;
below these, a noose and a sword are proclaimed in that order.
Having meditated thus upon Mahākālī, one should recite her mantra four hundred thousand times;
then, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with bilva leaves smeared with blood, using a tenth part of that number as the offering.
And the means of accomplishment, O Great Goddess, one should perform as before.
Now, the first Gāyatrī is as follows:
Having uttered the word *kālikāyai*, one should say *vidmahe* immediately thereafter;
then one should speak *dhīmahi*, ending with *śmaśānavāsinī*.
Having uttered that "Tanno Ghore," one should then recite "Pracodayāt.
Merely by the grace of this [mantra], millions of great sins [are destroyed].
They undergo immediate dissolution for the practitioner and not otherwise;
indeed, even Rāmacandra was deluded by the death of Rāvaṇa.
By her grace, Paraśurāma was liberated from the sin of matricide,
as were Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Dattātreya from the drinking of liquor.
"And by the severing of Brahmā’s head, I, Rudra, was liberated;
thus is this Gāyatrī, the goddess, the beautiful Great Vidyā."
Even if one is burdened by great sins, O Great Goddess, if one recites [the mantra] ten times, it is the truth, the absolute truth— that one becomes liberated at that very moment.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin truly crumble into pieces;
there is no knowledge equal to this, and no recitation equal to this.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a knowledge equal to this.
Now, [the mantra] of Tārā:
Having uttered the word "Tārāyai," one should then say "vidmahe";
after that, having pronounced the word "nagogrāyai," one should then again say "dhīmahi."
Having uttered that word "devi," one should subsequently say "pracodayāt."
Now, regarding the severed [vow].
"Let us know Vairocanī, and let us meditate upon Chinnamastā;
may that Goddess impel us toward her state. Thus one should recite and apply [the mantra].
Now, [the mantra] of Tripurasundarī:
One should first utter the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable] and then say, "We know the Goddess Tripurā"; thereafter, having pronounced the Kāma-bīja, one should say, "and we meditate upon Kāmeśvarī."
Having uttered "tannaḥ" and "klinne padaṃ," one should thereafter say "pracodayāt."
Now, [the mantras] of Bhairavī:
One should extract the word "Tripurā" ending with "aṅge," then utter "bhairavyai," and thereafter say "dhīmahi."
Then, having uttered the word "Devī" and the word "pada," one should pronounce "pracodayāt.
This is called the Gāyatrī of the Tripura; one should extract the Vāgbhava syllable as the beginning.
Now, [the ritual] for Kamalā.
Having uttered the word "Mahālakṣmī," one should then say "vidmahe";
having spoken the word "mahāśriyai," one should utter the word "dhīmahī."
From that word "tat" comes the syllable "śrī," and from "naḥ" one should give the word "pada"; then [from "tat"] comes "pracodayāt."
Now, [the procedure] for Bhuvaneśvarī.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should recite "vidmahe" for Bhuvaneśvarī;
then, having uttered the word "ādyāyai," one should recite "dhīmahi" immediately thereafter.
Having uttered that word "Devī" for us, one should then give [the mantra] ending with "pracodayāt."
Now, Mātaṅgī.
Now I shall declare the Gāyatrī that bestows boons upon the practitioner:
"We know Śukapriyā; we meditate upon Śrī Kāmeśvarī."
May Śyāmādevī inspire us in this matter.
Now follows Dhūmāvatī.
Having uttered the seed-syllable *dhūm*, one should recite "Dhūmāvatī" and then the word "vidmahe"; from the word "vivarṇādevī," one should extract the phrase "dhīmahī."
The Gāyatrī of the goddess Dūmā is: "Tanno ghora pracodayāt."
Now follows Vagalāmukhī.
Having recited "Sthiramāyā," one should utter the words "Vagalāpadatomukhī"; then, after "vidmahe," one should recite the word "duṣṭayadataḥstaṃbhinī."
At the end of the word "dhīmahi," one says "tanno devī pracodayāt.
O Maheśānī, this is proclaimed to be the Gāyatrī of Vagalā.
Now, [the hymn] of Gaṇeśa.
"Let us know that Tatpuruṣa; let us meditate upon Vakratuṇḍa; may He impel our intellect"—having thus uttered the word "Tanno Danti," one should thereafter say "Pracodayāt."
Now, [the ritual] of Āditya.

From the word *saptaturaṃgāya*, one should extract the word *pada*; then, from the word *padam*, one should extract [the syllable] *ud*. Then, from the word *sahasrakiraṇam*, one should take [the syllable] ending in *ṅe* (*ṅe*), and again from the word *dhīmahi*, [one should take the syllable] *pa*.
Having uttered the word "tanno raviḥ," one should then know that [the word] "pracodayāt" follows.
Now, [the ritual] for Nārāyaṇa.
We know Nārāyaṇa; we meditate upon Vāsudeva.
May that Viṣṇu inspire us.
Having recited the mantra, one should offer it after praising and bowing to one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā);
then, one should place the deity from the solar disc within one's own heart.
Then one should bow to the Guru; this is the Tantric Sandhyā.
Thus, the three-fold Sandhyā has been described, which bestows success upon those engaged in ritual action.

In this manner, the twilight rites should be performed at all three times; for there is no fruit from the omission of the twilight rites. One should never, under any circumstances or at any time, neglect the twilight rites.

The morning twilight, together with the stars and the sun, is said to last for twenty muhūrtas; beyond that, it is no longer twilight, but day. As for the evening twilight, it lasts for five muhūrtas after the sun has set. Thus it is according to the respective times.
The time near the Abhijit [nakṣatra] is most excellent;
likewise, it is most excellent within a three-nāḍī interval even when the primary time of the twilight (saṃdhyā) has been omitted.
However, as an atonement,
one additional *arghya* offering is presented when the time has passed beyond the subsequent period of twilight (*saṃdhyā*).
In that case, one hundred and eight recitations of the Gāyatrī are prescribed for a king, a person afflicted by disease, or for any necessary ritual act.
Having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), one should recite the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times;
however, when the deity is Tantric, one should then mutter the root mantra one hundred times.
Having performed the expiation prescribed for the occasion, one should perform that which has arrived according to the established rule.
Now, the libation (tarpaṇa).
Having performed the Vedic libation (tarpaṇa), one should then begin the Tantric rite;
having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the root mantra.
Then, in front of the triad beginning with the Ṛṣi, while reciting "vaṃ," he consecrates the water into nectar by means of the Dhenu-mudrā; there, he [visualizes] the Cakra.
Having meditated on the King of Mantras in the water and placed the goddesses therein,
and having offered libations to the lineage of gurus, one should satisfy Vaṭuka and the others.
Having satisfied the Root Goddess (Mūladevī), one should satisfy the members of her retinue;
likewise, one should satisfy the gatekeepers and the deities of the limbs (aṅga-devatās).
One should worship Śaṅkhikā in the west, the supreme Guru in the north,
Parāpara in the southeast, and Parameṣṭhin in the southwest.
One should offer libations to the lineage of gurus starting from the northwest (Vāyavya) and ending at the northeast (Īśa);
one should offer libations to the limbs in their respective locations and to the Goddess in the center.
At the end of the root mantra, [one says] "I satisfy the goddess Amukī," and thereafter follows the mantra ending with the wife of Vahni (svāhā); this is prescribed for the libation of the goddesses.
Now, concerning men.
One should join the word "tarpayāmi" (I satiate) at the end of the mantras, using one's own names in the accusative case; this is considered the mantra for the rite of libation (tarpaṇa).
Whether twenty-one times, ten times, or even three times,
one should satisfy the attendants by offering water in single handfuls.
One should satisfy the deity with the waters of sacred fords (tīrtha), perceiving them as nectar;
however, one may use animal sacrifices and the like through the Vāmā path and other such means.
In case of inability, one should recite the root mantra and satisfy the Goddess alone,
while recollecting the god Bhairava, known as Mārtaṇḍa, the lord of Umā.
One should worship the deity with the root mantra, or else with the mantra of the Sun;
having extracted the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), one should then place "So'ham" in reverse order.

The mantra of the Sun is declared to be "Mārtaṇḍa Bhairava" ending in the dative case (mārtaṇḍāya), conjoined with the light (prakāśa) and the power (śakti); one should prepare the arghya offering three times.
O Queen of the Gods, one should not worship Viṣṇu or Śaṅkara until the arghya offering has been presented as an oblation to the Sun.
Having satiated the Goddess within his own heart, he should dismiss the Tīrtha and the Sun;
then, having bowed to the Guru, the lords of the directions, and the birds, he should hold the vessel in his hand.
Carrying a vessel full of water, remaining silent, and remembering his chosen deity within his heart,
he should go to a secluded, solitary place that is pleasing and free from defects.
He should not look toward the horizon until he reaches his home.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of Morning Duties and Other Rites," in the *Śrītantracintāmaṇi*.
Now, the procedure for the daily worship of Sarvadhāraṇī is written.
O beloved, it is called "Pūjā" because it pacifies past lives, wards off birth and death, and bestows the full fruit [of one's actions].
Having circumambulated the sacrificial enclosure and having washed his feet and hands,
he performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and stood at the threshold of the house for worship.
Standing at the doorway of his home, he should mentally bow to his guru,
and having bowed to his own chosen deity (iṣṭadeva), he should also pay homage to the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) within his mind.
Whatever sin was previously accumulated, whether on that very day or on another,
one should recite these two mantras for the purpose of purifying that sin.
O God, this mind of mine is ordinary and this intellect is overcome by evil;
therefore, extract that evil from my mind—phaṭ phaṭ! And salutations to you.
The Sun, the Moon, Yama, Time, and the five great elements—
these nine are the witnesses here in this world of one's auspicious and inauspicious actions.
Uttering "huṃ phaṭ," one should gaze at both sides with a wrathful look;
when this has been done, it is the first [step] in the rite for the eradication of evil.
Since that sin is so exceedingly firm, let it remain far away;
yet, once the place of worship has passed, it shall return to you once again.
Because even the slightest evil is brought to destruction by worship, one’s desired object shall be attained in an instant once that evil has been cast off.
Then, having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with care, he should offer the arghya to the Lord of Day; the method for that is stated here.
Having prepared a mandala on ground smeared with cow dung,
one should then sit upon one's own seat using vermilion.
Facing the east, the knower of mantras, intent on devotion,
should bow to his chosen deity after performing three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas) with the Sūrya mantra.
"Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Saḥ" is said to be the three-syllabled mantra of the Sun;
having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and likewise meditated upon Indra and the other deities, one should contemplate the Sun with undistracted mind.

I worship Bhānu, the supreme non-dual one, who holds the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting with his lotus-like hands; who wears a crown of rubies, whose body has a reddish luster, who possesses three eyes, who sits upon a red lotus, who is the sole ocean of all virtues, and who is the mind of the entire universe.
One should worship with ritual offerings according to the procedure prescribed in that tantra,
having drawn a square mandala with water in front [of oneself].
Having placed there a copper vessel containing water along with its base,
together with scents, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, darbha grass, dūrvā grass, and mustard seeds;
He should place sesame seeds, unhusked grains, flowers, and barley into it,
touching that vessel one hundred and eight times while reciting the Sūrya mantra.
Having consecrated that vessel and risen from his seat with both hands,
the wise practitioner should offer the arghya water up to the head while reciting the Sūrya-mantra.
One should utter *hrīṃ hrīṃ saḥ sa* followed by the words for the planets (*graha*), zodiac signs (*rāśi*), and lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*),
and then the terms for the yogas (*yoga*), the karaṇas (*karaṇa*), and the revolution of the seat (*parivṛttāsana*).
The mantra for the offering of water (argha) to the venerable Sun is recorded as: *saṃsthitaḥ śrīsūryāya eṣate 'rghaḥ svāhā*.
This consists of thirty-four syllables and is used for the presentation of the argha to Sūrya.
Then, with one-pointed mind, the best of teachers should recite the Sūrya-mantra according to his capacity,
while meditating on the Sun submerged in that arghya water.
Having praised and prostrated, he should dismiss the Sun from the mandala;
then, having risen, he should duly commence the worship of the gateway.
Having sprinkled the door with water for the guest-offering (arghya), one should worship Vighna in its center,
Mahālakṣmī to its right, and Sarasvatī to its left.
And in the center of that [door], one should fashion the beauty of the door (dvāraśrī) upon the right and left branches,
divided into five sections each, from the upper part down to the threshold.
Having pronounced the first syllable of the name joined with a bindu, and the name ending in the dative case (ṅe),
one should worship these deities who have been drawn [into the heart].
Then [he should worship] Gaṇapati and Kṣetrapāla, joined with Vasundharā; and Śaṅkhanidhi on the right, accompanied by Sumati on the left.
Having worshipped Padmanidhi, he placed him to the right and left;
likewise, he placed Māyāśakti, Citśakti, Gaṅgā, and Yamunā.
Salutation to Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and salutation below to the threshold (dehalī).
First, however, the worship of the western door has been explained.
Having worshipped Nandī and Mahākālī at the right and left doors respectively, one should worship the northern door, and then worship [the deities] in the east and south.
The door-keepers among them are, in order, Gaṇeśa and Vṛṣabha,
as well as Bhṛṅgirīṭi, Skanda, Umā, and Caṇḍeśvara.
Viṣṇu’s attendants are Nanda, Sunanda, Caṇḍa, and Pracaṇḍaka;
Bala, Prabala, Bhadra, and Subhadraka.
Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadaṃṣṭra, Mahodara, Gajānana,
Lambodara, and Vikaṭa are the Gaṇeśas who serve as gatekeepers.
Vighnarāja, smoke-colored, [is positioned] successively from the western door;
these eight—the Goddess, Sūrya, and the Yoginīs—are the guardians of the gates.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
as well as Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Śrī.
Now I shall describe the meditation on the deities of the door, which is concealed in the tantras—
that which opens by itself the divine gateway and the deities of the door.
I bow to Vīra Vighneśvara, who holds a noose, a goad, and a fruit in his hands, whose face is like a trumpet-flower, who has an elephant’s countenance and three eyes.
She has four hands, two of which display the lotus and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
she possesses limbs as radiant as refined gold and has three eyes—[one should meditate upon] Mahālakṣmī.

One should meditate on Sarasvatī, who has three eyes, is white in complexion, wears white garments, sits upon a white lotus throne, and holds in her hands a rosary, a book, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting mudrā.
Shining like molten gold, adorned with divine jewels,
the Goddess of the Door stands upon an upward-facing lotus, her lotus-hands displaying the gestures of boons and fearlessness.
White-complexioned and elephant-faced, he stands upon a mouse, wielding an axe, a staff, a noose, and a trident in his four arms.
I meditate upon the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapāla), who bears a skull and a trident, who is compassionate yet possesses a dark form, who has three eyes, is fierce, and who has destroyed his enemies.
I worship Śaṅkhanidhi, who resembles a pearl, who is pot-bellied, and who embraces Vasudhārā with his right hand while holding a conch in his left.
The earth goddess embraces him on his forehead, which is marked with the lotus sign;
he holds the Padma-treasure, resembling a jewel, while holding a blue lotus in his left hand.
I worship Māyā, who is dark-complexioned, three-eyed, and the root of saṃsāra; she holds in her hands the boon-granting gesture, the goad, the gesture of fearlessness, and the noose.

I bow to Gaurī, who possesses the splendor of the rising sun, who has three eyes, who is radiant in her red garments, and who holds a noose, a goad, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness— she who is the embodiment of pure consciousness.
I worship the Great Goddess Gaṅgā, the supreme river of the gods, who bestows boons and fearlessness, who is gentle, and whose splendor is equal to ten million moons.
One should meditate upon Kālindī, who holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, whose form is dark,
who is mounted upon a black tortoise, and whose throat possesses the luster of a blue lotus.
I bow to the creator of the worlds, who holds the conch, discus, mace, and lotus;
who is mounted upon Garuḍa, the sustainer, whose form is Kṛṣṇa.
I salute the Creator, who is red in color, seated upon a red lotus, holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness along with a water-pot, mounted on a swan, and endowed with three eyes.
I bow to Sudakṣiṇī, who is mounted upon a lion, dark-complexioned, bearing a sword and a shield, and stationed beneath the threshold in the west.
Having reached the western door, preceded by three *tāla* hand-claps,
he should strike the door with the *astra-mantra* and [scatter] consecrated mustard seeds and unhusked rice grains.
The wise preceptor should scatter flowers within the pavilion with the *nārāca-mudrā* while reciting the mantra from the *anyatra-astra*.
But let the spirits, piśācas, pretas, and guhyakas depart,
as well as whatever other deities dwell here, established upon the earth.
Whatever beings are moving away, whatever beings are stationed upon the earth,
and whatever beings are creators of obstacles— may they perish by the command of Śiva!
Then, reciting the two verses and the Astra-mantra along with the Tārā-mudrā, he should cast [the oblation] into that pavilion; thereafter, those obstacles which have departed [should be dealt with].
By contracting his own left side and making way for it, he should cause [the opponent] to move away,
while recollecting the weapon-mantra (astramantra) and striking with the left heel three times.
One should dispel terrestrial obstacles with three claps of the hands, those belonging to the intermediate space with a side-glance,
and divine obstacles by looking upward.
One who follows the Śākta tradition should enter the temple of the deity placing the right foot forward,
while covering the door with his cloth using the left foot.
One should sprinkle the interior of the pavilion with the five products of the cow and with water for the arghya offering;
it should be made smooth like the surface of a mirror by means of sweeping, smearing, and other such preparations.
This purification of the site is considered to consist of stainless incense, lamps, and so forth; adorned with garlands of flowers and variegated with powders of five colors.
One should worship Vāstupuruṣa in the southwest with salutations and other offerings;
in that very place, one should also offer obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the site, with the words "Obeisance to Brahmā."
Having worshipped Dīpanātha Bhairava, who is red in color and endowed with twelve red-colored śaktis, one should pray as follows:
O you of exceedingly sharp fangs and massive body, who are like the fire at the end of an eon—
homage to you, Bhairava; you should deign to grant me your permission.
Then, with the mantra "Aḥ Phaṭ," one should enter the altar of worship;
one should consecrate the place for the seat by means of the four [purifications], beginning with inspection (vīkṣaṇa).
There, during the ritual of consecration (saṃskāra), one should worship the deities of the seat (pīṭhadevatā) ending with the altar (vedyanta);
beginning from the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), one should then install one’s own seat there.
Then, one's own seat for worship should be prepared with cloth, deerskin, and a layer of kuśa grass on top,
or else upon a woolen blanket, or a red or black tiger skin.
A celibate student (brahmacārī) seeking renunciation should enter upon the skin of a black antelope;
for the attainment of all perfections, he should use a tiger skin, while the deer skin leads to the perfection of knowledge.
A seat made of cloth removes disease; one made of cane increases affection; a silken seat is said to bestow nourishment; and a woolen blanket grants all perfections.
Today is white (lunar day), the day is bright; specifically, there is a red blanket.
On a white blanket, there is success in Dharma; on a red one, the successes of Artha.
In yellow, Kāma grants [boons] to others besides the twice-born; in black, he bestows liberation;
when dyed for the sake of release from suffering, he is red; however, blue-dyed is not auspicious.
Now, the prohibited postures.
Grass, sprouts, wood, stone, as well as that made of clay,
a bamboo seat, a cloth, or the bare ground alone may serve as a seat.
O Goddess, one should thus avoid these eight kinds of seats;
having sat there according to the rule, one should joyfully remember Viṣṇu and the Guru.
Merupṛṣṭha is declared as the seer (ṛṣi), Sutala is said to be the meter (chaṃdas),
Pṛthivī is declared as the deity (devatā), and the application (viniyoga) is for one’s own seat.
The earth was supported by you, O Goddess, and you were supported by Viṣṇu;
therefore, O Goddess, support me and make this seat pure.
In the four corners of the seat, one should worship Gaṇeśa and Sarasvatī, as well as Durgā and Kṣetrapati, and likewise Brahmā and the others.
Facing either north or east, seated in the svastika posture,
or even in the lotus posture, with the body straight, he remains steady and composed.
Now, the characteristics of the Svastika and Padmāsana postures.
Having properly placed both soles of the feet between the knees and the thighs,
sitting with the body erect— that is declared to be the Svastika posture.
Placing the left foot upon the right thigh and likewise the right foot upon the left thigh,
holding them firmly from behind with both hands according to the two-fold method,
placing the thumbs at the heart, and looking at the tip of the nose— this is Vyādhi-bandha.
The lotus posture (padmāsana) is said to be that which causes the destruction of the enemies [of yoga].
One should place one's own articles of worship on the right side,
and on the left, a beautiful water-pot filled with well-perfumed water.
To wash his hands, he should place the vessel behind his back;
he should then set up auspicious lamps filled with ghee and other substances, burning brightly, all around.
Having placed the mirror, the fly-whisk, the parasol, the palm-leaf fan, and the sandals each in their proper place, he should consecrate them as he would himself.
One should look upon the flowers, the food offerings, the perfumes, and so forth with the mantra *hāṃ hīṃ hrāṃ phaṭ*,
using the *nārāca* mudrā and the gaze, and likewise look upon the *samayī*.
Whether it be the sight of flowers and such things known by oneself to be defiled,
or even the touching of that which is untouchable, or whatever else has been acquired.
Likewise, whatever has been touched by the remains of offerings (nirmālya) or climbed upon by insects and the like—
all that shall go to destruction through the sight of the food offering (naivedya).
Then, with the mantra "Ram," one should touch the crest of the lamp;
that lamp will be auspicious, free from the smell of raw flesh, and a bestower of happiness.
From the burning of moths, insects, hair, and the like, it is joined with a collection of carnivorous creatures;
and it is employed through substances such as clarified butter produced from fat, marrow, and so forth.
All that which is of unknown form perishes through the defect of impurity;
the mantra-practitioner, uttering the seed-syllable *kṣraum*, should touch [the body] with the *devatīrtha* [part of the hand].
Having seen the water-vessel situated in the middle, the practitioner,
holding the jar located at his left side with his left hand, should act correctly.
Consecrating it with the mantra for the bowl-support (pātrādhāra), one should touch the blazing [fire];
[the fire] is joined with its own name-initial syllable, provided with a bindu and the half-moon (ardhacandra).
The name of that vessel should end in the dative case (ṅe), and this is the mantra for that vessel;
through ignorance of which, contact with impure substances and the like has occurred here.
Whatever other defilement may arise from a vessel or water through ignorance—
whether from contact with a corpse in a reservoir or from the water itself— is likewise removed.
Such refutations perish when one worships the deity for his sake;
then, with palms joined in *añjali*, [one should worship] on the left and right sides.
Having bowed to the Guru, Gaṇapati, and one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) in front of oneself,
the knower of mantras takes fragrant flowers smeared with sandalwood paste.
One should rub [the hands] with the *hyauṃ* mantra and with the weapon (*astra*) mantra;
then, taking those flowers with the left hand, one should place them upon the head.
Having smelled it again, one should rotate the wide [vessel] all around while reciting the mantra;
then one should first recite "Hauṃ Oṃ," and this verse is proclaimed as follows:
May all those destroyers who harm me go to destruction;
may death, disease, fear, and afflictions fall upon the heads of my enemies.
One should cast the *nārāca* weapon toward the northeast with the *astra-mantra*;
thereafter, one should perform the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*) with the *astra-mantra*, followed by the recitation of the three *tāra*s.
One should perform the binding of the directions (digbandha) with the Astra-mantra, directed higher and higher;
and by that [mantra], one should transform the generated splendor into fire using the Prākāra-mudrā.

One should protect oneself with the root mantra and perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma). Thereafter, one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi); I shall now describe its procedure.
From the feet to the knees, it is square and marked with a vajra;
joined with the syllable *laṃ*, yellow in color, it is the ground-element whose presiding deity is Brahmā.
The place presided over by the power known as Nivṛtti is called the station;
one should contemplate the single form of that reality from which living beings arise.
From the knees up to the navel, my station is white in luster;
it resembles a half-moon and has two peaks marked by lotuses.

One should meditate upon this [disc], which has six corners, is endowed with six dots, is joined with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, is united with the *pratiṣṭhā* kalā, and has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity.
From the navel up to the throat, the region is reddish, has Rudra as its presiding deity,
is joined with the seed-syllable *Raṃ*, and is endowed with the digit known as Vidyā.
One should contemplate the external element of fire, which is endowed with blazing svastikas, has assumed a triangular form, and possesses the configuration of the great dissolution.
Extending from the throat to the space between the eyebrows, it assumes the form of a hexagon;
it is marked with six dots, encircled by a circle, and is black in color.

One should contemplate the station of air, presided over by the power of peace (śāntikalā), having Śiva as its deity, joined with the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, and existing in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of all beings.
The space situated between the middle of the eyebrows and the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) is called the abode of space;
it is circular in shape, smoke-colored, and marked by a great, lofty thunderbolt.

Having meditated upon this as being presided over by the Śakti called Śāntyatītā, having Śiva as its deity, and joined with the seed-syllable *haṃ*, one should thus perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the elements within the body.
Having produced [the self] from the bulb of Dharma, beautifully adorned with the stalk of knowledge,
one should place it within the pericarp, resembling the flame of a lamp.
The practitioner, through the method of yoga-yukta, should unite the individual soul with the Supreme Self by means of the Suṣumṇā path, using the mantra "So'ham."
Therein, one should contemplate all beings as dissolved;
and within the body, specifically in the left side of the abdomen, one should contemplate the personification of sin (pāpapūruṣa).
The personification of evil, with the luster of soot, stands in the left side of the belly;
he has the murder of a Brahmin for his head and shoulders, and the theft of gold for his two arms.
The drinking of liquor is associated with the heart; violating the teacher’s bed with the two hips;
association with such persons with the pair of feet; and minor offenses with the limbs and sub-limbs.
One should contemplate the sinful protector as being covered in hair from minor transgressions, with red beard and eyes, cruel, and bearing a sword and shield.
O Śivā, one should remember the form of the sin in the Śaiva and Śākta [traditions] by means of the right hand;
in the Śaiva [tradition], by the right hand in sequence, and in the Śākta, by the left hand.
In the Vaiṣṇava [tradition], meditation on that [deity] as being of equal size is proclaimed;
likewise, one should indeed dry up this [body] through the sequence of inhalation (pūraka) and so forth.
One should contemplate charcoal or smoke at the region of the navel;
by that, one should indeed dry up the *liṅga* and the body for sixteen measures.
Having encapsulated the karma-nature with sixty-four [units], one should perform the practice;
or again, according to the opinion of Deva, one should excise it within thirty-two measures.
One should contemplate the red-colored seed-syllable of fire at the base of the penis;
one should burn the body with that linga, which consists of the seat of impurities.
According to the previously mentioned sequence,
the instructor should exhale through the right nostril by means of the mental count, using the abbreviated number.
Having visualized the syllable *vaṃ*, the seed-syllable of Varuṇa,
at the throat, one should produce nectar from that thousand-petaled lotus.

Having performed the inhalation and other breath-control exercises (pūraka, etc. down to the soles of the feet, one should visualize the syllable *laṃ*, the seed-syllable of Earth, at the root of the anus.
By that very same sequential method, the wise one should completely immerse the supreme Śambhava body, which is liberated from both sin and merit, with his intellect.
By that very same previous path, one should accomplish the entire body;
once the whole body has been brought into being, one is capable of the worship of the deity.
Then, one should cause the principles (tattvas) dissolved within the self to return to their own respective places;
thereafter, one should lead the self into the heart-lotus of the Supreme Self.
Having consumed the body, which is of the nature of light, according to the rules with the Haṃsa-mantra, the deity should worship the Deity; for one who is not a deity should not worship the Deity.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, one should contemplate that one's own true nature is realized within oneself;
one should contemplate that what has arisen is fit for the propitiation of the deity.
A worship performed by one who is devoid of the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is like black magic;
it yields a contrary result, just as worship performed without devotion does.
Having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should perform the installation of the vital breaths (prāṇasthāpana).
The sages, the lords, and the lotus-born Brahmā [have declared this] to be the mantra for the consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).
The meters are the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda; the vital breaths (prāṇas) are the powers, and these are the deities.
The seer is on the head, the meters are on the mouth, and the deities are on the heart.
"Āṃ, salutation to the Seed-syllable at the secret place; Hrīṃ, salutation to Śakti at the feet;
Namaḥ Krauṃ, salutation to the Kīlaka at the navel—thus is the yoga of firm establishment."
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ; having uttered the nasalized *aṃ* class along with the sky as the face and the five principles, one should place *āṃ* upon the heart for oneself.
Oṃ āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ iṃ, and likewise the five beginning with the letter *ca*; having uttered "ātmane īṃ," [one places] the consort of fire upon the head.
Having uttered those seed-syllables— *uṃ*, *tāṃ*, *ṭa-varga*, and the sense organs beginning with hearing— and having said *tadātmane ūṃ*, one should utter *śikhāyai vaṣaṭ*.
One should say "eṃ" for those seeds, "tuṃ" for speech and the others, and "ai" for the self;
then one should say "kavacāya hūṃ" immediately thereafter.
The four seeds previously mentioned, the *oṃ* and the labial class (*pavarga*) likewise,
as well as the words beginning with "vacana" and so forth, should be followed by "to the Eye, *vauṣaṭ*" (*netrāya vauṣaṭ*).
One should utter the four seed-syllables, the *y*-group beginning with the last [letter], the mantra beginning with *manu*, the vowel for that self, and finally *astrāya phaṭ*.
One should indeed extend the deity from the thumb and so forth to the palm of the hand;
likewise, from the navel down to the throat, and from the head down to its end.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the syllables *āṃ*, *drīṃ*, and *kroṃ* in sequence upon the eight petals of the heart-lotus starting from the east,
one should place the syllables ending with *hṛt* in the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

One should place *laṃ*, *raṃ*, *haṃ*, *saṃ*, *vaṃ*, *ca*, *yaṃ*, *saṃ*, *śaṃ*, and *kṣam* in the directions according to their respective groups; thereafter, one should meditate upon the vital power (*prāṇaśakti*) residing in the heart.

I bow to the Goddess who has red feet, who stands upon a fresh lotus, who holds a noose, a goad, a spear, a trident, and a skull-cup in her lotus-like hands, who is red in complexion, and who possesses three eyes.

Placing the hand upon the heart, one should recite the seed-syllable of speech (Vāgbīja), the eight syllables beginning with *yā*, and the mantra "Haṃsaḥ So'haṃ mama prāṇā iha sthitāḥ" (I am that; my vital breaths are established here).
Having spoken thus, and likewise saying again, "My life-breath remains here," and having said that once more, he should then say, "And all my sense-faculties."
Furthermore, in that same way, my speech, mind, and eyes shall go forth;
and having come here through the ears and nostrils, they shall remain for a long time within the mouth.
Having recited "tiṣṭha" up to the word "vahnijāyā" (svāhā), one should then release the Tāra and perform the recitation;
one should meditate on the body as consisting of light—this is the stabilization of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Now, as for breath control (prāṇāyāma), it is as follows.
Having taught the three types of breath control (prāṇāyāma), the practitioners of Vedic yoga recite the hymn;
the results are, respectively, the perfection of mantras, the destruction of sins, and the attainment of yoga.
It is considered to be of two kinds: that which is called Mātṛkā and that which is called Mantra.
If that which is called Mātṛkā is performed at the beginning and at the end of the recitation (japa), [it is the former].
Listen now to how the remaining defects, such as the transposition of syllables and so forth, are destroyed:
one should fill the breath with the vowels and the consonants beginning with *ka* through inhalation (*vāmaya*), and then perform the retention (*kuṃbhaka*).
One should inhale through the right nostril with the *yādi* [consonants] and the *mātṛkā* [vowels],
and having restrained the vital breaths as much as possible, one should mutter the mantra with the mind alone.

Holding the nose with the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb, one who possesses the measure [of breath] performs what is called *prāṇāyāma*, wherein whatever was done by another is performed by the mind.
Recitation, worship, and other such rites remove only his fault;
[one should recite] the Gāyatrī together with its Śiras, preceded by the seven Vyāhṛtis.
This Vedic method is considered to be performed three times, joined with each *praṇava*;
it consists of pressing the middle finger from its base to its tip with the thumb.
That is declared to be a *mātrā*, which bestows the desired result through six applications;
it is the time taken by the hand to circumambulate the knee.
The duration of a breath is likewise measured by that same amount of time;
the shortest [breath] is the length of a cow's lowing, while the middling is the length of a Jina.
This sixfold group is the most excellent, the true accomplisher of the three yogas;
when *kumbhaka* alone is mastered, the perfection born of *rājayoga* shall arise.
There is firmness of vigor, long life, and the destruction of wrinkles and graying hair;
when pūraka and kumbhaka are mastered, the perfections of one fit for practice arise.
And as previously stated, neither cold nor heat, nor hunger, thirst,
or fatigue arise when the inhalation (pūraka) and the retention (kumbhaka) alone become equalized.
Hatha Yoga is always established in the eightfold powers, such as *aṇimā* and the rest;
its fruit is slight in the lowest [grade], middling in the middle, and complete in the highest.
Through practice for three continuous years, all the fruit shall be attained;
having performed three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the ritual placement of the Mother-letters (mātṛkānyāsa).
The seer (ṛṣi) is on the head because of his gravity; the meter (chandas) is on the mouth because of its nature as syllables;
retention (dhāraṇā) is said to be in the heart because it is attained through the mind's object of knowledge, which is the deity.
The verbal root *ṛ* in the sense of "going" is considered to be the bringer of the vowel *ṛ*;
however, that which is below the vowels *i* and *u* is consciousness (*vijñāna*), and therefore it is the bringer of that [consciousness].
The verbal root *chat* means "to desire" and belongs to the first class (*adādi*), having the sense of giving;
therefore, *chandas* is that which bestows desire, distinguished by its specific arrangement of syllables and phonemes.
The word *devatā* is fully derived from the verbal root *div*, meaning "to play";
those who bestow [attainments] upon the practitioner are proclaimed as *devatās*.
This heart, which is the self of consciousness, is the very Self that is to be protected;
therefore, one should pay homage there and touch it with the thumb.
Since the withdrawal of the sense objects is properly performed by means of *svāhā*,
by whom will it be sprinkled with those [objects] drawn in by the ring finger and the forefinger?
The syllable *śekha* is the limb of *vaṣaṭ*; the planet is the body of the self through the crest (*śikhā*).
Therefore, the *vaṣaṭ* is performed with the middle finger.
For the purpose of grasping, the armor-element is seized with the hand of smoke;
however, that armor from the body is [grasped] by the bent forefinger.
The knower of the true meaning [knows] that from the two [fingers] in the six-mantra, it is produced by these two;
therefore, *vauṣaṭ* is said to be there, and it is traditionally taught to be performed with the index finger and so forth.
From the single syllable [of the seed-mantra], one should utter the deity beginning with Kuvera and ending with Indra;
for Viṣṇu and others it ends with *bhyām*, but for Rudra and others, it consists of the *tantra* (the mantra-formula).
That weapon which destroys the internal and other forms of the practitioner,
born of ignorance— that is elaborated by the two *tāra*s [oṃs] followed by *phaṭ*.
Having performed the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) of the Mātṛkā, one should perform the ritual placements (nyāsas);
these are said to be twenty-one, according to the distinctions of one's desires.
That secret is now being expounded according to the distinctions among qualified practitioners, as well as by way of its eternality and the differences among deities.
O Goddess, within the Puruṣa resides the eternal, absolute Mātṛkā of vowels;
through her placement (nyāsa), the practices such as celibacy and other virtues become perfected for the practitioner.
The seer is Brahmā, while the deity is Sarasvatī known as Mātṛkā;
the consonants are the seed-syllables, Gāyatrī is the meter, and the vowels are said to be the power (śakti).
Manifestation is designated as the *kīlaka* (stake), and its application is for the sake of attaining one's desired goal;
it is [to be performed] on the palm of the right hand, on its back, and likewise on the wrist.
One should place [the letters] beginning with the thumb on the left hand in reverse order;
joined with the *bindu*, this is the first arrangement of the vowels (*svaranyāsa*) in their proper sequence.
This reverse arrangement is called the *saṃhāranyāsa* (dissolution placement);
one should perform this ritual at the beginning for the sake of destroying sins, enemies, and so forth.
That which is performed with the vowels together with their visargas, arranged in the manner of a placement (nyāsa), is the Sṛṣṭinyāsa;
it should be performed at the beginning of a ritual application for its successful accomplishment.
One should place the eight vowels, beginning with *ḷ* and ending with *ḹ*, upon his left palm from the little finger to the base; likewise, one should place them upon the right palm as well.
This [syllable] beginning with 'a' and joined with the bindu and visarga is called Unmana;
it is known as Sthiti (Maintenance), and like the previous ones, it is employed for the maintenance of the gods, sages, and others.
Indeed, these fifteen letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṇa* are placed upon the joints of the right hand,
starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger.
One should place all [the letters] joined with the moon (bindu) on the left side as well, starting with *tā* and so forth;
one should also perform the placement on both hands, from the thumb to the little finger.
One should utter the five syllables beginning with *yugapadyāti*, ending with *namaḥ* and followed by the [specific] name;
placing the hand on each respective location, this is the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhi*).
Aṃ and āṃ are in the middle of the ka-group; i and ī are in the middle of the ca-group;
uṃ and ūṃ are in the middle of the ṭa-group; and e and ai are in the middle of the ta-group.
Oṃ Auṃ: the *pa*-group should be in the middle; likewise, the letters beginning with *ya* are in the middle of *aṃ* and *aḥ*.
With these [letters] accompanied by the bindu (*m*), one performs the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the fingers and so forth, as well as on the heart and other [limbs].
For the sake of its accomplishment, the assignment of the seers (ṛṣis) and other elements must also be performed for this [mantra];
likewise, the purification of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) is for the cessation of sins born from anger and other [afflictions].
One should perform the binding of the directions for three *tāla*-measures with the Astra-mantra;
thereafter, one should meditate upon a white lotus of syllables situated upon one's own head.

One should contemplate one's own mantra in the pericarp (karṇikā) and the eight filaments (keśara); likewise, one should place pairs of vowels in the eight vessels and the consonants beginning with 'ka' in the remaining eight.
One should contemplate the seven groups in this manner up to the eighth lac;
for one who contemplates thus, minor diseases and even death are destroyed.
Now, I shall describe the internal placement of the Mātṛkās (antarmātṛkā-nyāsa), which brings about purification;
by performing which, the mind of the Yoginī proceeds [freely] from sin.
Having heard the sound of the *mūlādhāra*, the *kuṇḍalinī* power awakens;
she blazes like glowing embers, exceedingly subtle and consisting of radiant energy.
Touching the lotus of the head from the *mūlādhāra*, she is like a flash of lightning;
having touched the lotus of the head, she is the embodiment of the rising flood of nectar.
Having caused the letters of the Mātṛkā, which have emerged from the body via the path of the Suṣumṇā, to be established [within],
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) while meditating upon them as thus situated.
In the throat is the lotus called the Viśuddhi-cakra, possessing sixteen petals;
it faces upward, and the sixteen vowels are situated there, beginning from the eastern petal.
Having reflected thus, one should utter the mantra beginning with Tārā and so forth, joined with the bindu and ending with *namaḥ*,
along with the vowel for all these letters, according to the ritual manual.
One should meditate on the heart as the unstruck (*anāhata*) wheel with twelve petals;
one should arrange the letters beginning with *ka* on those petals starting from the eastern petal, just as before.
Then one should contemplate the Maṇipūra-cakra in the region of the navel;
there, one should contemplate the ten petals with the letters beginning with 'ḍa', as before.
The Svādhiṣṭhāna is said to be the six-petalled wheel at the base of the genitals;
one should meditate upon the vowels and the six syllables there, as before.
The wheel known as Mūlādhāra is lotus-shaped and has four petals;
there, one should contemplate the syllables Vaṃ, Śaṃ, Ṣaṃ, and Saṃ on the petals starting from the eastern direction.
The wheel called Ājñā, located between the eyebrows, is two-petaled and lotus-shaped;
one should meditate upon "Haṃ" and "Kṣaṃ" there, which is to be performed by the mind alone.
In one's own body, the rite should be performed with Vāmā; in the forms of the deities, it is performed with Puṣpā.
Its seer is Anādila, and its meditation is like that of Brahmā.
Now I shall describe the external nyāsa: one should meditate upon Sarasvatī, known as Mātṛkā, within the previously mentioned lotus of letters at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra).

I bow to her whose face, arms, feet, belly, and chest are adorned with the fifty distinct letters; who possesses radiant matted hair and wears a digit of the moon; who is white as the moon, jasmine, and snow;
whose excellent hands hold a rosary, a water-pot, and a lotus; who has three eyes and stands upon a lotus, appearing as if she were the very embodiment of the pure Vedic tradition.
I bow to that Goddess of Speech, whose weight is borne by her breasts, arms, and shanks.
One should place the vowels on the forehead, the face, the eyes, the ears, the nose,
the two cheeks, the two lips, the two rows of teeth, the head, and the mouth.
The wise practitioner should place the *va* group at the joints of the arms and at the tips [of the fingers];
likewise, the *ta* group on the feet, and similarly the *pa* group on the sides and the region of the back.
Then one should place the *pa*-group at the navel and the abdomen, followed by the *haṃsa* syllable and the *kuṃda*;
thereafter, one should assign the four letters beginning with *śa*, and then assign the six letters beginning with *ṣa*.
This assignment (nyāsa) is performed in the heart and other centers, in the hands, feet, belly, and likewise in the mouth;
it fulfills the recitation by supplying the missing syllables and measures.
Now he explains the Mātṛkā-mudrā.
One should place [the fingers] on the forehead, between the nostrils, and on the circle of the mouth;
and one should likewise place the index, middle, and ring fingers on the two eyes.
Having worshipped the index and ring fingers, the best of practitioners should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa);
having placed the thumbs on the ears, he should place the little fingers and thumbs on the nostrils.

Having placed [the ring fingers] on the middle of the cheeks, one should place the middle fingers on the middle of the lips; having placed the ring fingers on the corners of the mouth, one should place the middle finger on the crown of the head.
The ring finger, middle finger, and little finger should be placed on the face, the middle of the hand, the foot, and the two sides; likewise, they should be placed behind the back.
The practitioner should place all of them with the thumbs at the region of the navel, in the belly,
in the heart, and in the region of both shoulders.
Placing the palms upon the head, the hands, the feet, the belly,
and the face— these are proclaimed as the Mātṛkā-mudrās in their proper sequence.
If one performs the ritual placement (nyāsa) without knowing [the proper order], that placement shall be fruitless;
however, if the placement is performed beginning with the letter *kṣa* and ending with the letter *a*, [it is effective].
This placement of the names of the withdrawal [mantras] is called the *bindu*-placement (*bindunyāsa*). Now, the meditation upon the deities on the path to the left and the right is described.

Bow down to Varṇeśvarī, who is slightly bent by the weight of her breasts; she holds a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, a deer-skin, a raised ṭaṅka-axe, and a book beautifully adorned with jewels, possesses three eyes, wears the crescent moon upon her crest, is ruddy in hue, and is clothed in a red lotus.
The nyāsa of the mātṛkā with the visarga should be performed exactly like the simple mātṛkā;
however, the specific distinction is that the pronunciation of the letters should end with the visarga.
One should place the letters from *ḍa* to *ṭha*, joined with the nasal bindu (*m*) and the visarga (*ḥ*), during the phase of maintenance (*sthiti*).
In this way, those previously mentioned [mantras] are to be generated; now the meditation on the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-dhyāna*) is described.

One should meditate upon her with lotus-hands, who possesses the luster of vermilion, is adorned with immeasurable ornaments, has three eyes, and holds a book, a rosary, a young deer, and a boon-granting gesture; and one should also meditate upon the Goddess standing at her side, possessing the splendor of a forest fire.
Holding a book and a rosary of beads.
The nyāsas should be performed with four and six [syllables] for maintenance (sthitī), withdrawal (saṃhāra), and emanation (sṛṣṭi);
one who resides in the house should perform the nyāsas in sequence as withdrawal-emanation-maintenance.
The forest-dwellers and the self-controlled ones should perform the ritual depositions (nyāsa) according to the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
thus has the detailed procedure for the deposition of maintenance been proclaimed.
I shall describe the placement (nyāsa) of the Kalāmātṛkā; its seer (ṛṣi) is remembered as Prajāpati, and its meter (chandas) is Gāyatrī, while its deity is [the Goddess].
Sarasvatī shall be the Mother (Mātṛkā) for this [mantra]; her application leads to the fulfillment of one's desires.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the *tāra* (Om), using the vowels situated between the short and long [consonants].
She carries in her hands a lotus, a discus, a bow, a deer, a book, a rosary of beads, a bright axe, a skull-cup, a leaf, a vessel filled with nectar, and a jar;
she possesses five faces made beautiful by necklaces of pearls, lightning, silver, crystal, and coral.
I bow to Śāradā, whose face resembles the moon, and whose jar-like breasts are bent by the weight of her own eyes.
Having thus meditated upon the Mātṛkā beginning with *Ta* preceded by *Tāra* (Oṃ),
starting with *Ma*, joined with the *bindu*, ending in the dative case (*ṅe*), consisting of the first portion of the *kalās*, and conjoined with *Rāma* (Ra).
One should place the previously mentioned pure *mātrās* in the locations for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*):
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidya, Śānti, and likewise Īndhikā.
It is called Dīpikā, Recikā, Bhocikā, and the one with the excellent name; furthermore, it is Sūkṣmā, Asūkṣmā, Amṛtā, Jñānāmṛtā, and Āpyāyanī.
Pervasive and of the nature of space, she is the infinite source of creation who bestows prosperity;
she is memory, intelligence, beauty, fortune, austerity, and firm stability.
Siddhi, Jarāpālinī, Vakṣānti, Īśvarikārati,
Kāmikā, Varadā, another [is] Ākhyādinī, and Prīti joined with Saṃyutā.
Dīrghā, Tīkṣṇā, Raudrī, Bhayā, Anidrā, Taṃdrikā,
Kṣudhā, Krodhinī, and finally Kriyotkārī— these are the messengers of death.
Yellow, white, and red, followed by the one facing west; endowed with that [energy],
one should thus place the Mātṛkās of the Kalās in their respective locations, beginning with the letter *ka*.
The Svarajas, however, are born from Sadāśiva, who is of the nature of sound (nāda);
they hold a rosary, a book, a noose, and a skull-cup.
Holding [lotuses] in their hands, white-complexioned, and adorned with white garments and ornaments,
these ten digits (kalās) of the letter-group 'ka' were born from Brahmā, who is the letter 'a'.
Yellow in color, holding a rosary, a lotus, the gesture of fearlessness, and a water-pot in their hands, they should be meditated upon as being anointed with yellow perfumes and unguents.
The ten digits of the *ṭa* and *ta* groups are born from the syllable *u* of Viṣṇu;
they are described as being dark-complexioned, with hands holding the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*), the conch, the sword, and the boon (*vara*).
From the letter *ma*, nine digits of Rudra were born, resembling the autumn moon; with their hands, they display the gestures of fearlessness and the trident.
And the skull should be meditated upon as being held by the excellent [deities] by the practitioners;
from the letter *ṣa* onwards, the five [syllables] should arise from the Lord.

In the ritual placement consisting of the digits (kalās), they should be meditated upon as being red in color and holding the gestures of fearlessness, the deer, the axe, and strength with their sprout-like hands.
The deity to be realized (*sādhya*) is Nārāyaṇa, derived from the Mātṛkā beginning with Keśava;
the Gāyatrī meter begins with Amṛtā, and the deity is Lakṣmī-Hari.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the mantras repeated twice, [accompanied by] the desire for power and prosperity:
the conch, discus, mace, lotus, water-pot, mirror, lotus, and book.
One should worship Hari, who is radiant with the color of a flickering cloud;
his powers (śaktis) are seated upon his dear lap, their faces smiling.
Having meditated thus, one should install the Śaktis with the syllables encased by Śrī and Kāma;
these Śaktis, beginning with Tārā and ending with Hṛdayā, as well as those beginning with Keśava, [should be installed].
Those ending in *bhyām* and those ending in *namaḥ* should be uttered and placed in their respective positions beginning with the letter *a*;
for the Śākta practitioners, however, the measure is one *kalā*, while for the constant worshippers of Viṣṇu, it is one *mātrā*.
Keśava is endowed with fame; Kānti is united with Nārāyaṇa;
Mādhava is joined with contentment; and Govinda is joined with nourishment.
Viṣṇu is endowed with fortitude; Madhusūdana is joined with peace;
Trivikrama is united with action, and [he] is accompanied by truth.
Śrīdhara is endowed with wisdom (medhā), Hṛṣīkeśa with joy (harṣā),
Padmanābha with faith (śraddhā), and Dāmodara with modesty (lajjā).
Vāsudeva is joined with Lakṣmī; Karṣaṇa is joined with Sarasvatī;
Pradyumna is joined with Prīti; and Aniruddha is joined with Rati.

The wielder of the discus and mace is joined with Jayī-Durgā; the wielder of the Śārṅga bow is endowed with Prabhā; the wielder of the sword is united with Satyā; and the wielder of the conch is accompanied by Caṇḍī.
He is joined with the plow and the pestle, and is playful;
he holds the trident together with Vijayā, and his hands are endowed with Virajā.
Aṅkuśī was joined with Viśvayā; Mukunda was joined with Vinadā; Nandaja was joined with Sunadā; and Nandin was accompanied by Smṛti.

Nara is known as the conqueror of the world through his supernatural power (ṛddhi), Hari as the one endowed with purity through his prosperity (samṛddhi), Kṛṣṇa as the one joined with truth through his awakening (buddhi), and Aja (the Unborn) as the one endowed with wisdom (mati) through his skillful means (yukti).
Śauri with Kṣameśvarī, Uśan with Damayantī, Janārdana with Umā;
Bhūdhara with Kledinī, and Viśvamūrti with Klinnā.
Vaikuṇṭha is joined with Vasudhā; Vasudhā and Puruṣottama are [joined] together.
Valī, however, is joined with Parā; [they are] devoted to the destruction of Vala.
Vālasūkṣma, Vṛṣaghnastu, Saṃdhyāyukta, Rayāvṛṣa, and Haṃsa are the names; Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the deity, and Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter.
The Lord who carries away the Daughter of the Mountain (Śiva) is the injunction for the attainment of all perfections;
the seed-syllables of the plowman (Halāhala) are in the secret place, while the powers of the vowels reside in the feet.
Having placed the short and long vowels in between as before,
and having joined them with the six long vowels, one should install the six limbs and so forth upon the body using the syllables *ha-sau-ma-saṃ*.
Resembling the bandhūka flower and gold, holding a beautiful rosary, a noose, a goad, and the gesture of granting boons with his own staff-like arms;
adorned with the crescent moon, possessing three eyes, and having the hair of Umā half-bound upon his head— [I meditate on him] perpetually.
We take refuge in the body.
One should utter those Mātṛkās joined with the deities;
[the mantra] ending in "ṅe" and "ṅeṃtāṃ" for that Śakti, ending in "namaḥ" in the place of the Mātṛkās.
One should state skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and life-force;
likewise, one should state power, anger, and the self, ending with the dative case (ṅe), across all ten [limbs].
Śrīkaṇṭha is with Pūrṇodarī, Ananta is joined with Virajā;
Sūkṣma is with Iḍā, Trimūrtika is joined with Śālmalī and Lolākṣī.
Amaraśa is associated with Vartulākṣā; Ārvīśa with Dīrghaghoṇā;
Bhārabhūti with Dīrghamukhī; and Atithīśa is joined with Gomukhī.
Sthāṇvīśa is joined with Dīrghajihvā, Yugadhara with Kuṇḍodarī,
and Śobhautika with Vikṛtāsyā, who has hair standing erect and wears a garland of skulls.
The one born immediately is joined with Jvālamukhī and Ulkāmukhī;
in Akrūra, he is joined with Śrīmukhī on the great throne and Vidyāmukhī.
Krodheśa with Mahākālī, Caṇḍa with Sarasvatī,
and Pañcāntaka with Sarvasiddhi are proclaimed as being joined with Gaurī.
Śivottameśa should be installed, joined with the Trailokyavidyā;
Ekarudra with the power of the mantra, and Kūrmeśa joined with the eight Śaktis.
Ekanetra is joined with Bhūmāmā;
then that Varānana is said to be joined with Lambodarī, while Ajeśa is joined with Drāviṇī.
Sarveśa is joined with Nāgarī; Someśa is joined with Khecarī; Lāṅgalīśa is joined with Mañjarī; and Dārukeśa is joined with Rūpiṇī.
The Vīrīṇya [mantra] consists of half of the Ācāra-mantra;
it is joined with Umākānta and likewise with Kākodaryā and Āṣāḍhī, and is said to be conjoined with Pūtanā.
Daṇḍīśa is joined with Bhadrakālī; Yugatrīśa is joined with Yoginī;
Mīneśa is joined with Śaṅkhinī; and Meṣeśa is joined with Tarjanī.
Lohita is joined with Kālarātri, and Śikhīśa with Kurddinī;
Chagalaṇḍa is with Kapardinī, and Dviraṇḍeśa with Vajrā.
Mahākāla is joined with Jayā; Vālīśa is joined with Sumukhī; Bhujaga is joined with Revatī; and Pinākin is joined with Mādhavī.
Khaḍgīśa is joined with Vāruṇī; Vakeśa is joined with Vāyavī;
Śveta is joined with Vadhāriṇī; and Bhṛgu is joined with Sahajā.
Nakulīśa joined with Lakṣmī, Śiveśa joined with Vyāpinī,
and Saṃvartaka joined with Mahāmāyā— these are the Mātṛkās.
One should employ Īśa from Śrīkaṇṭha up to Īśāna;
all these Rudras are remembered as being red in color and bearing tridents and skull-bowls.
The Śaktis reside in the Rudra-pīṭhas, their forms as red as vermilion,
with lotus-hands adorned by a red lotus and a skull-cup.
By which the Great Vidyā is to be worshipped, she who possesses tenfold authority;
O gods, [this is] Bhuvaneśī preceded by the seed-syllable, upon the seat of the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
The seer is Śakti, the meter is Gāyatrī consisting of the Mātṛkās, and the deity is Bhuvaneśī; its application is for the attainment of one’s own desired goal.
With the six groups of consonants, both short and long, joined with their respective long vowels,
one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) as before, beginning with the thumb in the same manner.

May the Sovereign of the Universe bestow upon us [her grace]: she who is like ten million rising suns; who, though possessing the form of a bull, is yet adorned with the crescent moon, necklaces, girdles, and anklets as if she were a woman;
who shines with lotus-like hands holding a rosary, a noose, and a book.
The face of the three-eyed one is slightly lowered like a lotus.
Having first uttered the seed-syllable of modesty (lajjābīja), there is indeed the Mātṛkā-nyāsa;
for in that practice where the installation of the Mātṛkās is prescribed, Bhuvaneśī [is to be employed].
Those householders who desire prosperity should perform [this rite] preceded by the seed-syllable *śrī*.
Bhṛgu is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Gāyatrī is the meter (*chandas*), and the Mothers are the personification of the form.
Lakṣmī is declared to be the deity; perform [the assignment] in the place of Hara for the sake of the six-limbed nyāsa and so forth, preceded by the Śrī-bīja for the remainder.
She possesses a radiance equal to a streak of lightning, and with her four arms resembling the snowy mountains, she is being sprinkled by jars of nectar held aloft by her trunk-like arms;
she holds a rosary, a pair of lotuses, and a book in her lotus-hands.
One should meditate upon the Mistress of the World, whose youthful breasts are radiant with shining jewels.
For the sake of accomplishing all desires, the sage, considered to be the "Enchanter," should first perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa preceded by the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja).

The *gāyatrī* meter is prescribed, and the deity consists of the *mātṛkās*. The goddess named Saṃmohanī [is worshipped], along with the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) according to the previously mentioned method.

One should meditate upon the Mother of all beings, who has three eyes, and who holds in her lotus-like hands a rosary of crystal radiant as ten million rising suns, a bow made of sugarcane, the five arrows of Smara, and the sacred lore.
She who has the nine moons as her crest-ornament.
Through the nyāsa of the Mātṛkā, beginning with the Śakti, Śrī, Kāma, and other seed-syllables, men's defects regarding mantras—
such as hostility and the like— arising from many syllables, are destroyed.
The sage is declared to be Mahāsaṃmohana, the meter is Gāyatrī;
the deity is named Saṃmohanī, and the ritual placement (nyāsa) is the same as that of the Mātṛkā.

One should meditate upon her who holds in her own arms a rosary, a sugarcane bow, two nooses, two lotuses, a goad, five arrows, and a fresh book; she is ruddy in hue, alluring, three-eyed, and has nine moons as her crest-ornament.
For the purpose of dispelling all obstacles, one must certainly perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
In the *Gaṇeśamātṛkā*, the sage is said to be Gaṇaka.

Having remembered that the meter is Nivṛt-gāyatrī and the presiding deity is Vināyaka, one should perform the limb-protection (aṅganyāsa) enriched with long vowels and meditate upon the Elephant-faced One.

I worship Gaṇeśa, who is red in complexion, possesses three eyes, and holds a spear, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in his hands; he is embraced by his beloved, who holds a red lotus in her hand.
Having meditated thus, one should place one's own seed-syllable conjoined with the preceding letter:
Vighna (conjoined) with Hrīṃ, and Vighnarāja conjoined with Śrī and the others.
Vināyaka is endowed with nourishment and joined with Śakti; he is the supreme Śiva.
He is the creator of obstacles, yet when united with the power of emanation, he is the remover of obstacles, Sarasvatī.
Gamā is joined with Svāhā; Ekadanta is joined with Medhā;
Dvidanta is endowed with Kānti; and Gajavaktra is united with Kāminī.
Nirañjana is joined with Kāminī, while Kapardin is joined with Nadī;
Dīrghajihva is joined with Pārvatī, and Śaṅkukarṇa is joined with Jvālinī.
Vṛṣadhvaja was with Nandā, Sudyaśas with Gaṇanāyikā,
Gajeṃdra with Kāmarūpiṇī, and likewise Sūrpakarṇa with Umā.
Trilocana with Tejovatī, Lambodara with Satyā, Mahānanda with Vighneśī, and Caturmūrti with Svarūpā.
Sadāśiva is with Kāmadā; Yugmāda is with Unmada-dvijihvā;
Durmukha is joined with Bhūti; and Sumukha is accompanied by Bhautikā.
The division [of the mantra] is joined with Sitayā; Ekapāda is joined with Umā;
Dvijihva is joined with Mahiṣī; and for the trident as well, there is Bhujaṅginī.
Vīra is joined with Vikarṇī; Ṣaṇmukha is endowed with Bhṛkuṭī.
Vāmadeva, the bestower of boons, is accompanied by Rajjā or Dīrghakoṇā.
Dhanurdhara with Cakratuṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa joined with Jāminī,
Senānī conjoined with Rātri, and Kāmāndha joined with Ugrāmaṇī.
From me comes Śaśiprabhāyukta; from Vimatta, Lolalocanā;
from Mattavāhana, Cāñcalya; and from Jaṭī, Dīpti.
Maṇḍin is joined with Subhagā, and Khaḍgin likewise with Durbhagā;
Vareṇya is joined with Śivā, and Bhagin with Yugavṛṣaketanā.
Gaṇeśa, fond of his devotees, is accompanied by Bhaginī;
Meghanāda is joined by Subhagā; and Vyāpin should be conjoined with Kālarātri.
Gaṇeśvara and Kālikā are declared to be the Mother of Vighneśa;
the application of the skin and other [sheaths] for the vowels and so forth is proclaimed as before.
Now, the placement of the limbs of the ritual (prapañcayoganyāsa), which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, shall be described.
One should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) using the mantra of Mahāgaṇeśa.
The seer is said to be the calculator (gaṇaka) of the Prapañca-sacrifice;
the metre is Gāyatrī preceded by Nivṛt; and the deity is Mahāgaṇapati.
One should place those [syllables] on the head and other parts, and the seed-syllable *gaṃ* in the secret place;
the power *svāhā* is for the feet—this application is for the attainment of one's desired goal.
Having first uttered "Oṃ Śrīṃ Hrīṃ Klīṃ Glauṃ Gaṃ," joined with the six long vowels, one should perform the limb-assignments (aṅga) and likewise place [the mantras] upon the thumbs and other fingers.
Having performed the three claps with the Astra-mantra, one should perform the binding of the directions;
then, by the sound of the index finger and thumb, one should contemplate [the protection] in the ten directions.

The moon-crested Lord, whose face is like that of a lordly elephant, who has three eyes and is draped in saffron, is constantly embraced with passion by his beloved, who holds a lotus in her hand and rests upon his lap;
he is equipped with a citron, a mace, a bow, a trident, and a skull-staff.
I worship him who bears in his hands a discus, a lotus, a noose, a blue lotus, the tip of a grain of rice, his own tusk, and a jewel-filled flask.
Thereafter, one should recite the mantra of Mahāgaṇapati eight times; "Gam" is its single-syllable seed-mantra (bīja), and Gaṇaka is considered its sage (ṛṣi).
The Lord [taught] the Vighneśvaracchanda, consisting of three leaders,
in the Nivṛtti-kalā for the sake of achieving the completeness of the sacrifice known as Prapañca.
The application for the purpose of reciting forty-four times is as follows;
then, one should perform the ritual for the limbs (aṅga) with [the mantra] joined with the six long vowels.
Holding a noose, a goad, and a rosary in his excellent hands, he has four arms;
he is the color of vermilion, bears the moon upon his crest, is adorned with serpents, and drips with the ichor of rut.
One should recite it once, followed by the Vedic mantra "Gaṇānāṃ tvā.
Regarding the Gaṇeśa Mālā Mantra, the sage (ṛṣi) is traditionally remembered as Gaṇaka.
The meter is proclaimed to be Amita, and Gaṇapati is the deity.
Hrīṃ, Kroṃ, and Tāra (Oṃ), followed by Namaḥ and all [the names] ending in the dative case (ṅe), and then Vidyādhipa.
"To the giver of the accomplishment of all aims" and "to the pacifier of all suffering," and then "O Gaṇapa, come, come, O Blessed One, taste! and so forth.
"Staṃbhaya" (paralyze), the two [syllables] "hrīṃ gaṃ gāṃ," and "namaḥ" with the wife of Agni (svāhā)—
this mantra of fifty-five syllables is proclaimed as "kroṃ hrīṃ."
One should recite this four times and perform the placement (nyāsa) together with the sages and others;
first, however, the placement of the Mātṛkās should be performed three times preceded by meditation.
The vowels together with the *sa*-group are declared to be the planets;
Brahmā is proclaimed as the sage (*ṛṣi*) of the mantra of the Prapañcayāga.
The Gāyatrī is declared to be the supreme primordial meter, the most excellent;
the Great (Mahaḥ) is declared to be the supreme deity, whose nature consists of pure consciousness.
He is eternally awakened at the end, all-pervading and stainless;
by means of the five supreme [syllables] in reverse order, which are established within the human world, [the universe is perceived].

[The mantras are formed] with the short and long vowels, the semi-vowels, and the consonant groups beginning with ka, preceded by [the seed-syllables] such as Tāra (Om) and Māyā (Hrīm), and joined with the Astra-mantras and the syllables of Hari and Hara.
The instructor should perform the six ancillary rites (ṣaḍaṅga) conjoined with the [appropriate] birth-mantras (jāti).

Worship that supreme splendor— the single root of the universe, which is constantly being investigated by the five Vedas and other means of knowledge yet remains inaccessible to them; which is Being-Consciousness, all-pervading, eternal, and infallible—
a vast ocean of intense compassion.
Having pronounced separately the letters beginning with 'kṣa' along with the bindu at the beginning and end of the Vedas,
and saying "haṃsaḥ so 'yaṃ svāhā" within his heart;
One should visualize these phonemes and offer them into the fire of the self;
having thus offered those beginning with 'a' and ending with 'a', one should offer them once again.
One should place [the letters] ending with the visarga up to the letter kṣa in the locations of the Mātṛkā;
thus is described the Mātṛkā-nyāsa known as the Prapañca-yāga.
One should perform the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa) with the auspicious principles of self-knowledge;
the principle of the self (ātmatattva) is proclaimed to extend from the feet up to the navel.
The principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva) is proclaimed to extend from the navel to the heart;
the principle of Śiva (śiva-tattva) is proclaimed to extend from the heart to the point between the eyebrows (bindu).
One should duly place the root mantra at the end of each of the three sections;
then, having recited the entire mantra, O Śivā, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) over all the limbs.
This entire reality has been proclaimed as that which effects the state of divinity for all.
O Goddess of gods, the principles of the lunar days (tithi-tattvas) indeed reside within the principle of the self (ātma-tattva).
Indeed, the twenty-five principles become the principle of knowledge (vidyā-tattva);
indeed, the thirty-six Śaiva principles reside within the principle of Śiva.
Now, indeed, there are fifty principles within every principle;
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) known as the Yoga-pīṭha according to this other method of placement.
Having first performed that which was previously mentioned, the practitioner should then proceed with his own chosen mantra;
having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra.
One should assign the seer (ṛṣi), meter (chandas), and deity (daivata) according to the prescribed rule.
Now, he describes the locations and gestures (mudrās) in the sequence of the assignment of the seer and the others.
One should place the *ṛṣi* on the region of the head, the *chandas* in the lotus of the mouth,
the *devatā* in the heart, and the *bīja* in the secret region.
One should place Śakti on the two feet and Kīlaka on all the limbs;
O Goddess, one should assign the Ṛṣis and the others, ending with the fourth [syllable] at the heart.
Now follows its mudrā:

one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the sages, meters, and deities; the four fingers, excluding the thumb, are prescribed for this, and one should then place them up to the power-fingers (śakti).
The foremost of practitioners should drive the ritual stake (kīlaka) into all parts of the body using his two hands positioned apart.
Or alternatively:
One should place the Ṛṣi with the fingers joined together, excluding the thumb;
then, one should again place him in the lotus-face with those same fingers, using the tips of the left hand.

The wise one should place all [the syllables] previously recited in the heart, the anus, the feet, and likewise at the front; with both hands, he should perform the placement on all limbs, which the learned know as the *cakram* [placement]. This is the mudrā for the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
One who knows the mantras should place [the mudrā] on the heart with the three fingers excluding the little finger and the thumb;
one should place it on the head with the middle and index fingers.

Having performed the placement of the *śikhā* with the thumb, the Supreme Goddess should perform the placement of the *kavaca* with the ten [fingers] and the placement of the *netra* with those [fingers] directed toward the heart.
Then, O Dear One, the practitioner of mantra should place the weapon (astra) with the index and middle fingers;
he should perform the six-limbed placement (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) and utter "Homage to the Heart" (hṛdayāya namaḥ).

Having recited each respective mantra, one should place the consort of Fire (Svāhā) upon the head; thereafter, one should place it on the middle of the shoulders and also on the crest-lock with the syllable "vaṣaṭ."

One should utter the *kūrca* seed-syllable at the base of the arms for the armor (*kavaca*); then, ending with "vauṣaṭ," one should assign the eyes (*netra*) to the three eyes. Thus, one should perform the assignment of the eyes.
The practitioner should place [the mantra] on the two hands with "Astrāya Phaṭ" as well.
Now he states its meaning:
By the word "to the heart" (hṛdayāya), the embodied deity residing in the heart is denoted; by the word "obeisance" (namaḥ), the supreme knowledge having that [deity] as its object is expressed.
The word "head" (śiras) denotes the excellence of the deity;
with "svāhā," all objects of enjoyment are offered to the deity.
The very nature of the deity's crest (śikhā) is called *vaṣaṭ*;
the pervasiveness of the deity is designated as the armor (*kavaca*).
The *hūṃ* syllable also manifests the pervasive radiance of the deity;
by the word "eye," the luminosity of the god is revealed.
The word *vauṣaṭ* is declared by the gods for the purpose of appeasement through the sound of a mantra;
the word *phaṭ* is said to be the burning energy that destroys what is undesirable.
He who performs the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) after truly knowing the meaning of the maṅga-mantras,
his goals are all fulfilled and he is honored even by the gods.
One should perform other nyāsas as well, primarily the Kara-nyāsa and Aṅga-nyāsa;
he who constantly performs these nyāsas according to the path taught in the Āgamas [attains success].

O Dear One, he who performs the placement upon the womb (*yonyāsa*) and the armor (*kavaca*), and recites the mantra according to its meter, attains the state of the deity and achieves perfection in mantra.
Upon seeing him, obstacles flee just as elephants do upon seeing a lion;
yet that foolish soul who performs the consecration without having first established the array of ritual deposits (nyāsa).
He will certainly be oppressed by obstacles, just as a young deer is by tigers; yet,
through the abundance of deposits, there will also be an abundance of fruits.
The prescribed ritual placement (nyāsa) must certainly not be abandoned; one may perform further practices according to one's desire.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Procedures from Entry into the Worship Pavilion up to the End of the Network of Nyāsas," within the General Daily Worship in the *Śrī Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Now follows the internal rule.

Thus, upon the seat consisting of the body, the practitioner of mantra should contemplate his chosen deity and perform meditation according to the method prescribed in the respective ritual manual (kalpa).
That [state] is also said to be twofold: with attributes (saguṇa) and likewise without attributes (nirguṇa).
[It resides] in the lotus of the heart of the Self, amidst the filaments blazing within the pericarp.
In that place, which shines with the blossoming mandalas of the Moon, Sun, and Fire,
one should worship one's chosen deity as revealed by the Āgamas.
Thus, that which is feeling is indeed called meditation with attributes (saguṇa-dhyāna).
Now, I shall describe internal sacrifice (antaryajana), which bestows both seen and unseen fruits.
By which means yogis always give birth to men who are lacking in fortitude.
The Goddess said: "O Lord, how can there be internal worship without external worship?
When the knowledge of worship arises, then internal worship occurs."
Since the collection [of conditions] lacks knowledge, how can there be internal worship?
The illustrious Śiva said:
This is true, O Great Goddess; listen with diligence to this secret:
what fruit is there in external purity when one is filled with excrement within?
