Having attained internal purity, one should perform external purification;
O Goddess, in the ritual of external worship, people have become distracted and confused in this age of Kali.
It is true that in all worship of Śiva, a deficiency arises;
therefore, internal worship is proclaimed as the means for achieving its complete perfection.
Thus, one may conceive of millions of jewels accessible through meditation alone;
yet, that which is performed without internal worship shall be fruitless.
O Goddess, he who desires conception without union is like one who abandons internal worship and seeks external worship.
How can there be happiness here for one who is truly poor and most wretched?
Having performed the internal worship, one should then perform the external worship.
Having conceived worship within one's own heart, one should likewise perform it externally.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord Śaṅkara, what you have said is true; yet I have a doubt:
having performed the external worship, should one then perform the internal worship?"
In this manner, O Goddess of Gods, how will the worship not come to be performed in due order?
Śiva said:
O Goddess, just as a jar might be produced from uncooked clay, O Goddess,
what will become of that jar once it has been cooked from that very same clay, as before?
O Goddess, just as a pot is formed by taking unbaked clay,
it must then be baked so that it becomes beautiful.
Internally and again externally full, it becomes even more full externally;
through the union of mutual dependence, the worship becomes complete.
Having become a god, one should worship the God; a god should not worship the God [as a mere mortal].
Therefore, having attained divinity, one should worship through the path of internal worship and so forth.
The wise one should perform meditation on the Guru just as previously described.
Thus ends the duties to be performed during the Brāhmī-muhūrta.
Thereafter, the wise one should perform ablution for the sake of attaining Being-Consciousness-Bliss;
he should bathe in the pure sacred ford (tīrtha) situated within the heart, known as Puṣkara.
A man who bathes at Bindu-tīrtha shall not undergo rebirth.
Thus concludes the ritual bath.
Having raised Kuṇḍalinī from the Mūlādhāra, one should unite her with Śiva;
at whatever time the union of Śiva and Śakti occurs, [that is the moment for this practice].
That is proclaimed by them as the meditative absorption (samādhi) of those who have reached the end of the twilight of the kula.
Thus concludes the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā).
One should satisfy the Supreme Deity with that divine nectar which has flowed forth from the union of the moon, the sun, and fire.
In the lower portion of the aperture of Brahma (brahmaraṃdhra), there is an excellent lunar vessel;
having filled it with the essence of the digits (kalāsāra), one should satisfy the Khecarī with that.
Thus ends the libation.

In the foundation (ādhāra), the genitals, the navel, the heart-lotus, the root of the palate, and the forehead; in the two-petaled, sixteen-petaled, twenty-two-petaled, ten-petaled, twelve-petaled, and four-petaled [lotuses];
at the end of the dwelling, in the middle of the hair, together with the uvula and throat, and at the root of the neck.
That one of pure intellect should place the vowels and the letters *ha*, *kṣa*, and *au* in the middle of the bow for the sake of attaining prosperity and perfection.
Thus ends the internal placement of the Mātṛkās (Antarmātṛkānyāsa).
Now follows the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
In the thousand-spoked [cakra], resembling a jewel and adorned with all colors,
it is embellished by the three lines beginning with 'A', 'Ka', and so forth, and by the thirty-six consonants.
In the center of that, one should meditate with a concentrated mind upon the supreme bindu, which consists of creation, maintenance, and dissolution; this is the internal ritual placement (nyāsa).
One should meditate upon the Bindu, whose nature is consciousness, from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra);
then, satiating it with streams of nectar flowing from that Bindu, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkās.
Pronouncing each syllable individually from the *mūlādhāra* to the vicinity of the eyebrows,
ending with "namas"— this is proclaimed as the internal placement (*nyāsa*).

From the heart comes the mind, and this mind has the heart as its essence; thereafter, by means of the *hṛn-mantra*, that which consists of consciousness is established within the heart through the state of supreme devotion.

The teachers, by means of ritual action and the Śiromaṇi-mantra, effect the absorption of the objects [of perception] into the Supreme Self, which is exalted by qualities such as omniscience and whose nature is existence and consciousness.
The purification of the heart, head, and body, which has been perceived through meditation,
is performed upon one's own body by the teachers using the *śikhā-mantra*.
By means of the armor-mantra (*varma-mantra*), a protective covering is created on all sides with light outside the body that consists of mantra; thus, there is no concealment during the day.
That light which bestows supreme knowledge regarding the Supreme Self, whose nature is existence and consciousness,
and which consists of the heart and other centers, is designated as the "eye."
It destroys the internal and other forms of the practitioner;
that weapon is the net of ignorance, proclaimed as the supreme abode.
Now, as for meditative absorption (dhyāna).

Having brought about the dissolution of that which resides in the rays, that which resides in fire, and that which is situated between the moon and the sun into the Great Void, the king of yogis remains full.
The realization that "I am He," which is the unity of the individual soul and Brahman—
that alone is known by the knowers of the Vedas as meditation on the attributeless (nirguṇa).
Thus ends the section on meditative concentration.
Now, the ritual worship.
One should worship with various flowers; at that very moment, one becomes identical with That.
Nyāsa is the realization of identity with That; one should worship with the feeling of "I am He."

In forbearance, there is freedom from egoism, absence of pride, and likewise absence of intoxication; then, freedom from delusion, absence of arrogance, absence of hypocrisy, and freedom from agitation.
The wise know that non-miserliness and non-greed are ten flowers;
non-violence is the supreme flower, and the restraint of the senses is a flower.
With the flowers of compassion, the flower of forgiveness, and the fifth, the flower of knowledge—
with these aforementioned supreme flowers, one should worship the Supreme Deity.
Thus ends the worship.
The fifty-fold garland has been declared; the thread consists of Śakti and Śiva.
Kuṇḍalī-Śakti is strung upon it, and at the end of the Kalās, she resides upon Meru.
Thus is the recitation.
Now follows the fire-oblation (homa).
In the triangle situated at the *mūlādhāra*, which is conjoined with dharma and adharma and is intensely blazing, the fire of the deity [is established] preceded by the root mantra.
The wise one should offer oblations individually, saying "I offer, svāhā!"—
offering as the sacrificial oblation (havis) egoism, falsehood, backbiting, lust, anger, and so forth.
The mind alone is declared to be the sacrificial ladle (śruva), while the state beyond the mind (unmanī) is said to be the fire-pot (mugudī).
Now, at the end of the root [mantra]:
In the fire of the nature of consciousness at the navel, eternally kindled by knowledge, I offer the activities of the senses as oblations with the ladle of the mind.
"svāhā"—this is the first oblation.
At the end of the root [mantra].

Into the fire of consciousness—which blazes forth without dependence on internal fuel, which is the adversary of the darkness of illusion, and which is the ground for the unfolding of certain wondrous rays—I offer the universe, from the earth up to the sky;
Svāhā! This is the fourth oblation.
Having performed the internal sacrifice in this manner, one becomes directly composed of Brahman;
for such a person there are neither sins nor merits, and he certainly becomes liberated while living.
Thus ends the internal sacrifice.
Now follows the external sacrifice.
Therein, first is the placement of the water for honoring (arghya) and so forth.
Then, with the root mantra,
one should properly draw a triangle surrounded by a circle with sandalwood water in front of his own deity.
Outside of that, one should fashion a square using the *matsyamudrā*;
having worshipped it with perfumes, one should now offer salutation to the divine *arghya* maṇḍala.

Having worshipped the limbs (aṅgas) in the four corners starting from the southeast, as well as in front, and having worshipped the weapon (astra) in the cardinal directions, one should duly place the conch-vessel.
Without a support there is a fall, and the Mothers are not satisfied;
therefore, one should provide a support according to the rules, either three-legged or four-legged.
That arm [of the vessel] shall be lotus-like, or triangular, or resembling a vulva (yoni);
and at its base, I establish the supporting vessel (ādhārapātra).

Having spoken thus, one should first place the support consisting of the conch and other vessels upon the mandala; then, saying "O Giver of Dharma," one should speak of that which consists of ten kalās.
One should utter the word "Ṅe" at the end, followed by "of Fire," "mandala," "O God," and the name [of the deity].
Then, having uttered "Obeisance to the holder of the argha vessel," one should perform worship.
The ten kalās of fire are to be worshipped there, and circumambulation is prescribed;
then, with the Astra-mantra, [the vessel] fashioned from gold and other materials [is prepared].
Then, having washed the vessel for the *argha* offering—or the conch—with water consecrated by the *astra-mantra*, one says:
"I establish the *argha* vessel for [the deity named] so-and-so."
Having spoken thus, one should place [the mantra] upon that support and speak again as follows: "O bestower of wealth, twelvefold; O you whose self is the kalās."
Having uttered the solar disc and the name of the deity ending in "ṅe," one should worship the vessel for the *argha* offering with this mantra: "Obeisance to the *argha* vessel."
Then, one should visualize that very vessel as the circle of the earth;
there, one should worship the six limbs as before.
One should perform the circumambulation of the vessel twelve times for the Sun;
then, with water consisting of nectar, one should recite the Mātṛkā-mantra at the end of the root mantra.
The worshipper should fill that [vessel] in reverse order with this mantra:
"Oṃ, O bestower of fearlessness, joined with 'ṣoḍaśa' (sixteen), O self of the kalās."

"Namaḥ pañcadaśārṇo 'yaṃ mantraḥ śaṅkhaḥ prapūraṇe | gandhapuṣpākṣatadyavakuśāgratilasarṣapān ||" This fifteen-syllable mantra, "namaḥ," is for the filling of the conch shell with scents, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, tips of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds.
Dūrvā grass is declared to be one of the eight substances for the arghya vessel, O Goddess;
then, having worshipped it with water, sandalwood paste, flowers, and so forth, one should offer it.
Then, at the conclusion of the worship, the practitioner should perform the restoration of all the lunar digits (kalās) one by one.
Having invoked the Tīrtha as before, one should then unite it there with the Mūlamantra;
[one should place] the flower upon it with the Netramantra and the crest [of the deity] with this [mantra].
Having displayed the gālinī mudrā and consecrated [the substance] with the mudrā known as dhenu,
the practitioner duly renders it nectar-like by means of the seed-syllable of Sudhā.
Having meditated there upon one's chosen deity, one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa;
and by means of the assignment of limbs (aṅganyāsa) or the armor-mantra (kavaca), one should protect the ten directions.
Having gazed [at it] with the Netra-mantra and having stabilized it with the mudrā known as the conch (śaṅkha),
one should then [stabilize it] with the blazing mudrā in the form of a womb (yoni).
There, one should worship the chosen deity with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
having worshipped the six limbs, one should consecrate them with the root mantra.
Then, eight times, one should cover the arghya with the fish-mudrā.
The *mudrās* such as the *gālinī* and others are as follows.
The little fingers and thumbs of the two hands are joined to one another;
the index, middle, and ring fingers are held together, unbent, and straight.
This is declared to be the Āgālinī mudrā, maintained over the conch;
furthermore, the little fingers and ring fingers are joined with their tips facing one another.
Likewise, the *dhenumudrā* formed with the index and middle fingers bestows nectar;
it is made by placing the thumb between the left forefinger and the ring finger, while the other fingers are extended.
One should touch the right hand with the left thumb;
this is declared by the learned to be the conch mudrā (śaṅkhamudrā), highly esteemed by the wise.
The middle fingers should be curved and joined, with the index fingers placed alongside them;
likewise, the ring fingers and the little fingers should be positioned in the same manner.
Joining all [the fingers] together in one place and pressing them with the thumbs is declared to be the yoni-mudrā, the mother of the origin of the three worlds.
With the right hand, one should throw the palm of the left hand toward the back;
then, moving the two thumbs, this is the mudrā in the form of a fish.
Thus concludes the procedure for the special *arghya* offering.
Now, he states the number of vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings.
There should be three vessels for the *arghya* and likewise three for the *pādya*; similarly, there may be as many leaves as required, or there may be only one of each.
O Maheśvara, one should not use a single alms-bowl;
for if one does, calamities will come upon one from every direction and at every step.
In this world there is poverty, and after death one goes to hell;
therefore, the wise man should place the common vessel before him.
Beside that is the vessel for water for the feet (pādya), beside that the vessel for the offering of water (arghya),
beside that the vessel for water for sipping (ācamanīya), and to its left the vessel for the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Furthermore, one should place the water for sipping (ācamanīya) and the water for bathing (snānīya) in sequence;
then, one should pour a little of that water from the conch into the pitcher.
One should consecrate each vessel individually with the root mantra, making the eldest [vessel] the primary one;
the *madhuparka*, however, consists of honey and curd, if that is not available.
Curd, milk, jaggery, honey, and ghee have no substitutes;
that which is the supreme state of the gods is called "madhu" (honey).
Even then, that by which these [are offered] is called the *madhuparka*;
it may be made of bell-metal or silver, and the two [deities] Śiva and Viṣṇu are seated upon conch shells.
In the great conch on the left path, one should take a crystal [bead] for the leader of the planets;
on the right, taking the *prokṣaṇī* vessel, one should fill it with water.
Having taken a small portion of the *argha* water, one should pour it into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel;
thereafter, one should set out another vessel for the purpose of the *ācamanīya*.
The water for washing the feet (pādya) is said to consist of śyāmāka grain, dūrvā grass, and viṣṇukrāntā; the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) is prepared with jasmine, cloves, and kola fruit.
One should cause kuśa grass, flowers, barley, rice, and plenty of tamālaka roots to be placed in the prokṣaṇī vessel, along with sacred ash, while reciting the Praṇava.
The water for sipping (ācamanīya) should be prepared with pure water;
however, in the absence of such materials, auspicious washed rice grains should be offered instead.
Now I shall describe the auspicious and inauspicious results of the vessels for the arghya and other offerings:
gold bestows all desires, while silver grants long life and sons.
Good fortune is attained through a copper vessel, the increase of dharma through an earthen one,
and satisfaction of the gods through a vessel made of coconut shell or glass.
The attainment of fortune comes from the bilva leaf; brahminhood from that which grows on the Brahma-tree (the banyan);
killing and expulsion from iron; and immobilization occurs when it is made from stone.
In the worship of the mantra, according to the Vāmamārga and the Tāntrika tradition, there should be wooden vessels,
as well as vessels made of gems and other materials, all marked with auspicious lines.

One should prepare the water for honoring (argha), the food offering (naivedya), the materials for worship, and the sacrificial oblation (bali). One must show great care regarding the vessels; indeed, the vessels should be of the highest quality.
Indeed, without a vessel, the primary rites of *vali* and *homa* are not accomplished;
a vessel measuring thirty-six finger-breadths is proclaimed to be the most excellent.
The medium-sized [vessel] is three parts less than that, while the smallest is twelve finger-breadths;
one should never have a vessel made that is devoid of eight finger-breadths.
One should provide vessels shaped like the openings of lotus buds, fashioned like white lotuses, and having the luster of conch shells or blue water-lilies.

One should sprinkle the white and other [substances] in sequence upon the Brahmins and others; one should perform the sprinkling with water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel while reciting the root mantra and the *astra* mantra.
One should show oneself, the sacrificial materials, and the articles of worship within the maṇḍala, as well as the dhenu-mudrā; this is considered the purification of the substances.
One should worship the deities of the yoga-pīṭha-nyāsa in their respective locations;
then, one's own deities are to be worshipped through meditation upon the maṇi-pīṭha.
One should meditate on oneself in the form of the deity five times with the root mantra,
[placing the deity] upon the head, the heart, and the anus of the flower-offerings held in the joined palms.
One should worship the two feet and all the limbs with sandalwood paste and other offerings,
and one should present an offering of food (naivedya) along with four excellent garments.
One should complete all the remaining rites according to the procedure taught by the guru;
one should perform all this with a concentrated mind, using the water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
Having sprinkled water upon the worship-circle (pūjā-cakra), one should then perform the external sacrifice (bāhya-yāga);
in a vessel made of gold or other materials, one should draw the yantra as prescribed in the ritual manual (kalpa).

The diagram and the yantra are to be drawn in a clockwise direction for worship in the Dakṣiṇa tradition; however, in the Kaula and other traditions, they follow a counter-clockwise sequence. This which was kept secret has now been revealed.
One should draw the worship-diagram (pūjā-yantra) on the right-hand path using those respective eight types of fragrances,
or one may draw it with saffron, camphor, and gorocana.
If one first draws the yantra on the left-hand path with a flower,
and if it is obtained combined with the juice of *devalākṣā*, [it becomes effective].
Having formed a pill smeared with musk and saffron, the practitioner should conceal it;
and having duly drawn the King of Yantras, he should worship it.
By worshipping there for six months, one shall swiftly attain accomplishment (*siddhi*).
In the absence of a young woman who has not yet given birth, her menstrual blood (*rajas*) is taken [as a substitute].
In the absence of that [semen], the menstrual flow of a healthy young woman may arise from the water of arousal or from sexual union.
In the absence of that, the blood of a buffalo is recommended;
in the absence of that, the Aparājitā flower is to be taken.
Having placed red sandalwood offered there upon its upper part,
one should then draw the yantra with that [substance] along the path from the root.
In the absence of that, however, one should draw the yantra as prescribed using liquor and red sandalwood ground with ghee; then the deity becomes pleased.
O best of gods, there is no ninth manifestation in the Vāmamārga.
Now, he states the necessity of the yantra.
The yantra is said to consist of mantra, and the deity is the very soul of the yantra;
just as there is a distinction between the body and the soul, so too is there a distinction between the yantra and the deity.
O beloved, just as the body is to Saṃjīva, or as oil is to a lamp,
so too is that which is established within the yantra for all the gods.
First, one should draw the king of diagrams (yantra) and the form of the deity;
for it restrains all suffering arising from defects such as desire, anger, and the like.
They call it a *yantra*; in it, the deity is truly pleased.
Without a *yantra*, the deity is not propitiated during worship.
Some scholars also say that this [rule] applies to both the Kaula and Vāmamārga traditions.
And so it is.
In the left [tradition], worship is performed upon the Kaula yantra-pīṭha; in the right, it is performed upon the image (mūrti).
Now he describes the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjā).
Having thus fashioned the pedestal, one should worship the deity of the pedestal;
it should be worshipped with the six Gurus, and beyond that, Mahāgaṇapati.
One should worship the seven [elements] beginning with the Earth below the God;
above that are Maṇḍūka, Rudra, and then Kālānala.
One should again worship the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), the supporting power (ādhāraśakti), the tortoise, Ananta, and the Boar, as well as the Earth upon the tip of his tusk.
In that [ocean] is the ocean of nectar (sudhārṇava), and within it is an island made of the nine gems;
in its center is a golden mountain, and above that is the Nandana grove.
In the midst of that [he saw] wish-fulfilling trees, and in their midst a jeweled ground;
within that was a golden wall, and in its center a jeweled pavilion.
Within that [shrine], one should visualize a golden altar and, further, a jeweled lion-throne;
in the center of the altar, one should worship with sandalwood paste and other offerings.
One should contemplate the pedestal as the support for the wheel of worship (pūjācakra) and as a lion-throne (siṃhāsana).
Upon its legs, one should properly worship [the deities] starting from the southeast (āgneya) and ending with Śiva.
Dharma is red-bodied like a bull, Jñāna is black like a lion, Vairāgya is yellow like the earth, and Aiśvarya is black like an elephant.
One should worship Adharma and the others, of various colors, beneath the pedestal;
and in their midst, one should worship Māyā and Vidya, and Ananta, whose form is like that of a serpent.

Upon his head, one should worship a lotus with eight petals representing the primary elements (prakṛti), having bliss as its root, consciousness as its stalk, and the transformations (vikāra) as its filaments.

One should worship the Mother (Mātṛkā) in the form of the pericarp, and on its petals, one should worship in sequence the eight supernatural powers (siddhis), beginning with aṇimā and prakāmatā as they have been described.
Obeisance to the one who possesses lightness, lordship, greatness, and mastery over those who have attained weightiness.
Below and below the pericarp are the Moon, the Sun, and likewise Fire.
There, one should likewise worship the qualities beginning with sattva, as well as the three fires,
and then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa in the cardinal directions and in the center.
Jñāna, Māyā, Kalā, and Vidyā— these four principles, preceded by Parā—
are [to be placed] in the filaments and in the center, starting from the east and proceeding in due order.
One should worship the nine Śaktis of the seat (pīṭha) as prescribed by its respective mantra;
then, one should worship the center of the seat with the pīṭha-mantra, using perfumes and other offerings.
The practitioner should offer a handful of flowers in the center with the fourth mantra, joined with the respective names of the deities, using the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra).
Having recited the root mantra, followed by the name of the seat in the genitive case,
one should project it into the center of the form with the words "I fashion the form" (mūrtiṃ ca kalpayāmi).
Again, having recited the root mantra and then the name of the deity,
one should worship those [forms] with flowers, saying, "I worship the form."
Furthermore, for the sake of pleasing one's chosen deity, one should also worship the sacred abodes (āyatanas) with the following:
Īśa, Yajña, Īśaja, Śivā, Harā, Vīśā, Īśeśaja, and Enasā.

In the northeast, one should worship Rava, Avīśa, Īśaja, and Aujha; in the southeast, Viśi, Gabhā, and Āskarā; and in the other corners starting from the northeast, Gaṇeśa, Yeśa, and Bhādevī are to be worshipped.
He who performs separate worship on a single seat without a yantra incurs the curse of the deity and shall go to the Raurava hell.
If one worships the yantra using a single mantra for all [deities], one will always incur a curse;
having invoked a single deity, one should worship another deity.

O Śivā, whether it be another yantra or another form of worship, it may bring a curse upon the deity; therefore, O Auspicious One, one should install either a śāligrāma or a yantra as the sole object of devotion.
One should not worship both a Śālagrāma stone and a yantra in the same place;
however, according to the Pañcāyatana system, one should always worship a second deity.
When the divine wheel (divyacakra) is attained, the vital wheel (jīvacakra) is not;
and when the vital wheel is attained, one should not worship the Bāṇaliṅga.
When the Bāṇaliṅga was obtained, then the Śālagrāma was [obtained] by the demons;
when the Śālagrāma was obtained, then one should not worship this yantra.
In the Śālagrāma, one should worship all the gods within the wheel of living beings;
whatever disposition is proclaimed for each, he remains established in that very disposition.
If the worship of many forms is to take place upon a single pedestal,
then sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, lamps, and so forth must be provided separately according to the ritual manual.
When [the image] is broken, cracked, burnt, fallen, devoid of its vital parts, mutilated,
touched by a corpse, fallen, or situated on impure ground;
Furthermore, in those ten places— such as one where another has worshipped with mantras, or which is defiled by the touch of a fallen person— the dwellers of heaven do not manifest their presence.
The worship of Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viśveśa, and Devī is performed in sequence;
these ten locations have been established for the purpose of worshipping the deities.
The presence of all the deities will inevitably arise from the yantra;
for the mantra is said to be like the life-force, while the image and so forth are like the body.
Even when the assembly of conditions is complete, there is indeed no fruit without the mantra—
whether it be in a Śiva-linga, a gem, a yantra, a śāligrāma, a jar, or the sun.
One should worship them on a sacrificial mound, in fire, on the head, or in the heart;
even a worship performed upon the ground destroys neither sons nor long life.
The Lord said:
O my deities, listen to this most wonderful account of the origin of the Śāligrāma, which was obtained by me after performing penance at the Gaṇḍakī.
"May all sons be givers of happiness to people"—thus she gave her splendor.
Then, pleased by her asceticism, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara [appeared].
The Lord of Speech was prepared to grant him the boon of being his own son,
but being unable to grant that boon, he was then cursed by her in her anger.
"O gods, because you have repeatedly practiced deception against me, you shall enter the womb of insects; for you are consumed by anger and devoid of virtuous intent."
"Since you fled today out of ascetic fervor without having reflected upon this matter,
by the ripening of that karma, become a river of turbid black water."
Upon hearing these mutual curses, a great tumult arose;
the gods were shaken, and they, desiring to know the truth, approached Brahmā.
"O Brahman, save us from this great curse! We have fallen upon one another in anger.
Having heard these words of the gods, Brahmā spoke to Śaṅkara.
Śiva said to the Creator: "I am the one who causes the cycle of worldly existence;
you are the creator of the universe, while Viṣṇu is the protector and the most highly intelligent."
"He should be reconciled so that happiness may accrue to both.
Having heard these words of Maheśvara, Viṣṇu spoke.
Listen, O Brahmā; listen, O Mahādeva; listen, O Elephant-faced One, O Goddess! These two Brāhmaṇas, my attendants Grāha and Mātaṅga, have fallen here under a curse.
There will be liberation for those two; I shall bring about the dissolution of their physical bodies when that which is produced from their fat and marrow has become decayed.
"Insects dwelling within stones shall become known as 'Vajras' (diamonds).
From this day forth, the Gaṇḍakī, a great and meritorious river, shall be equal to the Gaṅgā."
To the south of the king of mountains, along the Gaṇḍakī river, extends ten yojanas;
that is the Manu-kṣetra, a meritorious region upon the surface of the earth.
It is renowned as Cakratīrtha, famous throughout the three worlds;
the gods reside in Śālagrāma, while Devadvārāvatī is their gateway.
Where there is a union of both, there is liberation; of this there is no doubt.
It is pleasing to all the gods and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
But, Bhava, all the gods who have entered into this stone,
except for their earthly portion, shall become diamond-insects within it.
By this very [means], you too shall attain the status of sons of the Gaṇḍakī;
and at the end of that time, there shall be a sign arising from that deity.
If they worship with full understanding, that deity will be pleased with him—
not from the worship of a mechanical image, nor of a statue, nor even of a tree.
"Satisfaction arises in them just as it does from bathing in the Gaṇḍakī.
Having heard these words of Viṣṇu, Brahmā spoke this speech:

Of what nature is the stone of Viṣṇu that is worthy of worship? What is its characteristic mark, and which is beloved by him? What is the fruit [of its worship], who is the qualified person, and by what path [is it attained]? Tell me that.
Having heard these words of Brahmā, Viṣṇu spoke:
"The stone of one's own caste should be worshipped by Brāhmaṇas and the others for the attainment of happiness."
Oily stones bring about the accomplishment of mantras, while dry ones cause failure;
those known as *pecaka* stones, when washed, destroy one's reputation like charcoal.
White [ash] pacifies [diseases]; black [ash] produces an evil mind;
yellow [ash] bestows the fruit of sons; and the color of the Arka flower removes [one's] children.
Blue bestows prosperity; smoke-colored takes away the intellect;
red-colored brings disease; and vermilion-colored brings great strife.
The Cakrāsana causes poverty yet accomplishes all goals;
indeed, the gross [breath] destroys [life], while the subtle breath wards off a premature death.
The fruit of worship is rendered fruitless by a marked [cow], and [the rite] is without fruit without a marked one;
the Kapilā causes mental agitation, and the Karvurā causes eye disease.
One should know that a wheel with many spokes is authoritative as it prevents breaking when broken;
however, one with a single spoke, lacking internal protection, leads to separation.
A large-mouthed [wheel] that destroys the family and has large rims will take away one's sons;
if the rims are joined together, there is happiness, but if it is crooked, there is a great disease.
A broken wheel indicates poverty; one facing downward signifies total ruin; one with a serpent’s mouth portends leprosy and other ailments; and an uneven one brings various calamities.
With a deformed whorl, one brings about many disorders;
in the case of the Nārasiṃhī [mark], the destruction of the lineage of householders occurs.
A line with a curl brings suffering; as it is subtle, so is the happiness. As it is glossy, so is the prosperity; hear now the distinctions between these.
He is to be known as Hari where there is Lakṣmī and a lotus, and a discus;
one who possesses only the forest garland grants the desires of householders.
He at whose gate there is a pair of wheels, either continuous or even, that white [conch] is to be known as Vāsudeva; it is the destroyer of sins.
He is to be known as Saṃkarṣaṇa; he is ancient and possesses a pair of wheels joined together, situated on his frontal part, large, red, and very beautiful.
Pradyumna has a subtle wheel; its aperture is long and variegated.
Vīta has a beautiful interior with a large aperture and bestows desired objects.
The fire [element] is obstructed, blue-black in appearance, circular, and exceedingly beautiful;
it has two lines on its back at the opening, marked with a lotus.
That [mark] should be known as Keśava; it may be either one or two [in number].
If the discus is positioned both before and after [the mark], forming a quadrangle, it brings good fortune.
Nārāyaṇa is dark-complexioned, has a sunken wheel at the navel,
and possesses a long, straight line on the right side that is broad and auspicious.
That door which has the form of Hari, whose upper opening faces upward,
and by which Hari is seen, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
He should be known as Parameṣṭhin; he has three [marks] endowed with a lotus and a wheel, is shaped like a bilva fruit, is white in luster, and possesses great happiness on his back.
Viṣṇu, however, should be black in color; on the large and very beautiful discus, a line is seen from the middle toward the top of the door.
The Narasiṃha [liṅga] is tawny, with broad wheels and a large mouth;
there should be three or five drops [of water] there, but not for householders.
Kapila Narasiṃha, however, should resemble molasses and lac;
he has two large wheels in the center and a very beautiful line at the entrance.
The Great Nṛsiṃha is to be known as endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics:
lines in the shape of a mane, and a long, terrifying face.
Lakṣmī-Nṛsiṃha is to be known as having four discs and three dots;
he is endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics and is resplendent with a garland of forest flowers.
This [liṅga] is Vārāha; it is found in a Śakti-liṅga and likewise in an odd-numbered Cakra-liṅga.
It resembles a sapphire, is thick, and is marked with three lines.
That stone, known by the name Pṛthivīvārāha, has the form of a boar;
it is slightly curved and possesses a single line that bestows sovereignty.
That stone should be known as Matsyākhyā when it is adorned with three dots;
resembling the luster of bell-metal or gold, and elongated, it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The stone known as Kūrma, however, is circular and elevated on its back;
it possesses a green color and is marked with the Kaustubha gem.
That stone which is shaped like a tortoise should be known as the Śilākūrma;
likewise, one that is circular and marked with a wheel, when worshipped, bestows the [highest] station.
Hayagrīva is shaped like kusha grass, situated near the wheel of lines,
joined with many dots, and its back is as dark blue as a rain cloud.
That auspicious Hayagrīva stone should be known as one that is level;
it should be marked by a long line, or the line itself should be of such a nature.
He whose face has the form of a horse should be known as Hayashirsha;
or alternatively, his head may be lotus-shaped, likewise accompanied by a rosary.
Vaikuṇṭha has the luster of sesame seeds, possesses a single discus as well as a banner,
and above the necklace there is a very beautiful line in the shape of a cake (pūpa).
Śrīdhara, likewise, O Lord, is marked with a garland of choice flowers; he has the appearance of a kadamba blossom and is adorned with five lines.
That which is short and round should be known as Vāmana;
it resembles the color of an *atasī* flower and is adorned with a dot (*bindu*).
The one named Dadhivāmana is endowed with wheels above and below;
he is of great luster, extremely short in stature, and the bestower of abundance and security.
Likewise, the god Sudarśana is dark-complexioned and possesses great luster;
he has a single discus on his left side and a single line on his right.
That which is named Sahasrārjuna consists of various lines;
where the arrangement is in the shape of a wheel, it bestows lost property.
The *sthūla-dāmodara* type is that in which a wheel is established in the middle;
it is dark-green like *dūrvā* grass at the entrance, narrow, and marked with yellow lines—it bestows wealth.
Rādhā-Dāmodara is to be known by the presence of upper and lower wheels;
with a mouth that is not too long and a line of "laṃ" and "vo" in the middle, he bestows enjoyment.
That [liṅga] which is marked with two discs and possesses a subtle aperture should be known as Dāmodara; when worshipped, it always bestows happiness.
It should be infinite and multicolored, marked with the coils of a serpent,
adorned with many wheels, and bestowing the fruit of all desires.
He whose name is Puruṣottama, and whose faces are seen in the cardinal and intermediate directions as well as above, is the bestower of the fruits of the goals of human life.
He whose linga is situated upon his head should be known as a Lord of Yoga;
he is the destroyer of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin and the bestower of the perfections of yoga.
Likewise, Padmanābha, who is red in color, holding a lotus and accompanied by a parasol—
if he is constantly worshipped with Tulasī, even a poor man shall become a lord.
It has rays like flames, a golden face, the luster of the moon, and resembles crystal;
or else it appears endowed with various streaks of gold.
That which is known as Garuḍa is characterized by two middle wings;
it appears as a very long line and is the destroyer of snake venom.
He on whose belly there are four distinct and clearly visible discs is to be known as Janārdana; he brings satisfaction to the ancestors.
Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa is to be known as having a garland of forest flowers, a marked belly,
a subtle opening, four wheels, and being the bestower of enjoyment and liberation.
He who has the form of a crescent moon should be known as Hṛṣīkeśa;
by worshipping him, one obtains heaven and all desired objects.
Lakṣmīnarahari is to be known as being dark-complexioned with a bindu;
with two equal wheels on his left side, he is the bestower of desired objects upon householders.
Trivikrama, however, should be known as dark-complexioned and of great luster;
he has a pair of discs on his left side, while there is a single line on the right.
Kṛṣṇa is to be known as black stone; he possesses a discus-marked mark on his chest, and he is adorned with a forest garland that curls to the right.
He should be known as four-faced; in the middle region there are two wheels, and the four side-lines are the bestower of the Vedas, Śāstras, and Āgamas.

These are declared to be the various forms of Viṣṇu; here itself one may take up Hari, and at the conclusion of the worship, one should perform the dismissal (visarjana), but one should not perform the ritual installation (pratiṣṭhā) here.
Śāligrāmas of equal size are to be worshipped, for two of equal size should never be worshipped together;
those of unequal size may be worshipped, yet among them, one that is most excellent is to be worshipped as supreme.
If a person constantly worships the twelvefold Śilā with devotion,
day by day there arises an increase in righteousness and the destruction of sin.
The man who worships the Śālagrāma stone with devotion for a hundred days achieves his desires and attains perfection.
Listen now to the characteristics of those whose essential nature is Śāligrāma;
by serving them, one's desired goals are attained both in this world and in the next.
He should be known as Śivanābha; having assumed the form of a liṅga, he possesses the shape of a self-manifested (svayaṃbhū) liṅga and is the bestower of the accomplishment of mantras.
He who is adorned with three drops (bindus) is to be known as Traiyambaka;
likewise, a line in the shape of a trident is the bestower of virility.
That [liṅga] on which three lines resembling matted locks (jaṭā) are visible should be known as Dhūrjaṭi; when worshipped, it bestows knowledge.
One who is capable should be known as pale-white; however, a black mark on the forehead, the size of a bilva fruit, radiant and worshipped, brings women under one's control.
He is to be known as the Lord (Īśvara), with a red drop upon his head;
he has one wheel or two wheels, and he is the destroyer of the path below within.
He should be known as Mṛtyuñjaya (the Conqueror of Death), who destroys even a slight death;
below is a wheel, and above it is a white line representing a trident.
This [mudrā] named Candraśekhara is shaped like a half-moon;
by serving its two central moons, diseases are destroyed.
He alone is to be known as Rudra; Kapila is at the crown of the head due to his brilliance.
A discus should be placed in the middle; it shall destroy the multitude of enemies.
Now I shall describe the Śāligrāmas, which originate from the Śaktikīṭa;
by worshipping them, the Goddess Bhavānī becomes well-pleased.
Śrīvidyā is on her forehead, and a parasol is seen above her head;
her head is marked by an external jar, she is glossy and dark-complexioned, and she grants all that is desired.
She should be known as Mahākālī, endowed with the mark of the yoni;
she is rough, thick, and wrinkled, and one should worship her by way of the left path.
Vārāhī, however, is endowed with the mark of a boar;
she is smeared with the blood of Bali, for whose sake she would devour him.
All stone slabs that have two holes or more, or those marked with a triangle, or when the upper part has the shape of a weapon— there, one should designate that as the Goddess.
One should worship Devīśilā on the path to the right of Cakrā;
she, along with Sāvitrī, brings happiness to both worlds by means of that path.
One should worship that stone goddess who is devoid of a disc on the left side;
it must not be touched by Brahmins, nor should it cause agitation to cows.
O gods, in the Kali age, the solar stone (*saurīśilā*) is generally difficult to obtain;
it becomes like crystal in appearance during the month of Sādhāraṇa, and it releases pearls.
When Tulasī stands upright and sprinkled with water during a rain shower,
it renders false any oath that has been uttered by one who has committed an act of abduction.
He who is marked by his own trunk should be known as Gaṇeśa;
or even a stone in the shape of a trunk, or one resembling the face of an elephant.
That stone upon which there is a great wheel in the center and a subtle wheel in a particular direction should be worshipped in that very direction; it bestows sovereignty.
Where two forms of Śaṅkara are seen in the shape of a half-moon, that is indeed a *candraśilā*; when joined with a triangle, it is considered a *bhaumaśilā*.
O gods, a stone of Mercury is to be known by a mark in the shape of an arrow;
a stone of Jupiter is considered to be long and quadrangular.
The [maṇḍala] of Venus is five-cornered, that of Mars is considered bow-shaped,
that of Rāhu is sun-shaped, and that of Ketu has the form of a banner.
When the terrible Kali age has arrived, mixed with left-handed practices,
devoid of devotion and the distinction between what is fit to be eaten and what is not, and crowded with barbarians.
When people are overwhelmed by lust, anger, and the like, and utterly conquered by women,
where is the disciple, where is the guru, where is the mantra, where is the recitation, and where are the spiritual accomplishments?
When ten thousand years of the Kali age have passed, one should abandon the earth of Viṣṇuśilā;
half of that [period] for the waters of the Jāhnavī, and half of that for the deities' stones.
In this age of Kali, chanting is indeed the best means for spiritual welfare, as is the worship of the Śāligrāma;
likewise, the Lord is pleased by even a thousand repetitions performed upon the Śāligrāma or the yantra.
O Maheśvarī, since the Śāligrāma and the Yantra both exist, where would the Lord reside? O Goddess, there must be two locations.
The Śāligrāma is the yantra, and the Śāligrāma is the house;
for it is said that the yantra is indeed the house, and the house is considered to be the deity.
Or else, an image should be fashioned according to the description, possessing auspicious characteristics,
[to be placed] upon a divine disc, a living disc, or likewise upon a śāligrāma stone.
O Maheśānī, in the case of a Bāṇaliṅga, there is neither invocation nor dismissal.
Now, the invocation and so forth.
At the time of offering the arghya to the Sun, one should give a gift according to one's means; furthermore, one should perform the invocation and other rites ninefold upon the image and so forth.
First, the invocation should be performed by reciting the root mantra three times;
then the deity, having arrived from his own realm in a subtle form, enters into the images.
Remaining thus, the wise one, having meditated, brings the light from his own seat back out through the nostril by way of the path of the *suṣumṇā*.
Having placed the handful of flowers in his hand, he should offer it thus upon the head of the deity;
by means of the mudrā called Āvāhinī, the splendor of the deity enters that image.
Reciting the root mantra, one should establish [the deity]; this is considered the invocation (*āvāhana*).
The wise have stated that "establishment" (*sthāpana*) is the placement of the Lord within the *yantra*.

Then one should perform the ritual of stabilization (*saṃsthāpana*), reciting: "Stay here, stay here! at the end of the root mantra, followed by the name of the deity, and finally uttering this [formula].
Having displayed the stabilizing mudrā, one should meditate [on him], thinking,
"He has become firm as a deity," and afterwards, one should offer a prayer.
O Lord of Gods, easily accessible through devotion, endowed with all your attendants:
remain steadfast for as long as I worship you.
Having thus offered this prayer, one should perform the rite of bringing [the deity] into proximity;
then, having received the worship being performed, as well as grace and so forth.
The capacity to perform that [action] is said to be due to her presence;
having recited the root mantra, one should address that deity.
Having said twice, "Be present here," one should satisfy the deity situated in one's own presence with the *sannidhāpana* mudrā.
O Ehibho, one should say "be present" from the time of the ritual action until its conclusion;
this is declared as the perfect restraint by men who know the mantras and act with devotion.
Then, having uttered the root mantra of the deity, one should effect complete cessation;
having fully uttered "May [the deity] awaken," one should say, "Be completely ceased."
One should recite [the mantra] twice, while contemplating that the deity— who is filled with compassion, restrained by the state of devotion, and firmly established within the image— is present.
One should effect the manifestation of the deity by reciting the root mantra;
first, one should say "May [the deity] awaken," and afterwards, "Be present."
One should meditate upon the deity directly facing oneself, with a most gracious lotus-face;
one should display the mudrā known as "bringing [the deity] face-to-face. This is what has been taught.
The reality that is the abode of bliss, characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss, pervades all this; it should be meditated upon as the veil [of grace].
Then, having recited the root mantra, one should perform the veiling of the deity;
one should show [the mudrā] with the words, "May you be fully awakened; become veiled."
One should display the *avaguṇṭhana* mudrā and meditate thus:
[upon] the God, who is enchanted by devotion, his eyes wide open with wonder.
One should perform the sakalīkaraṇa of the deity by placing the six-limbed mantras (ṣaḍaṅgamantra) upon the heart and other parts, and then, having uttered the root mantra, [worship] the deity.
From that conflict, it would arise.
One should perform the rite of immortalization (amṛtīkṛti) by joining the limbs with the possessor of the limbs.
I shall now describe the immortalization: having established the deity upon the seat (pīṭha), [one should proceed].
While visualizing that the rain of nectar falls upon the head of the deity through the proper formation of the *dhenumudrā* by the bride, one should [offer] water for the *arghya* oblation.
One should perform the *dīpanī* (illumination) three times with the root mantra *triśiñca*,
and again three times with the *mātṛkā* letters from *a* to *kṣa*.
Herein is the Dīpinī mantra as follows:
The Vāgbhava [syllable], a pair of Vak words, the Vāgvādini [syllables], and the Vāgbhava;
[then] *klīṃ*, *klinne*, *kledini*, *kledaya*, and also *mahākṣobha*.
The pair *kuru*, the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma*), the pair *sau-mokṣa*, the pair *kuru*,
the *prāsāda* mantra, and the *parā-prāsāda*— this consists of thirty-seven syllables.
The "illumination" (dīpanā) is said to be the mantra itself, which effects the increase of splendor;
the "root" (mūla) is the vocative address, and that [mantra] is rendered nectar through the name of the deity.
For one should indeed say, "May this be for my immortality";
the forgiveness of their offenses should be understood as the supreme act of transformation.
I shall explain the process of making [the offering] supreme and how to bind the Mahāmudrā; having recited the root mantra and the deity as before, one becomes the Supreme Nectar.
Having been told, "Let it be done," one should meditate on a shower of supreme nectar falling from the head of the deity, touching the heart of the deity.
One should perform the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), and likewise, one should utter [the mantra] in my place;
indeed, the entire name of the deity should be recited exactly as before.
Now, he describes the characteristics of the mudrās for the invocation and other rites in sequence:
having formed a *añjali* with both hands, [one places the thumbs] upon the root joints of the ring fingers.
One should cast down the thumbs; this mudrā is considered the Vāhinī.
When it is turned face downwards, it is indeed called the Sthāpinī.
When joined with the fist having the thumb raised, it is considered the *saṃdhāpanī*;
that same [mudrā] with the thumb inserted within is considered the *saṃrodhanī*.
With both hands open with palms upward, it is considered the *saṃmukhīkaraṇī* (gesture for summoning);
the left hand has its thumb extended and its index finger long and pointing downward.

When this *avaguṇṭhana* (veiling) mudrā is rotated all around the body of the deity, it constitutes the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), which is the act of making [the deity] complete (*sakalīkṛti*).
The rite of making [the substance] immortal (amṛtīkaraṇa) by means of the dhenumudrā has already been described.
O Dear One, with the thumbs interlocked and the other fingers extended,
this is declared to be the Mahāmudrā for the purpose of supreme unification.
One should employ these mudrās in the rite of invoking the deities;
thereafter, one should display the specific mudrās prescribed in the ritual manuals (kalpa) for each respective deity.
The binding with the mudrā is taught to be performed with the two seed-syllables *oṃ* and *klīṃ*;
one should display it with the root mantra and release it with the *haṃsa* seed-syllable.
Those *mudrās* which, through their own nature and their radiance, and by means of the body, diligently bestow joy upon the Self— those are indeed powers (*śaktis*). I bow to them.
Because they gladden and because they cause the flood of evil to flow away,
they are therefore proclaimed as *mudrās*.
Just as mothers rejoice upon seeing the performance of their child,
so do the deities rejoice upon seeing the mudrās performed by their devotees.
One should never display the mudrā in a gathering of many people;
the deities of that person become agitated—what fruit, then, could there be from such an act?
Then one should worship the God with whatever offerings can be obtained according to one's capacity:
a seat, a welcome, water for honor (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and water for sipping (ācamanīya).
The honey-mixture (madhuparka), as well as the seat, the bath, clothing,
ornaments, scents, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and sandalwood paste.
One should employ sixteen modes of service in worship;
the midday rite consists of ten modes of service, which is prescribed for householders.

The arghya, the pādya, as well as the madhuparka and so forth, along with the offerings beginning with fragrance (gandha) and ending with the food offering (naivedya)— these are remembered as the ten modes of service (upacāra).
Incense and the other offerings constituting the fivefold worship (pañcopacāra-pūjā) should be presented;
this must be performed by both householders and those who are not householders, provided they are devoted to that practice.
Worship is said to be threefold; one should resort to at least one of these. Among all the ritual services (upacāras), whatever may be difficult to obtain—
Having meditated upon all that with the mind, one should arrange it by casting flowers;
one should offer water at each of those various points during the intervals between the ritual services.
At the outset, one who follows the Vedic path should perform worship with Vedic mantras;
thereafter, a woman or a Śūdra should do so according to the Tantra with Tantric mantras.
"Ahaṃ haṃ haṃ iham idam idaṃ gṛhāṇa ṭha dvayaṃ"—
this fifteen-syllable mantra is to be employed in all ritual services.
A Vaidika person, however, should recite the Tantric mantra at the end of the Vedic mantra;
in all cases, a Śūdra should recite "namaḥ" in place of the "vahnijāyā" (svāhā).
Now, the seat.
On the left side of the deity, one should offer a seat with the root mantra;
it may be made of flowers, wood, stone, leather, grass, or metal.
The flower-made [rosary] is fashioned from flowers and the like, joined with *kuśa* grass threads and so forth;
it is of various colors, fragrant, soft, and the granter of all desires.
If a practitioner prepares a seat using only those flowers which have been declared forbidden for him, it destroys his spiritual aspirations.
Now, their subdivisions:
A seat (viṣṭara) made from sacrificial wood, or from bilva, or from sandalwood,
or from gambhārī, or from śrīparṇī, bestows one's desired objects.

One should avoid the *vibhītaka* tree that has thorns, is laden with sap, or lacks *tāla* and *sāla* trees; likewise, one should avoid those growing near a shrine (*caitya*) or in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*).
Garments are made from wool, bark, silk, or those originating from insects; clothing is of four kinds, the first of which is declared to be the most excellent.
With the skins of lions, tigers, hyenas, goats, buffaloes,
elephants, horses, and black-spotted deer.
An excellent seat has been prepared; one should avoid the skins of donkeys, dogs, jackals, wolves, cows, hares, and likewise monkeys.

Kuśa grass, kāśa grass, śara grass, granthi-parṇa, dūrvā grass, and bark-fibers; likewise, cow-hair, muñja grass, and the root of the uśīra—each subsequent one is to be used in the absence of each preceding one.
This is considered equal to the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha).
It is traditionally taught that there are ten types of *kauśa* (wool/cotton), each preceding one being superior to the next.
Gold, silver, copper, brass, and tin—each subsequent one among these is inferior; iron, bronze, lead, and brass are prohibited.
Now, welcome.
Having meditated thus: "The Lord, together with his limbs and coverings, has come here for the sake of worship," one should proclaim a welcome at the end of the root mantra.
Now follows the offering of the arghya water.
Then one should offer the *arghya* upon his head; for him, time is considered to be of three kinds:
for the one who has arrived, for the one during worship, and for the one seated for the bath.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should cause the arghya offering to be presented to the deity who desires the ball.
Now follows the offering of water for the feet.
With water mixed with the materials for the *arghya* offering, while reciting the ritual manual (*anu*),
one should perform the preliminary rites when the time for the bath arrives, as well as the commencement of the food offering (*naivedya*).
The time for the water for the feet (pādya) is threefold; the pādya consists of the washing of the feet, performed either with fragrant clay or with fragrant flowers and unguents.
First, there should be a thorough cleansing with cold water, followed by warm water.
Now follows the water for sipping.

The sipping of water (ācamana) is prescribed with pure water on six occasions: when receiving the guest-water (pādya), the honey-mixture (madhuparka), during bathing, when putting on the garment and the sacred thread (upavīta), and at the conclusion of a meal.
Now follows the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Having prepared honey in a bronze vessel, one should offer it to the lotus-like face of the God on that day,
joined with curd while reciting the mantra of worship.
Then, furthermore, the water for sipping.

One should offer water for a second round of *ācamana* (sipping) to the mouth of the deity, mixed with the powder of nutmeg (*jātīphala*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), cardamom (*elā*), camphor (*candraka*), and *kola*.
Now, the bath-powder.
Having anointed [the image] with golden oils and fragrant substances such as *malaka* and others,
and having removed the impurities, one should then bathe it with warm water.
One should perform the consecration according to one's ability with fragrant waters and the root-mantra,
as well as separately with milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and sugar.
Nor with coconut water, nor likewise with the juice of palmyra fruit;
nor with fragrant substances, nor with fire, nor likewise with scented water.
Even with water from a single sugarcane stalk scented with camphor and other fragrances, or even with the sweet-smelling juice of plantain, jackfruit, or mango;
One may consecrate [the image] with a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand [offerings] according to one's capacity;
however, if the conch is not filled, one should not bathe it, remaining single-minded in devotion.
The conch shell brings joy to all, but never to the sun-faced one;
may Śiva, who is consecrated with the five nectars and waters from sacred fords, grant us prosperity.
Then, one should obtain water from a conch shell and pure water;
the bath should be performed with the Puruṣasūkta, the root mantra, and the [five] "I" mantras (vāmibhiḥ).
Now, the garment.
One should offer yellow silk garments to Viṣṇu and to Vagalāmukhī; and white ones to Śiva, Sarasvatī, and Pārśvanātha.
Red is for the Śaktas and Vighnas, as well as for the Bhaumas and Saugatas;
black is for Bhairava, Kālī, and so forth; and blue is excellent for Āḍhā and the others.
It should be made of silk or wool—jambū or kauśeya is distinguished as superior—not of hemp; it must be flawless, free from stains, and worn with the six auspicious marks.
From oil and other such defilements, disease arises; from a cracked [vessel], there is suffering;
from that belonging to another, poverty; and from one that is worn out, the destruction of life occurs.
From a burnt [mark], misfortune occurs; from one that clings to the limbs, servitude is granted.
A needle-mark results in boils and the like, while from a dirty [mark], there is a loss of luster.
If the water is taken up while still warm, there is the loss of a son; if it is not washed, there will be wretchedness;
and if it is defiled by phlegm, urine, or the like, there occurs a false accusation.
Then one should offer the garment previously described, prepared according to one's means; even in the absence of the goddess, one may likewise offer merely a flower.
Without the offering of clothing, however, worship becomes fruitless;
therefore, O Goddess of the Gods, one should offer even a flower in the absence of clothing.
Then, [he performed] the sacred thread and the ornaments.
Then, having offered the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), one should present the ornaments;
in worship and other rites, one should employ the deity's name preceded by the dative case-ending (ṅe) and ending with "namaḥ."
These should be understood by the wise as being of various kinds, distinguished by differences such as crowns and so forth, and also according to the distinctions among women.
Now, regarding sandalwood:
Sandalwood produced in Malaya, never before smelled, most cooling, auspicious,
and sprinkled with camphor, agallochum, musk, and cold water.
Powdered incense, ground incense, incense essence, that which arises from the friction of animals,
and [natural] fragrance— these five types of fragrance should be known as bestowing liberation even upon the inhabitants of heaven.
Those which are praised among fragrant substances and consist of powders are called "fragrant" (gandha); this is known as the first type, that which is produced from powder.
Sandalwood ground with the fragrance of *malayaja*, *sarala*, *devadāru*,
black aloe-wood (*kṛṣṇāguru*), and *kadamba*— this is proclaimed as the second [type].
The third [preparation] is accomplished by means of the *piṭharī* apparatus in a glass flask, using sandalwood, aguru, and other ingredients immersed in the juice of the *śatapatrī*.
Black agallochum, sandalwood, deodar, kālīyaka, vālaka, bhadramusta, śilārasa, kundara, kokilākṣa, senantikā, ketu, rāsnā, and gahvareya; [these are the ingredients].
Having placed [the substance] in a crucible together with clay and rags, seal the opening with iron wires;
once the fuming mercury has been extracted from it, place it in a small vessel along with fragrant substances.
He who causes great joy, who brings delight to the asuras, and likewise causes terror to the hosts of bhūtas and serpents;
he who removes fever, loss of appetite, vomiting, and fear, and who dwells upon the forehead to remove all defects.
Just as various fragrant substances are ground with perfumed waters according to their respective portions,
that which constitutes the fourth part is celebrated as the *saṃmarda*.
One part of musk, two parts of mustaka,
and half of that [total] each of elā, jaṭāmāṃsī, tvak, kuṣṭha, and śilārasa.
One-fourth part of bālaka, likewise nakha fried in ghee,
as well as sugandhā, kokilākṣa, lohavāṇa, and rājavacā.
Eight parts of saffron, sixteen parts of *śūlā*,
and the medicinal herbs *kṛṣṇā*, *aguru*, *akasīra*, and *kālīya*.
Whose portions are they that one should rub with sandalwood paste? One should rub those called Kāmoda; by this rubbing, one pleases the King of the Devas.
The intoxication found in musk is said to be of animal origin;
this fifth fragrance pleases both gods and demons.
The eightfold fragrance is also threefold, consisting of Śakti, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
it comprises sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and gorocanā.
They know the eight fragrances of Śakti to be jaṭāmāṃsī,
kapi, candana, aguru, hrīvera, kuṣṭha, kuṅkuma, and sevya.
Jaṭāmāṃsī, māṃsī, and surabhi are known as the eight fragrances of Viṣṇu:
sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, tamāla, jasmine, and saffron.
Kuśīta combined with kuṣṭha is known as the eightfold Śaiva-gandha.
Now follows the ritual procedure for flowers.
Now, I shall provide a mere fraction of the greatness of Puṣpa;
knowing which, the practitioner will certainly attain success—of this there is no doubt.
Because it increases merit and wards off the flood of sins,
and because of the offering of oneself as a flower, it is called "puṣpa."
Through flowers the gods are pleased; in flowers the gods reside.
What more need be said? Flowers are exceedingly subtle.
The supreme light is joined with the flower; it is pleased by the flower alone.
The flower is the means for achieving the three goals of life (trivarga), and it bestows nourishment, prosperity, heaven, and liberation.
Brahmā resides at the root of the flower, Keśava in the middle of the flower,
Mahādeva at the tip of the flower, and all the gods are situated upon the petals.
Therefore, a person endowed with devotion should always worship the God with flowers.
Flowers are said to be of five kinds: the supreme (para) and the non-supreme (apara).
I shall describe the characteristics of those [types of disciples] as superior, middling, and inferior;
for the supreme one is like a golden flower, and he alone is always worthy [of the teaching].
That which is worthy of worship should first be given to a guest;
furthermore, silver and copper are prescribed for flowers.
This [offering] is always appropriate, whether it consists of three years' growth or one year's; likewise, *tulasī*, *ketakī*, lotus, *karavīra*, and *mālatī* [are suitable].
These five are said to be the most excellent, while the following ten are considered middling:
the jasmine (mallikā), kunda, mandāra, tagara, arjuna, and kiṃśuka.
Gold that is mixed with *pārijāta*, *aśoka*, *vilva*,
and *paṅka* is said to be of inferior quality, even if it is fragrant.
One should offer those things prescribed in the ritual procedures for their respective mantras,
along with various pleasing offerings, oblations, and diverse beautiful flowers.
She should always be worshipped with devotion using auspicious Apāmārga leaves and Bhṛṅga flowers, excluding Tulasī, for men to swiftly obtain the fruits of their practice.
One should worship with fragrant white and red flowers,
along with bilva, maruvaka, and other auspicious blossoms, excluding tulasī.
One should especially offer flowers mixed with *droṇa* flowers and *vajra* flowers;
likewise, one should present flowers that are red, black, and white.
O beloved, [the flowers] are white flowers, the hibiscus, the oleander, as well as tagara,
jasmine, Arabian jasmine, the sevaṃtī, and likewise the yūthikā.
Dhustūra, Aśoka, Vakula, white and black Aparājitā,
Bakapuṣpa, bilva leaves, Campaka, and Nāgakeśara.
Mallikā, ṛṅghikā, and that which is celebrated as raktakāñcī; arkapuṣpa, kokanada, and varvara—these are the flowers dear to Priyāmudā.
The fruits of the mango, jīvūka, and daṃva; the kumuda and āmrātaka;
flowers produced from all types of grain; and that which arises from the plantain tree.
On the eighth day, Kālikā is especially pleased;
all the deities are well-satisfied by a red lotus flower.
Whether she be black or white, and whether she appears at night or during the day, Dhūmāvatī becomes a granter of boons; she is indeed pleased by the *dhustūra* flower from a cremation ground.
She is always pleased by various wild flowers;
Pārvatī is pleased by the leaf of the āmalakī tree.
O Goddess, it is not possible for me to describe the fruit of Aparājitā;
there is no beloved more dear to the Goddess than Aparājitā.
In Aparājitā, Sāparṇā remained equal to Pūrveśanta;
having stayed there in the form of a womb, that auspicious goddess departed.
In the form of a *liṅga* within the *karavīra*, Śiva indeed dwells forever;
through the union of Śiva and Śakti, the *karavīra* is unconquered (*aparājita*).
One should worship with the union of those two mixed with red sandalwood;
O Supreme Goddess, she is pleased, and that worship is considered fruitful.
With flowers produced in the forest, or leaves grown on the mountain,
or with white and red flowers arising from one's own garden, [one should worship] at the three junctions of the day.
The five-colored karavīra flower is the sphere of Kālī and Tārā;
I shall now describe the cūḍāmaṇi, the most excellent among all flowers.
The Cūḍāmaṇi consists of ten types according to the classification of the nine gems;
the tenth, which begins with all the colors, is known as Puṣpeṃdra.
The ketakī is said to be of two kinds, according to the distinction between male and female;
within the male variety, two types are described based on the differentiation between yellow and white.
Even among women, they are said to be of two kinds, distinguished by being yellow or white;
among men, they are said to be hard, while among women, they are considered soft.
O Pārvatī, Mallikā is said to be of four types; hear their sequence:
Śvetā, Dvipuṣpā, Ṣaṭpuṣpā, and another, Puṣpagucchā.
The one called Navapuṣpā is supreme; Raktapuṣpā shall be supreme as well;
likewise Pītapuṣpā, Ekaikā, and Dhūsarā born of five colors.
Mālatī is said to be fivefold; hear its varieties, O beloved:
Gandharājā, Sarvagandhā, and likewise Śrīkhaṇḍagandhikā.
The fourth is considered to be the Ketakī, endowed with the fragrance of musk;
then there is Mālatī, Svarṇabhājī, Śvetā, and another, Raktāśilā.
The other is to be known as red in color, and likewise another is five-colored;
these divisions have been proclaimed by me, which were concealed in the Yāmala and other scriptures.
O Goddess, you were hidden in the Ḍāmara; out of affection for you, it has been revealed here.
O Maheśānī, it must be kept secret; that is the very essence in brief.
O Goddess, [these are] yūthikā, mālatī, jātī, mallikā, navamallikā,
kastūrī, gaṃdhikā, and likewise those produced from the fragrance of vāguru.
Nakhagandhā, Śalākā, and others are known as Mālatī and Vedagandhikā;
Mālatī is said to be found in heaven, while the red variety dwells in the netherworld (pātāla).
The *jātī*, *yūthī*, and *mallī* are proclaimed in the world of mortals;
the red *mallī* and yellow *mallī* possess the nature of the five colors.
O Goddess of the gods, in this world of the three powers, during the worship of all the deities,
one should worship Cīnasundarī by contemplating her in this very form.
This secret has been fully proclaimed, the nectar of the determination of merits;
O Lord of Gods, no satiety has arisen [in me], so please speak further with haste.
Sālatī, Rājamallī, Jātī, Yūthī,
Jayantikā, Mālatī, Laghuyūthī, and Mallī— this is the sequence as it is traditionally remembered.
The *jāti* flower spoken of by Śvetāśrīmālī is known as *raktatalā*;
the *mālatī* has petals like leaves and is intensely flavorful, being both red and white.
O Maheśānī, the *rājamallī* has many petals and is fragrant;
the *śatapatrā* is the *rājamallī*, while the *mallikā* has petals of artistic design.
The *jātī* flower has five petals, while the *mālatī* has seven;
the *yūthī* is delicate, and these various types are enchanting with their flavor and fragrance.
Mālatī, svarṇabhājī, śvetā, and raktaśilā are considered [the first four];
the fifth is said to be red in color, while the others are known as five-colored, yellow, and black.
O Goddess, there is Kastūri-gandhikā, likewise Aguru-gandhikā,
the one called Aśvagandhāmalākā, and Mālatī endowed with the Vedas.
In all rites for the gods, the campaka flower is praised as the means for accomplishing worship with its constituent parts;
by the offering of this flower, one obtains gold of many kinds.
By the gift of *nāgakeśara*, one becomes handsome and fortunate;
and by the flower of the *punnāga*, there shall always be the pacification of fever.
By the offering of *keśara*, one certainly destroys the enemy;
by the offering of *pārijāta* or *pāribhadra*, one's lifespan increases.
By the offering of a *kunda* flower, one certainly attains all desires;
by offering *jāti*, *mālatī*, and *kubjaka* flowers with devotion, one quickly prospers.
By the gift of a cuckoo, one may avert untimely death;
by the gift of an *odra* flower, the Supreme Goddess is pleased.
Just as one is certainly satisfied by goats offered to Bali, so too,
when one gives hibiscus flowers and silk cloth, one shall obtain the fruit.
Sins such as the killing of a Brahmin are certainly destroyed in an instant;
one should worship the Sovereign of the Universe with Karavīra flowers.
Having joined each flower with the mantra during the nights,
one indeed obtains all desired objects, and the perfection of the command is attained.
Whether it be red or crimson, the *karavīra* flower grants success;
by the offering of *vaṃdhūka*, one obtains fine silk cloth.
And he said to Puṣpamālā:
O beloved, a garland may consist of flowers of a single species or even of different species; likewise, it may be of a single color or of various colors.
That city is to be known as threefold according to its circumference;
it falls away, excluding the heart, for that [city] which is always impure and dual.
That *raikikā* is to be fully known as abiding in the state of all-encompassing obscuration;
appearing like something dissolved at the lower garment, it is called the garland of flowers.
The common [form] is to be fully known; the middle one is superior to the former.
But the one adorned with garlands reaching to the ankles stands upon the lotus of the feet.
The forest garland (vanamālā) is renowned as the most excellent of all garlands;
even though it possesses some slight distinction [over others], listen as I describe it to you.
With *karavīra* flowers, *javā* flowers, *vaka* flowers, and even *damanaka*; with blue lotuses, white lotuses, cloves, and *nāgakeśara*.
Garlands fashioned from jasmine, *mālatī*, *mallikā*, *campaka*, and other such flowers would indeed be most beautiful.
These flowers, distinct from other garlands, bestow delight upon the Goddess;
therefore, O lady of excellent complexion, rise up among these other blossoms.
One should exert effort in stringing these flowers for them;
one should worship the Vidyā with one's own materials, such as hibiscus, barley-gruel, and vermilion.
Sandalwood known as "red" (raktasaṃjña) is declared to be śāṇita.
Now, the secret flower.
O Maheśānī, the flower of the vulva is called the *varaja* flower;
that of an unmarried girl up to sixteen years of age is the best, granting all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
If she is married by force, the middle [period] increases enjoyment;
due to the influence of the union with the menses, another [period] bestows happiness.
O Goddess, the *svayambhū* flower is known to be of three kinds;
she should always be worshipped with all flowers, whether they are prescribed or not.
Devotion must be practiced toward all the gods; here, the yoga of devotion is the cause, not gold, nor the nine gems, nor auspicious touch-stones.
For Kālikā, who is affectionate toward her devotees, O Goddess of gods, is never satiated;
therefore, O Śivā, one should gather flowers born from the womb for the purpose of worship.
Now listen as the most secret of secrets is told:
the Avīrā is said to be fivefold, in the sequence of white, yellow, and red.
White-yellow, yellow-red, and red-white are considered the others;
thus, through these different variations, she alone is proclaimed to be ninefold.
A woman without a husband should not worship any deity with flowers;
rather, she should use the flower of passion, the flower of desire, according to the sequence of divine flowers.
Service is said to be of many kinds; hear their divisions, O Pārvatī:
white, yellow, and red—these three groups each consist of three.
Sindūra is of divine color, and another is haridrā;
this is declared to be the flower of Rati. Listen, O beloved, to the flower of Kāma.
The yellow cluster is her own form, and the red cluster is her essential nature;
yellow-red, red-yellow, and another subtle form, O Maheśvarī.
There are six divisions in the subtle division, and there are also six in the extremely subtle;
thus, O Maheśvarī, the flower of desire is of eighteen kinds.
I shall now describe the divine flower, by means of which, through the worship of the Goddess,
one attains a divine form that is white, red, and likewise resembles vermilion.
Furthermore, there is the white and yellow, and another of five colors;
the flower of delight is five-colored and within the range of vision for beautiful women.
The flower of desire is five-colored and is the domain of Kālikā;
the flower of the gods is the color of joy and is the domain of Tāriṇī in the world.
Regarding these two, he states the following as the primary [view]:
Pārvatī [is worshipped] with a thread, a silk cloth, and a hero's cloth;
Pārvatī [is worshipped] with a Kāśmīra cloth, a thread, and a silk thread.
Having offered musk, saffron, sandalwood, agallochum, and other various fragrant substances there, the practitioner should then combine them together.
One should bring flowers combined with the eight fragrances or with flowers; by means of this combination of unbroken rice grains (akṣata), one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
The wise know that flowers grown spontaneously are used for the purpose of a seat, for worship, and for the fire-oblation, respectively; such flowers are known as *siddhapuṣpa*.
O Goddess of the gods, garlands that are not stale are pleasing;
they are known as "perfected flowers" (siddhapuṣpa) and grant delight to the Gandharvas.
Taking all these fresh flowers, both pure and impure, day after day,
one should worship Tārā and Kālī.
One shall obtain a fruit ten million times greater than the fruit of the gift of flowers.
Now, that which is not prescribed.
One should discard that which has fallen on the ground, that which is eaten by insects,
that which is stuck to the body, that which is obtained at dawn, as well as that which is withered or stale.

That which has a pungent odor, lacks fragrance, is defiled by worms, hair, and the like, or is contained in an impure vessel, or is a part of a living being, or has been touched by those of contemptible character— such [food] is unfit for the Soma sacrifice.
That which has been brought [as an offering] is forbidden, as is that used for the midday bath;
likewise, flowers that have blossomed spontaneously and fallen of their own accord upon the ground [are acceptable].
One should avoid flowers that have fallen to the ground, with the exception of *sephālī* and *vakula*; likewise, buds should be avoided, except for those of the *aśoka* and the *padmaka*.
In the case of the *vilva*, the *khadira*, as well as the leaf of the *dhātrī* and the leaf of the *tamāla*,
being cut or broken does not cause any defect.
One should worship with Viṣṇukrānti, Javā, Nāgakeśara sprouts, and Bandhūka, together with a cluster of Mandāra flowers.
The worship of the Goddess should always be performed with both aquatic and terrestrial flowers,
whether they are prescribed or not, by one whose mind is endowed with devotion.
Whether it be a leaf or a flower, a fruit should not be offered with its face turned downward;
that is declared to be a source of suffering. It should be offered exactly as it was produced.
In all types of variegated worship, there is no fault in using what is not prohibited;
however, offering flowers face-down is not desired, nor is it [permitted] in the rite of the handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali).
There is no fault in using stale flowers in the case of tulasī, bilva, campaka,
water-born lotuses, vakula, agastya, or those grown in the gardens of garland-makers.
One should not worship with flowers that are stale, withered, or infested by worms and insects, nor should one perform fire-oblations with them; otherwise, one incurs the curse of the deities.
