O Maheśvarī, bilva leaves, tulasī, and the golden flowers that arise spontaneously do not become stale nor do they become *nirmālya* (worn-out offerings).
O Goddess of the gods, I have not proclaimed on earth [the worship] of these four:
one should not worship Nṛsiṃha and Śiva with a *ketakī* flower.
One should never touch the black variety of Tulasī with white Tulasī;
likewise, one should avoid the lotus for ten nights and the Jātī flower for three days.
The Campaka flower lasts for five nights, the Kiṃśuka for seven days,
the Karavīra for eight days, and the Ketakī for fifteen.
O Goddess, where is the day of the eye, the *munipuṣpa*, and the pomegranate?
Then, the *japā* flower and the grape are within the scope of two days.
O Maheśānī, the Śatapuṣpa, the Puṣparāja, the Gandharāja,
the Bhagapuṣpa, and the Vedarātra are not to be disparaged.
According to the opinion of Nārada, it is not stated at all; listen now:
the bilva, arka, āmalaka, and tulasī are the first thirty.
O Great Goddess, thirty [offerings] are for the *vaṣaṭ* call, and they must not be stale;
[this applies] to one, a hundred, or a thousand *karavīra* flowers.
O Goddess of gods, by worshipping me, a man shall become my very form;
O beloved, one should worship me even with a single karavīra flower.
By that, O Goddess, one should worship the world, both the stationary and the moving;
I myself dwell there in the Karavīra, at the point of power (śakti-bindu).
One should worship Īśa with ketakī and kuṭaja flowers, Hari with fresh barley and unbroken rice grains (akṣata),
Durgā not with dūrvā grass, and Divākara with bilva leaves.
One should offer a long-stalked tulasī leaf that is devoid of its stem;
it should be yellow or black in color, and especially so when offering to Sūrya and Śambhu.
One should worship with auspicious bilva leaves, maruvaka, and other such flowers, excluding tulasī;
however, one should avoid tulasī and mālatī during the rites for Kālī and Tārā.
The *vilva* and *maruvaka* are to be avoided in rites involving heroic deeds (*vīrakarman*);
for the goddesses, the *arka* and *mandāra*; and for the Sun, likewise the *tagara*.
He who worships Gaṇeśa and Sūrya with what is pleasing—
even in the absence of flowers, with young shoots, or in their absence, with buds— [attains success].

In the absence of those, one should offer fruits; in the absence of those, leaves; and in the absence of those, sprouts of grass—namely, plantain, pomegranate, jujube, rose-apple, tamarind, myrobalan, and mango.
The citron and the jambīra are said to be the most excellent;
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship with flowers, or in their absence, with leaves.
If even leaves are not available, one should use those produced from trees, shrubs, and the like;
if those are unavailable, one should worship with their fruit.
One should perform worship with unbroken grains or with water; in their absence, with white mustard seeds;
and if even those are unavailable, one should perform mental worship.
Henceforth, O lady of pure smiles, listen to the offering of flowers;
for even the name of that flower consists of only two syllables: "namaḥ."
Having recited [the mantra], one should offer it to those goddesses for the sake of accomplishing all desires and purposes;
with the thumb and forefinger, one should present the flower at the wheel.
O Goddess, this most beautiful flower, endowed with fragrance, has been offered by me with devotion; please accept this excellent flower.

Then, at the conclusion of the offering of flowers, one should perform the worship of the surrounding deities (āvaraṇārcana) using the letters of the Mātṛkā, each enclosed by the mantra and accompanied by the bindu.

One should worship the limbs of the deity in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings; thereafter, one should worship the Mothers in their respective positions on the limbs through the yoga of absorption (layayoga).
Having worshipped the first enclosure, one should then worship the deity;
having again worshipped the enclosure, one should likewise honor the deity.
Having thus worshipped all those aforementioned deities of the livelihood,
there then arises omniscience, contentment, and that which is known as the awakening of another day.
Independence, the other [the self], eternity, and unimpaired power—
these are proclaimed by name as the six-limbed deities.
One should worship the heart and the other limbs in the filaments, beginning from the southeast corner;
the eye in front, and the weapon in the cardinal directions; and these limb-deities should be meditated upon.
The principal female forms have bodies like frost and crystal, with dark blue, black, and reddish rays, and they hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should worship the lineage of gurus situated in order in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and the center, extending from the north-western direction onwards.
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, listen briefly to these gurus in all cases:
in every instance, O Lord of Gods, the first guru is the one who bestows the mantra.
You are indeed the supreme and subordinate gurus, while I am the Parameṣṭhin;
among all mantras and vidyās, I am myself the embodiment of Prakṛti.
Then the form of the Puruṣa was described, as well as the lineage of gurus,
and which specific groups of gurus are traditionally prescribed for each particular mantra.
Each of those is to be worshipped at the beginning of the ritual service; I have described this briefly.
In the worship of the enclosure, the eastern direction is to be understood as being in front of the deity.
Then begins the worship of the retinue in clockwise order;
however, for the worship, the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) end with "namaḥ," and likewise in the fire-oblation (huti).

Then, with the words ending in "svāhā" and directed toward the face of the deity, they remain poised; thereafter, one should worship the guardians of the world (lokapālas) stationed in their respective directions.
Their weapons are also described before them; now their meditation is taught:
Indra, the lord of the gods, is the powerful one, pleased and mounted upon Airāvata.
I worship the thousand-eyed one with two arms, who holds a yellow vajra;
I worship the Lord Agni, the sovereign of fire-energy, who is red and holds a white śakti in his hand.
I bow to Yama, the lord of the departed spirits, who is well-adorned, whose vehicle is a ram, whose eyes are red at the corners,
who is dark-complexioned, and who is seated upon a buffalo.
He holds the staff of Death (Kāladaṇḍa), is cruel, and is surrounded by terrifying messengers; he is the lord of the Rākṣasas, belongs to the southwest direction, and is seated upon a corpse.
Having the appearance of smoke, holding a sword in his hand, with a tawny beard and mustache,
he is seated upon a crocodile, his lotus-hand holding a noose that resembles lightning.
I bow to Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, who has white limbs and holds a water-pot;
and to Vāyu, the supreme lord of the vital breaths, who is smoke-colored and holds a red goad in his hand.
I worship Kuvera, the lord of the Yakṣas, who is white in complexion, holds a trident and a mace, and runs with great speed mounted upon Vātapramī.
[He saw] the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyādhipa), mounted upon a lion-throne, adorned with a garland of skulls, bearing a blue trident, and having a bull as his vehicle.
Three-eyed, with the moon upon his forehead, wearing a mass of matted hair,
fair-complexioned, and adorned on his head by the lord of serpents and a circle of skulls.
I worship the infinite Ananta, who bears the discus, who is all-pervading,
the lord of the worlds, the creator, auspicious, red in color, and holding a lotus in his hand.
I worship Him who is mounted upon a swan and is causing the Vedas to be recited;
having again uttered the root mantra, one should offer it along with the limbs (aṅgas) and so forth, preceded by "sa".
One should utter the name of Vārāhī ending in the dative case,
and the practitioner should worship the women with "namas" and with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Now, the offering of incense.
Because it holds all great defects and possesses the power of a putrid odor,
yet generates supreme bliss, it is called "incense" (dhūpa).
Then one should wash the incense burner with the Astra-mantra and worship it;
having worshipped the bell with the Hrdaya-mantra and the Astra-mantra, one should ring it.
In this manner, one should prepare the incense in an auspicious vessel made of copper, bell-metal, or similar materials, shaped like a lotus with two bases and curved stems.
With incense produced from guggulu and aguru trees cast upon glowing coals,
and with the rising fumes of resinous exudations and other prescribed substances.
One should offer incense to Gaṇeśa; guggulu is said to be his favorite.
For the Goddess, one should use sarja resin, and for Maheśa, the resin derived from devadāru.
Black agallochum is the cool [incense] of Viṣṇu, while it is considered dear to the Sun;
likewise, jaṭāmāṃsī, guggulu, sandalwood, and agallochum [are favored].
O Maheśvarī, one should offer incense to the Goddesses mixed with ghee, combined with camphor, honey, and saffron.
He should burn incense from below using guggulu, aguru, uśīra, white [sandalwood], clarified butter, honey, and candana,
by casting them onto the glowing embers of the hearth.
98b) I shall describe the ten-ingredient formulation of Śakti: one part each of śaileya, malayodbhava, nakha, kuṣṭha, and sarjarasa should be prepared.
Two parts each of śilārasa, aguru, jaṭāmāṃsī, and māṃsī;
six parts of honey and eight parts of sugar—this incense is considered the offering to Śakti.
One part each of harītakī, sarjarasa, and muramāṃsī;
four parts of lākṣā; and three parts each of śailaja and musta.
Nakha is said to consist of five parts, kuṣṭha is said to consist of six parts;
guḍūcī consists of twelve parts, and viṣṇukrāntā consists of ten parts.
Madhu, mustā, ghṛta, gandha, guggulu, aguru, śailaja, sarala, sihlaka, and siddhārtha constitute the ten-ingredient incense (daśāṅgaka) for Śeṣadeva.
Guggulu, sarala, dāru, putraka, mayalasaṃbhava,
hīvera, aguru, kuṣṭha, guḍa, sarjarasa, and śana.
Harītakī, nakha, lākṣā, jaṭāmāṃsī, and śailaja—
this sixteen-ingredient incense is prescribed for rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors.
Alternatively, one may offer aguru, camphor, sandalwood,
guggulu, honey, clarified butter, jaṭāmāṃsī, śailaja, and saffron.
This incense, mixed with these [ingredients], should be prepared as the favorite of Pārvatī;
iron and lead, in sixteen parts, are proclaimed in the Trividyā.
O Goddess, in the ritual of the Kālī-vidyā, agallochum (aguru) and the ten-ingredient incense (daśāṅgaka) are prescribed;
in the ritual of the Tārā-vidyā, sandalwood (śrīkhaṇḍa) with eighteen ingredients (aṣṭādaśāṅga) is traditionally taught.
O Goddess, for the rite of Chinnā-vidyā, the five-fold limb-offering consists of guggulu, black aguru, and yellow sandalwood; this is the mantra within the range of Brahmā.
Guru-candana mixed with beeswax is prescribed for the Mātaṅgī;
likewise, musk, camphor, and the eight fragrances are also recommended.
O Goddess, *namri* and *śilārasa* are proclaimed for Bhairavī;
*śrīkhaṇḍa* has been declared by me for Bhuvaneśī and Kamalamati.
O Śivā, in the rite of the perfected lore (siddhavidyā) for Dhūmrā, [one should offer] lac,
jaggery, honey, musta-grass, ghee, fragrance, guggulu, and rock-salt.
Sandalwood, musk, white mustard, and the ten-ingredient incense (daśāṅga) are desired as incense;
likewise, guggulu, agallochum, and sandalwood mixed with sugar, clarified butter, and honey [are used].
This six-limbed incense is always dear to all the gods;
having worshipped the incense, lamps, and other offerings with the Astra-mantra, one should then present them.
O Goddess, as with the fragrance, so should the wise one offer incense;
that which is produced from the essence of trees is the most excellent fragrance for incense.
"May this incense, which is to be smelled by all the gods, be accepted.
The incense is on the left, and likewise in front and on the right."
One should not offer incense on the ground, nor likewise from a seat into a vessel;
rather, having placed it properly within its container, one should present it.
Fat, marrow, and sinews are not desired; [the offering] for Viṣṇu arises from the essence of the Vedas.
Then one should offer incense preceded by the ringing of a bell.
By the sound of which all obstacles flee to the ten directions,
as do all diseases, evil planets, and likewise the foremost Vināyakas.
Bad dreams, rākṣasas, wicked vetālas, terrifying śivās,
ḍākinīs, hosts of bhūtas, and serpents such as karkoṭaka and others— [all these are overcome].
But those who desire the Valika [sandalwood] for the sake of passion, like others who desire pleasure,
shall have their vigor destroyed upon hearing the sound of the bells.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always bring [the deity] at the time of worship.
The mantra for the worship of the bell is as follows:
*Tāra*, *jayadhvani*, *pada*, *mantramātā*, and *agnige hinī*—
this eleven-syllable mantra of the bell (*ghaṇṭā*) bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Having worshipped with his own mantra, preceded by the ringing of the bell,
he should offer a lamp according to his means, accompanied by various musical instruments.
One should ring the bell during the invocation, the water offering, the incense, the flowers, the food offering, and the lamp; one should especially ring it for the incense and the lamp.
One should play this [instrument] elsewhere except at the time of worship;
those who desire accomplishment should not perform worship without it.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the lamps.
Because it completely abandons the great darkness of long-standing ignorance and egoism,
and because it illuminates the supreme reality, it is called a "lamp."
The first lamp should be made of ghee, or else produced from sesame oil, mustard oil,
resinous extracts of fruits, or derived from lotuses.
The seven types of wicks are proclaimed to be those made from curd, those made from food, and so forth;
they may be produced from lotus fibers or from darbha grass fibers.
Whether made from Jālā, Āvādarī, or even from cotton (tūlaka),
five types of wicks are always prescribed for the purpose of lighting lamps.
The wick should be white, or red, or neither yellow nor black;
it may be made without seeds, or from threads spun by virgins.
The wick of the lamp should be excellent; it may sometimes be a new, fine cloth, or cotton, wool, or even a worn-out and soiled garment.
One should never take back a wick that has been used;
a wise person should avoid the fringe, whether it be from a new cloth or one made of worn-out rags.
A lamp-vessel made of gold, silver, copper, brass,
bell-metal, coconut shell, or even bamboo is highly commended.
In this manner, one should prepare a lamp, which is the cause for the delight of the eyes;
however, until the conclusion of the sacrifice, one should arrange the lamp with its flame facing downwards.
If the protection of a lamp is obtained even from a depth of four finger-breadths, that lamp is not said to be "extinguished" here; rather, it is considered to have increased today.
One should display a lamp high up, using either cow’s ghee or oil with a wick containing a moving core, or sometimes with fresh butter and other such substances.
One should not offer lamp oils such as ghee and the like by mixing them together;
having mixed the oil, one shall go to the mixed hell.
The lamp-vessel should be fashioned in the shape of a lotus like that of incense;
and on each petal, one should offer a lamp smeared with ghee as an act of renunciation.
Now, he describes the taking up of the incense burner and the lamp vessel.
One should place [the lamp] with the tip of the thumb between the middle and ring fingers;
O Dear One, the archway should be made threefold, and the lamp should be near the eyes.
O sweet-spoken one, one should show the smoke reaching as far as the tip of the nose;
one should show the lamp, shaped like the circling of a pigeon, at the eyes and other parts.
On the right, a lamp with ghee; on the left, one with sesame oil. A white wick is for the right, while a red wick is for the left.
A lamp should be offered upon trees, but never on the ground;
for the earth endures everything, yet it cannot endure these two together.
That man who offers a lamp shall cause distress to the earth, as well as heat to the lamps and heat to the feet of those who do not perform [the rite].
He surely attains the hell of torments; of this there is no doubt.
One must never extinguish lamps, for it causes the destruction of prosperity.
One must never extinguish a lamp prepared for the sake of the deities;
the one who steals the lamp will become blind, while the one who extinguishes it will become sightless.
O Goddess of the Gods, holding [the vessel] with the tip of the thumb, one should offer it while lighting it;
likewise, one should perform the *uttoraṇa* rite by means of the union of the three roots of the limbs.
One should whirl and display the form resembling the flight of a pigeon, showing all the limbs of the deity; thereafter, one should recite a single verse.
That light is the great lamp which dispels darkness everywhere;
that light which is both internal and external—may this lamp be accepted.
Now, the food offering (naivedya).
One should draw a mandala on the right, in front, or on the left;
it may be a triangle or a circular representation of the earth, serving as the support for the worshipped Śakti.
One should present perfume, flowers, and ornaments in the front;
one should offer lamps to the right, or in front, or to the left.
The incense should likewise be on the left; the one skilled in giving [the offerings] places them in front;
the food offering (naivedya) is on the right or the left, in front, but never behind.
One should offer the liquor from behind and never from the front;
likewise for the perfume, flowers, incense, lamp, and food offering.
Whatever garment, ornament, gold, or other such thing is given,
one should recite the name of its presiding deity and perform the rites of sprinkling and worship over them.
Having offered [the oblation] with the root mantra, one should present it to the image;
likewise, one should perform the ritual services (upacāra) using the special arghya water alone.

The Great Goddess does not accept that which is offered by others, even if it is presented according to hundreds of ritual procedures, if it has been discarded by those other than [the authorized officiants] or if it is contained in anything other than the arghya vessel.
Having offered water for the feet and water for sipping, one should present the food offering (naivedya),
placing it upon a golden vessel with its stand within the mandala.
Having established it within a square, one should consecrate it according to the path of the scriptures;
having sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra, it should be protected by the Cakra and Mudrās.
Having brought the two hands together facing each other, joined and fully extended,
with the little fingers and thumbs joined together— this is the mudrā known as the Cakra.
Having perceived the defects such as touch, sight, and so forth, one should dry them up with the seed-syllable of wind (Yam);
touching [them] with the tip of the right hand, one should burn them away with the seed-syllable of fire (Ram).

Having rendered it nectar-like with the seed-syllable *vaṃ*, one should touch it before [the deity] with both hands according to the rules while reciting the root mantra, and having performed the creation, one should consecrate it with mantras.
Then, having displayed the *dhenumudrā*, one should worship with perfumes and flowers;
having worshipped the deity, one of undistracted mind should perform the *puṣpāñjali* offering.
Accept this divine, well-prepared, and exquisitely seasoned supreme rice-food (paramānna), contained within a golden vessel,
endowed with five types of textures and six flavors, for the sake of my spiritual accomplishment.
Having recited the root mantra ending with "svāhā," one should offer water;
touching the vessel with both hands, one should say, "Salutations to you" regarding the food offering (naivedya).
Having offered water into the right hand of the deity, one should recite this:
"Thou art the spreading of the nectar, svāhā," ending with the syllable *bhava*.
One should display with the left hand [the gesture] resembling a half-blown blue lotus;
having displayed it, one should perform the five breath-offerings (prāṇāhuti) while making the *grāsamudrā*.
The union of the little finger, the ring finger, and the thumb is the mudrā of prāṇa.
Having taken a morsel with it, one should say: "Svāhā to prāṇa."
By joining the index finger, the middle finger, and the thumb, one should utter the word for apāna;
then, ending in "ṅ" and concluding with "svāhā," one should likewise utter it for vyāna.
Svāhā! Then, for the Vyāna breath, one should offer with the middle fingers joined to the thumbs; omitting the little finger, one offers to Udāna with all the fingers, O wife of Agni.
Having offered with "svāhā" to the aggregate of all [deities], one should present it upon the seat;
then, [the water] which has been drawn from a vessel made of gold or other materials by means of the *dhenumudrā*.
Having consecrated [the offering] as nectar, one should offer it to the deity while reciting this mantra:
"Salutations to you, O Goddess of the lords of gods, the excellent bestower of complete satisfaction."
Accept this excellent water, which has been offered by another, pure, in its natural state, very cool, and filled with supreme bliss.
Having spoken thus, the deity should place a water vessel on the left;
cooked food for the sake of the deity is to be offered with three syllables.
What kind of sugarcane product— prepared by frying in ghee, cooked in milk, or processed solely over an open fire—
is recommended for a Śūdra?
Then, one should offer a handful of flowers and perform the binding of the directions with the Astra-mantra; having done so, one should place a curtain all around the deity.
One should again utter "Namaḥ" over the nectar-like food offering (naivedya);
then, having displayed the Dhenu-mudrā, one should meditate upon the deity residing in the arms.
Having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times, one should offer water;
then, after offering water for sipping at the conclusion of the food offering, one should perform the rite of the fire sacrifice (homa).

Now, he describes the mudrās for the sixteen services (upacāras) in their proper order: For the seat, one should form the lotus-mudrā with both hands facing downwards; this same mudrā is used when inquiring about well-being, but then it is turned upwards again.
The *svāgata* (welcome) gesture should be the *arghya* mudrā, which takes the form of joined palms (*añjali*);
that same gesture, through the joining of the ring finger and the thumb, is declared to be the *pādya* mudrā.
The wise one, having placed the right hand face upwards,
should join the four fingers— excluding the little finger— and keep them raised.
O fair-faced one, this mudrā with the palm facing downward has been taught by me for the Sātvatas during the rinsing of the mouth;
when the thumb is touched [to the lips], it becomes the mudrā for the *madhuparka*.
With the palm facing downward and the right hand formed into a fist with the little finger released,
this is declared by the Supreme Goddess to be the *snāna-mudrā* (bathing mudrā).
Having placed the right hand palm upwards, one should then touch its middle finger with the thumb; this is proclaimed as the mudrā of the garment for the deity.
This very ring finger, when touched, is known as the mudrā of ornamentation;
indeed, the little finger, when touched, is the mudrā of the sacred thread.
One should touch the tip of the little finger with the tip of the thumb; this is the mudrā of fragrance. Having turned the hand downward, one should join it with the tip of the index finger.
This mudrā, known as Puṣpā, belongs to the Supreme Goddess;
with the tip of the thumb, Maheśvarī should touch the tip of the index finger.
This is declared to be the mudrā for incense, which is pleasing to all the gods.
One should touch the tip [of the incense] with the tips of the *jyeṣṭhā* fingers, while the *madhyamā* fingers are directed toward the deities worshipped by the asuras.
This is the auspicious Lamp Mudrā, the refuge of all the gods;
O Goddess, the instructor should touch the tip of the ring finger with the tip of the thumb.
The mudrā that is not to be given is proclaimed as the *tattvamudrā*.
Now follows the procedure for the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma).

I shall describe the procedure for the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma), by which one attains all goals; O Supreme Goddess, having made a formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should perform the procedure for the daily fire-oblation.
Having brought the fire according to the prescribed rule, one should set aside the flesh-eating portion;
then, having uttered the mantra, [one should offer] either in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or likewise upon the altar (sthaṇḍila).
Or, having spread fire upon the ground with the three *vyāhṛtis*,
one should offer three oblations and then perform the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) oblation.
Then, having invoked the Goddess and performed the sixfold rite with the root mantra alone,
one should offer twenty-five oblations with the root mantra.
With honey and clarified butter as the oblation, or with sesame seeds, or with auspicious milk-rice,
or with rice mixed with sesame, or even with flowers alone.
One should offer one oblation for each of the limbs and the protective deities;
then, having bid farewell to the deity and the fire, one should proceed to the place of worship.
Having sat upon the seat, the practitioner of mantra should then offer the bali-oblation to the spirits;
those who follow the left-hand path (vāmīs), however, should perform the libation with liquor at the conclusion of the ritual services.
For them, however, the fire-oblation is optional, but the service of libations is constant;
having offered, praised, and bowed, one should dismiss them within the circle of the twice-born.
Now follows the offering of the bali to the spirits.
Having drawn a mandala in the northeast, one should place there a vessel with its base;
in this [vessel], one should place a bowl filled with flowers and the like, along with condiments, water, and so forth.
There, having dismissed the spirits, one should then offer them an oblation:
"To those who are fierce, whose deeds are fierce, and who dwell in fierce places."
The yoginīs of fierce form, those who are lords of the gaṇas,
those who move upon the earth, those who move through the sky, and those who dwell in the intermediate space;
"May all these beings, with joyful minds, accept this offering;
he should offer a stream of water from his left hand into that vessel."
Having taken up a handful of flowers, one should pray to the elemental beings (bhūtas).

To all those beings who dwell here upon the earth, having received this offering presented according to the rite, may they attain satisfaction and depart; may they all be gracious to us—salutations to them!
Having offered a handful of flowers and bowed down, one should dwell in the Vihara as is pleasant;
then, one should dismiss the Bhūtas and others with the Nārāca-mudrā.
O beloved, make your hand like a bow held in the hand;
this is declared to be the arrow-seal (*vāṇamudrā*), which cuts down the host of enemies.
Having meditated that the deity has reached satisfaction, and having considered the food offering to be devoid of essence,
one should then place the vessel in the direction of the Rakshasas (the southwest).
The purification of the place for the food offering (naivedya) should be performed with cow-dung water while reciting the Astra-mantra;
then, taking the remains of the deity's meal (nirmālya), one should say: "Salutation to the consumer of the nirmālya."
Having cast [the water] toward the northeast, one should then wash one's hands;
thereafter, one should again offer water for sipping (ācamana) as well as a hand-rubbing powder (karodvartana).
Having offered pure water for sipping, one should scent the hands with fragrant substances.
Now, the betel-leaf offering.
Then one should offer betel leaf (*tāmbūla*) consisting of twelve ingredients to Viṣṇu:
catechu (*khadira*), cardamom (*elā*), cloves (*lavaṅga*), camphor (*indu*), lime powder (*cūrṇa*), betel leaf (*parṇa*), and *tamālaka*.
A betel nut combined with the inner bark, petals, and rind of the *jātī* flower, along with musk and saffron,
is declared to be the ten-ingredient offering for the Sun.
The five-fold offering for Vighneśvara consists of musk, two garlands,
powdered khadira wood, betel leaf, areca nut, and camphor.
Then he should offer a mountain to the Goddess together with a box of jasmine flowers for the Great Lord;
thereafter, he should present ornaments such as a crown and the like.
And one should likewise show the moon, fashioning an umbrella and chowries;
having placed dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and a purifying thread upon the head of the deity.
Then one should perform the *ārātrika* rite for the sake of attaining the goals of dharma, kāma, and artha.
Now follows the *ārātrika* rite.
Upon a vessel made of gold, silver, or bronze— which is as captivating as the eyes of the world—
one should draw a beautiful eight-petaled lotus with saffron.
A wise person should perform the ārātrika ceremony with ten lamps, twenty, five, or nine; or with eight lamps, according to the number of the principles (tattvas).
One should cause a triangle and a hexagon to fall within [the circle],
with petals consisting of that particular vidyā or of the special arghya.
First, one should display the *cakra-mudrā* in the Bhairava-vessel, saying:
"O Deity, accept this *ārātrika* for the sake of your pleasure."
O Goddess of the gods, with this mantra the wise one should perform the ārātrika ceremony using black gram,
sesame seeds, rice, wheat, or even barley.
One should carefully prepare lamps from molasses, such as those made from rice-gruel, sugar, turmeric, saffron, the eight fragrant substances, and cow's milk.
With red and yellow lamps, the results are known as subjugation (vaśya) and immobilization (stambha);
one should place a great lamp in the pericarp and eight desired lamps upon the eight petals.
[Offerings] made of barley and wheat, combined with sugar and milk,
adorned with the beauty of circular arrangements, and filled with ghee.
Then the mantra-practitioner, having consecrated [the object] with the Ratneśvarī mantra, does not recite it beyond the syllables *śrīṃ*,
*hrīṃ*, *glūṃ*, *mlūṃ*, and *mayai* as before, followed by *śrīṃ* and *hrīṃ* in sequence.
Then, having been instructed by the Mistress of the Petals (daleśvarī), one should worship her with the root mantra;
thereafter, lifting that vessel again and again up to the top of the head.
One should rotate [the vessel] nine times and display the *cakramudrā*;
then, having prostrated to the deity, one should perform three rounds of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
Then, with the root mantra, one should perform all the previously mentioned nyāsas;
[one should recite it] one thousand and eight times, or half of that, or three hundred times.
Or one should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times without sloth;
when the recitation is completed, one should place the rosary upon one's head.
Now, he describes the one-hundred-and-eight-bead rosary for the purpose of daily recitation (nityajapa).
Alternatively, one may perform the recitation (japa) with finger-garlands; that is now described.
Each of these two types is further divided into two according to the distinction between emanation (sṛṣṭi) and withdrawal (saṃhāra).
Starting from the middle finger, [it reaches] the root joint of the ring finger;
it consists of three joints of the little finger, ending at the tip of the ring finger, O Maheśvarī.
O Śivā, when the middle finger tips slightly exceed the root joint of the index finger,
this is called the Śaktimālā mudrā; through its withdrawal, it becomes Vaiṣṇavī.
Starting from the middle [finger], the Supreme Goddess [proceeds] from its tip;
then the ring finger follows, moving clockwise around the middle one.
The goddess named Śivā has beautiful joints and ends with the tips of the index fingers;
so too does the Saṃhārabhairavīmālā, provided it ends with the tips of the index fingers.
The solar garland is thus proclaimed; through the process of withdrawal, it becomes the Gāṇapī.
O Śivā, beginning from the ring finger and the middle finger, the middle [finger] is in the center.
O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, the rosary of Gāyatrī is said to end with the tip of the index finger in the ascending order; it is called Vadukā when counted in the reverse (descending) order.
Starting from the middle of the ring finger and reaching the middle of the middle finger,
one should proceed clockwise around the base of the fingers in due order.
The Cīnamālā is proclaimed as being born from the Kṣetrapāla through the process of withdrawal;
it begins from the middle of the middle finger and extends to the middle portion of the index finger.
O Goddess of the gods, O Śivā, the Gāndharva-mālā of the dweller of the Saṃhāra-vaṭa is said to begin from the root of the index finger in reverse order.
Starting from the base of the index finger and proceeding gradually to its tip,
one should then follow the same clockwise sequence to the first joint of the middle finger.
In the rite of Mañjughoṣa, however, Mālikā is used; in the rite of Khecarī, it is for the purpose of withdrawal.
Beginning from the tip of the little finger and proceeding in order to the tip of the thumb.
The rosary extending as far as the base of the index finger is called Sāṃbhavī;
the Vāruṇī rosary is proclaimed to belong to Dhanada (Kubera) because of its nature of withdrawal.
Starting from the base of the little finger and proceeding in the manner of a snake’s hood, O Goddess, the rosary is considered to extend to the tip of the index finger; this is the Yakṣiṇī rosary.
Through withdrawal, she is the supreme one who forms a great garland of Kinnarīs;
beginning from the little finger at the base, she proceeds in order along the path of the row.
The Jaina-mālā is proclaimed to end with the little finger (kaniṣṭhā) for the Goddess;
it becomes the Jaina-mālā through withdrawal (saṃhāra). Now hear [the sequence] from the base (anāmā) onwards.
Following the clockwise sequence, with the index finger marked by the middle finger,
this is declared to be the lunar rosary (mālācāndrī), the method of the rosary for reabsorption (saṃhāra).

One should always perform the daily recitation (japa) with the hand, but never the optional (kāmya) recitation. However, if no rosary is available, one may perform even the optional recitation with the hand.
Taking water from the *argha* vessel into his hand, he should recite this again:
"O you who protect the secret of secrets, accept this recitation performed by me."
O Lord of the World, may success be attained through your grace;
O Śiva, let the fruit of constant recitation be granted by the Goddess into the left hand.
Having offered water into the right hand of the deity, one should present [the offering];
and the prayer-bead rosary used for recitation should then be placed in a secluded, auspicious spot.
Then, preceded by the sounding of bells and hymns of praise to the heroes,
the Brāhmaṇa [should perform the rite] with Vedic mantras and so forth, while the Kṣatriya [should do so] with the *sahita* and other [mantras].
The Vaiśya should partake with those such as the Paurāṇikas, and the Śūdra with those such as the Prākṛtas; the Kaulikas, together with their Śaktis, should consume his leavings.
A Śūdra who, out of delusion or through desire, recites the Purāṇas or the Smṛti-saṃhitās,
becomes a doer of evil and attains hell along with his ancestors.
If a Śūdra should intentionally listen [to the Vedas], or if a twice-born man should cause them to be heard,
both of them shall become miserable denizens of hell in this world.
But he who, out of pride in his authority or even pride in his wealth,
allows a Śūdra to hear the Veda, shall become destitute and penniless.
If the Veda has been heard from or recited for a twice-born man out of ignorance, he shall perform three *prājāpatya* penances; then those two will become pure again.
Then, having taken the vessel for the *arghya* offering and reciting the root mantra, the knower of mantras [should say]:
"Whether my action has been well done or ill done, whatever has been performed by me."
"O Blessed One, O God, accept all this as my supreme worship.
Having spoken thus, he should pour out some of the arghya water to the right of the deity.
Then the wise one, having completed the worship, should offer it into the hand [of the deity];
having bowed with devotion to the Lord of Gods, he should ask for forgiveness with these verses.
Whatever leaf, flower, fruit, or water is given with mere devotion,
and whatever food offering is presented— accept that out of compassion.
I do not know how to invoke you, nor do I know how to dismiss you;
I do not even know how to perform worship. You alone, O Supreme Lord, are my refuge.
By deed, by mind, and by speech, there is no other refuge for me but you;
therefore, O Supreme Lord, you are the desired goal of all beings through your pervasive presence.
O Lord, in whatever wombs among thousands I may be born, may my imperishable devotion always abide in You alone.
The God is both the giver and the enjoyer; God is this entire universe.
God triumphs everywhere; indeed, I am that very God.
Now, regarding prostration and circumambulation.
Bowing is declared to be *māna* (reverence), consisting of both physical and verbal acts;
though homage is threefold, the physical is considered the most excellent.
Furthermore, that which is performed by means of Purāṇas or Vedas is vocal;
this is the middling salutation, whereas the verbal [salutation] is as follows.
When a salutation is performed by oneself, endowed with devotion, through both prose and verse composed together, it is therefore known as vocal (vācika).
Having gone to the ground on one's knees and touched the earth with the head,
the prostration that is performed is considered the highest form of physical homage.
Having joined the palms together above the head, they are likewise placed at the feet;
and having touched them with both knees and the head, it becomes another form of salutation.
With the two feet, the two hands, the two knees, the chest, the head, the eyes, the speech, and the mind— this is declared to be the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma).
With both arms, the knees, the head, and speech—this is the five-limbed prostration; these two are the most excellent among forms of worship.
One who, with a steady mind, performs the eight-limbed prostration upon the ground while Kṛṣṇa is present,
shall abandon the sins accumulated over a thousand births and attain Vaikuṇṭha.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by giving land to those learned in the Vedas,
that same fruit he obtains through devotion by performing a circumambulation of Kṛṣṇa.
A conch in the hand is prescribed everywhere for the right [hand].
One should offer one [flower] to Caṇḍī, seven to Ravi (the Sun), and three to Vināyaka.
One should perform four circumambulations for Keśava and half (two) for Śiva;
however, it is taught that for all [deities] except Triśakti, the circumambulation should be in the form of a triangle.
The half-moon is said to be behind Maheśa;
the practitioner of mantras should perform the circumambulation of Śiva in the sequence of the half-moon.
One should not cross the *somasūtra* by way of either the right or the left;
rather, having performed three circumambulations clockwise, one should offer five prostrations.
One should perform circumambulation once more; then rebirth no longer exists.
Having touched the testicles of the bull with the right thumb and forefinger, [one attains liberation].
Having seen Śiva in the middle of the peak, there is no rebirth;
[one sees] Vṛṣa, Caṇḍa, Vṛṣa again, the Soma-thread, and Vṛṣa once more.
In the Kali age, devoid of straightforwardness, one should move from step to step, then to another step, like a broken moon-path, then again broken, and then like a bull.
Vocal praise, mental meditation, the fourfold circumambulation,
the two Soma-thread lines, or wherever there may be a temple of Viṣṇu.
One should not perform the *apasavya* (leftward) rite; having done so, one must perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. One should extend the right hand and not release it again by oneself.
One should show the right side [of the deity] and perform circumambulation even mentally;
one should properly perform the circumambulation of the deity three times with body, speech, and mind.
Even a single circumambulation measuring one cubit,
or an unseasonable visit to Viṣṇu, destroys previously accumulated merit.
Having circumambulated clockwise, one should go to the western direction, and from there to the north-eastern (Sāṃbhavī) direction;
then, having offered salutation to the southern direction, one should perform prostration in the manner of a triangle.
Then, with the mantra beginning with "Oṃ," one should perform the offering to Brahman (brahmārpaṇa);
preceded by the syllable Om, one should recite "prāṇabuddhi... and so forth.
Regarding the domain of the body and its attributes— namely waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—
one is then situated within through standing, moving, mind, speech, and action.
Whatever you utter with devotion, whatever you hear, whatever is remembered, whatever is spoken, and whatever is done— let all that become an offering unto Brahman.
And this mantra, "Tursvāhā," is declared to consist of six syllables;
then one should dismiss the deity along with the hosts of his attendants.
Having thus offered a handful of flowers and prostrated,
one should contemplate that entire multitude of rays as having completely dissolved into the body of the deity.
Having meditated upon Śiva in the form of light and having repeatedly asked for forgiveness with the words "Forgive me," one should dissolve the deity into one's own heart after the meal.
Now he describes the *saṃhāramudrā*.
Having placed the two hands so that they touch and adhere, with the fingers interlaced in the middle,
one should then rotate them and make the two index fingers straight.
The mudrās proclaimed by means of dismissal are designated as "reabsorption" (saṃhāra):
"Go, go to the supreme place, your own abode, O Supreme Lord!"
These gods, beginning with Brahmā, do not know the supreme state;
[one should realize it] by means of this mantra and the breath of inhalation (pūraka).
Meditating with this mantra and having visualized her, one should establish her in the heart:
"Stay, stay in the supreme abode, O Supreme Lord, in your own place!"
"Wherein all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, reside within my heart"—
having thus established and worshipped one's own self, one should contemplate that wine as such.
In the northeast, one should prepare a mandala devoid of gates and lotuses;
it is used for worship with the remains of previous offerings during the worship of the five deities (pañcāyatana).
Indeed, five [deities] must be worshipped; one should worship Īśa and the others up to Madhya.
Laṃbodara is the splendor of Gaṇeśa, and Caṇḍa is that of Vivasvat.
The mantra of Caṇḍeśvarī for Hari is proclaimed as "viśvakteto," while that of Maheśī is "hareḥ"; the mantra of Caṇḍeśvara for Bhavānī is "maheśituḥ. One should perform the ritual in such a manner.

By the command of Śiva, Daśamiśrī offers to you— who consume the remains of offerings— the various foods such as those to be licked, sucked, and drunk, as well as the floral garlands and unguents used for worship.
Thus, having offered the remainder of the *naivedya* and bowed, one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*). Then, again, with this [mantra] joined by the seed-syllables *hrīṃ hrīṃ saḥ*:
One should announce the worship of the Sun with the mantra for the sake of ensuring its flawlessness:
"Obeisance to you, Vivasvat, the eternal one, the splendor of Viṣṇu."
To Savitṛ, the progenitor of the world, the pure one, the bestower of action;
then, having steadied the mind with hands joined in añjali, one should recite as follows:
Whatever flaw there may be in my sacrifice, whatever flaw in my austerity, and whatever flaw in my worship of me—
may all that become flawless through the grace of Bhāskara.
Then, having stirred with the root mantra a small amount of the water for the *arghya* offering and the remaining fragrance from the worship, one should consecrate it eight times again.
One should sprinkle oneself with this water while reciting the root mantra;
the practitioner should then place the *nirmālya* upon his head while reciting the root mantra.
After drinking the water for washing the feet, one should then distribute the food offering (naivedya) again among His devotees;
having eaten oneself, one should dwell happily, absorbed in Him.
A Śaiva, however, is entitled to the grace of the *nirmālya* of Śiva;
another [who partakes of it] goes to hell, yet there is no fault in the union of the five.
Whether they be non-Śaivas or Śaivas, those who with devotion visit the Svayaṃbhū Liṅga Tīrtha or even [partake of] the Prasāda, are liberated from a multitude of sins.
A Śūdra may worship a Liṅga installed by him, or he may cause it to be worshipped;
by accepting its related prasāda and other offerings, he shall attain freedom from debt.
This primary method of worship has been fully revealed to you.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Ritual from the Inner Worship to the Final Dismissal," in the General Daily Worship within the *Śrī Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Now, he describes the daily worship of Kaulavāminī.
In that regard, he first describes the arising of that path:
"O Goddess, when your body was cast off at the sacrifice of Dakṣa,
I took it upon my shoulder and prepared to enter the funeral pyre."
Wherever that submarine fire might go in search of the cows,
there it was swiftly extinguished by Śakra with waters.
Thus wandering for a year, my perspiration became great;
were those drops to fall upon a vessel, they would burn the very earth.
Then Viṣṇu, being entreated for the protection of the earth,
swiftly cut through your limbs with his swift arrows.
Having divided him into eighty-four pieces, he cast them upon the earth;
fanned by that [wind], I was then entirely pleased.
And Viṣṇu, having manifested once more, raised me up from my feet;
I was embraced by him, and my grief was forgotten.
Then Brahmā and the other gods, along with Nārada and the great sages, praised me; at that time, Viṣṇu spoke these words to Pārvatī.
O Great Lord, you who possess the light of knowledge, how have you fallen into delusion as to enter the fire along with the bodies of these virtuous women?
"A woman should follow her husband, but a man does not go to her"—
disregarding this scripture, O Lord, how have you been so deluded?
When the Lord of Gods spoke thus, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hari likewise praised him along with Vidhi using external ornaments of poetic figures (śleṣālaṃkāra).
O twice-born ones, when we two had then declared that you were to choose a husband,
those brahmins replied, "This subversion of dharma has occurred."
The Śaivas, relying on Dakṣa’s sacrifice, caused the twice-born to fall from their Brahminhood;
and all those twice-born who had come to the sacrifice were cursed by the Śaivas.
If this surface of the earth were true to Viṣṇu’s words regarding these limbs,
then at every spot, through the touch of the corpse, it would be devoid of the rites of Brahman.
Therefore, act in such a way that the purification of the earth, the purity of the Brahmins,
and the truthfulness of Brahma’s word may all be realized.
Then, having reflected and having reached an agreement with Viṣṇu, I declared:
"Wherever the ritual application of the Vedas has been destroyed, there let the Tantra be set in motion."
For those Brahmins who have been consumed by curses and have abandoned the Vedic rites,
this Kaula dharma is the means for attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Those Brahmins born in Pīṭha whose brahminhood has been consumed by a curse— they alone,
within their lineage, possess the qualification for this path.
Because it is honored within that very family (kula), this path is called Kaula;
the Vāma path is inferior to it, as are those belonging to the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya castes.
The authority for those two [rites] is declared here to belong to the sacrificers;
according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), anyone inferior to them— including Śūdras— is not entitled to perform them.
Those who, having known the lineage of the Kaula dharma, do not practice it, are devoid of the succession of breaths and are afflicted by disease; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, he who, being unestablished in the knowledge of the Kaula, desires to enjoy the substance,
is a great sinner and is excluded from all ritual acts.

For one who is devoid of the conduct of the samaya, who acts according to his own whims, and is evil-minded—there is no attainment due to the fall from the kula; therefore, one should not associate with such a person.
He who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, acts according to his own whims,
attains neither perfection in this world nor the supreme goal in the hereafter.
He who, having resorted to the [Jaina] doctrine, consumes the property of the community,
is reckoned as an *aṅgāra* (ember) and is born among the origins of elemental beings (*bhūtayoni*).
And if one whose self is stumbling with pride understands nothing at all—
neither meditation, nor the practice of austerity, nor reflection, nor dharma, nor virtuous action— then what?
If there is no reflection upon the deity, the guru, or oneself within the Kaulika path, one who is merely attached to sense objects will surely fall; of this there is no doubt.
Having correctly understood the Vāsas from the Kula scriptures of the venerable Guru, one should practice the five mudrās; otherwise, one becomes fallen.
He who does not worship the lineage of gurus, the circle of deities (āvṛtti), and Vaṭuka and the others— even if he is a Vīra— will,
due to such fruitless exertion, incur the curse of the deity.
Now, the method of worship for those who dwell in the Kaula tradition is described:
one should perform the purification of the deity by means of the offering of oneself and the ritual substances.
The ritual bath, the twilight devotions, the purification of the elements, and breath control are established;
the purification of the self occurs through the placement of the Mātṛkā letters upon the vital breaths and other such rites.

This purification of the site is considered to consist of sweeping, smearing with unguents, and so forth, making it like the surface of a mirror, as well as the use of canopies, incense, lamps, and the like.
The syllables of the root mantra, strung together with the letters of the Mātṛkā,
repeated three times in both direct and reverse order— this is considered the purification of the mantra.

Having sprinkled the articles of worship with the root-mantra and the weapon-mantra, the one who knows the ritual procedure should display the *dhenumudrā*; this is considered the purification of the substances.

Having established the deity upon the pedestal and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should sprinkle it with arghya water while reciting the root mantra; then, one should display the dīpanī mudrā three times.
Having thus performed the purification of the deity, one should thereafter commence the sacrifice;
that worship is to be known as fruitful, otherwise it would be fruitless.
First, having stationed oneself in the water, one should wash the feet;
then, having sipped water twice and tied the topknot, one should perform the worship of the Lord of the Door.
Having cleared away the Brahmins and performed the purification of the flowers and other materials,
one should then sit in the vīrāsana posture and consume vijayā.
Having placed the Śakti at one's side, one should perform the network of ritual placements (nyāsa);
then, having purified the Kula substances, one should establish the vessels.
Now, regarding the heroic posture (vīrāsana):
One should not use as a seat a monkey that is soft and supple, or one fallen in battle,
or even one killed by a creature or already dead.
O Śivā, one should perform worship using either a Tārīṇī image that has fallen from the womb, or one not born from a womb,
or even an image made of wind (a subtle form), O Auspicious One.
Or one should prepare a seat covered with cloth dyed with seasonal colors,
or a pedestal fashioned from the wood of a cremation ground, or made from sacrificial timber.
One who has been initiated should never enter [the fire] wearing the skin of the black antelope;
the householder [should wear it] one or two cubits in width and four finger-breadths in height.
One should perform the ritual of installation and worship on a pure seat; such is the procedure.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the most secret of secrets;
please speak of the purification rites and the means of accomplishment, beginning with the *muṇḍa* and ending with the *vīra*.
The illustrious Śiva said:
This is a secret, even a most profound secret, which I have never revealed anywhere;
out of love for you, O Great Goddess, it is now being told—listen!
First, there should be a soft seat; the second should be one without a crest;
the third should be soft; and the fourth is said to be the "shaven" (muṇḍa) type.
The fifth is considered the corpse posture (mṛtāsana), and the sixth is held to be the hero posture (vīrāsana);
O Goddess, the seventh is proclaimed as the great hero posture (mahāvīrāsana).
The Goddess accomplishes the purification of the seven [substances], as well as the purification of the rosary and the vessel;
the purification of the yantra and everything else has been fully explained previously.
Now, O Pārvatī, listen to the means for accomplishing the postures as well.
Now he states the definition.
The wise say that a fetus aborted within six months is "mṛdu"; they know one who dies before the tonsure (cūḍā) and initiation (upanayana) rites as a "cūḍaka."
A child who has undergone the tonsure ceremony but whose initiation (upanayana) has not yet been performed,
if he dies in his fifth year during an auspicious time, they know him as "Komala."
O Goddess, that which is attained through ordinary death is called the seat of death (mṛtāsana);
when it arises in the form of a hero, they know that as the hero’s seat (vīrāsana).
O Goddess, the Great Hero’s posture (mahāvīrāsana) is considered to consist of the piercing (āveśa), the trident (śūla), the noose (pāśa), and so forth;
it is a corpse with unbroken limbs, O Goddess, provided that the head is not severed.
That skull upon which a garland and so forth have been mentioned is prescribed for the purpose of the alms-bowl.
Now follows the consecration of the seat.

O Goddess of the gods, if one treats as a corpse a child born from the womb— whether it be Indra himself, or one situated in the seventh or eighth month, or even a tender infant who has just had his tonsure ceremony.
Having diligently purified the site, he, filled with joy and wearing the attire of a mendicant,
then performed the consecration rites and established [the deity] in a pure place.
Having taken up the eight perfumes, one should first sprinkle [the area]; then,
with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the five products (pañcagavya), consecrated by the five kalās.
With the root mantra, one should establish there the seat, the wheel, and the earth beneath;
[one should draw] a triangle, a bindu, and māyā within the square, and a triangle within that.
Outside of that, one should draw a triangle and an eight-petalled lotus;
outside of that, a sixteen-spoked [wheel], followed by three circles endowed with the three qualities.
And one should worship Mūladevī in the center with the root mantra;
it is circular and threefold, and one should not join the first [syllable] with the first.
There, in the lotuses at the beginning of the letters and in all rituals, are the ten kalās of Vahni; likewise, they are in the triangle and in the eight-petaled lotus.
One should worship the sixteen digits of the moon within the threefold sixteen-spoked [mandala];
and right there, one should diligently establish the hero known as Mṛdu.
There, one should draw the yantra preceded by the common power (sādhāra-śakti),
as well as the ocean of nectar, the island of jewels, and the house of the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).
The cremation ground and the Pārijāta tree, and at its root the funeral altar;
thereafter, the [four powers of] dharma, jñāna, vairāgya, and aiśvarya.
Then, from *adharma* onwards, there is a pair [of limbs] beginning with the mantra-less and ending with the handless and footless;
this is the form of the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*, consisting of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*.

The practitioner of mantra should worship that in its proper place; he should perform the heart-assignment (hṛnnyāsa) and so forth, and then the practitioner of mantra should perform the hand-assignment (karanyāsa), worshipping with both hands thereafter.
Having placed the deceased with his face downward, one should speak sweetly into his mouth:
"O Hero, O Supreme Bliss, O Śaṅkara upon the couch of the Goddess!"
"Grant me the eight siddhis and always bestow peace upon me.
Having said this, O Lord of Heroes, one should place gold into the mouth.
Along with cardamom, cloves, and nutmeg, together with fruit and betel leaf;
and ginger, jaggery, and camphor, bound with a red thread—these six [ingredients].
There, with the root mantra, one should fashion a firm-fisted tuft of hair,
like a lamp-wick made from the fibers of the sun, moon, and white lotus.
Then the practitioner of Śakti should invite the seven [deities] in due order;
he should worship the Goddess on his head with salutations, perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Then the practitioner of mantras should perform the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa) by means of the prāṇamantra at the anus,
the genitals, the navel, the stomach, and the secret region.
Likewise, the thighs, knees, shanks, ankles, and the soles of the feet;
as well as the head, throat, nose, the two eyes, and the two ears.
On the crest, the armor, and the cheeks, as well as on the upper and lower lips,
on the two cords, on the tongue, and on the head, the back, and the two sides.

One should likewise perform the unsurpassed deposition of the divine seat (devapīṭha-nyāsa) upon the heart and other [limbs], as well as upon the two arms and the two feet, and indeed upon all the limbs.
There, the solar disc consists of the digits (kalās) beginning with Tapinī;
[one should worship] the corpse (mṛtakāyaśava) here, followed by the word "namaḥ" at the end.
Bathing [the deity] with the root mantra, one should worship with the eight waters;
one should conceive of the seat as consisting of the nature of the sun and moon, having the form of fire.
Merupṛṣṭha is the seer, the Sūktam is the meter, and immediately after that is Sutala;
then follows Kūrmoda, and thereafter [the section] for accomplishing dharma and artha.
Furthermore, for the sake of accomplishing the mind's liberation,
it is proclaimed that one should display the tortoise mudrā (kūrmamudrā), followed by the weapon (astra) and the veiling (avaguṇṭhana).
O Śivā, one should then display the Matsya-mudrā, the Śakti-yoni, and the Dhenu-mudrā; and upon snapping the fingers, one should display the Caturasra-mudrā.
Having held [the vessel], one should contemplate the root [mantra] in sequence as "earth-ness" (pṛthvītva),
and then with the mantras beginning with "vajrodaka," numbering according to the [five] desires.
First, having extracted the Praṇava, then the word "sahasrāra," and at the end of that,
"hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should then say "rakṣa rakṣa."
O Mahāpratisarā, cut through all obstacles immediately!
Having extracted [the mantra] ending with *hūṃ phaṭ*, one should utter the *vahnijāyā* (the fire-born wife, *svāhā*).
The worship of the guardians of the directions (dikpālas), beginning with Indra, should be performed in their proper sequence,
using the formidable mantras of Vīrārgala as well as those of Pāśupata.
One should perform the binding of the quarters there with the mantras of the great maṇḍala;
O beloved, one should also offer an oblation to Śivā there during eclipses and other such occasions.
The offering to Śivā should be made three times—at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end;
however, at the time of seizing the head, the offering to Śivā must be performed in every way.
O Supreme Goddess, having worshipped Śiva and Śakti, one should worship the guardians of the directions along with their offerings,
together with their weapons and so forth, in due order.
In this manner, O Lord of Heroes, one should sequentially offer oblations to all [the deities],
pronouncing "Vāk Māyā Kamalā," followed by "O Goddess, such-and-such [name]," and "This is the Vedic mantra."
This sequence proceeds; however, one should take two [verses] as a pair. 87.
Likewise.
Having uttered "Stay here! Homage! (atra tiṣṭha namaḥ), [one says] "astute hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Then, one should recite the letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet from 'a' to 'kṣa', joined with the bindu.
The best of practitioners should wrap [it] from the head down to the feet in a clockwise direction,
encircling it with three and a half coils.
Having applied various fragrant substances, red sandalwood, sandalwood, saffron, and aloe-wood,
one should encircle it with a yellow thread.
One should bind it with various substances mixed with alkali and turmeric;
one should tie it with either a red thread or a silk thread.
Now he states the qualification [for practice].
Free from dualities and free from egoism, surrounded by a pure multitude of channels,
devoid of sectarian bias and lacking worldly intellect, he is devoted to the welfare of all living beings.
Completely purified in all his limbs, proficient in all the scriptures,
having received consecration, a knower of the Vidyā-mantras, and devoted to recitation, worship, and other such rites.
He should dwell on a soft seat; otherwise, he shall go to hell—he who, out of ignorance, delusion, or hypocrisy, performs what is seen or unseen [as prescribed] improperly.
They go to a terrible hell or may attain the state of a piśāca;
those great fools fall into disease and lead a life of very short duration.
But a hero who knows the scriptures, is devoted to the conduct of the observances,
is a knower of mantras, a seer of the tantras, and is expert in yantras and mantras, may enter.

Capable of both restraint and favor, he delights in the four aims of human life; endowed with supernatural powers, he bestows success upon the world and is able to grant grace to the lords of the world.
Death undoubtedly comes for one who performs [the practice] while being incapable;
this is declared to be the soft seat (mṛdvāsana). What else do you wish to hear?
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear about the purification of the *acūḍaka*;
for in the seat of the *acūḍaka*, O Goddess, all the *siddhis* reside.
Taking up that seat, which is endowed with the five *akāras*,
on the eighth or fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight, or on the new moon day, during the festival of lamps.

O Goddess of the gods, even in the case of a Kula-Ṛkṣa, there should be a seat without a crest; O Pārvatī, having performed the binding of the directions, the purification of the elements, and so forth with diligence.
Having begun with the Vajrodaka rite and performed the protection ritual for Śivā,
one should diligently master the mantras and accomplish the desired sādhanā.
Everything else shall be as before, but it is indeed the same even in the *komala* [posture].
I shall now describe the *suṇḍāsana*; listen, and be attentive.
On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days of the earth-born [fortnight],
on Tuesday, during the festival of lights (Dīpotsava), on the full moon day of Phālguna, and also on the day of the eight-night rite (Aṣṭarātra).
When one-third of the night has passed, having completed the preliminary rites,
one should be dressed as a hero, endowed with compassion, devoted to the Lord, and with senses subdued.
Possessing great strength and great intelligence, with his senses conquered and learned in the scriptures,
he held a sword in his hand, had disheveled hair, and was adorned with a mark of vermilion.
Having taken the authentic substances, the supreme practitioner— possessing great delight and firm devotion—
prepares the requisites for the heroic accomplishment (*vīrasādhana*).
Having offered a row of jackals at the end of the rite, one should perform the *muṇḍasādhana*;
there, the Goddess herself in the form of a jackal will certainly remove all obstacles.
Otherwise, gods, demons, and humans will become creators of obstacles;
therefore, for the sake of destroying all obstacles and for the sake of attaining success, one should worship Pheravī.
One should accomplish [the practice] in a cremation ground, a cave, by a river, or even in an empty house.
O Maheśānī, if it is in a cremation ground, the ritual procedure there is like that of a cremation ground.
Elsewhere, the accomplishment of all goals should be performed like that of a hero;
one should drive eight *kīla* pegs made of *kādira* wood into the ground while reciting the mantra.
One should dispel all obstacles with the mantras of the great mandala;
having diligently brought forth a severed head, one should cast it away without the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having performed her bath with milk and then with scented water,
Pārvatī then diligently performed her bath with wine at the conclusion of that rite.
Having anointed that shaven head with oil, and likewise applied vermilion and collyrium,
and having worshipped it with perfumes and flowers, one should dig a hole measuring half a cubit in depth.
In the case of Tārā, Kālikā, and even Chinnamastā, Pārvatī may be the seat,
or it may be Muṇḍaka and so forth, or indeed Ādhāra and so forth.
There too, within the power of Daśaśakti, the Great Goddess is divided into three;
likewise, whatever seat (pīṭha) one may worship, it resides within the power of Ṛtumatī.
Now, the limit of the time for sitting is as follows:
O Goddess, the seat of seasonal garments is proclaimed as *sūtrānta*;
the seat of the shaven-headed (*muṇḍāsana*) is likewise known as *majjīta*, and so too, O Beloved, is the seat of the corpse (*śavāsana*).
The kuca-āsana, the jāpātta,
and the surata-āsana have been proclaimed as consisting of the stages beginning with the soft and tender *cūḍā* and ending with *cūrṇa*.
Likewise, O Goddess, having diligently assumed the heroic posture (vīrāsana),
one should cast the impurities of the heart far away and purify the heart once more.
Having covered the ground with cloth or having placed a human skin seat thereon, one should remain and perform the recitation.

The cloth-seat (vastrāsana) ends with "bhaṅga," that with body-hair (sa-lomānta) consists of human hair; the essence of consciousness (saṃvid-rasa) is called "go-ja," and that called "tūrṇa" ends with "troṭana."
O Goddess, Maheśvarī, the vulva-skin is the āsana up to the edge of the pubic hair;
that which ends at the living organ (jīva) is the yogya-āsana, and that which ends at the perineum (pāta) is the surata-āsana.
O Goddess, the inverted posture is proclaimed to end with its fall;
at its conclusion, O Goddess, one should abandon it if another [posture] follows in succession.
O Goddess, that which is proclaimed as the "Poison-Bow" (Viṣarāsanaka) is known as the "Severer" (Chedanā);
O Goddess, it bestows success in due order and accomplishes all tasks upon this earth.
O Ambikā, some say the tiger posture (vyāghrāsana) is with hair, while others say it is without hair;
thus it has been briefly described. Now listen, O beloved, to the duration of time [for each].
O Goddess, for a woman in her menses, sitting [in this manner] for three days produces a triple effect;
O Goddess, sitting on a menstrual garment for three nights bestows fruit.
The muṇḍāsana is accomplished in six months, while the śavāsana is accomplished in one day;
the naracarmāsana is said to yield excellent results within a month for the Goddess.
O beautiful one, the fruit [of practice] is attained in two months on a low seat; O Great Goddess, the fruit shall be attained within half a month on the Ratāsana.

O Goddess of the Gods, on a soft seat (mṛdvāsana), the fruit is that of a month; on a comfortable seat (komalāsana), it is that of a year; and on one called ūrṇā, O Mistress of the Gods, it occurs after ten years.
In the Acūḍaka [tantra], by means of the Viṣṇu-tattvas, as well as in the Vīra [tantra] and the Mantra [tantra],
a throne is attained in five years with a cloth-seat and in five months with a lion-throne.
O Goddess, if one sits on a seat made of deer-skin for six years, or on one made of wool for ten years,
no fruit shall be obtained within seven days.
In the *yoni-āsana*, at the end of that fortnight known as *surata*, [the practice lasts] for eight days;
in the *viparīta* [position], it lasts for six days, provided there is the sensation of the tongue's touch accompanied by the two-fold awareness.
If a man applies the goddess Kālikā to the seven kisses,
he should be known as a resident of hell for as long as the dissolution of the world at the end of the kalpa.
Now, he states the alternative procedure in the absence of a soft seat and other such requirements.
In the absence of a corpse, one should imagine kuśa grass as the form and a seat;
the seat known as the *viṣṭhara* is to be worshipped, and the supreme consciousness is the one to be worshipped.
The seat of the Goddess Śrīdevī is the stream of nectar (amṛtadhārā), and its covering is the Sphaṭa.
Now, the seat of the practitioner is being described; listen at this moment.
In that [rite], indeed, leaves of the *bhūta* tree are prescribed instead of *kuśa* grass.
Ten white [syllables] and so forth are prescribed for each hand and foot; twenty in number are declared for the heart-lotus, which grants all boons;
and on the head, in the secret place, the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the ears, the breasts, the penis, and the anus, they are measured by pairs.
And the *yojanīya* and *akuśa* [plants] as well.
Thus, this is known as the *viṣṭara*, which bestows all accomplishments;
O Supreme Goddess, the binding should be performed with *kuśa* grass or with a cord.
Then, having prepared a seat with a thread mixed with blood or else with silk thread, one should perform the recitation upon it.
I have explained to you the ritual procedure for the lotus-seat of Brahmā;
by assuming the form of a corpse, a man shall become a poet and an eloquent speaker.
The Sūtra spoken by the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) must be performed by oneself for the sake of all accomplishments.
In the absence of a corpse, however, a seat (viṣṭara) is proclaimed to be the form of the corpse.
Indeed, the seat (viṣṭara) is proclaimed to be the manifest form of Śiva;
the seat is the very form of Śiva, while the conceptualization of one's own self as his Śakti [is the other aspect].
What on earth cannot be accomplished through the union of Śiva and Śakti?
The supreme garment of the Hero (vīra) is considered the second seat.
O Goddess of the gods, hear the third [mantra], which bestows all accomplishments:
the *viṣṭara* (seat), whose form is Śambhu, is the seat of both Śivā and Śiva.
The lion-throne, the couch, and the seat are the third; O Great Goddess, on the four legs are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara,
while Īśvara is the fourth, and Sadāśiva is in their midst.
In the center, however, is the place of the seat, which consists of the great state of aesthetic flavor (mahāsamarasa).
Then, O Goddess, having fashioned the hands, feet, head, and likewise the heart— having thus fashioned the corpse with all its limbs, both she and we [should do so].

O beautiful one, having placed either a bone or a portion of the corpse there, he should [perform the rite] on the foot with a hundred-vessel [vessel], a vessel of elements, or with *kuśa* grass, in due order.
A woman should perform the tying with a thread stained with menstrual blood,
or with silk thread, or with ordinary thread, as appropriate.
Having performed the placement of the vital breath (*jīvanyāsa*) there and meditated upon Tārā, one should perform the recitation (*japa*).
By means of this sequence and yoga, what on earth cannot be accomplished?
Sadāśiva in the form of a preta is described by me as the seat (viṣṭara).
Now he states the consecration of the seat (viṣṭara).
The breaking [of the thread] should be performed with the Gāyatrī, and one should carry out the tying with the root mantra. O Tārikā, listen now to that procedure where the Gāyatrī is not specified.
That name ending in "devī" is considered Gāyatrī;
that name ending in "devī" is the Gāyatrī Tāriṇī by me.
Having formed the resolve, the practitioner should grasp the soft [flower] with his left hand using the *kūrca* seed-syllable,
and perform the sprinkling with the *astra-mantra*.
Having uttered the Praṇava and Vaneśī, one should say that:
"O you who have the form of a corpse, O great preta, grant me the eight siddhis!"
Having praised him thus correctly, one should cause him to be placed in the midst of *kuśa* grass;
indeed, in his house, there should be a triangle made of red sandalwood.
Having drawn the Māyā [syllable] in the center of that, one should fashion a small maṇḍala outside;
then [one should write] the Praṇava, *Āḥ*, *Sa re rave*, and *vajra re rave*.
The *kūrca* (hūṃ), the weapon (*astra*) (phaṭ), and that which consists of the wife of fire (svāhā) are in the mandala;
then the mantra is: Oṃ, Āṃ, Māyā (hrīṃ), Krauṃ, and Haṃsa.
Having uttered the wife of Vahni (Svāhā), one should say the word "śava-prāṇāḥ" (the life-breaths of the corpse).
Then the word "iha-prāṇāḥ" (life-breaths here) is proclaimed; [then] "śava-jīva" (the life of the corpse) and "ihasthitaḥ" (stationed here).
All the sense-faculties of the corpse— speech, mind, sight,
hearing, and smell— having returned here, experience both pleasure and pain.
The mantra for installation consists of the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) joined with *tiṣṭha* and *svāhā*.
Having first uttered the *praṇava*, one should then recite the word *ādhāraśakti*.
One should worship that [seat] with the word "komalāsana" followed by "padaṃ ṅentaṃ" and ending with "namaḥ";
the salutation consists of the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and the words "kāmapīṭhāya namaḥ."
With three *māṣas* of gold, an image of a corpse should be fashioned upon a cloth;
having placed it upon a seat (*viṣṭara*), one should perform everything as previously prescribed.
Having performed the purification of the *samaya*, one should perform the purification of the *śakti*;
having performed the purification of the *śakti*, one should perform the purification of the liquor.
The gods, having performed the purification (*saṃśodhana*), should perform the purification of purity (*śuddhi-śodhana*).
Having performed the purification of purity, one should purify the *mudrā* through sexual union (*maithuna*).
Now, he states the acceptance by the twice-born.
Between the corpse and consciousness, the Goddess of Consciousness is the more important;
therefore, the best of practitioners employ consciousness here in worship and other rites.
And a great worship should be performed with well-uttered mantras;
the Brāhmaṇī [mudrā] consists of white flowers, while the Kṣatriyā consists of red flowers.
A Vaiśya woman has yellow flowers, while one born of a Śūdra has black flowers;
O Maheśānī, her Ṛṣi is considered to be Ānandabhairava.
By means of the three seed-syllables of Vāla, there is the seed (bīja), the power (śakti), and the pin (kīlaka).
O Maheśānī, the application for purification is performed in sequence;
the wise know that the six limbs are to be applied in order with those same two or three seed-syllables.
Now, as for meditative absorption (dhyāna).
I bow to the perfected Śivabodhinī Bhairavī, who holds a noose and a goad shining in her hands, who is skilled in granting the desired boons to her devotees, who severs the bonds of saṃsāra,
and who is like the nectar produced from the churning of the ocean of wisdom.
One should meditate upon the world-enchanting Suvijayā, whose sandals are worshipped by heroes.
Having consecrated it seven times with mantras, everything will certainly become purified.
O Consciousness, born of Brahman, daughter of Brahman, eternally stainless!
Grant me the bliss of Bhairava; may you be my purifier forever.
Oṃ, homage to Brāhmī, svāhā!
"One should purify the Brāhmaṇī."
O Goddess, you are the root of accomplishment and ritual action; you awaken those of deficient understanding, bring kings and subjects under control, and slay the throats of enemies.
Aiṃ! Homage to the Kṣatriyā; Svāhā!
Then he should purify a Kṣatriya woman.
O flame of fire whose nature is knowledge, for me who am blinded by ignorance,
grant the arrival of bliss, joy, and perfect wisdom.
Hrīṃ, obeisance to Vaiśyā, svāhā!
And then he should purify the Śūdrā.
I pay homage, I pay homage to you, O Mother who reveals the path of Yoga;
O Conqueror of the Three Worlds, grant me the fruit of meditative absorption.
Klīṃ, salutation and svāhā to the Śūdra woman.
The supreme mantra is now being told.
*Amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi*, then the word *padaṃ*; then the pair *amṛtam ākarṣaya*; then the word *siddhiṃ dehi*.
Then one should say "sarvam etat" followed by "vaśam ānaya";
this mantra, ending with the word "svāhā," is declared to be for the purification of all four.
One should apply the root mantra seven times over it;
then follow the mudrās beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), and after that, the Dhenu and Yoni mudrās.
One should dispel obstacles by binding the directions with snapping sounds preceded by three high-pitched notes,
as well as by divine vision and strikes of the heels.
One should satisfy [the deities] seven times in the aperture of Brahma while reciting the root mantra;
likewise, one should satisfy the Guru in the thousand-petaled lotus by means of the mudrā known as Tattva.
The practitioner, whose mind is intent on attaining perfection, should satisfy [the deities] with devotion in three ways;
he should utter the word "Aiṃ," then the phrase "vadavada," and thereafter the word "vāgvādini."
"O you who bring all sentient beings under control, become firm upon the tip of my tongue; then [recite] the entire mantra, ending with *svāhā*, and offer it into the mouth."
Accompanied by Ānanda, O Goddess, worship should be performed according to the prescribed rite by one who has consumed the *samaya* substances and likewise consorted with the *samaya* woman.
He is Śiva, he is the yogi, the one of true austerity, and the best among the virtuous;
he stands upon the path to liberation by whom the *samaya* has been consumed.
And having consumed this pledge, whatever mantra a person recites, he obtains the fruit of all [mantras]; this is the truth, the truth, O fair-faced one.
