Now follows the purification of the power (śakti).
He who is intent on purification is a practitioner among the three types of aspirants;
yet even when performed, there may be a loss of accomplishment, for Caṇḍikā becomes enraged.
O Maheśānī, power arises from consecration; it arises through the hearing of the mantra's recitation at the time of sexual union and at the time of initiation for a maiden.
Or, at the end of a *kalā*, one should perform the consecration with effort, even if it be in vain,
using wine, semen, or water, according to the ancient mantra.
First, having uttered the syllable *vā*, one should utter *tripurāyai*;
then, having uttered the word *namaḥ*, one should thereafter speak this *śakti*.
"O Dear One, purify [me] at the end of the word; empower my power.
Having uttered this along with the wife of Vahni (the *svāhā* mantra), it is proclaimed as the purification mantra (*śuddhi-mantra*).
By this rite, O Goddess, women who are always consecrated and constantly take delight here shall attain all perfections.
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, one shall attain liberation in the next;
for the purpose of piercing her ears, one should utter the seed-syllable of Māyā.
By that, a woman shall become pure and always indeed worthy of worship.
Now, he states the specific nyāsas for the left and right hands.
If the placement (nyāsa) beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with 'kṣa' is performed, it is called the Saṃhāra-nyāsa; it is also described as the Bindu-nyāsa.
For those engaged in the left-hand path who practice the service of Śakti,
the retention of semen is achieved through the internal placement (antarnyāsa) and, beyond that, through the placements of the bindu.
As long as the power remains moistened, so long is enjoyment known;
the meditation on the deity is said to be on the left or the right path.

Bow down to the Mistress of Colors (Varṇeśvarī), who holds a rosary of beads, a young deer, and a magnificent crest-jewel; who possesses three eyes and is incessantly adorned with sprouts of wisdom; whose head is crowned by the crescent moon, who rests upon a red lotus, and who is bent low by the weight of her breasts.
When the power's desire is fulfilled, one should perform the emission (visarga);
then the bindu falls from that, and thus these two, the bindu and the visarga, arise.
When the two deposits (nyāsau) of the left-hand Kaulika or the Śākta have been performed,
even without the emission-deposit (sarganyāsa), the semen is not lost and remains satisfied.
Then he goes to hell for as long as the moon and sun endure;
even in this world, he shall be without lineage, deprived of Brahmanic luster.
Those who, with the desire for enjoyment or liberation, strive to fall into the left-hand path,
are like those striving to seize a snake's jewel without the use of a mantra.
The nyāsa of the Mātṛkā with the visarga is exactly like the [nyāsa of] the Mātṛkā alone;
the distinction, however, is that the pronunciation of the phonemes should end with the visarga.
One should place those letters beginning with *ḍa*, adorned with the bindu and the visarga, during the stage of maintenance (*sthiti*).
These very same letters previously mentioned are to be generated; now the meditation on the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-dhyāna*) is described.
One should meditate upon the Goddess, who possesses the luster of vermilion, adorned with ornaments, three-eyed, holding a book, a rosary, a deer, and an excellent fruit,
and who stands at one’s side, radiant as gold, with her lotus-like hands.
The book of ghee and the garland of phonemes.
In the arrangement of the Mātṛkā-nyāsa, on the left path of the Kaulikas, one should perform the nyāsa known as Prapañcayoga; that is now described.
In the Śrīprapañca, the Īśvarasaṃhitā, the Kamalākhaṇḍa, the Jala-dhi-khaṇḍa,
as well as in the Girivallabha and Viṣṇuvallabha, she is described as the lotus-bearing one who is intent upon that [Lord].
The daughter of the ocean is on the seat; the pair of fields is the Mother of the World;
the forest is for the two Dwellers in the Lotus; and likewise, Indirā is the hermitage.
One should not seize Amānadī, Padmā, Catvarakā,
Nārāyaṇapriyā, Udbhijjā, Svedajā, Siddhi, and Lakṣmikā.
The egg-born is Mahālakṣmī, and the womb-born is Ājalakṣmikā;
in the place of the vowels there are sixteen pairs, and likewise those born of the consonants.
Āryā, Alavā, Uttruṭi, Mā, Caṇḍikā, and Kalānvitā; Kāṣṭhā, Durgā, Nimi, and the one called Vākhyā; Śiva and Aparṇikā.
Aṃvikā, Ghaṭikā, and Muhūrta joined with Sanī;
then Īśvarī, Prahara, and Śāṃbhavī accompanied by Divasa.
Having first established the one endowed with all auspiciousness (Sarvamaṅgalā),
he should thereafter establish Dākṣāyaṇī along with Vārāhī and Himavatī.
Then one should place the asterism conjoined with Mahāmāyā through yoga;
likewise, the instrument is assigned to Māheśvarī, and the lunar fortnight to Mṛḍānī.
Rudrāṇī is conjoined with the months and associated with all the zodiacal signs;
furthermore, the two supreme goddesses are Kālī and Anayā.
One should place Kātyāyanī together with Vatsara, and Bhavānī together with Gaurīyuga, or else in the places beginning with Pralaya.
Brahmī is endowed with the five elements; Vāṇī is joined with the five subtle essences (tanmātras);
thereafter, Vāgīśvarī is possessed of the five organs of action.
She is the faculty of perception, Sāvitrī, that dark-blue Sarasvatī;
she is Gāyatrī endowed with the qualities, Speech manifest and possessed of the instruments of action.

One should install the pervasive [deity] by means of the Vidyā, [visualizing her] as Śāradā endowed with the states (avasthā), as Bhāratī endowed with the elements (dhātu), and as Priyā endowed with the humors (doṣa).
At the end of the triple-starred root-vidyā, one should then utter the letters of the Mātṛkā in sequence, followed by: "Obeisance to Śrī, whose form is the universe."
Having set aside [the letters] through the *prapañca* and other methods, one should apply the manifestation of the phonemes (*varṇavyakti*).
Thereafter, the *mātṛkānyāsa* is prescribed for the respective locations.

One should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) by uttering "Obeisance" (namaḥ) to the Goddess Āryāvārā, who is by her very nature the root of the triple world and of the entire phenomenal universe.
Thus, the placement of the phenomenal world (prapañca-nyāsa) is completed; it is called the placement of the worlds (bhuvana-nyāsa).
Without the preliminary consecration of the ritual materials (dravyādhivāsa), one should neither meditate nor recite [the mantra].
Those great fools who long for these find suffering at every step;
there is no liquor without the mantra, and no mantra without the liquor.
Since they are mutually contradictory, how can worship be prescribed?
Having understood the resolution of that doubt from the mouth of the Guru, one should perform sacrifice.
Through purification by means of gazing, touching, meditating, mantras, and mudrās,
the substance becomes fit for libation and causes delight to the deity.
Now, regarding the acceptance of the substance, he states the distinction of the qualified person:
A Brāhmaṇa should never worship Śivā with a material substance belonging to a Sāttvika;
by giving liquor, a Brāhmaṇa falls away from his very status as a Brāhmaṇa.
A Brāhmaṇa who performs even a secondary rite [of this kind] would fall into the state of a Cāṇḍāla;
likewise, a Kṣatriya too should never give an image made of flour.
Coconut water, [water from] bell-metal or copper vessels, products of the cow, and likewise honey—
these are gifts for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, but never for a twice-born Brāhmaṇa.
Thus, by the mere act of giving, a Brāhmaṇa may become short-lived;
however, copper, cow-products, honey, and molasses do not cause harm when offered on the third lunar day (triyācya).
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, a copper vessel is taken up during the fire-oblation;
likewise, it must be performed by a Brāhmaṇa, so that his Brāhmaṇahood does not perish.
Furthermore, there are distinctions among substances according to the sequence of the castes:
Brāhmaṇas should be gratified with milk, and those born of the royal lineage with ghee.
The best of Vaiśyas [should offer] honey-wines, while those of the Śūdra caste [should offer] fermented liquors;
wherever the taking of the finest liquor is specifically prescribed.
A Brāhmaṇa should prepare the five products of the cow in a copper vessel,
following the true sequence with the four castes, using milk, clarified butter, honey, and flour-based preparations.
In the Tretā age, the Goddess was worshipped with clarified butter by all castes;
in the Dvāpara age, she was worshipped with honey by all social classes.
In the Kali age, the Goddess is to be worshipped at night with pure liquors alone;
she should always be drunk by Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas during the arrival of the [astrological] *caraṇa*.
If the scent of liquor should ever arise from the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa, it may be due to the activities of Vaiśyas with wealth, or perhaps even by a Śūdra.
Either he, being a follower of the Mīnakaulika path, should be cast out like a Caṇḍāla,
or a Brāhmaṇa established on the Vedic path should not touch liquor.
A Brahmin endowed with the five characteristics is indeed Time itself;
I, Brahmā, and likewise Viṣṇu, are all subject to his command.
If he has reached the left path and is born again as a dog,
yet is endowed with the four characteristics, he should be known as a mediocre Brahmin.
If, by the power of fortune, some Tantric mantra is bestowed upon them by those two,
it bears fruit immediately for him through either his speech or his ritual action.

One who is endowed with these three characteristics possesses both Vedic and Tantric [authority]; through the performance of the prescribed practices alone, he bestows the fruit, whereas the left-hand path (vāmaka) does not.
If both his left and right [eyes] are endowed with the two characteristics, they shall yield equal results; never, according to the Vedic tradition, shall there be a discrepancy.
Endowed with the single characteristic and bestowing all fruits,
a Brahmin may drink wine in the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice and in the Kula tradition.
Except when drinking out of desire, a man must perform penance;
however, it may be drunk by Kaulika Brahmins for the sake of satisfying the deities.
The deities abide in the mouths of the Vāmins and the Kaulikas;
they carry away that fragrance, and such a person is worthy of worship even by Hari himself.
He in whose mouth the deity does not reside is indeed a Cāṇḍāla;
if he should consume honey and meat out of craving, he is a sinner.
O beloved, for those people who drink the family substance (kuladravya) purified by mantra and offered to the Guru and the Deity,
the drinking from the breast occurs once again.
O Goddess, what is the use of much speaking? He who gives Kuladravya according to his ability for the purpose of worship to the Kula-teacher is a knower of Dharma.
In the Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Śākta, Saura, and the systems that show the good path; likewise in the Bauddha, Pāśupata, Sāṃkhya, Mantra, and Kālāmukha [traditions].
O Pārvatī, in the traditions of the six right-hand and left-hand paths, as well as in the Vedic and other systems,
worship performed without vermilion and saffron becomes fruitless.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the conduct of the Kaulikas:
he whose hand trembles at the sight of blood and semen would feel revulsion toward them.
One who perceives impurity in what is pure, and harbors suspicion of sin regarding sexual union, is fallen;
how can such a person worship the Goddess or recite the Caṇḍī mantra?
Now, he states the necessity of the ritual substances.
The goddess Kālikā is not pleased by offerings of wine and meat,
nor even by thousands of jars of honey or hundreds of loads of flesh.
The Goddess would not be satisfied at all without the nectar of the bhaga and liṅga.
Now, he states the results of the *kāmarāśis* in their respective order.
He who drinks liquor becomes liberated while living;
for that mortal who eats meat, whence can there be fear of death?
He who eats fish is Śiva; there is no doubt in this matter.
He who eats the *mudrā* shall become the lord of the *siddhis*.
He who performs *surata* (divine union) is capable of creating the three worlds;
his purpose is threefold: *sāttvika*, as well as *rājasa*.
And there is the *tāmasa* [path]; among these, the first is described as being for those such as Rāma.
Those who understand that path are liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Now he explains the threefold nature of the corpse.
Madirātri is said to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior is that which is produced from grain in one's own house; the middling is that which is produced from grain in another's house.
She who has been purchased by means of a low price—thus she is considered to be of three kinds.
Śiva said:
In a former kalpa, when the great ocean was being churned by the gods and asuras,
the goddess Śyāmā appeared there, bearing a jar of liquor.
The goddess, who deludes even the three worlds, has a fair complexion and wears reddish garments; she possesses a shining green bodice and white upper cloth.
Seeing that, all the Dānavas forcibly defeated the gods through Śukrācārya,
seized her, and drank the liquor from her jar.
Seeing that the gods had fled, the Śaktis who were stationed there offered that auspicious wine to the Mothers of the Devas.
The mothers of the gods may grant even many boons to those men who satisfy them with liquor and accept the remainder out of fearlessness.
They are of such a form, without a doubt, the sole vessel for the enjoyment of power;
they are the celestial Gaṅgā, the ocean of wine, and the goddess Sarasvatī.
Surā, Godāvarī, Revā, and Surī are indeed the supreme state;
those fools who censure Surā are fools in birth after birth.
Those Śaktis and those Dānavas were being praised by the Gandharvas;
their origin has been told, and now I shall describe the drinking of the Goddess.
Starting from the root of the tongue and extending to the heart, that beautiful [channel] is to be known as sixteen finger-breadths in length; its location is the station of the nectar of taste.
O Goddess, endowed with sixteen digits and sixteen finger-breadths in length,
the deities drink the wine which is of the nature of nectar.
The Fire-god drinks the first; the Moon drinks the second;
Viṣṇu drinks the third; and Varuṇa drinks the fourth.
The prince should drink the fifth [cup], the queen the sixth,
Vāsava the seventh, and Gaṇeśvara, along with all the sages, should drink the eighth.
One should drink the ninth with the King of Dharma, and the tenth with the Maruts;
O Dear One, one should drink the eleventh in the station of Brahmā’s sons.
The twelfth belongs to Kaumāra, and the thirteenth to Vaināyakya.
On the fourteenth day, [one should worship] Paśupati.
Having drunk these fifteen [verses] with ten [lines each], one should not reveal them;
they were not drunk by humans, O blessed lady, but were drunk by the gods who have come into existence.
And having drunk what was thus declared, O blessed lady, now hear concerning the deities:
that which is the essence is the goddess Umā, and that which is the wine is Maheśvara.
That which is color is Brahmā himself; that which is fragrance is Janārdana;
that which is taste is indeed Soma; and that which is motion is Pavana himself.
O Mistress of the Mind, she who is endowed with both primordial wisdom (jñāna) and discerning consciousness (vijñāna) [is] liquor.
Now, he describes the method of preparation:
Twelve *prasthas* of water and half a *prastha* of rice are prescribed;
the sprouts should be of that same measure as the rice.
Having placed it for two days in a place free from cold and other such elements,
one should afterwards mount it on a fire and cook it until it resembles charcoal.
One should throw into it a *prastha* of *daṇḍula* stalks of that same measure;
having let it sit for two more days, one should prepare it in this very manner once again.
Taking half of that [flour] and mixing it with rice, one should divide it into three parts;
that rice-mixture is known as *surā*.
This alone shall be the Soma that bestows the fruit of the Soma sacrifice;
the yoga of the dūtī-yāga is known as the drinking of the Soma.
That goal which is attained by the Kaulikas through the Soma sacrifice is achieved by non-dualists (vāmīs) through this [practice] without hardship or even without wine.
Thus, that which arises from barley flour is known as the god Soma;
and that which is produced through the combination of rice grains is called Śaktisoma.
Wheat that has been steamed and ground, mixed with equal parts of unrefined flour,
fermented for twelve days, and matured in a vessel of Varuṇī liquor.
That liquor is known as Sūrya; it is the constant nourisher of the Yoginīs. If that is drunk at the conclusion of the worship, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
This very leaf, prepared in three ways along with an abundance of wine, becomes fire;
by drinking it, one obtains the fruit of the Agnihotra sacrifice.
When fire is placed within the Vāruṇīyantra seven times,
it becomes equal to the submarine fire (Vaḍavānala) and is the destroyer of great sins.
Ten *prasthas* of jaggery are prescribed, as many of *dhuttūra*, and half that amount of rose-apple bark and *dhātakī* flowers; [the quantity] of coconut is half of that.
The flower should be half of that, and the myrobalan (harītakī) half of that;
the bibhītaka is said to be the same amount, and the three pungents (kaṭutraya) one-fourth part.
At that time, one part of *citraka* and twelve parts of jaggery should be taken;
one should thoroughly rotate it with the hand in both clockwise and counter-clockwise directions.

By reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times at the three junctions of the day every day, purification occurs within twelve days; the Vāruṇī [impurity] should be cooked away by means of the yantra.
This is renowned as Gauḍī, considered to be greatly intoxicating;
it was created by Śiva in the past and drunk by the Bhairavas themselves.
One should add double the amount of water called *makaranda* to the jaggery;
the cooking will not be complete until the sixteenth day; the rest is as previously stated.
This is beloved by all the gods, a marvelous means of subjugation;
it brings even the powers of the gods under control, so what need be said of non-human women?
Harītakī, citraka, marīca, and likewise dhātakī,
as well as madhūkapuṣpa and honey, increased by one part each.
Mixed with eighty pieces of jaggery, the remainder is as previously described;
this captivating substance is the supreme drink for the Yoginīs.
O gods, I shall now describe the substitute for liquor when it is unavailable:
one should take buffalo curd and prepare a liquor fourteen times its quantity. This is known as *vindumadya*.
Likewise, the juice of ripe, crushed plantain fruit should be taken, along with a fourth part of curd; having mixed these together, one should place them in a jar.
Having placed it for forty-eight days in mud thick with lotuses,
one should extract it and thoroughly dry it with the rays of the sun.
When that has become solid, one should likewise fashion an auspicious handle;
when it is filled with water, one should place it in a vessel.
This is praised for Brahmins even more than *surā* itself;
indeed, *surā* is traditionally held to be of three kinds: *gauḍī*, *sādhvī*, and *paiṣṭī*.
This lineage is suitable for Śūdras, as well as for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas;
it is pleasing to the Brahmananda-suras and to the Kaulika Brahmins.
This divine liquor, which increases their wisdom, does not cause them madness;
the liquor made from flour produces all accomplishments, while that made from molasses bestows enjoyment.
Madhvī should be known as the bestower of liberation; Drākṣā is considered the giver of sovereignty;
Ikṣurī-hālā is the sole bestower of knowledge; and Khārjūrī is the destroyer of enemies.

The one born from the palmyra tree is the Mistress of Stambhana; the branch of the Tāpana tree bestows auspiciousness. The one born from the coconut grants prosperity, while the one born from the Nimba tree destroys disease.
That which is born from the Madhūka tree bestows knowledge; that from the Vaileya destroys sin;
it is blissful, appetizing, fragrant, and captivating to the mind.
That supreme liquor is the deity that brings delight to the gods;
Brahmā resides in its moisture, Viṣṇu in its fragrance, and Rudra in its sound.
The Supreme Self resides in that bliss; therefore, O beloved, this should be served.
Having first seen and bowed down to the digit of Vāruṇī who possesses that form, [one should proceed].
The goddess worshipped by Varuṇa is renowned as Vāruṇī;
because the gods drink her constantly, she is remembered by the name Surā.
This wine is proclaimed as being eternally honored by Madana;
yet, in the ultimate sense, she is proclaimed as the Supreme Power (Parā-Śakti) who has arisen.
Just as nectar is, so is wine declared when consumed at the proper time;
born together with nectar, wine acts as nectar in its appropriate place.
Even though it arises together with poison, through that [association], the liquor becomes like poison.
Now he states what is prohibited:
Offerings made with substances that are spoiled, stale, leftover, foul-smelling, or devoid of fragrance,
or those offered from another's vessel, shall be fruitless.
One should not give the substance contained in one's own vessel nor the *hetu* to Bhairava;
for it has been ordained by the Śaṅkaras that if these are given, there will be a loss of spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*).
The propitiation of the goddesses with substances that are most delicious, intoxicating with joy, resembling nectar, and captivating to the mind shall become fruitful.
Meat is said to be of three kinds: that of aquatic creatures, that of sky-dwellers, and that of land-dwellers.
Aquatic creatures include tortoises and the like; sky-dwellers include chickens and the like.
Those that move on land are deer and the like; there are eight varieties of them, originating from the cow, man, elephant, horse, buffalo, boar, goat, and deer.
The eightfold great meat is said to cause delight to the deities;
rabbit meat is said to be a hundred times more effective, and that of the iguana is four times that.
The meat of peacocks is especially beneficial for them; likewise, the merit derived from the meat of tortoises, buffaloes, and rhinoceroses accrues both in this world and in the next.
O Lord, the deer is more meritorious than that;
the ram is even greater than that; the goat is twice as [meritorious] as the ram, and the boar is four times as [meritorious] as the goat.
An ox is eight times [the value] of a hare; an elephant is twice that of an ox;
a horse is six times that of an elephant; and a dog is greater than a horse.
Onion is specifically equal to Rajas;
likewise, fish is said to be of three kinds: superior, inferior, and middling.
O Goddess, the three kinds of fish—śāla, pāṭhīna, and rohita—are excellent; likewise, the prācīnashāka, when free of thorns, seasoned with oil, and prepared with savory ingredients, is supreme.
That which brings pleasure to the Goddess is declared to be the middling;
all those minor ones are the lowest, O most excellent of gurus.
It is made of rice, circular in shape, auspicious and resembling the orb of the moon;
it is beautiful, ripe, captivating, and filled with sugar and other ingredients.
At the time of worship for the goddesses,
it is proclaimed that there should be two portions of rice along with methi, asafoetida, and cumin.
And salt, having been thoroughly crushed with wine as appropriate,
is made into a ball and wrapped with betel leaves.
That which is cooked in a water-machine is called the Śakti-mudrā;
it is the Kāla-khaṇḍa of the goat, cooked by means of the Vādya-yantra.
A mixture of black gram, pigeon pea,
and lentils, combined with equal parts of powdered *vaṭaka* and joined with *hiṅgu* and other spices.
Fritters cooked in pungent oil constitute another type of mudrikā;
indeed, for all Śūdras, this applies to both water and land-based food.
Then, one may take *surā*, *madya*, or *āsava*, or something other than those;
one should thoroughly mix these with wheat flour and meat that has been cooked.
Having kept it in water for three days until it becomes sour,
one should mix in small pieces of cooked fish.
Having placed that [substance] in the center of the flatbread and having cooked the bread,
this indeed bestows supreme satisfaction upon the powers of the Paramamudrās.
Or rather, at the very moment of sexual union, one should maintain this understanding:
the *liṅga* is Śiva, the *bhaga* is Śakti, and the water from the *gaṅgā* is considered the water of the vulva.
By cultivating this meditation, one who engages in sexual union with a woman is liberated;
otherwise, by engaging in sexual union with a woman, one is cooked in hell.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) produced from the union of a Saturday is supreme and bestows prosperity;
the globular vessel (gola) produced from the union of a Sunday is pure and grants spiritual accomplishments.

O Goddess, one who deprives the lineage-sustaining substances of their essence renders mantra-recitation, worship, and likewise religious observances fruitless, just like an oblation poured into ashes.
Now, he states the secondary alternative for these [options] in the absence of the primary one.
One should not pour coconut water or honey into a vessel of bronze or copper;
likewise, cow's milk placed in a copper vessel is equal to liquor, with the exception of clarified butter.
Buttermilk, milk, molasses, honey, curd, clarified butter, sesame seeds, sugar, oil, and a cat’s tail— these are recorded as the ten types of substances.
Or alternatively:
In the absence of the substance, however, one should satisfy [the ancestors] by dissolving a *vaṭaka* (ball of food) in water,
or with buttermilk mixed with jaggery, or with a vessel of honey.
Or else, one may perform it with Sauvīra; one must not let this ritual action be omitted.
Just like a medicinal bolus.
One should prepare a meatball (*vaṭaka*) well-mixed with wine, meat, *vijayā*, and the eight fragrant substances (*aṣṭagandha*), and set it aside for the purpose of libation (*tarpaṇa*).
O Great Goddess, salt, fresh ginger, oil-cake, onion, the five types of meat,
and garlic are recorded as substitutes for meat.
In the absence of fish, however, one may use areca nut, betel leaf, or whatever constitutes meat;
in the absence of the ritual hand-gesture (mudrā), one may use rice or roasted grains, but not salt and the like.
On the left forearm, the best of practitioners should draw a triangle with red sandalwood paste;
in its center, he should indeed inscribe the seed-syllable of Śakti.
There, one should worship his beloved Pārvatī with this mantra,
either one hundred and eight times, or half of that, or half of that again.
In the triangle, the practitioner should recite the mantra with the power known as Gāyatrī;
within that power, he should perform [the rite] with power, and he must not allow any omission of the ritual action.
If there should be a Brahmin present who is devoted to the worship of his lineage,
then he should perform the rite arising from the essence of the lineage according to this procedure.
O Goddess, within the Aparāpuṣpagarbha there is a captivating family abode;
in the Hayāri flower, Sadāśiva himself is ever present.
Having meditated upon that very center, and having placed sandalwood or a red flower in the middle of the flower, one should meditate upon oneself as being of the nature of the Kula.
One should unite that Śiva with Śakti, contemplating their oneness with the intellect;
having reflected for a moment right there, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
Having recited that very substance known as *kuṇḍa*, which is most difficult to obtain;
or else:
O beautiful one, listen to how one should perform the bath in the absence of substances produced from a cow in the vessel,
for the sake of pleasing the deity.
Having quickly and with effort taken a flower from whichever tree [is chosen],
one should then grasp two of them between the hands while focusing the mind upon them.
In that case, a person should duly perform the fifth [rite] for both;
then, having rubbed red sandalwood [with water], he should cast it into the water.
One should perform the supreme bathing of the deity with that water;
one obtains the desired fruit—this is the truth, the truth, O fair-faced one.
In the absence of Svayambhū flowers, one should scatter red sandalwood;
O Dear One, in the absence of the five "M" substances, one should employ the five "M" substitutes.
O Goddess, in the absence of the fifth [element], one should perform the fifth mentally.
Now, he states the letter *ma* regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Having gone repeatedly from the mūlādhāra up to the brahmarandhra,
the awakening of the face [of the deity] occurs through the mudrā of the consciousness-moon-kuṇḍalinī energy.
One should become intent on drinking the nectar flowing from the lotus of the sky;
this is declared to be the drinking of honey, while others are merely drinkers of wine.
Having destroyed both merit and demerit with the sword of knowledge, the knower of yoga leads the mind to dissolution in the Supreme; he is called a "consumer of the leaves" (palāśī).
One who restrains the group of one's own senses with the mind and yokes them to the Self is called a "fish-eater"; all others are said to have the livelihood of fishermen.
The power of one whose fame is unawakened becomes awakened for the Kaulika;
he who serves that power shall be a true servant of Śakti.
Thus, I have declared the secret reality of the five mudrās;
he who, having correctly understood this from the mouth of the Guru, practices them, is fully liberated.
Now, he states the necessity of performing these consecrations (saṃskāras).
The unrefined daughter, having drunk [of this], brings about quarrels, disease, and suffering;
she is the destroyer of longevity, prosperity, fame, good fortune, dharma, and learning.
Therefore, having consecrated it according to the rules with family substances, one should then worship it;
well-consecrated liquor removes disease, suffering, and misfortune.
It increases longevity, prosperity, fame, good fortune, dharma, and knowledge;
otherwise, both the giver and the consumer go to hell—of this there is no doubt.
Just as wine that has the color of fire destroys great sins,
so too that mantra, when purified, is a divine fire that bestows heaven and liberation.
The gods, having been consecrated by the sage Dattātreya, by the high-souled Śukra,
and by the wise Balabhadra, drank the liquor.
When the cause is accompanied by ritual action (saṃskāra) and offered, the deities are pleased;
indeed, by the mere recollection of the mantras, there is the destruction of great sins.
From that [Sanskrit], one obtains longevity, prosperity, beauty, good fortune, and knowledge;
through the [proper] performance of the rite, the eightfold sovereign powers and the ability to travel through the air are attained, whereas from its neglect, there is a fall.
O beloved, for those people who drink the kula-substance joined with mantras and offered to the Guru and the Deity, not even a trace of sin exists.
Now, he describes their consecration in sequence.
In that regard, first is the establishment of the lineage, as follows:
O Maheśānī, on the left side, having drawn two [lines] within a square mandala, one should then draw the Brahma-aperture (brahmaraṃdhra) in between them.
Having measured it with a cord and encircled it with a square,
one should sprinkle it with *arghya* water and place the yantra there.
There, one should worship the circle of fire, which is pervaded by ten digits (kalās).
Now, he states the etymology and the definition of the *kalaśa*.
Since this was fashioned by the gods through Viśvakarman, having taken a portion from each of them, it is therefore called a *kalaśa*.
The measurement of the pitchers is fifty finger-breadths in width and twelve finger-breadths in height;
likewise, the mouth is eight finger-breadths.
The practitioner, placing upon a base a vessel made of gold,
silver, bell-metal, or even clay, which is flawless and beautiful;
A golden vessel is said to bestow enjoyment, while a silver one is traditionally held to grant liberation;
a bell-metal vessel brings about peace, and an earthen one shall provide nourishment.
Brahmā resides at the base of the jar, Keśava within the middle of the jar,
Nīlakaṇṭha at the neck of the jar, and the goddess Śakti at the top of the jar.
In the installation of the jar, there is no need for the ritual action of the deities;
for Śiva is everything that has been described, possessing every form, and consisting of all the gods.
Behold Ānandabhairava incessantly within the center of the jar;
he is said to be the very nature of light, a jewel consisting of the wish-fulfilling creeper.
The tongue consists of the essence of nectar, overflowing with the flow of immortality.
The announcement to the deities.
O Goddess of the gods, he himself performs it; having personally brought a full jar, by the mere act of going to his house, Sarasvatī speaks like a mute.
One who possesses a hundred streams [of knowledge] and is uplifted by hearing the scriptures—
this is declared to be the "Success of the Jar" (ghaṭasiddhi), which consists of all the scriptures.
Where Pārvatī is present, two types of arghya are taught: the general (sāmānya) and the special (viśeṣa);
because it takes the form of the eyes, the vital breaths, and so forth, the water-pot (ghaṭa) is therefore indispensable.
O Goddess of the gods, just as a triangle becomes devoid [of its essence] without the *bindu*,
so too, O Goddess, worship everywhere is rendered void without the *ghaṭa*.
O Sovereign of the Gods, one should thoroughly wash the pitcher with the Astra-mantra and then place the pitcher,
which is smeared with abundant sandalwood paste, upon the base for the water-pot.
Wrapped in a red cloth and adorned with a red garland,
one should place there a water-pot decorated with gold and other precious materials.
The practitioner of mantra should worship the solar disc here, joined with twelve digits,
and should complete the rite with the pure root mantra as the cause.
One should worship here the lunar disc, which is completely pervaded by sixteen digits.
Now, the seed-syllables of the kalās are stated elsewhere:
In the mandala and the vase, the mantra-practitioner should worship the threefold image of the Goddess— consisting of the fire, sun, and moon mandalas— with the three syllables of the *tāra* (om).
The practitioner should protect it with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), veil it with the armor-mantra (tanutra),
gaze upon it with the root-mantra (mūla-mantra), and sprinkle it with that same mantra.
Having worshipped thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, one should meditate upon [the disciple] as being of the nature of the deity.
Listen further, O Goddess of gods, regarding how this is done in rites such as those of the Kula lineage.
O Goddess, no loss occurs; listen, O beloved, to those mantras:
"The Supreme Brahman alone is eternal, consisting of both the gross and the subtle."
By that [act], I pacify the sin of killing a Brahmin born from my hair;
O you who are born from the solar disc, O you who are born from the abode of Varuṇa!
O Goddess, may she be freed from the curse of Śukra;
for the seed-syllable of the Vedas is the Praṇava, which consists of the bliss of Brahman.
"By that truth, O Goddess, may your sin of Brahman-slaughter be dispelled. Having thus consecrated the auspicious family with these three mantras, [one should proceed].
One should offer the food offering (naivedya) to Kālikā and withdraw it into the belly;
[one should recite the mantra] beginning with the Vedas and ending with Varuṇa, differentiated by the six long vowels.
Salutations to you, O Goddess Sudhā, who were liberated from the curse of Śukra;
one should recite this mantra twelve times for the sake of release from Śukra’s curse.
The young girl, who was of three colors, was delighted by Māyā and Rāmā;
in order to release herself from Śukra’s curse, she again assumed those same colors as her luster.

The mantra of sixteen syllables, encased by the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of that [deity] whose worship is performed, is declared as such; it should be recited one hundred and eight times for the purpose of consecration (*maṃtritā*).
It renders the object of accomplishment free from curses and makes one a sole vessel for both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
it is the Vāruṇa seed-mantra of the Vedas, differentiated by the six long vowels.
Salutations to Sudhādevī, who was liberated from the curse of Brahmā;
one should recite the mantra ten times for the sake of liberation from the curse of Brahmā.
Māyā, Śrī, and Aṅkuśa, combined with the six long vowels and differentiated by the vowels; O you who have the form of the god Kṛṣṇa, liberate me from that supreme sin.
Having uttered "amṛtam" followed by the pair [of seed-syllables] and then the wife of Vahni (svāhā),
the practitioner, by means of this mantra, shall release [the deity] from the curse of Kṛṣṇa.
Pavamāna is supreme bliss; Pavamāna is supreme essence;
Pavamāna is supreme knowledge—with that, I bathe you.
Afterwards, one should recite these verses: "O lamp of the deceased soul!
O embodiment of the nectar of the Self, whose body is the unbroken, singular bliss of rasa!"
She is the sovereign, whose form is the manifestation of the treasure-store of the Self;
she is of the nature of nectar, established in Akula, and is the supreme one who brings about purity and the knowledge of consciousness within the form of that nectar.
Place the state of immortality within this;
O you whose form is moist, having made the hand of that one whose form is such, become one whose very nature is this.
Having become so, perform a vibration even in the form of the deceased;
or else, having uttered the root mantra, [perform it] by way of the base of the *suṣumṇā*.
Having caused Kuṇḍalinī to drink [the offering], this is the purification of the substance;
furthermore, by this very procedure, one should perform the purification of the hero (vīra).
The meditation on Bhairava and Bhairavī in the midst of the substances.
Resembling ten million suns and as cool as ten million moons,
the god has eighteen arms, five faces, and three eyes.
He stands in the midst of the ocean of nectar, seated upon the lotus of Brahman;
he is mounted upon the bull, blue-throated, and adorned with all ornaments.
The god who holds a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, who sounds a bell and a ḍamaru drum,
who bears a noose and a goad, and who carries a mace and a pestle.
[He holds] a sword, a shield, a paṭṭiśa, a mallet, a trident, and a spear;
[he holds] a variegated shield and a severed head, with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The best of practitioners should meditate upon Lohita, the Lord of the Gods;
having thus visualized him, he should offer three handfuls of flowers with his own mantra.
Then one should meditate upon Ānandabhairavī.
On his lap [he saw] the goddess Surā, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons,
white as snow, kunda flowers, and the moon, five-faced, and three-eyed.
Endowed with eighteen arms, intent upon bestowing all bliss,
smiling, large-eyed, and facing the God of gods.
Alternatively, one should remember the Lord of the gods of gods, Ardhanārīśvara;
having meditated thus, the best of practitioners should worship him with his own mantra.
Śiva and Candra, ending with Mātṛkā; likewise Kṣa, Ma, La, and Vahni;
then Vāyu adorned with the left ear [the letter U] and followed by the Bindu.
Having uttered that seed-syllable, as well as Nandabhairava ending in "ṅ",
one should write the seed-syllable of the crest (śikhā) joined with the weapon (astra), preceded by the previous seed-syllable.
One should first perform the *caṃdrahitvā* [mantra] and join it with the left eye (*vāmākṣi*) and the ear;
then, for the goddess Surādevī, one should utter *vauṣaṭ*, [and finally] *iyam ānandabhairavī*.
With this pair of mantras, preceded by meditation, one should worship in the sacrificial fire;
one should offer oblations combined with black gram, rice, and so forth, joined with the *vahnimāyā* [syllable].
At the end of Paramasvāminī is Paramākāśa and Śūnyā;
at the end of Vāhinī and Candrapadā is Sūryāgnibhakṣiṇī.
One should recite the mantra ten times: "O Bowl, enter, enter, svāhā.
At the end [of the mantra], one should add: "Vāṅ-māyā-kamalā, we meditate upon Ānandeśvarī."
The wise one should mutter the Gāyatrī ten times: "We meditate upon Surādevī," "That is Nārīśvarī," and "May she inspire us."
Then, O Dear One, one should visualize the substance as nectar,
red-hued, arranged in three rows starting with 'A', 'Ka', and so forth, adorned with the three syllables of Hara (HŪṂ).
During the union of Śiva and Śakti in the previously mentioned Yonimudrā,
one should contemplate the substance as nectar and recite the Amṛtā mantra eight times.
The mantra for Amṛtā.
Having uttered "aiṃ klīṃ hrauṃ ju saḥ," one should then recite the words: "O Amṛte, O Amṛtodbhave, O Amṛteśvarī, O Amṛtavarṣaṇī."
"Amṛtaṃ prāvaya yugaṃ svāhā"—this is for the purification of the substance;
it is called Amṛteśī-mantra, consisting of thirty-five syllables.
The illuminating mantra is as follows:
The seed-syllable of speech (vāgbhava), the pair of seeds, Vāgvādinī, the seed-syllable of speech, *klīṃ*,
*klinne kledini kledaya mahākṣobhaya*— thus it is said.
The pair "kuru," the seed-syllable of desire (KĀM), "sau" for liberation, and the pair "kuru" again;
[this is] the Prāsāda mantra, the Parā-Prāsāda, consisting of thirty-seven syllables.
The Manu known as Dīpinī has been declared; now the purification of substances is prescribed.
Now follows the purification by another method.
In the context of the continuation [of the ritual], one should fill the jar with the causal substance;
there, having first drawn the yantra, whatever originates from the Kula [should be placed].
Having meditated upon one's chosen deity there, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
then, having visualized the *dhenu* and *yoni* [mudrās], one should contemplate that which has issued forth.
Upon seeing the corpse brought forth, the hosts of Yoginīs indeed dance;
all the Bhairavas dance, and the hosts of Bhairavīs dance as well.
Whatever family [of deities] has arisen, one should worship them in their respective yantras;
having meditated thus, the best of practitioners should recite the two vidyās.
At the end of the pair "Māyā" and "Lakṣmī," [one says] "namo bhagavati";
at the end of the form of Maheśvarī, [one says] "sarve paśujana."
Perform the dismissal of Manas and Cakṣus, as well as the pair Ṭha and Dva;
likewise, perform the dismissal of Anyatiraskariṇī, Lajjā, and Kāmeśvarī thereafter.
Then, "vāṇīglau tiraskaraṇaṃ sakalajana," and likewise "vāgvādinīti sakala paśuvratajana."
The mantra for the head consists of *manaścakṣuḥśrotrajihvāghrāṇokṣitiraskaraṇam*, followed by two *kuru*s, two *ṭha*s with the *visarga*.
One should recite one's own root mantra and the Varuṇa mantra seven times over that;
by this procedure, one should perform the purification of the ritual substances.
Now follows the purification of meat.
One should employ the mantra "pretaviṣṇu" for the purification of the vessel;
one should perform the purification of the fish with the mantra of Tryambaka.
With the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ" and likewise with "tad viprāso vipanyavaḥ," the practitioner of mantras should purify the mudrā, which causes delight to the deity.
The practitioner should employ the mantra "Viṣṇur yonim" and likewise "garbhaṃ dhehi" for the purification of those born from a *kuṇḍa* or a *golaka*.
Thereafter, one should perform the purification of the flesh; by means of that, one shall attain accomplishment.
Oṃ! By that very heroic power, Viṣṇu is praised; like a formidable wild beast, he roams the mountains, destroying obstacles.
In whose three strides across his broad [thighs], all the worlds become purified.
With this mantra, the practitioner of mantras should purify the meat in three ways.
Now, the purification of fish.
Oṃ. We worship the Three-Eyed One, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity;
may He release us from death, even as a cucumber from its stalk, for the sake of immortality.
The practitioner should perform the purification of the fish three times with this very mantra.
Now, the purification of the meat.
Oṃ. The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu, like an eye stretched across the sky. The learned, seekers of the divine, being ever-watchful, kindle it together.
That which is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
The purification of the mudrās should be performed three times with this mantra.
Now follows the purification of the family substances.
The mantra of Manu is prescribed for the purification of self-arisen flowers and other such items.
Oṃ! May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms.
May Prajāpati pour [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you.
O Sinīvālī, bestow an embryo; O Sarasvatī, bestow an embryo.
"O Aśvinī devas, you who wear lotus-garlands, bestow the embryo!
Having extracted the *tāra* (oṃ), the *kūrca* weapon (*huṃ*), and the three syllables beginning with *śiva* (*śrīṃ*) joined with the *bindu*.
O beloved of amorous play, [the mantra consists of] the wife of fire (svāhā), ramā (śrīṃ), and māyā (hrīṃ) as the seed-syllable;
then the om, māyā (hrīṃ), ramā (śrīṃ), and the weapon (phaṭ), followed by the wife of fire (svāhā) and the four-faced one (caturmukha).
Then, [the mantra] for Mṛtodbhavā is "Amṛtavarṣiṇī," and following that,
O Dear Goddess, the pair of words "padaṃ yuktaṃ śāpamocaya" [is added].
One should perform the purification of semen (śukra-śuddhi) with the mantra ending in the fire-born wife (svāhā), reciting "amṛtam ca" for the couple and "amṛtam kuru yugmakam" for the pair.
glūṃ mlūṃ plūṃ nlūṃ klūṃ svāhā | oṃ, O Immortal One, O Source of Immortality!
O showerer of nectar, cause the nectar to be heard, cause it to be heard, svāhā!
Or else, the practitioner should effect the purification of the flower by means of the threefold repetition.
Thus is the purification of the vajra-flower.
For the purification of all [the elements], one should recite the mantra seven times over the root;
by this very procedure, one should perform the fifth purification.
Having fully worshipped the Supreme Deity, one shall accomplish everything that is otherwise unattainable.
Now follows the placing of the vessels.
One should place all the vessels between the *śrīpātra* and the *ghaṭa*;
the vessel of the venerable Guru (*śrīguru-pātra*) is at the *ghaṭa*, and the vessel of enjoyment (*bhoga-pātra*) is near it.
At the end of that is the vessel of Śakti, and near it is the vessel of the Yogins;
at the end of that is the vessel of Vīra, and near it is the vessel of Bali.
They know that the water for the feet (pādya), the water for sipping (ācamanīya), and the water of honor (argha) as the ninth;
nine vessels are considered superior, while seven vessels are middling.
Some experts in mantras say that there are five vessels for the central [deity],
three inferior vessels, and likewise a pair of vessels.
One should not use a single vessel even if it is the Lord of the Family himself;
the mantras turn away and the beautiful goddess becomes angry.
In this world there is poverty, and after death one goes to hell;
such is the rule regarding the three vessels concerning the vessels used for the enjoyment of the venerable Guru.
The vessel for worship and the vessel for *bali*—this is the procedure for five vessels. The vessel for power (*śakti*) and the vessel for the hero (*vīra*)—this is the procedure for seven vessels.
The ritual procedure involves bringing water for the feet and placing it in nine vessels;
this is to be known as the vessel of worship, and one should perform the worship of the Yoginīs with it.
One should cause the water for the feet (pādya) and the water for sipping (ācamanīya) to be offered from the vessel for the sacrificial oblation (balipātra);
and all items beginning with the water for the feet should be caused to be offered from the vessel of enjoyment (bhogapātra).
O Great Goddess, listen attentively to the determination regarding the two vessels:
the vessel of enjoyment (bhogapātra), the vessel of power (śaktipātra), the vessel of the hero (vīrapātra), and that of the Yoginī.
One should prepare the vessel for the Guru and the vessel for the Vali offering using the Śrīpātra;
O Maheśvarī, the general arghya and the Śrīpātra are one and the same.
O Goddess of gods, the sprinkling of the ritual substances should be performed with the general *arghya*;
worship should be conducted with the *śrīpātra*, and Śiva is informed of everything.
In the case of the general *arghya* and the door *arghya*, there is indeed a distinction;
however, the general *arghya* consists of the common [water] or even just a single *śrīpātra*.
Nevertheless, O Goddess of the gods, if a jar-vessel is indispensable,
or if it is a skull-cup, O Mistress of the gods, one should employ that single vessel.
Elsewhere there is the state of being a single vessel; in the skull-cup (kapāla) there is the state of being all vessels.
O Goddess of the Gods, in the vessel that is the skull-cup and the skull-bowl, the accomplishment of the Kāpālika exists.

Whatever desires one may wish for— the accomplishments of the pill and the collyrium, the perfected substance, the power of moving at will, and the art consisting of the fulfillment of every heart's desire— [all these are attained].
Let it be seen that desire, enjoyments,
and the act of polishing anew are all contained within the wish-fulfilling gem, which is considered to be Time itself, and everything else resides in the worthy recipient.

In the Kāpālinī [tradition], there is the attainment of the fourth state (turyasiddhi), which is the domain of the skull-attainment (kapālasiddhi). Having brought together a single vessel, it is divided into three parts.
Now, [the author] states the definition of pride (māna).
It should be four finger-breadths in height and twelve finger-breadths in length;
it should be eight finger-breadths wide so that it holds one droṇa of water.

Likewise, O Maheśānī, the vessel for the full initiation (pūrṇadīkṣā) and for the offering of water to the Sun (sūryārghya) and so forth has been proclaimed; the special offering (viśeṣārghya) of the mental [worship] has also been proclaimed.
It should be six finger-breadths wide and shaped like a supine person;
or else, O Goddess of the gods, the vessel may be made circular.
The vessel may be in the shape of an *aśvattha* leaf, or indeed in the shape of a *kuta*,
or it may be a triangular vessel provided with three *triyonis*.
In the center, there is a vessel joined with a *bindu* and provided with the banner-sign (*dhvajacihna*);
or else it has the form of a vulva (*bhaga*), with the banner, the *bindu*, and the filaments (*kesara*).
Having thus brought forth the vessel, one should worship Mahācīneśvarī.
Now he speaks of the bowl.
The materials [for the vessel] are coconut, gold, copper, śakti, stone,
conch-shell, fine wood, tortoise-shell, skull-born, and earthen.
The superior, middling, and inferior [qualities] have been proclaimed for the Brahmins and the other castes;
one should avoid [a bamboo that is] too thick or too thin, or one that is broken.
One should not have a vessel made of metals such as copper, bell-metal, and the like;
all success is attained through gold, and effort bears fruit through a palm-leaf vessel.

Peace is attained from a stone slab; a pillar made of clay brings subjugation and other powers; knowledge is gained from one made of coconut shell; and that which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation is found in one made of tortoise-shell.
The skull-cup made from a sacred tree (puṇyavṛkṣa) destroys sins and brings about the end of death;
through a human skull (kapāla), one attains the perfection of a hero (vīrasaṃsiddhi); and through a bottle-gourd (alābu), the perfections of yoga (yogasiddhi).
For Śiva, [the rosary] may be made of bell-metal or silver; for Viṣṇu, it is the conch-shell;
on the Vāmamārga path, it is the great conch (mahāśaṅkha); and for the Lord of Planets (the Sun), it is crystal.
In the case of Viśvāmitra, however, the skull is the most excellent of all vessels;
it [absolves] sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, as well as treachery against a friend.
Upon seeing an unworthy recipient, even a coconut vessel is entirely destroyed;
likewise, the gift of ten million maidens and hundreds of gold pieces [perish].
O Maheśānī, whoever offers this during an eclipse of the sun,
the fruit thereof is multiplied ten millionfold by means of a coconut vessel for the arghya offering.
If that bowl is not available, one should worship with another bowl.
This also is another [instance] other than the great conch.
And so it is said:
A vessel made of a great conch shell should be known as the most excellent of all;
that called coconut, O Goddess, should be known as excellent-middle.
O lady of beautiful hips, the red vessel should be known as belonging to the highest category.
Now, he speaks of the taking of the great bowl.
At the beginning, the procedure for the *muṇḍa* was taught; that is now being told, so listen.
This rule applies to all *muṇḍas*; listen to [the rules] regarding those pierced by a trident and so forth.
Young, beautiful, and heroic, standing face-to-face on the battlefield,
devoid of any other refuge, and free from the eight letters beginning with 'ka'.
When [the staff] is pierced by weapons such as a club, or struck down by a trident,
or overcome by outcasts and the like, it swiftly bestows accomplishment.
O Ambikā, whether on a Saturday or a Tuesday, or when death occurs to the body,
or during the Night of Time (Kālarātri), the Night of Heroes (Vīrarātri), or the Night of Delusion (Moharātri);
On the Mahārātri, on the fourteenth and eighth days of both fortnights,
on the fourteenth day of the festival of lights (Dīpotsava), during an eclipse, or at the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti).
Assuming the attire of a hero, with disheveled hair and naked as the directions,
bearing a mark of vermilion and kūrca-ashes on his forehead, he bestows the knowledge of the liquor.
O Goddess, having gone to the site of the stake equipped with all the necessary materials—
betel leaf, vijayā, a sword, vermilion, and likewise vijayā—
O Pārvatī, having prepared the complete collection of materials such as stone, meat, wine, and so forth, and having purified them in the house on dry land, contemplate the causal factors.
O Goddess of the gods, having performed this with effort preceded by the worship of Śivā,
and having worshipped Śivā with diligence, one should then worship Śūra.
O Goddess, one should worship Śūla and then perform the ritual of formal undertaking (samādāna):
"O King Śūla, you who are most fierce and the bringer of joy to all beings!"
"O Goddess Vajraśūla, salutations to you! Grant the success intended by my resolve. Having performed this, one should keep watch over the hero; at its conclusion, there is the worship of the sword.
One should worship that corpse situated upon the stake with offerings of incense and lamps,
as well as betel leaf, cardamom, cloves, and the like, combined with camphor and agallochum.
O Goddess of gods, having worshipped with ritual substances and having carefully worshipped the sword,
[one should know that] Kālī is born from the sword and is the bestower of all accomplishments.
Obeisance to you, the wish-fulfilling jewel of poetry, the sword, and the shaven head;
O hero of heroes, the great hero, the demonstrator of the sixty siddhis.
And being propitiated, quickly become the *Kavikalpalatā* (the Creative Imagination Vine);
having thus prayed with this root mantra, one should perform the cutting [of the obstacles].
He himself should perform the rite of valor and offer the *brahmāṇḍa* oblation;
or, having covered the severed head with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), he should carry it away.
O Goddess of the gods, having brought [the skull] into the house and placed it on a spot measuring half a cubit,
one should first prepare all the ritual materials and then establish the life-force (prāṇa) within the skull.
One should drive stakes made of khadira wood and other such materials into those ten directions;
remaining there, having offered the bali-oblation, one should be devoted to recitation and worship.
O Maheśānī, from the vision of that [reality], there arise the Ghoramantras such as the Pāśupata and others, as well as Jayadurgā and Vīrārdana immediately thereafter.
O Goddess of gods, having first established these and the other thirteen locations upon the ground, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and level the sites.
Having established [the image], remained [there], performed the recitation, and worshipped Maheśvarī in that place,
one should recite two hundred thousand [times] during the course of day and night, O Śivā.
O Śivā, having performed the fire-oblation, the libation, the purification of the Goddess, and the feeding of the twice-born, the severed head becomes accomplished; it becomes a perfected head.
Thus, when the fruit of the *muṇḍa* has been accomplished, the eightfold supernatural powers (*aṣṭasiddhi*) are in one's hand;
with that fully perfected *muṇḍa*, one should fashion the rosary, the vessel, and so forth.
He who acts otherwise does not attain success;
likewise, the rosary, the yantra, and the vessel [are perfected] at the end through the *siddhimuṇḍa*.
Therefore, O Goddess, one who is intent on the practice of the samaya should cause [the ritual] to be performed;
thus kindled, he shall become a wish-fulfilling tree in this world of strife for the sake of attaining siddhi.
If one possesses knowledge of the meaning of all the scriptures, no further deliberation is required here;
[the purification] applies immediately for that which has been made [recently], as does that which has remained for three nights or seven nights.
Listen now to the sequence for the intermediate [rite] lasting twenty-one nights,
which is classified as superior, middling, inferior, and even the lowest of the inferior.
The *muṇḍa* performed immediately is proclaimed as the best;
that which occurs after six nights is proclaimed as the middling *muṇḍa*.
That which has remained for three weeks is proclaimed as the lowest of the low;
however, a head that has been freshly severed is prescribed for all rites.
The muṇḍamālā yantra is proclaimed to be for a period of three nights;
one should prescribe the muṇḍa for a vessel for a period exceeding six nights.
Now follows the characteristics of the great bowl (māhāpātra).
O Goddess of the gods, now hear the characteristics of the *māhāpātra*:
it has the face of a cow, the back of an elephant, and likewise the frontal globes of an elephant.
The back of a tortoise, the hip, and likewise the vessel of power (śaktipātra)—these are known as the khaṇḍapadma; hear now their defining characteristics.
O Goddess, that which has a long shape, a back [that is curved], and a sharp point at the tip is called Gomukha; it is a Kapāla, of this there is no doubt.
Long and elevated in the middle, yet not well-proportioned at the sides,
and likewise broad at the back— such is the shape of your back, resembling that of an elephant.
That skull which is elevated in the middle, circular in shape,
and resembles the back of a tortoise is called "tortoise-back" (kūrmapṛṣṭha).
From the forehead down to the caulaka, where the lines and junctions arise—
if it consists of six sections, they know that to be the vessel of Śakti.
If the back is level and the horn, or even the tip, is likewise elevated,
and the center is also level, it is declared to be a lotus-vessel; of this there is no doubt.

O woman of excellent complexion, those who have a cavity within the crest [of the hair] belong to the four castes beginning with the twice-born, according to whether there is one, two, three, or four [such cavities].
A Brahmin is said to have one opening; a Kṣatriya is traditionally held to have two openings;
a Vaiśya is said to have three openings; and a Śūdra has four openings.
Indeed, those that have holes or belong to other species are merely skull-bones;
one should discard even a flawless one, for it is proclaimed to be a mere skull-bone.
A vessel belonging to any of the four castes that is endowed with the proper characteristics should be accepted;
practitioners should avoid vessels of other origins.
A dark complexion indicates a great disease; with a black complexion, death occurs;
with a red complexion, there is suffering; and with a mixed complexion, some minor affliction.
The crystal belonging to the fire element (āgneya) should be red in color in all respects;
that which is to be grasped by the practitioner bestows the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
That which resembles fresh butter and is glossy in its luster bestows liberation;
indeed, that which is white in color is proclaimed for those seeking release.
A female skull should be circular and have two partitions; it bestows liberation.
Single-partitions are highly praised, though they are indeed rare to find.
Indeed, those possessing two layers and endowed with the proper characteristics should be accepted;
however, a single-piece skull, O Lord, is difficult to obtain even for the gods.
By that very [means], one situated in the hand attains the state of a Vidyādhara;
the two sections and the three sections are proclaimed as leading to worldly enjoyment and liberation.
That bowl which has four sections bestows the four aims of human life;
likewise, those with five, six, and seven sections follow in succession.
O Goddess, that which ends in a hundred fragments is certainly not obtained through mere fortune.
Now, he describes the placement of the vessel for women.
Between the object of proof (sādhya) and the means of proof (sādhaka), there should be thirty-six finger-breadths (aṅgula);
twelve finger-breadths above and likewise twelve finger-breadths below.
The wise one should place it there, situated in the middle of twelve finger-breadths;
for his own sake he should leave aside twelve, and for the sake of the deity he should abandon the twelfth.
One should place the arghya offering there, situated in the center of a twelve-finger span.
Now, he states the definition of the mandalas, preceded by their necessity.
Worship without a maṇḍala is proclaimed to be fruitless;
therefore, having drawn the maṇḍala according to the rules, one should perform worship therein.
That which is of unbroken circular form, established pervading the universe,
and by which the three worlds are adorned— that is the Maṇḍala of Sadāśiva.
The garden (udyāna) should be square, while Kāmarūpa is circular;
Jālandhara is a half-moon, and Pūrṇagiri is considered full.
After worshipping the maṇḍala, one should subsequently place the support in the proper sequence.
Now he states the substances for the *arghya* offering.
By offering wine as an *arghya* oblation, one becomes dear to the *yoginīs*;
O Goddess, by washing the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) with these waters, one becomes a great yogi (*mahāyogī*).
Now follows the purification of the great vessel.

O Goddess, listen now with care to the purification of the vessels; at the very beginning, one should cleanse them with this mantra, "Indro dadātu... and so forth, along with the moon (the *saṃ* syllable).
One should construct a circular subterranean chamber (bhūgṛha) joined with fire using the Dhruva-maṇḍala mantra;
there, one should worship the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) and the Tortoise (kūrma).
Accompanied by the sky (0), fire (3), and power (H), one should praise that [seat] beginning with Dhruva;
by means of this mantra, the knower of mantras should establish the support there.
Immediately after that, one should worship the fire-maṇḍala within this [space],
auspiciously washed by the seed-syllable of Wrath (Krodhabīja) and the seed-syllable of the Weapon (Astrabīja).
The great mantra-practitioner should establish the Great Conch and recite that [mantra];
[he should also recite] the Śikhā-mantra, which is endowed with the three long vowels and joined with Kālī, Brahmā, Rāmā, and Agni.
The long [vowel] Śacīpati (ai), Vāyu (ya), and the heart (hr) near Manmatha (kṣa);
endowed with the three longs, Tāriṇī follows as before.
Śiva, endowed with the three long vowels, is as before from the word "nīla";
then Māyā, the final portion of the arrow (five), Śambhu, conjoined with the moon of the left ear (the letter *u*).
He who possesses all desires, the Night of Time, whose body is long; thereafter, he who is the support of all, who is everything, and who arises from all—by way of sound.
Then, from the position of all the asuras, [he offered] a vessel for the gods, consisting entirely of purity,
red as blood, and white in its destination.
The mantra for Āyadevī is considered to be from *kapālāya* up to *hṛdayam*.
One should worship the Great Conch with these four mantras.

There, the practitioner, perceiving the mandala— which is devoid of essence and filled with fierce poison— to be nectar through his intellect, should fill it with water according to the prescribed rite while reciting the root mantra.
Having cast perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), one should then display the three-part gesture (trikhaṇḍā);
O Goddess, one who delights in nectar should worship the maṇḍala there.
The power of speech, the power of the unmeasured, endowed with the human tone, the root, that third [seed] of Bhairavī, the blazing seed-syllable of Krodha.
With this mantra, the practitioner of mantras should meditate eight times upon each [offering];
having poured nectar according to his capacity, he should display the conch and the *yoni* mudrā.
Everything is exactly as previously described, according to the procedure for the special *arghya* offering;
thus, by the aforementioned method, the skull-bowl is the most excellent vessel.
With this excellent vessel, one should accomplish the desired practice:
the attainment of one's wishes, the power of flight (khecarī), and the entry into another's body.
One may likewise accomplish the fulfillment of desires, divine vision, the Vetāla-mantra, alchemy, and elixirs through this desired means of attainment.
Or the sandals empowered by the seed-syllable of Vāparṇa, the host of Yakṣiṇīs,
the perfection of the sword, the perfection of the spear, or even the noose and the power over people.
O Śivā, the accomplishment of creation, the eight Bhairavas, and Mahākapālinī [are attained];
O Goddess of gods, by means of the skull-offering (kapālārghya), all [powers] are certainly accomplished.
Now follows the ritual for placing the arghya water.
Then the practitioner should place the *arghya* vessel on his left, O beautiful goddess;
and to the right of the *kalaśa*, he should draw a triangle combined with a circle.
Having drawn a hexagon and a square, one should draw within its central portion a radiant full moon and a gandharva.
One should worship the seat (pīṭha), such as the *ojāpūpa* and others, in its four directions;
and in the hexagon, one should worship the limbs (*aṅga*) with their mantras, and the Śakti in the center with the threefold root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
Having worshipped the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) as before, one should likewise worship the triple vessel,
the great conch, the coconut, and the shining golden vessel.

One should place there a vessel made of copper or even one produced from a *śakti*; having worshipped it as before, the practitioner of mantras should fill it with the substances for the water-pot (*kumbha*).
They say the support is of three kinds: having six parts or four parts;
or else, O Goddess, one should make it circular in shape and beautiful to the mind.
It may have the luster of a lotus, or be triangular, or resemble a womb; it may be made of metal or born from living beings.
Without a base, there is a risk of falling, and the deities will certainly not be pleased.

Therefore, O Mistress of the Kula, one should prepare the support according to the rules; having worshipped the Weapon-mantra in the cardinal directions, one should place the conch-vessel. Having washed the conch-vessel with the Root-mantra, one should establish it.
In that same manner, he should extract the letter Kāla (Ka), along with Viṇḍuka (Au) and the arm (U), as well as Śeṣa (Sa).

Having recited "to the one who maintains the mandala," likewise "to the bestower of dharma," and "to the one whose self consists of the ten kalās," one should worship with perfumes and other offerings while uttering "namas."
Having washed the conch with a blade and placed it there, one should worship it;
its height should be a span (prādeśa) and its width four finger-breadths (catur-aṅgula).
Having declared "This is the arghya vessel," one should say with the mantra, "I place [it]," and then say,
"To the twelve [suns], not to the solar orb."
Having uttered the *pada* for the self of the *kalās*, the heart-mantra (*hṛnmanu*) for the *arghapātra*,
and having worshipped the conch with this [mantra], one should worship the *kalās* of the Sun.
Having worshipped as before, the practitioner should fill the conch with the ritual substance;
then, having touched the vessel of worship, he should worship it with the *hetu-mudrā*.
One should offer the nectar of immortality, which fills the great vessel, equal in measure to all the essences produced from the fragments of the cosmic egg.
Having worshipped the brilliantly radiant syllables of the root mantra in reverse order as before, one should draw a circle there and within it a hexagon.
From the beginning of the *akathādi* [mantra] up to the end of the three lines, one should worship the triangle within the circle;
then, with the three root sections, one should worship the triangle.
In the hexagon, one should worship the six limbs and then contemplate the Tīrthamaya;
having meditated upon Ānandabhairava and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship the five jewels and cast in the substances of one's lineage;
therein, one should cast meat, fish, and so forth, in the measure of a *māṣa*.
Having taken the nectar of the family (kulāmṛta), the wise one should pour it into that argha offering;
thereafter, the lunar digits (somakalā) should be worshipped by practitioners of pure intention.
One should perform the remainder as before; this is remembered as the procedure for the *argha* offering.
We shall now describe the swift sacrifice of the *kulāmṛta* during worship.
Bhauvaneśī, Amarāmā, Kāmā, Yoginī, and thereafter Śākinī; these seven seed-syllables (bījas) indeed possess stability in their proper sequence.
The eighth, however, is to be known as the seed-syllable of the Sovereign of the Three Worlds;
it is the first letter of each respective world, surrounded by the vowels.
Going to heaven and the mortal world, as well as to the netherworld (pātāla) and to the nāgas—
this is indeed accomplished by grasping the word *hṛt* with the genitive case-ending (*ṅasi*).
Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Śikhinī,
Svarūpā, Kapilā, Havyavāhā, and Kavyavāhā.
The ten digits (kalās) beginning with Āgneyī and starting with the letter *ā* bestow the ten qualities:
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Sūṣmā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, and Kṣamā.
Suṣumṇā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Vodhinī, Dhāriṇī, Kṣamā,
Kalā, Ādyā, Vasudā, Saudā, and Phaḍantā— these twelve are proclaimed.
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati,
Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Aṅgadā.
O Kulavāpikā, Pūrṇā and Pūrṇāmṛtā are said to be the sixteen digits born from the vowels; they are gentle and bestowers of desires.
Having invoked the holy ford (tīrtha) as before, and having united it there with the tīrtha-mantra,
one should place a flower upon it with the netra-mantra and [place] the crest-lock (śikhā) with this [mantra].

Having displayed the Gālinī mudrā and having consecrated [the offering] with the Dhenu mudrā according to the rule, the practitioner [should consecrate it] with the nectar-seed syllable (sudhā-bīja) to make it nectar.
Having meditated there upon his chosen deity and performed the ritual integration (sakalīkaraṇa),
the practitioner should protect the ten directions with the weapon-mantra (astra) through the assignment of limbs (aṅganyāsa).
Having gazed [at it] with the Netra-mantra and with the mudrā known as Śaṅkha,
one should worship the chosen deity there with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having fully worshipped the six limbs, one should consecrate them with the root mantra;
in rites of sorcery (abhicāra), one should recite [the mantra] in reverse order.
Likewise, one should offer the arghya eight times while concealing it with the form of a fish;
the little finger and the thumb of the two hands should be joined together.
With the index and middle fingers joined and unbent, this mudrā is called Āgālinī; it is moved over the conch.
One should arrange the series of vessels according to the procedure prescribed for the *kalaśa*;
having drawn forth the drop (*bindu*) from the nectar in the conch with flowers and other offerings.
One should place everything into all the bowls and contemplate it all as divine;
having set aside one bowl, one should not perform the libation with those [remaining ones].
Here, first of all, is the propitiation of the deities residing within the body.
With that pure substance, as well as with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains,
and likewise with all the mantras prescribed for the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should thus bathe oneself.
One should first satiate the lineage of the venerable Gurus at the crown of the head and the *pādukā* at the *mūlādhāra*;
[then] one should satiate the Divine Current (*divyaugha*), beginning with Ādinātha Sadāśiva.
Īśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā, together with their wives, become twelve; one should satisfy them by offering bells.
The four beginning with Sanaka, Suvrata adorned with beautiful ornaments, Sanatkumāra, Vyāsa, Vāmadeva, and Sakas; likewise—
One should satisfy Dattātreya, Raivataka, and these twelve Mānavas; furthermore, one should satisfy Nṛsiṃha, Maheśa, and likewise Bhāskara—these six.
One should employ the names Maheṃdra, Mādhava, and Viṣṇu at the end [of the lineage];
likewise, Mahāśiva in the Siddhaugha and Sadāśiva in the Mānavaugha.
Then one should perform the worship of the pedestal, which is supremely auspicious and divine.
These are the common gurus for both the Kaula and Vāma traditions.
At the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), the wise practitioner, using his own mantra and the mudrā known as Tatva,
should satisfy the three lineages (oghatraya) with the substance from the vessel of the Guru.
Having especially gratified his own gurus three times or once,
[he should contemplate her] within the lotus of his own heart, surrounded by a circle of attendants.
The Goddess, the mistress of the Kula, should also satisfy her with the nectar from the vessel;
having taken the pure substance, she should perform the libation with the *tattva-mudrā*.
Having taken up the purification between the thumb and the forefinger on the left side,
the wise practitioner should satisfy the Goddess with the left hand or even with the right.
Then, one should perform the purification of reality (*tattvaśuddhi*).
Oṃ! May Prāṇa, Apāna, Vyāna, Udāna, and Samāna be purified within me; may I become light, stainless, and free from evil—svāhā!
Oṃ! May earth, water, fire, air, and space be purified for me; [Jyoti].
Oṃ, may my primordial nature, ego-sense, intellect, mind, and ears be purified.
Oṃ, may my skin, eyes, ears, tongue, nose, and speech be purified.
Oṃ, may my hands, feet, anus, genitals, and ears be purified.
Oṃ! May my touch, form, taste, smell, and space be purified.
Oṃ, may my wind, fire, water, and earth elements be purified.
Having grasped the seventh *trā* with both hands, [he should do so] again seven times.
The practitioner of mantra should touch all the limbs; this is considered the purification of reality (tattva-śuddhi).
Now follows the offering of the *bali* to the *vaṭuka*s and others.
One must certainly perform the worship of Vaṭuka at the beginning, at the outset of the left [path], and so forth;
on this path, Vaṭuka is the primary deity, established between the gods and the ancestors.
Without him, the gods do not accept [offerings]; therefore, his worship is essential.
If one should worship a deity out of delusion without first honoring Vaṭuka, [the rite is fruitless].
There is no fruit from worshipping him alone, and Vaṭuka becomes angry;
therefore, one should worship Gaṇa with perfumes, flowers, and various kinds of meat.
Through those respective mantras and according to the prescribed rite, one shall obtain the favor of the deities;
[one should worship] in the corners of Īśāna, Vahni, Nairṛtya, and Vāyu, as before.
Then, O Dear One, having prepared the mandalas, one should worship as before;
and for the sake of all prosperity, one should offer the bali-oblation as previously described.
O Maheśānī, beloved of the Yoginīs, one should offer the bali-oblation to Vaṭuka,
Gaṇeśa, and Kṣetrapāla as before.
One should offer the *vaṭuka* offering to the south, the *yoginī* offering to the north,
the *sarvabhūta* offering [to the center], and the *kṣetrapāla* offering to the west.
The offering for Vaṭuka is prescribed with the thumb and ring finger;
one should present the offering for the Yoginīs using the little finger and the thumb.
One should offer the bali to Kṣetrapāla with the thumb and forefinger; then, having uttered "Tāra" three times, one should say "Devīputra" and "Vaṭuka."
"O Lord! O you who are tawny and radiant with a mass of matted hair like Kapila, O three-eyed one whose face is ablaze with fire! [He] should utter this: 'Accept this worship and offering.'"
Seize, seize! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
He is the beholder of forty-six.
Having thus recited the mantra, one should then recite this verse:
"May Vaṭuka, who bestows all accomplishments, be well-pleased by this offering of bali."
May he who is served by spirits and vetālas grant me constant peace.
One should utter the three *tāra*s first, followed by "sarva," and then say "saṃtāni" in sequence.
The Yoginī, the Bhūta, the Bhūtādhipati, and the Ḍākinī.
Śākinī, dweller of the three worlds, accept, accept this worship and offering! HŪM PHAṬ TATHĀ SVĀHĀ.
This mantra consists of fifty-one syllables. Whatever yoginī there may be—whether fierce, gentle, or most terrible—[is addressed by this].
May Khecarī, Bhūcarī, and Vyomacārī always be dear to me.
Whether situated above the cosmic egg and its waters in the expanse of the sky, or upon the earth, or in the partless netherworld (pātāla), or in fire, or in water and wind, or wherever else;
or having taken their place in sacred fields (kṣetra), seats (pīṭha), and secondary seats (upapīṭha)— may the Goddesses always be pleased with us by means of flowers, incense, and other offerings.
But those who follow the method of the Śubhavali are equal to the lords of the gods.
At the end of this, O Maheśānī, one should write the seed-syllable *yāṃ*, then *yoginībhyaḥ svāhā*; at the end of all these syllables, one should write the word *yoginām*.
