Having written the armor (*kavaca*) and the weapon (*astra*), one should write the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*, *svāhā*) again;
then, O Goddess, having bowed with the mantra, one should offer the oblation (*bali*) to the Yoginīs.

Perform three claps of the hands, and likewise say: "Come, come, O son of the Goddess, O young ascetic! To the one who takes away the remnants [of the offering], hūṃ hūṃ phaṃ hūṃ vāṃ—utter these two syllables."
"O Kṣetrapāla, O All! Destroy the obstacles!"—with these two [verses], one should offer this oblation of worship accompanied by all ritual services.
*Gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This mantra of sixty-four syllables is proclaimed as belonging to Kṣetrapāla; it bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
May he, who dwells in the Kṣatra realm and is the servant of the Kṣatrapāla,
being pleased by this offering, grant me protection from all [harm].
With this mantra, one should offer the bali-oblation to the goddess Kṣetrapāla.
Having written the triad gāṃ, gīṃ, and gūṃ, one should utter Gaṇapati ending in the letter ṅa;
after "vara," after "varada," and after "sarva," one should write "jana."
Having joined [the mantra] with *mevaśam* and *balim gṛhṇa dvidhāpadam*,
this mantra, ending with the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*), one should offer the oblation (*bali*) to Gaṇeśa.
Then, having drawn a mandala on the left side, one should encircle it;
there, one should worship the support and the vessel provided with food and water.
Having consulted with one's own retinue, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, one should offer the bali-oblation to all beings three times with the sixteen-syllable mantra.
Then, O Bhuvaneśānī, [utter] the syllable *tāram*, followed by the words *sarvavighnapadebhyaḥ*,
then *kṛdbhyaḥ* and *sarvabhūtebhyaḥ*, the syllable *hūṃ*, and the beloved of fire (*svāhā*).
While reciting [the mantra], one should offer the bali-oblation with the mudrā known as Tatvasaṃjñā;
one should then utter "Tāratrayam" for all beings and for everyone.

The heart-mantra for the five lords of the elements consists of seventeen syllables: "bhūtā ye vividhākārā divyabhaumāntarīkṣagāḥ. These beings are of various forms, dwelling in the heavens, on earth, and in the intermediate space.
Those residing in the netherworld (pātāla) were addressed by means of Śiva-yoga;
Dhruva and others, who are true to their vows, as well as Indra and the other gods, are firmly established [in their positions].
May the spirits with hungry minds be satisfied; accept this bali offering.

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Ritual from the Origin of the Kaula Path up to the Installation of the Śrīpātra and Other Vessels," within the General Daily Worship of the Kaula and Vāma traditions in the *Śrī Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Now he describes the worship.
The place of worship is considered to be threefold, according to the divisions of Paśu, Vīra, and Divya;
that which is secondary, primary, and supreme shall now be described.
For ordinary people (paśus), worship is proclaimed as secondary when performed upon a constructed yantra;
for heroes (vīras), it consists of the installation of the Śakti within the bindu of a drawn yantra.
Having meditated upon her as having the form of one's own chosen deity, she attains preeminence through worship;
moreover, worship within the divine wheel (*divyacakra*) is considered the most excellent among all divine forms of worship.
O Maheśānī, she is eternally gracious within the *jīvacakra*;
indeed, one who possesses the realization of the *jīvacakra* is extremely rare in the Kali age.
Oil might be produced from sand, a barren woman might give birth to a son,
a sky-flower might come into being, and a man might be born without a womb.
In the Kali age, no one who knows the wheel of life will be afraid anywhere;
abandoning his primary station, the foolish man wanders about for alms.
Likewise, having abandoned the individual soul (jīva), it runs and hastens about;
oh, the man who possesses knowledge of the soul becomes equal to Śiva!
Or, having mentally visualized [the deity], one should worship the Great Goddess along with her limbs and her retinue,
after having performed the worship of the pedestal up to that point, upon that very lion-throne.
O Goddess of the Gods, having established the unbroken rice grains with the realization of non-duality, one should worship them;
having performed the worship of the pedestal, one should honor [the deity] with the fivefold offerings.
Having worshipped [the deity] and established her upon the lion-throne, one should worship her within the ocean of nectar.
That single pedestal shall indeed be the supreme pedestal for all of them.
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship the primary seat (pīṭha) within the yantra;
O Śivā, one should establish that yantra upon a lion-throne (siṃhapīṭha), which is the seat itself.
O Goddess of gods, that *pīṭha* there shall be the presiding deity of the livelihood (*vṛtti*);
whether it be called *pīṭha* or *vṛtti*, this is declared to be the doctrine of all.

O Maheśvarī, there upon that seat, one should meditate upon the great yantra, which is the essence of one's chosen deity; or else, O Great Goddess, the yantra should be visualized or drawn within the wheel of life (jīvacakra).
He states the place of worship in the absence of these:
Worship is proclaimed as being of ten kinds: in a *liṅga*, in a *sthaṇḍila* (sacred mound), in a vessel, on a fruit, on a slab, on the head, on a mandala, in an image, on a wall, and in the heart.
Having made the formless appear as having form, people devoted to the ritualistic section [of the Veda] would produce milk from the mouths of cows and elephants, as it were.
Thus, for this reason, O Lord, when an image or similar representation is resplendent, the deity is present there;
this is especially true for worship performed with a face-to-face orientation toward the reflection.
Through the faith of the practitioner, the deity attains presence;
just as the heat inherent in all bodies does not cause itself injury.
Whatever good deed was performed or given should nourish those very same [beings];
thus, if the Supreme Lord resides within all bodies, [He should do so].
O Goddess, without worship, [the deity] does not bestow fruit upon men.
Now, the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjā).
The wise one should worship the seat according to the prescribed rite for the worship of the seat (pīṭhapūjā).
Then one should invoke the Goddess with two mantras and likewise worship her:
"O You who abide within the forest of great lotuses, whose form is the infinite cause!"
O Mother, who acts for the welfare of all beings, come here, O Supreme Goddess!
O Queen of the Gods, who are easily attained through devotion and endowed with all protective coverings.
"Remain steadfast here for as long as I worship you.
Having meditated thus and displayed the mudrās, one should then [worship] with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and so forth.
The conceptualization of forms for Brahman— which is composed of consciousness, immeasurable, devoid of qualities, and bodiless— is for the benefit of spiritual practitioners.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the infusion of limbs) for its vital breaths and its sense organs, one should install and worship the deities; otherwise, it is considered fruitless.
Whatever may be performed deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in tantra—
whatever it may be that is accomplished, it will be deficient in its constituent parts accordingly.
O Śāmbhavī, for those who know the pervasion of the yantra of the Lord in the form of mantra, all their worship and other rites become [sources of] bliss.
One should worship [the Goddess], together with her limbs and her retinue, by means of the sixteen services;
one should perform the worship with each respective name preceded by the *praṇava* and followed by "namaḥ."
Now, in order, the mantras for the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra):
This seat has been offered by me, O you who are worshipped by the best of gods;
please sit upon it while I perform your worship.
O Great Goddess, accept this water for the feet, which removes all suffering;
O Goddess, granter of boons, protect me from this terrible ocean of existence.
O beloved, one should offer water for bathing, clothing, and food offerings, as well as water for sipping (ācamanīyaka);
and that should be offered with the utterance of "svadhā," as should the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
When all else has been completely offered with the word "svāhā" for the *arghya*,
it should be accompanied by *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and *bilva* leaves.
O beloved of Hara, accept this beautiful *arghya* placed in a conch vessel;
[accept] the water together with camphor, nutmeg, cloves, cardamom, and *kakkola*.
"Accept this water for sipping, offered by me with devotion;
and accept the madhuparka, O Great Goddess, prepared by Brahmā."
I have offered this to you; accept it, O Sovereign of the World!
After the presentation of the honey-mixture (madhuparka), there is again the water for sipping (ācamanīya).
At the conclusion of the consumption [of the food], that which remains as his leavings (ucchiṣṭa) should be given;
this water is cool, fragrant, excellent, and indeed moderate.
"O Queen of the Gods, bathe with this which has been offered by me with devotion—
a cloth made of various colors such as silk thread and the like."
O Sovereign of the Thirty-three Gods, accept these garments— both white and red—
which beautify the body, are pure, and are dyed with color-fast dyes.
The nurse should respectfully offer the garment that has been presented;
after the putting on of the garment, there is again water for sipping (ācamanīya).
It should be given with a spirit of devotion, as it is prescribed by the Smṛtis, like [the gift] to a human being;
it is endowed with divine jewels and possesses a radiance equal to fire and the sun.
The Queen of the Gods adorned her own limbs with ornaments;
however, that which was born of the serpent was the cause of a splendor exceeding even her forehead.
O you who possess excessive passion, please accept this sindūra produced from mercury;
it is smooth, brilliant, most pleasing to the eyes, and a source of beauty for you.
Having immediately taken soot, Parvati anointed her eyes with it,
making them as beautiful as the luster of your feet, O Lord.
"O Goddess, please accept this uncolored [garment] given by me;
it is exceedingly fragrant and cool from my own ointment."
"O Goddess, take this fragrant flower that I have offered, which grows both in villages and in the forest, and smear it upon your limbs."
Please accept this heart-pleasing nasal ointment offered by me,
produced from the essence of trees and blended with camphor and agallochum.
O Goddess of gods, please accept this incense offered by me;
you are the sun, the moon, the stars, and likewise the lightning and fire.
You alone are the light of the worlds; please accept this lamp, as well as these various kinds of delightful, delicious, and flavorful foods.
O Goddess worshipped with wine, take what has been offered by me,
such as the sacrificial oblations and all fruits and roots grown in the village forests.
O beloved of Hari, accept these various forms of fragrant offerings;
O Goddess, this fourfold food is endowed with the six flavors.
Please accept this delightful food, which brings eternal satisfaction,
consisting of cow’s ghee mixed with milk and blended with various sweets.
"O Veda, please accept this supreme food offered by me;
it is divine, composed of nectar, and fashioned from ghee and sugar-candy."
O beloved of Hara, accept these various kinds of delicious flour-cakes,
and this sweet, beautiful *modaka* confection seasoned with camphor and other ingredients.
Having accepted the mixture of various ingredients, let it be eaten;
or else, the sidhu liquor contained in a copper vessel may be consumed here.
O beloved of Śaṅkara, having taken water from a coconut in a bell-metal vessel—
cool, clear, limpid water mixed with camphor—
O Goddess who brings satisfaction in food, may you graciously accept this;
at the conclusion of the meal, water for sipping (ācamanīya) should be offered once again.
O lady of pure smiles, in every case, one should offer [the substance] combined with fruits and leaves, well-perfumed with camphor and other fragrances, using the very mantra previously mentioned.
Please accept this betel leaf, which beautifies the face and is pleasing to the heart.
Then, according to the path taught in the scriptures, one should satisfy the *ali* with drops,
lifting it up silently with the nails of the thumb and ring finger.
One should offer libations to the deities at their mouths using three handfuls from the water-vessel;
having performed this libation once, one should recite the root mantra and the *pādukā* mantra.
Recalling the internal power (antaḥśakti), one should satisfy the deities of the body:
the thumb is the station of Bhairava, while the ring finger belongs to Caṇḍikā.
Therefore, one should offer libations with those two [fingers] where this is pleasing to them;
and for the rite of subjugation (*vaśyakarma*), one should offer libations with the thumb and the middle finger.
One should perform the libation for malevolent rites (ābhicārika) by joining the index finger with the thumb;
one should perform the libation for the rite of immobilization (staṃbhana) by joining the little finger with the thumb.
Having thus satisfied [the deities], one should worship the lineage of gurus before the gods.
One should worship her who holds the *cinmudrā* and a human skull raised aloft with her two hands;
who is adorned with garments and unguents like the color of refined gold and fresh flowers;
whose side-glances are full of compassion, whose eyes are reddish, and whose hair is matted; and who is attended by the Siddhas and other celestial beings.
The lineage of gurus has perfected their minds.
Having thus worshipped oneself with incense, lamps, and food offerings,
as well as liquor mixed with meat and various kinds of edibles;
One should likewise offer plantain fruits and betel leaves;
having thus addressed Vaṭuka and the others, one should display the family lamps (kuladīpas).
When slightly cooked, one should fashion lamps four finger-breadths high from well-ground [clay],
shaped like hand-drums (ḍamaruka), triangular, and very beautiful.
One who is capable of drawing [the breath] should perform nine, seven, or five [restraints];
having unified the internal light and the external light into immeasurable radiance.
Having whirled the family-lamp three times above the Goddess, one should offer it, saying:
"O Goddess, Mistress of the entire wheel, together with the lords of the wheels, [I offer this] in your presence."
"O Goddess, accept this *ārātrika* for my spiritual success.
Then, having displayed the family lamps (*kuladīpa*), one should perform the worship of the Śakti.
Now, he states its necessity:
Having attained the Kaula lineage within the Kaula tradition,
those who abide by this doctrine perform the daily worship of Śakti; thus spoke the Enemy of Cities (Śiva) to me.
When the Śakti-worship has been performed, the daily worship becomes fruitful;
but for men, when it has not been performed, the daily worship is fruitless.
Therefore, after the daily worship, the ascetic, having honored her according to his capacity,
should worship her with the thought that she is the Goddess herself, and not with the thought that she is an ordinary wife.
Having worshipped the deities with a focused mind, one should offer the vessel of enjoyments;
at the conclusion of that, one should also offer young maidens and captivating women.
Having worshipped the deity with a focused mind, one should offer the vessel individually for each.
However, he who partakes of the family substance (kuladravya) without first offering it to Śakti [commits an offense].
The worship of such a person is fruitless, and the deity does not become pleased;
[only] one who is fully endowed with the mantra and maintains the conduct of the samaya [is successful].
Whether she be a maiden, one established in a vow, or even one bearing the yoga-mudrā,
if she arrives spontaneously at the time of worship, she should be immediately honored by the wise.
Then, preceded by the mantra-water, the practitioner of mantras should offer all the rites beginning with worship,
starting from the east, to the Goddess while reciting the mantra.
One should perform the remainder of the rites as in the *dakṣiṇā* [rite], and likewise dispose of the leftovers and so forth.
A worship performed without the requisite capacity is in vain; a ritual of worship devoid of Śiva is in vain.
The worship of Śiva and Śakti together is that worship which grants all desires;
in the absence of devotion, even when possessing ritual materials, one should worship the power of the mind.

That which is to be given as the remnant (śeṣika) after being consecrated with mantras is called "for the Remnant" (śeṣikāyai). One should utter the word "Aiṃ," then "hṛducchiṣṭacāṇḍālini," and then the term "Mātaṅgī."
With this mantra, "Sarvevaśaṃkarī Svāhā," which consists of twenty-one syllables,
one should offer the remains of the floral offerings (*nirmālya*) to Śeṣikā.
One should meditate upon the goddess Mātaṅgī, who is the sole enchantress of the world and is characterized by the remnants of the divine offering.

Mātaṅgī, who delights in the playing of the lute and sweet singing, radiant in her blue silken garment, with lips like the bimba fruit and feet moist with fresh lac, whose clothing reaches to her ears,
whose limbs are charming, who is as white as a conch, a jasmine flower, or snow, and resplendent with ornaments of rubies.
I bow to the goddess with a beautiful smile on her face, who is dark as a parrot.
One should partake of that which has been left over by the Kaulikas together with their Śaktis;
[one should serve] one's own Śakti or the Śakti of a Vīra, who is initiated and embodies the form of the Guru.
"Having caused [the disciple] to drink the middle [portion], this is the certainty of the scripture.
Then, [one should offer it] to the venerable Guru, who is the manifest form of Paraśiva himself."
Having lifted the vessel with both hands, he should offer it a second time;
in the absence of the guru, he should cast that vessel into the water.
The vessel for the venerable Śakti is for the Śaktis; the vessel for the heroes (vīra) is for the heroes;
the vessel for the Yoginīs is for others; and the vessel for enjoyment (bhoga-pātra) is for one's own sake.
The Kuṇḍalinī should perform the ritual of offering (tarpaṇa) using the vessel of enjoyment;
recollecting the internal Śakti, one should satisfy the deity of the body.
Now, I shall declare here the manner in which they should accept the supreme vessel, exactly as it was spoken by Rudra.

Having performed the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma), one should then perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with those respective mantras out of a spirit of devotion, as well as [the worship] of the tree and so forth according to one's ability.
Then, having smelled each of those vessels, one should place it in the right hand;
one should join the thumb with the ring finger of the left hand.
This mudrā is indeed proclaimed as the propitiatory (tarpaṇī) and of pure form;
by this mudrā, O Goddess, the withdrawal (saṃhāra) of all things occurs in due order.
Having taken the substance with the vessel, one should satisfy [the ancestors] with the prescribed mantras,
as far as the nails of the thumb and the ring finger touch each other.
Indeed, the mudrā should be established with the fluids of the Kaulika;
closing one's eyes, one should meditate upon Kālikā in that very form.
Having entered the lotus of my inner heart, she who bestows success;
while reciting the root mantra, one should apply the tilaka-mark of a bindu upon the forehead.
One should offer the five *prāṇāhuti*s while drawing in the essence of the flesh;
first the *tāra* (Oṃ), then the *śiras*, and finally, in the middle, those [syllables] divided by the fourth case-ending.
While reciting the mantra to be described hereafter, one should silently drink that liquid, which consists of the various forms of prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.

One should offer the sacrificial substance along with the mantra into the form of Kuṇḍalī, whose nature is consciousness, which arises from the triangle that is the root of one's own self, and which possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns.
This supreme nectar, filling the vessel of the infinite,
is characterized by the acceptance of the oblation into the fire of my supreme *ahaṃtā*.
I drink this purifying nectar, the medicine for existence,
which is the cause for severing the bonds of the individual soul, as proclaimed by Bhairava.
While others were reciting mantras here at the crown of the head, the Sovereign of the World,
with her mind as the sacrificial ladle, offered the oblation of dharma and adharma into the blazing fire of the Self.
"By means of the path of the Suṣumṇā, I constantly offer the functioning of the senses as an oblation;
I shall now recite to you the mantra deposited by the Kāpālikas."
I bathe the Goddess residing in the heart with the nectar-like juices;
by this, may this bond of worldly existence come to an end for me.
Thus, these three mantras have been declared for the rite of accepting the vessel;
one should not drink the substance without the mantra, for a penance is prescribed [for doing so].
One should never drink liquor, nor should one drink it without a mantra;
to drink liquor without a mantra is declared to be the same as drinking wine.
Holding the full vessel in his hand, the practitioner should recite: "I offer";
then he should utter the mantra: "O all you hosts of heroes, partake! (juṣasva).
Having made each other the *caṇḍālī*, one should drink [the wine] with the other's permission;
according to the ritual rule, one should take it while reciting the mantra with the second [partner].
A piece of flesh the size of a black gram and wine measured by a handful should first be accepted by the Guru; he shall then become the bestower of the remainder to the disciples.
Free from hesitation, pure, steadfast, shameless, and full of curiosity—
one who has ascertained the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras may drink the excellent Varuṇī.
Having worshipped the gods and the ancestors according to the path prescribed by the Vedas and the Śāstras,
one who drinks liquor and eats meat while remembering the Guru incurs no fault.
Perceiving with his intellect the oneness of the Guru, the Deity, and the Mantra,
he should drink the substance up to the throat and then perform the chewing.
One should worship meat, fish, mudrā, and sexual union in their proper sequence;
one should perform the worship together with heroes who are joined with one's own tradition.
Because the mind has autonomy as its essence, it consists of bliss;
therefore, one should cultivate meditation upon that which consists of it, while the emotional state remains within the latent aesthetic flavor.
Wine is drunk by that [adept] for the sake of expanding his own sovereignty;
therefore, I offer the Goddess Wine, who is the fullness of I-consciousness, as my desired oblation.
O Goddess of the Gods, the knower of mantras,
with an undisturbed mind, should slowly perform the drinking of honey using this root mantra.
Drinking wine with appetizers until he was completely intoxicated,
he then let a drop of the liquor from his vessel fall upon the ground.
One should offer the leavings here to Bhairava while reciting the mantra:
"Maidha-māyā-ramā-vīje, ehyeṣi ucchiṣṭa-bhairava. (O Bhairava of the leavings, come, come!)
Taking the unjoined portion of the *bali* offering with the mantra "yugaṃ svāhā," one should rub it upon the ground in the western direction and perform the painting as before.
This same sequence applies even to those who would take up the vessel;
it is characterized by the manifestation of the fruits of the various types of drink and the established state of the valid means of knowledge.
He who acts without understanding will not reach the goal of the stages.
Five kinds of drink are proclaimed, distinguished as the Great Divine and so forth.
The Great Divine, the Divine, the Hero, the Great Animal,
and the Animal to be Worshipped who is Pure— thus it is proclaimed as fivefold.
Having brought the prāṇa and apāna breaths into equilibrium, with the mind steady through withdrawal (pratyāhāra),
one should enter the solar orb situated within the lunar orb.
Flowing constantly through the path of the Suṣumṇā, this supreme support of the gods is drawn forth;
O Maheśvarī, hear this which is called the Great Divine and the Divine.
The divine drink before the Goddess, the supreme heroic seat of softness,
and the abandonment of all fetters at the root within the accumulation of the pure Vāma.
One should satisfy [the deities] through the yoga of the Kaulika conduct by means of the five tattvas;
one should offer the substance accompanied by mantra according to the sequential division of the six cakras.
O Goddess, the supreme state of meditative worship and the unsurpassed drinking of the hero's liquor (vīrapāna) are called "hero's drinking" after the ritual dismissal [of the deities].
The drinking of heroes (vīrapāna) is said to be of two kinds; listen, O beloved, to the drinking of beasts (paśupāna).
In the drinking of heroes, the former is a hero, while the latter is a beast.
Being attached, greedy for wealth, or engaging in conversation for the sake of mantras;
being like a bow in the direction of one's task—this is called "drinking the cattle."
O Goddess, when that which is drunk is done by all those of noble birth who remain arrogant without performing worship, it is called the drinking of the bound (paśupāna).
Furthermore, listen, O Goddess of gods, O Śivā: this is the sequence for the Paśupāna [vow].
O Beloved, one who drinks wine should be alone, and one who consumes the Śakti should be alone.
If one never forms an association with Maheśvara,
this is called "drinking like a beast," which brings about great poverty.
O Dear One, that drinking which is performed by fools without mantra, without initiation, and without the instruction from the mouth of a Guru, the wise know as the drinking of cattle.
O Dear One, listen: Kaulavāma is declared to be Mahāpaśu.
On the left is a beautiful woman who captivates the mind, while on the right is the vessel for the offering (colipātra).
O Maheśānī, the Mahākaula practitioner, while offering libations with his left hand from the drinking vessels,
should place them on the ground and perform the libation, O Maheśānī.
O Goddess, if [the hands] are joined with both hands, it is called Kaula;
by the reversal of the left and right, it is proclaimed as Vīra-kaula.
One should offer libations from the vessel of wine held in the left hand using the right hand;
this is proclaimed as Kāmagauḍa, and it is indeed that which is called Caitanya.
O Great Goddess, having placed [the vessel] on the ground, one should offer libations with both hands;
this is declared to be the "Bliss" (Ānanda) rite, and it is prescribed as the left-hand (vāma) method.
But the fruit is as follows:
Purified by the consecration of mantras and by drinking the nectar, Pārvatī becomes the divine state that liberates one from the bonds of worldly existence.
Bliss is the form of Brahman, and that is established as liberation;
the substance that manifests it is drunk by the yogis.
The hero who delights in divine drink shall attain union with the Goddess;
indeed, by means of the hero’s drink, the teacher goes to the world of the Goddess.
The practitioner who drinks the animal-sacrifice liquor shall go to the Raurava hell.
[The stages of life are] infancy, childhood, youth, and maturity.
Beyond that is the state of Unmanā, and the seventh is indeed the state of Avasthā.
Now, their characteristics:
O Mistress of the Kula, the commencement is said to consist of three vessels;
at its conclusion is the Youth, O Dear One, who bestows happiness upon the Youth.
O beloved, youth is said to be the perfect blossoming of the mind;
the faltering of sight, mind, and speech is designated as maturity.
The mature stage is proclaimed as that in which one’s own desired and cherished veil [of ignorance] is cast off;
it is characterized by falling down, rising up, and fainting again and again.
One who lacks mastery over the body and the senses is said to be unstable;
at the end of a meal, wine is poison, and at the end of drinking wine, food is poison.
One should know that to be nectar which is at the end of wine;
wine accompanied by chewing is always declared to be nectar.
Drinking without chewing is merely consuming poison;
therefore, having praised and paid homage, one should perform the union of enjoyment.
In the presence of the deity, during the enjoyment, there shall be the pleasing of the deity;
having understood these [mudrās], one should then [place them] within the circle of the womb.
Having worshipped the Great Goddess, he should then engage in sexual union,
offering the oblation of dharma and adharma into the fire of the self with the ladle of the mind.
"By means of the path of the Suṣumṇā, I constantly offer the activity of the senses;
this great mantra, ending with 'svāhā', is proclaimed at the beginning."
Then, while walking along a pleasant path, one should mutter the mantra of the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Three Worlds,
who is heard in the sky, supported by the hands of the luminous ether.
"I offer into the fire the entire essence of both dharma and adharma, filled with affection;
this great mantra, ending in 'svāhā', is proclaimed for the renunciation of all that is white (pure)."
If it should be omitted through negligence, that deity becomes enraged;
[this occurs] by eating without [offering], by drinking without [offering], and by performing the fifth [act] without [offering].
How can that most wicked one say, "I am chanting the Kālī-mantra"?
Therefore, O beloved, one should accomplish the fifth [mantra] with every effort.
If it is not done at all, there is no suffering for him at every step;
if, however, there is attachment through anxiety, then [suffering arises] from the application of subsequent conceptualization.
The rite must be performed for the sake of its completeness; otherwise, it is said to be fruitless.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Worship of the Sacred Seats and the Consumption of Kula Substances," within the general daily worship of the Kaula and Vāma traditions in the *Śrī Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Having emerged from the house after receiving worship, one may then roam about according to one's own will.
Listen now, O beloved, to what must be done at the time of eating with honey.
One who desires to live for a long time should eat facing the east;
one who faces the southern direction, O Goddess, attains fame.
One who desires abundant prosperity should eat facing the west;
one who aspires for spiritual perfection and liberation should consume food facing the north.
This being the case on the path of Dharma, specifically the Śakti-upāsaka,
should always eat his food facing the northern direction during both twilights.
The Blessed Lord Śiva has said that the cause therein is valid cognition;
by whatever means of sitting and upon whatever seat one may sit.
Having sat down, one should eat food, but never upon the bare ground;
first, having placed the sacred grass (ācamana) on the right, one should set down water.
O Sovereign of the Gods, one should indeed place the water for rinsing the mouth and the mantra within the speech; and one who [offers] a lamp before her at night and fire by day.
By that, his digestive fire shall be eternally perfected for consumption,
and the presence of bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas does not arise.
The Rākṣasas tear away that food and that sacrificial oblation;
therefore, one should draw a line from the south-west to the north-west with a stream of water.
Having recited the Rodharāva weapon-mantra, one should, with the right hand, [draw] the western line,
and likewise the northern and eastern lines immediately thereafter.
Starting from the northeast corner and ending in the southeast, and immediately thereafter,
one should visualize it extending from the tip of the southeast to the southwest at the very end of all.
One should draw the maṇḍala outside, with a central bindu, an argha-vessel, and a rākṣasa in the corners;
and in the north-west corner, a vajra and a crescent moon-mark together with a bindu.
One should draw this *kuśa* in the northeast corner;
then, one should subsequently draw a line from the southeast corner toward the west and north, meeting in the center.

Caitanya, Praṇava, Māyāpāśa, Kāma, Śākinī,

Henceforth, O Goddess, listen attentively as I describe in due order the twelve Tantric mantras that are about to be spoken by me.
Tāra, Māyā, Carāva, Kūrca, Kuṇḍa, Karṇikā, Surasa, Phetkārī, and Ghaṭī— these indeed do not exist here.

place these two in me as well, O Inner Ruler of all."
Then all this [universe] became perspiration for you, and immediately thereafter,

With this mantra, one should offer sacrificial food (bali-anna) to the Goddess;

When being recited with the nasal vowel (anusvāra), one should offer [the oblation] after having released [the breath];
she is Sarasvatī, Ramā, Kāmā, Prasādā, Aṅkuśā, and Kālikā.
The nine seed-syllables of the Ḍākinīs, Pretas, and Bhairavīs are indeed in front;

One should say "anunayam anna-bali" to the Yoginīs and Ḍākinīs, and then say "I offer it; O gentle ones, eat and be satisfied."
"May they grant me accomplishment; may they bestow compassion upon me"—thus one should recite.
Then, one should clearly inscribe the series of seed-syllables beginning with *Prabhañjana* (the Wind).
Aḍākinī, Mahārātri, and Roṣamastra—these three are the heads.
Now, having abandoned slaughter, offer the auspicious *bali* to Vināyaka.
Having offered the bali-food at the end of the mantra within the mandala as before,
one should offer it to Gaṇādhipati with the mantra that is about to be spoken.
Vedādi, Pāśa, Garuḍa, Yoginī, Candra, Dakṣiṇā, Bali, Padme, Taṃdrā, Kūṭā, Siddha, and Prabhānavā.

To the Great Lord of the Host (Mahāgaṇādhipati) and to the King of Obstacles (Vighnarāja), one should likewise offer this oblation along with the pedestal; thereafter, one should take up a pair of vessels.
Devour the pair as well, and thereafter all obstacles;
destroy the two, O beautiful one, and burn the two, O Amāriṣṭa!
Vīja, Āpsarasa, Māścarya, Vaiśvadevaka,
and Ṛṣabha— these five one should employ in succession.
The third [syllable] is declared to be *astrāya* followed by *svāhā*;
O beloved, now hear the fourth mantra of Vaṭukanātha.
Having placed the lumps of food within the maṇḍala as previously described,
one should offer them to Vaṭuka while reciting the final mantra.
One should not again utter these seed-syllables: Tāra-caitanya, Pāśahṛī, Bhāruṇḍā, Kūrcakākinī, and Kālāditya.
Immediately after those three peaks known as Raudrā, Nandā, and Calā, one should address Mahāvaṭukanātha, saying: "Come, come! (ehy ehi).
Accept this offering and grant both types of all accomplishments;
destroy my enemy twice and slay him twice over.
Bestow the pair that grants all sovereignty, and likewise grant the second pair;
thereafter, [grant] the four beginning with Sauraṅga and Carpaṭa.
Having uttered "Rauḥ" three times for each of the three [groups], one should say "Śiraḥ" at the end of all;
now listen to the supreme bali offering for Kṣetrapāla.
Having first offered a piece of cow-horn, one should recite this mantra:
"O you who possess consciousness, the power of illusion (māyā), the lotus-born Brahmā, and a girdle of a thousand [rays]!"
One should not place the seed-syllables *tāṭaṃ* and *kamaṃdasvārṇā* before [the mantra];

Having uttered the words beginning with "hetukādi" and ending with "bhīṣaṇebhyaḥ," one should likewise offer this bali to all the kṣetrapālas.
One should write "may she be gentle" after omitting "my success," and then one should state "grant [it]" and "destroy my enemies."
Having said, "HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ, let the remainder remain," one should release [the water].
Now, O lady of pure smiles, I shall declare the mantra for the sixth power;
this is recited by those seeking its fruit when it is bestowed upon the retinue.
Caitanya, Tārakamalā, Pāśa, Roṣa, Vadhū, Smarā,
Trāsāda, Śākinī, and the nine seed-syllables (bījas) of the Puras.

from the single word "Guhyakālī" onwards, they proceed as companions.
The words for the retinue are also just two, thus they are not measured;

O Goddess of the Universe, these six *vali-mantras* have thus been declared;

Below these, I have previously described six cities consisting of bindus;

Jātavedas, Āditya, Śanaiścara, and Agastya after him;

However, one should gradually deposit [the offerings] from the Vedas and so forth up to the heart; having offered those various portions of cooked rice to the respective deities with these mantras, one should release them.

The youngest [wife] remains [there], and silence is likewise prescribed;

Indeed, one should not perceive any deficiency or excess among the flavors, nor should one offer anything else;

At that very moment, the practitioner should consume all of that which has become the great prasāda;

One should have them sit together there in private where one eats oneself;

One should gradually fill three parts of the stomach;
one part should be left empty for the movement [of food] with the water of the womb.
Food that begins with bitter [tastes], has sour in the middle, and ends with sweet,
has been proclaimed in the Āyurveda and other treatises by great sages such as Ātreya.
Having thus finished the entire meal himself,
the practitioner should lift the vessel and slowly place it elsewhere while reciting the mantra.
One must certainly place whatever food remains in a vessel;
having formed that food into a ball (piṇḍa), one should take it along with water in the right hand.
O fair-faced one, one should place the *bali* offering beneath the vessel in both cases;
first, one should set it out for Ucchiṣṭabhairava in the western direction.
In the same manner, [one should offer] to the Ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī in the east according to the sequence;
now one should attend to this pair of mantras for these two.
Maidha, Māyāyoginī, Carāvarāmā, Smarāśaruṭ,
Kulyāyoṭo, Muṃtālā— these indeed are the ten seed-syllables (bījas).
Having invoked Ucchiṣṭabhairava, one should likewise utter the offering for the remnants:

Now hear further of the mantra by which [the offering] is given in the east:
maidhaṃ, pāśaḥ, smara, rāvaḥ, kūrcam, and kṣetrapatākinī.

and "Ehyehi ucchiṣṭacāṇḍālī anughaṃsadhivarjitam."
Having assumed a hideous form and addressed the seeker of liberation, O Piśācinī,
having spoken thus, take this offering of leavings for a pair [of years].

O Goddess, there is the *sāmarthya* (efficacy), then the pair, and then the three of the *piśācinī*;
here too, the final one should be understood as the four-syllable mantra, as before.
O Dear One, having thus offered this pair of *valis* with these two *manus*,
one should immediately thereafter perform the six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*) ritual right there.
O gracious one,
this betel leaf and its fragrance—
by chewing this betel, a mortal becomes supremely pure and auspicious.
Betel nut is auspicious for all castes, providing supreme purification of the mouth;
it stimulates digestion, improves appetite, and alleviates all disorders caused by Vata.

One should avoid that which has turned yellowish-brown, that which is discolored, that which has red eyes, and that which is spotted; one should likewise reject leaves with broken tips, leaves with dark backs, and powdered leaves.
A disease may arise from the base of a leaf; sinful thoughts from the tip of a leaf.
A powdered leaf takes away one's lifespan, and a veined leaf destroys the intellect.
Taking the betel powder with the index finger, one should not eat the betel leaf;
if that foolish soul becomes distressed by it, he shall go to the Raurava hell.
The nut is Brahmā, the leaf is Viṣṇu, the lime is the god Maheśvara;
the wood is the Goddess herself—thus, betel (tāmbūla) is exceedingly rare.
By the gift of these, the abundance of one's fortune increases;
O Goddess, now hear the proper time for betel-leaf in its due order.
O Goddess of the Gods, one hundred leaves are for the supreme universal monarch (cakravartin),
and thirty-two leaf-rolls (vīṭikā) are to be presented to the gurus.
O beloved, one should give eighteen ripe leaves to twenty-eight kings and kinsmen, and twelve to the son-in-law.
To the twenty-five Śaktis, he gave as many sons as there are principles (tattvas);
and to his enemies, he gave six-leaved [leaves]—this was the fourth, most excellent gift.
Three leaves are for the side of the enemy; ten leaves for those to be brought under control;
sixteen for heroes; and for Śivā, the divine lineage, there are eight [leaves] joined with the sacred seats (pīṭhas).
Half of that again is for the Siddha lineage, half of that for the Mānava lineage;
seven leaves are to be honored by others, and twenty-five for the maiden.
O Maheśānī, fifteen [shares] including Candra were for the grandsons;
thirty for the daughter-in-law, and fourteen indeed for Śivā’s mouth.
O Supreme Goddess, one should cause twenty leaves to be given to others:
Pariputrī, Dāsī, and Dāsa as the fourth.
The elder brother who marries before his younger brother, the younger brother who marries before his elder, those who give betel-leaf to six people,
the giving of the first offering to enemies, and the giving of a wheel to a good friend.
One should apply the horizontal gift (tiryagdāna) to servants and others, as appropriate to the circumstances.
One should avoid [food] from the hand of a barbarian (mleccha), from the hand of an enemy, and likewise from the hand of one who bears a staff;
furthermore, betel leaf from the hand of a clever person (vaidagdha) is indeed forbidden.
The first betel-roll should be offered to the accuser;
the second, to the witness; and from the third roll onward, three pieces at a time should be taken in succession.
The leaf, the fruit, the resin of the Kadir tree, and powder as the fourth;
the fifth is said to be "pleasure," and passion is declared to be the sixth.
It is proclaimed as having six limbs and being endowed with the six sovereign powers;
having grasped that, O lady of excellent hips, one may then wander at will.
Alternatively, consider the task that pertains to the evening.

Having indeed performed the Vedic twilight worship (saṃdhyā) as at the time of the midday rite, one should then perform the Tantric worship of the Goddess; however, if he belongs to the three castes, he may do so otherwise.
But the fourth [state] is indeed tantric;
it is like the firmament at the time of the setting of the sun, or like the night.
Now follows the daily offering of the Śivāvali.

Whether at the root of a bilva tree, in a wilderness, or even in a cremation ground, the practitioner— whether established, victorious, constant, or engaged in rites for specific desires— is [successful] in both the Kula and Akula traditions.
At the time of twilight, one should offer a primary oblation of meat;
when the name "Kālikālī" is uttered, she then assumes the form of Śiva.
Taking the form of a beast, it approaches accompanied by its own retinue;
when it raises its face toward the northeast and cries out with a beautiful sound after eating, [it portends success].
At that very moment, it brings him auspiciousness; otherwise, it is a defilement of the family.
By the giving of food, one must certainly and invariably satisfy Śivā.
Just as the daily śrāddha, the twilight prayers, the application of sandalwood paste, and the libations to the ancestors are obligatory,
so too are the worship of the family deities and the service of those worthy of the lineage constant duties.
If one does not worship the Goddess who assumes the form of a beast in a secluded place,
everything of his will certainly and swiftly perish due to the howling of jackals.
Taking whatever merits there may be from the performance of recitation and worship, as well as other good deeds,
she utters a curse and weeps in a secluded place.
O Kulabhairavī, where one is enjoyed by Śivā alone,
there indeed lies the supreme and most rare delight of all the Śaktis.
Since the power of animals, the power of birds, and the power of humans are, respectively,
twice as effective in ritual action when worshipped, the practitioner thereby becomes endowed with qualities.
With every effort, one should perform this great worship when faced with dangers such as those from kings and the like, or fears of migrating to another land.
Having reflected upon auspicious and inauspicious actions, one should offer the bali-oblation:
"Accept it, O Goddess, O highly fortunate Śivā, you who have the form of the fire of time!"
"Clearly declare the auspicious and inauspicious results; accept this offering for you.
Having spoken thus, O beloved, the offering (bali) should be given by the members of the family.
Therefore, O Queen, it is not eaten by us; otherwise, it would not be auspicious.

Knowing this, O Great Goddess, one should perform rites for peace and prosperity.
Thus ends the offering of the Śivāvali.
Having performed purification and likewise rinsed his mouth, he should again enter the house of worship,
bringing with him a collection of flowers, garlands, incense, food offerings, sacrificial oblations, lamps, and so forth.
During the time of worship,
O beloved, one should perform the *ārātrika* for the practitioner engaged in the ritual according to one's means, as well as the offering of rows of lamps.
Closing his eyes for a moment, he should practice meditation as previously described;
then, with palms joined in *añjali*, he should recite the two lotus-mantras.
The Yoginīs, the Mothers, the Siddhas, the Kṣetrapālas, and the Vināyakas;
likewise Vaṭukanātha, Cāmuṇḍā, and the hosts of Bhairavas.
May the Vetālas, Bhūtas, Kumbhāṇḍas, and others who follow Kālī, manifest their presence here; I perform this nocturnal worship.
Having recited thus, one should then perform the sixfold ritual application (ṣaḍaṅga) beginning with the seers (ṛṣi);
thereafter, O Dear One, one must perform the placement of the faces (vaktranyāsa) as a necessity.
One should also perform other [rites] as far as possible according to one's own will;
the placement on the mouth (*vaktranyāsa*) is obligatory, while the others are performed for specific desires (*kāmya*).
Having thus performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and other rites according to one's own desire, O Goddess worshipped by the gods,
one should again recite a single verse with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*).
O Guhyakālī, Sovereign of the Universe, Mother of the World, whose form is consciousness, who art ever equal to Sadāśiva and Jīva—
I perform this evening remembrance here, in order to destroy the accumulation gathered throughout the day.
Having recited this, O beloved, one should then take a flower in the hollowed palms or with the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā, and perform the rite with eyes opened by meditation.
Now, as for the trikhaṇḍā mudrā: [it is as follows].
One should turn the two hands over so that the thumbs touch and are made equal;
having placed the two index fingers in a curved shape within the ring fingers.
The Great Goddess should place [her fingers] on their respective positions starting from the little finger;
this is declared to be the "Three-Parted" (trikhaṇḍā) mudrā for the rite of summoning Tripurā.
One should not meditate according to the sequence of the two verses mentioned in the previous hymn;
rather, [one should meditate on] the first as "O you who possess the rays of the sun" (yāvat-sūrya-kale) and the second as "O Brahman and Indra" (brahmendra).
If one has the capacity, one should perform the rites beginning with the invocation, using the sixteen services with the very same mantras previously mentioned.
In case of inability, [one may worship] with flowers, garlands, incense, lamps, offerings made for three nights,
food offerings, oblations, hymns, recitations, and even through silent repetitions (japa).
The practitioner should prostrate like a staff and also perform circumambulations;
beseeching with plaintive cries, he should pray for the fulfillment of his own desires.
O Goddess, if an image or even a yantra is available,
one should prepare it and cover it with a soft cushion.
Having set aside her pillow, she should recite there the *Tatra-kālikā* [mantra],
as well as those medicinal substances that are required for the nocturnal worship.
One must certainly partake of those [offerings] together with capable practitioners;

Then, he should perform the evening meal as previously described;
thereafter, he himself should lie down with his beloved wife.
One whose head is turned westward, or whose right side is toward the head, or whose head is toward the west,
should be known [to bring] longevity and wealth when lying with the head toward the east or the south.
In the west there is great anxiety, and likewise death in the north;
having performed purification with the hands and feet and having sipped water (ācamana), one should remain well-composed.
While the lamp was burning, he was not rendered blind by darkness; he was not a wind-eater (a snake); his hand was not motionless like a statue; he was neither naked nor clad in a bodice.
O beloved of the Wind-god, one should recite the following verses to be spoken for the destruction of bad dreams:
"O Mother of the World, O Great Illusionist, O Kālikā, O Destroyer of Time!"
O Hara, O Rudrāṇī, take away my bad dreams; protect me, your devotee, always.
O Bhīma, O God, [protect] this man from ghosts, spirits, piśācas, and the like.
May the Rākṣasas, Dānavas, and Daityas who cause the interruption of my sleep,
whatever defects arise from bad dreams, and whoever seeks to harm me, [be destroyed].
But those serpents, birds, scorpions, and creatures born from thorns, who have been brought to destruction by the thunderbolt of remembrance of you;
Those whose limbs are afflicted by poison, those who possess venom in their horns,
insects whose bodies are filled with poison, and those who cause agitation;
Having heard of that flight in the ten directions of those named Kālikās,
Kālī, Karālī, Cāmuṇḍā, Chinnamastā, and Bhairavī [pursued them].
Hara-siddhā, Siddhi-lakṣmī, Dvāmarī, Vābhravī,
as well as Mahāmārī, Tāmasī, Mātaṅgī, and Īśavareśvarī.
Carcikā, Śivadūtī, Mahāmahiṣamardinī,
Ugracaṇḍā, Kubjikā, Phetkārī, and Guhyakālī.
These are your forms, both terrible and gentle, O Sovereign of the Asuras;
O Mother, protect him as he sleeps and destroy his bad dreams.
Discus, noose, sword, trident, spear, mace,
iron club, tomara, thunderbolt, mallet, lance, bhuśuṇḍī, noose, and paṭṭiśa.
O Goddess of gods,
O Maheśvarī, may those weapons which you hold in your hands protect me myself.
By your command, may Nārasiṃhī protect me in the eastern direction,
Vārāhī in the western, and Kālikā in the southern.
And may Cāmuṇḍā, most exceedingly terrible, protect me in the north; likewise above and below, in the cardinal and intermediate directions— protect me everywhere!
O Goddess, may those powers of yours and those hosts of attendants protect me,
your servant, everywhere and at all times.
O Goddess of gods, by your command alone, may both gods Viṣṇu and Rudra, the lords of all deities, assuming various forms, protect me.
May Varāha, Nārasiṃha, Vāmana, Ananta,
Trivikrama, and Hayagrīva— these six— protect me always.
The conqueror of death, the blue-throated one, the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
the slayer of Tripura, the one with tawny beard, the wielder of the Pināka bow, and the blue-and-red-hued one.
May these eleven Rudras— Pramatheśa, Kīrtivāsas, Virūpākṣa, and Maheśvara— who assume fierce forms, protect me.
"O Guhyakālī, always harbor fear toward me;
O beloved, having thus performed the protection with these eighteen verses, fix your mind [upon this]."
Lying down, he thought of Kālī with a mind free from worldly attachment; the entire night passed for that knower of yoga as if in a state of yoga itself, through sleep.
Rising again at dawn with the desire to perform the morning rites,
one should carry out the daily observance as before, according to the path prescribed in one's own ritual manual.
Now follows the procedure for the daily worship of the intermediate [deities].
Now I shall explain another [method] by which she may obtain freedom from suffering:
having risen in the morning, she should remember her guru and others, and then perform the purification rites.
Having performed the ritual bath, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and the libations (tarpaṇa)— both Vedic and Tantric—
one should then return home and perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should perform the Mātṛkā-nyāsa as well as the Nyāsa of the Chandas and the Devas;
then the Nyāsa known as Kara-aṅga for that mantra, and the placement of the conch and the arghya vessel.
The ritual bathing of the deity with mantras, the five-fold theft in worship,
and the honoring of the surrounding enclosures with sandalwood paste and flowers alone.
There, after the Vaiśvadeva offering, one should offer five oblations with the root mantra;
first, one should perform the recitation one hundred and eight times.
At the conclusion of the Vedic recitation, worship is performed and the leftovers are eaten;
thereafter, one should pray to the God and perform the evening twilight ritual (sāyaṃ-saṃdhyā).
The offering of lamps in a temple is declared to be the summary of the daily ritual.
Now follows the daily ritual for inauspicious places, such as places of exile or prisons.
Now I shall describe the afternoon [rite], which occurs in ten locations:
on a road, while traveling, in a difficult place, when not at home, upon arrival, or when there is fear in the mind.
In a prison, in an auspicious place, or when there is fear arising from snakes, tigers, and the like,
or upon the arrival of a hostile army, one should perform purification and other rites however one may.
Having contemplated and performed the mantra-bath and other rites, as well as the mental worship,
one should mentally visualize within the heart the seat known as Yoga.
In that very center of the earth, one should perform the worship of the deity,
just as worship with flowers and other offerings is prescribed in the outer region.

Likewise, all those [rites] should be performed mentally in the heart for the sake of practice, as well as in the stomach during fire-offerings (homa), in times of distress, and in the daily ritual (āhnika).
Now follows the daily observance for those who are ill.
Now I shall describe the daily regimen for the sick person who is generally healthy,
provided that no disease is observed in him that would require fasting as its ultimate treatment.
At that time, worship should not be performed on the sacrificial ground (sthāṇḍila) or upon images;
nor should one perform bathing, use a tooth-stick, or even blow the fire.
Having gazed upon the solar disc or else upon the image,
one should recite the root mantra once and cast forth a flower together with unbroken grains of rice.
Exhausted by extremely fierce diseases and with his senses impaired by old age,
or even by his own companions, he should nevertheless complete his own duty.
Then, having performed the fire-ritual and having worshipped the fire and the deities,
he should address his teacher and the lineage of knowledge in their presence and utter these words:
"By your grace, may there be no fault in this worship that has been interrupted for so long"; having obtained this assurance, one should perform the rite again as before.
But whatever fault has arisen by the power of disease, one should perform its purification through recitation,
or through giving, or through fire-offerings, or even through wealth.
Now, the section on fire regarding the atom.

Now, regarding those subject to birth-impurity (sūtakin), the Vedic rites prescribed by the Smṛtis are to be performed constantly; first comes the impurity due to birth, and at its conclusion follows the impurity due to death.
O Goddess, during the birth-impurity of a twice-born man, one should not perform the eradication of deities;
rather, having meditated upon the Supreme Goddess, one should perform the mental *saṃdhyā*.
O beloved, one should never touch a Śālagrāma stone or its image; by touching it, a man becomes a sinner, for there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Having performed the Tantric worship and so forth, one should carry it out with the mind alone;
however, if the practice is for the sake of a specific desire, then one should perform it as previously described.
Having abandoned the house of death through the practice of the left-hand path (vāmācāra),
and having cast aside desire, one attains the dharma of the Kula lineage preceded by knowledge.
By practicing the Vāma dharma, one is born as a deity;
he who performs the rites taught by the guru with devotion follows the Vāma path.
The reality of the scripture and the reality of the deity are not external; that [reality] is indeed the Guhyaka.
Having known it thus, one who worships it for the sake of happiness is born therein.
A hungry ghost (preta), deluded by hunger and thirst, should contemplate that dharma;
for if one does not possess it, there will be no means for one's livelihood, such as travel and so forth.
The offering of water should be performed with ritual water; however, if no water is available at all,
then one should worship the deity with mental visualizations, flowers, and so forth.
Devotion, faith, and contemplation are said to be the life-force of worship.
Now follows the section on the dull-witted.
I shall describe the daily ritual for the insentient [deities], as well as the procedure in brief:
the jewel-pavilion, the fourfold [principles] beginning with Dharma, and the serpent-king’s path.
The primary form and the six limbs—their worship is thus prescribed.
Indeed, when none of the ritual materials are available, one of steady mind should perform the meditation alone; one should not perform the worship with anything other than pure water.
In general, worship is threefold—superior, middling, and inferior;
yet it is further divided into a hundred ways by way of the qualified practitioner and the specific occasion.

That worship which is performed with all the necessary implements and is considered the most excellent is the highest; however, worship performed with whatever materials are obtained or prepared is the middling one.
In that place, worship performed with flowers and water is designated as the lowest form,
as ordained by the stainless Brahman-sages who have mastered all the Vedas.
But that worship which is performed with a pure nature (sāttvikī) bestows liberation;
it was practiced by royal sages who were devoted to it and who knew the true reality of the Blessed One.
That worship which is performed correctly by women, children, the elderly, the ignorant, and others who are devoted with noble minds, is royal and bestows happiness.
That worship which is performed constantly is proclaimed as tāmasī.
In the forest, worship is beneficial for those with few desires for the sake of attaining spiritual perfection;
however, for householders free from desire, worship is beneficial within the home.
The path of the Vedas, born of delight, is always maintained by the twice-born;
for those who have fallen away from the Vedas, both the status of a Brahmin and even divinity are difficult to attain.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Varieties of Worship Beginning with Feeding, from the Sāttvika to the End," in the *Śrī Tantracintāmaṇi*.
O wise ones, I have already spoken of that which is common to all;
now, however, I shall describe the ten kalpas of the Vidyā in their proper sequence.
Now, Śyāmā states the specific sequence.
Having performed all [rites] such as bathing and the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) as before,
that yogi, free from external pride, should likewise enter the sacrificial ground (yāgabhūmi).
Now he states the location.
Staying at a solitary linga, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, or at a crossroads,
the yogi should accomplish the vidyā that liberates from the three realms of existence.
He states their defining characteristics:
Where no other *liṅga* is found within a distance of five *krośas*, that is declared to be *Kaliṅga*; there, the highest accomplishment (*siddhi*) is attained.
When it is surrounded by vultures, jackals, crows, and others, greedy for flesh;
It was known as Tachmaśāna, frequented by hosts of piśācas,
filled with crows, vultures, and the like, and teeming with worms, insects, and so forth.
That which is abandoned from afar by the citizens, devoid of the cause for any agitation,
and filled with women dwelling in palatial mansions, is called an empty house.
Where the meeting of four roads occurs simultaneously, that is called a crossroads; at night, it bestows what is desired.
Each preceding one is mixed with [the previous], while each subsequent one is more excellent;
this may be performed on Mount Urjaṭa, or even in a secluded place or at a crossroads.
In a temple devoid of deities, at the foot of a bilva tree, on a riverbank, in one's own home,
in a secluded place, O Rāma, or likewise in the vicinity of an aśvattha tree.
In the absence of that [image], one should worship in a celestial abode adorned with vermilion and other substances,
and furnished with a sword, trident, mace, scimitar, chowries, fans, and so forth.
In a place filled with canopies and incense, fragrant with black aloe-wood,
and beautified by the dancing of young courtesans intoxicated with wine.
Resounding with the sounds of conchs and bells, and adorned with rows of lamps,
the worship of Kālikā in the son’s house was thus most beautiful.
Now, he states the time.
Every moment is indeed auspicious; no inauspicious time exists anywhere.
There is no distinction between day and night, nor between the twilight and the night.
There is no distinction between day and night, nor between twilight and the night;
however, if all the offerings, worship, and so forth are performed during the night, [the result is superior].
That [merit] attains imperishability through the grace of Kālikā,
provided it is performed from the first watch until the end of the third watch.
The family worship should be performed by those well-versed in the family scriptures;
having taken a water-conch in hand, one should go to the door of Maheśvarī.
And one should wash one's hands and feet according to the method that will be described.
Then, having brought water with his right hand while reciting the mantra "Oṃ vajrodake hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," the knower of mantras should purify the seat.
Having first extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ) and likewise the seed-syllable *jaj*,
one should then [utter] "viśuddhānte sarvapāpāni śamaya" (at the end of purification, pacify all sins).
After that, one should say, "Remove all conceptual constructions without exception.
Then, having performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana), one should prepare the general water offering (sāmānyārghya).
Then, one should fashion a triangular mandala upon a circular base;
having worshipped the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti), one should place the support (ādhāra) therein.
Having purified it with the Astra-mantra, one should fill it with the Hrdaya-mantra;
having invoked the Tirthas, one should pour them in while offering perfumes and other articles with the Pranava.
One should indeed display the bow-mudrā; this is known as the general arghya.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should worship those stationed at the entrance with the general arghya.
One should then enter Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, Vaṭuka, and likewise Yoginī, as well as Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Lakṣmī, and Vāṇī.
Then [one should worship] Gaṇeśa beginning with *gāṃ*, likewise Vaṭuka beginning with *vāṃ*,
Kṣetrapāla beginning with *kṣāṃ*, and thereafter the Yoginīs beginning with *yāṃ*.
Thus they are proclaimed as being in the upper, left, right, and lower directions.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, followed by "sarvavighnān," then "utsāraya," then "hūṃ phaṭ," and immediately after that, "svāhā."
With this very mantra, the wise one should dispel all obstacles.
Having first extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ), and then "rakṣa rakṣa" (protect,
protect), followed by "hūṃ phaṭ svāhā"— with this mantra, one should purify the ground for worship.
Then, when the vajra and other [mantras] have commenced, one should first extract the syllable Om (praṇava);
thereafter, "carmayaṃ," and immediately after that, "phaṭ svāhā."
And with this very mantra, one should perform the consecration of the ground.
Furthermore, regarding the consecration of Puṣya, one should first extract the *praṇava* (oṃ);
then the word *ṭhātābhiṣeka*, and thereafter the word *ṭhātābhi*.
The word "Ṣeka" is proclaimed, followed by "hūṃ phaṭ svāhā";
with this mantra, one performs the consecration of flowers for the Goddess.
Having uttered the Praṇava, then "Puṣpaketu," likewise "Rājārha," and "Ṭhātāyasasya," followed thereafter by "Saṃbuddhāya."
Puṣpe puṣpe mahāpuṣpe supuṣpe puṣpasambhave | puṣpe ca yāvakīrṇe hūṃ phaṭ svāhā ca tataḥ param ||
With that pure flower, one should take up water as before.
Seated on a soft cushion or upon other gentle seats,
one who is well-seated shall accomplish the supreme perfection.
O Goddess, if a man recites the mantra of Kālikā without the corpse-seat (mṛtāsana),
he shall remain a denizen of hell for as long as the dissolution of the world (saṃplava).
Having then established the seer and the meter, one should cause kusha grass to be placed right there,
having uttered the seed-syllable of Maya preceded by the Support-Energy (Ādhāraśakti).
Having drawn the lotus-seated one, one should worship him with the mantras ending in *ṅeṃ* and *oṃ*;
then [worship] *Surekhe* ending in *ākāra*, and after that, *Vajrarekhe*.
One should indeed perform the maṇḍala on a corpse-seat with the mantra "hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," and sit in the vīrāsana posture after having worshipped the seat itself.
Now, as for the heroic posture (vīrāsana), it is as follows:
Placing one foot upon one thigh while remaining seated,
with the other [foot] likewise [placed], this is declared to be the beautiful Vīrāsana posture.
Now he describes the sipping of water with mantras (mantrācamana).

Having sat upon the seat, the sipping of water (ācamana) with the mantras bestows all accomplishments; having drunk with the three *kāli* mantras, one should perform the ritual rinsing (*upaspṛśet*) with the *kālyā* and other mantras.
Having wiped the two lips twice with two [fingers] and washed the hand once with one,
one should touch the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, navel, chest, and arms.
He who performs this ritual sipping (ācamana) in this manner shall behold her after one year;
thereafter, having carefully brought a sixteen-year-old woman, he should proceed.
A young woman, charming and intoxicated with passion, well-attired and sweetly smiling; ever longing for the aesthetic delight of love, her forehead marked with vermilion.
The wise practitioner should place a woman of loving character on his left side.
Without having tasted the *kama* [wine] according to the prescribed cause, the Great Goddess Maheśvarī becomes agitated;
one should not perform worship, nor recitation, nor meditation, nor even contemplation.

Therefore, having eaten and drunk, one should worship the Supreme Goddess with the *kūrca* mantra joined by *viyat* (the letter *h*) and the *bindu* (the nasal dot), as well as with *śaktyastrāya phaṭ*.
With this mantra, one should perform the binding of the directions by means of finger-snaps and other gestures;
first uttering the Praṇava (Oṃ), and immediately thereafter—
"HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ" is declared as the mantra for purifying body, speech, and mind;
"RAKṢA RAKṢA HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ" is the mantra for one's own protection.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, one should mentally place the Guru and Gaṇapati on the left and right sides, and one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) in front.
Having taken fragrant flowers smeared with sandalwood paste,
the knower of mantras should rub them on his two hands with the *hyauṃ* mantra and the *astra* mantra.
Taking that flower with the left hand,
one should whirl it around the head while reciting the *tāra* mantra, and then smell it again.
Oṃ! This verse is recited at the beginning of the chapter:
"May all those harmful ones who indeed injure this [mantra] go to destruction."
"May death, disease, fear, and afflictions fall upon the head of the enemy!
With this weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), one should cast [the offering] toward the north using the nārāca-mudrā."

Then one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), uniting the self with Kuṇḍalinī; having joined the individual soul (jīva) with the Haṃsa-mantra by means of the central channel (madhyamā) and the others, [one should merge it] into Śiva.
One should dry up the cruel sin residing within the belly by means of the syllables of wind (ya), fire (ra), and wind (ya); having burned it within, one should wash it away and exhale it outside.
One should lead that very [consciousness] back to its proper place with the *so'ham* mantra;
thereafter, having a purified body, one should perform the *jīvanyāsa*.
Now, he explains her purification, which is of the nature of mantra.
Then one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) through the application of the syllables of one's own mantra;
as is Kālī, so is Tārā, and as is Tārā, so is Unmukhī.
One should perform all the rites, beginning with the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), in the same manner as for Tāriṇī.
Thereafter, one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) for a duration of twenty-four minutes.
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), Uṣṇik is cited as its meter (chandas),
Kālikā is declared to be its deity, and the seed-syllable of modesty (lajjā-bīja) is its seed-mantra (bījaka).
The Śakti is the Kūrca-bīja, the Kīlaka is the Udyat-bījaka;
O Maheśānī, the Viniyoga is for the attainment of the four aims of life.
The ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) are now described according to the rule:
one should perform them using the seed-syllable (*bīja*) preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and endowed with the six long vowels.

One should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) using the Praṇava as the initial seed-syllable, differentiated by the six long vowels, and also by means of the three sections of the root mantra.
Then one should perform the deposition of the letters (varṇanyāsa), which bestows the fruit of divine nature,
by placing the letters of the Mātṛkā along with the bindus upon the heart, the two arms, and the pair of feet.
Thereafter, one should arrange [the mantras] row by row and perform the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa);
one should perform the pervasive placement with both arms while reciting the root-vidyā.
Having thus performed the placement once— from the feet to the head and from the head to the end of the feet— the practitioner becomes one with that.
Now follows the placement of the phonemes (varṇanyāsa).
One should place the ten syllables beginning with *a* in the heart,
and the ten beginning with *e* on the right arm.
Having placed the ten syllables beginning with *ṅa* on the left arm,
one should place the supreme ten syllables beginning with *ña* on the right leg.
One should place the letters beginning with 'ma' and ending with 'kṣa' upon the left shank.
Thus ends the placement of the letters (varṇanyāsa).
Now follows the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
I shall describe the sixfold nyāsa, which is difficult to obtain in the three worlds;
by performing which, the best of practitioners becomes equal to Bhairava himself.
One should first arrange the Mātṛkā; this is remembered as the first nyāsa.
One should place each syllable encapsulated by Śrī, and Śrī encapsulated by each syllable.
Having thus arranged them in sequence, the second [mantra] is proclaimed;
it consists of Lakṣmī encased by Kāma, and that [Kāma] encased by Lakṣmī.
One should place it in the locus of the Mātṛkās; this is declared as the third [method]:
Lakṣmī encapsulated by Lajjā, and Hrī encapsulated by Śrī.
The practitioner of mantras should perform the placement as before; this is declared to be the fourth placement (turyanyāsa).
Mounted upon the circle of the mouth are the two pairs of the letters *lajjā* (hrīṃ) and *namaḥ*.
Having placed [the syllable] mounted on the crescent moon in the position of Kāma and Śakra,
one should enclose the root mantra within that enclosure.
One should perform the placement according to the stated path; this shall be the fifth nyāsa, consisting solely of the letters in their places, both in direct and reverse order.
Having placed the root [mantra], the wise one should mutter the root mantra one hundred and eight times and then distribute it throughout the body; this is declared to be the sixth nyāsa.
This sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa) of the King of Mantras of Kālikā has been declared;
having performed this placement in such a manner, that practitioner of mantra becomes equal to Bhairava.
It removes death caused by poison, destroys the afflictions of planetary influences and diseases;
all the wicked perish, and enemies turn into friends.
The succession of grape-juices of his poetic waves is established;
indeed, the eight supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā), reside in his hand.
Whatever misdeed has been committed— whether physical, verbal, or mental—
all of it goes to destruction through the contemplation of the Nyāsa.
The killing of a Brahmin and whatever minor offenses there may be go to destruction; and whatever form is seen by whomsoever, he assumes that very form.
O Great Goddess, he whom those whose bodies are folded in the six ways salute shall immediately become short-lived; even the deity trembles with fear.
He is Hara, he is Hari manifest, and she is the Goddess herself; there is no doubt in this matter.
One should perform this ritual placement (nyāsa) for Tārā and likewise for Unmukhī.
Such a person shall become a lord of the eight supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā).
Now follows the secret sixfold deposition (guhya-ṣoḍhā-nyāsa).
The Lord said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim this secret sixfold [mantra], O beloved;
this must not be revealed anywhere if one desires one's own welfare.
O Pārvatī, one should place camphor enclosed by the letters of the Mātṛkā in the locus of the Mātṛkā;
by that very [enclosure], one should install the letter enclosed within it right here.
O Goddess, the pair of *kūrca* seeds should be carefully placed;
likewise, O Goddess, one should place the *śakti* seed and the root mantra at the beginning.
On the right, one should place the three preceding seed-syllables for Kālikā,
the three Kūrca seed-syllables, O Goddess, and the two Lajjā seed-syllables.
In that manner, O Goddess, the Mīlita [mudrā] should be placed by the one born of fire (Svāhā);
then, O Goddess, having performed the placement of all [the limbs], it should be done as a pervasive [placement].
In this mantra of twenty-two syllables, the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa) has been proclaimed;
it bestows success in this world as well as among the gods and the asuras.
This must necessarily be performed every day; neither worship nor recitation is required.
Even when this is done, the practitioner becomes excellent and equal to Mahādeva.
Thus, O Ghoradākṣiṇī, I have told you a certain secret;
it must never be disclosed, whether among the gods or among men.
Now follows the assignment of the principles (tattvanyāsa).
One who knows the self should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the reality (tattva) by means of the auspicious principles (tattvas).
p. 135b) Now, the placement of the seed-syllables (bījanyāsa).

Then, one should place the seven seed-syllables in the space between the eyebrows and the Brahma-locus, on the forehead, at the region of the navel, in the private parts, in the mouth, and upon all the limbs.
Now follows the placement of the mantra syllables (mantravarṇanyāsa).
On the head, the eyes, the forehead, the pair of eyebrows, the ears and cheeks, the mouth, the teeth, the region of the tongue, the shoulders, and the necks;
One should place the mantra syllables on the arms, heart, both sides, back, navel, Rudra (the genitals), waist, belly, and feet, and everywhere else.
O Dear One, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) nine times with the root mantra;
or likewise five times, nine times, or seven times with the root mantra.
Then he should assume the dress of a woman, with his forehead marked with vermilion;
adorned with erotic ornaments and a radiant costume, his mouth filled with betel leaf.
In this manner, one should likewise cause all [the attendants], beginning with the courtesans, as well as the women, to be fashioned;
thereafter follows the ritual placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa), preceded by the foundational power (ādhāraśakti).
Prakṛti, Kaṭha, Śeṣa, and likewise Pṛthivī;
the Ocean of Nectar, Maṇidvīpa, and likewise the house of the Cintāmaṇi jewel.
The preeminent practitioner should place a cremation ground and a *pārijāta* tree there, and at its base, a jeweled altar; upon that, he should set down a throne.
In the four directions, [he visualizes] sages, gods, corpses, and skull-bearers;
and likewise, the principles beginning with Dharma (Dharmādi) at the four parts of the body, starting from the feet.
Likewise, O Maheśvarī, within the heart-lotus there is a lotus, as well as the sun and moon,
and likewise Vaiśvānara, along with sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Having first established the self, one should place the Śakti in the heart-lotus;
she is indeed Will, Knowledge, and Action, the beloved who bestows all desires.
Ratī, Ratipriyā, Ānandā, Karṇikā, and Manonmanī;
having first uttered the Vāgbhava [bīja], one should then say "to Parā."
For that which is to be expressed beyond this is indeed *yauṃ*.
Then, "Sadāśiva-mahāpreta-ṅenta-padmāsanāya namaḥ"— this is declared to be the mantra for the placement of the seat (pīṭha-nyāsa).
Then one should perform the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjā), with the primary [deities] being one's own Śaktis:
Ugrā, Ugrā, Caṇḍā, Cāmuṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Vikaṭā, and Utkatā.
Saṃkaṭā, Caṇḍogrā, and likewise Maṅgalacaṇḍikā.
Herein is the internal sacrifice.
In this manner, one should meditate upon the chosen deity within the seat consisting of the body.
Now follows the external departure.
Having thus disposed his body, he should extract the King of Yantras from a copper vessel,
a skull, or one fashioned from the wood of a cremation ground.
On a Saturday or a Tuesday, when death occurs in the body,
the wheel should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite with gold, silver, or iron.
"Āsurekhe vajrarekhe hūṃ phaṭ vahnivallabhā"—
with this mantra, one should draw the captivating king of diagrams (yantra).
Svayambhū flower, the substance produced from the *kudagola* plant, *rocanā*, *guru*, saffron,
musk, lotus, and sandalwood from Malaya.
This fragrance has been fully described, O beloved Caṇḍikā;
with this application of fragrance, one should draw the yoni-cakra.
O beloved, listen now to the yantras of Śrī Kālī according to the division of mantras;
