first, having generated the Power (Śakti), there is a quartet of powers.
O Śivā, one should draw the bindu in the center according to the sequence of the outer and inner [circles].
O Queen of the Gods, having drawn this, it should be joined with a single *bhūpura* (fortress-square).
In some places, the term *bhūpura* is proclaimed to mean a square;
here, by the term *bhūpura*, it should consist of four gates.
Having drawn three triangles and a hexagon above them, one should then draw a circle,
an eight-petaled lotus, and another circle, all provided with an outer enclosure of walls (bhūpura).
In the center of the Bindu is the Yantra of Śrī Māyākālī, which bestows perfect accomplishment.
Listen to another mantra, O wise one: a person of intelligence should draw a *yonicakra* (womb-diagram).
Having drawn two wombs, there should then follow a hexagon.
Then, O Maheśānī, this yantra, consisting of an eight-petalled lotus together with a house of earth, bestows great sovereignty.
First, having drawn a yoni, one should draw another yoni outside of it;
then, three yonis outside of that, and thereafter, one should draw a circle.
Then, having drawn an eight-petalled lotus and a circle above that,
as well as the abode of Dharaṇī, this yantra has been described by me.
Having first generated Śakti, one should then draw two Śaktis;
having generated Vahni-Śakti, one should cause the external Śakti to be divided.
One should extend the fire downward according to the sequence of breaking the knots;
likewise, one should pierce upward through Śakti according to the sequence of the divisions of fire.
One should differentiate the fire above by division and likewise differentiate the fire below;
with three [units] of the womb and two of the fire, this is the Kālīyantra, which bestows perfect accomplishment.
A hexagon, a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, a hexagon marked with vajras, and outside that a square enclosure (bhūpura)— this is the yantra, provided with three enclosures.
By means of the *śakti* and the fire-mantra (*agnibīja*), a hexagon is formed, within which there should be three *yoni*s;
then a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, and the earth [square] adorned with four gates.
In the center of the yantra of Śrī Dakṣiṇakālī is the Māyā-bīja (Hrīṃ) as its ornament;
listen as the determination of the seed-syllables according to the division of mantras is now described.
If it is joined with the Nāda and Bindu, it is proclaimed as the Power of Consciousness (Cicchakti).
One should meditate upon the Virāḍ-bīja in due order within the Bījayantra.
Then one should perform the worship of the *pīṭha*, beginning with the worship of the foundational power (*ādhāraśakti*).
Then [one should meditate on the Goddess] flashing like lightning within the heart-lotus.
The wise practitioner, using the mantra beginning with "Deveśī" and so forth, should perform the invocation;
then, through meditation on the *kāmakalā*, he should invoke the auspicious Kālikā.
One should place flowers in the center of the cakra using the mudrā known as kūrma.
Meditation on the Kāmakalā.
The face has the form of a drop (bindu), and below that is the pair of breasts, filled with the nectar of all vidyās; it bestows all diseases and worldly existence.
It accomplishes all aims and causes all people to rejoice;
beneath that is a well-adorned maṇḍala extending for a parārdha.
He is the source of all beings, including the gods; he is saluted by all the gods;
he is completely fulfilling to all and the cause of delight for everyone.
This meditation on Kāmakalā, which accomplishes all aims, brings all deities under control, and sets everything in motion, must be kept strictly secret by the most excellent practitioners.
As for the tortoise mudrā: ||
Then, with the index finger of the left hand and the little finger of the right,
as well as the index finger of the right hand, one should join them to the thumb of the left hand.
One should raise the right thumb and join the middle and other fingers of the left hand to the back of the right hand.
One should perform [the offering] with the left hand using the *pitṛtīrtha*, with the middle and ring fingers likewise;
then, one should turn those two downward and use the right hand.
A tortoise held in the hands bestows such universal accomplishment;
one should place it near the heart while closing both eyes.
Keeping the body, head, and neck straight, the wise practitioner, remaining most steady,
should begin meditation— the destroyer of all sins.
Now, as for meditative absorption (dhyāna).
Now I shall describe the meditation upon the Goddess, adorned by all the deities—
the auspicious Goddess whose face is formidable and who resembles collyrium and other such substances.
She is adorned with a garland of severed heads, her hair is disheveled, and her face is smiling;
she stands upon the lotus-heart of Mahākāla, her breasts full and firm.

She who delights in the perverse, who is attached [to her passions], whose fangs are terrible, who indeed has a serpent as her sacred thread, and who has the crescent moon as her crest-ornament— by Śiva [she was embraced].
Adorned with every ornament and decorated with pearls and gems,
she had a thousand dead hands bound as a girdle and was naked.
She is resplendent with thousands of crores of Śivās and Yoginīs;
her lotus-like face is filled with blood, and she is intoxicated by the drinking of wine.
She has eyes like fire, the sun, and the moon; her face is quivering with redness;
she is adorned with colorful ornaments made from two lifeless young birds.
One should meditate upon the divine Kālikā, who has a terrifying face, is formidable, has disheveled hair, possesses four arms,
and is adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Her head is severed instantly; her upper left lotus-hand holds a sword,
while her lower right hand displays the gestures of fearlessness and the granting of boons.
She has the luster of a great cloud, is dark-hued, and likewise naked;
she is smeared with blood dripping from a garland of severed heads around her neck.
She had made the pair of Śiva’s ears her earrings;
she was terrifying, with fierce fangs and a gaping mouth, and possessed full, elevated breasts.
Her waist girdled by the hands of corpses, her face smiling,
with streams of blood flowing from both corners of her mouth, her countenance radiant.
She of terrible form, most fierce, dwelling in the abode of the cremation ground,
with protruding teeth, auspicious, divine, and with her mass of hair loose and hanging down.
O Mahādeva in the form of a Śava, she is seated upon your heart,
surrounded on the four sides by Śivās who utter terrible roars.
Together with Mahākāla, she is intent upon the supreme delight;
her face is serene and her eyes are bright, her lotus-face smiling.
Having thus reflected upon Kālī, who dwells in the abode of the cremation ground,
Having meditated and invoked the Goddess, one should display the *yonimudrā*;
indeed, one should display the great *yonimudrā* characterized by the sword, the severed head, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Now, he describes the sequence of mudrās beginning with the sword (khaḍga).
Having bound the little and ring fingers with the thumbs on the right side,
while the remaining fingers are extended and touched together, this is the sword mudrā (khaḍgamudrikā).
Having formed a fist with the left hand, with the thumb inside,
one should likewise carefully grasp the two middle fingers of the right hand.
O Lord, the practitioner should place the middle finger of the right hand upon the tips of the thumb and index finger of the left fist.
This is called the Muṇḍa-mudrā when shown on the right side;
the right hand placed below and extended is the Vara-mudrā.
The left hand is raised and extended in the *abhaya-mudrā*;
the index, ring, and middle fingers are [extended], while the little finger is bent toward the wheel.
One should join the two hands by separating the bases of the little fingers;
having placed the tips of the thumbs [therein], it is proclaimed as the Mahāyoni.

Now, since the universe consists of the nature of both [Śiva and Śakti], and because there is no fruit in the worship of Śiva without Śakti or of Śakti without Śiva, he speaks of the worship of both as a single deity.
And so it is said:
O Goddess, without Prakṛti, saṃsāra does not exist anywhere;
and O Goddess, without Puruṣa, knowledge does not bestow perfection.
Mahākāla is the deity of Kālikā, Laliteśvara of Sundarī,
Akṣobhya of Tārā, and Vikarālaka of Chinnā.
Mahādeva resides in Bhuvanā, Kālabhairava in Dhūmrā;
Nārāyaṇa is in Mahālakṣmī, and Vaṭuka is said to be in Bhairavī.
From Mātaṅgī, Mataṅga shall arise, or else Sadāśiva;
Mṛtyuñjaya is proclaimed to be from Vagalā-vidyā.
Therefore, O Goddess Śivā, for that reason one should worship the second [deity];
one should first worship Mahākāla and afterwards worship the Goddess.
One should worship Mahākāla to the right of the Goddess; he is smoke-colored, holding a staff and six limbs, with fangs and a terrifying face like a child.
His waist was covered with a tiger skin; he was pot-bellied and wore red garments;
he had three eyes and hair on his head, and was adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Having meditated thus upon Mahākāla— fierce with a sword, possessing matted locks and a radiant crescent moon, and blazing as if on fire— one should worship him with the very mantra of Mahākāla.
Having extracted the armor (*kavaca*) from *sphauṃ*, the discus (*cakra*) is considered to be *yālārāvāṃ*. [The mantra continues with] "O Mahākāla Bhairava, O destroyer of all obstacles."
By reciting it again, one destroys illusion (māyā) and uplifts prosperity (lakṣmī).
This mantra, joined with *phaṭ* and *svāhā*, accomplishes all aims.

Then, having again meditated upon the Goddess, the wise and intelligent practitioner should worship Her with all ritual offerings while reciting the root mantra, offering the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Kālikā.
Having satisfied her with three offerings of betel leaf and having bowed down, one should display the yoni-mudrā;
one should worship the Goddess, holding a sword and a severed head in her left upper and lower hands.
One should worship the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting on the upper and lower parts of the goddess's right hand.
Having informed the Goddess, one should likewise worship her attendants;
then, at the conclusion of the six-limbed worship (ṣaḍaṅga-pūjā), one should worship the lineage of gurus.
Thereafter, one should likewise worship the deities of the limbs with water for the feet and other offerings;
in all mantras, they bestow success everywhere when placed at the beginning.
O God, I shall now briefly describe before you the divine lineages of gurus, as well as the lineages of the Siddhas and the human lineages of gurus.
In that regard, O Goddess Kālikā, listen to the lineage of her gurus:
Mahādevī, Mahādeva, Tripurā, and Bhairava.
The Gurus of the Divine Current (divyaugha) have been declared; now I shall describe the Siddhas of the Siddha Current (siddhaugha):
Brahmānanda, Pūrṇa, Calacitta, and Calācala.
Kumāra, Krodhana, Varada, and Smaradīpana;
Māyā and Māyāvatī—listen, O beloved, to [the names of] the multitudes of Mānavas.
Vimala, Kula, Bhīmasena,
Sudhākara, Mīna, Gorakṣanātha, Bhojadeva, and Prajāpati.
Mūladeva, Raṃtideva, Vighneśa, Hutāśana,
Samaya, Ānanda, and Saṃtoṣa are remembered as the Gurus of Kālikā.
The divine goddesses are eternally present here on the ground of accomplishment (siddhābhūmi);
and among humans, the multitudes of men always bear my own form.
The gurus ending with the word "Ānandanātha" bestow all spiritual accomplishments;
even women, if they are in the form of a guru, are proclaimed to end with the suffix "-ātma."
At the conclusion of the multitude of human beings, the Goddess should worship her own Guru;
having first meditated upon her own Guru, she should then [meditate upon] the fourfold lineage of Gurus.
Having performed worship, one should sacrifice to the God and perform the nine-fold contraction (navasaṃkoca),
as well as to the Guru, the Paramaguru, and likewise the Parāparaguru.
Parameṣṭhin and the Guru—these have been declared as your gurus.
Now, he states the position of the preceptors.
O Maheśānī, the Gurus are always present behind Vidyā;
[the ritual] proceeds by way of three rows along the back of the Goddess.
Following the sequence beginning with the divine [mantras], one should place one's own three gurus below that;
then, one should draw three lines toward the south, north, and west.
The divine stream consists of the deities on the back [of the seat]; the other two, however, are on the ground and in the heart.
In the division of the Vidyā, O Śivā, one should worship one's own guru.
O Great Goddess, you alone are proclaimed to be the station of the Guru.
Now, he states the necessity of this.
O child, if one should commence worship without first performing the worship of the Guru,
one should perform the worship of Śakti in order to pacify that fault.
Wherever anything may be defective, it becomes endowed with qualities through worship of the lineage;
likewise, upon beholding the lineage, where indeed is there any need for cleansing as prescribed?
Where is bathing, where is purity of speech, and where is purification by the month?
If there is initiation, a master, and those of noble lineage—if the lineage itself is Vaṭukeśvara—then all is complete.
Having brought the Guru into that body, one should meditate upon the Guru in the form of the Kula;
for as the Guru is the Kula there, so is the Kula-practitioner not [the Kula].
The lineage of the gurus has been told, which must be guarded with great effort; and by no means should their names be uttered even by the foremost among them.
Then, the deities of the enclosure [are placed] in the fifteen corners.
And so it is said:
Then, having invoked the Goddess in all the corners, one should worship her.
Then, one should worship in the corners starting from the east, proceeding counter-clockwise.
Kālī, Kapālinī, and Hullā are in the first triangle;
Nīlā, Aghanā, and Valākā are in the second triangle.
Kurukullā and Virodhinī are in the third triangle, Vipravittā in the fourth; Ugrā, Ugraprabhā, and Dīptā are in the fourth triangle.
One should worship Mātrā, Mudrā, and Mitā, and the fifth in the triangle;
all of them are dark-complexioned, holding swords in their hands, and adorned with garlands of severed heads.
Holding the index finger with their left hands, they are well-proportioned;
the practitioners should perform the worship for all of them three times each.
Now, on the eight-petaled [lotus].
One should worship Brahmā and the others on the petals, and worship the Bhairavas at the tips of the petals;
then one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) outside of that, and their weapons further outside.
Furthermore, outside the maṇḍala are Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Māheśvarī,
Cāmuṇḍā, Kaumārī, and Aparājitā.
Vārāhī should likewise be worshipped, and Nārasiṃhī in the same way;
then Tārā, Pāśā, Śrī, Brāhmī, and thereafter the venerable sandals (Śrīpādukā).
One should worship her and likewise meditate upon that beloved of Brahmā—
Brahmāṇī, mounted upon a swan, golden-hued, and four-armed.
She has four faces and three eyes, and she bears a beard, a lotus, a staff, a rosary of lotus seeds, and a sacred thread; she possesses a beautiful smile.
The best of practitioners should meditate upon the Goddess who wears a mass of matted hair;
having thus contemplated the consort of Brahmā, O Beloved, according to one's capacity and with devotion.
O Dear One, having first uttered "Oṃ," then "Ismṛtvā Nārāyaṇī Śrīpādukām," and thereafter "Pūjayāmi," one should meditate upon that Vaiṣṇavī form.
Nārāyaṇī is greatly radiant, dark-complexioned, and mounted upon Garuḍa;
she is adorned with various ornaments, possesses beautiful hair, and has four arms.
Holding a bell, a conch, a skull-cup, and a discus, she is supreme;
her gaze is rolling like that of one intoxicated with honey, and she is beautiful in every limb.
Having reflected thus, O Great Goddess, one should then meditate with effort;
having worshipped the Great Goddess, one should worship Māheśvarī once again.
O Dear One, having uttered "uṃ" with the bindu, then [utter] "Māheśvarīm," then say "Śrīpādukām," and then "I worship" (pūjayāmi), [one worships] the head.
O lady of beautiful hips, listen as I describe her meditation:
she is the consort of Maheśvara, mounted upon a bull, white in complexion, and endowed with three eyes.
The goddess, adorned with various ornaments, holds a skull-cup, a hand-drum, the gesture of granting boons, a trident of fear, and an axe.
And having performed meditation upon Maheśvarī, one should worship her according to one's ability.
Having uttered the seed-syllable *ṚM* and [the name of] Cāmuṇḍā, "I worship the Śrī-pādukā";
having thus worshipped the Great Goddess, one should then perform meditation.
And Cāmuṇḍā, who possesses a fierce laugh, whose face is revealed, whose countenance is terrifying, who has three eyes,

and who has the luster of a blue lotus; she whose body is joyful, who wears a garland of human heads and skulls, who holds a sword, a trident, a skull-cup, and a shield fashioned from a human head, and who is mounted upon a corpse.
And one should meditate upon her as being intoxicated with wine, joyful, and of fierce form.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the goddess Cāmuṇḍā, the sovereign of the world;
and having worshipped Kaumārī with the syllable *Ṛṃ*, one should perform the visualization (*dhyāna*).
Kaumārī has the luster of saffron, possesses three eyes, and is seated upon a peacock;
she has four arms and bestows fearlessness while holding a spear, a noose, and a goad.
One should contemplate her as being adorned with various ornaments and in a state of playful intoxication;
having performed meditation upon Kaumārī, one should worship her according to one's capacity.
One should worship the great goddess Aparājitā with the Vāgbhava [syllable] according to all the previously mentioned rites; thereafter, one should perform the meditation.
And one should meditate upon Aparājitā, who is yellow in color, bestows boons, displays the mudrās of the rosary and the gesture of granting boons, and holds a lotus and a citron.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, the practitioner should worship with devotion;
O Queen of the Gods, he should then worship Vārāhī with the syllable *au*.
O Parameśvarī, know that this Vārāhī is the state of being free from fear;
Vārāhī has the luster of smoke-colored hue, possesses the face of a boar, and is auspicious.
One should worship this supreme goddess Vārāhī according to the prescribed rite, who holds a shield, a sword, and a mace, and possesses four arms.
The foremost of practitioners should worship Nārasiṃhī with the Visarga;
Nārasiṃhī bears a body resembling that of Nṛsiṃha.
O Goddess, I shall now describe her meditation; listen to it from me.

With her tongue flickering in rage, her own mouth wide open, and eyes like the moon, sun, and fire; with her feet reddened by the blood of the lord of the Daityas whose body she has pierced, standing upon his chest;
holding a discus, a conch, a noose, a goad, a thunderbolt, a mace, and an elephant—she is truly terrifying.
I eternally praise Nṛsiṃhī, who has sharp-pointed fangs and a crown made of jewels.
Having meditated thus, one should worship Maheśvarī according to one's ability.
Then, on the tips of the eight petals, [one should worship] the Bhairavas and Bhairava himself.
Asita, Goruru, Caṇḍa, Krodha, Unmatta, Bhairava, Kapālī, and Bhīṣaṇa; Saṃhāra is remembered as the eighth.
Now follows its meditation.
May they grant [blessings], those who have the dark-blue hue of a mass of people, who possess excellent vetālas, skull-bowls, and trident-staves,
who are joined with small drums, who have three eyes, and whose staff-like arms are as fierce as the trunks of elephants.
With their foreheads knit in frowns that turned away from the fourth state, they possessed the tips of hair as lovely as swarms of bees;
with joyful inner hearts, they were in the bloom of youth and the like.
The mantra for these is as follows:
The short vowel joined with the bindu, preceded by Vāṅmāyā.
Then, in the place of the Bhairavas, the Bhairavīs are to be worshipped.
And Bhairavī, Mahāsiṃhī, Dhūmrabhīmā and the others—these four;
then Unmattabhairavī, and after that Vaśīkaraṇabhairavī.
On the tips of the petals, the practitioner of mantras should worship the goddess Bhairavī known as Mohanā;
he should worship these three times each with red garlands and ointments.
Now, their meditations:
I bow to the Goddess who possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns, who wears a crimson silk garment and a garland upon her head; whose breasts are smeared with red pigment;

who holds in her lotus-like hands a rosary, the Vidyā, the gesture of protection, and the gesture of boon-granting; who has three eyes, whose face is radiant, who possesses the beauty of the sun and moon, and who is adorned with a crescent moon.
I bow to her who wears a jewel crown and possesses a gentle smile.
Then, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) above the bhūpura.
Beginning from the east and ending with the northeast, the wise one should worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas),
having first uttered the seed-syllable of Indra (indrabīja) and then [the name] "to Indra."

Having spoken thus to the Lord of Suras (Indra), together with his limbs (attendants), and immediately thereafter to him along with his retinue, and then likewise to him equipped with weapons and vehicles;
He should not then offer salutations or worship to that vehicle.
One should worship the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) with their respective seed-syllables and so forth: Laṃ, Raṃ, Yaṃ, Kṣaṃ, Vaṃ, Yaṃ, Śaṃ, Haṃ, Aṃ, Kaṃ. Thus [one should worship].
But as for meditative absorption (dhyāna):
I worship Indra, the lord of the gods, who is yellow in color, mounted upon Airāvata, all-pervading, possessing a thousand eyes, two arms, and holding a yellow thunderbolt.
I salute Agni, the lord of splendor, who is red in hue, the sovereign holding a white spear, beautifully adorned, mounted upon a ram, and possessing blood-red eyes.
Yama, the lord of the pretas, is black, seated upon a buffalo;
he is cruel, bearing the staff of death, and surrounded by terrifying messengers.
And [he visualizes] Nirṛti, the lord of the Rākṣasas,
seated upon a corpse, smoke-colored, with a sword in his hand, and possessing tawny beard and fine mustache.
I bow to Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, who is seated upon a crocodile, whose lotus-like hand holds a noose resembling lightning, and whose body and tusks are brilliant white.
I meditate upon and worship with fervor the supreme Dhūmra, the lord of wind and vital breath, who is red in color, holds kusha grass in his hand,
and is mounted upon a Vātapramī deer.
And [he saw] Kuvera, the lord of the yakṣas, white in color, bearing a trident and a mace,
seated upon the throne of Narasiṃha, together with Medalā and Citriṇī.

One should visualize the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyādhipa), holding a blue trident, mounted upon a bull, possessing three eyes, with a moon upon his forehead, white in complexion, and wearing a mass of matted hair.
I worship Ananta, the pale-complexioned lord of serpents, adorned with a circle of hoods upon his head, possessing full and lofty coils, bearing the discus, and emitting poison.
I worship him, the Lord of the World and the Creator, who is red in color, holds a lotus in his hand, is auspicious, is mounted upon a swan, and is engaged in the recitation of the Vedas.
Likewise.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship everything according to the procedure taught by Indra;
one should worship the serpent Śeṣa between Rakṣas and Varuṇa.
Then, one should worship Brahmā between Īśāna and Śakra.
Now, the mudrās of the world-protectors are as follows:
When the hands are joined at the roots of the palms and all the fingers are extended, this is the *mudrā* of the World-Protectors; one should perform their worship by displaying it.
Now, outside the *bhūpura*, are the weapons of the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*).
Outside of that, O Goddess, one should worship the thunderbolt (vajra), the spear (śakti), the staff (daṇḍaka),
the sword (khaḍga), the noose (pāśa), the goad (aṅkuśa), the mace (gadā), and the trident (triśūla).
Likewise, the discus (cakra) should be worshipped between Kuvera and Varuṇa;
thereafter, one should worship the lotus (padma) between Īśāna and Śakra.
Now, in the absence of specific [mantras], he states the general mantra for the attendants:
The seed-syllables of the letters of the name today [should be used], ending in *ṅe* and followed by *namaḥ*. Having first extracted the word *śrī*, one should then extract the word *pādukā*.
I worship; after "namas," one should worship the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās). Then, one should indeed bestow the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) in the form previously described.
Accompanied by the circle of Yoginīs and joined with Mahākāla.
One should then worship Mahākāla on the right side of the Goddess;
having worshipped the Root Goddess with water for the feet and other offerings, one should thereafter satisfy her with libations.

Then, with devotion, one should offer incense, lamps, and likewise food offerings (naivedya) to the goddesses; then, with the water of the special arghya and unbroken grains (akṣata), one should offer three handfuls of flowers.
One should worship the Goddess’s upper left hand with a sword and her lower left hand with a severed head;
one should worship the upper right hand of the Goddess with the gesture of fearlessness and her lower right hand with the gesture of granting boons.
Again, having recited the root mantra,
one should utter "sāṅgāyai saparivārāyai" and then pronounce the name of the goddess ending in the dative case.
Now, the offering of food.
O Maheśvarī, one should offer the bali oblation at the conclusion of worship and at the beginning of meals.
Therein, first is the offering of the bali to Mahākāla; his mantra is as follows:
At the end of "hūm," [recite] "mahākālāc chmaśānādhipa" (O Mahākāla, Lord of the Cremation Ground).
At the end of this, [say] "gṛhṇa yugam" (accept the pair), followed by the offering of food with meat.
Then, cause my two feet to be grasped; thereafter, ward off all obstacles, grant me success, and bestow it upon me, accompanied by the *svāhā* exclamation.
One should cause [the offering] to be given to the deity Mahākāla with [the mantra] beginning with the Praṇava (Om).
Now follows the offering of the oblation (validāna) to the Goddess, along with its mantra.
Come, come, O Mother of the worlds, likewise O Birth-giver of the worlds;
accept, accept this constant offering of the bali-oblation from me henceforth.
"Grant me accomplishment, O pair of feet; thereafter, bring about the destruction of my enemies!
Having thus uttered the sound "vāyu," one should repeatedly recite the pair of *kūrca* mantras (*hūṃ*).
First, the two *hṛllekhās*, and again at the end, the two *ṭha*s;
having thus extracted the mantra, [one adds] *phaṭ* at the end for Vahnisundarī.
This wonderful rite of offering is concealed in all tantras;
one should cast the bali-offering according to the name [of the deity] in all the Kālī-vidyās.
Liberation is accomplished through offerings, heaven is accomplished through offerings;
therefore, O King, let that king recite the Śatruñjaya mantra while making offerings.
Having thus first performed the worship at the root according to the prescribed rule,
one should repeatedly offer food offerings and other gifts to the deity according to one's ability.
Then one should perform the *nīrājana* rite ten times with lamps;
thereafter, the practitioner, being composed, should bow to the Guru situated at the crown of his head.
One should recite the great mantra of Mahākāla one hundred and eight times.
The illustrious Lord said:
Having meditated upon the *kullukā* at the crown of the head, one should contemplate the bridge (*setu*) in the heart;
then, for the sake of purification, one should extract the great bridge (*mahāsetu*) in the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*).
In Maṇipūra is Nirvāṇa; according to the Mahākuṇḍalinīmata, Kāmarāja is in Svādhiṣṭhāna, and Kākinī is situated at the crown of the head.

Having meditated according to the rules, one should contemplate the Goddess as being thinner than a lotus fiber, extending from the vicinity of the *mūlādhāra* up to the *viśuddha* at the crown of the head.
The all-pervading Lord, surrounded by the root mantras, extends from the station of the Vedas to the end of the double-tongued one.
Now follows the Dīpanī-vidyā.
The beloved one, the seed-syllable of life, adorned with three feet and endowed with the nasal vowel (anusvāra) as its digit—
this is declared to be the triad of seed-syllables.
Then one should give Tuṃvuru, and after that, Saṃhāra;
O Goddess, one should join these at the beginning of the Vidyā, endowed with the three dots (bindus) and the Kalās.
This is the illuminating vidyā, saluted by all the traditions;
one should visualize the tongue as ablaze with the banners of its splendor.
If one should employ the supreme Kālikā mantra without knowing the illuminating Vidyā,
he shall meet death before long, and upon dying, he shall go to hell.
Now, the meditation on the mantra.
I shall now explain the meditation on the mantra, which bestows omniscience through recitation;
O Great Goddess, through meditation on the mantra, one attains success even beyond the Vedic path.
One should contemplate the entire Vidyā, from the base to the aperture of Brahma,
resembling ten million suns and previously beheld by yogis.
Perceiving with his intellect the identity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra, he—
contented and of steady mind— should recite the mantra along with its underlying impressions (vāsanā).
With a rosary of teeth and with a *nameru* tooth from a king's mouth,
one should then perform all the previously mentioned ritual placements (*nyāsa*) using the root mantra.
With a one-pointed mind, one should daily recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times, or half of that, or thirty, or even one hundred and eight times.
One should offer the fruit of the recitation, consisting of radiant light, into the hand of the Goddess;
then, praising her and circumambulating her, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff.
Then one should recite the armor-rite (kavaca) named Śrī Galanmaṅgala.
Now, the southern [altar].
Then, having placed a flower upon his head and prostrated with the eight limbs of the body,
he should extend his right hand while again bowing his face low.
One should show the right side [of the deity] and mentally circumambulate;
one should properly perform the circumambulation of Kālikā three times.
That circumambulation should be known as auspicious, bestowing satisfaction upon the entire host of gods;
so too for one who performs one hundred and eight circumambulations of Kālikā.
One attains all desires and thereafter shall attain liberation;
likewise, that which is spoken by the mind is declared to be equal to what is vocal and physical.
The entire procedure is to be performed as before, according to the distinction between the left and the right;
this specific detail has been stated, while the general rule was explained previously.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Determination of the Daily Worship of Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Now he speaks the Camphor Praise (Karpūra-stava).

Those who recite three times your seed-mantra— which consists of the letter *ka* (Karpūra), the middle vowel (*i*), the final vowel (*au*), devoid of its inherent vowel, joined with the moon (*i*) and the left eye (*i*)—
their speech, whether in prose or verse, flows spontaneously from the cavity of their mouths.
Resplendent with the beauty of a mass of dark clouds, [this is] for those who have attained all perfections.
O Great Goddess, if a person of dull intellect should ever recite even once this seed-syllable mantra, which begins with Īśāna, followed by the Moon, Vāma, Śravaṇa, and ends with Dvandva—
then having conquered the Lord of Speech and long deluded even the Giver of Wealth, he shall captivate the multitude of lotus-eyed women.
When he whose crest is the crescent moon, who possesses a great and most terrible roar as his ornament, prevails;

Those who recite the mantra "ĪŚO VAISVĀNARASTHAḤ ŚAŚADHARAVILASADVĀMANETREṆAYUKTO BĪJAṂ TE DVAṂDVAMANYADVIGALITA CIKURE KĀLIKE YE JAPAṂTI," they bring their enemies to ruin and lead even the three worlds into a state of subjugation by means of the pair of corners of their mouths.
In the two faces bearing the continuous stream, and in the one with three syllables on the right.
Above, in her left [hand], upon the palm of her lotus-like hand, is a severed head with a sword; below that, in her right, are the gestures of fearlessness and boon.
O Kālikā, who bestows the fruit of the three worlds!
Having recited this mantra of yours, which is the manifestation of your power, one should meditate for that purpose upon you in your left-facing form.
Of those [eight], eight are located in the hands; O lady with manifest teeth, these are the eight siddhis of Tryambaka.
Having joined the first of the classes [Ka] conjoined with fire [Ra], the moon [I], the three-fold *lalita* [Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Hrīṃ], the pair of *kūrca* [Hūṃ Hūṃ], the pair of *lajjā* [Śrīṃ Śrīṃ],

and thereafter the smiling face [Haḥ] along with the two below it [Phreṃ Phreṃ]; those who, O Mother, mutter this while contemplating their own true nature as the destroyer of Smara, they behold Lakṣmī in her entirety.
Those with eyes like the petals of a playful lotus become capable of assuming any form at will.
Whether individually, in pairs, or even all three together, they recite while constantly contemplating everything as being joined with your name— the supreme seed-syllable that is utterly secret.
O Goddess, when their eyes leave the sun— the bright orb with a lotus-face— Vāgdevī [appears] upon you,
who are rich with thick breasts and a neck adorned with a garland of severed heads.

O Mother, one should meditate upon you— residing on a couch in the cremation ground, with a girdle fashioned from the multitude of arms of the lifeless, your hips resplendent, clad in the directions as your garment, the creator of the three worlds, possessing three eyes, and intent upon amorous union with Mahākāla within your heart.
Even one of dull intellect is a poet.
I meditate upon you, the youthful consort of Hara, who have entered a funeral pyre that is intensely crowded with multitudes of corpses and heaps of skulls and bones—
both auspicious and terrible— and who, being ever satisfied by celestial union, never turns her gaze elsewhere.
Their contempt.
What shall we say to you, O Lord? This multitude of people are of dull intellect; neither Brahmā, nor Īśvara, nor Hari knows your supreme nature.
Nevertheless, our devotion to you makes us loquacious; therefore, this [fault] of ours must surely be forgiven by you.
The wrath of a beast is appropriate.
If a devotee, at night, while attached to the pleasures of youth with a woman whose breasts and hips are full on all sides, recites your mantra while meditating upon you,
then all the hosts of Siddhas, their hair disheveled and thirsting for him, shall become entirely subject to his will.
The poet lives for a very long time on this earth.
If one always recites the *viparītā* [mantra] while contemplating you, who possess the supreme erotic play of Mahākāla, and remains composed and healthy,
then for that wise man dwelling upon the surface of the earth, the consort of Hara shall become submissive at his lotus-hand.
The multitudes of great siddhis.
O Mother, since you produce this entire cycle of worldly existence, sustain it, and withdraw the whole world— beginning with the earth— at the time of dissolution;
therefore, even the Creator, the Lord of the three worlds, the Lord of Śrī, and indeed Maheśa as well, along with almost everyone else, [worship you].
He praises you.
Many serve the celestial vehicles that carry you, O Mother; yet they are deluded, for they do not know anything of the Supreme who is superior even to them.
Having propitiated the Primordial Goddess, who is worshipped at will by the gods beginning with Hari, Hara, and Viriñci,
I have taken refuge in her who is ever intent upon the great bliss of the essence of Rati.
The earth, the water, the pure fire, the wind, and the sky—you alone are the auspicious one; O Kālī, beloved of Śiva, you are everything.
What praise can there be for you, O Mother? Be gracious toward me, who am helpless.
May existence be favorable to me, and may my birth be fruitful.
Staying in a cremation ground, with hair flowing down from his well-set neck and wearing a garment of bark, he [offers] a thousand suns as a flower by means of his own emitted semen.
O Japan, having destroyed even each individual mantra, he becomes intent on the great *sālikhira* and becomes a beholder of the earth.
On a Tuesday at midday, when the sun is in Scorpio (Kuja-dine) and the moon is in Libra (Tulā), if one combs the hair that has lost its luster from being brushed in the house,
and while reciting [the mantra] even once with focused vision, he shall go forth mounted upon an elephant, surrounded by the earth.
The Gatekeeper of Good Poets.
If a devotee, meditating upon the great palace of the Flower-Bowed God (Kusumadhanu), strewn with his own flowers, mutters your mantra,
he becomes like a chief of the Gandharvas— a lord of rivers through his poetic flow— extending to the very ends of the earth.
Absorbed in the supreme state, he becomes manifest.

O Mother, may that person who meditates upon you— seated on a five-triple-spoked pedestal (tripañcāra-pīṭha) upon the heart of a corpse-Śiva, her face radiant with the essence of the nectar of passion and beauty, intensely united with Mahākāla,
and herself delighting in the bliss of union— even at night— be truly blessed.
The destroyer of Smara.

O you with sparse teeth, why would there not be every possible supernatural power (siddhi) for one who offers you as an oblation in worship hair, bones, meat, or even a cat, or at most a mouse, a ram, a man, a buffalo, or even a goat?
The unprecedented word comes forth.

One who is self-controlled, intent on eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), devoted to meditating upon your lotus feet during the day, and furthermore, at night, naked and engaged in the pleasure of sexual union— such a person should properly recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, O Supreme Goddess.
Equal upon the surface of the earth.
O Mother, this hymn of yours, known as the *Manusamuddhāraṇa-japasvarūpa*, which includes the ritual for worshipping your pair of lotus feet—
if one recites it at midnight or during the time of worship, even his mere prattle shall spread [with grace].
The nectar-essence belongs to the poet.
A herd of fawn-eyed women follows him, trembling with love; even the lord of the earth, a veritable representative of Kuvera, remains under his sway.
His enemies cast themselves into prison through the mere play of his amorous dalliance, while the devoted worshiper prevails as one eternally liberated.
The formal proposition.
Thus ends the Karpūra-stotra composed by the illustrious Mahākāla.
Now follows its preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa).
O Śaṅkara, please explain the application of this hymn called Kapūra, which was previously mentioned by you as the means for accomplishing the six rites (ṣatkarma).
The illustrious Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the ritual practice (*sādhana*) of the Karpūra-stava;
O Queen of the Gods, even if performed but once, Kālī shall always be pleased.
O Goddess, having bathed on a Saturday or a Tuesday with a restrained mind,
one should worship the goddess Kālikā and properly perform the formal ritual resolve (saṃkalpa).

O Goddess, having performed the preliminary rites such as the sixteen-fold service, the wise one should recite this unsurpassed hymn ten thousand times and offer oblations amounting to one-tenth of that number.
Then one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and the ritual ablution (abhiṣeka), and feed the Brāhmaṇas;
afterwards, for the sake of accomplishing one's own purpose, one should then carry out the ritual applications (prayoga).
O Goddess of the gods, for the sake of all undertakings, one who is imbued with specific desires should perform the practice one thousand and eight times.
In matters of attraction, subjugation, killing, and expulsion,
as well as when fear of a king has arisen, during famine, or in the face of an enemy's threat.
O Maheśānī, when fear has arisen, as well as in times of disease, grief, or danger, one should recite this hymn of Mahākālī; it bestows all-pervading peace.
At the conclusion, the worship of a maiden should be performed with a well-concentrated mind;
O Maheśānī, when this is done, perfect success will certainly be attained.
Now follows the Jaganmaṅgala-kavaca (The Armor for the Auspiciousness of the World).
Bhairavī said:
O Lord, O Master, I have heard of the worship of Kālī and various vidyās;
now I wish to hear the armor (kavaca) that was previously mentioned.
You alone are my refuge, O Lord; protect me from this peril of suffering.
The illustrious Bhairava said: Listen, O Bhairavī, beloved of my life-breath; I shall declare the secret, the armor named Śrījaganmaṅgala, which is the very embodiment of mantras.
Having recited and mastered it, one may delude the three worlds in an instant;
even Nārāyaṇa, having assumed a female form, [deluded] Maheśvara.
That yoga which the scion of Raghu brought to such agitation caused him to slay, as it were,
the night-stalkers such as Rāvaṇa and others who were arrogant due to their boons.
By whose grace even the Lord, the all-pervading conqueror of the three worlds,
as well as Kuvera the lord of wealth, the lord of the gods, and the lord of the earth, [attain their sovereignty].
Thus, O beloved, those gods who are masters of all supernatural powers (siddhis) are but a fraction [of its power];
Śiva is the seer (ṛṣi) of this armor (kavaca) known as the Śrījaganmaṅgala.
The meter is Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Kālikā, proclaimed as the Southern [Face];
she is for the enchantment of the worlds, for victory over the wicked, and for worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Its application is proclaimed for the attraction of women.
May Kālikā, the supreme single-syllabled *krīṃ*, protect my head.
KṚĪM KṚĪM KṚĪM: may Kālikā, the wielder of the sword, protect my forehead;
HŪM HŪM: may she protect the pair of my eyes; HRĪM HRĪM: may she protect my two ears.
On the right, may Kālike protect the pair of nostrils; O Maheśvara,
*krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ* protect the tongue, and *hūṃ hūṃ* protect the skull.
May she whose form is the syllable *hrīṃ*, who is the embodiment of the mantra *hrīṃ hrīṃ svāhā*, protect my entire face.
May the Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*) consisting of twenty-two syllables bestow auspiciousness upon my shoulders.
May Kālī, who bears a sword and a severed head and bestows boons and fearlessness,
protect me on all sides with all her vidyās throughout every limb.
May the three-syllabled *cāmuṇḍā*—*krīṃ hūṃ krīṃ*—protect my heart;
*aiṃ hūṃ oṃ aiṃ* protect my pair of breasts; and *hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā* protect my collarbone.
May the Great Vidyā of eight syllables, together with the *kartṛ*, protect my two arms;
may the six-syllabled mantra—*krīṃ krīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ*—protect my two hands.
*Krīṃ*, together with *dakṣiṇe kālike*, protects the region of the navel;
*krīṃ svāhā* protects the back—this is the ten-syllable *Kālikā*.
HŪM HRĪM, O Kālikā in the south! KRĪM HŪM, may she protect both hips! Kālikā, the twelve-syllable mantra, SVĀHĀ—may she protect the pair of my thighs!
Oṃ hrīṃ krīṃ me svāhā; may Kālikā always protect my knees.
This Vidyā, named Kālī-hṛdaya, bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.
*Krīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ*, may Kālikā protect my right ankle;
*krīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ svāhā*, may this fourteen-syllable mantra protect me.
May Kālī, who bears a sword and a severed head and holds the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness,
protect me on all sides with all her sciences and arts throughout every limb.
Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kuru-kullā, Virodhinī, Vipracittā, as well as Ghoraghorā, Prabhā, Dīptā, and Aghanatviṣ.
Nīlāghanavalākā, Mātrāmudrāmitā, and I—
these are all holding swords in their hands and adorned with garlands of severed heads.
May Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Māheśvarī, Cāmuṇḍā, Kaumārī, and Aparājitā protect me in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
May Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, and all those adorned with immeasurable ornaments,
protect me with their weapons in the cardinal and intermediate directions, in every way.
Thus has been told to you this divine armor, most wonderful by name, the auspiciousness of the entire world, which is the very embodiment of mantra.
Having performed the worship of the Guru according to the prescribed rules, one should then recite this Brahma-kavaca, which attracts the three worlds, as uttered from my own mouth.
One may recite this armor-mantra (kavaca) three times, once, or even throughout one's entire life;
by repeating it fifty times, one shall become a conqueror of the three worlds.
By the grace of this armor-mantra, one truly agitates the three worlds;
within a month, one becomes a great poet and a master of all supernatural accomplishments.
One should recite the root mantra once while offering handfuls of flowers to Kālikā;
one shall obtain the fruit of worship performed for hundreds of thousands of years.
If a wise person should wear this written on birch bark, placed within gold,
on the topknot, on the right arm, or around the neck,
he shall, through his wrath, enchant the three worlds and crush the three worlds with a mere glance.
One shall possess sons, wealth, and glory, and become a treasury of various sciences.
O Goddess of the Gods, by the mere touch of his body, weapons such as the Brahmāstra and others are destroyed; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Whether a woman is barren, or one whose children have died, or one who has no sons at all— by wearing this armor (kavaca) around her neck or on her hand, she becomes possessed of immortal offspring.
She who possesses many offspring indeed becomes endowed with life; of this there is no doubt.
This [teaching] must not be given to the disciples of others, and especially not to those who lack devotion.
Otherwise, he would meet his death; having cast aside rivalry, Kamalā and Vāgdevī took up residence in the temple of his mouth for the sake of his devoted disciples.
Having adopted steadfastness toward her grandson, she certainly dwells [there];
knowing this armor, whoever worships Kālīdakṣiṇā [shall attain success].
Even if recited a hundred thousand times, his spell will not succeed;
he shall suffer a blow from a weapon and shall meet death before long.
Thus ends the Śyāmākavaca in the glorious Bhairavatantra, within the dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī. Now follows the hundred names (Śatanāma).
Bhairava said:
O Mahākāla, I shall proclaim the auspicious one hundred and eight [names] of the Goddess,
which are supremely secret, meritorious, and the destroyer of fear everywhere.
The great Māyā, the Great Goddess, the Sovereign Maheśvarī;
she of great intellect, the greatly fierce one, Mahākālī, the Great Kalā.
The Great Seal, the Great Awakening, the Great Sleep, the Great Arising;
the Great Auspiciousness, the Great Lakṣmī, the Highly Fortunate One, and the Great Prosperity.
She is Great Delusion, the Vision of Delusion, Greatly Nourished, and Great Victory;
she is Great Fortitude, Greatly Terrible, Great Fangs, and Great Splendor.
To Mahākānti, Mahāpadmā, Mahāsiddhā, Mahātapā,
Mahāsvadhā, Mahotsahā, Mahābodhā, and Mahāsudhā.
She who destroys great bondage, she who annihilates great fear,
she with great eyes, great faces, a great tongue, and great arms.
He whose hand holds the great tree, the great living being, and the great serpent;
he who possesses great splendor, great forbearance, great affection, and great intelligence.
She who has great breath, great wisdom, and dwells upon the great mountain;
she who consists of the Great Brahma, the Mother, of great body and great roar.
She is the great-sounding Śrī, the great Pārvatī, Caṇḍikā, and Śivā;
she is of noble lineage, greatly fickle, highly esteemed, and possesses great wealth.
She who is deep blue, the great mountain, the great stream, and possessed of great strength;
she who is the great anxiety, the great mind, the great cause, and the illustrious one.
She is the great lore, the one of great accomplishment, the one of great intelligence, and the one of great wisdom;
she who wields the great trident, the one of great nobility, and the destroyer of great evil dreams.
She who bestows great liberation, she who is liberation itself, she who is accompanied by great skill and has no companion,
she who is supremely skillful, she who possesses a great voice, and she who destroys the great horse-demon.
Mahākālā, Mahādhārā, Mahāmāyā, Khecarī,
and she who is known as Mahākṣemaṃkarī, the bestower of great sovereignty.
The great destroyer of poison, the remover of venom, the annihilator of great difficulties;
the Great Durgā, the one of vast intellect, who dwells upon the great Kailāsa.
Mahāsutatvī, Subhagā, Mahejyā, Mahāsatī,
the eternal Mahāpratyaṅgirā, and Mahāpretakarālinī.
Whoever recites this with devotion— even if situated in a state of distress— shall attain great peace, great liberation, and the source of all great auspiciousness.
For one situated within an iron cage, the bondage perishes;
kings attain a state of servitude, and he shall become beloved by all people.
He attains unshakable prosperity, his afflictions perish,
and he conquers enemies in battle as well as those who move through the air.
Poison does not affect his body, nor do death, fire, or water;
for him, untimely death will never occur at any time.
Whatever desire one may wish for, that very thing one obtains constantly; what is the use of saying more here? It bestows all perfections upon men.
Thus ends the hymn of one hundred and eight names of Śyāmā from the *Śrī Rudrayāmala*, in the dialogue between Bhairava and [the Goddess].
Now begins the Thousand Names beginning with the letter *Ka*.
On the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, surrounded by various hosts of gods,
filled with diverse trees and creepers, and resounding with the cries of various birds.
Situated within a pavilion of aesthetic splendor, joined by four mandalas,
he remains established in meditative absorption, peaceful, sporting, and beloved by the yoginīs.
There, seeing Śaṅkara observing a vow of silence, the Goddess questioned him.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, what do you recite? What do you constantly remember?
Where has the creation dissolved, and where, O Progenitor of Creatures, will it appear again?"
O Śiva, what is the cause of the cosmic egg? What is that primordial, great cause? Is it the accomplishment consisting of mental desire, or is it the fulfillment of one's longing?
The third is the accomplishment of conceptualization, which consists of the mastery of the ten powers (*siddhīśvaratva*),
the eighteen descents of power (*śaktipāta*), and the movement through the cities of the moving and the unmoving.
Likewise, the Mahendra-net consists of the construction of nets such as those of Indra and others;
as well as the power of atomization (aṇimā), the ability to travel through the air (khecaratva), and the entry into another's body (parakāyapraveśana).
The creation of a new world, the drying up of the ocean,
the appearance of the moon on the new-moon day, or the shining of the moon by day.
O Śiva, there is likewise a group of eight moons in the eight directions;
and in water, there is the nature of being composed of water, while in fire, there is the nature of being composed of fire.
The supreme creation of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others, as well as the making of Indras;
likewise, the fivefold [attainments] of the sandals, the pill, the bird, and the Vetāla.
The elixir (*rasāyana*), likewise its protection, and the people of Vilā;
the accomplishment of Mahāmadhumatī, as well as Padmāvatī, O Śiva.
Likewise, by what mantra and austerity can the attainment of Bhogavatī and whatever other siddhis exist be achieved in the Kali age, which is so filled with sin?
Tell me, how does it come to be for one who is devoid of longevity and merit?
Śiva said:
Without mantra, without hymn, and indeed without austerity, O beloved;
without offering, without practice, and without the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), O beloved.
Success will indeed be attained quickly; that very light is described [as such].
Others, however, say there are fifty auspicious [degrees] within the sphere of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍagola).
Tārā resides at the end of the five voids, and Kālikā resides at the very end of all;
O Śivā, the infinite millions of cosmic eggs rest upon the tip of your upper incisor.
Having established the empty abode and having rendered it black in color,
she is indeed the form of the Great Attributeless (Mahānirguṇa), transcending speech, the supreme power.
In play, she would imagine her husband to be of an empty form;
then, for the purpose of beginning the work of creation, she perceived his shadow.
That power of will (icchā-śakti) was born, and by her time (kāla) was fashioned;
a reflection was seen therein, and she became known as the element of knowledge (jñāna).

When this very [reality], characterized by both knowledge (*jñāna*) and discernment (*vijñāna*), becomes distinguished, then action (*kriyā*) arises in two ways; this is what is intended, O Maheśvarī.
O Goddess of the gods, that which was situated as the royal gift within the sphere of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍagola),
she, Kriyā, established it in its own respective places according to the proper order.
Right there, by her own will, the Goddess is devoted to the state of supreme equanimity;
O Goddess, listen as I describe what she desires.
O Goddess, at the time of the beginning of the Yuga, Śiva is supreme in his excellent qualities;
by His will, He is beyond attributes (nirguṇa), peaceful, and the embodiment of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss.
Eternal, beautiful, pure, endowed with all divine qualities, supreme, the primordial lord who transcends all attributes, the Sovereign united with Kālī.
To the god who delights in the unconventional, the ultimate refuge of aesthetic union (sāmarasya),
[he spoke] to the hosts of gods, gandharvas, and apsaras who had arrived for the purpose of worship.
Seeing her, who was Tilottamā—the foremost of all yakṣiṇīs, kinnarīs, and mortal women—created by his own māyā, he said: "O beautiful one, O beloved of my life!"
O Beauty of the Three Worlds, O Mistress of my life, O Delighter of my life! What has come about that your feet have arrived? My ocean of fortune is now vast indeed.
Having spoken thus, the hosts of Apsarases worshipped Śambhu, who remained observant of silence.
The Gandharvas said:
O God, beloved by all people, you have rescued me from the dissolution;
O Great Lord, you are now joined with me for the purpose of the work at the commencement of creation.
This *pragāyaṇa* is for subjugation; it is a song of auspiciousness for the gods,
to be sung at the time of departure, at festivals, and at the commencement of an undertaking.
O Mṛḍa, O Śaṅkara, for this is indeed the time of the commencement of the Yugas;
there are millions of Indrāṇīs who have arisen from the drops of her perspiration.
Millions upon millions of Brahmāṇīs, Vaiṣṇavīs, and Māheśīs have arisen for the sake of beholding the bliss of your nectar-like essence.
O Maheśvara, we have been born and have come before you, an ocean of bliss;
having abandoned delight in amorous women, there is no other happiness for us.
That essence has been seen by us as something that brings about great happiness and purpose;
in this very same way, we must act toward her together with our husbands.
Having heard this, Mahādeva, with his mind established in meditation,
abandoned that meditation and, through his illusory power (māyā), spoke to Kālikā.
O Kālikāli, garlanded with severed heads, beloved of Bhairava and his roar;
you who assume the form of a jackal, cruel and terrifying with your formidable fangs!
O beloved Śivā, at the time of action, Sundarī beheld before her the beautiful goddess Trailokyābhakṣaṇakarī.
"O Great Goddess, abandon your meditation; O Mahākālī, our lives do not return home. Your form, O beloved, is my very time."
"Their beautiful form brings delight to the three worlds"—
thus spoke Mahākāla, possessed by the delusion of Māyā.
Having heard these words of Kāla, Kālikā,
concealing herself through her illusory power (māyā) and assuming the form of his own wife, spoke to Kāla.
From this time forward, O Goddess, in age after age, all that is merely female shall become medicinal herbs at the beginning of the Kalpa; by day, they shall take the form of creepers.
Having assumed the form of women at night, they will sport with one another;
and there shall be ignorance among all people in age after age.
Having thus pronounced the curse, Kālikā spoke again:
"Those who, having engaged in inverted sexual union, worship while reflecting [upon me in that state]..."
"I shall grant them boons, and there I shall always abide.
Having spoken thus, the Kālikā-vidyā vanished right then and there.
In the *nikharva* unit there are thirty-six *vṛnda*, ninety *arbuda*, and ten million *koṭi*s;
O beloved, where indeed has she gone, who performed such penance for the sake of a vision?
"My queen is dearer to me than life, she is my very life-breath;
what shall I do? Where shall I go?"—thus was he overwhelmed by confusion.
Then Kālī’s grace arose, for Śiva is intent upon my welfare;
indeed, Kālī quickly bestows the intellect for the arrangement of the yantra.
From the time that the yantra was first mastered, it has not been within the range of those previously perfected;
one should be intent upon the practice of the arrangement and construction of the Śrīcakrarāja.
Wandering here and there within the wheel that encompasses the three worlds,
he went for millions and billions of ages in order to see the further shore of the wheel.
The Goddess, whose life-breath is her devotee, is the sovereign of the Great Śrīcakra;
there, within that Bindu, is her supreme form, beautiful and most enchanting.
O Great Goddess, when form was born, she became Tripurasundarī in her waking state;
upon seeing that form, Mahādeva indeed became Rājarājeśvara.
By her mere sidelong glance, Śiva, assuming her form,
then became Maheśvarī, endowed with the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra).
Without Kālī, O Goddess, the world of the moving and the unmoving would not exist;
O Maheśvarī, neither beauty nor power exists anywhere at all.
Requested by Sundarī, the pleased Kālī said:
"The eyes, hair, and ears of all shall become mine."
O Queen of the Gods, O Beloved, in my previous states a portion of mine remained; however, in that state called Aruṇa, no part of me remains at all.
O Great Goddess, it is certain that [my power] always remains with my devotees;
yet, O beautiful one, their power has become blunted, and likewise their form [is no longer radiant].
There, Sundarī became overcome with anxiety and grew dejected;
after remaining for a moment absorbed in meditation, she became intent on contemplating the supreme time.
At that moment, O Lord, Kālī certainly became pleased;
she said respectfully, "Choose a boon, choose a boon, choose a boon!"
Sundarī said:
"Grant me supreme power; this is the boon requested by me.
Tell me such a means by which that power shall come to be."
Kālī said:
And a thousand names of mine were previously composed by me,
[describing] my own form known as "Ka," the leader of the great empire.
Recite that which is named "The Bestower of Boons," for it grants boons within half a moment; O Mahāmāyā, through this, devotion shall arise within you.
From that time forward, Śrīvidyā became intent upon reciting His name;
that very thousand names is the bestower of power for Sundarī.
O beloved, with supreme devotion, the practitioners should worship their own Great Goddess with wines,
meats, semen, and all kinds of blood.
One should satisfy and worship Kālī and practice the inverted sexual union (viparītarati).
O Goddess, in the inverted sexual union, Kālī is eternally present.
Mādhvīkā is Śukrapuṣpā, who is dispassionate toward sexual union;
she is the Vaiṣṇavī pervading Vidyā, the supreme one who dwells in the cremation ground.
Satisfied by the heroic practice (*vīrasādhana*), resounding with the clapping of heroes,
her soul delighted by the rows of jackals, Caṇḍikā possesses the form of a female jackal (*śivā*).
O Praise-worthy One, she who surpasses the bliss of desires, who is beloved by those of fierce minds, who is the supreme,
dense bliss of Brahman, and who is satisfied by the bliss of sexual union.
The lord of yogis is the abode of the heart, while day and night are reversed;
the gods are the opposite, for their delight is in the reversal of day and night.
In an instant, she became visible and pleased—she who wears a garland of teeth and is fond of reciting prayers;
[he was] with sword in hand, with disheveled hair, naked, and adorned with ashes.
While reclining on his bed, delighting in kisses and devoted to the company of courtesans,
he should recite the *Sahasranāma* known as *Medhāsāmrājya*.
Just as the divine [speech] becomes clear for a mere moment by means of divine nectars,
so too does Samākālī become clear through the mere recitation of this [text].
The Thousand-Name Hymn is now being recited; listen with an attentive mind to this Thousand-Name hymn known as the "Wisdom of Universal Sovereignty."
The sage (ṛṣi) is declared to be Mahākāla; the meter (chandaḥ) is proclaimed to be Uṣṇik;
the deity is Dakṣiṇakālī; and Māyā is proclaimed as the seed-syllable (bīja).
HŪM is the Śakti; the seed-syllable of Kālī is proclaimed as the Kīlaka.
Kālī, through her bestowal of boons, is employed for the sake of one's own desired aim.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with camphor, preceded by the six long vowels;
then, having performed the meditation as before, one should accomplish one's desired goal.
Oṃ Krīṃ! Kālī, Karālī, Kalyāṇī, Kamalākalā, Kalāvatī, Kalākhyā, and Kalā—the one whose essence is the arts—are worthy of worship.
One part is joyful, one part is nourished, one part is afflicted, and one part is the creator;
she is the embodiment of ten million parts, and is worshipped through the play of the arts.
She who consists of the arts, who is the support of the arts, who transcends the arts, and who is the source of the arts;
she who is the support of the arts, the lotus-born one, whose name begins with the letter 'ka', and the mine of compassion.
She whose every limb is the color of the letter *ka*, adorned with millions of digits of beauty;
multiplied by millions of *ka*-syllables, she is adorned with millions of *ka*-syllables.
Her heart is the letter *ka*; she is adorned with the mantra of the letter *ka*.
She has the letter *ka* as her crown; she is decorated with the letter *ka*.

Ka-ka-ka-ka, she whose form is the color Ka; Ka-ka, she who is devoted to the sound Ka; Ka-ka, she who delights in the brandishing of heroes; she who is worshipped by the creator of the lotuses (Brahmā).
She is the mistress Kamalākara, she who assumes the form of Kamalākara;
she is established in the perfection of Kamalākara and bestows the transcendence of Kamalākara.
Abiding in the midst of a lotus-pond, she is delighted by the lotus-pond;
how can she engage in other talk, and how can she be devoted to anything else?
How can you stand at the end of a word, and how can you be at the beginning of a word?
O lotus-eyed one, born from a lotus, you are worshipped by the lotus-eyed Lord.
Kamalākṣī, Varodyuktā, Kakārā, Karvurākṣarā,
Karatārā, Karacchinnā, Karaśyāmā, and Kalārṇavā.
She who is worshipped by the hands, who delights in the hands, who bestows the hand, who is honored by the hands;
she who is the Karatoyā river, who touches the hands, who destroys karma, and who is dear to Kana.
Her life depends on her hands; she is born from her hands; she dwells within the hollow of her hands;
she has the form of a mass of hailstones; and she is resplendent with a garland of hailstones.
Kakāra is the daughter of the Moving One (Cala), and Karakā is Toṣiṇī;
Karakā resides in the house of Cala, and she is the protectress of Karakācala.
Honored by Karakācala, she who brings about Karakācala;
she who is rich in the rain of Karakācala, and she who is delighted by Karakācala.
She whose forest is Mount Karakācala, who is garlanded by Mount Karakācala,
who is enriched by the splendor of Mount Karakācala, and whose form is like a lotus-hand.
She who resides in the *karāmalaka* fruit grants the accomplishment (*siddhi*) of the *karāmalaka*;
she who protects from the *karāmalaka* should be worshipped in the play of the *karāmalaka*.
She who holds a myrobalan fruit in her hand, she whose eyes are like myrobalan fruits,
the mother of the myrobalan-in-hand, and she who partakes of the essence of the myrobalan.
She who is like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand, she who bestows the myrobalan fruit upon the palm;
she whose eyes are like lotuses, whose path is like a lotus, who dwells in a lotus, and who holds a lotus.
She who wears a garland of lotuses, she who acts for the beloved, she who has the form of a lotus, and she who is born from a lotus;
she who belongs to the lotus lineage, she whose path is the lotus, and she who is devoted to the lotus-oblation.
Seated in the center of a lotus mandala, adorned with lotus ornaments,
devoted to honoring the lotus, she is the source of the lotus and its ultimate refuge.
She has a form like a heap of *kaṃja* flowers, she dwells in a forest of *kaṃja* trees;
she stands amidst *karaṃja* trees and resides within *karaṃja* trees.
Abounding in the ornaments of karañja fruits, dwelling in the karañja forests,
adorned with garlands of karañja flowers, she stands amidst the moon-like faces of the celestial hosts.
She whose form is shaped like a headless trunk, who is adorned with headless trunks,
who is delighted by the sound of headless trunks, and who makes her seat from a headless trunk.
She who dwells within the house of the trunk, she who resides in the movement of the trunk,
she who makes the trunk her garment, and she whose ornament is the moon upon the trunk.
She who bestows victory upon those with headless trunks, she who dwells within the bodies of trunkless beings,
she whose seat is the garland of headless trunks, and she who wears a garland of beautiful forms.
She dwells in the midst of a garland of skulls, gratified by the vow of the skull;
she is content with the lamp of the skull and has the form of that skull-lamp.
She who grants boons with the skull-lamp, she who resides in the soot of the skull,
she who bestows victory with the garland of skulls, and she who is pleased by the recitation of the skull-mantra.
Contented with the perfection of the skull-cup, intent upon eating from the skull-cup,
established in the vow of the skull-cup, she has her abode in the lotus of the skull-cup.
She whose essence is poetry, who is the ocean of poetry,
who rejoices in the perfection of poetry, and who bestows the gift of poetry.
She who is worshiped by poets, the path of poets, the form of poets, and beloved by poets;
she whose form is the universe of poets, and who is gratified by the vow of poetic composition.
Residing in the minds of poets, she fulfills the desires of poets;
stationed upon the throats of poets, she is *hrīṃ kaṃ kaṃ kaṃ*, the bestower of completion for poets.
She whose mind is intent on the gift of collyrium, who is fond of collyrium,
and who is worshipped by the Lord of Collyrium (Kajjaleśa), who is equal to the collyrium in the skull.
Abiding in the midst of the ocean of collyrium, she is the embodiment of the bliss of collyrium;
she is satisfied by her beloved who loves collyrium, and she brings satisfaction to that beloved who loves collyrium.
Adorned with a garland of skulls, decorated with skull ornaments in her hands,
enriched by the embellishments of skull-attributes, and adorned with a circle of skulls.
She whose abode is ten million skulls, she who creates the fortress of skulls;
she who resides on the mountain of skulls, she who dwells upon the mountain of skulls.
Content with the skull-bowl as her vessel, devoted to the skull-offering,
her life-breath dear to the skull-offering, she is intent on the boon of the skull-offering.
She is the form of the skull-cakra and consists solely of the form of a skull;
she is the plantain tree, having the nature of a plantain, and dwells in the plantain forest.
Delighting in the flower of the plantain tree, her mind fixed on the fruit of the plantain,
satisfied by the oblation of the plantain, she is intent upon the leaf of the plantain.
She dwells within the heart of a plantain tree, beautiful as a grove of plantains;
she resides in the kadamba flower and stands in the midst of a kadamba forest.
She whose fragrance is like that of the kadamba flower, who delights in the kadamba forest,
who is to be worshipped with kadamba blossoms, and who grants the offering of kadamba flowers.
She who dwells amidst kadamba flowers, she who feeds on kadamba fruits,
she who resides within kadamba forests, and she who abides in the kadamba groves.
She who is worshiped by Kacchapa and Akacchapa, she who is seated upon the throne of Kacchapa,
the ear-ornament, the destroyer of the ears, the woman from Karṇāṭa, and Kālabhairavī.
Karaprītā, Kalahadā, Kalahā,
Kalahātarā, Karṇayakṣī, Karṇavārtā, Kathanī, and Karṇasuṃdarī.
She who is the female ghoul of the ear, the cluster of blossoms for the ear, and the giver of *kapikacchū*;
she who is rich in form within the *kapikacchū* plant, and whose very nature is that of the *kapikacchū*.
She has the form of the musk deer, she possesses the appearance of the musk deer;
she brings joy to the musk deer and dwells in the midst of musk deer.
Her body is dark as indigo and perfumed with musk; she is delighted by the scent of musk;
her life-breath belongs to the worshipper of musk; she is dear to the worshipper of musk.
Kastūrī is satisfied with love; Kastūrī is the bearer of love;
Kastūrī is the bliss of those who worship her; Kastūrī is the embodiment of fragrance.
She who takes the form of a musk garland, she who is fond of worship with musk,
she who rejoices in the musk tilaka, and she who is dear to the musk tilaka.
Kastūrī is satisfied by the fire-oblation; Kastūrī is intent upon the libation;
Kastūrī is engaged in purification; Kastūrī is worshipped by the circle [of deities].
She is to be worshipped with musk and flowers; she is intent on chewing musk;
she dwells within the very heart of musk; and she wears garments of musk.
She possesses the fragrance of musk; she dwells in the musk-deer forest;
she is the protector of the musk-deer forest; she bears love for the musk-deer.
Musk is the abode of power; musk resides within the central pool;
musk is bathed in the musk-pool; musk is the immersion that kisses [the divine].
Musk is satisfied by an offering of water; musk is the sustainer of life;
musk possesses supreme fragrance; musk is capable of sustaining existence.
The state of being musk is the essence of the nutmeg; she is kissed by the fragrance of musk, and the ground of her forehead shines, resplendent with the beauty of the scent of musk.
She who dwells within the *kastūrī-damanā* plant, she who bestows the joy of the intoxication of musk,
she who is the primordial source of the musk-perfumed canopy, and she who resides in the center of the musk-house.
She whose life is the touch of musk, who brings an end to those who revile musk,
who delights in the fragrance of musk, and who is intent on playing with musk.
She is intent on the gift of musk, the bestower of the boon of musk,
capable of establishing musk, and the delighter of the abode of musk.
She who is praised by the musk of inquiries after welfare, she who is extolled by the musk of hymns,
she who is the support for those who worship musk, and she who dwells in the abode of musk.

She whose form is "Ka," who is enriched by "Ka," who is the bliss of "Ka," and who is born from "Ka"; she who is worshipped by "Ka," whose name is "Ka," whose neighing is "Ka," and whose very self is "Ka."
With a rosary as her neck-ornament, she is intent on the recitation of mantras;
she remembers the Name, and she is solely devoted to the Name.
She is devoted to the recitation of the *Kaha*, she is the Goddess Kaha, she is the Mistress Kaha;
she is the cause of the *Kaha*, she is the bliss of the *Kaha*, and she is devoted to the sound of the *Kaha*.
Where is her mother? Where does she reside? What are her mantras? Who are her lords? What is her lineage? What is her wealth? And what is she devoted to in meditation?

She whose essence is narrative, who is devoted to the discussion of "what," "how," and "wherefore," whose conduct is narrative, whose movement is narrative, and who performs the cosmic dance of narrative.

She whose forest is the letter *ka*, whose movement is the letter *ka*, whose power is the letter *ka*, who is the supreme refuge; she whose royal duty is the letter *ka*, whose action is the letter *ka*, the beautiful one.
She is the knowledge of karma, the course of karma, and one who is devoted to the mechanism of karma;
she is the measure of karma, the body of karma, and one who is intent upon the vital points of karma.
The line of karma is the destroyer of karma; the line of karma is the dispeller of karma;
the line of karma is the deluder of karma; the line of karma is the delighter of karma.
The line of karma is delusive, devoted to the fame of karma;
it is the science of karma, the essence of karma, the stream of karma, and the field of karma.
Karmakārī, Karmakarī, Karmakautukasundarī,
Karmakolī, Karmatārā, Karmacchinnā, and Karmadā.
She is the Caṇḍālī of karma, the mother of the Veda of action, and the field of action;
she is infinite, delighting in the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa), and is inferred through the ritual section.
Her body is as broad as the ritual section (Karmakāṇḍa) of the Vedas; her form is like that of a female tortoise;
she is another heart-pleasing goddess worshipped by Kamaṭha; and she is beautiful with a neck like a tortoise.
She is to be served by those seated on tortoises, who are intent upon the rites of the female tortoise;
she is the beloved of Karuṇākara and is saluted by Karuṇākara.
She holds a rosary of hard seeds, possesses firm breasts,
wears matted hair, is free from deceit, is a grinder of the wicked, and is adorned with herons.
With thighs like the trunk of an elephant, she possesses a garland of rays as hard as the sun;
she consists of sweet speech, she is the conceptualization beyond all conceptualization, and she is the bestower of the Kalpa.
She is a garland of lotus-filaments, she has a lotus-face, and the radiance of her ears;
she is the preeminent one, she is full of austerity, she is honored in every marshy place, and she is the unborn one.
Her body was adorned with hair, she bore beautiful locks of hair,
her breasts were pressed against her throat, and she was resplendent with a waist-string.
She who is dear to Kaṇabhakṣa, the bulbous root, likewise the movement of the bulbous root, the Kali age, the destroyer of Kali,
the messenger of Kali, and she who is worshipped by the leader of poets.

*kaśā* means "whip" and *kakṣā* means "waistband"; *yaṃtra* refers to a "mechanism" or "instrument," while some [forms] are honored by the best of poets; *kartrī* and *kartrikā* mean "knife"; *bhūṣā* means "ornament"; and *karaṇī* and *karṇaśatrupā* refer to tools or instruments.
The mistress of the senses, the bestower of the senses, adorned with the collyrium of creative ideation;
she is the mistress of the senses, the source of the senses, and the treasury of all arts.
She whose support is movement is black, with hands like those of an elephant;
she is the heap of pebbles at the sound of time, and the heap of pebbles is most highly honored.
The sign of Virgo, the maiden, the girl who speaks sweetly,
she who brings joy to those who give a daughter in marriage, and she who bestows the desired fruit upon the house where a daughter is given in marriage.
She is satisfied by the gift of a maiden, she is pleased by the offering of a daughter;
she is the one who burns the thicket of worldly existence, and she whose seat is unmeasured.
Karamālā is the creator of joy; Karamālā is fully satisfied;
Karamālā is the bliss of the corpse; Karamālā is the union.
The rosary of the hand bestows success; the rosary of the hand is dear to the hand.
She is dear to the hand, she is the creeper of the hand, and she is devoted to the giving of gifts with the hand.
She is the bliss of action, the course of the Kali age, worshipped in the Kali age, and the progenitor of the Kali age;
she is the locus of the resonance of sound, and the bestower of boons through that resonant sound.
She is the one who causes the assembly to sound, Kahola, and the giver of Kahola;
she resides in the abode of Kahora and is the bestower of boons upon Kahora.
The stream of Kahora’s poetry, the infinite honor of the sage Kahola,
worshipped by the mind of Kahola, she who acts according to the words of Kahola.
Residing in the center of the house of Kahola, she is the maker of the excellent Kahola;
she is the agent, composed of agency, the mother of agents, and the hand-axe (kartarī).
She is the youngest, worshiped by Kanaka, whose story consists of the essence of the eyes;
she is the abode of the smallest bliss, pleased by the joy of Kanaka.
She who draws the ocean of stories with the hook of her finger-ring,
she who is accessible by elephant, whose gait is like an elephant’s, and who is devoted to the one whose banner is the elephant.
The beloved of Kalinātha, who delights in the stories told at her throat,
is lovely, desire-granting, and adorned with beautiful ornaments.
She is the beloved of the lovely assembly, fond of lovely vows,
worshipped for her lovely qualities, the tawny-hued one, the sovereign lady of Kapila.
Worshipped by Kapila, she is the heart-essence; Kapila is the bestower of boons.
Ka-e-ī-la-hrīṃ is Svarūpā, and Ka-e-ī-la-hrīṃ is Varapradā.
Ka-e-ī-la-hrīṃ is the bestower of perfection; kala-ha-hrīṃ is she whose form is the essence;
ka-ha-la-hrīṃ is the phoneme of the mantra; and kala-ha-hrīṃ is the creative power.
Kavargā resides at the door-panel and is capable of opening the door-panel;
she is Kaṅkālī, Kapālā, and she who speaks kindly to Kaṅkāla.
She is worshipped by Kaṅkālabhairava, she resides in the mind of Kaṅkāla;
she is intent on the delusion of Kaṅkāla and bestows the delusion of Kaṅkāla.
She who destroys impurity, she who removes impurity, she who annihilates the suffering of impurity;
she who is worshiped in the Kali age, she who bestows arts and knowledge, she who is the nourisher of the earth, and she who is adored by Kaśyapa.
Kaśyapā, Akaśyapā, Ārādhyā, Kali, Pūrṇakalevarā,
Kalevarā, Karikacā, Kaṭavargā, and Karālikā.
She is worshipped by Karālabhairava; she is the sovereign lady of Karālabhairava;
she is the support for the hand of Karāla; she is Kapardīśa, the bestower of boons.
