Kapardīśa is delighted by love; Kapardī is adorned with garlands;
Kapardī is richly endowed with a rosary; and she is the giver of Karavīra flowers.
O Karavīra, you whose life-breath is dear to me; O Karavīra, you who are fully worshipped; O you who possess a form like the Karṇikāra flower; O Karṇikāra, you who are fully worshipped.
Abiding in the fire of dried cow-dung, she bestows gold by the measure of a karṣa;
she is to be worshipped with jars and non-jars, she is the astringent, and she is the bliss of the elephant-singer.
Kapilā is considered Kalakaṇṭhī and Kalikalpalatā;
she is Kalpalatā, Kapamātā, Kalpakārī, and Kalpabhū.
She is beautiful with the fragrance of camphor, she bears the scent of camphor;
she is adorned with garlands of camphor, and she bestows the fulfillment of camphor.
She who bestows the garland of camphor, who dwells in the midst of the ocean of camphor,
who delights in the libation of camphor, and who wears the excellent camphor.
She who is worshipped as Kapaṭeśvarī, she who possesses the form of Kapaṭeśvara; she who is adored by Kadru, Kapidhvaja (Hanumān), and Ārādhya; she who takes the form of a multitude of flowers.
Resplendent with *kalāpa* flowers, honored by *kalāpa* flowers,
and worthy of worship through the cries of peacocks— how can this tree be so formidable?
How is she liberated from time? Where is Kālī, the beloved of Kāla? Who is the passionate woman (Kāminī) worthy of worship? And who is the passionate woman who bears flowers?
The beloved is worthy of worship with flowers; the beloved is adorned with flowers;
the beloved has flowers as her tilaka mark; the beloved kisses the *kuṇḍa*.
Satisfied by union with Kāminī, she bestows the yoga of Kāminī;
she is immersed in the lotus-pool of Kāminī and dwells in the midst of the pool of Kāminī.
She is the beloved to be worshipped by the mind, she who is satisfied by the pride of the beloved;
she whose movement is within the minds of the beloved, she who is dark as Time, and she who is the primordial darkness of Time.
Kāmā, Kāmadevī, Kāmeśī, Kāmasambhavā,
Kāmabhāvā, Kāmaratā, Kāmārtā, and Kāmamañjarī.
She whose anklets resound with desire, she who is dearer than the beloved of Kāmadeva,
she who is Kāmakālī, she who is the Kali of the arts of love, and she who is named Kāmakalā.
O Kālī, you who are the essence of the art of desire (kāmakalā), whose splendor is equal to the fire of cosmic destruction;
beloved by the one who consumes the end of the eon, you who speak with affection even in the midst of the wilderness.
She who is to be worshipped at the [proper] time, she who delights in the [proper] time, the garland of time, and the dark one;
she who is formidable with the [proper] time, she who has attained perfection through the [proper] time, and she who bestows the [proper] time.
She who has the appearance of black collyrium, who dwells in Kālīñjana,
who possesses black supernatural power, who increases the power of Time, and who liberates from the prison of rebirth.
The Kādividyā, the Mother of the Ka-series, residing in the Ka-series, the beautiful one beginning with Ka;
she who is Kāśī and Kāñcī, the consort of the Lord of Kāñcī, the bestower of boons upon the Lord of Kāśī.
The seed-syllable *krāṃ* and likewise the seed-syllable *kāṃ* are remembered as "salutation to the heart" (*krāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*).
She is the goal of both the desirable and the undesirable, the bestower of the attainment of all desires, and the source of the perfection of *ka*.
She who is Kāmākṣā, who can assume any form at will, who releases the bow of Kāma;
she who is the delight of the arts of Kāmadeva, and the abode of the arts of Kāmadeva.
She is the Night of Time, the bestower of desires, dwelling in the mountains of the wilderness;
she is the form of Time, the movement of Time, and devoted to the yoga of desire.
Delighting in the crushing of desire, she who expands the abode of desire;
she is the wife of Kālabhairava and the beloved of Kālabhairava.
Established in the yoga of Kālabhairava, she bestows the enjoyments of Kālabhairava;
she is the wish-fulfilling cow, the milker of desires, the mother of desire, and the giver of what is beloved.
She who is fond of lovers, who is worshipped by lovers, who increases the bliss of lovers;
she whose seed is the *kārtava* flower, who is Kārttikeyā, and who is fully adored by Kārttikeya.
She is the giver of effects from causes, yet she produces no effect; she is distinct from other causes.
She is attainable through splendor, she is composed of splendor, and she is like Kātyāyanī in her brilliance.
She was the essence of desire, a native of Kashmir devoted to the customs of Kashmir;
she delighted in the conduct of Kāmarūpa and was as sweet-spoken as the goddess of Kāmarūpa herself.
She who can assume any form at will, who has accomplished her desires, whose form is at her own command, and who is mind-made;
she who is the full moon day of Kārtika, who is to be worshipped in Kārtika, and whose birthplace is the Kāñcanāra flower.
She has the luster of a *kāñcanāra* flower, she is worshipped with golden lotuses;
she is the form of glass, the ground of glass, and she who eats from vessels of bell-metal.
Consisting of the sound of bell-metal, she is Kāmasundarī, who kisses with passion;
resembling a kāśa flower, she has come from the wish-fulfilling tree.

She whose flowers are desire, the ground of desire, the object of worship for desire, and the giver of desire; she whose body is desire, whose home is desire, and who is devoted to the passion of desire.
Mounted upon the banner of desire, established upon the banner of desire;
worthy of worship by the descendants of Kaśyapa, she who bestows joy upon the Kaśyapas.
Who is she who resembles the waters of the Kālindī, who is worshipped by the waters of the Kālindī,
who is devoted to the worship of which deity, and which deity is the giver of the supreme goal?
By her action she has the form of the *kārmaṇa* [body]; she acts according to her will through the *kārmaṇa*;
she is the destroyer of the *kārmaṇa*; she is Kākinī, called by the name "Cause."
She is the nectar of poetry, she is the Kaliṅga plant, she is intent on the passion of Kaliṅga;
she is enriched with the ornament of black aloe-wood, and she bestows the prosperity of black aloe-wood.
She is fragrant with black aloe-wood, she is satisfied by black aloe-wood,
she is the Kāverī, she is delighted by the blue [lotus], and she dwells on the banks of the Kāverī.
She whose form is the whirling wheel of time, who dwells within the wheel of time,
whose body is the support of forest and non-forest, she is composed of compassion.
Kāmpilyavāsinīkāsthā, Kāmapatnī, Kāmabhū,
Kādaṃbarī, Pānaratā, and likewise Kādaṃvarītalā.
She is the one to be venerated by desire, the Mistress of Desire, worshipped by the King of Desire;
she is the Vidyā who is the Sovereign of the King of Desire, the delight of the festival of desire.
Desiring the Kāmbojas, she then became the city of Kāśī, the maker of gold;
she has the form of the Golden Mountain (Meru) and bestows the treasures of the Golden Mountain.
She whose fame is desire, she whose hair is desire, Kālikā, who takes refuge in the forest;
she who pierces desire, she who destroys the affliction of desire, and she who is the ground of desire.
She is the destroyer of the enemy that is Time, the wife of Kavi, and she who can assume any form at will.
She dwells within desire, she is the blazing flame of wood, the bestower of poetry, and the beauty of love.
The mistress of wood, the cause, the wretched one, and the enemy of desire, she is intent on worship;
she is enriched with the ornaments of girdles and anklets, and endowed with saffron-colored adornments.
Kālacakrā, Kālagati, Kālacakra, Manobhavā,
Kuñjamadhyā, Kuñjapuṣpā, Kuñjapuṣpapriyā, and Akuśā.
She whose mother is the Earth, she who is to be worshipped by the Earth, she who holds an axe as her excellent weapon;
she who is seated upon an elephant, she who delights in the *kuśa* grass, and she whose eyes are like lotuses.
Kunaṭhī, Kurarī, Kruddhā, Kuraṅgī, Kuṭajāhvayā, Kumbhī, Nadyavibhūṣā, and Kumbhī, who is intent on slaying Namava.
She who delights the mind of Kumbhakarṇa, the crest-jewel of the Kula,
the one belonging to the Kula, the daughter of the potter’s house, and the beloved of Kulacūḍāmaṇi.
She is the worship of the family, she is adored by the family, and she is devoted to the worship of the family;
she is the ornament of the breasts, likewise the belly, and she is the one who serves the host of celestial nymphs.
She whose flower is the Kula, who delights in the Kula, who is devoted to the Kula as her supreme goal;
she whose garment is the Kula, who is worshipped by the Kula, who is the sacrificial pit, and whose splendor is equal to the Kula.
She is the radiant manifestation of the Kula-vessel, devoted to the flower of the vessel;
through the flow of the flower of the vessel, her very self is born from the *kuṇḍa* and *goḷa*.
She is the source of those born from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, she consists of the *kula* and *gola*, and she is the *kuhu* [new moon] night;
she holds the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* as her dear life-breath, and she is worshipped by the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*.
She who delights the mind of Kuṇḍagola, she who bestows boons upon Kuṇḍagola,
she who is devoted to the deity of the Kula, she who is wrathful, and she who is the supreme bringer of Kula-siddhi.
Equal in form to the *kulakuṇḍa*, with ground equal to the *kulakuṇḍa*,
they possess the perfection of the *kuṇḍa* and the power of the *kuṇḍa*, intent upon the worship of the *kumārī*.
The life-force of the Kumārī-worshipper, residing in the womb of the Kumārī;
she who is satisfied by the time of the Kumārī, whose very self is the worshipper of the Kumārī.
Content with the vow of a maiden, assuming the form of a maiden,
pleased by the feeding of maidens, she is a maiden and the bestower of maidens.
The Mother of the Kumāra, born from the source of the Kula and the Dākula,
the Mistress of the Kula, possessing the Linga of the Kula, the Bliss of the Kula, the Delight of the Kula, and the vision of the Kula-logic.
Kuntī, Kulakāntā, and she who is devoted to the path of the noble;
Kullā, Kurukullā, Kullukā, and she who grants the desires of the lineage.
Kuliśāṅgī, Kubjikā, Kubjikā, Nandavardhinī,
Kulīnā, Kuñjaragati, and Kuñjareśvaragāminī.
She is the protector of the family, possessed of noble lineage, and likewise the illuminator of the family;
she is the sovereign of the yogis of the family, the sacrificial pit, and her form is as red as saffron.
She who is the bliss of saffron, she who is contented, she who dwells in the ocean of saffron;
she who is fond of saffron flowers, the source of the lineage, and the beauty of the lineage.
She who has teeth like jasmine buds, she who is like the night-lotus, she whose abode is auspiciousness,
the sovereign mistress of the Kula, the one from the sacrificial pit, the wanton woman, and she who is gratified by the Kula.
Kulaṭā is intent on kissing, Kuśāvartā is the ocean of the Kula;
Kulārṇavā delights in conduct, while Kuṇḍalī has the form of an earring.
She was of dull intellect yet foremost in her lineage, devoted to the wheel of the family;
she was immovable, possessed of a fierce gaze, and her form was as beautiful as a mass of curly locks.
She is of virtuous form and possesses a beard and seed;
she has breasts and delights in the sounds "kuku" and "kuku"; she is devoted to the supreme "krūṃ krūṃ krūṃ krūṃ."
Ku ku kuṃ is the abode of sound; she dwells in the lair of dogs,
is joined in union with dogs, and her very form is the bliss of dogs.
She moves within the *kūrca*, she whose seed is the *kūrca*, she who is devoted to the recitation (*japa*) of the *kūrca*;
she is of noble lineage, established in the *kula*, and her supreme goal is the *kūrca-kuṇḍa*.
She whose seed-syllable is *kūrca*, who possesses the *bhāla-daśā* (the state of the forehead), and is adorned with the *kūrca* on her head;
she who resides in the *kulavṛkṣa* (the family tree) and dwells upon the mountains of Kūrma and Akūrma.
She is the essence of the Kula, the auspiciousness of the Kula, and is devoted to the supreme Śakti of the Kula;
she is renowned as the jewel of the Kula-essence and dwells within the saffron tree.
Content with the massaging of her breasts, devoted to the recitation of her breasts,
satisfied by the touching of her breasts, she is intent upon the embracing of her breasts.
She who destroys evil destinies, she who is worshipped by Kubera, she whose birthplace is the breast, the leader of her clan,
she who sings beautifully, the bearer of breasts, she whose song is sublime, and she whose tusks are like jasmine buds.
Kugeyā, Kuharābhāsā, Kuśoṣā, Kughnadārikā,
Kīrti, Kirātinī, Klinnā, Kiraṇā, and Kinnarīpriyā.
She whose enemies are conquered by the syllable *krīṃ*, who is intent on the recitation of *krīṃ*, whose form is the mantra *krīṃ hūṃ strīṃ*;
she whose side-glances are variegated, who is worshipped as a youth, and who wears a crown.
She is the speech of insects, the womb of insects, the mother of insects, and the giver of monkeys;
she is the *kiṃśuka* tree, the language of insects, the essence of action, and the possessor of action.
She whose supreme sound is "kī kī," who takes the form of the mantra "krāṃ krīṃ krūṃ kraiṃ krauṃ," whose essential nature is expressed by "kāṃ kīṃ kūṃ kaiṃ," and who embodies the mantra "phaṭ."
She who finds joy in the ketakī ornaments, she who is endowed with a profusion of ketakī flowers;
she whose hair is curly, she who possesses beautiful locks, she who is the slayer of Keśin, and she who is intent upon the destruction of Keśin.
Keśarūpā, Keśamuktā, Kaikeyī, and likewise Keśikī; Kairavā, Kairavāhlādā, Keśarā, and Keturūpiṇī.
She who is worshipped by Keśava, whose heart is [his], whose mind is attached to Keśava;
she who destroys impotence, and who is pleased by the recitation of the *klaiva* seed-syllable.
Kośalā, Komalākṣī, and likewise Kośā and Komalā;
she who dwells in Kolāpura and is the destroyer of the demon Kolāsura.
She whose form is a hollow, who possesses the nature of a hollow, the wrathful one, she whose form is like a crow,
the *kekā* sound of the cuckoo, the pinnacle (*koṭi*), and she who is devoted to the *koṭi-mantra*.
Possessing a form endowed with ten million infinite mantras, she dwells in Kerala;
she is skilled in the Kairala way of life and resides in the home of the Lord of Kerala.
Established at Kedārāśrama, she is worshipped as Kedāreśvarī;
she is Krodharūpā, Krośapādā, Krodhamātā, and Kauśikī.
She who holds the bow, she who dwells on the *krauñca* mountain, the princess of Kośala, she of delicate limbs;
she who belongs to the *Kula*, the support of the *Kaulikas*, and she who resides in the hearts of the *Kaulikas*.
The curious one, the moonlight, the follower of the Kula, the maiden, the one worshipped by the Kauravas;
she who belongs to Kauṇḍinya, the descendant of Kuśika, the wrathful one, the flame, she whose form is radiant.
She possesses the flames of ten million cosmic fires, her form is that of ten million suns;
she is Kṛttikā, black in color, the dark one (Kṛṣṇā), a malevolent spirit (Kṛtyā), and distressed by her own activity (Kriyā).
O slender-limbed one, you who have accomplished your purpose, Cakra Phaṭ Svāhā, you whose nature is the essence of sound!
Kroṃ Kroṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ, you whose syllables are the mantra, Krīṃ Krīṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ, obeisance, Svadhā!
KRIṂ KRIṂ HRĪṂ HRĪṂ TATHĀ HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ—she whose very nature is this mantra.
Thus ends the thousand names called *Śrī-sarvasāmrājya-medhā*.
The [tantra] called Śaktidāna, as well as that named Svarūpa,
were spoken by Dakṣiṇakālī to Sundarī out of a spirit of affection.
In the context of granting boons, even the secret has been revealed;
it should always be kept hidden with devotion and recited as the supreme among the supreme.
It should be recited especially at the time of worship and at the conclusion of the recitation, during the morning, at midday, and also at dawn, midnight, and twilight.
The supreme master of practitioners who recites this for a year indeed becomes the very form of Kālī;
having recited it, or caused it to be recited, or heard it, or caused it to be heard.
Or he who might satisfy the reciter shall become the very body of Kālikā; or whatever man should recite it with ease or with grace.
Completely liberated from all suffering, the poet is the conqueror of the three worlds;
yet the barren woman, the woman whose sons die, the woman who bears only daughters, and the woman who is childless—[all these are overcome].
A woman barren of flowers or barren of children should listen to this supreme hymn,
which bestows all accomplishments, grants true poetic inspiration, and ensures a long life free from disease.
One obtains a lord of scholars endowed with fame; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever desire one has prepared for, having meditated upon Kālī, one should recite the hymn.
Having performed each respective act according to one's desire, the mantras become effective; it is not otherwise.
[This applies] with flowers from the vulva, flowers from the penis, or even those produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *gola*.
With the nectar-flowers of union, with the filling offerings for the deity Vastu,
with Kālī-flowers, with the waters from the sacred seat (pīṭha), and with drops for the cleansing of the womb;
The Goddess [is worshipped] with musk, saffron, and the sequence of black aloe-wood and camphor,
with the eight fragrances, and with incense, lamps, and *javā* mixed with barley-meal.
With red sandalwood and vermilion, with fish, meat, and the like, with mice, with honey, milk-rice, milk, and even purified blood;
Having worshipped Mahākālī, who is cherished by Mahākāla, with great services and offerings of food endowed with the six flavors, [one should proceed].
O Śivā, having recited the Vidyārājñī and the Kullukā,
one who is devoted to Kālī, single-minded, and adorned with a vermilion tilaka, should chant the hymn of praise.
With his mouth filled with betel, his hair disheveled, and naked as the sky, the hero,
situated within the womb of a corpse, is engaged in the sexual union of the cremation ground.
In the empty abode, upon the seat of the *bindu*, strewn with flowers in the forest of Śiva—
by knowing the Lord who moves there, one shall obtain the vision of Kālī.
Whatever action is performed there, its fruit shall be infinite;
in sovereignty, Kamalā herself resides, and in spiritual accomplishment, the form of Śrī Kālikā.
He was equal to Kavitvatāriṇī in poetic skill, like Saundaryasundarī in beauty, and like Vasordhārā in his poetry; in hearing, he was like one who possesses the Vedas.
Like the Brahmāstra, difficult to withstand, and like the weapon for conquering the three worlds,
he shall be the destroyer of enemies and the accomplisher of tasks, equal to Śiva in the Kali age.
The creator of the moon in every direction and intermediate point, he who causes the reversal of day and night, Mahādeva is a yogin equal to him, capable of paralyzing the three worlds in an instant.
In battle, he would be as directly formidable as Karṇa;
skilled and successful, he was the master of elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, and secret counsel.
By means of the *bhuśuṇḍī* at the time of the flower [mantra], one becomes sixteen years old for all time, O Maheśvarī, and there is the destruction of the graying of hair caused by water.
O Goddess of the celestial sphere of the universe, nothing is difficult for him to attain anywhere;
everything shall come into his hands—of this there is no doubt.
Having seen her adorned with family flowers, having meditated there upon Kālī,
and having fully worshipped the Queen of Vidyās, one should recite the Thousand Names.
Success consisting of the fulfillment of his desires shall always remain in his hand,
having embraced and kissed the Supreme Goddess, the wife of another.
Having joined hand to hand and performed the recitation, one should chant the hymn;
having recited the hymn at the Yonivṛkṣa, one shall become superior even to Kuvera.

O Maheśānī, having taken the substance produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* and smeared it with leaves, one should perform the fire-oblation at night; then, on the ground of the ancestors, one should erase the lines of the ritual diagram.
Having diligently brought a young woman who is restless, charming, beautiful, and proud of her beauty, and having purified her through the yoga of ritual placement (nyāsa).
Having placed [the deity] upon a bed of flowers, one should traverse the blossoming earth;
then, one should contemplate the root-cakra together with the enclosure of the Goddess.
O Parameśānī, having worshipped Maheśvarī with offerings up to the end of the *svalya*,
and having recited the mantra and offered praise, O Śivā, one should meditate upon Drāviṇī, O Maheśānī.
Having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times over the vulva and having kissed it with effort,
that yogi should recite it again; he shall become the master of all vidyās.
In an empty house, in a cremation ground, in a temple of Śiva, likewise in a desolate place,
by a lake, within the Ganges, or at a crossroads.
In a cremation ground, on a mountain, at a boundary, at a solitary linga, in a corpse, in a mouth,
on a shaven head, in a vulva, in the house of one who has bathed after her menses, and likewise in the house of a prostitute;
Whether in the middle of a brothel or always in a plantain grove,
one should recite the hymn known as the *Sahasranāma* for the accomplishment of all goals.
In the forest, in deserted forts, in battle, or when encountering powerful foes,
one should meditate upon Kālī, recite the mantra, and chant the Thousand Names.
May he become the lord of all accomplishments; may he attain the fulfillment of his desires.
[He should touch] the vulva of the two soft, tender, and youthful ones.
Having meditated upon Kālī upon a seat of grass, a cloth, or even a seat of flowers and cloth, one should then recite the Thousand Names.
Having become filled with the fivefold bliss, Kālikā herself recites [the mantra] while standing upon a bed,
with disheveled hair, wearing the quarters as her garment, and engaged in sexual union.
Having recited [the mantra] of Kālī, one should recite the hymn; thus one becomes a possessor of the *khecarī-siddhi*.
Having attained the *cikura-yoga* and the extraction (*sāraṇa*) of semen, [one attains success].
Having recited the mantra of Śrī Dakṣiṇakālī, one obtains hundreds of descents of divine power (śaktipāta).
Even by reciting while touching a creeper, or even while meditating upon Kālikā, [the same result is attained].
Beholding the directions and especially the supreme power (Paraśakti) residing within them,
and having praised Śrī Dakṣiṇākālī, one should place the Yoni-mudrā in one's own hand.
Whoever recites the Thousand Names shall become even superior to Śiva;
having praised Kālī, one should chant the *latāratas* without agitation.
Within just one month, the practitioner becomes possessed of tenfold concentration,
especially on the Night of Time, the Great Night, and the Heroic Night.
O Maheśvarī, [the time for worship is] on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days,
at the transit of the sun, during the new moon (kuhu), the full moon, and on Fridays, Tuesdays, and Sundays, at the beginning of night.
On the ninth lunar day, on a Tuesday, as well as on an auspicious *kulatithi* and under a favorable *kulanakṣatra*,
one should diligently recite the Thousand Names.
One shall quickly become endowed with the sixfold vision and attain the siddhi of the Kinnarīs;
there is an ancient linga facing west, devoid of a bull.
O Śivā, staying there, one should recite the hymn for the attainment of all desires on a Tuesday at midnight,
or on an auspicious new moon day.
An offering of black gram rice, a goat, kṛśara rice,
milk-rice, burnt fish, blood, curd, milk, jaggery, and fresh ginger.
Having offered the bali-oblation there, one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times;
thus attended by hosts of gods, gandharvas, and siddhas, [one attains] Purasundarī.
O Goddess of gods, within a month he shall attain the destruction of his latent impressions (vāsanā);
he will rise three cubits high—of this there is no need for doubt.
A man who praises Kālī with ease, playfulness, and devotion—
the Goddess Māheśī can instantly paralyze even Brahmā and the other gods and delude them.
One will certainly and surely cause eradication and indeed create a new creation by means of [the mantras of] the ram,
the buffalo, the cat, the goat, the donkey, and so forth.
With the flesh of rhinoceros, boar, pigeon, lapwing, and rabbit;
with blood, along with bones and meat; and with the causal substances of milk and milk-rice (pāyasa).

She [should be worshipped] with *kādambarī*, *siṃdhu*, and liquors, along with *ariṣṭas* and all [other] juices; with the wash-water from cleansing the vulva, and with the nectar of the vulva and the phallus.
Having worshipped with flowers of its own season at the conclusion of the recitation, one should satisfy Śiva;
then, having praised and bowed according to one's ability, one should honor all [the goddesses] by the name "Sovereignty."
During the recitation of the *śakti*, one who has assumed the form of Kālī should recite the hymn for three days;
Kālī herself, as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), will abide in his house—there is no other way.
Having gone to a bower of creepers with a courtesan, intent on kissing her,
and placing his mouth upon her vulva while tasting its flavor, he should perform the recitation.
Then, one who is devoted to worship should recite this thousand-name hymn to you;
for him, a vision of Kālikā will surely occur within three nights.
Having gone to the house of the dancing girl, honored by her with the fifth letter *ma*,
and having established the *prasūca* (the sacrificial vessel), he was devoted to the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *śakti*.
Having arranged the vessels, one should perform that [rite] while wearing garments in the direction of the quarters;
having honored the Cakra at its root, one should worship it there along with its enclosures.
O Maheśvarī, there are a hundred [dots] on the forehead, a hundred in the mass of hair, a hundred in the circle of vermilion,
two hundred on the pair of breasts, and a hundred at the navel.

O Maheśānī, having risen, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred times at the birth-place and three hundred times there; O Maheśānī, at the conclusion of that, one should recite the hymn of praise.
O Śivā, within merely a month the practitioner becomes capable of a hundredfold concentration;
having summoned Mātaṅginī or perhaps Kāpālikī.
A rosary of teeth should be used for recitation; one made from three skulls should be worn around the neck.
One should visualize the yoni-cakra on the lotus of the eyes, and the śakti-cakra on one's own face.
Having performed this, O Maheśānī, one should recite the mantra and worship the Muṇḍa-yantro.
The hero, seated upon the Muṇḍa-throne, is endowed with the five *makāras*.
Embracing one woman, he should mutter [the mantra]; kissing another, he should recite [it] with kisses;
honoring another there, he should recite [it] while massaging another.
Having bestowed Śiva upon another womb, one should perform the rite once again as before,
even amidst thousands of attentions and hundreds of descents of power (śaktipāta).
O Goddess of the gods, by practicing this yoga for five months, one becomes a king;
having brought a young woman [as a consort], he is devoted to the power of Gaṇeśa.
One should cause her vulva to open according to the sequence of family tradition;
having placed the tongue there, one should recite the Thousand Names.
Having placed a lamp there in a human skull, one should indeed recite [the mantra] without effort;
one shall become a supreme great poet—of this there is no doubt to be made.
O Supreme Goddess, O Śivā, having brought the power (śakti) afflicted by time and having drawn the root-cakra within the womb, one should write the mantra there.
The Goddess, who knows the true meaning of all scriptures, should mutter the *tallihā* mantra;
she will certainly cause one to recite even those scriptures not yet heard, such as the Vedas and others.
O beloved, without practice, without exertion, and without recitation or the like,
one shall possess the intellect of the four Vedas and become a knower of the three times within three years.
And fourfold scholarship shall come into his hands in an instant;
the Śivāvali should always be offered in the void-mandala.
The meditation on Kālī, the practice of the mantra, the sādhana of Nīla,
the recitation of the Thousand Names, and the glorification of Kālī’s names [are prescribed].
For a devotee, this much is the duty; others know it to be exceedingly compassionate:
the rite of *vīrasādhana*, the worship of Śiva, and likewise the offering of oblations (*bali*).
O Goddess, there was a vermilion tilaka, constant conversation with courtesans,
and likewise wandering at night and frequenting the houses of courtesans.
Performing the worship of Śakti with the vision of the Yoni, sword in hand, naked,
with hair disheveled, dressed as a hero (vīra), and his mouth filled with betel.
The Goddess becomes a devotee of Kālī; otherwise, she would not experience agitation.
She tastes the milk, licks the vulva, and is completely intoxicated by consciousness.
Through union with the creeper of a courtesan, one becomes oneself a wish-fulfilling vine within a month;
through union with the circle of courtesans, one becomes oneself equal to the circle of Kālī.
Through union with the body of a courtesan, he himself becomes composed of the body of Kālī;
when shall I see that heroic practitioner situated within the midst of a courtesan?
Thus spoke that Kālī; therefore, she was a courtesan of excellent limbs. Likewise, the courtesan girl belonged to the Pīṭha lineage according to the distinctions of caste and family tradition.
O Dear One, having understood the Kumārikā through the division of the Akula lineage,
one should worship the Kumārī with devotion like a deity at the conclusion of the recitation.
He who recites the Thousand Names shall become one who beholds Kālī;
he should worship with devotion a young girl, even if she is a courtesan born of a low family.
O Śivā, having gratified [the deity] with garments, gold, and other offerings, and having performed the recitation, one should chant the hymn:
"May he become a conqueror of the three worlds, and may I see the moon on the new-moon day."
Whatever is given to a Kumārī shall yield infinite fruit;
the merit of worshipping a Kumārī cannot be described by me.
Whatever has been said out of fickleness, please forgive it; no formal salutation is offered.
If one young girl is honored, both are honored.

The maidens and the powers—all this world of the moving and the unmoving—is brought by the Possessor of Power; one should then duly perform the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsa) upon His body.
Having established [the image] on one's own left side, one should recite the Thousand Names;
one shall become a master of all accomplishments—there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
One should dwell in a cremation ground, remain well-composed, and let one's hair fall loose; clad in the directions as one's garment, one should gather a thousand *sūryapuṣpa* flowers.
Having endowed [the mantra] with one's own vigor, one should recite and offer oblations for each individually;
having worshipped and meditated with great devotion, the king of men should recite it.
Nails, hair, and one's own semen— whatever has fallen upon the broom—
he should offer while with disheveled hair and wearing the quarters as his garment, preceded by the root mantra.
Having performed a fire sacrifice (homa) in a cremation ground at midnight on a Saturday,
he who recites the Thousand Names shall effect the summoning of the lords of the earth.
O Goddess, when the vulva is joined with flowers,
one intent on the bliss of union should again take hold of the hair and recite the root mantra, O Śivā.
Having diligently cast the *vīrya* into the fire of the funeral pyre at midnight,
one should worship Kālikā there and recite the *Nāmasahasraka*.
One should perform the attraction of the lord of the earth; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Having reached a grove of plantain trees, a person should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
Served by the goddess Madhumatī herself, he was like the god of love;
and thus, having spoken of the illustrious Madhumatī, [he described] the world of moving and unmoving beings.
Having uttered "Karṣaṇī," one should then utter "Ṭhaṭha Svāhā.
This Vidyā, the Attractor of the Three Worlds, shall reside in his hand sevenfold.
O Minister, he draws forth rivers, cities, jewels, mountains, and trees from the ocean, from Mount Sumeru, and from every direction.
And objects that are unattainable, even from a distance or from the surface of the earth;
as well as the conduct of those standing before one, and the secrets even of enemies.
And tell it to those kings into whom truth may quickly enter;
by reciting it for a second year, one shall become the husband of Padmāvatī.
Oṃ hrīṃ Padmāvati, speak of that place named Trailokya and tell me the news; this mantra, ending with svāhā, is thus proclaimed.
O Goddess of gods, the auspicious sage, who knows the three periods of time, speaks of everything— whatever may exist in the three worlds concerning Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others.
O Goddess, by reciting the Trivarga, one may obtain the portion of the Bhogavatī [Kalā],
even if seen by Mahākāla or even without having entered the path of smoke.
By the mere sight of it, a person becomes long-lived;
having uttered the *Mṛtasañjīvanī* mantra, one who has died shall rise up.
The mantra is said to end with "svāhā"; thereafter, one shall attain success in dreams.
With "Oṃ hrīṃ," one should invoke Svapnavārāhī Kālī so that she may speak in the dream and deliver [the seeker].
The mantra is considered to end with "svāhā," preceded by "amukasya" and "amukam dehi krīm.
Once she has attained success through dreams, she remains present in his dreams after four years.
By the study of a four-year-old [child], a man becomes a master of the four Vedas;
and through contact with the water from his mouth, even a tree composes poetry.
By the power of his words, the form of stone spoke the speech of Sarasvatī;
placing his hand upon the rock, he said, "Speak! and the voice emerged.
Whatever a practitioner performs with desire shall come to pass exactly so; whatever is sought on this earth within the sphere of the universe, that too shall be fulfilled.
O Goddess, all accomplishments (siddhis) arise from the root of the Kalās;
whatever measured accomplishments there may be, they come to the practitioner merely by his recollection.
They come before one of their own accord; what need is there to mention recitation and other rites? Acting as if under command, they remain like servants.
On the new moon day, there was the appearance of the moon and likewise a lunar eclipse;
on the eighth day, the fullness of the moon, as well as the eightfold [manifestation] of the moon and sun.
Likewise, the Great Goddess indeed effects eight [powers] in the eight directions:
atomization (aṇimā), the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva), and the ability to enter the bodies of all moving and stationary beings.
The sandals, the sword, the vetāla, the yakṣiṇī, the guhyakas and so forth; the forehead mark, secrecy, visibility, and the narrative of the moving and the unmoving.
The accomplishment of reviving the dead, the medicinal pill, the elixir of life,
the accomplishment of flying upward— O Goddess of Gods, these constitute the state of being a lord of the sixty accomplishments.
O Goddess, it shall be in his hand; there is no need for deliberation here.
Whether on a banner, a drum, a garment, a canopy, a binding, or in a house—
A painting on a wall, a wooden panel, or a pedestal should be worshipped with great care;
it should display the central wheel endowed with its ten limbs, surrounded by the inscription of the name.
By warding that off, O Great Goddess, one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds;
indeed, alone upon the field of battle, one may defeat hundreds of thousands.
And Pārvatī returns happily to her own home;
for indeed, one who perceives the hundred worlds becomes certain [of his goal].
Having carefully established the water-pot, one should recite the *Nāmasāhasraka*;
O Maheśānī, this should be performed as the warding off of all calamities.
O Skanda, [one should offer oblations] to the bhūtas, pretas, grahas, and so forth; to the rākṣasas, brahmarākṣasas, vetālas, bhairavas, and the leaders of the nāyikās.
It shall destroy [the affliction] in a mere instant; no deliberation is required here.
Having consecrated ashes with mantras, one should smear them upon one seized by a planetary spirit.
O Goddess, by sprinkling ashes, there is warding off of all seizing spirits; O Maheśvarī, having consecrated butter with mantras, one should give it to women.
O Goddess Śivā, by wearing [this] on the neck, on the left arm, or in the womb, a barren woman becomes possessed of sons; there is no need for deliberation here.
A woman who wears it on her left side will certainly become blessed with many sons and auspicious;
a man should wear it on his right side for the attainment of all success.
One should wear [the amulet] on the neck, the arm, the head, the heart, the field of vision,
the waist, and the crest-lock for the sake of attaining all perfections.
He will be powerful, renowned, blessed, righteous, successful, and accomplished;
he will have many sons, be a lord of chariots and elephants, and live in happiness.
Intent on attracting beautiful women, the reciter of the name should chant ten thousand times the mantra: "O Dakṣiṇakālikā! Krīṃ! Svāhā! (krīṃ ca dakṣiṇakālike krīṃ svāhā).
O Goddess, one should perform the rite of attraction for those who move through water, through the air, or on the earth;
indeed, for the purpose of subjugation, one should utter *hūṃ hūṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ* in the right [hand].
Reciting the seed-syllables of the *kūrca* mantra at the proper time as before, one shall bring even Urvaśī under control; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
A person should recite "KĪM, O Kālikā of the South, SVĀHĀ" joined with the mantra,
and by reciting the Thousand Names, one will certainly cause the destruction of the three worlds.
It should be given to a virtuous son who is well-versed in the Queen of Knowledge (Vidyārājñī),
who is well-disciplined, peaceful, self-controlled, and possessed of excellent qualities.
To the devotee who is his eldest son, who is supremely devoted to his guru,
who is a devotee of devotees, who is worthy, and who is exclusively devoted to Śakti.
This work called the Thousand Names should be given by Kālī herself to a pure Vaiṣṇava who is devoted to Śiva and to ritual offerings.
To the one engaged in the worship of courtesans, to the worshiper of virgins,
to the devotee of Durgā, to the Śaiva, and to the progenitor of Mahākāla.
To one endowed with the state of non-duality, devoted supremely to Kālī,
and [dedicated] to the Guru, the Deity, the Mantras, and even to Maheśa and Pārvatī.
One should remember the mantra without making any distinction; he is Śiva, there is no doubt about this.
The practitioner who meditates upon the mantra is Śiva himself, and he is indeed the singer of the hymns.
He is indeed a Śākta and a Vaiṣṇava; he alone is fully initiated here.
This [initiation] must not be given to an unworthy person, for it would result in the obstruction of spiritual attainment.
Furthermore, for one who reviles a prostitute or reviles a woman who knows the secret of wine,
the mantra *surāmukhī*— having been recollected— will descend like wine.
One should utter "vāgvṛttāghore āḥ saḥ" and "paramaghore hūm";
then one should utter the words "ghorarūpe", "haḥ", "ghoramukhi", and "bhīma".

The mantra is formed by [the syllable] *bhīṣaṇya*, ending with the sixth vowel (*ū*), followed by *hetu* (the letter *ha*) and *mayuta* (the letter *ma*), then *pivā* (the letter *va*), *śivaṃ* (the letter *sa*), *vahni* (the letter *ra*), the *yuga-astra* (the letter *pha*), and finally *hūṃ haḥ phaṭ*. Thus it becomes the mantra.
O Goddess, by the mere remembrance of this [mantra], liquor shall descend into the mouths of the wicked; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
To one who is wicked, dependent on others, devoted to reviling others,
fallen, of evil nature, and intent upon slander;
O Goddess, one should not show this hymn to a devotee who is wicked or devoted to the wives of others; [if one does so], it would result in the sin of killing Śiva.
He whose heart is blissful with Kali, whose mind is attached to Kālī,
and who is a devotee of Kālī— he indeed is the one of blessed form.
In the Kali age Kālī, in the Kali age Kālī, in the Kali age Kālī alone;
in the Kali age Kālī, in the Kali age Kālī, in the Kali age Kālī is the bestower of boons.
One should worship with thousands of bilva leaves and likewise with karavīra flowers; by worshipping according to their respective names, the boon-granting Kālī becomes well-pleased.
O Goddess of the Gods, having worshipped the wheel, one should offer a thousand lotuses according to their respective names; thus one shall obtain the boon from Kālikā.
O Goddess, by sprinkling with the water contained in the divine jar while reciting mantras accompanied by the *kṣobha* syllable,
and by pronouncing the [recipient's] name, one brings about the destruction of all disturbances.
Likewise, O Goddess, the observer of the vow should bring a thousand *damanaka* flowers;
having worshipped Kālikā with her thousand names, he shall obtain a boon.
Having drawn the wheel situated within the body, one should maintain the form of Kālikā;
O Śivā, one should consume whatever remains after it has been offered to Kālī.
Having assumed divine bodies, Kālī shall abide within their forms;
seeing the wicked who revile the food offering, the Bhairavas dance.
And the great heroines, the yoginīs, are always intent on drinking blood;
they are engaged in chewing flesh and bone and devour them, without a doubt.
Therefore, one should not revile [it] in thought, deed, or word—how much less so otherwise!
For he who acts contrarily shall suffer a downfall.
Success comes for those who are devoid of initiation only through the gradual [process], and not otherwise;
otherwise, there may be agitation of the mantra, or one's lifespan will certainly be diminished.
One will certainly become a stealer of sons, a stealer of women, and a stealer of kingdoms;
O Goddess, one who possesses the Krama initiation shall, however, obtain a kingdom through the sequence.
O Goddess, one who recites it once destroys all sins;
indeed, he who recites it twice constantly attains his desires.
He who recites it three times shall attain equality with the Lord of Speech;
O Goddess, he who recites it four times shall become the sovereign of the four castes.
O Goddess, by reciting it five times, one becomes the lord of the five desires;
O Goddess, by reciting it six times, one becomes possessed of the six sovereign powers.
O Goddess, by reciting it seven times, one obtains whatever desires one has contemplated;
O Goddess, by reciting it eight times, one certainly becomes a lord of the quarters.
If one recites it nine times, O Goddess, one becomes equal to the Nine Lords (Navanātha). He who recites it ten times becomes a lord of the Dāśārhas and a master of the sky-farers.
He who recites it twenty times shall become possessed of all sovereignty;
by twenty-five times, he becomes the destroyer of all anxieties.
By reciting it fifty times, one becomes the lord of the five elements;
he who recites it a hundred times attains a mind equal to Śatānanda.
By reciting it five hundred times, O Goddess, one becomes the Lord of the Kings of Kings in the Kali age;
by reciting it a thousand times, Lakṣmī herself encompasses him.
Enveloping the triple-thousandfold world system, he possesses a splendor equal to that of the Three-eyed One;
by five thousand recitations, he becomes the deluder of millions of Kāmas.
By reciting it ten thousand times, one becomes the Lord of Ten Faces;
by twenty-five thousand, one enjoys the twenty-four accomplishments (siddhis).
By merely reciting it one hundred thousand times, one becomes equal to the Lord of Lakṣmī;
by reciting it three hundred thousand times, however, one shall conquer Mahādeva.
Encompassing five hundred thousand [recitations] and joined with the five kalās,
the supreme attainment of the ten Vidyās results from the clockwise rotation of one hundred thousand.
By twenty-five hundred thousand [recitations], one becomes a Lord of the Ten Vidyās;
by completing fifty hundred thousand, one becomes equal to Mahākāla.
Whoever should behold Kālī with their eyes at the end of ten million [revolutions],
she who is intent on granting boons and accompanied by Mahākāla;
One perceives Śivā directly; she dwells eternally within his body. One should recite this regarding the subject of the three powers: Śrīvidyā, Kālikā, and Tārā.
O Goddess, the Krama initiation is proclaimed for the domain of the three powers;
one who is endowed with the Krama initiation certainly becomes a king of the goddesses.
Having wiped away the writing of destiny and having cast off the state of being an instrument, one attains great sovereignty; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O Goddess, for one devoid of the Krama initiation, the fruit described as "Fullness" (Pūrṇama) is said to be [merely nominal];
however, one endowed with the Krama initiation is Śiva himself and nothing else.
One who is endowed with the Krama initiation shall partake in the accomplishments (siddhis) declared in the Kalpa;
for one devoid of the Krama initiation, there is a loss of accomplishment at every step.
Oh, how blessed is the land of Varta in the midst [of the world], and how blessed is he who possesses the Krama in the Kali age!
Even there, O Mistress of the Gods, most blessed is the reciter of the Thousand Names.
In the ritual of Daśakālī, O Goddess of the gods, one should always recite this hymn to me;
one attains perfection—of this there is no doubt.
In the Kali age, Kālī is the Great Vidyā; in the Kali age, Kālī indeed bestows accomplishment; in the Kali age, Kālī is perfectly perfected; and in the Kali age, Kālī grants boons.
In the Kali age, Kālī is prepared to appear before the practitioner; in the Kali age, Kālī alone shall exist—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
In the Kali age, there shall be no other knowledge, no other knowledge, no other knowledge; for whoever desires success in the Kali age must abandon Kālī.
O Goddess, he who desires pleasure and sexual enjoyment without Śakti, or whoever in the Kali age desires to accomplish any task without Kālī, [is like one who seeks fruit without a tree].
Having abandoned the practice of Nīlasādhanā, he wanders everywhere; for in the Kali age, whoever seeks liberation must first abandon Kālī.
The practitioner who desires accomplishment while abandoning meditation on the Guru is like someone who, in the Kali age, desires a kingdom while forsaking Kālī.
He who, having renounced all food, desires only the cessation of hunger—
he is blessed, he is wise, and he alone is worshipped by the gods.
He is initiated, happy, virtuous, truthful, and one who has conquered his senses;
he is a speaker of the Vedas, devoted to sacred study, and intent upon the bliss of all.
Having meditated upon Kālī within oneself, one should worship the Mother of the Universe;
one shall become a conqueror of the three worlds—of this there is no need for deliberation.
Having meditated upon Śiva in the form of the Guru, one should remember the Guru as being Śiva;
he shall indeed become Sadāśiva himself—of this there is no need for doubt.
It must be guarded, guarded, guarded with great effort;
it is a secret, a most profound secret, a secret beyond the most profound.
O Goddess, one should recite even half a verse, a single quarter-verse, half a quarter-verse, half of that, or even half a name; one should not let a day pass in vain.
One should worship the book with devotion for the sake of attaining livelihood and the fulfillment of desired fruits;
there, the fear of new women, as well as that arising from the nine fires and the wind, shall cease.
There, no fear arises from spirits or other such things; everywhere, happiness increases, just as saffron becomes even more intensely red through the application of yellow pigment and aloe-wood.
"Write this mantra on birch bark for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
Thus has been declared in its entirety the form of the letters of Kālikā.
If one recites this with devotion, one shall become a lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis),
possessing ever-new happiness and delighting in all branches of knowledge.
There occurs the attainment of all perfections and the prosperity of all heroes.
Thus it has been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the thousand-name hymn beginning with the letter *Ka*, titled "The Bestowing of Boons upon Sundarī," from the dialogue between Kālī and Kāla within the *Mahākālasaṃhitā* composed by the illustrious Ādinātha.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Determination of the Hymn, Armor, and Other Elements," within the daily worship of Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Now, as an ancillary part of the Śrī Dakṣiṇāmūrti [Tantra], he describes the individual worship of the Nityās, beginning with Mahākālī.
The Goddess said:
Speak the two-fold determination of the Mahākāla and Ādinityā deities.
The illustrious Śiva said:
Beginning with Mahākāla, hear the determination regarding the Nityās:
Mahākāla is most formidable, resembling the fire of universal destruction.
Born from the illusion (māyā) of Kālī, Śiva is the mental essence of Kālī;
Mahākāla is the supreme Śambhu, the source of qualities beyond the highest.
I shall proclaim his mantra, by which one may protect the three worlds:
"Kūrca" twice, followed by "Mahākāla" and the two words "prasīda."
The sixteen-syllable mantra consists of the pair of *lajjā* (the two *hrīṃ*) joined with the wife of fire (*svāhā*).
Just as this sixteen-syllable mantra is primary within the entire mandala of the Śrīcakra, so too is it supreme.
Likewise, this Mahākāla is proclaimed to be present at all times;
Kālikā is declared his seer (ṛṣi), and Virāṭ is proclaimed as his meter (chandas).
The deity is Mahākāla, who possesses all forms and is stainless;
likewise, the *kūrca* seed-syllable and the power of *māyā* are proclaimed here.
" Svāhā" is designated as the *kīlaka*, and its application is for the purpose of Kālī.
Now hear, O fair-faced one, the meditation on the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) performed through *māyā*.
He has the appearance of ten million Kalās, possesses four arms and three eyes,
stands in the midst of eight cremation grounds, and is adorned by eight severed heads.
The god stands upon five corpses, holding a trident and a hand-drum,
as well as a sword and a skull-bowl, in the order of the left and right hands.
Bearing a beautiful body adorned with the ashes of the cremation ground,
playing with various corpses, and dwelling in the heart of Kālikā.
Lusting and intent on passion, devoted to terrible kissing,
he was surrounded by vultures and jackals, accompanied by a pack of female jackals.
Śiva is richly adorned with the beauty of his mass of matted locks, standing as the protector of all beings;
he is the emptiness of all things, adorned with a skull, and possesses a serene countenance.
O Supreme Goddess, one should meditate upon the Yantra of Rati, that very Yantra;
the triangle is known as the Yoni, and that wheel is the Kālacakra.
One should worship the god Mahākāla, together with his fivefold enclosure, either in the vulva, the heart, the forehead, or upon the circle of the breasts of a beloved woman.
O Goddess, one should worship Kālikā and the others in the triangle;
the six limbs are worshipped in the six-petalled [lotus], and the powers beginning with Nābhau are considered to be in the pericarp.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship the twelve Ādityas in the heart, the sixteen Nityās in the throat,
and Kālakālī on the two petals.
During inverted sexual union, one should worship the Goddess;
during [ordinary] sexual union, one should worship the supreme Kālikā, having turned the Śakti toward oneself.
O Supreme Goddess, one should fashion the cakras from the mūlādhāra up to the end of the two petals,
and worship them preceded by the worship of the Guru.
Having arranged the ritual vessels, one should worship [the deity] like Kālī;
having thus performed the worship, O Śivā, one should then recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should perform the oblation with *karavīra* flowers of that same proportion,
consecrated with the seed-mantras (*bīja*) spoken by Svayambhū, or with the *kāraṇa*-mantras, for the sake of subduing.
One should perform all [rites]— the daily (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and those for specific desires (kāmya)— just as one would for Kālī.
The procedure for the Vidyā of Kālī, who brings an end to ignorance, is now declared;
having first performed the visualization of her form, which is adorned with all its limbs.
One should worship Gaṇapati at the base of the support, Gaṇapativallabhā on the liṅga,
Vaṭukanātha at the navel, and Vaṭukavallabhā in the heart.
One should worship Udyānapīṭha on the throat, Pradīptamaṅgala on the eyebrows,
Karavīra on the forehead, and Kṣetrapālaka on the hair-tuft.
One should worship Kālikā, ending in the dative case (Kālikāyai), upon the head;
likewise, one possessing the sovereignty of space (Vyomaiśvaryā) on the head, and Khecarī on the forehead.
One should place Dikcarī between the eyebrows, Gocarī likewise in the heart,
Bhūcarī in the navel, and Khagamūrtikā in the generative organ.
The best of practitioners should worship the variegated [deity] on the root-leaf;
likewise, he should worship the Sun on the forehead and the Lord of Kalās on the right eye.
One should worship Vaiśvānara with the left eye, Kālikā in the throat,
Dāsayoni in the heart, and Tāsasiddhaka in the navel.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
as well as Vārāhī, Aindrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Mahālakṣmī are considered supreme.
Maṇṭhānabhairava, as well as Ṣaṭcakrabhairava,
Ṣaṭkālabhairava, and Ravibhakṣakabhairava.
Vīreśa Bhairava, Śrīmantraīśvara Bhairava,
Hemagarbha Bhairava, and Caṇḍikeśvara Bhairava.
The wise one should perform worship on the crown of the head, the forehead, the throat, the heart, the navel region, the linga, the mūlādhāra, and all the limbs.
The learned one should recite [the mantra] according to his capacity and offer the bali-oblation according to the prescribed rule:
"Oṃ Kṣauca Kṣetrapāla, [he] should utter these words regarding the bali."
"Take, take! This offering, joined with the pair, is intended for Kṣetrapāla.
Thus, O Goddess, is the procedure for worship considered for Śrī Kālī and Kāla.
Through the procedure of internal meditation, the inverted sexual union (viparīta-rati) is considered [attained];
even the secret has been revealed through the context of Mahākāla.
O auspicious lady, you must keep this most secret of secrets hidden;
it must be guarded, guarded, just as one guards one's own private parts from others.
Now listen as the mantra of Kālīnityā is being told:
first the poison-seed (viṣa-bīja), then Māyā (hrīṃ), and one should utter the pair "Kālī" twice.
Having uttered the word "Mahākālī," one should speak the word "Kaumārī";
then the words "bhagaṃ dehi" (grant [me] fortune) and "dehi" (give), followed by "ṭhaṭha"—this is considered the mantra.
The twenty-one-syllable Vidyā is proclaimed as the eternal Kālī.
Paraśurāma is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas) is proclaimed to be Anuṣṭubh,
Kālikā is declared to be the deity, and Māyā is proclaimed to be the seed-syllable (bīja).
The Śakti shall be Kālikā, and the pair of Ṭha-s shall be the Kīlaka;
the application of Kālikā is proclaimed for the purpose of propitiation and so forth.
O Goddess, one should perform the six-limbed practice with the Māyā-mantra joined with the [appropriate] birth-syllable;
thereafter, O Maheśānī, one should meditate within the circle of the extinction of the funeral pyre.
Dark-complexioned, most terrifying, with a dreadful roar and formidable appearance,
she is richly adorned with a garland of severed heads and brandishes a sword in her right hand.
She should hold a threatening gesture with her left hand while dancing in the realms of the pretas;
having meditated thus, O Maheśānī, listen to that yantra, O Pārvatī.
O Goddess of gods, having worshipped Kālī within the *bindu* of a diagram consisting of two triangles, a circle, an eight-petaled lotus,
and a square enclosure, one should worship her again within the pair of triangles.
The three qualities (guṇas), those situated therein, and their powers are considered to follow in sequence;
likewise, the eight Mothers beginning with Brāhmī, and the world-protectors (lokapālas) together with their weapons.
O Goddess, one should worship [the deities] in the Bhūpura with offerings of incense, lamps,
and various kinds of food, especially the five types of solid foods.
One should offer it to Kālikā; then she will become pleased.
Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājanīta), one should then recite the mantra for exactly one hundred thousand times.
One should perform the fire offering (homa) according to the prescribed rite with milk-rice (pāyasa) ten times [the number of recitations],
or alternatively, one should offer karavīra flowers for the attainment of all perfections.
O Goddess, he indeed becomes the lord of all accomplishments; of this there is no doubt.
I shall proclaim the divisions of the mantras; listen attentively as they truly are, O Maheśānī, each one according to the sequence of the Praṇava, beginning with its mere name.
O Maheśānī, one should employ the three mantras as the three seed-syllables;
furthermore, O Goddess, the three vidyās are formed by the employment of the Dhruva and Māyā syllables.
O Maheśānī, each of the three Vidyās consists of nine mantras;
they are for those who are unfortunate, the wretched, the cruel, and those who perform sinful deeds.
One who recites this mantra shall become possessed of all sovereignty;
he will surely become wealthy, famous, and blessed—of this there is no doubt.
Having seen a beautiful woman who is a mistress of love, one should speak of her *bhaga*;
by the recitation of the mantra on the word *bhaga*, that slave girl becomes possessed of that *bhaga*.
She indeed becomes agitated and desires enjoyment according to her own will;
one should place the Vidyā on the forehead, the heart, and the center of the womb in due order.
If a wise person recollects the name of this vidyā preceded by mindfulness, he attracts her; what is the use of much further talk?
O Goddess of Gods, he would be Kālīputra in person; there is no need for deliberation on this point. This secret is being told, which has not been proclaimed anywhere else.
Kapālinī is the great vidyā; hear now her second mantra.
First, having uttered the syllable *sa* with its vowel portion (*a*), followed by *kāma* (the letter *ka*) situated on the "fire-place" (*ra*),
and then *indirā* (the letter *i*) adorned with the dot (*bindu*), one obtains the seed-syllable (*bīja*) which is the very nature of Kālī.
One should recite in the mind: "O Kapālinī, you who are fond of the great skull-cup, grant me the accomplishment of the skull-cup! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā! What is this mantra?
The king of mantras, consisting of thirty syllables and a half-syllable, is the most supreme;
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and Triṣṭubh is cited as its meter (chaṃdas).
The deity is Kapālinī; the seed-syllable is said to be Anukālikā;
Svāhā is declared to be the Śakti; and Hūṃ Phaṭ is declared to be the Kīlaka.
The application for the attainment of the Kapālinī-siddhi has been proclaimed;
with the seed-syllable possessing the six long vowels, the six limbs beginning with the *kūrca* [mantra] are assigned in sequence.
One should meditate upon her who is adorned with collyrium, possessing a pair of full,
milk-white breasts, moon-like face, bimba-red lips, loose hair, and is naked.
She is surrounded by four severed heads, adorned with conch shells and bracelets,
and possesses four hands holding a sword, a trident, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should thus meditate upon the supreme goddess Mahākāpālinī, who bestows [boons] in succession and is devoted to song and laughter.
Three triangles, a circle adorned with eight petals,
surrounded by a perimeter of earth (bhūpura), and beautified by four gates.
This yantra of the goddess Kāpālinī bestows universal sovereignty;
it likewise [concerns] Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī.
In the second [triangle], one should worship Rati, Prīti, and Kānti;
likewise, in the third triangle, one should worship Icchā, Jñānā, and Kriyā.

Having worshipped Kapālinī in the center, one should perform the worship of the Mātṛkās on the eight petals; thereafter, one should sacrifice to the eight Bhairavas, the lords of the directions, and the Śāstrakas.
Having worshipped with the five offerings, the practitioner, devoted to the family tradition (kulācāra),
should mutter [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with flowers sacred to Hayagrīva.
Or one may offer oblations with honey for a month to accomplish the desired goal;
then the goddess Kāpālinī will certainly grant success.
Without the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), how can there be success with the goddess Kapālinī?
A man, seated upon a skull-throne, should always remain with his mind fixed upon her.
Having performed the great garland, the great vessel, the great terror, and so forth,
according to the ritual procedure, O Goddess, one then becomes a practitioner (sādhaka).
Now I shall also describe another feat of the Kāpālinī:
on a Saturday at the onset of night, she [gathered] skulls from the heroes of battle.
O Great Goddess, having gathered [the materials] together, endowed with the five-fifths [mantras],
one should perform the binding of the directions, the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), and so forth, along with the offerings to the guardians of the quarters and others.
The practitioner, having become composed, marked with a tilaka of vermilion,
sword in hand, clothed in the directions (naked), with disheveled hair, and filled with joy;
Being such a practitioner, endowed with a sense of accomplishment,
and having set aside the means of practice at a great distance, [one should proceed] with a flower-wick soaked in ghee.
The Goddess should cause the lamp to flicker; there, one should mutter the mantra of Kapālinī.
Through good fortune, the accomplishment of Kapālinī may perhaps arise.
Nevertheless, Kālikā will appear before her devotee;
she will appear if, by the power of fortune, a skull is ever obtained.
Then, having obtained the skull-bowl siddhi and having collected that soot,
one should indeed place that soot in the skull-bowl and recite the mantra.
O Maheśānī, that which is called the great "ointment of delusion" has been proclaimed by people;
yet what is that which resides in the skull, rather than in the hand?
This Kapālinī is eternal, and Kālikā is the second;
thus it has been briefly declared. Now hear of Kullā, the third.
She who is known by three names— Kālikā, Kullukā, and Kullā—
has therefore attained the status of being worshiped by the Kula through the name "Kullā."
Because she is worshipped by the Kula among the sciences (vidyās), she is celebrated as Kullukā;
because she is worshipped by the Kula, she is the Mistress of the Kula (Kuleśvarī) by the name of the Kula.
I shall proclaim her mantra; listen attentively as it truly is.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, one should extract the seed-syllable (bīja) of Kālikā;
"Kullāyai" is the heart-mantra (hṛnmanu); this seven-syllabled mantra is declared to belong to the Goddess.
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is said to be the meter (chandas),
Kullākālī is the deity here, and Kālikā is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja).
The power known as Kullāśakti is saluted; it is proclaimed as Kālaka, and its application is celebrated for the accomplishment of all aims.

One should worship on the *pīṭha* that which was spoken by Kālikā; indeed, it is the *yantra* itself. One should worship the Goddess in the *kumārī*; Kullā will certainly become accomplished (*siddhā*).
One should recite the mantra two hundred thousand times while eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), remaining pure by day;
likewise at night one may remain impure, being eager for the vision of Śrī Kullā.
Sometimes resembling a cloud, sometimes like a light,
possessing four faces and three eyes, adorned with a magnificent crown.
One should visualize Kullā seated upon a corpse-couch, resting atop ten severed heads;
her left hands display the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, while her right hands hold a book and a rosary.
Or one should contemplate Kullā, who is skilled in various amorous graces;
for one contemplating her in this way, the digit consisting of the ten sciences arises.
O Maheśānī, by the power of Kullāyanī,
[the desired result] indeed comes to pass through oblations of karavīra and javā flowers performed in the tenth part of the number of recitations.
One should satisfy it with fragrant water in the tenth part of that amount and also perform the ritual sprinkling;
at the conclusion, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and the Kumārī.
O Supreme Goddess, by worshipping [her], the Kullā-vidyā becomes perfected.
O Great Goddess, the Kullā-vidyā is the illuminator of all vidyās.
O Goddess of gods, for the ritual of the single-minded vow (ekāmyakarma), one should employ this yantra,
which consists of two raised triangles and is adorned with circles and eight petals.
It is provided with four gates and joined with a single outer square (bhūpura);
in the center, one should place the seed-syllable of Kālī, which is most excellent when conjoined with its seed-mantra.
One should worship Dhṛti, Puṣṭi, Medhā, Prajñā, and Japā within the two triangles; and on the petals, the eight Mothers and Bhairava.
One should worship the World-Protectors (Lokapālas), joined with their respective scriptures, in the Kullukā-enclosure;
or else, O Goddess of the God of Gods, [one may worship them] entirely as in the case of Kālikā.
On both Navarātras, during both lunar eclipses,
at the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), and on the most excellent lunar days, one should worship this wonderful yantra.
As soon as a task has arisen, one must immediately perform the worship of Kullukā;
for without the worship of Kullukā, one does not attain the perfection of knowledge.
One who is joined with the first [syllable] shall attain the perfection of the vidyā;
however, that teacher who does not know both the first and the last is a destroyer of his disciples.
Indeed, a mantra that possesses its initial and final syllables conjoined with ritual action is eternally perfected;
for one who is devoid of the initial and final [syllables], there can be no vision of that deity.
The world is joined by these two—affection and fear;
this method I have taught must not be disclosed to anyone anywhere.
In the case of the Nityās beginning with Kullādevī, the recitation (japa) extends up to the second couplet;
if it is not accomplished by those two, that mantra is not fit for recitation.
Kullā has been declared by me to be eternal; in her is established the entire essence of the world. Kullā is the concise mode of worship.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the most secret of secrets;
because she is the object of worship for the Kula among all vidyās, Kuru-kullā is superior to the Kula.
Because Kullā is also worthy of worship, Kuru-kullā brings great prosperity;
O Great Goddess, her mantra is the most excellent among all mantras.
Having extracted *kālīṃ* and *dhruvam*, one should utter *samuddhṛtya*, *kuru*, *kulle*, and *padam*.
Then follow *kālīṃ*, *māyā*, *mama*, *padam*, and *sarvajanapadam*.
Having uttered *vaśamāna*, [one says] *kālī* and *kurukulluke*; having extracted the word, O Goddess of Gods, the mantra ends with *māyā svāhā*. This is the *go-manu*.
O Goddess, the mantra of this celestial tree consists of twenty-seven syllables; its heart-mantra is the nine-syllabled Kuru-kullā.
O Great Goddess, O Sovereign of the Gods, Śrīvidyā is distinct from the subject matter of Kurukullā;
O Goddess, Śrīvidyā [contains] the Kālī-aṅga-vidyā and Kurukullā.
This is the great, distinct Vidyā, Kālī, the eternal Fourth;
O Goddess, without the heart-mantra, Kurukullā is not accomplished.
Having learned the heart-mantra of Kurukullā with diligence, Pārvatī should first utter the Praṇava (Oṃ) and then recite the word "Kurukulle."
O Goddess, the mantra ending in *hrīṃ svāhā* belongs to Kurukullā Kumārikā;
it is declared to be her heart-mantra (*hṛnmanu*), the most excellent of all mantras.
Kālabhairava is its seer (ṛṣi), and Vṛhatī is declared to be its meter (chandas);
the deity is Kurukullā, the supreme one who consists of all vidyās.
*Krīṃ* is said to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hrīṃ* likewise the power (*śakti*), and *svāhā* the pin (*kīlaka*).
Kurukullā is the maiden (*kumārī*), while Bhairava is the reverse.
The Virāṭ meter is proclaimed, the Kūrca seed-syllable is celebrated,
Svāhā is designated as the Śakti, and the application is according to one's desire.
Kurukullā, the friend of the Kula, Kurukullā who dwells in the heart; O Kālī, O Kurukullā, may the syllables *dhruva*, *krīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, and *hrūṃ* protect me from all sides.
"Janavaśaṃ krīṃ kuru yuk kurukulle triviṣṭayā svāhā"—
this mantra is taught, for Bhairava is indeed the Virāṭ [meter] therein.
The seed-syllable is *hrīṃ*, and likewise *svāhā* is considered the power (*śakti*); *klīṃ* is regarded as the pin (*kīlaka*).
The application for all purposes (*sarvārtha-viniyoga*) is proclaimed to be as before in some traditions.

The application (viniyoga) shall be as before; listen now to the ritual arrangement of the limbs (aṅga-kalpanā). One should perform the six limbs in sequence using the six long vowels as seed-syllables for Kālī.
Then one should meditate upon the Great Goddess Kurukullā, the Great Vidyā,
seated upon a corpse and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Holding a skull-bowl and a chopper in her hands, bearing a sword and a shield,
resembling a mountain of collyrium, divine, with loose hair, and four-armed.
She possesses a pair of full and elevated breasts, a broad chest, and shapely hips;
she is intent on bestowing bliss upon her devotees and grants the desired objects of her practitioners.
One should thus contemplate the goddess Kurukullā, who brings great prosperity, whose eyes are filled with nectar, and who fascinates all people.
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while partaking of the three sweets;
O Dear One, one should also perform the fire sacrifice with bilva leaves and bilva flowers.
One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part [of the recitations], and the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) with a tenth part of that;
O Brahmin, one should also feed ten [Brahmins], and by that means the mantra becomes perfected.
One should worship in the seat of Kālikā, which is radiant with three triangles,
enriched with the ornaments of a circle and an eight-petaled lotus, and beautified by two enclosures of earth (bhūpura).
One should write the seed-syllable (*bīja*) within the *bindu* and worship the triad of the three powers (*triśakti*) of Kālī—
namely Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, Vālā, Vagalā, or Rasā.
Ugraprabhā and Ugravīryā are the third;
the worship of these three in a triangular formation is proclaimed according to the sequence.
One should worship the eight [deities] beginning with Brāhmī and Bhairava upon the eight petals;
the Supreme Goddess should worship those ending with the world-protectors and their weapons.
In a cemetery, a cremation ground, a forest, or a wilderness teeming with spirits, one should worship Kurukullā; he shall obtain all accomplishments.
Whatever the practitioner desires in his heart, that he shall obtain;
he should worship all the goddesses, as well as Brāhmaṇas and married women.
What need is there for anything else when it resides within the mere propitiation of the Brahmins?
Through rice one attains victory; through wheat, the arrival of wealth.
Through oblations of black gram (māṣa), one brings about the death of an enemy; through mung beans (mudga), one attains liberation;
and by offering oblations of sesame seeds and rice, he finds great joy.
By means of an oblation of salt and *rājī* seeds, one will certainly attract a passionate woman;
with mustard seeds and salt, one brings about the destruction of the mind of a divine woman.
By an oblation of ghee and salt, one wins over a loving woman;
by means of turmeric, poverty is surely destroyed—of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, the Nityā known as Virodhinī is said to be more secret than the secret;
understand correctly this fifth Nityā.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, one should extract "Kāli" followed by the Praṇava;
then Māyā, Kāma, and Kūrca are declared, followed by the word "Virodhinī."
The mantra for uprooting enemies is: "O you who speak of hostility, destroy the enemy!
HŪM PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. This mantra is said to cause the destruction of the foe.
This supreme king of mantras, consisting of thirty-two syllables, is declared to be the Great Mantra;
its seer is said to be Bhairava.
The Gāyatrī meter is prescribed for this [mantra], while its deity is Virodhinī;
Kālī is its seed-syllable (bīja), and Māyā-śakti is proclaimed as its power (śakti).
The seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) shall be the *kīlaka*; the application (*viniyoga*) is according to one's wish.
One should perform the pair of six-limbed rites for Kālī using the six long vowels as the seed-syllables.
One should meditate upon her, resembling a mountain of gold, appearing about sixteen years of age,
with a pair of full and elevated breasts, and adorned with a garland of snakes.
Four-armed and three-eyed, she stands upon a corpse and a lotus,
holding a trident, a snake-noose, a bell, and likewise a hand-drum.
He bore the Great Goddess, who was successively endowed with four arms,
clad in smoky-colored garments, with a yellow body, and a slightly smiling face.
"Do not fear, O hero; choose a boon, for I shall grant you every truth.
Whatever task has come before you, I shall perform that very task for you."
Thus spoke the goddess, who possessed a beautiful smile and was captivating to the mind;
she was intent on creating discord and was the bringer of destruction to her enemies.
One should worship on the seat described by Kālika, which is beautified by three triangles,
enriched with the ornaments of a circle and an eight-petaled lotus, and adorned with a single outer square.
In [the mandala] richly adorned with four gates, its pericarp radiant with the seed-syllable Śrī,
Virodhinī is in the pericarp, and in the triangle, the triad [of goddesses] in successive order.
Then one should worship Dhūmā, Pūṣā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilī, and thereafter Havyavahā.
Then, one should worship the tenth [digit], Virodhinī, upon the head;
and on the eight petals, the eight Bhairavas together with Bhairava.
Outside that, [one should place] the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons within the Bhūpura;
then, having performed the lustration rite (nīrājana), one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should offer a tenth part as oblations into the fire with *nimba* wood according to the prescribed rite;
and having fashioned a garland of *ariṣṭa* fruits, the man becomes seated upon the great *muṇḍā*.
One should diligently offer the fruit of the *ariṣṭa* tree for the destruction of enemies;
one should offer *vibhītaka* for the eradication of all foes.
A wise man should cause enmity among his enemies by means of *dhuttūra* flowers;
with the flesh of a crow or an owl, he slays his enemies in an instant.

The wise practitioner should offer oblations into a fire made from the wood of that tree using the flowers of the *rājasu* tree; thus, Dhūmāvatī and the others will become accomplished and [the deity] will become favorable.
Combined with wood from the *arka* tree and other such materials, this [mixture] causes enmity toward enemies;
facing the northwest (vāyavya), one should offer water produced from *vada* and cumin.
O Great Goddess, one should drink it lukewarm; thus the enemy shall become afflicted with fever.
This is the procedure for the purpose of destroying hostile sorcery and for one's own protection.
In a solitary place, in a mother’s house, at a cemetery, or in a temple of Śiva,
one should recite the Vidyā of Virodhinī ten thousand times according to the prescribed method.
One should offer oblations with fuel-sticks of the *vibītaka* tree for the warding off of enemies;
having entered water reaching to the navel, one should likewise [offer] with *marī* wood combined with water.
One should satisfy the deities with water and perform the rite that causes hatred in the three worlds;
then, if one desires to effect attraction, one should bring earth from an anthill.
Having taken earth from a cremation ground, one should fashion an image of the Supreme Goddess in the form of the person to be accomplished, using wheat, asafoetida, and cumin.
Having placed a ring upon the nose and performed the stabilization of the vital breath (prāṇa),
one should recite the Virodhinī mantra there and worship with Karavīra flowers.
Having fashioned an effigy with milk, one should heat it in a fire of *vadarī* wood according to this sequential method for fourteen days.
The most excellent man who performs this, the performer of universal attraction,
draws toward himself by means of yoga a woman rich with the fire of passion.
Having reflected, one should perform the drawing-in [of the deity]; it may or may not occur. Having meditated upon the noose at her throat and the swift goad upon her head.
Having reflected thus, O Goddess of gods, one becomes the attractor of the three worlds.
O Goddess, even this secret is being told to you out of affection for you.
Formerly raised for the sake of slaying the wicked ones such as Vipracitti,
she became renowned as Vipracittā, the destroyer of the Vipravittas.
O Pārvatī, listen to the mantra of that sixth eternal Great Vidyā:
one should utter the Praṇava, the Lotus-born One, Kāma, and the roar of Cāmuṇḍā.
Having uttered the word "Vipracitta," one should then pronounce "O slayer of the wicked.
Having pronounced "Destroy the enemies," [one should continue], O beloved, until this day.
Having uttered "grant me success" (siddhiṃ me dehi), the mantra ends with *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*;
this great mantra of Vipracitta consists of thirty-four syllables.
Īśvara is its seer (ṛṣi), the goddess Jagatī is said to be its meter (chandas),
Vipracitta is its deity, and Cāmuṇḍā is declared to be its seed-syllable (bīja).
The power is declared to be Kamalā, while the Kāmabīja is the pin (kīlaka).
One should perform the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) with Kāma preceded by the six long vowels.
Mounted upon a lion, situated in the midst of a skeleton cage,
