she has four arms, three eyes, and full, elevated breasts.
Clad in space, with disheveled hair, with a lolling tongue, terrifying,
with fearsome fangs and a gaping mouth, her corners of the mouth flowing with blood.
She holds a sword, a severed head, a skull-cup, and a trident in her hands; she has a large belly, is dark-complexioned like a blue lotus, and bestows grace upon her devotees.
Having thus meditated upon the Queen of the Gods, Vipracittā, the beloved of Śiva, who is intent on destroying the Daityas and grants fearlessness to her practitioners.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with white water-lilies (kumuda) ten times that number;
then, one should offer libations (tarpaṇa) with water scented with the eight fragrances ten times that number.
The cleansing is one-tenth of that, the consecration is one-tenth of that,
and the feeding of Brahmins is one-tenth of that, for the sake of success in the *vipracitta* rites.
A triangle, a circle, a hexagon, adorned with a circle and an eight-petaled lotus,
joined by a circle and a square fortress, and embellished with the seed-syllable *bindu*.
One should worship Vipracitta at the drop (bindu), worship the triple-guṇa in the triangle,
the six limbs in the hexagon, and the Mothers and Bhairava on its petals.
Outside of that, one should place the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons within the Bhūpura;
then, having performed the lustration rite (nīrājana), one should offer the recitation (japa) to the Goddess.
One who is engaged in the preliminary rites (puraścaryā) is fit for the practical application (prayoga), and not otherwise;
O Goddess, the practitioner should perform the fire-oblation with all its components during rites for pacification (śāntikarma).
One should offer oblations with *mālatī* flowers for subjugation, with *ketakī* for the attainment of speech,
with *karavīra* for enchantment, and with *kiṃśuka* for immobilization.
One should prescribe enchantment with the flower of the *coḍru* plant, and killing with *dhuttūra* flowers.
Protection from great fear [is achieved] with the *vṛhatī*; the eradication of enemies with the *girikarṇikā*, and the arrival of wealth with the *dhanvayāsa*.

One should perform the rite of subjugating enemies with *kāśa* flowers, and for inciting enmity, with those born from the *karṇikāra*; one should indeed offer oblations of wild rice (*nīvāra*) to the Goddess for the sake of attaining success in grain.
By offering *kalāpa* flowers or *tulasī*, one attains all prosperity;
by offering safflower (*kausumbha*) blossoms, a woman desiring a lover shall obtain her wish.
One should certainly offer oblations with Madhūka flowers for the attainment of one's desired goal;
by offering oblations with Dhātrī, the Goddess [bestows] wealth, and one shall become a lord of riches.
Whatever medicine is for a particular disease, by that very means is that disease destroyed;
though it is a secret and an even greater secret, it is nevertheless told—listen.
The Praṇava, the seed-syllable of the bride (Vadhū), the seed-syllable HŪṂ, and then Bhuvanā;
again the former [syllables], then HŪṂ PHAṬ—this is the seven-syllabled mantra of Ugrā.
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and the Vṛhatī meter is proclaimed;
the deity is celebrated as the fierce (ugrā) seventh Nityā.
The seed-syllable *kūrca* (huṃ) and *phaṭ* are declared to be the power (*śakti*) and the *vadhūlīlaka*;
their application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the sake of attaining all desired goals and so forth.
Then, with the six limbs [consecrated] by means of the seed-syllable called Māyā, which begins with the six long vowels,
one should meditate upon the supreme, fierce goddess standing in the pratyālīḍha posture.
Four-armed, three-eyed, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
naked, with a gaping mouth, possessing terrible fangs, and fearsome.
Sporting on the lap of a corpse, dwelling in the abode of the cremation ground,
dark-complexioned, with loose hair, and bearing a sword and a blue lotus.
One should meditate upon the fierce Mahāvidyā, who holds a skull and a sword in her hands and is devoted to the granting of boons; one should perform the recitation of two hundred thousand [mantras].
One should perform a fire-oblation with lotuses mixed with ghee using one-tenth of that [number];
the libation (tarpaṇa) should be one-tenth of that, and the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) one-tenth of that.
By feeding ten Brahmins with a tenth part [of that], she certainly bestows fierce accomplishment (ugrāsiddhi) on a mountain,
in a desolate wilderness, in a forest, or on the bank of a river.
One who has performed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) should practice in a solitary linga or a cremation ground.
Now, listen as the worship of this [goddess] and her yantra are duly explained.
A triangle, a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, a circle adorned with a square enclosure,
enriched with the ornament of eight petals, or perhaps adorned with a thunderbolt.
Within a triangular circle, one should draw the supreme seed-syllable *kūrca*;
there, one should worship the blue Tārā Ekajaṭā within that triangle.
Then, O Goddess, on the eight petals, one should worship the eight Ugras and Ghoras;
having worshipped the eight Vairocanas, one should likewise worship the Padmāntakas.
Then one should worship the world-protectors and their weapons according to the prescribed rule;
thereafter, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and offered the recitation (japa) to the Goddess.
O Lord of the Gods, always remaining upon a corpse-seat (śavāsana), one should constantly recite [the mantra],
always bearing a vermilion tilaka smeared with the powder of saṃvid-liquor.
With disheveled hair, clad in the directions as his garment, endowed with devotion, and having conquered his senses,
he should prepare the great *mahācīna* tree and creeper for the Supreme Goddess.
Constantly beholding the triangle with his mind fixed upon it, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; then he will certainly attain mastery over the fierce [deity].
Everything else regarding the Goddess of the World has been proclaimed as being like that of Tārā:
the ritual placement (nyāsa), worship, meditation, the preliminary rites (puraścaryā), and the prescribed procedure.
Thus should Mahogratārā be known; what more do you wish to hear?
Having first extracted the Praṇava, one should extract the seed-syllable of Śiva.
Having uttered the two seed-syllables— Nāda and Bindu mounted upon Fire (Ra), adorned with the sixth vowel (Ū)— one should contemplate the form of Ugraprabhā.
"O Goddess Kālī, Great Goddess, show me Your true form!"—
this mantra, joined with *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, is declared to be the one of fierce radiance.
The mantra beginning with "Pañcaviṃśati-tattva" is declared to be Ugraprabhā;
Mahākāla is said to be the seer (ṛṣi), and Triṣṭubh is proclaimed as the meter (chandas).
The deity is proclaimed to be Mahākālī of fierce luster;
"Raṃ" is the seed-syllable, "Oṃ" is the power (śakti), and "Phaṭ" is declared to be the pin (kīlaka).
The application of Kālikā for the purpose of visualization and so forth has been proclaimed.
The six-limbed [rite] is performed with the seed-syllable known as Ugraprabhā and the six long vowels.
One should meditate upon the divine Ugraprabhā, who possesses the luster of a celestial blue lotus,
has four arms and three eyes, and is seated upon a corpse-lotus.
Clad in the directions, with disheveled hair, her breasts full and uplifted,
with a most serene countenance, she who feeds upon the flesh of the corpse of Bhoja.
Her waist is girdled by a multitude of corpses; her face is smiling;
she holds a sword and a severed head in her left hands, and a skull-cup and a chopper in her right hands.

O Śivā, having thus meditated upon the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), who bestows supreme bliss, who deceives Time (Kāla), and who is the Mother, one should recite her mantra two hundred thousand times.
As stated by Kālika, one should worship on a pedestal (pīṭha) that is radiant with two triangles,
enriched with a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, and adorned with two enclosures of the earth (bhūpura).
One should first worship Ugraprabhā, Kālī, Tārā, and Rocanī in the center of the bindu; in the first [circle], one worships the Goddess, and in the second, the host of Tāriṇīs.
In the second triangle, one should place Tārā and Ekajaṭā, both blue;
on the eight petals, the eight Mātṛkās; and at the tips of the petals, the eight Bhairavas.
The world-protectors (lokapālas) should be worshipped on the base of the temple (būpura), and their weapons outside of that;
the preceptors must perform the worship for all of them three times each.
Having thus worshipped Ugraprabhā, one should perform the recitation (japa) two hundred thousand times;
one should then offer oblations (homa) of vajra-flowers smeared with liquor, numbering one-tenth of that amount.
One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of that [quantity] using milk, or honey, or curd,
or sugarcane juice, or whatever else is available from the pedestal (pīṭha).
One-tenth of that amount is for sprinkling [the ground], and one-tenth is for feeding the Brahmins;
thereafter, one should worship a young girl and also worship Śakti.
Having fashioned an image of Ugraprabhā upon a banner and maintaining it,
one shall become a conqueror of the three worlds after defeating the gods and the asuras in battle.
Having recited [the mantra] over a drum, a wooden board, or a sword, and having attained all perfections through the fierce and radiant Śivā, a man shall become the very form of Kālī.
Having beheld the Mālinī-maṇḍala, one should mutter the mantra of Ugrāprabhā;
Kālikā shall become the bestower of siddhi—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having smeared the vulva with one's own semen, the practitioner should recite the supreme mantra of fierce radiance;
O Goddess of Gods, what is there that the practitioner cannot accomplish by meditating upon her therein?
Having visualized Kālī with the two [mantras] Ugra and Prabhā, one should recite [the mantra] for one month, O Śivā;
by practicing for just one month, Kālikā will become a granter of boons.
She who is concealed in all tantras, radiant, eternal, and of great prosperity;
she who is the ninth among the eternal ones, the eternal essence, and of great exaltation.
I shall proclaim her mantra; listen attentively as it truly is:
the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Kālikā, and likewise that of Kaulinī.
Having extracted the *kūrca* seed-syllable (*hūṃ*), one should thereafter utter the word "to the Radiant One" (*dīptāyai*) and then "bestowing the fruit of all mantras" (*sarvamantraphaladāyai*).
The supreme mantra ending in *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā* consists of twenty syllables;
it is proclaimed to have the number of its syllables reduced by half.
Mahādeva is proclaimed as its seer (ṛṣi), the Uṣṇik meter is celebrated as its meter (chandas),
and the ninth Nityā, named Dīptā, is proclaimed as its deity.
The seed-syllable of Kālī is indeed her seed, for she is the power (śakti) of Kaulinī;
"svāhā" is said to be the kīlaka, and its application is for the purpose of Kālī.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual with the six long vowels joined to the letters of Kālī;
one should meditate upon her as blazing like a great sapphire, possessing a large belly.
Four-armed, three-eyed, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
naked, with disheveled hair, possessing terrible fangs, and formidable in appearance.
Seated upon a corpse-lotus, with full and elevated breasts,
she is adorned with bracelets made of human bone and bangles of conch shells.
One should meditate upon Kālikā, who is eternally bestowing boons upon her devotees, who laughs while lolling over a corpse somewhere, and who is intoxicated with passion.
At night, she is adorned with a meditation-band (yogapaṭṭa), seeking the path of yoga;
she holds a sword and a severed head in her left hands, while bestowing the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting in her right hands.
O Śivā, having thus meditated upon her who has beautiful fangs, who is exceedingly fierce, who dwells in the cremation ground,
and who possesses a blazing radiance, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
One should perform the oblation with coconut for one-tenth of the total;
the oblation with plantain should be performed for the sake of attaining universal radiance.
One should perform the oblation (havana) with a tenth part of the [substances] from the pedestal;
and the sprinkling (mārjana) should be done with a tenth part of that, using water mixed with the eight fragrant substances (gandhāṣṭaka).
One should feed Brahmins and indeed a young maiden with a tenth part of that;
then the practitioner, having perfected the mantra, becomes fit for its application, and not otherwise.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and preceded by the recollection of the Guru,
one should meditate upon the Guru in the *sahasrāra* according to the previously described method of meditative yoga.
From the *mūlādhāra*, one should contemplate the supreme *mūlavidyā* within one's own tongue—
Sarasvatī in the form of a lamp, whose nature is that of the root seed-syllable (*mūlabīja*).
Having recited the complete Mātṛkā, one should utter the Root-Mantra;
having again recited the Mātṛkā, one should once more utter the Mantra.
O beautiful one, he who [recites] the root-vidyā three times according to this sequence through the mantra,
should then meditate upon it as being in the form of a lamp on the tongue.
O Śivā, O Goddess of the Gods, one should drink that water while it is in the form of light and accompanied by weapons;
by this yoga, O Mistress of the Gods, a man shall become a knower of the three times.
O beloved, without exertion, without practice, and without study or the like,
the fourfold scholarship is established within his hand.
O Goddess of the gods, by means of the *jātī* flower, poetic skill becomes subject to one's control;
O Goddess of the gods, by means of the *kandapuṣpa*, mastery over all scriptures is achieved.
With *durvā* grass, one performs the homa for pacification; with *guḍūcī*, for the warding off of death;
with wine, it is said that enchantment is achieved; and with plantain, immobilization is proclaimed.
Through the mango, the accomplishment of subjugation (vaśya) occurs; through the thorn-apple (dhuttūra), great prosperity;
through the oleander (karavīra), eradication (uccāṭana); and through the fruits of the cucumber (karkaṭī), inciting enmity (vidveṣa).
One who has mastered the mantra should perform all such rites as summoning by means of a blue flower or attracting by means of *marīca*.
She is collyrium, a pill, the alchemy of the sword, an elixir, sacrificial porridge,
a forehead mark, a drum, and a skull-bowl.
For in this way, the rite indeed becomes radiant with success through the mantra;
O wise one, listen to the extraction of the mantra by which one attains perfection.
O Great Goddess, having extracted the pair of *kūrca* mantras, likewise the two *kālī* seeds,
the two *māyā*s, and the essential form consisting of *ha-sa-ka-la-rī*.
Then there is Nīlapatākā, and Maheśvarī ending with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*;
and Nīlānīlapatākā, the supreme bestower of all accomplishments.
Ugracaṇḍālajjihvā, Sā, Siddhakarālikā,
Nīlā, and Mahānīlapatākikā— thus Nīlā is said to be fivefold.
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), and Vṛhatī is said to be its meter;
the nature of the Kūrca seed-syllable is indeed designated as its power (śakti).
O auspicious lady, *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* are the *kīlaka*; they are to be employed for the purpose of Kālī.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs using the six long seed-syllables of Kālī.
Then one should meditate upon Mahānīlā, who has the luster of a mountain of blue collyrium,
four arms, three eyes, and is adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Seated upon a corpse, with eyes rolling from intoxication,
possessing eyes like those of a young deer and a serene lotus-face;
She was adorned with beautiful earrings made of human skulls,
with a dangling tongue, a gaping mouth, and terrifying, formidable fangs.
Always blue and fierce toward sinners, most excellent toward the meritorious,
intent on the destruction of the wicked, and the bestower of boons upon the practitioner.
Resounding in the four directions with packs of jackals and flocks of vultures,
she was thus the primordial form, blue as a lotus and the bestower of boons.

O Goddess, one who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should perform the recitation (japa) according to the sequence of family tradition and by means of the prescribed method of practice.
One should perform oblations in a triangular sacrificial pit on a well-prepared ground, using *karavīra*, *javā*, *bilva*, *mallikā*, and other flowers, accompanied by clarified butter.
One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) ten times with milk and also with wine;
one should then sprinkle [the deity] with red water and feed the Brāhmaṇas.
A mantra perfected through preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) bestows all desired goals when accompanied by a married woman, a maiden, or a virtuous Śakti— these three being auspicious.
The preliminary rite (puraścaryā) for practitioners consists of [offerings] corresponding to the substance [of the deity], such as kings and so forth;
one who has completed the preliminary rite is fit for the ritual application (prayoga), and not otherwise.
I shall now describe her yantra, by means of which one becomes a master of supernatural powers (siddhi):
one should write the *kūrca* mantra in the center of a point, and above that, a triangle.
The auspicious yantra of Nīlāmānu is composed of a circle, a hexagon, a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, and a square enclosure (bhūpura) enriched with four gates and secondary ornaments.
O Dear One, the deities of the gates, beginning with Vaṭuka, are at the four doors;
their weapons are outside of them, and on the petals, O Beloved, are the eight Bhairavas.
In the filaments are the eight Mother-goddesses (mātṛkāḥ), and in the circles, the Siddhis in succession;
in the hexagon are the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅgāni), and in the triangle are the three deities.
Kālarātri, Mahārātri, and Moharātri are worshipped in sequence within the triad;
having propitiated Nīlā in the center, one should then satisfy her with an offering of food.
Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and having offered praise, prostration, and dismissal,
one should diligently accomplish the rite for Nīlā and the host of thirty-six yakṣiṇīs.
Whenever one should cause the goal to be known, [one should invoke] the host of thirty-six Yakṣiṇīs,
with Kālī, Kūrca, Vadhū, and Māyā in the midst, [and then] "O such-and-such Yakṣiṇī!"
At the end, O Dear One, these seed-syllables, accompanied by *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, constitute the limbs;
thus the thirty-six Yakṣiṇīs have been extracted in their proper order.
In the same way, O Yakṣa, for Valin, with *spheṃ krīṃ hūṃ hrīṃ* and the *puṭa*,
all the Yakṣas are proclaimed to be eighty-four in number, ending with *hūṃ phaṭ*.
Having attained the accomplishment of the yakṣiṇī, the practitioner shall obtain happiness;
O Pārvatī, he becomes a king in this world through the sovereignty of wealth.
He who treats even a man of little knowledge as a scholar, and likewise a fool as a learned man,
and so forth— even if he does this hundreds of times— [is a fool].
Whosoever indeed gives [an offering] to a Sādhya, a Yakṣiṇī [is attained]—of this there is no doubt. The womb is proclaimed to be twofold: divine and human.
Having attained that respective form, one achieves its specific accomplishment;
as for the fruit, it is the attainment of a Yakṣiṇī—what then is the fruit of attaining a Yakṣa?
Tell me that, O you who are beyond the further and the near; salutations to you!
[Grant] the gold coin, the pill, the sword, the vetāla, the sandals, and the collyrium.
Elixir, elixir-therapy, concealment, the tilaka-mark, and likewise invisibility;
the skull-cup, the conch, the trident, and the hand-drum (ḍamaru).
Attraction, subjugation, as well as delusion and expulsion,
and likewise the creation of Indra’s net and other such nets.
The supernatural powers such as Khecarī, beginning with the practice of ascending upward (ūrdhvotkramaṇa), must be kept secret, must be kept secret; what else do you wish to hear?
O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear about the worship of the sequence of the eternal Ghanā;
she who is the eternal Ghanā, possessing the form of rising, dense clouds, and who is of great exaltation.

O ocean of compassion, you must always grant me the mantra-worship of her who has the clouds as her abode, who possesses a resonant voice, who arises from the water-jar (ghaṭikā), and whose form is manifest.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, and likewise the two syllables from Kālikā,
[the mantra] "ghanālaye ghanāghane hrīṃ hūṃ" is considered the Mantra.
May this mantra, which is a celestial wish-fulfilling tree for the destruction of the multitude of sins of the world, be auspicious.
Aghorabhairava is proclaimed as the seer (ṛṣi), and Virāṭ is the meter (chanda).
The seed-syllable is *kālī*, likewise *māyā* is the power (*śakti*), and *hūṃ phaṭ* is the pinning (*kīlaka*);
this application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the pleasure of the goddess Kālikā.
With the seed-syllable possessing six long vowels and camphor, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) for Ghanā Nityā,
the Great Vidyā, who resembles a dark blue cloud.
With the luster of a drunk cuckoo’s eye and the radiance of a ripe rose-apple fruit,
she has very long toes and is free from the burden of hanging locks of hair.
Four-armed, with three eyes, delighting in the naked state,
with a formidable face and terrifying fangs, and possessing full, elevated breasts.
Her face was made to quiver by streams of blood flowing from the corners of her lips;
she was adorned with the bracelets on the arms of heroes, and her form was terrifying.
She should be meditated upon by the heroes as holding, in sequence, a sword, a shield, a battle-axe, and a mallet—
a dwelling place for the clouds of great heroes.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with the lotuses as prescribed;
O Dear One, the libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed with scents, milk, and other substances for one-tenth of that number.
One-tenth of that amount should be used for sprinkling with cool water,
and one-tenth of that should be offered as a meal to Brāhmaṇas.
Thus, being endowed with such ritual action, he attains the accomplishment of the mantra.
I shall now describe the dense yantra and the manner in which its worship should be performed.
A six-cornered [diagram], adorned with a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, and a perimeter of earth-fortresses;
in the six corners are the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and likewise the deities.
On the eight petals are the eight Mothers; then follows the worship of Bhairava.
The world-protectors are in the outer square (bhūpura), and their weapons are outside of that.
Having recited [the mantra] according to one's ability, one should then perform the lustration (nīrājana) for this [deity].
O Goddess of Devas, having offered praise, bowed down, and bid farewell [to the deity], one should conclude with the lustration ceremony.
O Goddess of the gods, listen; I shall describe the sequence for the worship of Valākā.
Valākā is the eternal Nityā, who brings all things under her control.
Through sacrifices, she attained the various branches of knowledge and reached her own respective station;
O Maheśānī, her mantra is now being told—listen.
One should extract the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Kālikā, the Kūrca, and Māyā;
then Valākā, followed by the word Kālī, for she of most wonderful prowess.

"Grant me the accomplishment of my desired goal, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā"—this is considered the mantra. The seed-syllable (bīja) of Kālikā’s mouth is *kāli*, and the thunderbolt (*kūrca*) is proclaimed as her power (*śakti*).
The Māyākīlaka has been taught; having performed the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the kīlaka and having applied the six-limbed placement (nyāsa), Maheśvarī should perform meditation.
Resembling a boundless mass of collyrium, possessing the brilliance of ten million fires of cosmic destruction,
four-armed and three-eyed, she dwells in the fortress of Muṇḍa.
Clad in the directions, with a formidable face, possessing full and elevated breasts,
wearing a girdle fashioned from a collection of corpses' hands, and seated upon a corpse;
With disheveled hair and rolling eyes, her lotus-face is serene;
she possesses a brilliance equal to ten million suns and is adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Holding a sword and a severed head in her left [hands], and a skull-cup and a raised index finger in her right,
Mahākālī assumes the form of a crane.
It was a terrifying cremation ground and hell, filled with bhūtas and pretas,
surrounded by jackals howling with dreadful cries, and resounding with a terrible noise.
"Do not fear; O hero, speak what is in your heart, and I shall accomplish it for you.
Having meditated thus, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, and one will certainly become perfected in the mantra.
The wise one should offer oblations with ten parts of bilva leaves smeared with ghee;
he should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of that, and the sprinkling (mārjana) with a tenth part of that.
The feeding of Brahmins is proclaimed to be one-tenth of that [total];
by the mere propitiation of the Brahmins, every limb [of the rite] attains completion.
O Maheśānī, whatever limb may be deficient, that should be made complete by feeding the twice-born; all else one should perform exactly as in the Kālikā ritual.
O Maheśānī, listen as I describe the mantra of that which is called the eternal Mātrā— the most excellent among all that is eternal.
The Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Kālikā, Māyā, Kūrca, and Mātṛkā;
again, the letter of Mātṛkā with the Bindu—these are indeed the four seed-syllables.
Furthermore, O Maheśānī, the syllables of the Mātṛkā and the four seed-syllables, as well as that [syllable] ending in *kṣāṃ*, are proclaimed as the great measures (*mahāmātrā*).
"O Goddess of gods, likewise, grant me success quickly with these four seed-syllables: *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is considered the supreme mantra of Mātrā."
O Śiva, one should place the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Kālikā, the Kūrca, and Māyā; in the middle, one should give the name of the Nityā, ending in the vocative case and standing alone.
O Pārvatī, eternal mantras arise in various forms;
furthermore, they are proclaimed to end with the seed-syllables *hūṃ*, *phaṭ*, and *svāhā*.
Through the initial conjunction or through the *saṃpuṭa* method, ending with *hūṃ phaṭ*,
there arise thus ninety variations of the mantras for the Nityās.
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), Uṣṇih is proclaimed as its meter (chandas),
and the goddess Mātrā is celebrated as its deity (devatā).
*Krīṃ* is declared to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hūṃ* likewise the power (*śakti*), and *hrīṃ* the wedge-syllable (*kīlaka*).
Their application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the sake of the great goal, namely for the purpose of Kālī.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual application (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) joined with the six long vowels and the syllable Māyā;
likewise, one should meditate upon the Great Vidyā, who possesses the luster of a mountain of black collyrium.
Four-armed and three-eyed, seated upon a severed head-lotus,
holding a skull-cup and a chisel in her hands, and bearing a sword and a severed head— she is the Supreme Goddess.
She has protruding teeth, is exceedingly fierce, and is terrifying with her violent roar;
she is mounted upon a corpse’s chest, licking [her lips], and seated upon a corpse.

O Goddess of the gods, having thus contemplated her who is of such a kind, the glorious one, and the utterer of most terrible sounds, one should perform the recitation of the mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should perform the oblation with bilva fruits, or else with plantain fruits;
or one should perform the oblation ten times the [mantra] count with grapes or with milk-rice (pāyasa).
O Brahmin, one should diligently perform the libation (tarpaṇa), the ritual sprinkling (mārjana), and the feeding of the twice-born;
for whatever limb of the rite may be omitted, the recitation (japa) must be performed double that number of times.
O Goddess, just as Kālīvallī is like a mother to you regarding recitation, worship, ritual applications, and so forth,
even her secret is now being told to you; listen.
The ritual procedure for the eternal Mudrā is the most excellent of all essences;
the eternal one named Mudriṇī is indeed Mudriṇī within the Śrīvidyā.
The goddess named Mudriṇī and Daṇḍinī possesses a majestic form;
she is the one who effects the seals (mudrās) of the mantras beginning with Mahāvidyā and others.
Therefore, this mudrā is called Nityā; it is the supreme Parā, the bestower of all accomplishments (sarvasiddhi).
It consists of the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Kālikā, and the Kūrca syllable in their proper sequence.
Having uttered the pair of seed-syllables as previously taught, one should utter the word *mudrā* or extract the word *pada*.
[The mantra is: "O Mudrā, you whose nature is the form of the syllable *bhauja*, grant me success (*siddhi*) and the *mudrā*."
The auspicious mantra for subjugation is *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā* joined with *vīti vaśa*. Mahādeva is declared to be its seer (*ṛṣi*), and the *gāyatrī* is said to be its meter (*chaṃdas*).
The Mudrā is proclaimed as the eternal Great Goddess, the deity;
the seed-syllable of Kālī is proclaimed as the seed of the seed, the power of Māyā.
The *kūrca* and the *kīlaka* are said to be joined with the six long vowels of Kālī;
having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should meditate upon the Great Goddess with the proper measure.
Resembling a mountain of collyrium, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
naked, possessing terrible fangs, and extremely terrifying due to her fierce roar.
She faces south, with disheveled hair, delighting in nakedness;
she has tawny eyes, blazing tongues, terrible fangs, and is fearsome.
Her waist was bound by a girdle made from the joined hands of corpses; her face was smiling, streams of blood flowed from both corners of her mouth, and her countenance was radiant.
Holding a skull-cup and a flaying knife in her hands, and bearing a sword and a shield, she is joined with Mahākāla, intent on blood, and afflicted by hunger.
"Choose a boon, choose a boon, choose a boon," thus speaking,
O Goddess of gods, one should worship the yantra with devotion after reflecting in this manner.
A triangle, a circle, a hexagon, a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, and a square enclosure;
it is enriched with four doors and secondary ornaments, and likewise, Gaṇeśa is situated at its entrance.
One should worship the Yoginī, the Kṣetrapāla, and Vaṭuka as the fourth; then the Lokapālas with their weapons, and the Lord of the World (Lokeśa) within the Bhūpura according to the sequence.
Having worshipped the Mother-goddesses (Mātṛkās) on the petals and the eight Bhairavas in the filaments,
one should worship the eight Siddhis at the tips of the eight petals and the six limbs (Ṣaḍaṅga) in the hexagons.
Having invoked her as the giver of sovereignty, the giver of enjoyments, the giver of liberation and victory, and likewise the giver of fear,
one should worship the sixth goddess, the giver of success, in the six corners in due order.
One should worship Will (icchā), Knowledge (jñāna), and Action (kriyā) within the triangle;
and having worshipped the Mudrā in the center with all five types of offerings.
Having thus completed the worship, one should then perform the *nīrājana* rite;
at the conclusion of the *nīrājana*, O Goddess of Gods, preceded by the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
One should recite the mantra of the two Rakṣas with white oleander flowers;
having performed the fire-oblation (havana) consisting of a tenth part [of the recitation], one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) consisting of a tenth part of that.
One should perform the ritual sprinkling and provide a meal for the Brahmins;
in this way, the mantra-practitioner attains success, and the mantra is fit for application, but not otherwise.
Whatever one fixes in the heart, that very thing one indeed performs as an action;
everything has been declared like that of Kāli, though I have stated the specific distinction.
Thus it has been briefly explained; what else do you wish to hear?
The Goddess said:
O Goddess of gods, I desire to hear the sequence of the ritual for the Mitā-nityā;
O lady of excellent hips, please tell me respectfully about this Mitā, which is the foremost of all vidyās.
The illustrious Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess of gods, I shall declare the most secret of secrets:
the Great Queen of all vidyās, known by the name Mitā, who brings great prosperity.
I shall proclaim her mantra, which is wondrous in all its parts:
having first extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should extract the seed-syllable of Kālikā (Klīm).
One should extract the seed-syllable Kūrca, as well as Māyā and the seed-syllable Vāgbhava;
having uttered the word *mite*, one should likewise utter the word *parimite*.
Furthermore, for the sake of valor, one should extract the words and the seeds again:
*so 'haṃ hūṃ phaṭ* and likewise *svāhā*, consisting of twenty-seven syllables.
O Goddess, this mantra has been declared; now hear its seer, meter, and other details.
Mahākāla is the seer of this, and Triṣṭubh is proclaimed as its meter.
O Maheśānī, the deity is Mitānityā and Kālikā; the seed-syllable (bīja) has been declared, as well as the kūrca, the śakti, and the māyā-kīlaka.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual with the *kīlaka* mantra preceded by the six long vowels;
one should meditate [on the deity] resembling a blue mountain, like a dark blue cloud.
Clad in red garments, seated upon a corpse, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
she possesses a pair of full, elevated breasts and has swelling bosoms and hips.
She is facing south, with her hair loosened, delighting in the state of being unclothed;
she dwells in the heart-lake of Mahādeva, adorned with a conch-shell bracelet.
Resembling the fire at the end of an aeon, dwelling in the cremation ground,
holding a sword and a severed head in her left hands, and bestowing fearlessness and the boon-granting gesture in her right hands.
She dwells in the heart of the practitioner, granting boons to the seeker;
she resides densely within his mouth, delighting in joy and overwhelmed by intoxication.
One should meditate upon the divine Dakṣiṇā, the protector of the wretched, who is adorned with eyes and other features that are intensely red and beautiful.
Having meditated thus, O Goddess, one should perform the recitation three hundred thousand times;
the fire-oblation should be performed with *kiṃśuka* flowers or with *jyotiṣmatī*, O Beloved.
The fruit is considered to be like that of the *kiṃśuka* with the flower of *jyotiṣmatī*; one should offer oblations with the reddish *karavīra* for the sake of mantra-siddhi.
One should perform oblations in a triangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) prepared with firewood of *khadira* or other trees;
by means of an oblation of betel leaves, one brings Kālikā under control.
And by means of the *nāgavalī* flower, a female serpent-spirit (*nāginī*) shall attain accomplishment;
one should offer oblations with *vajrapuṣpa* for a *ḍākinī* or a great goddess (*maheśvarī*).
By offering *dhūmūra* one brings about the destruction of enemies; with *kunda* flowers, one should dissolve poetic obstacles.
Through *jāti* flowers, victory is attained; with sesame flowers, there is an increase in strength.

Through *punnāga* one attains the goals of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*); through *ketakī*, a woman shall obtain a lover; through *caṃdana*, there is the destruction of the sun, enemies, and sins, and one is always victorious.
In that very way, O Goddess, one shall obtain the status of a king of kings through the Guru;
by means of an oblation of red sandalwood, one should perform the enchantment of all.
The attainment of the maiden Girikarṇī by Sevaṃtī through her Śiva-form;
the destruction of enemies by Puṇḍrī; and the supreme attraction by Marīci.
Great fortune is attained through betel nuts (*pūgīphala*), likewise wealth through nutmegs (*jātīphala*);
subjugation is achieved with *campaka* flowers, and the pain arising from the calves is destroyed.
Thus, having directed his desire toward various kinds of objects,
the practitioner should then perform a fire-oblation (homa) amounting to one-tenth [of the recitation], followed by a libation (tarpaṇa) from the pedestal-vessel.
One should perform the libation with water scented with the eight fragrances, as well as with saffron water; then one should carry out the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) using a tenth part of that.
One-tenth of that amount should be used for feeding Brahmins, as well as for the Śaktis and Kumārikās;
O Goddess, he who worships and feeds them attains all perfections (siddhis).
Now, the yantra according to the ritual of worship is described; listen.
Having drawn three triangles, one should enclose them within a circle joined with six spokes.
Adorned with a circular eight-petaled lotus, endowed with a boundary wall (bhūpura),
enriched with the beauty of four gates, and decorated with a bindu in the center.
One should worship Kālī, Karālā, and Śrīghorā in the first triangle;
and in the second triangle, Jyeṣṭhā and Raudrikā on the left.
In the third triangle, however, are Will, Knowledge, and likewise Action. Then, O Goddess, one should worship the Goddess; first, one should worship Vārtālī.
O Goddess of gods, in the second part one should worship Laghuvārāhikā;
O Goddess of gods, in the third part one should worship Svapnavārāhikā.
O Goddess of the gods, having worshipped Tiraskāriṇī in the fourth part of the auspicious [area],
one should worship the four gates within the six-cornered circle.
In the hexagon, one should worship the six limbs; likewise, the eight Siddhis in the circle. On the eight petals, the Mātṛkās are to be worshipped, and at their ends, the eight Bhairavas.
Outside that, on the Bhūpura, one should worship the world-protectors (Lokapālas) and their weapons;
thus having worshipped the immeasurable, eternal Vidyā Amitrā, who is stainless.
A person who is thus devoted and disciplined shall attain the accomplishment of mantra.
Alternatively, listen to another method for the sequence of constant meditation:
all [the goddesses] resemble the Añjana mountain and are adorned with garlands of severed heads.
O Goddess, holding a sword in her right hand and a raised index finger in her left, the auspicious Kālī shines with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
This is known as the general meditation in the ritual of the Name-mantra;
that which is taught in the secret mantra is of various forms for the two types of accomplishment.
Eye-salve, a pill, a sword, a vetāla, a host of yakṣiṇīs,
sacrificial porridge, a forehead mark, clothing, a skull, and likewise sandals.
The staff, the Kinnarī, the Siddhījāmi, and whatever great arts there may be,
as well as the power to move through all things moving and unmoving, and the qualities of minuteness, lightness, and so forth.
Entering another's body, all elixirs and alchemy,
removing affliction by touch, and likewise the movement among the elements;
The raising of the dead is divine; the siddhis reside in his hand.
Having extracted the great seat (mahāpīṭha), the Nityās should be established in due order.

Alternatively, while reciting the root mantra, one should meditate upon one's own deities in the midst [of the practice] by means of the kula-substances, for the sake of attaining the success of the mantra as prescribed.
One should worship and satisfy [the deity] according to one's ability with food, clothing, and so forth;
then, one should fumigate with the ten-ingredient incense (daśagandha) and descend from the divine state.
One should be a certain Śakti with red eyes, whose body has eyes like those [of a peacock], and whose lotus-face is serene; others are situated at her mouth.
At that moment, having prepared an auspicious image made of mung beans,
one should fashion a figure made of meat cooked in ghee for the purpose of consumption.
At every morsel, one should offer wine, fish, and gold;
having uttered the primordial seed-syllable, likewise for the eternal [goddess] Krūramukhī.
"O you with cruel fangs and lolling tongue, this theft from the mouth is prepared;
eat the pair of yugas as food—svāhā at the end, followed by two *ṭha*s."
Having uttered the first seed-syllable, one should likewise meditate upon the enemy as dead;
at that very moment, O Goddess of the Suras, he takes away the limited life-breaths.
One should first feed that bestower of boons while reciting "śrūyate saumṛta," and afterwards, one should fumigate her with incense made from the five limbs [of the tree].
Having laughed and granted a boon, she departs from her body as Śakti;
or else, having been worshipped in the cremation ground, she possesses a radiance equal to the submarine fire (vaḍavāgni).
For the destruction of an army's king, one should use human flesh as the ritual substance;
for subjugation, in gardens; and for eradication, on a riverbank.
There is no knowledge higher than this, which provides immediate conviction;
it is renowned in the new Āgama and has been worshipped by me in a hundred ways.
Though this is more secret than the most secret of secrets, it has been revealed by me to you.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Determination of the Rituals Ending with Mahākāla and the Mitā Nityās," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*. 23.
Now, he explains one of the procedures for Ugratārā, Ekajaṭā, and Nīlasarasvatī.
First, having taken one's stand in the water, the washing of the feet is prescribed;
then, having sipped water twice and tied the topknot, one should form the Brahma-granthi.
Having prepared the *arghya* at the door, one should sprinkle the doorway with those waters;
[one should likewise worship] Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, and Yoginī.
Having performed worship and returned to his home, the best of practitioners should sacrifice to Brahmā, the Lord of the Site (Vāstveśa),
in the southwest, using a mantra beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ."
Having purified both speech and mind, one should thoroughly purify the ground;
having dispelled all obstacles, one should perform the consecration of the ground.
Having prepared a mandala on his seat and worshipped it, the wise practitioner should ascend;
then, having inscribed and empowered the yantra, he should perform the purification of the flowers.
Having taken a soft seat, one should write the Māyā-bīja on the eastern petal.
Now, he states their mantras in sequence.
The mantra for the acceptance of water begins with the syllable Om and ends with the wife of Agni (Svāhā).
*Tāra* (Oṃ), *vajrodake*, *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*: thus the water is consecrated.
With *tāra* and *lajjā* at the end of the purification, all sins indeed [are purified].
At the end of *samaya* and at the end of *aśeṣa*, one should extract the word *vikalpa*;
at the end of *apanaya*, [the words] *varma phaṭ svāhā*—thus the foot is purified.

Oṃ, *māyā*, and *vahnijāyā* (svāhā) are remembered as the mantra for sipping water (*ācamana*). [The mantra for] the jewel-wearing goddess (*maṇidharaṇī*) and the thunderbolt-bearing goddess (*vajriṇī*) consists of the *praṇava* (oṃ) followed by all the aforementioned words.
With "vaśaṃkarī hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," one should bind the topknot (śikhā). Then, with "Tāra" (Oṃ), the word for "sage" (muni), and "vajriṇī" at the end of "Dharanī" (Earth), [one should bind it].
With this mantra: "O Mahāpratisarā, protect me from the end of the pair! Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā," one should perform the protection and tie the knot.
Having sprinkled [the vessel] with *phaṭ* and worshipped it with the heart-mantra, one should consecrate it ten times with the *tāra* mantra.
One should sprinkle the stream of water with *phaṭ* syllables and worship it with perfumes and flowers.
One should worship Gaṇeśa above the door, Vaṭuka on the left with the syllables *vāṃ* and *vāṃ*, Kṣetrapāla with ten eyes, and Yoginī below.
Now, regarding the specific feature of their mantras: at the end of all [mantras], they are enriched with the *dhruva* (the syllable *oṃ*) and the *dīrgha* (long vowels).
Preceded by the seed-syllable of power (śakti-bīja), the names should be in the dative case, ending with "namaḥ," and joined with the initial seed-syllable.
Then the practitioner should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) according to the [prescribed] syllables.
Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ cāstraṃ svāhā—this nine-syllable mantra;
then, with this thirteen-syllable mantra, one should dispel all obstacles.
Oṃ dāraya dāraya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā, the shatterer of obstacles.
Oṃ sarvavighnānutsāraya hūṃ phaṭ— this thirteen-syllable mantra of Vahni-gehinī destroys obstacles with a kick of the heel.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, followed by the syllable ĀḤ,
and then HŪM PHAṬ SVĀHĀ— this is declared to be the mantra for purifying body, speech, and mind.
Then, for the sake of worshipping the Goddess, one should certainly consecrate the earth with this mantra consisting of twelve syllables:
*Pavitra vajra me hūṃ svāhā*.
Having drawn a triangle on the ground, one should perform the worship of Ādhāraśakti;
then, having uttered the Māyā-bīja, [one worships] for Ādhāraśakti.
Having drawn the one seated upon a lotus, one should worship with the mantra ending in *namaḥ* and preceded by *ṅe*;
then, after *surekhe* and *vajrarekhe*, it ends with the syllable *āḥ*.
One should perform [the rite] with "hūṃ phaṭ svāhā" upon a corpse-seat (śavāsana) in the maṇḍala;
there, O Goddess, one should worship a soft seat with the *pīṭha-mantra*.
Oṃ aiṃ klīṃ; for the Kāmapīṭha, water is declared to be the heart. Therein, O Hero, having prepared the seat for the consort, one should then purify oneself.
One should thoroughly purify the flowers with the fourteen-syllable mantra;
then, one should utter the words "yathāgatābhiṣeka" and so forth.
The mantra consisting of the syllables beginning with *tārādi* and ending with *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā* is said to be the "mantra-colored" one;
the wise should know that the purification of the flower is further [performed] as in the case of Śyāmā.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) in detail.
One should contemplate the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, resembling a hibiscus flower, at the navel.
One should burn the body along with one's own sins by means of the fire produced from that;
then the knower of mantras should meditate upon the seed-syllable *strīm*, which has the luster of gold, within his heart.
One should scatter the ashes of sin upon the earth with the wind arising therefrom;
and with devotion, one should meditate upon the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, which resembles the moon's orb, on the forehead.
One should wash the body with the nectar arising from that, making it resemble a deity;
through this purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one attains similarity with the Goddess.
Now follows its meditation.
Having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should contemplate the universe as empty,
[and then] the self as stainless, pure, subtle, and composed of the deity.
Then, one should meditate upon a red lotus arising from the syllable *ĀḤ* in the intermediate space;
furthermore, one should meditate upon a white lotus above that, arising from the syllable *DĀṂ*.
Then, one should meditate upon the syllable HŪṂ, dark blue in color, above that;
then, one should meditate upon a flaying knife adorned with a seed-syllable above that.
Above him is Mahādevī, short-statured, with the luster of a dark blue cloud,
pot-bellied, her hips covered by a tiger skin.
She possesses full and elevated breasts heavy with milk, eyes that are red and round, tawny-colored eyes, and a single matted lock; she is adorned with blue serpents as her sacrificial thread.
She has a terrifying appearance with a mass of matted hair like a blooming blue lotus upon her crown;
she is adorned with five skulls joined by a band of white bones.
She who has made an ear-ornament from a red serpent on her forehead,
and who is most brilliantly radiant with a necklace fashioned from a great, exceedingly white serpent.
She has a sacred thread made of serpents as dark as the blades of dūrvā grass,
and she possesses four arms, one of which holds a fist filled with pieces of red flesh.
Adorned with a mass of matted hair and a sacred thread,
and graced by a sharp-edged sword held aloft in her right hand, she is the one who utters the roar of heroes.
Below that, one should fashion the supreme [consort] in the form of a seed-syllable,
beautiful with her own voice, possessing a red stalk in her left half.
Holding a blue lotus, and beneath that,
a skull-born [flower] resembling a water-pot, which contains the world joined with dullness.
Her true arms are adorned with armlets made from a multitude of smoke-colored serpents;
she possesses a golden-hued serpent as a bracelet, and her hands are radiant with light.
O Mahādeva of brilliant white complexion, seated upon the heart of a corpse,
likewise contract the tips of your feet with a gaze fixed by the *niryaṃtra* [mudrā].
She stands upon the heart of a corpse with her left foot, smiling-faced,
adorned with a girdle of serpents as white as kunda flowers, and possessing three eyes.
Her anklets were made of slightly blood-stained serpents,
and she was adorned with human heads whose throats had been recently severed and from which blood was still flowing.
The Supreme Goddess was adorned with a great garland of fifty [heads], whose lotus feet hung down while their hair was intertwined with one another.
Seated in the midst of a blazing funeral pyre, clad in an upper garment of leopard skin,
with a mass of matted hair bound by a serpent the color of lac, she is the bestower of boons.
Having thus meditated upon her, whose face is smiling with a slight frown, whose tongue is lolling, and who bestows boons,
the wise one, a great poet, should contemplate her as "I am he."
Now he speaks of the secret of meditation.
For the purpose of subjugation, she is blue-colored; for attraction, she has a yellow form;
for killing and expulsion, she is smoky-colored; and black is used for purposes other than those.
One should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess, visualizing her as seated upon a corpse.
Then the mantras and the mind-speech [arose].
Having first performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should perform the divine sipping of water (ācamana).
Having drunk [the water] with the three variations of the Tārā mantra, one should wash the hands with the Māyā mantra.
With *strīṃ hūṃ*, having twice wiped the lips, one should wash the hands with *phaṭ* syllables;
[one should likewise cleanse] the mouth-lord, the ears for a moment, the navel, the chest, the head, and the arms.
Having been touched by Vairocana and the others, one is liberated from all sins;
having sipped water and become Bhairava, one beholds her within a year.
Now, immediately after the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), he states the sequence.
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) in this manner, one should perform the placement of the arghya and other offerings;
thereafter, one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) and perform the ritual assignment of the seers (ṛṣi) and so forth.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs, and then meditate upon oneself as Tāriṇī.
Now, he describes the general establishment of the arghya offering for these [deities].
Then, having performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana), one should prepare the general offering water (sāmānyārghya).
Thereafter, one should fashion a mandala consisting of a triangle, a circle, and the representation of the earth.
Having worshipped the power of the support (ādhāra-śakti), one should place the vessel upon it;
having purified the vessel with the Astra-mantra, one should fill it with the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having invoked the sacred ford (tīrtha), one should cast [the water] forth with the *praṇava* while offering perfumes and other articles;
one should indeed display the *dhenumudrā*. This is considered the procedure for the general *arghya*.
The Goddess proceeds with the ritual placement (nyāsa), preceded by the sixteen-fold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
Now he speaks of her Great Sixfold [Nature].
I shall proclaim the sixfold Tārā, which is concealed in all tantras,
the pacifier of all obstacles and the destroyer of all sins.
She who pacifies great poverty, she who bestows everything at present,
she who grants all desires eternally, and she who bestows universal sovereignty.
To a disciple who is endowed with devotion, humble, high-souled,
generous, of noble birth, and devoted to pure conduct.
Having performed it in this manner, O Goddess of gods, one should cause the practitioner to enter;
otherwise, there would be a loss of accomplishment, for such is the command of Śambhu made regarding the self.
And so it is said:
Then one should perform the sixfold placement (ṣaṭkanyāsa) of Tārā, which bestows all accomplishments.
Among those, first is the initial placement beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha, as previously described.
Having uttered the letters of the Mātṛkā, one should speak preceded by *hrīṃ*, *strīṃ*, and *hūṃ*;
at the places of the Mātṛkā, one should utter the names beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha and so forth, together with their consorts, ending with *namaḥ*.
One should place [the mantra] ending in the dative case; this is remembered as the first nyāsa.
While performing this nyāsa, one should meditate upon the Goddess in this manner.
Seated upon a corpse-throne, possessing a blue luster, three-eyed,
with the crescent moon as her crest-jewel, enriched with various ornaments, and four-armed.
One should perform the second placement of the planets (grahanyāsa) and recollect it with that mantra;
this placement of the planets is declared to be preceded by the three seed-syllables.
One should place the red Sun, preceded by the *ya*-group, in the heart;
and the white Moon, preceded by the *ka*-group, on the earth; and likewise Maṅgala.

One should place the red [syllable] on the three eyes; you shall state that the first of the *varga* [consonant group] is yellow. One should place the dark-blue Mercury (*budha*) and the yellow Jupiter (*guru*), the first of the *ṭa*-group, on the limbs.
The first letter of the *ta* group, white in color, is Bhārgava in the *ghaṭikā*;
the first letter of the *pa* group, blue in color, is Śanaiścara in the region of the navel.
Having meditated upon the first letter of the *śa*-group, which is smoke-colored, one should place it on the face of Rāhu;
then, one should again place the first letter of the *la*-group, which has the luster of smoke, at the navel.
I shall now describe the third nyāsa, preceded by the triad of seed-syllables (bījas). Having first uttered the corresponding phonemes, [one says]: "Obeisance to you, Indra."
Having uttered the *si* and the diphthongs (*sandhyakṣara*), one should say "Salutation to Agni" in the southeast;
"Salutation to Yama" in the south; and the first letter of the *ka*-group on the forehead.
The first letter of the *ca*-group is in the southwest; [one should say] "Salutation to Nairṛti" at the mouth.
The first letter of the *ṭa*-group is on the ankle in the west; [one should say] "Salutation to Varuṇa.

One should place the first letter of the *ta*-group at the heart; [the mantra] "vāyave namaḥ" with the first letter of the *pa*-group should be placed on the right hand, ending with "namas" for Kuvera.
One should place the mantra "Ya-varga-ādi-Īśānāya Rudrāya Hṛt" on the left hand;
then one should place the mantra "Śa-varga-ādi-Urdhva-Kāmāya Namaḥ" on the navel.
One should perform the placement with "HŪṂ, protect today the earth" and "from the heart to the chest.
Now, the fourth [placement], called the placement of Śiva and Śakti, is described.
Preceded by *hrīṃ*, *strīṃ*, and *hūṃ*, one should perform the extraction of the senses and so forth;
[one should place] Brahmā joined with Ḍākinī in the east, preceded by the letter *tā*.
One should place at the *mūlādhāra* a four-petaled [lotus] endowed with the letters beginning with *va*, *di*, *la*, and *aṃ*, together with Śrī Viṣṇu and Śākinī.
One should place Rudra, joined with Lākinī and preceded by the letters from Ḍa to Pha, within the six-petalled lotus located at the Svādhiṣṭhāna, which is situated on the linga.
One should install a ten-petaled lotus in the Maṇipūraka located at the navel,
preceded by the syllables from 'ka' to 'va', together with the letter 'la', and conjoined with Kākinī, wherein resides Īśvara.
One should place Sadāśiva and Śākinī, preceded by the sixteen vowels, in the Anāhata center located at the heart, which has twelve petals.
One should place [the deity] in the sixteen-petaled lotus at the throat known as Viśuddha;
one should place Paraśiva, conjoined with Hākinī, in the Ājñā-cakra.
The syllable *hakṣa* is situated between the eyebrows; it is heart-entrancing.
One should now describe the fifth placement (*nyāsa*), which destroys all misfortunes.
One should utter "aṃ āṃ kavarga hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ tārāyai namaḥ" and then place it in the *brahmarandhra*, as well as "iṃ īṃ" and the *cavarga*.
One should also place *hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ nama ugrāyai* on the forehead;
one should utter *uṃ ūṃ ca varga strīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ mahogrāyai namaḥ*.

One should assign [the letters] between the eyebrows; at the throat, the *ṛ*-group (*ṛ*, *ṝ*, and the *ṭa*-class); and also *hrīṃ*, *strīṃ*, and *hūṃ*, ending with "namo vajrāyai," in the joints as well.
One should place *hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ namaḥ kālyai* at the heart for the *ṭa*-group and *ḹ* and *ḹ̄*. And one should place *hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ sarasvatyai* at the navel for the *pa*-group and *e* and *ai*.
Oṃ auṃ śa [the *śa*-group], hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ cāmuṇḍāyai ca liṅgake;
aṃ aḥ rakṣau ca hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ cāmuṇḍāyai namaḥ—one should thus perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
Having gone from the *mūlādhāra* to one's own chosen [deity], one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
At the *ādhāra*, one should place the seed-syllable of Kāmarūpa preceded by the short vowels.
One should place the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Jālandhara, preceded by the long vowel [Ā], in the heart;
the wise one should then place the seat named Pūrṇagiri, beginning with the consonant group 'ka', on the forehead.
One should place Uḍḍīyāna, beginning with the *u*-group [of consonants], at the junctions of the hair;
and one should place Vārāṇasī, the sacred seat (*pīṭha*), beginning with the *ṭa*-group, concentratedly upon the two eyebrows.
One should place the letters preceded by the *ta*-group upon his two eyes;
one should place the *māyāpūri* seat, preceded by the *pa*-group, upon the mouth.
One should place the Mathurā-pīṭha, beginning with the letter 'ka', on the throat; and one should place the Ayodhyā-pīṭha, beginning with the letter 'śa', on the navel.
One should then duly place the tenth seat, Kaṭaukāñcīpurī;
this sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa) of Tārā is declared to be the bestower of all desired goals.
Now, the sixfold mantras.
Having separated them with the mantra, one should place the Mātṛkā six times;
O lady of excellent hips, these are proclaimed as the sixfold Tārās, both in direct and reverse order.
When this ritual of placement (nyāsa) has been performed, all sin is destroyed;
he becomes worshipful to the Yoginīs—a god, and not a mere mortal.
O Maheśānī, he whom those purified in body by the sixfold [initiations] salute shall immediately become short-lived; even the deities tremble with fear before him.
In this world, there is no prior connection for him with father or mother.
Now he speaks of the secret sixfold [mantra].
This should not be disclosed anywhere regarding the protection of the minister’s body;
the Praṇava and the letters of the Mātṛkā are purified in the locus of the Mātṛkā.
O Pārvatī, one should place that very same purified syllable right there;
likewise, O Goddess, the Māyā-bīja should be carefully deposited.
Likewise, the goddess, being composed in meditation, should place the *vadhū* seed-syllable;
and in the same way, the *kūrca* seed-syllable should be placed without exception.
And immediately after that, he shall perform the *astra-mantra* and the *mūla-mantra*.
O Goddess, this sixfold secret [mantra] must never be disclosed.
It must necessarily be performed every day; neither worship nor recitation is required in that regard.
Furthermore, its sixfold common classification has also been stated in the Śyāmā-prakaraṇa.
In the ritual procedure for the Tārā-vidyā, the Goddess is to be visualized as the fourfold group of six activities.
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras).

Having placed [the letters] beginning with 'a' in forward order, then [the asterisms] beginning with Rohiṇī in forward order, and again in reverse order, one should apply these four; as for the remainder, one should not join it.
Having performed the great Nyāsa beginning with Rohiṇī, the wise and excellent man will certainly become like the son of Rohiṇī on earth, beyond the reach of mourning.
If one should worship Tāriṇī without performing the *tārakā-nyāsa*,
then even if the mantra is recited a hundred times, it will not bestow accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the ṛṣi and other components.
The seer is Akṣobhya, its metre is said to be Bṛhatī,
and the goddess is Nīrasarasvatī, who is concealed within the three worlds.
HŪṂ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Māyā (HRĪṂ) is the power (śakti), and STRĪṂ is known as the pin (kīlaka);
this yoga, O Goddess, should be practiced for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life.
Now follows the ritual assignment of the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa).
Therein, first, by means of the five-and-a-half-syllable vidyā.
The ritual of the six limbs is declared to be performed with the six long syllables of the Māyā-bīja.
Now, the six-syllable [mantra] of the two triple-ignorances.
Having uttered "the embodiment of all speech," one should say "salutation to the heart" (hṛdayāya namaḥ);
and [having uttered] "the unbroken embodiment of speech," [one says "salutation to the head"] with the beloved of fire (svāhā).
Having uttered "Brahmavāgrūpiṇī," one should pronounce "Hūṃ" for the armor;
likewise, "Rudravāgrūpiṇī netratreya vauṣaṭ."
Having released [the mantra] "Sarvavāgrūpiṇī," one should recollect "Astrāya Phaṭ.
One should join the seed-syllable with the six long vowels and the Māyā-bīja at the end of each seed-syllable.
Now follows the Vidyā consisting of four and a half syllables.
At the end of the seed-syllable, "Ekajaṭāyai" is proclaimed as the heart-mantra;
likewise, "Tāriṇyai" is for the head, and similarly, "Vajrodake" is for the crest-lock.
The *ugrajaṭa* and the *kavaca*, as well as the *mahāparisana*;
likewise, the *piṅgāgraika-jaṭa*—these are proclaimed to be the weapons of the eyes.
Now follows the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa).
O Dear One, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) nine times with the root mantra;
one may also perform it seven times, five times, or even fewer than that.
In this regard it has been said: "The wise man should practice this; he should not cause anything else to enter here."
Now, he describes the drawing of the yantra.
Then, the yogi should prepare the yantra with saffron and vermilion on a surface made of gold,
silver, copper, crystal, or likewise of wood.
The Goddess should be worshipped by the best of men according to the prescribed rite upon a mandala consisting of a bindu,
a triangle, an eight-petaled lotus, and a square enclosure marked with thunderbolt symbols.
O Great Goddess, that yantra of mine is the most secret of secrets;
it consists of a bindu, a hexagon, and a circle, adorned with a lotus and a square enclosure.
O highly wise one, the yantra is said to consist of two pairs of *bhūpuras*,
followed by a point (*bindu*), a triangle, a hexagon, and three circles in succession.
Then, having drawn a square, a circle, and above that an eight-petaled lotus,
one should then draw three circles followed by three enclosures of the earth (bhūpuras).
The yantra marked with the trident belongs to the mantra of the illustrious Mahātāriṇī.
The dot (bindu), the triangle, the hexagon, adorned with circles and eight petals,
the sixteen-spoked [wheel], the tooth-lotus, and likewise the sixty-four-petaled [lotus].
The yantra of the mantra of Śrītāriṇī is joined with three enclosures of earth (bhūpura).
Then he spoke of the fanning machine.
Then, having carefully constructed a pedestal out of *kula-rasa* [mercury], one should recite:
"Oṃ Āḥ Surekhe Vajrarekhe Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā."
With this [prescribed] method, one should draw the beautiful Tārā yantra:
a lotus situated within a hexagon, and again, two earth-fences (bhūpura).
In the center of that, the practitioner of mantra should indeed inscribe the Tārā-om (the Praṇava).
Or alternatively:
Furthermore, one should draw a lotus situated within a hexagon, possessing the luster of the orb of the earth;
then, one should write the syllable *māyā* on the eastern petal and a second one on the southern petal.
Then, in the north and the west, one should place "hūṃ phaṭ" and the syllable "tāra" (oṃ) in the center;
[one should draw] a very beautiful eight-petaled lotus with its yoni-mark made of cow dung.
The city of the earth (bhūpura), rich with excellent vajras, is a single-crested yantra;
one should place the *māyā* [syllable] on the eastern petal and the second seed-syllable on the southern [petal].
Likewise, one should then write the syllable *phaṭ* in the north and the west;
having written the central seed-syllable, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
There are seven types [of mantras]: those consisting of weapons, those consisting of seed-syllables, and those consisting of both.
The Kuleśvara doctrine is proclaimed in the north-east and the west;
likewise, "phaṭ" is recorded in the western Vikarāla doctrine and the north-east.

In the sky [the letter *ha*], with the moon [the vowel *ī*], and the letter of taste [the vowel *ra*] as its pericarp; it is the radiant Keśava, whose petals are the pairs of vowels, shining with the unfolding of the consonant groups, and which is encircled by the house of Sumati [the syllable *ya*].
This supreme yantra of the Lord of Waters, shining with the colors of the ocean and adorned with eight corners,
is declared to bestow the accomplishment of all goals.
One should make [the site] empty with flowers; one should indicate obstacles in an empty [place].
A short witness brings fear; the white Lord is the one whose face is Madana.

O beloved of Kālī and Marut, having likewise spoken of their consecration, Bhṛgu [instructed that] one should cast an offering of flowers (puṣpāñjali) into the yantra with the mantra "Kūrcāstra vahnibhāryā."
Now he describes the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjā).
Having meditated upon Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, Kṣetrapāla, and Yoginī within the house on the four directions, one should worship them perfectly.
One should conquer the fierce Kṣetrapāla in the west, who is black, naked, and holds in his hands a noose, a goad, a trident, and a skull-cup.
And on the right, one should worship the beautiful Vaṭuka, adorned with serpents, surrounded by his own retinue, and holding a skull and a trident in his two hands.
One should worship the Yoginī in the north, holding a hand-drum, a skull-topped staff, a trident, and a skull-cup in her hands, adorned with red garlands and wearing red garments.
Having visualized the cremation ground there, one should at that time recollect the tree;
and at its root, a jeweled pedestal adorned with various gems.
Abundantly adorned with various ornaments and graced by sages and gods,
its interior was filled with jackals greedily devouring much flesh and bone.
In the four directions, one should worship the corpses— shaven-headed and adorned with glowing coals and bones—
and then, subsequently, worship the powers of the seat (pīṭhaśakti) equally upon the filaments.
One should worship the seat (pīṭha) of Dhāriṇī, the bestower of boons, with this [mantra].
It is as follows:
Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Rati, Prīti,
Kīrti, Śānti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi— these are the eight Śaktis.
In the midst of that, one should worship the vehicle of the Goddess, which is indeed a corpse.
Now, he states the Pīṭha-mantra.
Having pronounced "viyat" (ha) intensely, followed by the mantra (sa), endowed with the bindu and the kalā; then the word "mahāpreta," ending with "hṛdaya"—this is the mantra.
p.
172b) Now follows the ritual for placing the *arghya* offering.
One should prepare the ground for the mandala with the previously mentioned mantra;
there, one should recite the mantra over the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), the tortoise (kūrma), and Śeṣa.
One should place the base there with the mantra "Oṃ Hrīṃ Phaṭ," and then worship that base and the fire-maṇḍala.
At the end of "namaḥ," with the syllable "namaḥ," and then having washed away the wardens of hell with the mantra "hūṃ phaṭ," one should establish [the deity] with the seed-syllable "strīṃ."
Then one should worship the human skull and recite the fourfold mantra.
One should utter "Namo Kālīkapālāya Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Hūṃ" preceded by [the syllables] Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Hūṃ;
this eleven-syllable mantra is prescribed for worship and other rites.
Having uttered "strīṃ strīṃ strūṃ tāriṇī," the skull [mantra] ending in "namaḥ" becomes the twelfth;
by this, the second worship of the skull is performed.
Having uttered "hāṃ hīṃ hūṃ," [the mantra] "nīlā kapālāyai namaḥ" consists of eleven syllables; thus is described the third worship of Kapālā.
*Māyā* (the Illusion), *strī* (the Woman), *hūṃ*, and for *svargakapāla* (the Skull of Heaven); one should utter [this] for all calamities.
Then, for *dhārāya* (the Stream), for *sarvāya* (the All), and likewise for *sarvodbhavāya* (the Source of All).
"Salutation to the goddess who consists of all purity, who has slain all the asuras, and who holds a skull"— this is declared to be the fourth mantra.
This fifty-sixth letter, *ka*, is for the worship of the skull;
thereafter, one should worship the solar mandala within that skull.
Oṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya namaḥ— this nine-syllable mantra is intended for worship of the solar disc when using a human skull.
Reciting the root mantra, one should cast a blade of *kuśa* grass into it with the visualization of nectar;
having offered scents, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one should display the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā.
In the Kali age, however, she makes the mudrā with the two thumbs separated and made equal;
having placed the two index fingers inside the ring fingers, they are made curved.
In the rite of summoning Trikhaṇḍā, one should place the little finger in its own position;
then, within that wine, one should worship the lunar maṇḍala.
Then, one should consecrate the water in the conch with the eleven-syllable mantra.
Having uttered *hrīṃ śrīṃ hrauṃ oṃ*, one should then utter *hrīṃ strīṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
With *hyoṃ huṃ* as the beginning, this mantra consisting of eleven syllables is preceded by the seed-syllable of speech (*vāgbīja*).
Then, with the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, one should pour a little wine into the remaining water;
one should display the conch-mudrā and the yoni-mudrā to the water in the conch.
There, having meditated upon an eight-petaled lotus within a hexagon, one should contemplate the Goddess;
having worshipped her as previously described, one should satisfy the Lord with the root mantra.
With the index, middle, ring,
and little fingers together with the thumb, one should perform the rite four times over the water contained in the great conch for Maheśvara.
Afterwards, one should satisfy Ānandabhairava with the five-syllable mantra:
*Tāraḥ* (Oṃ), *Hrauṃ*, *Hyauṃ*, and *Namaḥ*; this five-syllabled mantra is that of Bhairava.
Then, with that [water] by which one should sprinkle the implements of worship, one should not offer the *arghya*;
rather, having displayed the *yonimudrā*, one should prostrate before Bhavatāriṇī.
Now he describes the worship.
Having performed the invocation and established [the deity], one should meditate and display the mudrā;
having displayed the mudrā, one should worship according to the rules with the ritual offerings.
Now, as for meditative absorption (dhyāna).
She stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, fierce, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
short-statured, with a protruding belly, terrifying, and her hips wrapped in a tiger skin.
Endowed with fresh youth, adorned with the five mudrās,
four-armed, with a protruding tongue, most terrifying, and bestowing boons.

One should meditate on her holding a sword and a knife in her right hands, and a severed head and a blue lotus in her left; she has a single matted lock with a tawny tip upon her crown, and she is adorned with ornaments upon her chest.
Adorned with three eyes shaped like the orb of the rising sun,
she is terrifying with fangs protruding from the midst of her blazing forehead.
She indeed has a smiling face, is adorned with ornaments of serpents,
and stands upon a white lotus within the waters that pervade the universe.
Now he explains the mudrās.
In the worship of Tārā, one should especially display the five mudrās:
the Yoni, the Bhūtinī, the one called Bījā, and the Daityadhūminī.
And *lelihā*; these are proclaimed as the five well-guarded mudrās.
The wise know them in sequence as Yoni, Māyādharā, Adhyenu, Vadhū, and Kūrca.
I shall now describe the characteristics of their seed-syllables (bījas) in sequence:
[they are located] on the index finger, the ring finger, the middle finger, the little finger, and also on the wheel [of the thumb].
One should join the two hands by separating the roots of the little fingers;
having placed the tips of the thumbs [there], it is proclaimed as the Mahāyoni.
One should display this downward-facing mudrā preceded by the seed-syllable;
having indeed formed the yoni-mudrā, make the two middle fingers curved.
When the thumbs are at their tips, this mudrā is considered Dhūtinī;
having crossed the hands and touched the pair of thumbs and index fingers.
One should simultaneously and evenly form the logic of the half-moon shape;
having drawn down the little finger, one should join it with the middle finger.
This goddess, known as the Seed (Bījā), whose nature is wisdom, has been described;
having crossed the hands and placed the little fingers, the ring fingers, and the middle fingers [within].
The two ring fingers are placed below, and the pair of index fingers is held separately;
having joined them closely together, the ring fingers rest upon the tips of the thumbs.
O beloved, this mudrā is called Dhūmaketvā, belonging to the Daityas;
having expanded the *cakra*, one should move the tongue downward.
With her two fists held at her sides and licking [her lips], she is thus described as "Lelihānā."
Now, he describes her worship.
Having uttered "Śrīmadekajaṭe," say "O Vajra, accept this flower";
then, having recited [the name] beginning with Tārā and ending with the fire-born wife (svāhā), one should perform the worship.
Having satisfied them with the five mudrās, one should pay homage unobserved.
The five mudrās are as follows:
Facing forward, square, circular, and likewise "cow-mouthed"—
this is declared to be the *yoni-mudrā*, and this *mudrā* is used for salutation.
Now he states their protection:
Having placed the añjali upon the ground and again resting the head there,
O Maheśānī, this mudrā of these [deities] is known as the Saṃmukha.
Having placed her left hand palm-upward on the ground, Maheśvarī,
the best of practitioners, should join her right palm upon it.
Having touched the backs of the fingers of both hands with one another, and by joining the heads [of the index fingers] there, this shall be the *catusrikā* mudrā.
O Śivā, O Great Mistress of Yoga, when one places both fists with the thumbs turned upward on the ground and holds them at the crown of the head, it is known as the Vṛtta mudrā.
Having placed both hands on the ground with the fingers spread and joined together like a casket,
and by joining the head to that position, this mudrā is known as Gomukha.
The previously mentioned *yonimudrā*, when joined with the head to the ground,
is called *yonimudrā* for the purpose of saluting the goddess Tārā.
Then, one should worship Bhairava upon her head.
And so it is said:
Then, one should worship the one known as Akṣobhya upon the head of the Goddess with the twelve-syllable mantra of the Sage; that is what is declared.
Akṣobhya and Vajrapuṣpa receive [the offering] from Analavallabhā.
The mantra, meditation, and other practices for its worship shall be described hereafter.
Then, one should worship the six limbs of the Goddess in the six corners.
Now, the gurus beginning with Divyaugha.
Now, O Tārā, I shall describe the gurus who bestow both seen and unseen fruits:
Ūrdhvakeśa, Vyomakeśa, Nīlakaṇṭha, and Vṛṣadhvaja.
Then, O child, one should worship the divine lineages (divyaugha) that have been described, as well as the perfected lineages (siddhaugha):
Vasiṣṭha, Kūrmanātha, Mīnanātha, and Maheśvara.
And Harinātha [overcomes] the floods of pride; listen, I shall name the true gurus:
Tārāvatī, Bhāsvamatī, Jayā, Vidyā, and Mahodarī.
Sukhānanda, Parānanda, Pārijāta,
Kuleśvara, Virūpākṣa, and Pheravī— thus has the Tāriṇī-kula been described.
The wise practitioner should worship his own guru in the center of the triangle, in front of the Goddess;
Kāmeśvarī and the others are to be worshipped within the triangle in the fire-mandala.
Kāmeśvarī, Dikkaravāsinī, and Caṇḍalāyikā.
Then, in the downward-facing triangle.

In the northeast corner, one should worship Gāyatrī, the mother of the mantras, holding a radiant staff, water-pot, rosary, and the gesture of fearlessness, as well as Brahmā, who is likewise endowed with these same attributes.
Thus, this is the distinction regarding the six-cornered and three-cornered [mandalas] according to the Upaniṣads.
In sequence, one should worship Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, and Māheśvarī with the three seed-syllables in the three corners.
Now, the worship of the enclosures for this [deity] is performed by circling only counter-clockwise.
And thus:
One should worship the deities of the limbs in sequence, proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction.

Then, on the eight petals starting from the east, the root deities such as Mahākālī and the others are to be worshipped. Thereafter, the eight Yoginīs are to be fully worshipped on the outside, starting from the base of each petal.
Mahākālī, then Mudrāṇī, Ugrā, and likewise Bhīmā;
Ghorā, Bhrāmarī, and Mahārātrī as the seventh.
Bhairavī is declared to be the eighth; one should worship those Yoginīs.
Then, one should worship Rocanā and the others on the four petals starting from the east.
The mantra-practitioner should worship Vairocana, Śaṅkhapāṇḍara, Padmanābhaka,
and Asitābha on the four petals starting from the eastern direction.
