Then, on the four petals beginning with the southeast, the offerings are made to those whose names begin with the respective letters.
Thereafter, one should worship in the intermediate directions, starting from the southeast corner in sequence:
Nāmakā, Nāmakā, Pāṇḍarā, and Tārikā.
Now, he describes the meditation on Vairocana and the others.
Vairocana has two arms and holds a staff and a *ṭomara* weapon;
he is yellow in color, seated upon a bull, possesses three eyes, and is affectionate toward his red [attendant].
The god Śaṅkha, who has three heads, is dark-hued yet golden, holding a book, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting mudrā; he is stainless and has the moon as his vehicle.
One should meditate upon the auspicious, three-eyed Lord Padmanābha, who bestows boons, holds a book, the gestures of granting boons and protection, and a noose.
One should visualize my [form] as white, with three eyes, bestowing boons, holding a book and the gesture of fearlessness,
and accompanied by Baladeva.
[He saw] Kṛṣṇā, with a terrifying face, and Akā in the prime of youth;
[he saw] Tālakā mounted upon a lizard and seated upon a peacock.
One should meditate upon her as pale white, endowed with four arms through the white seed-syllable, red in color, pot-bellied, and seated upon five corpses.
Now, he states the specific mantra for the worship of Vairocana and the others, ending with Narakāntaka, within the Tāyī ritual.
First, having uttered the *praṇava* (oṃ), one should utter the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the name;
then the name itself in the vocative case, followed by "Vajra" and "pratīccha" (accept).
The mantra is said to end with "svāhā"; this is the sequence for the twelve [syllables].
Then, on the tips of the eight petals starting from the east, the eight Mothers beginning with Brāhmī are to be worshipped.
And on the tips of the petals, O Great Goddess, one should worship Brahmā and the others.
Then, one should conquer Padmāntaka and the others at the four gates, beginning with the eastern one.
At the gate, starting from the east, one should subsequently worship Padmāntaka and Yamāntaka;
having worshipped Vighnāntaka, one should then worship Narakāntaka.
Then, having worshipped the guardians of the directions (Dikpālas) in the ten directions of the outer enclosure (bhūpura), and having duly honored its eight petals,

one should worship the Sun in the eastern direction of the bhūpura, in the space between the syllables *Bhū* and *Pura*. To the north of the Goddess, within the lineage of the Gurus, one should conquer the Vīras.

And outside that very bhūpura, one should worship Indra and the other guardians of the directions, as well as the vajra and the other weapons, in the ten directions in due order immediately thereafter.
Then, within the circle of the earth, one should worship the Sun to the north of the lineage of gurus;
further to the north, one should worship the Buddha, and thereafter worship the Goddess.
The wise one should offer three handfuls of flowers and recite the mantra according to the prescribed number.
Now he states the weapon-mantra for the common sacrifice that removes all obscurations.
Having first uttered the *praṇava* (Oṃ), followed by the name accompanied by the vocative case,
and then the mantra "Vajrapuṣpaṃ pratīccha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," [the offering is made].
By this mantra alone, the nyāsa is indeed distinct; of this there is no doubt.
With this mantra, one should worship all the members of the retinue.
Furthermore, in the case of Vairocana and the others, [the seed-syllable] is preceded by the first letter of their names.
Now follows the offering of the bali-oblation.
Then, at the conclusion of the daily worship, one should offer a bali-oblation to the Goddess every day.
On the left side, there should be a triangle, a circle, and a square.
Having prepared red garlands and other offerings, one should worship according to the prescribed ritual.
Having uttered "Śrīmadekajaṭā," "Nīlasarasvatī," "Mahogra," "Tārādevī," and "Khakha," [one becomes] the devourer of all spirits and piśācas.
Seize, seize! Cut, cut! Render [the mind] free from dullness, making it equal to the state of awakening.

The mantra beginning with *tāra* (oṃ) and *māyā* (hrīṃ), followed by *śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *phaṭ*, and ending with the wife of fire (svāhā), consists of fifty-two syllables; when worshipped in this manner, it attains perfection.
Now he describes the recitation (japa).
Therein, first [the mantra] of Bhairava, then that of Kullukā, and then that of one's own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā).
If one abandons the mantra of Akṣobhya and recites the mantra of the goddess Tārā,
there will be a loss of accomplishment for that person, and he shall go to the Raurava hell.
O Brahmin, the mantra of Akṣobhya is the armor, the most excellent essence;
it is the supreme secret and the great meditation, the highest among all meditations.
First I shall proclaim the mantra, and after that the meditation;
thereafter, I shall relate the armor-mantra (kavaca) in due order.
Having extracted the unsurpassed [seed-syllable] adorned with *prapañca*,
the great mantra begins and ends with *akṣobhya* and *svāhā*.
He himself is declared to be the Sage (Ṛṣi), the Virāṭ meter is proclaimed as his Metre (Chandas),
and Akṣobhya is declared as the Deity (Devatā), who possesses three forms and assumes the shape of a serpent.
Its application, however, is invariably restricted to the four aims of human life.
Now I shall describe the meditation that bestows all prosperity—
the auspicious form of the serpent, radiant as a thousand suns.
His face is like lightning, his eyes are radiant with fire,
he is endowed with three folds [of skin] on his chest, and his matted locks stand upright and prominent.
Endowed with a great forest, saluted by gods and asuras,
and radiant like the sun or lightning, there was a great jewel upon his head.
O goddesses, you too should worship this great-bodied one with perfect veneration.
The illustrious Śiva said:
For this armor of Akṣobhya, Brahmā, Viṣṇu,
and the Rudras are declared to be the seers (ṛṣis), and Virāṭ is cited as the meter (chandas).
Akṣobhya is the deity, Śrī is the seed-syllable, and [the letter] V is indeed the seed;
Svāhā is the power (śakti), and its application is for the four aims of human life (puruṣārtha).
May the seed-syllable *Śrī* protect the head; may *Ādi-vijita* protect the crown-lock (*bhāraka*). May the letter *A* protect the shoulder, and may the letter *Kṣa* protect the heart.
May the syllable *Bha* protect my navel, may *Eka* protect the secret region; may the power of the mantra protect all my limbs, and may the seed-syllable protect my three eyes.
One should always protect the two upper arms with all the [other] deities;
Brahmā protects the two feet, and Viṣṇu protects the two knees.
May Śivomā protect my *mūlādhāra*, and may Vṛṣa protect my *svādhiṣṭhāna*;
and may the consort of Śiva always protect my *maṇipūra*.
May the unstruck lotus protect me; may the ten deities beginning with Indra, who are spread throughout the Viśuddha-cakra, grant me protection; and may the Sun protect me.
May Maheśvara always protect the most beautiful wheel of command;
may he protect my semen and Brahmā, and may Bhairavī protect my navel.
In the *Divya* and other [tantras], as well as in the lineage of gurus, Akṣobhya is mentioned everywhere;
thus, according to the prescribed sequence, the wise one should recite the armor-mantra (*kavaca*).
Whoever recites this daily at the three junctions of the day, endowed with faith and devotion, shall never suffer a loss of accomplishment; of this there is no doubt.
Now, he states the necessity of the *kullukā*.
If one applies the Tāriṇī mantra without having recited the Kullukā mantra and without remembering Hari, the Lord of Śrī, it leads to Narakeśariṇī (the hellish lioness).
Having recited the Kullukā-mantra one hundred and eight times, the wise practitioner should thereafter recite the Tāriṇī mantra; otherwise, he shall not attain success.
Having held the *kullukā* in her hand, one should worship the Great Goddess;
or else, having placed it upon her head, one should worship and also recite [the mantra].
He states the number of recitations for the impermanent [mantra]:
With single-minded concentration, the practitioner of mantra should daily recite the mantra one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times, using the secret rosary.
And so it is said:
If one recites [the mantra] of Indrāṇī a thousand, a hundred, or twenty times with the secret rosary, she becomes the deliverer and bestower of success, as heard in the Śruti.
Therefore, one who desires accomplishment should fashion a garland made of great conch shells, constructed from fifty beads, with that [mantra].
This secret garland has been fully proclaimed; it must be concealed with great effort.
A rosary for recitation made of human bone fragments is known as the *calamālā*.
It should be known as made of a great conch shell; in its absence, it is considered to be made of crystal.
Now, the meditation on the mantra.
I shall now proclaim the meditation on the mantra, which accomplishes all goals through recitation;
O Maheśānī, by means of this meditation on the mantra, even a slayer of a Brahmin is purified.
One should meditate upon Hṛllekhā at the mūlādhāra-cakra, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns; and one should visualize the second [syllable], yellow in color, at the svādhiṣṭhāna-cakra.

One should meditate upon the eighth mantra in the heart, which resembles ten million suns, possesses great radiance, and has the splendor of the fire of universal destruction. It is the seed-syllable *kūrca*.
One should visualize the entire Vidyā, from the base (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
resembling ten million suns and previously beheld by yogis.
Merely by placing [the mantra] upon the tongue, even a mute person becomes a great poet;
having thus offered the recitation, one should then perform the ringing of the bell.
Having praised them properly with hymns, the practitioner, endowed with devotion, [should proceed].
Now, as for the hymn of praise: as follows.
If the supreme form of Viṣṇu did not manifest itself through its own divine play, how could the Moon-crested Lord exist?
Therefore, one should worship the Three-eyed One, from whose lotus-feet flows the stream of water that is the eternal seed of the universe.

O Kṛṣṇa, if Parā had not existed, how could the three-eyed Lord— whose face possesses the luster of the sun and whose eyes are curved like lotuses— have attained the state of being a *bahuvrīhi* compound for the god of love (Smarāgni) within the name of Kṛṣṇa, and how could he worship her, the eternal seed of the universe and the three-eyed goddess?
The five-faced one (Śiva) became intoxicated by the honey-like nectar from her lips, which were moistened by the essence of truth;
therefore, having attained the name "Ever-Blissful" (Sadānanda), one should worship that three-eyed goddess, the eternal seed of the universe.

If, having thoroughly drunk her nectar with my senses, I were to remember it in my mouth, in ambrosia, or in sandalwood paste and the like, why would I feel loathing? Having consumed the Kālakūṭa poison, may I instead worship the Three-eyed One, the eternal seed of the universe.

When the Creator himself does not exist, how could he be self-born? Thus, the one whose name is praised as "the Unborn" (Anutārā) was not born; may she, the eternal seed of the world, who sports in the celestial sphere, grant her grace to the Three-eyed One.
Then there is the "portion of that" (tadaṃśa), which is equal and has two seed-syllables; thereafter comes the "three-footed" (tripāda), which the Vedāntins proclaim.
One should worship the three-eyed goddess, whose single syllable is the seed of Brahman, and whose "kūrca" is the eternal seed of the universe.
Then, when she was together with the weapon-mantra consisting of five syllables, she became renowned as Ugratārā because of her rescuing of the world;
without that *tāraka*, she alone is the supreme one, and from her matted locks she should worship the three-eyed goddess who is the eternal seed of the universe.
Devoid of weapons, consisting of five syllables, Kullukā herself is the silent voice and the supreme nature of consciousness;
one should worship her, the three-eyed goddess, who is the eternal seed of the universe and the cause of perpetual liberation even when remembered for but a single moment.
Those people who recite this king of hymns, renowned in the context of both prose and verse,
are quickly liberated from sins and the like that take the form of the world, and they go to the presence of Tārā in another body.

He who, during a time of misfortune, at midnight, at the conclusion of his recitation, or at dawn, shall recite with devotion while contemplating its meaning, will become like a blue lotus; he is a living swan within the lotus-feet of the Lord, a living soul, not merely a lifeless one.
Thus ends the Stotrarāja named Maṃtrārthavivaraṇātmatātmaka, consisting of the exposition of the meaning of the mantra within the Śrī Advaitanirūpaṇa.
Now, he speaks of the Kavaca.
Long ago, on the peak of Kailāsa, Śaṅkara questioned Tārā:
"O Goddess of gods, speak with respect in confidence."
By what means, O beloved of the wise, may the body suddenly become very firm? Or how, in this matter, may there be incomparable success?
Śrītārā said:
For this is indeed most secret, having issued from my lotus-like mouth;
O beloved, I shall tell you this supreme mystery.
Listen with careful attention to that armor which issued from his mouth,
as it was recounted by the Lotus-born One during the battle with Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
O Lord of Gods, it is because of that power that Viṣṇu does not meet his destruction;
you previously spoke of this, yet you do not remember it due to your *māyā*.
This armor, extracted from the essence of all things for the sake of virtuous yogins,
must not be spoken of to anyone, nor should it be revealed in any way whatsoever.
O Lord of Gods, if you have affection for me now, take an oath;
then listen with full attention to this armor, the compendium of the essence.
Truth, truth, again truth, truth, truth, again and again:
one who worships the divine beings for even a moment without the armor-mantra [is lost].
I eat that most terrible crocodile, as firmly determined by the Yoginīs.
Protect the root-seed of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa;
and above that, protect the seed of Śakti and the Liṅga with great effort.
May the seed-syllable *Vadhū* always protect Maṇipūra, especially;
may the seed-syllable *Varma* protect Anāhata for me from all sides in every way.
May the weapon always protect the pure [heart], adorned by the throat;
may Śeṣa, however, eternally protect my command-center, the two-petaled [lotus].
May Tārā protect my head, and may she always protect my face;
may Nīlasarasvatī protect my heart forevermore.
May Akṣobhya protect all my limbs; may Vṛhatī protect my forehead;
may the deity Ugratārā always protect my throat.
May the Māyā-bīja always protect my feet in their entirety;
may the Vadhū-bīja always indeed protect my thighs at all times.
May the *kūrca* mantra, the destroyer of obstacles, always protect my two breasts;
and may the eternal Goddess Lakṣmī protect my tongue and my seat.
May Sarasvatī always protect the tip of the tongue with effort;
may Rati always protect the seed-syllable, and may Prīti always protect my mouth.
May Kīrti always protect Kīrti; may Śānti always protect Śānti;
may Puṣṭi protect me with nourishment, and may Puṣṭituṣṭi always protect [me].
May Vairocana protect the conch, and likewise may Śaṅkha protect the eastern [direction];
may Pāṇḍara always protect my cheek, eternally and in every way.
May Padmanābha always protect the navel;
may Medaspatra protect [the body]; may Asitābha protect the genitals; and may Nāmaka protect the eyes.
May Māmakī protect my arms; may Pāṇḍara protect my neck;
may Tāraka protect my heart; and may Padmāntaka protect my vision.
May Yamāntaka and Narāntaka always protect my two sides;
may the one known as Vighnāntaka protect my feet forever.
May Tārā, the Supreme Goddess, constantly protect my eight limbs.
O God, this armor (kavaca) has been told; it issued from her very mouth.
O Lord of Gods, if through negligence this [teaching] is revealed anywhere by the Yoginīs, then I myself shall be the bringer of death.
If it is obtained by some practitioner through the power of fortune,
then for him great accomplishment will certainly arise in his very body.
It must not be given to those who are forbidden, nor should it be revealed under any circumstances;
if I were to give it to those who are forbidden, then I would be a bringer of death.
One should bestow it upon a peaceful disciple, accompanied by the tantra and the mantra;
when it is enclosed within the lineage of gurus, then there is unsurpassed accomplishment.
The entire secret has been told, which bestows infinite fruit;
it must be guarded, O Lord, and never revealed at any time.
Thus ends the *Ekajaṭā-kavaca* as spoken in the *Śrī-yoginī-tantra*.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Daily Worship Common to the Three Varieties of Tārā," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*.
The twenty-fifth chapter is unavailable.
Now, the sequence of the Śrīvairocanī-vidyā is written down.
Taking a water vessel in his hand, he should then proceed to the place of worship;
having washed his feet and hands and put on two clean garments.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules, O Lord of Teachers, the Goddess [should sit] on a comfortable seat facing east,
or facing north, or especially facing south.
To the left of one's own house, one should construct the beautiful temple of the Goddess;
it is formed with the Praṇavas, the syllable of modesty (lajjā), and the letter 'sa' followed by the visarga.
For the sake of protection against the destruction of the Asuras, [one should recite] "rakṣamāye phaṭ" ending with two *ṭha* syllables (*svāhā*).
Having washed one's feet with this, one should discard the water toward the northeast (Īśāna).
Now, the sipping of water with mantras (mantrācamana).
Meditating on the Goddess in the lotus of the heart, the practitioner should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with mantras;
having drunk the water with the three syllables *lakṣmī*, *māyā*, and *kūrca*.
Having drunk water with the three seeds— *lakṣmī*, *māyā*, and *kūrca*— the practitioner,
having worshipped [it] eight times with the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable, should rinse his mouth twice with the two *māyā* syllables.
One should wash the hand with the *kūrca* [mantra] and perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with these mantras:
Śrī, Māyā, Kūrca, Vāk, Kāma, the Tripuṭā, and the syllables Bhaga.
Having performed the *kāmakalā* with the two *kuśa* blades at the mouth, nose, eyes, ears, navel, heart, and head— these eight— one becomes a reciter (*japtṛ*) in an instant.
Having sipped water (ācamana) in this manner, the wise man beholds Chinnamastā for a year;
he should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) and then offer the general arghya.
The door should be sprinkled with water, and one should worship the deities of the door:
Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, and thereafter Kṣetrapāla.
O Maheśānī, [one should worship] Vighnarāja, Gaṅgā, and Yamunā,
followed by Vasudhārā, Śaṅkhanidhi, Padmanidhi, and Vasumatī.
Having paid homage to the glory of the gateway, the wise one worships it in due order.
The best of teachers should perform worship beginning with the syllable *Oṃ* and ending with *Namaḥ*,
slightly contracting the left side of the body while placing the left foot forward.
The wise one should enter the place of worship while reciting "Astrāya Phaṭ."
Then, having prepared the vessel, the wise one should bow to Kṣetrapāla;
[he should visualize] Brahmā above, Ananta below, and then the Ādhāra-śakti beyond that.
The tortoise, Ananta, the earth, the Kalpa tree,
and beyond that the jewel-goddess, the golden lion, and thereafter the eight Śaktis.
One should bow to the bulb of bliss (ānandakanda), then to the stalk of consciousness (saṃvinnāla),
then to the petals of primordial nature (prakṛti), and finally to the filaments consisting of the transformations (vikāra).
The lotus is the single quality of all principles: sattva, rajas, and tamas;
beyond that are the orbs of the sun, the moon, and fire.
The wise one should bow to the pericarp joined with the fifty seed-syllables,
as well as to the individual self (ātman), the supreme self (paramātman), and the inner self (antarātman).
The wise one should prostrate like a staff upon the ground before the filament (Keśara);
with divine vision, he should drive away the non-divine obstacles, but not the former ones.
With the mantra "Astrāya" and also with the mantra "Hūṃ," the wise and beautiful woman should protect herself by means of the application of a wall of fire.
O Maheśvarī, you wear a corpse, elephant skins, and human skin;
you have a tiger skin upon your breast, and you possess ash produced from charcoal.
O Maheśānī, the wise one should prepare a seat of shrouds from a corpse;
with great effort, he should clothe himself in a blue garment.
O Great Goddess, the most excellent practitioner should especially worship [it];
the wise one should enter the Kūrma-cakra at the mouth for the sake of all prosperity.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, the wise and pure man should then enter;
having especially purified the seat above, the wise man should sit upon it.
Having worshipped the seat, the wise one— possessing the support through the union with power (śakti)—
should take white mustard seeds and, being well-discerning, expel all obstacles.
In heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld, may all obstacles and Vināyakas vanish from this tortoise of mine by the command of Śiva.
Then, recollecting the mantra *phaṭ* for the weapon (*astra*), one should bestow the three *tāra*s (oṃs),
having placed the two hands upon the head in successive order.
Having meditated upon the Guru in the thousand-petaled lotus and having prostrated with deep reverence,
the wise one should then indicate the Guru’s sandals in that very place to the left of the Guru.
Having meditated upon Gaṇeśa to the right, one should prostrate for the pacification of obstacles;
one should prostrate before the goddess Chinnamastā and Vasundharā who face oneself.
The practitioner should perform *prāṇāyāma* while seated above the one who desires pleasure,
and then perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) for the seeker with the *Haṃsa* mantra.
Having diligently ejected the life-force from the head of the corpse with the syllable Oṃ,
one should burn the lifeless body with the forms of the seed-syllable of fire.
By that very seed-syllable of wind, those ashes should be reduced to nothingness;
by that same [syllable] in the form of a cloud, one should contemplate the dissolution therein.
Having meditated upon that very [deity] as a rain of nectar, one's body is rejuvenated,
assuming the previously described form of the deity, free from all impurities.
One should hold the *karakacchapikā* flower in the hand by means of the root-mantra;
thus, this purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) brings benefit to the worlds.
Having performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should practice the Mātṛkānyāsa;
one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the sixteen-syllable root mantra.
One may perform [the rite] through illusion (māyā) by means of numbers equal to the moon, the Vedas, and fire;
or, in all the sciences (vidyās), by means of the teeth of the science of transformation (vikāravidyā).
Then one should perform the mantra-installation (nyāsa), including the seers (ṛṣis) and other elements previously mentioned. Bhairava is the seer of these; by name, I am Krodhabhūpati.
The Samrāj meter and the deity Chinnamastā have been proclaimed;
the seed-syllable Māyā and Svāhā as the Śakti were taught by Padmayogin.
The application [of this mantra] is proclaimed for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
One should first utter the Praṇava (Om), followed by the letter Ā joined with the Bindu.
The mantra "khaḍgāya hṛdayāya svāhā" is joined with the youngest [vowel];
the letter *i* from the *praṇava*, O Goddess, is endowed with the moon-bindu (*candravindu*).
After saying "sukhadgāyata," one should say "śirase," and thereafter say "svāhā" joined with the sacred fingers (pavitrāṅguli).
The letter *ū* from the *praṇava*, with its head adorned by a bindu,
is joined with "Śrīvajrāya," and after that, [the word] "śikhāyai."
Then, O Goddess, one should place [the mantra] ending in "svāhā" upon the middle finger;
after that, having uttered the twelve-mora measure (mātrā), one should thereafter utter "apāsayat."
Then "Kavacāya" should be recited, and immediately after that, "Svāhā";
the Goddess, being composed, should place [the mantra] on the index finger during the rites of union.
The goddess [utters] the letter *au* from the *praṇava*, followed by "for the goad" (*aṅkuśāya*),
joined with "for the three eyes" (*netratrayāya*), and immediately thereafter, "svāhā."
Then, for the sake of excellent protection, one should place the Goddess upon the thumb, preceded by the Praṇava,
followed by the syllable *tryaḥ*, and joined with the *visarga*.
One should place [the mudrā] joined for the destruction of the Asuras upon both hands,
and [the mantras] at the heart, the head, the crest, the armor, and the two eyes.
One should assign [the mantras] in due order throughout the cardinal and intermediate directions, ending with that called the Weapon (astra).
Now follows the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
Then one should perform the sixfold mantra (ṣoḍhānyāsa), which brings the three worlds under control:
the venerable Vārāhī, Tripuṭā, Yoni, Prāsāda, and likewise Praṇava.
One should perform [the rites] sequentially with the goads (*aṅkuśa*) of the arts of desire (*kāmakalā*), the tufts (*kūrca*) as weapons,
and the sixteen syllables of the mantra, each consisting of eighteen letters.
One should place the letters of the Mātṛkā with these seed-syllables in their respective locations;
indeed, this is the nature of Brahman, proclaimed as the sixfold seed-syllables.
Indeed, by abandoning other [practices], they all become vajra-bodies;
endowed with all sovereign powers, they are liberated while living for ten years.
Now he describes its yantra.
Now I shall describe her mandala so that one may understand it as it truly is—
the great goddess who bestows initiation and is the impeller of all ritual actions.
One should first make the eastern petal white, the southeastern red,
the southern black, then yellow, then white, and finally black.
Then one should make it yellow, with a pericarp situated in its center;
there, in the middle of that, one should fashion a mandala of the fiercely radiant one (the Sun).
The lines of rajas, sattva, and tamas are red, white, and black respectively;
in their midst is the pair of māyās, accompanied by the syllable phaṭ.
One should construct the outer and inner circles provided with three gates;
first red, then yellow, white, and red, in due order.
It was provided with four gates and presided over by the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas).
Now it is said: Vairocanī, the Great Sovereign, is the King of Yantras.
First, there is a hexagon; in its center is a triangle.
Then one should offer the solar disc, and after that, a square;
then one should offer the terrestrial globe, and after that, another square.
Then the preceptor should provide an eight-petaled lotus according to its proper position;
after that, he should provide the lunar disc, and following that, the solar disc.

Then one should offer the terrestrial globe (bhūgola), and then three enclosures of the earth (bhūpura); one should place the thunderbolt (vajra) and the trident (śūla), and fix the corner-markers (koṇetaṅka) at the corners.
One should place the filaments and the stamens within the triangle according to the syllables of the mantra;
O messenger, one should meditate upon the auspicious goddess Vairocanī seated above Kāma.
I shall proclaim the great [teaching] spoken by Bhairava, the yantra that bestows prosperity.
First, a triangle should be drawn, and it should be surrounded by six corners.
Then one should offer the triple-image, which effects the transformation of the qualities;
one should construct three square enclosures (bhūpuras) provided with vajras and spikes.
Then, in a corner, the wise one should place the beautiful Ṭaṅka weapon;
he should draw the auspicious Kartṛkharparaka in its proper place.
One should meditate upon the goddess Rati, the auspicious Vairocanī, seated above Kama.
Then, immediately after the drawing of the yantra, the ritual placement of the arghya and other offerings should be performed.
And so it is said:
One should prepare the vessel for the respectful offering (arghya) and so forth, and one should perform the mandala before oneself.
Now he describes the worship of the seats (pīṭhapūjā).
Having invoked the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) and worshipped up to the ultimate reality (paratattva),
on that seat (pīṭha) reside Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Parājitā.
The powers Nityā, Vilāsinī, Ṣaṣṭhī, Dogdhī, Ghorā,
and Maṅgalā are to be worshipped in the cardinal directions and the center, according to the procedure for the sacred seat (pīṭha).
Then, having meditated upon the Goddess within the circle of one's own navel and worshipped her with mental offerings,

and having brought the flower and unbroken rice grains (akṣata) situated within the yoni-mudrā according to the prescribed method, and having meditated again and invoked her into the center of the yantra, one should worship her.
Now, meditation.
One should meditate on a pure, blossoming, and radiant lotus within one's own navel;
in the midst of its filaments is the mandala of the fiercely shining sun.
Resembling a hibiscus flower and similar to a red bandhūka blossom,
it is adorned with the lines of rajas, sattva, and tamas, and embellished by the circle of the womb (yonimaṇḍala).
One should meditate on Rati and Manobhava standing in the posture of inverted union;
and one should meditate on the enchanting Goddess Rati seated upon Kāma.
And in their midst was the Great Goddess, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
who held her own severed head in her left hand as Chinnamastā.
With her mouth wide open, terrifying, and licking with her fierce tongue,
she was drinking a stream of blood arising from her own throat.
Her mass of hair was disheveled and adorned with various flowers;
in her right hand she held a razor, and she was decorated with a garland of severed heads.
The goddess is sky-clad, most terrible, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture,
wearing a garland of bones, and having a serpent as her sacred thread.
Always sixteen years of age, with full and elevated breasts,
she is joined as a Ḍākinī and a Varṇinī through the union of the left and right.
One should meditate on Varṇinī on the right and Ḍākinī on the left side;
Varṇinī is red, gentle, with loose hair, and naked.
With hands joined in the left and right [positions],
holding a skull-bowl, they perform the drinking of the stream of blood gushing from the neck of the Goddess.
On the left side is the goddess Ḍākinī, who wears a garland of bones as her garment and a serpent as her sacred thread, resembling the blazing fire at the end of an aeon.
Her eyes flashed like streaks of lightning, her rows of teeth resembled a flight of cranes,
her face was formidable with fangs, and her breasts were full and elevated.
The Great Goddess, most terrible, with disheveled hair and naked,
pot-bellied, the Night of Doom, wearing a serpent as her sacred thread.
Licking her great tongue, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
she holds a skull-cup and a chopper in her left and right hands respectively.
She is exceedingly terrifying, drinking the stream of blood gushing from the goddess’s throat with a skull-cup held in her hand that is itself most fearsome.
The wise practitioner should meditate upon the Goddess as she is being consecrated by these two;
having thus meditated, one should worship the Goddess with humility through the yoga of devotion.
Then one should perform the external worship with flowers, food offerings, and incenses.
Now he speaks of the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
I shall declare the meditation taught by Bhairava, which bestows all prosperity:
one should properly meditate upon a white, fully blossomed lotus at one's own navel.
Having meditated upon Saṃkara as before— possessed of passion and pride—
one should meditate upon the captivating Goddess seated above Rati and Kāma.
In the midst of that [mandala], one should visualize the Great Goddess Chinnamastā, who resembles a cloud of the letter *ma*,
holding her own severed head in her left hand.
The Goddess has her mouth wide open, licking with her fierce tongue,
and drinking a stream of blood arising from her own throat.
Her mass of hair was disheveled, she was adorned with various flowers,
held a small knife in her right hand, and was decorated with a garland of severed heads.
A garland of fifty human heads is fashioned as a wreath,
beautifully captivating, with the locks of hair from each head interwoven with one another.
The goddess, naked and of magnificent form, stands in the pratyālīḍha posture,
wearing a garland of bones and having a serpent as her sacred thread.
Always sixteen years of age, with full and elevated breasts,
adorned with various armlets, serpent-girdles, and serpent-anklets.
Adorned with serpent-earrings and accompanied by eight serpents—
namely Ananta, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Karkoṭa, and Padmaka.
Mahāpadma and Śaṅkha are proclaimed as the two Kulikas; Ananta and Kulika, being variegated, are placed at the base of the ears.
Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla are Kṣatriyas of yellow complexion,
each resplendent with seven hundred and fifty fruit-like hoods.
The *nāgahārā* and *nāgakīcī*, arranged in their proper places—
these two are declared to be Takṣaka and Mahāpadma, the Vaiśyas.

The two [serpents] are blue in color, endowed with five hundred hoods, and complete with their limbs; this is described as the armlet (aṅgada) of the Goddess, which is captivating when joined by those two.
Padma and Karkoṭaka are declared to be Śūdras of red complexion;
they possess thirty hoods and are beautiful with anklets.
One should meditate with focused concentration on Chinnamastā held by those two,
accompanied on her left and right sides by Ḍākinī and Vaṇinī.
Having meditated on Varṇinī to the right, one should meditate on Ḍākinī on the left side of the deceased;
one should visualize Varṇinī as dark-complexioned, with loose hair and naked.
With her left and right hands joined, she holds a skull-cup and a knife;
the goddess places it to her right mouth and performs the drinking.
The goddess wears a garland of severed heads and has a snake as her sacred thread;
she is adorned with ornaments identical in form to those of the Goddess herself.
On the left side, however, is the Ḍākinī, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon,
arisen from lightning-fire, three-eyed, and exceedingly beautiful.
Adorned with a row of teeth resembling pomegranate seeds,
she possessed a formidable countenance and full, elevated breasts.
The great goddess with disheveled hair, most terrible, naked, with a protruding belly,
the Night of Doom, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
She has a tongue that lolls out and is adorned with a garland of severed heads;
she holds a skull-cup and a chisel in her hands, positioned on the left and right respectively.
She is performing the drinking of a stream of blood from the right arm of Vāmana;
she is exceedingly terrifying, holding a skull-cup in her hand that is itself most fearsome.
While practicing these two, one should meditate with the concentration of dhyāna-samādhi;
having thus meditated, one should worship the Goddess mentally through the yoga of devotion.
Then the preceptor should perform the external worship with food offerings, flowers, and incense;
he should diligently perform this meditation as taught by Bhairava.
It bestows all accomplishments and, as is witnessed, destroys even the greatest of sins.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, should remember [the Goddess] even during her worship, for that person the Goddess—who bestows desired objects—shall grant success;
she grants wealth, grain, sons, a wife, elephants, horses, and indeed everything else.
He shall obtain the great vidyā, the bestower of wealth, and attain the eight siddhis.
Alternatively, in the case of mantras, the seed-syllable and so forth are to be meditated upon according to their specific phonemes.
And so it is said:
That meditation which is performed with this very seed-syllable is called *dhyāna*.
One should meditate on her as dark-complexioned in the beginning of *kāma* and so forth, and likewise as red-complexioned in the beginning of *lajjā* and so forth.
In the case of illusion and the like, it would be black; in the case of speech and the like, it has the luster of lightning.
Then, having formed the *yoni-mudrā* and placed red sandalwood, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and hibiscus flowers in its center, one should meditate there once more.
Having assumed the *yonimudrā* and holding unbroken grains along with red flowers,
one should meditate upon the Goddess Mahāmāyā, the performer of all auspiciousness.
And on the island in the ocean of nectar, one should remember a wonderful garden;
on its shore, at the landing place, is a beautiful red pavilion.
It is endowed with four gates, adorned with rows of pillars,
possessed of ten apertures for the movement of air through its latticed windows, and provided with filaments.
One should visualize four *kalpa* trees spread out, resting upon a bed of nectar and supported by pillars of jewels, and there one should meditate upon one's own tutelary deity.
One should meditate upon her seated on a corpse, with severed hair,
large-bellied, four-armed, mounted upon a corpse, clad in red garments, and three-eyed.
Adorned with a magnificent crown, she holds a sword in her right hand;
with her two other hands, she holds a lotus and a book.
Having severed their own heads with swords, they drink much blood;
she has the splendor of the rising sun and wears the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
She who is constantly served by yogins and who wears a serpent as a sacred thread.
Now, the mantra for invocation (āvāhana) is as follows:
And there, the practitioner, the best of adepts, should first utter the invocation with this mantra: "O bestower of all accomplishments! (sarvasiddhiprade).
Then the word "varṇanīye" (to be described) should be uttered; then "sarvasiddhiprade" (bestower of all accomplishments);
then the word "ḍākinīya" should be uttered; and after that, the name of the goddess.
Then one should utter "Ehi ehi" (Come, come), and immediately after that, "Mahā" (Great).
Then, one should utter "Tiṣṭha tiṣṭha" (Stay, stay), followed by the pair of Māyās (Hrīṃ Hrīṃ).
Combined with the syllable *phaṭ* and followed by *svāhā*—
this is declared to be the invocation (*āvāhana*), together with the ritual of installation (*sthāpana*).
Now, he states the specific mantra for the offering of a seat.
Then the practitioner, having performed the invocation, should offer a seat with this mantra:
first uttering the Praṇava, followed by "O bestower of all accomplishments."
Then one should speak the name to be described; thereafter, one should utter the *praṇava*.
Then one should speak "Ḍākinī," and thereafter, one should utter the *praṇava* again.
In this rite, one should recite "iha śabda asti tiṣṭha tiṣṭhāmi phaṭ svāhā" ten million times;
then, having meditated, one should worship the goddess who is youthful and moon-like in form.
Now, he describes the worship.
Having worshipped the Maṇḍala with the root mantra, O Great Goddess,
one should then worship it with ritual offerings and with red flowers.
Having taken her younger sister, one should worship Aṅgadevā;
then, likewise, one should worship Varṇinī residing in the southern region.
From the *praṇava* [oṃ], one should worship the seed-syllable of Sarasvatī according to its name and nature;
thereafter, a person should worship the Ḍākinī situated on the left side.
As before, beginning with the syllable *praṇava*, one should likewise say "Salutation to Ḍākinī."
First, one should worship in the triangle, ending with "phaṭ," using the armor-mantra (kavaca),
[worshipping] Kālikā, Bhuvaneśī, and Mātaṅgī according to their respective positions, O Lord.
Thereafter, in the subsequent petals starting from the north and proceeding in order,
[one should worship] Kāmākhyā, Bheruṇḍā, and likewise Nīlasarasvatī.
One should worship with the seed-syllable *māyā* using extensive displays of great magnificence;
one should worship the god Bhairava before oneself according to the method taught by the sage.
The wise practitioner should worship Samrāt-chanda in the south, the mantra-syllables likewise in the north, and the seed-syllable and power (bīja-śakti) in the direction of the Rakṣas, in due order.
The Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, who bestow all accomplishments, are situated in the center of the lotus;
likewise, the world-protectors beginning with Indra and ending with [Vaiśravaṇa] are to be worshipped, together with their weapons.
One should worship them in the Bhūpura (the outer square) according to the sequence starting from the east;
one should worship Rudra upon the pedestal and Manohara all around it.
The best of practitioners should worship at the four gates, starting from the east;
above each gate he should worship Mahālakṣmī, and in front of them, Brahmā.
Furthermore, one should worship Kṣetrapāla, Karāla,
and Vikarāla with [mantras] beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, using the dative case for the name.
Let what was previously stated stand; now he states another internal [distinction] regarding the reverse order (*pratiloma*).
p.
181a) Beginning with the outer enclosure, one should perform worship in reverse order;
one should worship the vajras and other [emblems] in the outer regions of the square enclosure.
In the interval between those, one should worship the King of the Gods and others at the gates;
and within the gates, Karāla, Vikarāla, Atikāla, and Mahākālaka.
And Ekaliṅgā, Yoginī, Ḍākinī, Bhairavajendrākṣī, Asitāṅgī, and Saṃhāriṇī.
One should worship the six limbs in the six corners; in the triangle, one should worship Chinnamastakā, Ḍākinī, Varṇinī, Tārā, and Vāgīśvarī on her two sides.
In this manner, the worship should be performed; thereafter, one should proceed with the offering of the bali-oblation.

Then, first having worshipped the vajras and so forth on the exterior of the *bhūpura*, as well as the moon and other [deities] above, one should worship the gatekeepers in order, starting from the east.
Karāla and Vikarāla are at the eastern gate; Atikāla and Mahākāla are likewise at the western and northern gates respectively.
One should perform their worship beginning with the syllable Om (praṇava) and ending with "namaḥ."
Now, he describes their meditative absorption (dhyāna).
Karāla is red in color, two-armed, and situated on an island;
and in the west is Vikarāla, resembling a blue lotus.
One should meditate on him who holds a goad and a book in his left hands, whose complexion is like the hibiscus flower,
who is mounted upon Garuḍa, possesses a massive body, has three eyes, and bears the crescent moon upon his crest.
Likewise, Mahākāla is likewise two-armed and clad in yellow garments.
Then, on the eight petals in order starting from the east, the Bhairavīs, beginning with Ekaligā, are to be worshipped.
O you of excellent vows, [worship] Ekaliṅgā, Mahādevī, Ḍākinī, Yoginī,
and likewise Bhairavī preceded by "Mahā," and then Bhairavī.
Indrāṣī, Masitāṅgī, and then Saṃhāriṇī are to be worshipped in sequence on the petals starting from the east, according to the proper order of the Śaktis.
Beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, joined with the seed-syllable of *lajjā*.
Now he explains meditation according to its sequence.
I shall describe again the sequence: the red, the fair-complexioned, likewise the black, the red, and the tawny; the yellow, the pearl-white, and the smoke-colored.
She holds a trident and the gesture of granting boons, is clothed in a tiger skin,
possesses three eyes, has slender limbs, and wears a serpent as her sacred thread.
The second [form] is Sundarālokā, holding a staff and a conch in her hands,
clothed in red garments, and wearing a red serpent as a sacred thread.
The goddess wears a garland of bones, sits in the bound lotus posture,
possesses a third eye, has a terrifying form, a lolling tongue, and a large belly.
Holding a skull as a weapon in her hand, wearing a black serpent as a sacred thread,
possessing terrible fangs, most formidable, intoxicated with pride, and exceedingly cruel.
The fourth [form] has the luster of fire, is adorned with a garland of severed heads,
holds a skull-cup and a chisel in her hands, and is equipped with a sword and a trident.
She has a mass of hair that is tawny-brown, she possesses a fierce and loud "aṭṭāṭṭa" laughter,
she is the fifth [form], has the luster of the rising sun, possesses six arms, and likewise stands upon two feet.
She has three faces, is most formidable, and her faces are red, yellow, and blue;
she holds a skull-cup and a chisel in her hands, and is endowed with a sword and a trident.
Having brought the Goddess— who possesses a mass of matted hair and a half-moon, who has three eyes in each face,
and who dwells upon a corpse— she took her place in her station.
She was clothed in a leopard skin and equipped with the hero’s bell.
She possesses a golden luster like that of refined gold, radiant with a thousand eyes,
her hands busily holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus— she who is enchanting to the mind.
Seated upon a lotus, established in the lotus posture,
wearing yellow garments, with smooth eyes and a most beautiful form.
And I shall describe the eighth [form], who resembles a dark rain-cloud,
the three-eyed goddess Ḍākinī, the bringer of destruction.
One should always meditate upon the Goddess, the mother of the three worlds, who is united with her own consort;
one should worship her according to the prescribed rites in due order, from the east to the northeast.
Now follows the offering of food.
Having thus performed the worship, one should then arrange the offering of the bali;
one should give as the bali milk-rice and rice mixed with sesame and honey.
O Goddess, a vessel filled with honey as well as a *raṃbhā* flower [is offered],
and at intervals within, the gift of a beast (*paśu*) is prescribed.
Having thoroughly honored [the deity] with offerings, incense, flowers, and prostrations in the east,
one should then display the *dhenumudrā* and touch [it] with the thumb of the left hand.
Having performed the purification with the mantra "Yaṃ," one should then place [the substance] within the mantra;
one should contemplate it as nectar with the mantra "Ṭhaṃ" and flood it with the mantra "Vaṃ."
One should recite the mantra twenty-four times; one should offer the root mantra ending in the syllable *ṅ*.
Having displayed it before [the deity], one should then perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) once more.
Now, the mantra for the offering of food.
One should utter the word "saṃbuddhyamāna," then the words "dehi" and "ehi";
thereafter one should say "gṛhṇa gṛhṇa imam," followed by the word "bali."
Having uttered the word "mama," one should say the two words "siddhiṃ dehi";
then, having spoken the two words for the armor (kavaca), one should thereafter utter the word "karālike."
The great mantra ending with "phaṭ svāhā" is prescribed for the ritual offering of the bali oblation.
O Maheśvarī, the practitioner of mantra should perform the recitation one hundred and eight times or even a thousand times, according to the prescribed rule, beginning with the *kulluka* mantra.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should offer praise and place the rosary upon one's head;
having thus completed the recitation and worship, and having offered praise, one should recite the armor (kavaca) mantra.
Therein, first of all, the mantra of Krodhabhairava should be recited.
And likewise:
Having first recited the mantra of Bhairava, one should then recite the mantra of this Wrathful One;
having taken up a garland of bones, one should recite the Vajra-Vairocanī mantra.
Now he states the mantra of Krodhabhairava.
Now I shall declare the Krodha-mantra, by which even the impossible is accomplished.
Having taken the Hālāhala seed-syllable, thereafter follows the Krodha seed-syllable.
Having addressed the terrifying ocean that stands upon blood with its darkened limbs,
and having addressed the great flame of the fire of universal dissolution, one should extract the mantra.
When thus uttered, the Wrathful One becomes spontaneously accomplished.
Now follows the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
Then, with the Krodha-mantra, one should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa). One should place Viṣa, Vajra, Yuta, Bodhi, and Mahākāla within the heart.
One should place the pair Viṣaṃhana and Yuga, as well as Vajra and Kūrcādi, on the exterior;
one should place Hālāhala together with Deha on the body, and Vajrakāla on the crest-lock (śikhā).
One should place the weapon-vajra joined with the *viṣa* mantra as armor;
one should place the weapon-vajra joined with the *tāra* seed-syllable as armor.
The Vajra for Mahākāla is joined with the seed-syllable *tāra* (OM) at the two eyes;
it takes up "viṣaṃ hanaya" and is followed by the words "gṛhya daha gṛhya."

Likewise, one should employ Krodhavajra and Yuga for all malevolent beings; furthermore, there are the six limbs ending with the binding of the directions: *talomāraya*, armor (*varma*), and the weapon (*astra*).
Now he explains meditation (dhyāna).
There, in the center, one should place Bhīma, who is filled with glowing flames,
laughing with a loud roar, most terrible, and resembling crushed collyrium.
Standing in the pratyālīḍha posture, with four arms,
holding a discus in the right hand and making the threatening gesture (tarjanī) with the left, his face is made terrifying by sharp fangs.
Wearing a crown of skulls as a jewel, the leader of the three worlds,
resembling ten million suns, and adorned by eight nāgas.
The Aparājita Padākrānta mudrā is formed by joining the two ring fingers and curling the two index fingers,
while the little fingers are extended.
The little finger, the middle finger, and the thumb [of the right hand] should be placed respectively against the [corresponding fingers of the left];
this glorious holder of the mudrā is the accomplisher of that which is to be accomplished in the three worlds.
Now follows the praise.
Having thus performed the ritual of worship according to one's ability,
One should recite this hymn for the sake of accomplishing one's desired aims.
At the navel is a pure lotus, shining with a bandhūka flower as red as merit;
its interior is a radiant solar orb, which is the great yoni-cakra.
In their midst is the reverse union of Parapradyumna and his beloved;
behind them stands Śivā, whose radiant form shines with the splendor of ten million rising suns.
In her left hand she holds a severed head, and in her upper right hand a large knife;
she stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, with the quarters of the sky as her garment, and her hair disheveled and entwined with snakes.
She drinks the gushing stream of blood from her own severed head, and she shines, illuminated by three eyes that gleam with a brilliance equal to the rising sun.

To her left is her own power (ātma-śakti), of fierce form and red complexion, with reddish hair, naked, and wearing bone ornaments; she is drinking deeply from many streams of blood flowing from the channels [of the victim] with the lotus-hand of her hand shimmering with a chopper (kartṛkā). She stands in the fierce pratyālīḍha posture.
The Yoginī with reddened feet and eyes, performing the yoga-mudrā.
Clad in the directions as her garment, with disheveled hair, possessing a form as terrible as a mass of clouds at the time of universal dissolution, she is fierce;
her mouth and the cavity of her belly are difficult to behold due to her fangs, and she is formidable with the blazing luster of her flickering tongue darting out from within.
With tongues flickering like lightning and fierce radiance.
[He beheld] his own form as a Ḍākinī, whose pair of eyes flicker like lightning, who is terrifying with the serpent coiling upon the slope of her heart,
and who nourishes herself with the blood flowing from her own neck, which she has just severed.
I entered daily that city which is the very form of consciousness, whose lotus feet are placed upon the heads of Brahmā, Īśāna, Acyuta,
and others, and which is meditated upon by the foremost of yogis who have received the command of the Self.

With my mind, I meditate upon Chinnamastā, who is the essence of saṃsāra, the mother of the three worlds, the most praiseworthy, the one who bestows desired fruits even at the end of life, and the remover of the impurities of the Kali age.
He assumes a threefold form to effect the creation, maintenance, and destruction [of the world];
because the universe arises from his three qualities (guṇas), he is Brahmā, Acyuta, and Bhūmabhṛt.
I remember the primordial nature (prakṛti), beginning with Māyā, which is all-pervading for the sake of accomplishing every purpose;
the pair of whose lotus feet the virtuous always worship.
I am one who delights in the yoga-worship of wine, meat, and women; I am one honored by the undertaking of various kula-observances.
I am Bhairavī, withdrawn from the state of ordinary beings;
I abide as the one devoted to the feet of the Guru; I am Bhairava; I am Śiva.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, should recite this hymn of great merit spoken by Brahmā in the past— whether in the presence of the Goddess or otherwise.
O Goddess, his success shall be granted by you, bestowing his desired objects—
whether wealth, grain, a son, a wife, a horse, or even an elephant.
One will certainly obtain the eight accomplishments (siddhis), including the great vidyā of Vasundharā.
Thus ends the hymn to the Goddess as proclaimed by Bhairava.
Now, the armor.
Bhairavī said:
This primordial Vidyā of Chinnamastā, which is most secret, was spoken by you, the Lord Jīva; it was heard by me and has now been related by me.
Now I wish to hear the armor previously mentioned;
O Lord, please tell me out of compassion that which is named Trailokyavijaya.
Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess of gods, who are saluted by all the deities; I shall declare the armor known as Trailokyavijaya, which deludes the entire universe.
Consisting of all vidyās, it directly bestows victory upon gods and asuras;
by wearing or reciting it, the Lord becomes a conqueror of the three worlds.
O Queen of the Gods, because of its retention and recitation, Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Rudra become the creator, the protector, and the destroyer of the worlds.
It should not be given to the disciples of others, and especially not to those who lack devotion;
it should be given to a devoted disciple who is dearer to one than even one's own life.
For the armor (kavaca) of the Goddess Chinnamastā,
Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), Samrāṭ and Virāṭ are the meters (chandas), and Chinnamastakā is the deity (devatā).
The application for liberation through Trailokyavijaya has been proclaimed.
May the syllable HŪM, possessing the splendor of Chinnamastā, protect my head.
May the three-syllabled mantra *hrīṃ hūṃ aiṃ*, clad in red garments and other colors, protect the forehead;
may she who bears a severed head and a sword, *śrīṃ hrīṃ hūṃ aiṃ*, protect the eyes.
May that Vidyā, beginning and ending with the Praṇava, protect the pair of Śrutis forever:
*vajra vairocanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, preceded by the Dhruva.
May Chinnamastā, who holds her own severed head and a sword, protect the nose;
[the seed-syllables] Śrī, Māyā, Kūrca, Vāg-bīja, Vajra, Vairocanīya, and Hūṃ.
"HŪM PHAṬ SVĀHĀ! The sixteen-syllable Great Vidyā, whose form is Brahman—having sprinkled water with this mantra upon the entrance itself, [one should place it] on the right and left sides."
Above and below, at the ends of the three stars, from the seed-syllable consisting of the first letter of one's own name,
one should [place] Gaṇeśa, Kṣetrapāla, and likewise Dvāraśrī again.
Having also worshipped the threshold, one should enter the sacrificial hall.

In the directions starting from the southeast (Āgneyī) and so forth, in the middle, one should worship Gaṇapati and the others in their proper order, preceded by the three-syllabled mantra and their respective seed-syllables.
Having worshipped the four— Gaṇeśa, Durgā, Vaṭuka, and Kṣetrapāla— as well as the jeweled pavilion together with Kāma and Rati.
O Goddess, having first worshipped Sarasvatī together with Vasantaprīti,
and afterwards Śrī, one should scatter handfuls of flowers.
Alternatively, having worshipped the ten Śaktis in the ten directions, one should worship Vāgīśvarī in the center, offer a handful of flowers, and then worship Dīpanātha.
Then Sarasvatī, Śrī, Māyā, and Durgā;
likewise Bhadrakālī, Svastī, Svāhā, and Śubhaṃkarī.
And Gaurī, the Sustainer of the World, as well as Vāgīśvarī;
together with the twelve red Śaktis, [he worships] Dīpanātha.
The conjunction of the three stars (tritārayoga) should be understood everywhere by the most excellent practitioners;
other matters should be performed by the most excellent practitioners according to the general procedure.
Having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should perform the deposition of the Mātṛkās;
having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should perform the other depositions.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the supreme nyāsa of Śrīvidyā.
Now, first, the ritual placement of the seers and so forth (ṛṣyādinyāsa).
O Maheśānī, its seer is the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
Paṅkti is declared to be the metre, and the goddess Tripurasundarī is the deity.
The seed-syllable is said to be Vāgbhava, while Śakti is the Śaktikūṭa;
Kāmarāja shall be the Kīlaka—this is declared as the Ṛṣyādinyāsa.
Now follows the ritual assignment of the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa).
The seed-syllables *aṃ*, *āṃ*, and *sauḥ* are declared to be the various supreme mantras;
having repeated this seed-syllable twice, [one should place them] on the middle and the other fingers.
One should perform the purification of the hands, the palms, and the backs of the hands as well,
using the four mantras joined with the word "namas," each separately.
The middle finger, the ring finger, the little finger, the thumb, and the index finger— O Maheśvarī, these are the names of the fingers explained in their respective order.
Now, he describes self-protection or the binding of the directions.
O Tripurasundarī, having first recited the Vālī seed-mantra three times,
one should perform protection by touching the heart while saying, "Protect me, protect me!"
In the same manner, one should then perform the binding of the directions using the weapon-mantra and the mudrā.
Now follows the placement of the seats (āsana-nyāsa).
Then, the mantra preceded by the word "amṛtārṇava" is for the seat; thereafter, one should place the mantra ending with "bālā" at the feet of Tripureśvarī.
One should place the knees upon the lotus-seat of one's own self, saying "namas."
Having joined *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ* with the word *Tripure*, one should then [join] the word *Sundarī*;
ending in the feminine suffix *ṅī*, it is placed upon the seat of the Goddess, and at the end, one should install the two "maddu" syllables.
Haiṃ Hvrīṃ Hsauḥ Teṃ, and [the mantra] Tripuravāsinī.
With this [mantra], "cakrāsana," one should place [the hands] upon the two buttocks.

*hyai& hstrī& hstrau&* [repeated] ... at the end of *sarvamantrāsanāya*, one should duly place "namo guhya". Then, after *hrīṃ klīṃ tripuramālinyai*, one should utter the word for the target (*sādhya*).
Then, one should place the perfected seat (siddhāsana), ending with "ṅeṃ," in the region of the navel;
thereafter, the mantra "hsraiṃ hśrīṃ hsrauṃ" and the word "Tripurāmbā."

One should place [the mantra] on the chest: "Salutation to the one seated upon the throne of the Śakti-pīṭha in the form of a couch (paryaṅka)," followed by the seed-syllables of the three-peaked Vidyā and the name Mahātripurabhairavī.
One should install Sadāśiva Mahāpreta at the location of the Brahma-randhra with the mantra: "Obeisance to him who is seated upon a lotus."
Now follows the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
Omniscience, eternal perfect satisfaction, beginningless awakening, and autonomy;
imperishability, power, and infinity—these are the six auspicious attributes of Śiva and Śivā, beginning with Śiva himself.
Having joined the name at the end of the seed-syllable, together with the caste-designation and the six marks.
One should contemplate the complete Vidyā in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), possessing a reddish luster;
one should remember it as having sixteen syllables, dripping nectar, and bestowing great good fortune.
Then, O Dear One, one should cause Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī to revolve on the region of the left side;
thereafter, one should place the Viśvajihvāgrahaṃ mudrā from the feet up to the root with the mantra.
Having meditated thus, "I am the creator of the three worlds," one should place the *kīlaka*;
one should place it in its entirety within the mouth as a surrounding encirclement.
Again, one should place the full [mantra] on the face and half on the throat; again, with the full mantra, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-vinyāsa) upon the body.
Having placed the *yonimudrā* upon the mouth at the end of the pervasive [assignment] and having offered praise,
this placement (*nyāsa*), which is the perfect form of Śrīvidyā, increases good fortune.
Having donned his armor, he shook the three worlds with his battle-ready form.
Now, the staff mudrā (daṇḍinīmudrā).
Holding a fist while moving about with the index finger extended like a staff, the practitioner of mantra then becomes known as Saubhāgyadaṇḍinī; she punishes enemies in an instant.
Now, the seizing of the enemy's tongue.
One should place the thumb within the fist; this becomes the "seizing of the enemy's tongue" (ripujihvāgraha).
Now, as for the *yonimudrā*: [it is] as follows.
O Goddess of the Gods, having joined the hands, one should worship with the index finger and the ring finger;
likewise, having joined them with the left hand, one should arrange them in the shape of a womb (yoni).
O beloved, one should rotate the ring fingers around the head.
Now follows the Saṃmohana Nyāsa.
One should conquer the Goddess at the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) and then place her at the base of the jewel (maṇibandha);
the wise one should form a garland on the forehead and meditate upon the sixteen syllables.
Meditating on the three worlds as crimson, one should recall Śrīvidyā in the mind;
O Goddess of the Gods, this installation called Sammohana is the cause of agitation.
Now follows the ritual placement of reabsorption (saṃhāranyāsa).
On the two feet, the two calves, the two knees,
the two elbows, the back, the navel, both sides, the two breasts, and likewise the two shoulders.
Pārvatī [placed] the *andhūs* on the two ears, the *brahmaraṃdhra*, and the face;
thereafter, she placed them in the region of the hands in sequence, encircling the human body.
This great assignment (mahānyāsa) is the withdrawal [mantra] performed sequentially with the sixteen seed-syllables;
by means of these sixteen-syllable assignments of Śrīvidyā, one becomes the Lord of the Universe.
O Dear One, for the purpose of emanation, one should install the Goddess Mātṛkā as before.
Now follows the placement of the Vasinyādi [mantras].
The Mātṛkā-syllable is her own essential form, endowed with eight phonemes;
she is the Veśinī who possesses the Mātṛkās and is endowed with eight seed-syllables.
O Dear One, one should write the seed-syllable at the end of the vowels, conjoined with the letter *pha* which is at the end of the fire-group (the *ra*-series),
enriched by the beauty of the left ear (*u*), and marked with the bindu and nāda.
O Goddess of excellent vows, one who has entered [the ritual space] should worship the deity of speech;
O Maheśānī, at the end of the braid [of hair], one should worship Kāmeśī, the supreme seed-syllable.
Having uttered "Merubhṛtam," one should then worship Vāgdevī;
at the end of the *ca*-group [of consonants], there is the syllable *dhvāṃ* (dhva), followed by *ra*, *āṃ*, and *takṣamāturya* accompanied by a vowel.
Thereafter, one should worship Mādinī, the deity of speech;
O Maheśvarī, at the end of the Ṭa-group is the seed-syllable of Vāyu situated upon the earth.
The first syllable consists of the moon (i) and the bindu (m) on the left ear, followed by Vimalā, the Mistress of Speech;
at the end of that group of consonants (ta-varga), there is Yamakṣmā (ya), adorned with the left eye (ī).
One should worship the seed-syllable (bīja) marked by the bindu and nāda with the mantra of Vāgdevī;
it is joined at the end of the 'pa' group with Vyoman (ha), Candra (sa), Kṣyāta (la), Jāni (ra), and Anila (ya).
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should worship Jayantī, the deity of speech, who is conjoined with the vowel *ū*, and whose nature consists of the *bindu*, the *nāda*, and the *kalā*.

One should worship Sarveśī, who is at the end of the class [of consonants], joined with the letter 'ra' at the time of dissolution, endowed with the left ear (the letter 'ya') and the moon-bindu (the nasal 'm').
One should worship Kaulinī Vāk, who is the sun situated within the fire, encircled by the seed-syllable, and pervaded by the Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā.
For the accomplishment of all aims, one should place the Great Goddess at the end of the *śa*-group [the letter *kṣa*] upon the head,
the forehead, between the eyebrows, the ears, the heart, and the region of the navel.
O Dear One, one should install the goddess Parā as far as the foundational body (ādhāradehaka).
Now follows the sixfold deposition (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
Then one should perform the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa), by which [the practitioner] becomes the upholder of the form of the universe;
there is no doubt that Śiva himself, whose nature is the Virāṭ and whose essence is the phonemes, is directly present.
Gaṇeśa is the first assignment (nyāsa), the destroyer of all obstacles;
he resembles the rising sun, has the face of an elephant, and possesses three eyes.
O Dear One, one should place these goddesses, endowed with nooses, goads, gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and spears, according to the Mātṛkā-nyāsa.
Vighneśvara is endowed with glory (śrī), Vighnanātha is possessed of modesty (hrī),
Vināyaka is likewise contentment (tuṣṭi), and Śivottama is joined with peace (śānti).
Vighnahṛt is joined with Puṣṭi, and Sarasvatī is the creator of obstacles;
Vighnarāja is joined with Rati, as are Medhā and Gaṇanāyaka.
Ekadanta, Cakrānti, Dvidanta, Kāminīpati,
Gajavaktra, Mohanī, Nirañjana, and likewise Jaṭā.
Likewise, O beloved, Kaparddhabhṛt, Tīvrā, and Dīrghavaktra;
then Jvālinī, followed by Nandā and Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Vṛṣadhvaja and Surasā were joined with Gaṇanātha;
Kāmarūpānikā was followed by Gajendra together with Guha.
Śūpakarṇa is joined with Japinī; Trinetra is united with Satyā; Lambodara is with Vighneśī; and Mahānāda is with Svarūpiṇī.
Then there are Caturmūrti, Kāmadā, and Sadāśivayutā; likewise Madavihvalā, Mahānāda, Āmoda, and Vijayā.
Durmukha, as well as Ghūrṇā, Sumukhā, Bhūmidā, and likewise Pramoda, Bhūmi, Ekapāda, and Satī.
Dvijihva joined with Ramā, Śūla joined with Dhvajinī,
Vīra joined with Karṇa, and the Śailas joined with Makaradhvaja.
Then Ṣaṇmukha, Vikarṇa, Varada, and likewise Bhrūkuṭī; then Vāmadeva, Lajjā, and after that Vakratuṇḍa.
Afterwards, there are Dīrghaghoṇa, Anvita, Dviraṇḍaka, and Dhanurdhara;
joined by Senānī and Yāminī, and accompanied by Grāmiṇī and Rātri.
Tamas accompanied by Candrikā, Vimala joined with Śaśin,
Mattavāhana with Lolā, and Jaṭī with Capalākṣiṇī.
Muṇḍī is endowed with supernatural powers (ṛddhi), and Khaḍgī is thereafter joined with Śubhagā;
Vareṇya and Garbhā are likewise situated upon Vṛṣaka, as is Śivā.
Bhaktapriya and Satvadā, Meghanāda and Cakāriṇī, Gajeśa and Kālakubjā, Gaṇeśa and Vighnahāriṇī.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the goddess with the letters of the Mātṛkā; thereafter, the placement of the planets (grahanyāsa) occurs:
red, white, likewise red, dark-blue, yellow, and pale-white.

One should contemplate [the deities] as smoky, black, and likewise smoky, or reddish-smoky; they are the foremost among those headed by Ravi, capable of assuming any form at will, and adorned with all ornaments.

One should assign the Sun to the heart with the vowels; then Saturn to the navel with the *ya*-group; Mars to the center of the earth with the *ka*-group; and one should assign [the other planets] to the eyes three by three.
The wise one, having placed Jupiter with the *ca*-group on the belly,
should place Venus with the *ta*-group on the throat.
O fair-faced one, one should place Saturn at the navel with the *pa*-group, Rāhu in the mouth from the *i*-group,
and Ketu in the anus with the two *la*s.
Then one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the hosts of constellations, which bestows happiness;
they resemble the blazing fire of time (kālāgni) and are adorned with all ornaments.
Mati, Pāṇi, and Aśvinī are the foremost, granting boons with hands held in fear;
likewise, Rohiṇī is joined by pairs, pairs, pairs, and pairs.
One [mark] is thus, and likewise two [marks] are said to have the luster of a single flower;
they are located on the forehead, the two eyes, and subsequently on the left and right ears.
O Goddess of gods, one should likewise place [the seed-syllable] on the non-dual [place] and then sequentially on the throat;
having placed that which has the luster of a flower, one should place the one named "phlegm" (śleṣman) with the two birds (khaga).
Dakṣa is on the shoulder; Maghā is on the second shoulder;
and Pūrvaphalgunī is situated on the right elbow.
O Dear One, one should place the constellation Uttarā-phalgunī on the left elbow;
the hand, situated in the syllables Ū and Ña, is placed upon the right wrist.
O Dear One, one should place Citra, Aṣāḍhā, Parā, and Ātmā at Maṇibandha;
likewise, Svātī and Viśākhā reside at the end of the letter Ḍa and the letter Sa respectively.
O Goddess Pārvatī, one should place Ta, Tha, Da, and Dha, along with Anurādhā, in order upon the two breasts on the right and left; likewise, one should place them at the navel.
O Dear One, one should place Jyeṣṭhā, joined with the syllable *dhakāra*, on the right hip;
likewise, O Dear One, one should place Mūlā, consisting of *na-pa-pha-dya*, on the left hip.
Then one should place Pūrvāṣāḍhā on the right thigh with the syllable *va*,
and immediately thereafter, Uttarāṣāḍhā on the left thigh with the syllable *bha*.
One should place Śravaṇā, conjoined with the letter *ma*, on the right knee;
and one should place Dhaniṣṭhā, situated beyond it, on the left knee.
O Dear One, with the letter *la*, one should install the Great Goddess Śatabhiṣā;
thereafter, one installs Pūrvabhādrapadā, which resides in the right calf.
One should place the syllable *va* on the left calf in sequence;
likewise, one should place the syllable *ṣa-sa-ha* on the right foot, corresponding to the constellation Bhādrapadā.
O Dear One, [one should worship] Revatī with the two syllables *rakṣā* (ra-kṣa), along with the bindu and visarga; likewise,
[one should worship] Revatī with the letter *kṣa*, followed by the bindu and visarga.
Having placed [the hand] upon the left foot, one should perform the Yoginī-nyāsa;
one should contemplate the eyebrows as white, black, and red, and the [other parts] as variegated and yellow.
Having four arms, with symmetrical faces, and adorned with all ornaments;
having uttered the two seed-syllables "Ḍāṃ" and "Ḍīṃ," one should choose the ḍamaru, O Dear One.

In the left ear, one should say "endowed with the moon and the sound" (vāmakarṇendu-nādāḍhya), followed by "homage to Ḍākinī" (ḍākinīṃ namaḥ); at the end of one's own name, the two words "protect" (rakṣa) should be uttered at the conclusion.
O Dear One, one should place [the syllable] for the self of the skin in the region of the throat within the Viśuddha [cakra];
and one should place Ākinī with the letters beginning with *ka* and the single letters beginning with *ra*, respectively.
As before, one should deposit the blood-nature together with the seed-syllables;
thereafter, one should deposit the Anāhata [cakra] with the letters beginning with *da* and ending with *pha*.
Likewise, the goddess Rākinī is in the maṇipūraka cakra;
and Kākinī, with excellent colors, is likewise designated in the svādhiṣṭhāna.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, one should place Mada in the form of her own nature, and with six syllables,
place Kiṅkiṇī in the form of bone at the mūlādhāra.
O Maheśānī, one should worship the white Hākinī with the syllables *hakṣa* and *va*;
this is the sequence of Nyāsa for the Yoginīs in the Brahma-randhra.
Then one should perform the placement of the zodiac signs (*rāśinyāsa*), which always provides complete protection:
one should place those that are red, white, green, pale yellow, variegated, and black.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should assign the four letters beginning with 'a'— namely *piśaṅga*, *piṅgala*, *babhru*, and *varvara*— to the states of smoke (*dhūmatāṃ*).
One should place a ram on the right ankle; then, by means of a pair, a bull at the knees;
and then a couple upon the testicles.
With two [dots] one forms a crab in the belly; with two, a lion on the shoulders;
and with the anusvāra, the visarga, and the *śa*-group, one forms a maiden (*kanyā*).
O you who are praised by heroes, one should place [the letters] with the *śa*-group on the right side of the head;
likewise, one should place the balance-scale with the *ka*-group on the left side of the head.
Likewise, O beloved, one should place Vṛścika in the shoulder with the *ca*-group;
and likewise, O beloved, one should place Dhanvin at the joint with the *ṭa*-group.
One should lovingly place the letter *ma* along with its group upon the testicles;
likewise, one should place the letter *pa* along with its group upon the left knee.
One should place the sign of Pisces with the group beginning with 'va' and the letter 'kṣa' at the ankle, which corresponds to Libra.
Then, O Goddess praised by the gods, one should install the seats according to the prescribed rite;
they are white, black, red, and dark-blue in sequence.
Furthermore, for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals, the wise man should repeatedly and in due order meditate upon the goddess and the fifty rows of sacred seats (pīṭhas).
Kāmarūpa is a great pīṭha, and then Vārāṇasī;
likewise Nepāla is a pīṭha, as well as Pauṇḍravardhana.
First is Puraḥsthita, then likewise Āpīṭha;
after that Carasthita, then the great pīṭha Pūrṇaśaila, and after that Narvuda.
Next is the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Āmrāṭakeśvara and then Ekāgra;
thereafter is the stainless Tisrota-pīṭha, and beyond that is Kāmakoṭi.
Kailāśa, Bhṛgupīṭha, Kedāra, Candrapūraka, Śrīpīṭha, and likewise Oṃkāra; after that, Jālandhara.
And likewise the Mālava-pīṭha, Kulānta, Devakoṭaka,
the great pīṭha Gokarṇa, and also Māruteśvara.
Aṭṭahāsa, Viraja, Pīṭha, and likewise Rājagṛha;
Mahāpīṭha, Kollagiri, and after that Melāpura.
Koleśvara is a great pīṭha; Jayantikā is a great pīṭha;
likewise Arjunī is a pīṭha, as is the wonderful one named Kṣīrikā.
Hastināpura-pīṭha, Uḍḍīśa, Prayāgaka,
Ṣaṣṭhīśa, as well as the pīṭha of Māyāpura and Jaleśvara.
Malaya, the great pīṭha Śrīśaila, Meru and Kaṅgiri,
Mahendra, Vāmana, and Hiraṇyapura as well.
The seat consisting of Mahālakṣmī is Oḍḍīyāna; beyond that is the supreme seat of Chāyāchatra, and likewise the Supreme Goddess.
O Dear One, one should arrange the fifty seats and then arrange the Mātṛkā.
The first assignment (nyāsa) is with the Gaṇeśas; the second is remembered as being with the planets (grahas);
the third should be with the lunar mansions (nakṣatras); and the fourth is with the Yoginīs.
The fifth is to be known by means of the zodiac signs (rāśi), and the sixth is declared by means of the sacred seats (pīṭha).
Thus is proclaimed the sixfold ritual placement (ṣoḍhā-nyāsa) of Tripurasundarī.
The Great Goddess, who is Sadāśiva himself, should perform the sixfold installation (ṣoḍhānyāsa).
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Tripurā.
Then, for the sake of attaining one's desires, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) known as Tripura;
the Great Goddess consists of the alphabet preceded by the three seed-syllables and ending with "ṅena" and "maḥ."
One should sequentially install the Goddess known as Tripurā in the positions of the Mātṛkā;
by the mere installation of this, a person becomes liberated while living.
Now follows the ritual deposition of Kāmarati.
Then the Goddess should place the Kāmas, who have the luster of pomegranate flowers,
accompanied by the Śaktis of their left limbs, and holding flower-arrows and sugarcane bows.
The Śaktis, resembling saffron in hue and adorned with all ornaments,
should be meditated upon as holding blue lotuses in their hands, capable of attracting the three worlds.
One should place Kāma and Rati behind him; then Kāmaprīti and Parameśvarī, followed by Kānteśa joined with Kāminī, and Bhrānta joined with Mohinī.
The lover is united with Kamalā (Lakṣmī), moving at will as a playful woman;
likewise, from that [state] comes the Karṇakalpalatā, tender and stainless.
Vijayā is conjoined with Kāmavardhana, and Caṇḍavismṛtā;
Tārā is joined with Vidyā, and Viśālākṣī is joined with Namaḥ.
Vimala, Lalitāyukta, Rātrinātha, Digaṃvara,
Ratipriya, Rāmā, Ratirātha, and Kubjikā.
Mala was united with Kāntā, Ramaṇa with Satyā,
Niśākara with Kalyāṇī, and Maṇḍana with Bhoginī.
Nandīśa was joined with Kāmadā, and the beautiful-eyed Madana was joined with Sulāvaṇyā;
likewise, the goddess named Nandāyitā was joined with him.
Then the night-stalker, his body deprived of the earth, was joined by her who is fond of strife; and Puṣpadhanvan desired her.
Mahādhanu is joined with Sumukhī, Grāmiṇī with Nalinī,
Bhīma with Jaṭinī, and Bhrāmaṇa with Yāminī.
Bhramaṇa joined with Śikhinī, O charming Śyāmā; after that, Bhrāmaṇī joined with Ramā; then Bhṛgu joined with Bhūmī.
Bhrāntabhrāmaralolā, Bhrāmāvahasuyaṃcarā, Mohanā, Dīrghajihvā, Sevaka, and likewise Satī.
And likewise, the charming and tremulous-eyed one, the color of delusion, the female bee,
the deluder, the basket, and the god of love are together with the Mistress.
Mataṅga is joined with Māriṇī, Bhṛṅganāda with Paṅkahaṃsinī,
Gāyaka with Viśvatomukhī, and likewise [the others].
Gaja was joined with Nandikā, and Gītī followed immediately after Madana;
Nartaka was accompanied by Sarañjinī, and Lekha was endowed with Kānti.
Unmattā, Karakaṇṭhī, Mattā, Vṛkodarī, Meghā, Śyāmānvitā, Devī, and Vilaṃvinī are the [mantras], O Dear One, in successive order.
O Dear One, one should perform the placement of the letters of the alphabet, beginning with 'a', in their respective locations;
