by this yoga of placement, one becomes a shaker of the three worlds.
Now follows the arrangement of the nine syllables.
One should perform the Nyāsa of the nine yonis using the three Vārā-bījas in sequence,
across three groups of three locations, according to the order to be described below.
Furthermore, one should place [the mantra] on the ears, the chin, the pavilion (maṇḍapa), and likewise on the two sensations;
then on the eyes, the nose, the shoulders, and again on the abdomen.
Then, [one should place them] on the two elbows, the two sides of the abdomen, the two knees, the top of the penis,
the two feet, the secret region, the two flanks, and the lotus of the heart.
One should place the seed-syllable individually at each of the two breasts and at the region of the throat;
O Supreme Goddess, this is declared to be the placement consisting of the nine wombs.
Now follows, in sequence, the placement of the Śrīcakra upon the principles of the sacred seats (pīṭhatattva).
Then, having again recited the *vālā*, one should visualize a square.
Furthermore, having recited the *bālā* mantra, one should contemplate it as a sphere (*golaka*).
Through the yoga of the sphere-assignment (*golaka-nyāsa*), one should thoroughly contemplate the *śrīcakra*.
O Goddess, thereafter one should assign the ritual intentions (saṃkalpa) to the nine locations: the six cakras, the forehead, the hairline, and the cavity of the head.
Now, the placement of the venerable Vidyā-gurus (śrīvidyāgurunyāsa).
One should sequentially place the sixteen syllables upon the head, forehead, eyebrows, mouth, tongue, and the joints and extremities, as well as in the mouth and the locations of the vowels.

One should then place the five [syllables] on the forehead, throat, heart, navel, and the root support (mūlādhāra); and the three seed-syllables in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the mouth, and one's own heart.
One should then place the three seed-syllables at the heart (the support), the *brahmarandhra*, and the hands and feet; one should assign the five seed-syllables to the heart.
One should make [the deity] pervasive and protective for the sake of attaining great good fortune;
the wise one should install the goddess Śrīvidyā in her entirety within the heart.
In the Śrīvidyā tradition, the gurus are situated in sequence behind the openings of the Brahma-randhra.
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the daily deities of the lunar days (tithi-nityā).
Then the goddess Nityā Tithi, joined with the vowels of the Mātṛkā,
bestows all prosperity when the Mātṛkā is placed upon the face.
Now follows the daily installation of the sixteenth [Nityā].
The first Vidyā is Mahātripurasundarī;
she is likewise known as Kāmeśvarī and Bhagamālinī.
Nityā, Klinnā, Bheruṇḍā, and likewise Vahnivāsinī; Vajreśvarī, Dūtī, Tvaritā, and Kulasundarī.
Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, Sarvamaṅgalā,
Jvālāmālinī, and Citrāntā are proclaimed as the fifteen [Yoginīs].
Now he states the mantras for these [goddesses] in sequence.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the supreme Nityā-maṇḍala;
it is the great vidyā of Kāmeśvarī, which brings all the worlds under control.
One should write the syllable *vā* (the seed-syllable of Brahmā), followed by *hṛt* (the heart), and at the end the word *Kāmeśvarī*.
Then, after the phrase "granting the fruit of all desires," one should write "O bestower of everything" (*prade sarvaprada*).
Then one should utter the *satvavaśa* mantra, which bestows everything upon the world; at the end of the agitation, one should utter the *kara* mantra and write the three *hūṃ* syllables.
Having drawn the five arrows in reverse order for the maiden,
this Kāmeśvarī-vidyā has been taught in this context, O beloved.
One should write the Vāgbhava syllable at the end of the word "bhaga," followed by "bhage," "bhagini," "bhagodarī," "bhaga," "bhagamāle," and "bhagāvahe."
In the secret place of the vulva, at the edge of the vulva, at the edge of the womb, marked by the vulva;
falling down at the very end of all, she is then the one who brings about mastery over the vulva.
Then, having drawn the form of the *bhaga* with large, lotus-like eyes,
one should draw everything in its true form, eternally moist at the edges of the *bhaga*.
"O Bhagā, come here, bring [him]!"—thus one should write, granting boons.
Then: "O Rati, O Surati, O Subhaga, O Klinne, O Klinna, O Drava."
O Mistress of the Bhaga, may you moisten and dissolve all sentient beings;
O Amoghabhagavicce, [grant] sight and the agitation of fear for all.
Bhageśvarī should speak to sentient beings: the Vāgbhava syllable *plūṃ*, [the word for] birth and so forth, *bhe*, *plūṃ*, *bhoḥ*, *vlūṃ*, *he*, *vlūṃ*, *hai*, *vlūṃ*, and then again *klinne*.
And at the end, he said, "Bring all the vulvas under my control," and at the conclusion of the woman's seed, he uttered the indestructible syllable (*akṣara*) which is one's own power.
Having written Bhuvaneśī, this Vidyā Bhagamālinī has been recounted here incidentally; it is the Vidyā that brings all the worlds under one's control.
Having uttered the seed-syllable *parā*, followed by *nityaklinne madadrave* and ending with the consort of fire (*svāhā*),
this is declared to be the mantra of Nityaklinnā.
She is the eternal bestower of all good fortune and the giver of all sovereign power.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, one should likewise write it joined with the goad (aṅkuśa);
in the middle of that, one should inscribe the syllable 'bhavoyām' of the Goddess.
And one should write it situated in fire (the letter Ra), devoid of the final letter of the group,
endowed with the fourteen vowels, and distinct as consisting of the bindu and nāda.
The mantra of Bheruṇḍā, joined with the word for "wife" (jāyā) and preceded by the fire-syllable (vahni), bestows the fruit [of the practice].
Having uttered Bhuvaneśī, Vahnivāsinī follows, ending in the feminine nominative suffix ṅi.
O Goddess, this Vidyā known as Vahnivāsinī is the Manu of the lake-water.
The Praṇava, Bhuvane, Śāntī, the syllable consisting of the fruit of the self,
followed by the Visarga and the Moon, and then "Nityaklinne Madadrave."
This Vidyā, joined with the wife of Fire (Svāhā), bestows all sovereignty;
it is the Mahāvajreśvarī Vidyā, which I have declared in this context.
Having uttered the seed-syllable of Parā, followed by Śivadūtī with the [dative] suffix ṅe,
and then the mantra at the end of the heart— this is the goddess Dūtīgrā, who grants all desires.
Having uttered the seed-syllable *oṃ*, one should write *vaḥ* at the end;
having written *khe-ca-che-khaṃ*, one should then write the seed-syllable of the woman (*strīvīja*).
The syllable *hūṃ* is the weapon that casts [the foe] away; this is the sixteen-syllable vidyā.
Or alternatively:
One should write *khe*, *strī*, *cai*, *cha*, *hū*, *cai*, *kṣe*, and the *visarga*;
together with the syllable *hūṃ* and the Supreme Goddess (*parādevī*), this is the twelve-syllabled *vidyā*.
This Vidyā named Tvaritā is difficult to obtain in the three worlds;
she is the very essence of all lion-thrones, a maiden who is the beauty of her lineage.
One should form the Vālayāpuṭitā [mudrā], as well as Caitanyabhairavī;
O Goddess of Gods, the five arrows and the Nityā [mantra] become the Śakrākṣarī.
The Vidyā Trailokyavimalā is the eternal Supreme Goddess;
O Beloved, she is the five-syllabled seed-mantra of the arrow, eternally dear to Parā.
The *praṇava*, the Mistress of the World (*bhuvaneśānī*), the syllable whose nature is the fruit, and the second short vowel; then the *kuśa* belonging to the Mistress of the World.
Having extracted the word *nitya* [and] with the vocative case ending for *madadrave*,
the goddess’s armor-mantra and goad-mantra are those of Nīlapatākinī.
Then, joined with *vāṃ* and followed by the vowel *a* (forming *vāṃ*) and the sound of Indra (*śakra*), [the mantra is] "Obeisance to the Goddess Vijayā; O beloved of Vijayā, you who are eternal."
Or alternatively:
After *vām* comes *kālāgni* (the letter *ra*) and *vāyu* (the letter *ya*), followed by that which is adorned by *śakra* (the letter *i*).
Joined with *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*, this *vidyā* becomes *vijayā*.
One should write the Moon (caṃ) conjoined with Vāruṇa (va), followed by the seed-syllable Tāra (oṃ),
and then "O Goddess Jvālāmālini," ending with "O Bhagavati."

Having uttered [the mantra] twice, and at the very end, having written the pair of feet blazing within the fire of the time of the dissolution of all beings (bhūtasaṃhārakālika-jātavedas), [one should worship].
One should write "jvāla" and "prajvala," followed by the pair of "hūṃ" syllables;
then, on the fourth [line], one should write the goddess Sarvamaṅgalā.
This goddess, who dwells within the heart, is eternal and the source of all auspiciousness.
Or alternatively:
One should write the seed-syllable of Tārā conjoined with the Moon (Ca) and Varuṇa (Va);
then one should write the goddess Sarvamaṅgalā in the dative case.
O Goddess, this mantra, which is eternally all-auspicious, has *hṛdayam* as its heart;
the mantra consists of the three fire-seeds (*hūṃ*), the weapon (*phaṭ*), and is joined with *svāhā*.
This is the eternal Great Goddess, the supreme Jvālāmālinikā;
she is adorned with the vowels ending in the *ka*-group and the final vowel, embellished by the fifth vowel.
The Supreme Goddess, Vicitrā, pervaded by the Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā,
should be worshipped in sequence within all the vowels beginning with 'A'.
The Mother of the Universe.
One should place Nityā, who possesses a beautiful voice, with eyes like lotuses.
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the manifest Yoginīs.
Starting from the Ādhāra and ending at the Brahma-randhra at the tip of the Nāda, one should subsequently place the [mantras] beginning with Prakaṭā; this is the Prakaṭayoginī-nyāsa.
Now follows the secret placement of the Yoginīs (rahasyayoginīnyāsa).

One should install the secret Yoginī in the head, the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, the throat, the heart, the navel, the crown, and extending as far as the foundation and the pervasive [centers].
Now follows the ritual placement of stability (sthitinyāsa).

Then, after that, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) for stability using the sixteen syllables of the Śrīvidyā mantra upon the five-syllable groups on the two hands, the brahmarandhra, the mouth, and the heart.
O Madrijā, having thus performed the placement starting from the head and ending at the feet,
one should then perform another, starting from the throat and extending to the navel.
Having placed one [syllable] from the aperture of Brahma (brahmaraṃdhra) down to the throat,
and having placed [the others] on the feet and the fingers, this ritual placement (nyāsa) brings about stability.
Now follows the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the order of emanation (sṛṣṭi).
Then one should perform the Sṛṣṭinyāsa, which bestows all accomplishments (siddhis),
[placing the mantras] near the aperture of Brahmā (the crown of the head), on the forehead, the nose, the eyes, the ears, and the lips.
O Goddess, [one should contemplate] between the teeth, above and below, on the tongue,
at the base of the throat, on the back, on all limbs, in the heart, on the breasts, in the belly, and on the linga.
The practitioner of mantra should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Śrīvidyārṇa upon the Goddess for the sake of all prosperity.

Then, having meditated upon the Kāmakalā as described within one's own body with the realization of non-difference from the Goddess, the placement of the weapons (āyudhanyāsa) should be performed; and it is as follows:
Having thus contemplated one's own body as consisting of the deity in the form of Kāmakalā, one should perform the ritual worship of the weapons of Śiva and Śivā.
*Drāṃ*, *drīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *plūṃ*, and *saḥ*—these are proclaimed as the arrows of Kāma;
and *yāṃ*, *rāṃ*, *lāṃ*, *vāṃ*, and *māṃ* are the five arrows of Kāmeśvarī.
One should extract the five starting with *drā*, the five starting with *yā*, and the seventh, *saṃmohana*;
then, ending with *ṅe*, [one takes] the bow of Kāmeśvara, ending with *ṅe namo*.
With this mantra, one should hold the arrows below the hand and the bow;
likewise, the reciter of the Vāmadevya mantra should hold the bow with the thumb.
O Kāmeśvarī, at the feet of the Lord, one should place that which arises from the letters beginning with *drā* and ending with *ya*,
saying "to the arrows, salutation," upon one's own right lower hand.
The practitioner should then duly place the arrows of the Goddess, beginning with *au* and ending with *ṣya*;
furthermore, he should place those beginning with *drā* and *iyā* upon the face, together with the nasal bindu.
Then, for the purpose of subjugation, one should place [the mantra] ending with "Obeisance to the Noose" (pāśāya namaḥ) on the upper left hand, which bestows the status of Kāmeśvarī.
If [the mantra] is for the purpose of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), then [one should add]: "drāvīṇi gaganaṃ vahnivāmākṣi vindumat syāt," and then "kāmeśvarī."
One should place [the mantra] "pāśāya namaḥ" on the upper left hand;
then [place] all the syllables beginning with *drā* and *yā*, followed by the word "sarvastambhanāya".
Afterwards, one should write "Kāmeśvarī-padaṃ" and "Aṅkuśāya namaḥ";
then, one should place the goad (aṅkuśa) on the upper right hand of the Goddess.
Then, one should write "drādiyādīni kroṃ" followed by the word "sarvastaṃbhanāya," and above the word "kāmeśvari," one should write "aṅkuśāya namaḥ."
Then, one should place the goad (aṅkuśa) in the upper right hand of the Goddess;
having performed the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the root mantra, one should display the mudrās.
Now follows the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa).
One should place the Vidyā upon all the limbs as the beautiful one who pervades everything.
Now he states the rule for the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Their application is distinct and separate during the morning time, at the time of worship, during the rite of fire-oblation (homa), or even at the time of recitation (japa).
At the time of worship, the best of practitioners should perform all [of these] together.
Then, one should display the nine mudrās.
And so it is said:
Having thus disposed the body, one should sequentially assume the mudrās with the two ring fingers,
the two little fingers, the two middle fingers, and the palms.
With the two thumbs and the two ring fingers joined like a staff, and the two index fingers [extended],
this is the Kṣobhiṇī Mahāmudrā, which is called Drāviṇī.
In the middle finger of this very same vidyā, joined with the index finger,
the second [vidyā] named Sarvavidrāviṇī is proclaimed.
The Supreme Goddess should join the index finger and the middle finger of this very vidyā in the form of a hook.
The third proclaimed vidyā is the Attractor of the Three Worlds.
One should form the hands in the shape of a hollowed bowl, with the two index fingers shaped like hooks.
Then, having been questioned in sequence, when that middle [finger] has gone below it,
by that same sequence, O Manu, the two— [the] little finger and the ring finger— [are to be joined].
Having joined [the hands], one should rub them together with all the fingers and the tips of the thumbs;
this is the fourth mudrā, the Supreme Goddess, which brings everything under control.
The two hands should be joined palm-to-palm, with the middle fingers following the hollows of the palms; the index fingers should be joined outwardly, and the ring fingers should be kept straight.
Then, with the middle nails at the base of the thumbs joined like a staff,
this is proclaimed as the fifth mudrā, named Unmādinī.
The mantras of the five arrows are proclaimed in sequence;
[they are assigned] to the two index fingers and the two middle fingers of this very vidyā.
One should form the two hands in the shape of a great hook; this is the Mahāṅkuśā mudrā.
The great seed-syllable known as Aṅkuśa is proclaimed to be its mantra.
Then the Goddess should place her right arm upon his left arm,
and she should gradually rub their hands together.
O Maheśvarī, one should join the little fingers and ring fingers together, place the middle finger behind them, and extend the index fingers in both hands.
Having joined both thumbs together, one should apply this [mudrā] upon the earthen [element];
this is the Khecarī Mahāmudrā, which causes the agitation of the three worlds.
The mantra of this [goddess] is proclaimed to begin with "Vijaya" and consist of the great seed-syllable;
she is celebrated as the Samaya-mudrā of all.
Then, having touched the two hands together in the shape of a half-moon,
one should likewise join the pair of index fingers and thumbs simultaneously.
One should join the little fingers below with the middle fingers;
and one should place the two bent ring fingers at the very bottom of all.
This is celebrated as the Seed Mudrā; its mantra is "haum. The previously mentioned Yoni Mudrā is proclaimed as the ninth.
Because she flashes forth within the multitude of powers (śaktis), she is therefore common to all;
her mantra is Vāgbhava, for she is the Mother of the universe.

Having thus disposed his body and having his form armored with the [proper] mudrās, he should perform the rite of internal sacrifice (antaryāga), by which the All-pervading Lord himself becomes manifest.
Having performed the rite of the internal sacrifice, one should perform the external worship;
having performed the installation of the *arghya* and other offerings, one should indeed manifest the *śrīcakra*.
Now he describes the Śrīcakra.
The point, the triangle, the eight-sided figure, the pair of ten-sided figures, the pentagon, the eight-petaled lotus, the sixteen-sided figure, the three circles,
and the three abodes of the earth— this is declared to be the King of Yantras of the Supreme Deity.
Some say this yantra is devoid of the three circles; and thus:
"Having produced the four fires, then the five powers in Śivā."
In the forward and backward sequence, there are the vital points (*marmas*), joints (*saṃdhis*), and so forth;
specifically, there are eighteen *marmas* and twenty-four joints.
And with four Śrīkarṇas and five Śiva-śaktis,
joined in the sequence of the cakras and interconnected with one another.
By means of the powers (śaktis) of Śambhu, [the mandala] takes the form of nine wheels;
it consists of forty-three angles, a circle, and likewise an eight-petaled lotus.
O Maheśvarī, beginning from the fourteenth [day], there is a circle, a digit (kalā), a petal, a triple circle, and three enclosures of the earth (bhūpura).
Listen indeed to the four auspicious wheels, the wheels of Śakti,
belonging to Maheśvarī, beginning from the fourteen-spoked wheel and ending with the triangle.
There are indeed five Śakti-cakras according to the tradition of Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Or alternatively:
O Maheśvarī, listen with diligence to the cakras according to the tradition of Ānandabhairava, beginning from the fourteen-spoked wheel and ending with the outer square.
O Supreme Goddess, listen attentively to the four auspicious wheels of Śakti, beginning from the outer ten-spoked wheel and ending with the point (bindu).
O Dear One, there are indeed five power-wheels (śakticakras) that are devoid of the triple-folded [structure].
Now he describes the method of writing.
Among those, pride is as follows:
One should fashion the yantra on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or on the ground measuring one cubit;
however, when constructing it from gems and such materials, the measurement may be according to one's desire.
The divisions have been described, O Goddess; now listen with care to the arrangement.
There, seated facing the east, one should draw the King of Wheels (Cakrarāja).
Then, on a level and delightful spot of ground, one should draw a wheel upon the earth using vermilion powder or powders such as saffron and the like.
Make the joint straight-lined, pleasing to the eye, and equal in its divisions;
then [fashion it] with silver, copper, or various other metals.
Having fashioned a cloth-strip from white sandalwood and red sandalwood,
O beloved, one should place it upon that cloth and write with a golden pen.
With yellow pigment (rocanā) and saffron (kuṅkuma), as well as musk (kastūrī), sandalwood (caṃdana), and so forth.
The preceptor should draw a straight line from Īśāna to Agni;
then, having drawn two lines from the tips of those [lines] at Īśāna and Agni, he should pull them [together].
And having unified [these] within the beautiful Śaktirekhā, O beloved of the Supreme,
one should draw the form of a triangle above it.
The two powers (śaktis) are described as having the form of a triangle;
one should perform the measurement of the measuring-stick (mānayaṣṭi) at the front tip of the eastern power, as previously prescribed.
O Supreme Goddess, one should then draw a line from the junction of those two powers toward the southwest corner (vāyurākṣasakoṇa), following the sequence for breaking the joints.
Having drawn lines from the two corners toward the front,
O Goddess praised by heroes, fashion this fire-maṇḍala extending toward the east.
O lady worshipped by the gods, listen now to what follows: at the end of those two wheels, there is a prior power (pūrvaśakti) from the two fire-triangles (koṇa).
Having extended the eastern lines from the western fire-corner likewise,
one should draw a line going westward from both the northwest and southwest corners.
The Goddess should extend [the lines] and join them according to the sequence of dividing the joints;
the tip of the womb [should be placed] in the eastern region, proceeding in order from south to north.
Likewise, by joining the lines situated in the womb (yoni) in the western direction with the two corners in due order, there will then be ten corners.
In the same manner, O Goddess of the gods, the second ten-cornered figure is formed by drawing lines from the northeast and southeast to the tips of the eastern yoni in due order.
O beautiful one, having extended two lines from the tip of the northwest corner,
the Goddess [then] should join them at the western tip to the direction of Indra, the lord of the quarters.
O Goddess of the gods, one should place the charming Cumbinī at the tip of the eastern corner in such a way that the [deity] becomes the leader of the row.
O Goddess of the gods, having left aside four corners of the ten-cornered [figure],
O Goddess, one should draw a line in the middle within the ten corners.
Likewise, in the southern part and similarly in the northern part,
there is a sequential division of the joints of the hexagon for the Goddess.
Having joined the *yoni* and the fire, just as the letter Śa is produced,
one should apply a straight line passing through the middle of the *kakṣā*.
O Goddess, it should be straight in its formation, as beautiful as a woman in childbirth;
facing forward with the tips of the five powers directed toward the front, and having four fires in the cardinal directions.
O fair-faced one, this wheel consists of a bindu in the middle portion of the triangle;
know that there is a wheel in the center, as well as a pair of ten-spoked wheels.
O Goddess, marked with the corners of Indra (the northeast), it shall consist of outer, middle, and inner [circles].
O Maheśānī, this wheel increases all auspicious fortune.
O Goddess, you are the bestower of universal sovereignty, the destroyer of all calamities,
and the fulfiller of many horses, rubies, and gold.
O Goddess, this great state of supreme liberation is the essence of the play of speech;
O Maheśānī, this external form is like the full moon.
O fish-eyed one, endowed with that [lotus], it is beautiful with eight petals;
then, O goddess praised by the gods, having drawn a sixteen-petaled [lotus] there—
O Supreme Goddess, it is square and endowed with four gates,
for there, O Great-minded One, are sixty-four crores of Yoginīs.
Indeed, in this wheel, those distinguished ones pay honor to the practitioner.
Now, he states the names, colors, and fruits according to the division of its parts.
A square [mandala], adorned with the letters of the Mātṛkā for the sake of attaining success, set with pearls and rubies, and shining everywhere with gems.
Named Trailokyamohana, it bestows the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree;
it has sixteen spokes, possesses the form of the lunar disc, and is the abode of all.
O auspicious one, it fulfills all desires; O Great Goddess, it is eight-petaled, resembling the hibiscus flower, and flows with an increase of nectar.
That which is named "Agitator of All" and that which "Fulfills All Desires"—
these two, O lady of excellent hips, are the Wheel of Emanation that bestows auspiciousness.
O Goddess of the gods, the fourteen-spoked [mandala] of the Goddess, which is adorned with all the traditions and bestows all perfections, has the luster of a pomegranate flower.
O blessed lady, it bestows infinite fruit and always grants all prosperity;
O beloved, the ten-spoked [cakra] has the luster of molten gold and resembles vermilion.
The wheel that accomplishes all aims is always meditated upon in the mind;
the second [wheel] is at the tip of the row, resembling a hibiscus flower in color.
The wheel that provides all protection... O Śivā, these three constitute the wheel of Maheśānī’s abode, which bestows happiness.
O lady of excellent hips, the worship of the Dakṣiṇāmnāya, which bestows desired fruits,
consists of an eight-cornered [diagram] as red as the rays of the rising sun.
Resembling a ruby in appearance, it always removes all diseases;
it possesses the brilliance of a thousand rising suns and the luster of the bandhūka flower.
The wheel that bestows all accomplishments is that sovereign who is the abode of all arts;
the triangle is the source of everything, the eternal cause that grants prosperity.
O lady of excellent hips, O beloved, the Bindu-cakra consists of all-bliss;
O Supreme Goddess, it is the leader of the cakras and is composed of Sadāśiva.
This wheel, however, is of the nature of withdrawal, eternally composed of Brahman;
it is to be served according to the Western Tradition (Paścimāmnāya), and here the triad is worshipped.
Because it bestows the glory of absolute liberation (*śrī-kaivalya*) and because it bestows the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*), it is called the *Śrīcakra*.
Now, he describes its nature as being composed of mantras that have the form of Mount Meru.
O Goddess of gods, there is no doubt that the Śrīcakra is also of the form of [the letter] La;
since the letter La is the seed-syllable of the earth, it is therefore called the "earth-diagram" (bhūvimbam).
O auspicious lady, the letter *sa* is the moon, which assumes sixteen forms as its digits (*kalā*).
Therefore, the sixteen-petaled [lotus] is indeed the letter *ha*, which is called Śiva.
O Subhadrā, because he is the eightfold-formed one (Aṣṭamūrti), there should be an eight-petaled [lotus];
the letter *i* is indeed Māyā, the binder of all, comprising the fourteen worlds.
O Dear One, they protect from the other side; thus the corner of Śakra (the northeast) is formed.
The line of power (śaktirekhā), situated in ten places upon the thread, sustains the three worlds.
Known as Viśvajyoti, she is Viṣṇu in her tenfold form;
from the letter Ra, O Supreme Goddess, she expands, pervading the Cakra.
Therefore, the ten-cornered [diagram] is the immutable light;
joined with the ten-fold divisions of the digits (kalās), it is the fire that sets the ten corners in motion.
From the letter *ka*, O Goddess, comes Mādana and Śiva, whose nature consists of the eight vowels; when the womb is pleasing, that wheel becomes marked with the eight wombs (*vasuyoni*).

Since the qualities of the elements, beginning with the form of agaru, abide in the half-measure (ardhamātrā), the womb (yoni) takes the form of a triangle; indeed, through the bindu, it becomes the lunar sphere (vaidava).
The essential nature of the Lord of Desire, whose very form is the support of the universe.
Now, the fruit of vision.
Whatever fruit one might obtain by performing a hundred perfect sacrifices,
that same fruit one attains through devotion by beholding the Śrīcakra.
Whatever fruit one obtains by performing the sixteen great gifts,
that same fruit one attains by constructing the supreme Śrīcakra.
Whatever fruit one obtains by bathing in three and a half crore sacred fords (tīrthas),
that same fruit one attains through devotion by performing the vision of the Śrīcakra.
Now, the fruit of worship.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to be obtained from the consecration of ten million liṅgas,
that same fruit one certainly attains from the worship of the Śrīcakra.
Now, the fruit of giving.
Whoever, having fashioned a Śrīcakra, gives it to a practitioner,
has indeed given the entire earth with its mountains, forests, and oceans.
Now, the fruit of the water used for washing the feet of the Śrīcakra.

In the interior of the vessel of the universe, [the merit of] bathing at ten million billion sacred fords (tīrtha)— including Gaṅgā, Puṣkara, Narmadā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Gomatī, Gaṅgādvāra, Gayā, Prayāga, Badarī, Vārāṇasī, Siddhi, Revā, Setu, Sarasvatī, and so forth— [is attained].
The water from the feet of the Śrīcakra bestows fruit.
Now, he states again that specific feature of this [goddess] which pertains to the general seat (pīṭha).
With a steady mind, one should visualize the configuration of the great wheel,
rising above the ocean of red nectar like the rising moon.
In the center, one should visualize a ground made of gold adorned with rubies,
and an island composed of the nine gems, whose masses of radiance illuminate the quarters of space.
With its mouths and blood-machines licking the expanse of the sky,
it is thus exceedingly vast, measuring a thousand yojanas in extent.
In its center is the great Nandana garden, which intoxicates even the God of Love;
it has a moat filled with the waters of compassion and is encircled by a golden wall.
It is resplendent with garlands of moonlight from the ever-risen full moon,
and is eternally protected by the god of love, Kāmadeva, who dwells there together with Spring.
At the edge [of the grove] were the five trees— bakula, punnāga, and nāgakeśara—
as well as pārijāta, mango, raṅga, nāgaraṅga, and atimuktika.
With cardamom, cloves, kakkola, jasmine, and mallikā flowers, and with citron,
honey-jambīra, pomegranate, and mātuluṅga fruits.
With *sephālikā* flowers, coconut trees, plantain trees, betel-nut trees,
betel vines, *muralatā*, *cakravallī*, and other such creepers;
With black aloe-wood, mahendra, moon-tree, wood-apple, breadfruit, and others;
with date-palm, palmyra, śrītālī, hiṃtālī, and devadāru.
With *pāṭalī*, *yūthikā*, *jātī*, *sallakī*, creepers, and the like; with *tomara*, *niṣpaṇḍī*, *kadaṃba*, and *udumbara* trees.
The ground was carpeted with the petals of madhuka, grapes, śyāmā, and kunda flowers,
as well as those of exceedingly radiant, magnificent, and divine kalpa-trees and the like.
It was surrounded by bees resonant with the sound of "hrīṃ," ever laden with fruit and everywhere radiant with blossoms, and filled with cuckoos singing.
The interior of that direction resounded with the intoxicated, warbling chatter of cuckoos,
and it was filled with the burgeoning warble of intoxicated parrots.
Its interior was filled with the sweet warbling of sarika birds,
and it shone with circles of cakoras, karandavas, cranes, and water-fowls.
It was radiant with pairs of swans intoxicated by the scent of *makaranda*,
and filled with masses of pollen from *jātī* and *puṇnāga* flowers intermingled together.
The three worlds were set in motion by the Maruts moving with my speed;
it was served by groves of trees resembling various flowering creepers.
It was perfectly attended by Malaya breezes and by the grey pollen arising from long-stalked, full-blown lotuses and water-lilies upon its couch.
Having thus meditated upon the Nandana garden, one should then contemplate the Praṇava within it,
adorned with sands of pure gold and camphor.
In the midst of that, one should meditate upon a pavilion frequented by many gods and siddhas eager for service, pervading the entire circle of the universe.
Resembling the rising sun, quadrangular and most beautiful,
it made the quarters of the sky tawny with a mass of radiance from the brilliance of jewels.
It was devoid of a central pillar, yet adorned with pillars at its corners,
and was constructed from great rubies, lapis lazuli, gems, and gold.
Richly adorned with canopies of pearl necklaces, embellished with jewel-studded stairways, level and swept by the wind, it was made fragrant by waves of incense and perfumes.
With *jātī*, *caṃpaka*, *punnāga*, *ketakī*, *mallikā*, and other flowers;
with fragrant blue lotuses, white lotuses, *mādhavī* vines, and snow-white jasmine.
It was adorned with celestial palaces fashioned from jewels, gold, lapis lazuli,
and pearls, featuring wings, precious yak-tail whisks, bells, and other ornaments.
Adorned with various garlands that had been strung together,
it was decorated with millions of jeweled figurines and was most wonderful.
One should meditate on a vast altar in its center, adorned with various divine jewels and other ornaments fashioned by Viśvakarman, and capable of feeding a hundred people.
Resembling a thousand [suns] and the like, constructed from a single ruby,
it was provided with four gates and featured gate-arches made of rubies at its entrances.
Having thus meditated upon the altar, adorned on all sides with lamps and full water-jars, and in its center, a pedestal consisting of the crescent moon;
It was fashioned from moonstone (caṃdrakānta) rock, adorned with four legs,
and made beautiful by various gems such as māṇikyas and other jewels.
The bed was exceedingly soft, strewn with garments as red as the Japā flower,
adorned with a great pillow, and covered with a pale-red cloth.
Having thus meditated upon the arrangement of the Śrīcakra, one should commence the worship.
O Maheśvarī, from west to center in reverse order,
there is an island composed of the nine gems, resplendent with nine divisions.
One should worship that [deity] with its name preceded by the Mātṛkā and ending with "namas."

Then, having worshipped the seat according to the method described above and meditated upon the Goddess preceded by the Kāmakalā, one should invoke her either into the Śrīyantra or the Bindu; for according to the scriptures, other [deities] do not possess the three Bindus of Tripura at all.
The Viśvamātṛkā consists solely of three dots and three measures (mātrās);
for that reason, the Goddess is called Tripurāśakti.
Through the union of the three drops, Tripurā resides within the triple drop.
One should visualize the bindu as the face, the two breasts situated below it,
the lower lip (aparārddha) below that, and the mouth below that.
Thus, she whose form is the aesthetic essence of desire (kāmakalā) is directly embodied in the imperishable;
she resides there upon the seat of the bindu, within the eternal lotus of kalās.
There, at the seat of Kāmeśvara, she is the consort of him who is proficient [in that place];
she is the sovereign of the three worlds of the Command, the teacher who dispels the afflictions of Brahmā.
Beautiful in her constituent letters from 'a' to 'kṣa',
she enters in her essential form from the root center (mūlādhāra) up to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra).
Resplendent like the rising sun, resembling the hibiscus flower,
possessing the luster of freshly smelted gold, and brilliant as the pomegranate blossom.
Her hair-dress was resplendent with fragrant flowers,
and her dark, curling locks shone like slender *ketaka* blossoms frequented by bees.
With a line of bees hovering over her face, radiant with a jeweled tilaka of rubies,
beautiful with shimmering strings of gems, and her crown resplendent with tiny bells.
Slightly reddish, with a face like the shimmering moon, her lower lip like coral,
radiant with the brilliance of a crescent moon as her forehead mark, and exceedingly resplendent.
Adorned with beautiful earrings that caused her dark locks to quiver as they tossed,
she shone with a radiant pearl necklace and glittering golden earrings.
Her cheeks were adorned with the luster of her ear-ornaments;
her face was like a radiant moon, and her nose was set with pearls as bright as pure silver.
She who surpasses the sweetness of a smile that bestows the essence of the knowledge of Brahman,
and who is resplendent with vine-like arms resembling rows of royal coral creepers.
Her lotus-like hands are as delicate as the petals of a red water-lily,
and the lunar radiance of her fingernails illuminates the expanse of the sky.
Śivā was languid from the weight of her well-rounded, firm, and lofty breasts;
her chest rose as a great necklace of fresh pearls fell upon it.
Śātodarī, with a beautiful waist that is deep and resembles a well-drawn bow,
wearing a girdle fashioned from priceless jewels with small bells attached.
She is beautiful with the orb of her hips, adorned with a line of hair;
she possesses the radiance of shimmering red garments that pervades the entire circle of the three worlds.
Resplendent with divine tunics adorned with various and wonderful gems,
she surpassed the delicate pillars of plantain trees with her tender thighs.
The goddess whose splendor flashes with the nine gems, who is adorned with tinkling anklets,
and whose lotus feet rest upon the shimmering crowns of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
Her face was perfumed with betel-leaf mixed with whole camphor;
she held a flute fashioned from a coral creeper and was adorned with silken garments.

And the second [arrow] has the crescent moon as its notch; it is capable of attracting, and by its excellent luster, it is the Bhramari-arrow that draws forth the qualities of the elements from the sugarcane bow.
She who bears the five arrows shining with the form of a lotus,
and whose body is ruddy with saffron and the abundant scent of great musk.
Richly adorned with the splendor of all ornaments, radiant with every decoration,
the Goddess who embodies all the gods, whose very form is the essence of all conduct.
Thus meditating upon the Great Goddess, the mother of all auspiciousness, the beauty of all auspiciousness, who dwells in the midst of the Kadamba forest.
Alternatively, one should meditate starting from the feet up to the head.
She possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns, the luster of the bandhūka flower,
resembling the javā flower, and having a radiance equal to a ruby.
The Supreme Goddess, resembling a mass of lightning, glowing like molten gold,
and resplendent with sprout-like feet shaped like the petals of a red lotus.
Her two feet are adorned with anklets set with priceless jewels,
and they shine with the brilliance of gems placed upon her toe-rings.
Her two thighs were as delicate as the graceful trunk of a plantain tree,
and her rounded hips were adorned with shimmering red garments.
She was adorned with a girdle of shimmering rubies and tinkling bells; she possessed slender thighs, a deep navel, and a waist so thin it could be encircled by the hand.
She was endowed with a body like a great fruit from the vine of Rāma’s lineage,
adorned by the dense and lofty circles of her breasts.
Adorned with a magnificent necklace of vast, priceless pearls,
and graced with the finest ornaments such as a radiant neck-ornament composed of the nine gems;

Adorned with the Vedas as her ornaments, captivating the mind, with clusters of blossoms upon the surface of her cheeks, she possesses the radiance of a beautiful face graced by earrings resembling the rising sun.
Her face was like the full moon, her lotus-like mouth was crimson,
her beautiful eyebrows were like a quivering bow of love, and her eyes were like lotuses.
Upon her forehead is a crest-ornament marked with a beautiful creeper of excellent gems, and upon the surface of her crown set with pearls and rubies are tiny bells.
She wears a crown shining with a throbbing crescent moon, possesses three eyes,
and has four vine-like arms resplendent like coral creepers.
She who holds a sugarcane staff, flowers, a noose, and a goad—these four—in her hands;
I bow to this Mother Ambā, who embodies all the gods and is the beauty of all auspiciousness.
The Goddess who embodies all sacred fords, who possesses the nature of all the gods,
who consists of all the scriptures, who is eternal, and who is saluted by all the immortals.
To the Goddess who consists of all sacred traditions, who is served by all beings,
who is composed of all bliss, who is the Mother of Knowledge, and who is the supreme bestower of perfection.
Then he spoke the invocation mantra and the three-part mudrā.
O Mother, who dwells within the Great Lotus Grove, whose form is the bliss of the primal cause,
who is devoted to the welfare of all beings— come, come, O Supreme Goddess!
Separate the previously mentioned *yonimudrā* into three distinct parts using the two thumbs,
the two little fingers, and the middle fingers of the hands.
This is the mudrā named Trikhaṇḍā, used for the rite of summoning Tripurā;
thereafter, one should contemplate the serpent-like [power] entering through the gateway of the two nostril-channels.
O Kulasuṃdarī, one should place Kāmeśvara upon the lap of Śiva with the Vidyā in the form of invocation and with the Trikhaṇḍā mudrā.
One should contemplate the venerable Śrīpīṭha established there, with the Goddess residing within it;
one should display the mudrās and worship her thrice with libations.
One should mentally conceive the body of the Supreme Goddess along with its limbs;
one should properly offer perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and other articles to the Goddess.
Having worshipped the Supreme Deity with the sixteen services,
one should again offer the arpaṇas three times with the root mantra.
At this time, one should worship the goddesses, the lunar days (tithis), and the eternal ones (nityās).
One should worship the Great Goddess, beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Nityā Vicitrā, in the form of the lunar days (tithis) from the first day of the lunar fortnight up to the full moon.
Having performed the great nyāsa in sequence from the top right to the top left,
one should draw five lines there in order, five by five.
One should contemplate the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa' on the right face;
then, on one's own eastern line, [one should place] Dīrghakarṇā and Vipaṃcaka.
Then, having drawn [the grid], one should write the powers (śakti) and so forth upon the northern line;
one should worship the sixteen vowels ending with the anusvāra, and the sixteenth [vowel] as the visarga.
O Goddess of gods, O Adrijā, the sixteen Nityās are proclaimed to proceed in counter-clockwise order,
beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) up to the full moon (paurṇamāsī).
One should worship each Nityā daily and shall attain great good fortune;
O Maheśānī, one should worship them within the circle of lunar days (tithis) during the dark fortnight.
O lady of excellent hips, from Vicitrā onwards until Kāmeśvarī is reached,
the Great Goddess is to be worshipped even in reverse order.
O Goddess of the gods, as long as there are sixteen digits (kalās) of the moon in succession,
that great goddess obtains good fortune through the eternal Guru.
Having worshipped the Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī in due order,
one should then worship the goddess Tithinityā in her three forms for the sake of good fortune.
Furthermore, one should worship the illustrious Tripurānityā for the sake of attaining good fortune.
At this time, O Goddess, the wise man should worship his gurus;
I shall explain this to you through the yoga of the closing of the flowers, O sinless one.
Having recognized more than a hundred rays of light from the gurus,
one should contract the flower; otherwise, it is the cause of the loss of success in my mantra.
By the contraction of the flower, one destroys twelve lineages;
O Dear One, through the destruction of the lineage, the form of the deity does not exist.
For this very reason, O beloved, the great flower is perfectly closed;
the wealth of the Guru indeed belongs to the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja.
In the center, one should first worship the lineage of gurus in three groups within a triangle;
first, one should worship those known as Parā, and then those distinguished as Parāparā.
Then, O Goddess, O Beloved, one should worship Parā as the Guru;
O fair-faced one, the divine lineage (divyaugha) is indeed the supreme accomplishment (siddhi), numbering seven.
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, [the sequence] should be known to end with the word Ānandanātha;
O Queen of the Gods, beyond that, Para-prakāśa is considered to be Paraśiva.
O Dear One, Parāśakti is likewise the Goddess Kauleśvarī;
O Kuleśāna, Śuklā Devī and the others, beginning with Kāmeśvarī, follow in sequence.
The gurus known as the "Man" (muni) are called Parā; they possess divine forms.
What use have we for enjoyments? Likewise, there are those called Veda, who are innate (sahaja) to both [traditions].
O beloved, hear now of the lineage of the Siddhas known as the Higher and the Lower, and the lineage of Men:
Gaganas, Viśvakamalau, and likewise Madanābhuvana.
O Naga, thereafter, the human [mantra] consists of eight syllables;
O Supreme Goddess, these are the secondary [mantras] composed of letters.
O Maheśānī, these three—along with another teacher for the sake of welfare—are certainly extracted by me; O beloved, the flower is now closed.
Afterwards, one should worship the three gurus of the lineage ending with Mānavaugha:
first the Parameṣṭhi-guru, then the Guru-guru, and finally the one known as Parama-guru.
O Maheśānī, one should worship one's own guru and the triad of gurus;
or else, at the end of the Mānavaugha, one should worship a single own-guru.
This method has been described; now another method is being stated.
The last [group] consists of all types of human multitudes, eight in number;
thus, the gurus indeed become nine in number.
Since the Mistress of the Nine Wheels (Navacakreśvarī) thus manifests the Flower within the human stream (mānavaugha), there are indeed seventeen goddesses [therein].
Afterwards, one should contract the flower and worship the ninth, the Śrī Guru.
O sinless one, having thus spoken to the disciple who has attained realization, he said:
"Having uttered 'Salutation to the Guru,' one should write 'Salutation to the Pādukās'."
One should likewise offer salutations to the sandals of the Guru, the Paramaguru, the Parameṣṭhiguru, and the Anteguru, as well as to the Ācāryas.
Having worshipped the lineage of gurus, one then becomes Śrī Tripurā herself;
however, a man devoid of the lineage of gurus is excluded from the assembly.
O beloved, O Supreme Goddess, by your grace and for the benefit of practitioners, I have attained perfection through the path of the closing of the flower.
Having worshipped the lineage of gurus, one should then worship the deities of the tradition within the wheel that fascinates the three worlds and fulfills all desires.
One should worship the Eastern Tradition (pūrvāmnāya) in the Sarvasaṃkṣobhaka-cakra,
as well as in the Sarvasaubhagyaka-cakra and the Sarvārthasādhaka-cakra.
One should worship the Dakṣiṇāmnāya in the Sarvarakṣākara-cakra;
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship the Kuverāmnāya in the nine cakras.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship the lion-throne in the center of the Vaiṃdava;
in this very manner, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
Śrīvidyā, as well as Lakṣmī, Mahālakṣmī,
likewise Triśakti, and Tvaritā— these are proclaimed as the five forms of Lakṣmī.
Śrīvidyā, Para-jyoti, Parānihvala-śāmbhavī,
Ajapā, and Mātṛkā— these are proclaimed as the five sheaths (pañcakoṣas).
Śrīvidyāpārijāteśī, Pañcavāṇeśvarī,
Trikūṭā, and Pañcavāṇeśī are remembered as the five Kalpalatās.
Śrīvidyā, the Mistress of the Root-Pīṭha, Sudhā, Śrī, and Amṛteśvarī—
these are renowned as Siddhi and Lakṣmī, remembered as the five who grant all desires.
Śrīvidyā, Annapūrṇā, Mātaṅgī, Bhuvaneśvarī,
and the Great Goddess Vārāhī are proclaimed as the Five Jewels (Pañcaratna).
In the place of worship of Śrīvidyā is the King of Wheels (Cakrarāja), O Great Goddess;
it is Mahālakṣmīśvarī, seated upon a throne adorned by the assembly [of goddesses].
Having uttered, "I worship Śrīvidyā, the mother of all auspiciousness," the wise one should worship the supreme light and the corners.
In this very manner, one should worship the five pentads.
Now, he states their mantras in sequence.
O Great Goddess, the Mūlavidyā is proclaimed as Śrīvidyā.
The word "Lakṣmīdevyai" is declared to be situated in fire (Ra), ending with Varuṇa (Va), and endowed with Bindu and Nāda; this is cited as the seed-syllable (bīja) of Lakṣmī.
Having first uttered the Praṇava, one should worship that which consists of the syllable Hrīṃ; then, with the Śrī-enclosure, [one should say]: "O Kamala, be gracious to Kamalāya."
One should assign the ground situated between the *lā* to the place of Rudra;
one should bestow the pair "pra-sīda," the seed-syllable of Śrī, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
Then one should give the seed-syllable of Śrī; Mahālakṣmī resides within the heart-mind.
This mantra of Mahālakṣmī is considered to consist of twenty-seven syllables.
One should inscribe the Śrī-bīja, the Parā-bīja, and the Kāma-bīja;
O Goddess, this Triśakti is difficult to obtain in the three worlds.
O beloved, in the course of conversation, the goddess Lakṣmī, adorned with long eyes, was respectfully described by Candra as the Vidyā Viṣṇukūleśvarī.
The three seeds, the supreme seed, and the one with desire are declared to be the Tripuṭā;
the Pañcakāmeśvarī Vidyā is prescribed for the practice of the arrows.
The Vāgbhava syllable, the left eye (I), ending with the Dhruva (M) and joined with the Bindu (Ṃ)—
this is the Vidyā of the Mistress of the Root-Pīṭha, which I have declared as well-guarded.
The seed-syllable of Parā is the Śrī-bīja (Hrīm), followed by the syllable "Makamaka" with strength;
then "Rājyāderājyalakṣmī," and the Moon (Oṃ) adorned with the creative emission (Visarga).

The seed-syllables beginning with *viloma* (reverse order), followed by *ādyabīja* (the first seed), the nectars (*sudhā*), and the venerable *sampramā*; then the *vāgbhava*, the goddess *bhuvaneśānī*, and immediately thereafter the *śrībīja*.
One should always write the eternal reality beginning with *vipatta* and ending with *khaphare*;
the mantra is considered to be *phroṃ*, beginning with *viyat* and ending with *tadādi*.
Having extracted the third and fourth letters of the *ca*-group joined with *māyā* (the letter *ī*), the letter *ra*, and the crescent moon (*indu*),
one should write the word "Mahāmakha" followed by the word "Saṃkarṣaṇī."
Having uttered "Kāli Mahādiru," which is joined with the moon (i) and the syllable "vipat" (vi),
the great mantra of Siddhilakṣmī, beginning with the seed-syllable of Māyā (hrīṃ), has been declared.
And Annapūrṇā, O Goddess of gods, is proclaimed in the Uttarāmnāya;
one should write the mantra for Mātaṅginī ending with two *ṭha*s, encased by *vāṅ*, *māyā*, and *śrī*.
This twelve-syllable Vidyā of Ātaṅginī has been proclaimed;
it is joined with the sky (ha) and fire (ra), and adorned with the moon (i) in the left eye (u).
Bhuvaneśī, who is difficult to reach even for Maheśa, [pervades] the three worlds.
Having first extracted the *vāṅmāyā* (the syllable *aiṃ*), [one should address] the Blessed Lady with the vocative case:
"O Vārtālī, O Deśavārāhī, O Yugmavārāhī, O Mukhyā!"
Blindness perishes by Andhāndhinī; thereafter, obstruction by Rundhīrudhinī; paralysis by Jambhājambhinī; and delusion was not even seized by Mohāmohinī.
O Stambhini, when joined with "staṃbhe" and "hṛdi," it should paralyze such-and-such a person;
it shall extract everything from all those who are wicked or malicious.
"Jihvā-stambhaṃ kuru-dvandvaṃ śīghra-vaśyaṃ kuru-dvayam | Vāg-luṇṭha-traya-vinduṃ ca mantraṃ pāvakavallabhā ||" (The beloved of Agni [the goddess Svāhā]).
This great vidyā is highly renowned and kept secret in all tantras.
In the place of worship of Śrīvidyā, within the sovereign wheel (cakrarāja), one should visualize Maheśvarī,
the Great Mistress of Desire, seated upon a throne adorned by the assembly of the Vṛnda.
Having uttered, "I worship the sandal that generates all auspiciousness," the wise one should worship the supreme light within the treasure-chest.
In this very manner, one should worship the Pañcapañcikā.
The Goddess should worship the Śaiva perspective within the Vaiṇava [circles],
while the Supreme Sovereign worships the Śākta perspective all around the Cakra.
O Goddess, O beloved, on the first square of the earth-mandala,
one should worship the Vaiṣṇava perspective to the left of Śiva's perspective.
O lotus-eyed one, the vision of the Sun occurs in the wheel of emanation (sṛṣṭicakra),
and after worshipping in the wheel of maintenance (sthiticakra), there is the supreme Buddhist vision.
Having thus worshipped the entire Śrīvidyā, one should worship her on all sides;
one should offer libations three times with the *tattvamudrā*.
Having propitiated [the deity] with all ritual services, one should display the mudrās in their proper sequence.
Then one should perform the limb-enclosure (aṅgāvaraṇa) arising from the mantra of Śrīvidyā;
the worship of the limbs is performed in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Asura, Vāyu, and in the center.
The seed-syllable consisting of Māyā and Lakṣmī is [formed] from the pair according to the previous sequence;
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, one should join it with either the triad or [the others].
Or else, O Goddess praised by heroes, having joined them all according to the method of the *saṃpuṭa* sequence, one should worship them in this manner, O fair-faced one, following the proper order.
In the Trailokyamohana-cakra, one should worship the manifest Yoginī.
O Dear One,
Aśusundarī, who has the luster of freshly smelted gold and holds a noose and a goad, shall be accomplished.
One should worship those with lotuses in their hands, who bestow treasures marked with gold and great jewels from the *bhāṇḍīra* tree upon practitioners.
Meditation on the source of accomplishments.
O Śivā, one should meditate upon her who wears variegated garments, who is awe-inspiring, who possesses the luster of the moon, who has three eyes,
and who bestows the great supernatural powers (mahāsiddhis) such as atomization (aṇimā) upon men.
In the square with four gates,
one should worship the Yoginī Aṇimā, the bestower of supernatural powers, at the western gate in the southern corner.
O Goddess, one should then worship Laghimā in the north;
O Śivā, one should worship Mahimā at the eastern gate in the north.
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship the power of mastery (īśitva) and the accomplishment (siddhi) at the southern gate;
one should conquer the power of control (vaśitva) and the accomplishment at the northwest gate in that same sequence.
Likewise, one should worship Bhuktisiddhi in the southeast according to that same sequence,
and one should worship Icchāsiddhi in the eastern quarter and the southwest.
Attainment is perfection; she who grants all desires is the Supreme Goddess.
O Goddess praised by the gods, she is to be known through the yoga of the downward and upward sequence.
Brāhmī and Māheśvarī are [the first two], and Indrāṇī is the third;
Kaumārī and Vaiṣṇavī are likewise, and Vārāhikā shall be the sixth.
And Cāmuṇḍā and Mahālakṣmī are on the other side.
O Dear One, Brahmāṇī and the others should be worshipped there in their proper sequence;
Brahmāṇī is yellow in color and adorned with four faces.
Māheśī is white in color, has three eyes, and holds a thread; her hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, while she honors the book and the syllables.
O Dear One, Kaumārī is red in color; she holds a garland of skulls and an axe in her hands, and she bears a spear and a javelin.
The Supreme Goddess Vaiṣṇavī, dark-complexioned, should be meditated upon with her hands granting boons and fearlessness, holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus.
Bearing [implements] with her lotus-like hands and adorned with divine ornaments,
Vārāhī possesses a dark complexion and is radiant with the face of a boar.
Holding a plow, a pestle, a sword, and a spear in her hands,
Aindrī is dark-green in color, with her hand radiant with a red lotus.
Cāmuṇḍā is black in color and holds a trident, a hand-drum,
a sword, and a vetāla in her right hands.
Mahālakṣmī, however, is yellowish in luster and holds a lotus, a mirror,
a mātuluṅga fruit, and a supreme vessel.
In the square [mandala], they are manifested in order starting from the west.
One should worship the Cakramātṛkā, beginning with Kṣobhaṇā, Drāvaṇā, Ākarṣaṇī, Vaśyā, Unmādinī, Mahāṅkuśā, Khecarī, and Vīrayoni, as well as Trikhaṇḍā.
Having worshipped [the goddesses] in a counter-clockwise direction starting from the northwest as before,
one should worship this supreme Tripurā, the Mistress of the Gods, after having worshipped her.
In front of the perfection of *aṇimā*, one should display the mudrā that accomplishes all desired aims and agitates all beings, O dweller in the lotus.
The wheel that fulfills all desires is situated within the secret womb;
therefore, O Goddess, one should worship it with sixteen spokes for the sake of accomplishing one's purpose.
The goddess Kābhākarṣaṇikā has the form of attracting the intellect;
she is the attractor of the ego and has the form of attracting sound.
She whose form is the attraction of touch, and she whose nature is the attraction of form;
she whose form is the attraction of taste, and she whose nature is the attraction of smell.
She is the form of attracting thoughts and the form of attracting fortitude;
she is the form of attracting memory and the form of attracting names.
O Goddess, these sixteen Nityās, endowed with vowels and situated within the lunar mandala, are arranged in order starting from the west in the sixteen-spoked [cakra].
One should constantly meditate on the Nityā who is joined with the vowels; she rains nectar upon the heart and bestows the gift of saffron jars filled with nectar, marked with the noose and goad.
O Dear One, one should worship the goddess Cakreśvarī, the Mistress of Tripura, who bestows prosperity;
one should fulfill the desires of her whose form is the attraction of all wishes.
Having displayed the mudrā that causes all to flee, one should present [the offering].
In the Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa-cakra,
the wise one should worship the most secret Anaṅgakusumā in the east with the *ka*-group.
And in the south, one should worship Anaṅgamekhalā with the *ca*-group;
then Anaṅgamadanā with the *ṭa*-group in the west.

Thereafter, one should worship with the *tavarga* [consonants] in the north, and then, in the southeast corner, one should worship the line of the limbs (*aṅga*) and the limbs of passion (*anaṅgamadana*) afflicted with love, using the *pavarga* [consonants].
One should worship Anaṅgavegā with the group of consonants beginning with *ya* in the southwest,
and likewise one should worship Anaṅgāṅkuśā with the group of consonants beginning with *śa* in the northwest.
In the northeast, one should worship Anaṅgamālinī with a hundred thousand [offerings];
these goddesses are most secret, possessing the luster of bandhūka flowers.
One should visualize her holding a noose, a goad, and a blue lotus with a stalk in her hands.
Then one should worship the goddess Cakreśvarī, who bestows universal sovereignty, as well as Tripurasundarī, Anaṅgakusumā, and the others.
And one should display the mudrā of universal attraction, O Goddess praised by the gods.
Having worshipped the Cakrapūjyā, one should then worship the fourth wheel—
the wheel that bestows great good fortune, resplendent with the letter *ka*.
Born from the source known as Saṃpradāya, she is adorned with all ornaments;
she holds a noose, a goad, a mirror, and a vessel for drinking nectar.
Vitraṃtya, Sarvasubhagā, and Vilohitā from the west;
likewise, the power Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī and Sarvavidrāviṇī.
She is the power that attracts all, she who causes the delight of all;
she is the power that utterly deludes all, and she whose form is the paralyzing of all.
She is the power that subdues all, the one who brings everything under her control;
she is the power that delights all, the soul of all who brings everything under her sway.
The power that accomplishes all aims, whose form is every prosperity,
the power consisting of all mantras, which brings about the destruction of all suffering.
There, one should worship the supreme Yoginī, the mistress of the wheel (Cakreśvarī), the bestower of accomplishments, who dwells in Tripura and embodies the supreme oral tradition.
Then, having displayed the Vaśya-mudrā and subsequently offered [the oblation] with the Sarvārthasādhaka-cakra, which is beautifully adorned with the letters of the alphabet;
Resembling the hibiscus flower, adorned with shimmering jewels,
she possesses great good fortune and deep, full, rounded, and firm breasts.
The practitioner, with a pure mind, beholds a divine jewel-casket placed before him,
containing various jewels and possessing smiling faces.
One should visualize the Yoginīs there as holding nooses and goads.
One should worship in reverse order, beginning from the west; she bestows all accomplishments.
Thus, the Goddess is the giver of all siddhis and likewise the giver of all prosperity.
She is the one who makes everything dear, the bringer of all auspiciousness,
the goddess who grants all desires, and the liberator from all suffering.
The goddess who pacifies all death, destroys all obstacles,
is beautiful in every limb, and bestows all prosperity.
One should worship these goddesses in the ten-spoked [cakra] in reverse order, starting from the west;
in front is the Goddess who bestows all siddhis, the Mistress of the Krama.
O Beloved, having displayed the *sarvānmādini* mudrā and having made the offering, one should worship the Goddess Tripurā, the bestower of all accomplishments.
In the wheel that is the source of all jewels, resplendent with the color of bees,
one should worship the Nigarbha Yoginī starting from the west in reverse order.
Possessing the brilliance of a thousand rising suns, adorned with ornaments of pearls,
they hold nooses and goads as weapons, and their eight hands grant knowledge, liberation, and boons.
One should worship these goddesses, who bestow the fruits desired on the path;
they are all-knowing, all-powerful, and likewise the givers of all sovereignty.
The Goddess consists of all-knowledge, she is the destroyer of all diseases,
her very nature is the support of all, and likewise she is the remover of all sins.
O Goddess, you consist of all bliss, you are the embodiment of all protection;
O Goddess, you are the secret bestower of all desired objects and the granter of the accomplishment of all aims.
One should worship in the sequence beginning from the west in the *paṅktiyonika* [arrangement];
in front of Sarvajñā, one should worship the Goddess, the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśī*), Mālinī.
Having displayed the great hook and the great mudrā, and having made the offering, [he should proceed].
O Maheśānī, O beloved Mistress of the Gods, one should worship the Yoginī in the central wheel;
she dwells in the eight-cornered wheel that removes all diseases.
In the wheel that removes all diseases, the eight groups [of letters] unfold;
one should worship the secret Yoginī in reverse order, beginning from the west.
Below Śrīkaṇṭha is [the goddess] whose luster is like the flower of the pomegranate tree;
she is clothed in red garments and anointed with red perfumes and unguents.
One should properly worship [the goddess] with red flowers and unbroken rice grains; she bestows all accomplishments.
[The attendants are] adorned with various ornaments, profound, and bearing the five arrows and the bow.
One should write the eight groups of great syllables, each standing in its own group, bearing a book and a boon-granting gesture, and marked with the bindu and nāda.
I shall describe the fruit at the end of the vowels, marked by the moon (the letter *u*) on the left ear (the letter *a*);
the goddess or deity to be worshipped is the beautiful one named Āveśinī.

At the end of the *ka*-group, one should write the supreme Kāmeśvarī joined with the letter *la*; then, at the end of the *ca*-group, one should write that which is enriched by the letter *va*, the left eye (*i*), and the moon (*u*).
After this, one should worship Ādinī at the end of the ṭa-group;
thereafter, one should worship Vāyu and Kṣmā, along with the vowel 'u' and the left ear (the letter 'i'), together with the bindu and the digit (kalā).

One should worship the goddess Aruṇā, who is characterized by the end of the *tavarga* (the dental class), the letter *ja*, and the digit of the moon in the left eye; now the end of the *pavarga* (the labial class) is being described.
Adorned with the sky-seed (ha), earth (la), water (va), wind (ya), and the moon-lord (sa), by this [mantra] Jayanī is to be worshipped; thereafter, the end of the *ya*-group is written.
With what should one worship her who consists of the letter *ra*, the wind, and the *praṇava*;
she who is the sovereign of all (*sarveśvarī*), situated at the end of the *la*-group, and endowed with *kṣama*, fire, Īśa, and the *bindu*?
With this, the wise one should worship the goddess Kaulinī on the eighth day;
at the conclusion of the Aṣṭakā, O Maheśānī, he should worship these deities of speech.
O Great Goddess, having uttered the five arrows consisting of Kāma and Kāmeśvarī,
one should worship the deities of the bow known as Bhañjanā.
One should worship the bow-deity named Mohanā, who belongs to Kāmeśvarī, as having Dharma, Artha, and Kāma for its strings, and the second string consisting of the self (ātman).
O Mistress of the World, the second pair of nooses is the subduer;
O Dear One, it is the weapon of Kāmeśa and Kāma that attracts the three worlds.
Having uttered the *aṅkuśa* (goad) mantra, one should utter it for the purpose of immobilization (*staṃbhana*).
One should worship the goad of Kāmeśvara and Kāmeśvarī in the proper sequence.
Outside the enclosure of the six limbs, one should worship the eight weapons;
in the three corners, one should worship the three goddesses endowed with the three peak-syllables (*kūṭas*).
One should worship in the four directions in order, beginning from the west;
one should first worship Kāmeśvarī, the power of Rudra, with the first *kūṭa*.
Having worshipped the power called Rudra, who belongs to Viṣṇu, at the southern corner with the second syllable,
one should worship her with the third syllable as well.
One should worship Bhagamālā, the power of Brahmā, in the north; Viśvamātṛkā, known as Cakreśvarī, in the west; and Kāmeśī in front.
Then, having displayed the seed-syllable mudrā (bījamudrā), one should offer the worship of the wheel (cakrapūjā).
Kāmeśvarī is white in color, adorned with white garlands and unguents.

Adorned with ornaments shimmering with pearls and decorated with various other jewels, she holds in her hands, in successive order, a book, a rosary, a face [representing speech], and the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya-mudrā).
Placing them at the forefront, they are worthy of worship and are proclaimed as the powers of Rudra.
Vajreśvarī is saffron-colored, adorned with shimmering jewels,
clothed in the morning sun, and her eyes kiss her dark ears.

Vajreśvarī, adorned with the *ikṣuka* flower and the staff-flower, and graced by the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*), is the Great Goddess (*Maheśvarī*), the power (*śakti*) of Viṣṇu, on the right side.
To the north is Bhagamālā, who instantly possesses the luster of molten gold;
she is the Mistress of the World, adorned with ornaments set with priceless jewels.
O Maheśānī, you who hold the noose, the goad, the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā), the boon-granting mudrā, the conch, the lotus, and the lute;
you are the power of Brahman and the cutter away of the threefold afflictions.
O beautiful one, listen: within the wheel consisting of all bliss, known as Rājavaiṃdava, there is the form of Brahmā; and within the form of Viṣṇu, there is the form of Śambhu.
One should worship Tripurā, the Yoginī known as the supreme and inferior secret,
having uttered the three peak-syllables (kūṭas), which constitute the essential nature of all vidyās.
One should worship Mahātripurasundarī, who is the form of all deities and consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, as she has been offered into the wheel (cakra).
Having performed worship, one should there worship her who dwells in the supreme and the non-supreme secret;
having honored her with ritual offerings such as perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains.
The eternal Yoginī, the bestower of accomplishments, for the sake of achieving the goals of enjoyment and desire;
indeed, the Śrīvidyā of sixteen syllables, which grants the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
To the Mistress of all wheels, who is saluted by all the traditions;
the Sovereign of all traditions, adorned with knowledge, whose form is Brahman.
Having worshipped thoroughly with ritual services such as perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains,
one should again offer libations three times with the root mantra.
Having displayed the *yonimudrā*, one should then display the mudrās in succession:
Tripurā, who has the luster of crystal, is adorned with pearls and jewels.
One should constantly meditate upon her, the destroyer of great sins, who holds a book, a rosary, a vase, and an excellent lotus.
One should meditate upon Tripureśī, who embodies all forms, beautiful, with the luster of saffron,
endowed with every ornament, and holding a book and a rosary.
Holding the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, possessing all power, and with a smiling countenance—
the Goddess Tripuravāsinī should be meditated upon as being identical to her.
O Śrī Maheśānī Tripurā, you whose eyes are slightly reddened at the corners and rolling with great intoxication, and who possess full, rounded, and firm breasts.
She possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns, is adorned with divine ornaments,
and holds a book and a rosary, while bestowing boons and granting fearlessness.
Now she who bestows a garland of all-bliss is described:
the Goddess Indragopaprabhā, who holds a noose, a goad, and a skull-cup.
This very moment, one should meditate upon the supreme sovereign goddess, the destroyer of fear, who is perfectly accomplished and who instantly removes the great terrors of practitioners.
Bestowing prosperity like Bhairavī, she grants great accomplishments;
together with the Cakra, she is the presiding deity of each individual Cakra.
Having understood that this wheel is indeed extremely profound, one should worship it;
or else, there may be a salutation with the thought, "I worship the sandals."
One should utter "svāhā" during a fire-oblation (homa), but during a libation (tarpaṇa), one should remember the words "I satisfy" (tarpayāmi).
Alternatively, O Supreme Goddess, one should contemplate all the rays in the form of goddesses within the Śrīcakra, each resembling her own [original] self in the Svatantra.
O auspicious lady, you must guard this [teaching] as you would your own womb, O Pārvatī;
it consists of the food offering endowed with the six flavors, the wish-fulfilling cow, and the purificatory thread.
Having offered betel-leaf mixed with camphor to the Supreme Śakti,
O beloved, they perform the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) according to the previously mentioned procedure.
And as before, one should offer the bali-oblation for the sake of all prosperity;
O Great Goddess, it is dear to Vaṭuka and to the Yoginīs.
One should offer the bali-oblation to Gaṇeśa and the two Kṣetrapālas as before;
then, one should scatter it around the left side of that maṇḍala.
There, one should worship the support (ādhāra) with an offering of food, water, and other oblations;
having consecrated it with the appropriate mantra, one should present the bali-offering to all beings.

O Goddess worshipped by heroes, O Sovereign of the World, one should [utter] the mantra of sixteen syllables three times, followed by the *tāra* (Om), and then the words "all obstacles" (*sarvavighna*).
Having uttered "hūṃ" and "vahnivallabhā" for all beings, one should offer the bali-oblation with the mudrā known as Tattvasaṃjñā.
The five-fold *vali* has been declared as the supreme means for constant protection;
one should perform the recitation and the hymn of praise to the Supreme Goddess according to one's capacity.
p. 199b) Now, the Makaranda-stotra.

O Mother, whose nature is the form of Time, consisting of the seed-syllable *Śrī*, the two—the *Nāda* and the *Bindu*—and the digit of the moon; O Sovereign of the helpless, who art the refuge of those suffering from the cold of ignorance, grant me increase!
Cast away my dullness, O Goddess whose lotus feet shine with true splendor, capable of destroying the darkness of nescience, and worshipped by Brahmā, Śiva, and others.
I bow to Śambhu’s beloved, who is surrounded by the hosts of gods and the lords of the immortals.

O Giver of Boons, protect that Śambhu-śakti, whose nature is the seed-syllable *Lajjā*, who dwells playfully throughout the three worlds, who has come to eternally sustain the universe and the Mother of the three worlds;
she who is the primordial source of worldly existence, composed of all virtues, whose form is Being-Consciousness-Bliss, and whose essence is radiant light.
I bow to the three-eyed one, the destroyer of the darkness of ignorance in the three worlds.

I bow to her whose seed-syllable is *klīṃ*, who holds the bow and arrows of the flower of passion (*kāmarāja*), and who is enriched with a noose and goad; she whose radiant form is like the sun, enchanting the three worlds with the beauty born of the moon;
she who shines with the ornaments of tinkling anklets, girdles, necklaces, armlets, crowns, and gleaming gold and rubies.

O Mother, you are the very essence of the seed-syllable of speech (Vāṇī-bīja), who destroys the darkness of inertia in the three worlds; you are the nature of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), and you alone are the Veda ever being sung. O Mother, grant me the intellect that brings about the cessation of the great agitation caused by dualities in this assembly.
I praise Your lotus feet, which surpass even the speech of Bṛhaspati with their manifold words.

O Śakti, you alone are the primordial cause in the production of effects such as jars and cloths; you are the primordial source in the transformation of the great principle (mahat) and the rest, which is seen as the cause aided by Māyā.
You are the Vidyā that serves as the cause for the cessation of the deluded mind regarding the expansion of various words.
O you whose movement brings about the destruction of the hosts deluded by ignorance, may you bestow upon me a state of pure being for all worlds.
Oṃ! Homage to you, Mother, whose form is the three-syllabled Brahman churned from the Vedas; protect me daily, for I am devoid of sense-control and have fallen into the blind well of false knowledge.
I am being tormented by enemies—the first host of delusion, anger, and greed.
Bound by his wife, sons, and other dependents, as well as by various people with chains.

O Mother, known by the syllable *Hrīṃ*, burn away my misdeeds, diseases, poverty, and the seeds of rebirth within my own form; I pray for devotion to take root at the periphery of your lotus feet in my heart.
You are eternal Lakṣmī, you are the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī), and you are the form of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods—thus I meditate upon you constantly.
O Refuge, here in this world, [all things] have been rendered worthy of protection by the multitude of your motherly glances alone.

O Śrī, whose nature is auspiciousness, O Mother of the Universe, you who are the embodiment of truth and endowed with meditation, grant your grace! All wealth, such as gold, rubies, and other jewels, is truly worthy for the worship of your feet.

O Goddess, grant me the knowledge that brings liberation; release this wretched one who is being scorched by the fires of worldly existence, while being attended by the lords of yogis who possess the luster of nectar.
The fourth source is desire; the seed-syllable of Bhuvaneśī belongs to the Lord of the ten vowels. I praise that which is not merely a sequence of letters, but which grants boons at Your feet.
Those who, having placed the pair of Your lotus-feet within the lotus of their hearts, meditate with single-minded focus—
The lords of sages have become liberated from the bondage of karma and the dualities of impurity.

O Mother, I have sought refuge in you, whose slender body is fashioned from the very forms of the syllables: Brahmā (Bram), Indu (I), Kāmadeva (Ka), Viyat (Ha), Amaraguru (U), and the seed-syllable known as Bhuvaneśī (E).
Upon the heads of Viṣṇu and Brahmā, she shines with the luster of a jeweled crown.
In that lotus emerging from the primordial source, which is brilliantly illuminated by the yogi-lords who have attained steadfastness through its practice;
The Moon (Indu), Desire (Kāma), the two Lords of the Gods (Sureśau), joined with Fire (Vahni) and the Abode (Ala), conjoined with the Half-Moon of the Left Eye (Vāmanetrārdhacandra)—
this is the Bīja-mantra which is also Your body, whose nature is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (Saccidānanda).
You are Vālā, Bhairavī, the Mother of the Three Worlds (Tribhuvanajananī), Tāriṇī, Nīlavāṇī, Gaurī, and Kālī.
She consists of all virtuous qualities and is the bestower of great liberation.

O Sovereign of Heroes, born from the syllable *Sauṃ* and known throughout the three worlds, you alone are the primordial Śakti; joined with you, this Śambhu is empowered to move, for without you he is inert. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva receive their heads [of power] merely by a fraction of your grace.
Established in Your state, O Cakrin, You perform the creation, preservation, and dissolution [of the universe] without ceasing.

O Mother, you who are the seed-syllable *aiṃ* known as Vāgbhava, the moonlight that dispels the darkness of dull-wittedness— protect me, who am bereft of a protector, with a glance that is a drop of the nectar of your stream of compassion;
for those whose minds are bound by your great *māyā*, O Mother, remain deluded even while they are being deluded.
The lords of sages, possessing knowledge of Your pair of feet, pray for Your compassion.

O best of men, O lady with beautiful teeth, the syllable *klīṃ* is your seed-form; in the central region, you are the manifest embodiment of Brahman. This body of Madana is the deluder of Brahmā himself. Within the Command (*ājñā-cakra*), your smiling lotus-face shines like the nectar-stream of the Vedas.
But when the daughter of the Himālaya mountain has attained the form of Mahendra, together with her limbs and so forth.
O you whose form is Time, you are here as the moon-faced one; O Hrīḥ, you alone are my own essential nature.
You are patience, and you are splendor; you alone are the forms of Hari, Hara, Kamala, and all beings.

You are accomplishment, you are supernatural power, and you are the consort of the enemy of Smara; deluding [the world], you are the sacred lore that is the cause of liberation. You alone are the destroyer of suffering for those who have entered the ocean of existence.
O Śrī, who are rich in beauty, whose seed-syllable is auspicious, and who are utterly indivisible from the mind of Madhuripu;
