by even a mere fragment of Your glance, this Lord of the Immortals attained his status as the Lord of Heaven.
Thus, this celebrated and excellent mantra of sixteen syllables is the sole cause for both heaven and liberation;
those who always worship this supreme mantra obtain the eight supernatural powers (siddhis).
Having worshipped Mahātripurasundarī according to the prescribed rite and having recited this hymn, one shall attain union with the Goddess.
Thus ends the hymn named *Makaranda*, issued from the lotus-mouth of Śiva, within the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara in the *Śrī Rudrayāmala Mahātantra*.
Now he speaks the armor (kavaca) of Mahātripurasundarī.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, you who bestow grace upon the worlds;
by your favor, O Mahādeva, many mantras have been heard by me in various ways.
O Lord, I have heard from you the various means of accomplishment (sādhana), as well as the extraction of divine pins (kīlaka) and the removal of defects such as curses.
O Lord, although the armor (kavaca) of the Goddess Rājarājeśvarī has been briefly indicated, I desire to hear it from you; please tell it to me as well.
The illustrious Lord said:
O Great Goddess, O beloved, though you have been restrained by me hundreds of thousands of times again and again, you persist in asking me about the nature of women.
O Goddess of gods, for your pleasure I shall describe this armor that is extremely well-guarded and bestows all desired boons; listen to it.
The sage of this armor-mantra (kavaca) of the glorious sixteen-fold knowledge (ṣoḍaśī-vidyā) is remembered as Mahādeva; Pañkti is declared to be its meter.
The Goddess is proclaimed as the Queen of the Kings of Gods, the Supreme Deity;
O Goddess, her application is proclaimed for the accomplishment of all aims.
May Bhairavī protect me in the east; may Bālā protect me in the south;
may Nālinī protect me in the west, and Trāsinī in the north.
May Mahādevī Mahātripurasundarī protect [me] above;
may the Goddess of gods, who dwells in the depths of Pātāla, protect [me] below.
May Vāgbhava protect the base; likewise, may Kāmarāja protect the heart;
and may Bhrāmara, the granter of all desires, protect her head eternally.
May the Blessed One, the Great Vidyā, the Supreme Goddess, protect me always at the aperture of Brahmā, in all my limbs, and in every location of the body's openings.
Aiṃ Klīṃ; may [the deity] protect me on the forehead; may he protect me.
Hrīṃ, Klīṃ, and Vlūṃ are for the two eyes; Drāṃ, Dreṃ, and Drīṃ are likewise for the nose and the two ears, as well as the chin.
May *sauḥ* protect my throat and heart; may *saḥ* protect the region of the navel;
may *kala hrīṃ klīṃ strīṃ* protect the secret place; and may *sa hrīṃ* protect my feet.
May he protect me everywhere with *hrīṃ*; may he protect my joints with *klīṃ*—in water, on land, as well as in the sky, in the cardinal directions, and likewise in the royal palace.
HŪM—may Khemā protect me swiftly; SA HRĪM SA KLĪM—obeisance to Bhava; and HAṂSA—may Mahādevī protect me; these are the supreme, partless deities.
May Vijayā, Maṅgalādūtī, Kalyāṇī, Bhagamālinī, Jñānā, Mālinī, and Vidyā— the auspicious Śivā— protect me at all times.
Thus, O Goddess, this armor, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain, has been declared by me out of affection for you; it must be guarded with great effort.
This is the supreme secret, dear one, more hidden than the hidden;
it is auspicious, bestowing wealth, fame, long life, enjoyment, and liberation.
O Goddess Śivā, it destroys the evil dreams of men, brings under control both men and women, effects attraction, and performs the rites of paralyzing and exorcism.
Having learned this armor-mantra of Śivā, the sovereign of the queens of kings, whoever worships her along with the hosts of Yoginīs shall be devoured by them; of this there is no doubt.
O Daughter of Śiva, for such a person, there shall never be success in mantra;
moreover, in this world, there will be poverty, disease, suffering, and fear.
Having gone to hell in the next world, one may be reborn in the womb of an animal;
therefore, through constant practice of this, one shall thereafter become qualified.
Whoever recites this highly meritorious armor (*kavaca*) that has issued from my mouth according to the prescribed rite before the ritual of worship,
shall enjoy fortune, pleasures, and auspicious delights, and at the time of death, he attains the abode of the Goddess.
Thus ends the complete Sixteen-Syllable Armor of Śrī Mahātripurasundarī from the Kulāntasaṃhitā.
Now, he states the mantra of Tripurabhairava.
The mantra of Tripurabhairava consists of the syllables *māyā* (hrīṃ), *lakṣmī* (śrīṃ), and *haṃsa*, followed by the seed-syllable *prāsāda* (hauṃ) and ending with the wife of fire (svāhā).
Likewise, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga), the offering of oblations (bali), worship, and so forth, with the root mantra (mūlamantra).
Now, meditation.
He has one face, three eyes, and is endowed with four arms;
in his right hands he holds a goad and a sword, and in his left hands a shield and a noose.
One should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord, red in color, seated upon a bull,
with hair standing erect, adorned with necklaces of human skulls and garlands of severed heads.
Having thus meditated upon Tripurabhairava in this manner, [one should proceed].
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Daily Worship of Śrīvidyā," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Now, the sequence of Tripurabhairavī is written down.
Now I shall describe the ritual procedure for worship, which is concealed in all tantras and specifically set forth by the Goddess Tripurabhairavī.
Having performed the *pīṭha-nyāsa* up to the end of the ritual placement, one should perform the *savyādi-nyāsa*.
O Maheśānī, the immutable Dakṣiṇāmūrti is the *ṛṣi* of this [mantra].
O beloved, one should place the *paṅkti* meter on the head because it is worthy of worship; the goddess Vālā Tripurā Parameśvarī is at the mouth of the *chaṃdas* and in the heart.

The seed-syllable *vāgbhava* is said to be the first; one should contemplate the third as *śakti*. Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) from the navel to the feet, one should perform another from the throat to the navel.
One should sequentially place the three syllables from the crown of the head down to the throat.
Now follows the placement of the Vidyā-mantra (vidyānyāsa).
Then, O Śivā, one should perform the placement of the Vidyā with the three seed-syllables in their proper sequence:
first, one should place them on the two hands at the wrists, the palms, and the fingers.
Having placed [the hands] on the right and left sides, at the belly, the elbows,
and the palms, one should likewise place them again on the right and left feet.
O Goddess, one should then place [the seed-syllables] at the end of the *nāda* upon the heart-liṅga;
O Queen of the Gods, one should place them upon these limbs according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*).
O Supreme Goddess, understand the creation of the Vidyā according to the sequence;
then one should perform the Nyāsa consisting of the nine wombs (navayoni) by means of the three seed-syllables.
This has already been explained previously, in the very sequence of the Śrīvidyā.
Now begins the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the *ṛṣis* and so forth.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the three seed-syllables of Mūla, Hrīṃ, and Prīṃ—representing the mind-born goddess—at these locations in reverse order: at the heart, between the eyebrows, and on the head.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of these [deities]— Amṛteśī, Yogeśī, and Viśvayoni— in their proper sequence using the seed-syllables in reverse order, one should then perform the placement of the forms (mūrtinyāsa).
One should first arrange [the seed-syllables] according to the sequence, joined with the fire (Ra) on the left of Bhṛgu (Sa);
this is proclaimed as the placement of the seed-syllables beginning with the five short vowels, starting with Sadyojāta.
Now follows the placement of the arrows (vāṇanyāsa).
O Supreme Goddess, one should place the five arrows in sequence upon the fingers of the hand,
starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger, in due order.
Then, one should place the objects of desire in those locations according to the proper sequence.
Now follows the ritual placement on the hands and limbs (karāṅganyāsa).
The ritual of the limbs (aṅgakriyā) is considered to be performed with the first seed-syllable joined with the six long vowels;
[it is applied] to the head, the feet, the mouth, the secret place, and the lotus of the heart.
Having written two final *tha*s situated in the fire [triangle] in sequence,
it is adorned on the left by a mouth-circle and an eye.

O fair-faced one, these two arrows are proclaimed: the *mādana* [arrow] situated on the earth, and that which consists of the form of the fourth vowel, the bindu, and so forth, together with the nasal sound (*nāda*).
O Dear One, the beloved [mantra] is mounted on Śakra (the letter *ka*), adorned by the left ear (the letter *u*), joined with the Bindu and Nāda, and possesses the Visarga; it is the Moon.
O Pārvatī, O Great Goddess, listen to the names of the five arrows:
Drāvaṇa, Kṣobhaṇa, and those known as Vaśya and Ākarṣaṇa, O Goddess.
Likewise, O Supreme Goddess, one should place the names in sequence:
Drāmādyā Drāviṇī on the head, and Drīmādyā Kṣobhiṇī on the feet.
One should place *klīṃ*, preceded by the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, for subjugation in the mouth and the secret place;
then, for attraction, one should again place it ending with the letter *sa* (the end of creation) and situated in *bhṛgu* (the letter *s*).
In this manner, the placement of the arrows (vāṇanyāsa) has been described as progressively deluding;
O Supreme Goddess, [the sequence is] the Parā-bīja, the central arrow, and the Vāgbhava [bīja].
O Dear One, the seed-syllable HŪM is [placed] in sequence.
O beloved, hear these names of the five deities of desire:
Kāma, Manmatha, Kandarpa, Makara, and he who is known as Dhvaja.
O Great Goddess, the fish-bannered one (Kāmadeva) is conceived as the fifth.
Now follows the Subhagādinyāsa.
The five stars beginning with Subhaga and others are located at the forehead, between the eyebrows, the face, the throat, the heart, and the two bases of the navel.
Vrūṃ, strīṃ, and saḥ—these five seed-syllables of speech and desire have been proclaimed.
Now follows the ornamentation, which is the ritual placement (nyāsa).
One should place [the vowels] on the head, the forehead, the eyebrows, the two ears, the two eyes,
the two cheeks, the two nostrils, the two rows of teeth, and the mouth.
On the chin, the throat, the neck, the two sides, the pair of breasts,
the two armpits, the two elbows, and on the regions of the upper arms and their backs.
Then [one should place them] at the navel, the secret place, the thighs, the shanks, and then the calves; afterwards, on the buttocks, the knees, and finally on the backs of the big toes of the feet.
Being composed, one should not place the letters of the *kādika* series in these locations:
first on the girdle and the necklace, then on the bracelet, the heart, and the secret organ.
The seventh preceptor should thus duly place twenty-eight *lavaśākṣarāṃhasas* on the two ears, the two cheeks, and the head.
Now, as for meditative absorption (dhyāna).

Oṃ! [I salute her] who possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns, who wears a red silken garment and a garland of lotus fibers, whose breasts are smeared with red pigment, and who holds a rosary, the Vidyā, and the gestures of fearlessness and boon-granting.
I bow to the Goddess Dakṣiṇā, who holds a hand and an eye, whose face shines with the splendor of three eyes,
and who wears a crown of fire, the moon, and jewels.
The one known as Yoni is renowned in the heart; she becomes the protector of the three worlds. The Supreme Goddess residing in the mouth is named the "Molten Flow of the Three Worlds."
O Great Goddess, when situated between the eyebrows, she becomes the attractor of the three worlds;
O Great Goddess, when situated on the forehead, she is the subduer of the three worlds.
Residing in the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), she alone is the supreme goddess who brings delight to all;
composed of the five mudrās, she displays the yoni-mudrā.
Then, having performed the ritual for arranging the vessels and other implements, one should draw the yantra;
thereafter, having performed the internal sacrifice (antaryajana), one should carry out the external worship (bāhyapūjā).
There, sitting facing the east, one should arrange the extraction of the yantra;
one should draw straight lines from Īśāna to Agni.
Drawing two lines from the tips of the eastern and southern [lines] toward the northeast, the preceptor unifies them at the western point;
this is the supreme Śakti-line, O Śiva.
O Śivā, this pair of powers has the form of a triangle;
one should draw them like a jeweled staff at the front of the eastern power.
O Supreme Goddess, one should then draw a line from the junction of those two powers toward the southwest corner (vāyurākṣasa-koṇa), following the sequence of dividing the joints.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, having drawn lines from the two corners toward the east, make them prominent; that shall be the fire-maṇḍala with its apex pointing east.
This king of wheels (cakrarāja) shall be enriched by the beauty of nine wombs (navayoni). Upon its periphery, one should draw a circle resembling the full moon.
O Śivā, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with six corners at the rising sign (lagna),
adorned with four beautiful gates, which always bestows all bliss.
Having drawn the yantra on a plate of gold, silver, or other materials,
or upon the ground, or on sandalwood pedestals with saffron, aguru, and sandalwood, one should worship it.
Just as [an image] fashioned from clay might be decorated with vermilion powder, musk, saffron, and the like, using a pen made of gold and jewels;
O Goddess of the gods, having drawn the yantra, one should prepare the articles for worship.
Then, with the power of the Ādhāra [cakra] and so forth: Hrīṃ, salutation to the Self of Knowledge (jñānātman).
Having thus fully worshipped [the deity], one should worship the nine powers, beginning with Icchā, in the filaments starting from the east and in the center.
She is Icchā, Jñānā, and Kriyā; she is the beloved of desire, the bestower of desires, the one dear to Rati, the infinite one, and the one who intoxicates with passion.
These are proclaimed as the Pīṭha-Śaktis of Tripurabhairavī. Vāgbhava, Lohitarāyai, Śrīkaṇṭha, Lohita, and Anala.
Dīrgharāva ai parāpaścādayarāyai hrauṃ; again:
Sadāśiva mahāpreta, ending with ṅa (ṅe), [is] Padmāsana, [ending with] namaḥ.
With this [mantra], one should offer a seat to the lineage of the venerable gurus;
thereafter, one should worship within the interval between the eastern and central yonis.
Having invoked the deity into that form with five *praṇavas*,
one should then [invoke] Vākśakti, Kamalā, Ha-sa-kha-phaṃ-sa-sau.
Then, at the end of the root mantra, one should perform the visualization of the Goddess's form within the bindu.

Having meditated upon the Goddess with the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā as before, and having invoked her, one should perform the worship of the surrounding deities (*āvaraṇārcana*) after propitiating her with all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*) according to one's capacity.
And so it is said:
One should perform the worship of the limbs starting from the center and the directions, such as the northeast (abhīśāsu) and the northwest (vāyavya).
There should be two goddesses in the north and likewise two in the south.
And first, one should worship the five arrows in sequence, one by one;
likewise, O Goddess, one should worship the five Kāmas after the arrows.
In the center, within the triangular yonis, in that very sequence,
are Rati, Prīti, and Manobhavā, according to the order of the bāla-seed syllables.
Then, in the eight birth-places starting from the east in sequence, are the eight Śaktis beginning with Śubhagā, preceded by their respective mantras.
O Maheśānī, at the end of one's own mantra, [the goddesses] Śubhagā, Bhagā, and likewise Bhagasarpiṇī are to be worshipped within the eight yonis.
Bhagamālinī, Anaṅgā, Anaṅgakusumā,
as well as Anaṅgarekhā and Anaṅgamadanā are thus proclaimed.
Then, on the eight petals in order starting from the east, [one should place] the eight Mothers, Brāhmī and the others, together with Asitāṅga and the rest.
The Mothers, who cause fear and are overwhelmed by the agitation of their speech and pride,
should be duly worshipped with flowers and other offerings upon the eight petals.
Outside of that, in the four squares, one should worship Indra and the other [deities], and outside of those again,
having worshipped their mantras, one should perform recitation according to one's capacity.
Now follows the hymn to Bhairavī.
By means of the *raktapāna* (red-drink) rite, one should propitiate the venerable Tripurā for the attainment of desired fruits;
by means of which men attain that Lakṣmī who is worshipped by the gods.

Even Brahmā and the other gods do not know her subtle form through hundreds of hymns— her world-originating, beginningless embodiment; therefore, O Subhaga, praise her who is the source of all speech, whose breasts are curved within and possess the luster of saffron.

I worship you in the city of Tripurā—you who possess the splendor of a thousand suns suddenly risen, whose hands bear the marks of the book, the rosary, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness; whose lotus-like face is adorned with three blue-lotus eyes, and who are radiant with a necklace of sapphires.

O Mother, those of dull intellect— whose minds are agitated by mutual strife and discord— do they know Your form, which is beautiful with streams of vermilion upon the weight of Your breasts, and which is attainable only through the fruit of merit earned in previous births?
Sages declare you to be gross, while those learned in the Vedas describe you as subtle;
others call you the root of the worlds, yet we worship you, O Bhava, as an ocean of boundless compassion.
I meditate within my heart upon you, who possess the crescent moon as an ornament, who are white with drops of nectar, who consist of fifteen syllables,
and who hold a book, a rosary, a jar filled with nectar, and the act of exposition.
Holding [the image] with her lotus-like hands, she possesses three eyes.
You are Śambhu, whose half-body is embraced by the Daughter of the Mountain; you alone are Viṣṇu, whose body is joined with Kamalā.
You are the one born from the lotus, the abode of speech; you alone are the ground for them and the triple city in this world.
Relying upon the four vowels beginning with *parā* which arise from the *vāgbhava* syllable and are assigned to the various parts of the body,
and through the organs such as the throat, I never at any time forget you, the Supreme Goddess, who consists of the *māṃsa* (flesh) element, within my heart.
Having drawn in the breath and conquered the six enemies, those of virtuous deeds meditate with an unwavering mind upon the tip of their own nose on Your form—
adorned with the rays of the moon as its crest-ornament, resembling the rising sun, and situated at the crown of the head.
"O Daughter of the Mountain, O sole Mother of the World, it is the Vedic teaching that you create the worlds by taking half the body of the enemy of Manmatha;
this is true, for were it otherwise, the very existence of the entire universe would not be possible."
Having performed worship with flowers from the celestial trees upon your throne, O Mother, in the golden caves of the mountain,
the wives of the Siddhas, together with the Kinnarīs, sing while their lotus-eyes are reddened by the sight of battle.

I worship the Goddess, who is sprinkled with supreme nectar within my heart— she who possesses a body radiant like a flash of lightning, who proceeds from her own celestial abode to the capital city of Śiva, and who causes the lotus-faces of Śambhu to blossom.
The Gāyatrī.
I take refuge in that whose body is pure consciousness, who is the source of infinite births and existences, and who is the ultimate support of all sacred scriptures;
O Tripurā, whose lotus feet are worshipped by Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu, and who is the abode of the birthplace of all good fortune.
As it truly is.
The Moon-form creates the world permeated by word and meaning; the Sun-form sustains it again through its own power;
and the Fire-form, being of the nature of fire, withdraws all that at the end of the age—I never forget that Śāradā within my mind.

The wise call you Nārāyaṇī, the one who carries across the ocean of hell; Gaurī, the pacifier of weariness; Sarasvatī, the bestower of knowledge; adorned with three eyes; and the daughter of the king of mountains.
Those who praise the Mother of the World with these twelve verses in their proper order—
Having attained you, they reach the supreme goal.
Thus ends the King of Hymns to Bhairavī.
Now follows the armor (kavaca) of Tripurabhairavī.
Homage to Tripurabhairavī.
The illustrious Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who are proficient in all scriptures;
have mercy, O Lord of the world, for you are a knower of dharma, O high-minded one!
The Vidyā beginning with "Tripura," which was previously proclaimed by Sundarī, contains within it a divine armor; tell that to me according to its true essence.
Having heard those words of his, the Lord of the World spoke:
"The wonderful armor of the Goddess has been described by you, beginning with Sundarī."
The illustrious Īśvara said:
I shall speak the armor of the Great Vidyā, which is difficult for all to obtain;
listen to it according to the prescribed rite, and having heard it, O sinner, you must keep it secret.
By whose grace I sustain the entirety of the three worlds;
from whom everything has arisen and in whom it remains even until now.
She is the mother and father of all births, the protector of the world in her true form;
she is the bestower of success and is perfected, yet she remains unaccomplished among wicked beings.
She is the one whose very nature is sound; the letter Ka is the goddess Pātumā, the passionate one who bestows all desires.
May the Goddess Ai, whose nature is the Mūlādhāra, protect me;
may the Goddess Ī, who bestows all the light of the sun and heavenly bliss, protect me.
May the goddess Lakārī, the beloved of Indra, protect me; may the goddess Hrīṃkārī, the beautiful consort of Śambhu who is everywhere, protect me.
May Mahāmāyā protect my head with these syllables;
may the goddess Sarvāṇī, the consort of Hara, protect me with the letter *ka*.
O Goddess, protect me at the letter *ma*, you who destroy all sins;
O Goddess, protect me at the letter *ka*, you who always assume forms at will.
May the Goddess who always delights in Śambara’s enemy protect me at the syllable *ka*;
may the Goddess who assumes the form of the earth-protector protect me at the syllable *la*.
May the Goddess Hrīṃkārī, whose body is half that of Śaṅkara, protect me;
may Mahāmāyā, the beloved of Kāmarāja, protect me with these syllables.

May the goddess Sāvitrī, the bestower of all things, protect me everywhere; may she whose form is the essence of the musical notes protect me in every respect. May the letter *ma* protect me, and the letter *ka* protect me everywhere.
May the goddess Lakṣmī, who possesses all auspicious marks, protect me with the syllable *lakāra*. May the goddess Tribhuvaneśvarī protect me everywhere with the syllable *hrīṃkāra*.
May Mahāmāyā, whose nature is Śakti, protect [me] with these very syllables.
May Vāgbhava protect the head, and Kāmarājikā protect the face.
May she who is the embodiment of power protect my heart, bestowing the perfection of mantras;
may Sundarī always protect me, and may Sundarī grant me complete protection.
May Sundarī, who is red in color and the bestower of all things, protect [me] always;
may Sundarī, adorned with various ornaments, protect [me] at all times.
May she who is beautiful in all her limbs, the bestower of auspiciousness everywhere, and the mother who generates joy for the world— she whose form is Śambhu— protect me always.
May she who consists of all mantras protect [us], the bestower of all prosperity;
may the Goddess who consists of all Lakṣmī grant supreme bliss.
The auspicious Goddess Pātumā is always the treasure-house of various conchs;
thereafter, the Goddess Sarvāṇī, the bestower of all things, is the treasure-house of lotuses.
May Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the sage, protect me everywhere on my head;
may she who is the very form of the Paṅkti meter, the all-agitating one, always [protect me].
May she who bestows all accomplishments protect me; may she who effects all summonings protect me;
may she who agitates always protect me; and may she who holds mastery protect me forever.
May Ākarṣiṇī always protect me; may Saṃmohinī always guard me;
may the goddess Rati always protect me; may Bhagā protect me at all times.
May Māheśvarī protect me always; may Kaumārī protect me at all times; may she who brings joy to all protect me; may Sarvavaśaṅkarī protect me.
May she who always bestows security, who is eternally beautiful in all her limbs,
the youthful maiden in every part of her body, and the giver of all good fortune, protect me.
May Vāgdevī protect [me] always; may she always protect [me].
May Vaśinī, the bestower of great siddhis, protect [me] always.
May Sarvavidrāviṇī protect me; may Gaṇanātha always protect me;
may Goddess Durgā always protect me; may Vaṭukā protect me at all times.
May Kṣetrapāla protect me always, and may Ādhāraśakti protect me;
may Ananta protect me at all times, and may Varāha protect me at all times.
May the Earth always protect me, as well as the golden lion-throne;
and may the red nectar protect me perpetually at all times.
May the Ocean of Nectar protect me always; may the Kalpa-tree protect me evermore;
O Madanodyāna, protect me constantly for the attainment of all perfections.
May all the guardians of the directions, beginning with Indra, protect [me] at all times;
likewise, may the vehicles always protect, and the weapons protect at all times.
May the weapons protect me at all times; may the Yoginīs protect me at all times;
may the Siddhas always protect the Goddess, and may she grant all accomplishments.
May the Goddess Sarvāṅgasundarī protect me everywhere and at all times;
she is the Goddess whose form is bliss, whose nature is eternal, and whose essence is consciousness.
May Sundarī, beautiful in every limb, protect you; O Sundarī, become auspicious! [Protect us] in the terrible abode of separate deities, in calamity, and on the inaccessible mountain.
Whether in a forest or even in a wilderness, may the beautiful Śivā protect me.
O Pārvatī, this is called the armor (kavaca), as well as the extraction of the mantra.
Whoever, having become restrained, disciplined, and pure, should recite this at the three junctions of the day,
for him there shall be the accomplishment of all aims, whatever dwells in his mind.
For Mars, one should worship with saffron or red sandalwood paste;
for Saturn, with white *svayambhū* flowers.
In a cremation ground, or in the wilderness, or in an empty house, or in a temple of Śiva,
having worshipped the yantra along with the Guru and the Śakti, [he should worship] the young maidens.
Having worshipped that mantra and especially the lineage of gurus,
one should worship according to one's capacity and praise them according to this rite.
Having worshipped the yantra with the Guru, the young girl should likewise maintain it.
Then, having offered an oblation to the Goddess with men, goats, cats, and boars,
and having worshipped her according to the prescribed rite with buffaloes and other animals, he should proceed.
Having placed it, with gold in the center, upon the neck, the head, or the arm,
on an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation, and likewise at sunrise.
Having worn this armor, a person shall obtain all accomplishments;
and as for the majesty of this armor, I could not describe it even in hundreds of years.
But I am able, O Great Goddess, to describe its fruit:
for him there is no fear of thieves, nor is there any affliction from disease.
There, there is no fear of famine, nor is there ever any oppression;
it pacifies all obstacles and destroys all diseases.
This [tantra] brings about all protection and bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life;
it must never be spoken of or given away here or there.
Having obtained the mantra according to the prescribed rite, the wise one should worship it constantly;
even there, O Goddess, I consider this armor (kavaca) in embodied form to be difficult to attain.
Having obtained the grace of the Guru and acquired the well-guarded lore,
one also acquires therein the divine armor, which is difficult to find in the three worlds.
Whoever, being restrained and pure, should recite this true verse, for him there shall be the accomplishment of all aims; so it was proclaimed by Śaṅkara.
The Guru is the god Hara himself, and Pārvatī is his consort;
for him who worships them without making any distinction between them, spiritual perfection is not far off.
Thus ends the Tripurabhairavī-kavaca in the Viśvasāra-tantra.
Now, for Vaṭuka.
And for the sake of rescuing from calamity, [one should recite] "māyā" (hrīṃ) followed by "vaṭukaṃ" with the dative suffix -ṅe;
perform this pair for Vaṭuka, where "hrīṃ" is the syllable representing his essential nature.

The Vṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad has the sage Śaunaka as its seer, the Anuṣṭubh as its meter, and Bhairava as its deity; *hrīṃ* is declared to be its seed-syllable (*bīja*), its power (*śakti*), its light (*bhās*), and its pin (*kīlaka*).
Now follows the ritual placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).

With the power joined to the six long vowels and with the syllable *kāra*— that is, the two of them— one should fashion the other [mantras] joined with their respective classes, beginning with the *praṇava*.
Having thus cast off that body, one should meditate upon [the deity] resembling pure crystal,
blazing white, displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and adorned with a network of small bells and anklets.
Adorned with jewels and a smiling face, with curved locks of hair,
she holds a spear in her right hand and a staff in her left, appearing in the form of a young brahmin student.
For the sake of accomplishing their tasks, twice-born Vaiṣṇavas should meditate upon this sattvic Lord as having two arms,
or else as having four arms and wearing matted hair and a crown.
One should contemplate him holding a trident, a noose, and a staff, as well as a water-pot;
in his left hands a skull-cup and in his right a staff.
And thus concludes this Krama of Tripurabhairavī.
Now, the sequence of Mahālakṣmī is being written down.
Then, having performed the ritual procedures up to the placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa), one should perform the placement of the seers and other elements (ṛṣyādinyāsa).
It is as follows:
The seer and other components of the Brahmagāyatrī are proclaimed as Mahālakṣmī;
having purified the hands with the mantra beginning with Oṃ and ending with the heart [syllable].
The practitioner of mantra should place the five seed-syllables on the fingers in sequence;
the remainder of the mantra, the practitioner should place upon both palms.
The practitioner of mantra should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) with the mantra from the crown of the head down to the feet;
he should then place the remaining seven-syllabled mantra within the heart and the bodily constituents (dhātus).
One should fashion the fifth [mantra] with the five seed-syllables, and the sixth with the remaining ones;
moreover, the six-limbed [ritual] should be joined with those primary mantras of knowledge in the dative case.

Having thus performed the placement (nyāsa) of knowledge, sovereignty, power, strength, valor, and splendor in their respective order, the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon his chosen deity.
First, one should visualize a magnificent garden, resplendent with the beauty of all seasons,
filled with charming birch trees, mango trees, and glorious forest trees.
It was adorned with those *tamāla*, *hintāla*, and *śāla* trees, as well as *vakula*,
*karkandhu*, *bandhujīva*, and *campaka* trees.
Adorned with gently swaying leaves of camphor plantain trees,
it was enchanting with Aśoka, Śara, Lāna, Nāga, and Kovidāra trees.
With *mallikā*, *yūthikā*, *kunda*, *madayantī*, and *sugandhikā* jasmine; with grapevines, betel vines, *mādhavī* jasmine, and *devadāru* trees.
It was adorned with *nameru*, *bilva*, *aṅga*, *vakula*, and *tilaka* trees,
as well as with *karṇikāra*, *candana*, and red *candana* trees.
It was auspiciously surrounded by vañjula trees, mātuluṅgas, pomegranates,
and lakuca fruits, as well as by coconuts, dates, betel-nut palms, and kuravaka flowers.
It was surrounded by *mālatī*, *ketakī*, *jātī*, *pāraṃtī*, and *tulasī* trees,
and made radiant with flowers of every season, including *saṃdāvarta* and *damana* blossoms.
It was adorned with *pramada*, *pijumarda*, and *mandāra* trees,
as well as tall *śirīṣa*, *panasa*, *śākhoṭa*, and dense *kuṭaja* trees.

The practitioner of mantra should visualize his desired object in the center of that great seat, which is touched by jasmine, fragrant flowers, and *vañjula* blossoms, and is approached with eagerness.
Its four quarters were adorned by swarms of bees wandering about,
it was filled with the cries of peacocks, and it was enveloped in the spray from the waters of the Lakṣmaṇā.
It was filled with flocks of excellent swans, radiant with ruddy geese and ducks,
and adorned with blooming lotuses, as well as other white and night-lotuses.
It was surrounded by clusters of blue lotuses and fragrant flowers,
radiant and adorned with groves of wish-fulfilling trees that are beautiful in every season.
Filling that space, in its center was a jeweled pavilion with a paved floor,
radiant and brilliant with the splendor of the rays from a mass of rising suns.
Extremely cool with nectar sprinkled by the multitude of rays from his hand,
it was most enchanting with its shimmering, refined golden ramparts.
It was surrounded by a wall of skulls fashioned from the nine precious gems,
and possessed lofty gate-towers constructed of newly risen great jewels.
It possessed a multitude of staffs and banners resembling masses of molten, flowing gold;
it was adorned with great jewels such as lapis lazuli and graced by magnificent pillars.
It was crowded with hundreds of windows fashioned from refined gold,
and it was most enchanting with thousands of islands shimmering with gold and jewels.
It was further adorned with various kinds of linen garments and golden [ornaments],
and it was covered with small bells and banners.
It was joined with the auspicious moonlight of autumn, fashioned like silken garments from the nectar-rayed moon, and further endowed with the variegated splendors arising from diverse raiments.
The auspicious golden ground was adorned with jewel-paved floors,
and further embellished with camphor, aguru, musk, and saffron.
One should visualize the pavilion with its four doors perfumed by tamāla trees and various other fragrant substances.
Then, within that pārijāta tree, she should contemplate a new lion-throne at its base, strewn with various multitudes of gems; upon it, the Goddess should be meditated upon.
Possessing a splendor like the rising sun, adorned with the moon upon his crest,
radiant with a necklace of pearls, and beautifully decorated with ornaments of jewels.
With her lotus-like hands, she holds a fresh cluster of śāli rice, a pair of lotuses, and the kaustubha gem; her lotus-face is graced with a gentle smile.
Adorned with three eyes as beautiful as blooming blue lotuses,
her two feet are like red lotuses upon which tinkling anklets resound.
Her hips are like a beautiful discus, adorned with a shimmering necklace of tongues; she is exquisitely beautified in her waist-region by the three folds that shine like goddesses.
Her navel was adorned with a circle of deep whirlpools,
and her full, elevated breasts were like jars smeared with yakṣa-paste.
Having obtained her— who was radiant with a necklace of pearls, wearing a fine linen upper garment, and beautifully adorned with garlands of flowers— the one born from the jar (Agastya) approached.
Resplendent with armlets of ruby, gold-inlaid lapis lazuli, and other gems,
she wears bracelets set with radiant golden rubies.
Her fingers were adorned with various kinds of shimmering jewel rings;
her neck was graced by a golden necklace and a sweet-toned ornament.
Her limbs were adorned with various and diverse ornaments; she was filled with great wonder, and she shone with a jeweled crest-ornament as radiant as the rising sun.
She has made an auspicious sprout of jewels her ear-ornament, like gold; her bud-like lower lip possesses the beautiful luster of shimmering coral.
Adorned with a row of teeth beautiful and gleaming like the moon,
she possesses a face as auspicious as the lord of stars on an unblemished autumnal full-moon night.
She possesses a nose that sports with the bow of the five-arrowed god [Kāmadeva],
and which is radiant with the splendor of a rising sesame flower.
It possesses the beauty of the cool-rayed moon adorned with its digits,
and it is distinguished by musk endowed with intense fragrance.
Her hair was slightly curled, glossy, dark blue, and beautiful;
her fine locks bore the fragrance of the flowers of the Pārijāta tree.
Crowned with a mass of various jewels set in refined gold,
she was the ultimate limit of beauty and the birthplace of splendors.
One should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī, the abode of the splendor of grace;
one should contemplate her beginning from the lower left hand up to the right hand.
The weapons of Mahālakṣmī rest upon her lotus-like hands,
while she is seated upon a pedestal fashioned from Dharma and the other virtues, adorned with a city-gate (bhūpura).
One should worship her upon the eight petals rich with filaments and in the pericarp;
[the goddesses] Vibhūti, Unnati, Kānti, Sṛṣṭi, Kīrti, and Sannati.
Vyuṣṭi, utkṛṣṭi, and ṛddhi are declared to be the nine powers (nava-śaktayaḥ).
One should offer the seat with the seed-syllable (bīja) and perform the visualization of the form (mūrti-kalpana) with the word "svā" followed by "anunā."
On the right side, one should likewise worship the five attendants of the Goddess;
one should honor him who holds a beautiful noose in his hand and is adorned with flower ornaments.
First, the knower of mantras should worship the limbs in their respective places;
Umā, Śrī, and Sarasvatī, who reside upon the eight petals, should be worshipped.
The goddesses Durgā, Dharaṇī, Gāyatrī, and Uṣas are the Śaktis;
they are enriched with various ornaments and hold two lotuses in their hands.
When the daughter of the Sun rose to wash his feet,
O venerable one, she held the fly-whisks with both hands and served him with great effort.
One should worship Nidhi and Pūjya, Varuṇa in the west, and Chatradhāriṇī;
one should sacrifice to the Rāśis all around, and thereafter worship the Grahas.
One who knows the excellent mantras should worship the world-elephants with four tusks in their respective directions;
furthermore, one should worship the world-protectors and their weapons outside of those.
Now follows the Lakṣmī Stotra.
Agastya said:

O Mother, I bow to you, O lotus-eyed one; O Śrī, dweller in the heart of Viṣṇu, O Mother of the Universe, residing in the lotus! O Lakṣmī, born from the Milk Ocean, fair as the tender interior of a lotus, be gracious to those who constantly bow to you, O refuge of all.
O Śrīrūpendra, you are the sole mother of Madana in his abode; you are the moonlight, more full than the full moon, with a face as enchanting as the moon;
you are the radiance of the sun and you shine throughout the three worlds. O Lakṣmī, be gracious, O refuge for those who constantly bow to you!

O Jātavedas, you are always the power whose nature is burning; through you, the Creator fashions this entire world. Even Viśvaṃbhara (the Sustainer of the Universe) would be able to support everything because of you, O Lakṣmī! Be gracious, O refuge of those who constantly bow to you.
O stainless one, this devotion of yours takes away even the sins of Śiva; protect me, for you bestow all accomplishments and are both the supreme and the non-supreme.
Through the attainment of you, O stainless one, Indra became [Indra] and Hari also [became Hari]; O Lakṣmī, be gracious to those who constantly bow to you, O refuge of all!
He alone is a spear [of valor], he alone is wise, he alone is virtuous, he alone is blessed, and he alone is worthy of honor through his collection of qualities, beauty, and arts;
indeed, he alone is a pure man in all the world upon whom your auspicious glance of compassion has fallen.

O lotus-eyed one, in whatever great man he dwells— whether in an elephant, a lord of horses, a woman, a blade of grass, a lake, a temple, a house, a lotus, a jewel, a bird, a beast, a bed, or the earth— it is that very lotus of his own fortune alone that exists here, and nothing else.

Everything created by you alone attains purity; everything abandoned by you becomes impure and wretched. Wherever your name exists, there is indeed auspiciousness; O Śrī, wife of Viṣṇu, Kamalā, whose abode is the lotus! Thus [it is said].

To those who constantly chant: "Lakṣmī, Śrī, Kamalā, Kamalālayā, Padmā, Ramā, and I, Nalinayugmakarā; Kṣīrodajā, Amṛtakumbhakareḍirā, and Viṣṇupriyā"— (Note: *Nalinayugmakarā* refers to the goddess holding a pair of lotuses; *Kṣīrodajā* is she born from the Ocean of Milk; *Amṛtakumbhakareḍirā* is she with a jar of nectar in her hand; and *Viṣṇupriyā* is the beloved of Viṣṇu.)
Where is suffering?
Having thus offered praise to the Blessed Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Hari, the sage, together with his wife, prostrated himself like a staff, performing the eight-limbed salutation.
Śrī said:
Arise, arise, may it be well with you; O Lopāmudrā of auspicious vows, best of sages, you were born from Mitrā and Varuṇa. You have fallen [into this state].
Pleased by this hymn of praise, I shall grant whatever is desired.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard this, O mighty-armed one, that sage then prostrated himself before Śrī and spoke these words filled with devotion: Thus he replied to Śrī.
Agastya said:
If a boon is to be granted to me, and if I am worthy of a boon,
then let those who shall recite this hymn always be your devotees and honored.
May they never experience distress; may there be no poverty; may there be no separation from their desired objects, and may there be no severance of their lineage.
May there be victory everywhere, and may there be no decline of prosperity.
Śrī said:
"So be it, O Sage; everything that has been spoken by you shall be so.
The recitation of this hymn brings about my presence."
Misfortune and Kālakarṇī shall never enter that house;
for the sake of pacifying elephants and cattle, one should always recite this hymn.
For those afflicted by hair-grasping spirits (vālagraha),
one should write this supreme pacification rite for children on birch bark and bind it around the neck.
This seed, which is a secret, must be guarded with great effort;
it should not be given to one lacking faith, nor should it ever be given to one who is impure.
Thus ends the complete Lakṣmīstotra.
Now follows the Lakṣmī-kavaca.
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall declare the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) which grants all desires;
by the mere knowledge of which one becomes Sadāśiva himself.
A person who performs her worship, adoration, and the recitation of her mantra shall become a son of Pārvatī, honored by all the scriptures.
One who seeks the entry into knowledge should especially serve her who is beloved of Viṣṇu.

Of this armor (*kavaca*) consisting of the glorious four-syllabled name of Viṣṇu’s consort, the Lord Śrī Śiva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandaḥ*), Vāgbhavī is the deity (*devatā*), the seed-syllable (*bīja*) is Vāgbhava, the power (*śakti*) is Lajjā, the bolt (*kīlaka*) is Ramā, and the armor consisting of the Kāma-seed-syllable is for my own poetic skill, scholarship, and all perfections (*sarvasiddhi*).
The application is for the sake of prosperity.
May the syllable *Aiṃ*, the source of speech (*vāgbhavī*) that bestows all accomplishments, protect my head;
may *Hrīṃ* protect the space between my eyes, and may the consort of Śaṅkara (*śāṃkarī*) protect my pair of eyes.
On the tongue, the perimeter of the mouth, the two ears, and the teeth;
on the upper and lower lips, the row of teeth, and again at the root of the palate, one should place the letter *ha*.
May Lakṣmī, the consort of Viṣṇu, who is the very embodiment of fortune, beauty, and splendor, protect me; and may Pārvatī protect my two ears, my two arms, and my two breasts.
In the heart, at the wrist-joint, on the neck, and again on both sides;
likewise in the region of the back, in the private parts, and similarly on the left and the right.
Again, [one should place them] on the lap, the hips, the navel, the two shanks, the two kneecaps,
the two feet, the two ankles, and the roots of the toes.
May the great goddess Kāmeśī protect my own element, my vital breath, my forehead, my head, and again all my limbs, bringing about my exaltation.
May Puṣṭi protect me; may Mahāmāyā protect me; may Utkṛṣṭi always protect me;
and may the goddess Ṛddhi, the beloved of Śambhu, protect me everywhere.
May Vāgbhavī protect me always; may the consort of Hara protect me;
may the goddess Ramā protect me always; and may Māyā protect me from destruction.
May Lakṣmī, the sovereign goddess of the gods and the illusory power of Viṣṇu, protect me in all my limbs;
may Vijayā protect me in my home, and Jayā always protect me.
May Śivadūtī protect me always; may Sundarī protect me at all times;
may Bhairavī protect me everywhere; may Bhāruṇḍā protect me forever.
May Tvaritā protect me always; may Ugratara protect me forever. May Kālikā protect me constantly; may Kālarātri protect me always.
May Vanadurgā protect me always; may Kāmākhyā protect me at all times. May the Yoginīs protect me always; may Mudrā protect me always.
May the hosts of Yoginīs, stationed upon the wheel of the Goddess, protect [us] always with their vessels—
everywhere, in all undertakings, in all rites, and at all times.
"May Lakṣmī, the Goddess of the lords of gods and the bestower of all prosperity, protect me.
Thus has this divine armor been told to you for the attainment of all perfections.
If one desires one's own welfare, O Maheśvarī, this should not be spoken anywhere to one who is deceitful, devoid of devotion, or a slanderer.
One should never show [the deity] with missing limbs or with extra limbs;
nor should one show the divine form while reciting a hymn, for by showing it thus, one becomes a destroyer of Śiva.
One should bestow this supreme armor upon one who is of noble birth, a great lord, devoted to Durgā, a Vaiṣṇava, and pure.
To one's own disciple who is peaceful, virtuous, and likewise wise;
on a Saturday or a Tuesday, with red sandalwood [powders];
One should write the mantra, endowed with all mantras, using barley-meal;
one should write the divine armor (kavaca) with auspicious, self-arisen flowers.
With one's own semen and the semen of others, endowed with various fragrances,
or with *gorocanā*, saffron, or red sandalwood;
On an auspicious lunar day or under a favorable yoga, on the day of the sun (Sunday), or under the asterisms of Śravaṇā,
Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, Phalgunī, or Maghā;
On Tuesday, during the conjunction of the asterism Pūrvabhādrapadā and the lunar mansion Svātī,
one should write out or recite this hymn in a temple during an auspicious yoga.
The Venerable One was especially engaged in the yoga of joy, the yoga of the Brahma,
the yoga of Indra, the auspicious yoga, and likewise the yoga of Śukla.
In Kaulava, Vālava, and the seventh, Vaṇija;
or in an empty house, a cremation ground, or especially in a secluded place.
Having worshipped the maiden, one should sacrifice to the eternal Goddess;
one should worship the Supreme Deity with fish, meat, vegetables, and winnowing baskets.
Having fed the Brahmins with offerings such as clarified butter and especially with incense and lamps, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
One should perform the Āṣeṭaka narrative there for three days;
then there will be great protection, as spoken by Śaṅkara.
One attains [the powers of] killing, inciting hatred, and so forth; of this there is no doubt.
Such a person would be a son of Pārvatī, yet cast outside of all the scriptures.
Hara is the Guru himself, and his wife is the beloved of Hara;
for one who worships them without making any distinction between them, spiritual perfection is not far off.
The mortal who here recites this mantra daily with a mind full of devotion shall obtain the fruit of its recitation according to the prescribed rite.
He becomes a supreme abode of all prosperities, bowing at the feet of kings and possessing the splendor of royal crowns.
The cessation of the characteristics.
Thus ends the Śrī Viśvasāra Tantra, the Lakṣmī-kavaca, in its entirety.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the great mantra of Nārāyaṇa:
"Namo nārāyaṇāya" (Salutation to Nārāyaṇa); this eight-syllabled mantra begins with the syllable "Tāra" (Om).
The meter is the goddess Gāyatrī, the sage is Sādhya Nārāyaṇa, and the deity is the Supreme Self (Paramātman); thus the procedure for the five limbs is declared.
With [the mantras] "Kujolka," "Maholka," "Avīcolka," and "Udyulka" as the fourth, joined with "Sahasrolka" at the end and ending with "svāhā" and "iti."
The five-limbed mantras have been proclaimed; one should also assign them to the thumb and the other fingers.
[One should visualize] the crown, necklace, armlets, and earrings shaped like sea-monsters (makara).
Holding a conch, a discus, a mace, and a lotus in his hands, he is clothed in yellow garments;
his chest is adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark, and he is accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi.
The light of the Self is fully kindled, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns.
And this sequence of Mahālakṣmī is completed.
Now, the ritual procedure for Mātaṅgī is written down.
Now I shall describe Mahādevī Mātaṅgī, the bestower of all accomplishments;
by merely serving her, one certainly attains perfection of speech.
The seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti; Virāṭ is declared to be the meter;
the goddess Mātaṅgī is the deity, the bestower of all spiritual accomplishments.
The practitioner, being composed, should perform the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa);
he should fashion these with the seed-syllable of the six long vowels preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ).
One should draw a beautiful yantra consisting of a six-cornered figure and an eight-petalled lotus;
upon this seat, one should worship these nine Śaktis in their proper order.
Vibhūti, Unnati, Kānti, Sṛṣṭi, Kīrti, Sannati,
Vyuṣṭi, Utkṛṣṭi, and Ṛddhi— these are the ten names that follow Mātaṅgī.
At the very end, "Śaktikamalāsanāya namaḥ"— this mantra,
enriched with the seed-syllables of Vāk, Śakti, and Lakṣmī, is known as the Āsana-mantra.
There, the knower of mantras should perform worship with hibiscus flowers;
being well-composed, he should recite the mantra eight times over each of the eight petals.
Rati, Prīti, Manobhavā, Kriyā, Śraddhā,
Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamadanā, and Madanālasā are the powers (śaktis).
Having thus worshipped the eight Śaktis together with the offerings,
the practitioner, with a steady mind, should then meditate upon the Supreme Goddess.

One should meditate upon her who has a dark-complexioned body, whose crest is the moon, who possesses three eyes, and who is seated upon a throne of excellent jewels; she is adorned with various jewel-encrusted ornaments, has a slender waist, full and rounded breasts, a smiling face, and holds [the attributes] in her hands.
In succession, with her four arms, she holds a goad, a sword, a whip, and likewise a noose and a shield.
Having meditated thus, [one should worship] the Great Goddess with captivating perfumes and flowers,
and offer to the Great Goddess an oblation of milk-rice mixed with sugar.
Now follows the hymn to Mātaṅgī.
Having propitiated her feet, O Mother, Brahmā and the other gods attain renowned fame and long life;
other lords of sages attain supreme power of speech, and others, through the weight of their devotion, attain supreme prosperity.
I bow to the Goddess Mātaṅginī, who wears the new moon upon her crest and is adorned with a digit of the moon;
she who, through the words of the Vedas, respectfully awakens Śuka to the meaning that has been established.
O Goddess, those who worship your lotus-feet— which are illuminated by the luster of the crest-jewels of the bowing gods and asuras—
attain with equal respect the status of lords of the earth.
O Mother, at the time of your playful gait, they worship your lotus feet with the pretext of jingling anklets;
O Mother, [I worship] your lotus feet, which are the very essence of unartificial words.
May that Mātaṅgiṇī— who makes the path meaningful with her feet as they move, their anklets tinkling,
and who strikes her lute held in her hand— shake my heart.

I bow to the consort of Śambhu, whose rounded hips are girt by a blue sash, who wears an ornament of bees placed upon a palmyra leaf, whose lotus-eyes roll from the intoxication of honey-wine, and who possesses full breasts.

O Sovereign of the worlds, with devotion I remember your orb-like waist, adorned by the three folds of skin, which for a long time remained unperceived due to its beauty like a streak of lightning, until it was finally visible through the line of fresh body hair.

We meditate in our hearts upon the daughter of the mountain king, who brings forth the splendor of blue lotuses with her beauty and the side-glances of her eyes, who possesses locks of hair adorned with garlands of *kadamba* flowers, and who is the very source of all lotus-like lakes.

O Great Goddess, I would meditate upon Your face, with cheeks lovely and slightly flushed, with a lower lip like a bimba fruit resting upon a row of teeth, with long eyes and a tremulous brow, and graced with a gentle smile.
O Śaṅkara, those men who, endowed with devotion, praise Mātaṅginī— the lawful wife of Śiva and the supreme deity of speech— constantly attain the highest prosperity.
Thus ends the complete hymn to Mātaṅgī.
Now, her armor:
The illustrious Bhairava said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the auspicious armor (kavaca) of Mātaṅgī;
it is effective without meditation, without mantra, without fire-oblation, and without sacrificial offering.
By the mere recollection of which, the practitioner becomes a lord of the earth.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
This divine armor of Mātaṅgī provides all protection for men,
as well as poetic talent, wealth, and the comforts of elephants and horses.
She is the bestower of happiness, the giver of auspiciousness, and the granter of the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā*;
she is the primordial Maheśvarī of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa.
Whatever man recites correctly even half a verse or a single verse, royal fortune always remains in his hand; of this there is no doubt.
Having made his face [as if] smeared with food remnants and seated upon a lotus throne,
he should form the *yonimudrā* with his hand, intent on meditating upon the Śakti.
Having brought [the breath] to the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra), one should constantly perceive the forehead as the abode of the one named Ucchiṣṭā, known as Mahācaṇḍālinī.
May the goddess Suṣṇumukhī protect [us] with her two eyes, may she protect the nose;
and may Mahāpiśācinī always protect us in the mouth.
May *lajjā* protect my teeth; *daṃ* [protect] my lips; *coṣṭaḥ* [protect] my hands during purification;
*ci* [protect] my chin and the region of my throat; and thereafter, the triad of *ṭha* syllables [protects] them.
May that Visarga, the Great Goddess, protect my heart at all times;
may Kālikā, whose eyes are red, eternally guard me at the navel.
May Cāmuṇḍā protect the belly, and likewise may Kātyāyanī protect the linga;
may Ugracaṇḍā protect the anus, and may Cāmbikā protect the feet.
May Śarvāṇī protect the two arms, and Caṇḍabhīṣaṇā the heart;
may Mātṛkā protect the tongue, and Puṣṭikā protect the east.
May Kṛttikā protect in the north, and may Vidyā protect in the west;
may Vijayā protect in the south, and may Medhā protect in the southeast.
May Prajñā protect in the southwest; may Lakṣaṇā guard in the northwest;
and may the goddess Mātaṅgī, the performer of auspicious deeds, protect in the northeast.
May the Great Goddess, who acts for the welfare of the gods, protect me above;
may Vāsukī, who possesses universal forms, protect me eternally in the netherworld (pātāla).

May she whose vowels reside in the region of the throat protect me; may she who is beloved by the devourers at the Ājñā-cakra protect me; and may she who is dear to the heart protect me with the consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha* at the twelve spokes.
May she whose nature consists of the ten syllables from *ma* to *pha* in the Maṇipūra-cakra protect me;
may she who consists of the six syllables from *va* to *la* in the six-petalled lotus always protect me.
May the Goddess always protect the end of the speech within the four petals.
Oṃ krāṃ śrīṃ prīṃ chrīṃ chrīṃ ṭhaḥ hrīṃ ṭhaḥ svāhā.
Having recited this mantra, one should wear it on the left arm.
Whoever wears it around the neck is indeed the god Maheśvara;
seeing him from afar, all the deities bow down to him.
By the power of his splendor, it is not even possible for Indra and the other gods to go there; that lord of beings treats them like servants.

For him, there shall be the fulfillment of his desires, as well as the powers beginning with *aṇimā*; likewise, fame, poetic talent, prosperity, and all such things as the rites of subjugation (*āraṇa*).
O Goddess, a man who, being well-disposed, should employ [this mantra] without knowing the armor (kavaca) might sometimes incur the devotion of kings through worship.
O Goddess of gods, his yoginīs will perish and devour him;
he shall be a partaker of suffering in this world and, in the next, he will become mute.

For ten million lifetimes, one who does not bow at the feet of the Guru remains perpetually mute and finds no accomplishment in mantra; however, when a wise person receives the mantra after prostrating at the Guru’s feet, [he attains success].
Then, O Goddess, having obtained that armor through service to the Guru,
he shall become a king in this world and attain liberation in the hereafter.
O Sovereign of the Gods, [this knowledge] should not be given to a new initiate, nor to the disciple of another, nor to a wicked person, nor to a slanderer,
nor to one of evil conduct, nor to one devoted to the injury of Śakti.
He who gives the auspicious armor of Mātaṅgī is the most wicked;
the Yoginīs drink his blood and devour him.
Therefore, they obtain all accomplishments through this supreme secret;
it is to be hidden more than the hidden, and is the doctrine more secret than the secret.
This must not be disclosed, O blessed lady, even at the cost of one's life-breaths.
A single recitation of this hymn is equal to ten million acts of worship; a single recitation of it is equal to ten million other hymns.
Meditation is equal to ten million recitations; dissolution is equal to ten million meditations.
This science of dissolution is never to be revealed.
Thus ends the Mātaṅgī-kavaca in the Śrī Guhyakālī-tantra.
Now, [the mantra] of Sadāśiva.
The five-syllabled mantra begins with the seed-syllable preceded by *tāra* and *māyā*;
its sage is considered to be Vāmadeva, and it consists of eight syllables.
The deity is declared to be Sadāśiva, and the meter is said to be Paṅkti;
[the mantra is formed] by the two seeds Māyā and Prāsāda, combined with the six vowels.

Then, with the six mantra-syllables accompanied by their respective seed-syllables (*jāti*), one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and meditate upon [the deity] who is crimson like vermilion, smiling, and three-eyed.
He holds a ṭaṅka and a deer; likewise, the Goddess embraces him, the bestower of boons, holding a deep-red lotus in her four hands.
Seated upon a red lotus, she has full, round, firm, and lofty breasts; she rests upon the left lap [of the deity], adorned with red garlands, perfumes, and unguents.
And this Mātaṅgī-krama is completed.
Now, the sequence of Bhuvaneśvarī is written.
There, having performed the ritual procedures up to the placement of the seats (pīṭhanyāsa), one should perform the placement of the seers and other elements (ṛṣyādinyāsa).
O Bhuvaneśvarī, the sage is Śakti, the metre is Gāyatrī, and the deity of the mantra is said by the host of gods to be Manu, who is served throughout the world.
One should perform the six limb-projections (aṅga-nyāsa) in sequence using the seed-syllables joined with the six long vowels,
following the path of both withdrawal (saṃhāra) and emanation (sṛṣṭi), having performed the placement of the Mātṛkā upon one's body.
Then one should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantra-nyāsa) for the sake of attaining the state of the deity:
[one places] Hṛllekhā on the head, Gaganā on the face, and [Khecarī] in the lotus of the heart.
One should visualize the red Karālikā at the secret place and Mahocchuṣmā on the two feet;
and [the remaining goddesses] in the upward, eastern, southern, northern, and western faces.
One should first install the Bhūtaśakti, enriched with short seed-syllables such as *sa* and others;
afterwards, one should place the six limbs (*aṅga*) in their proper sequence, conjoined with the [six] *jāti* mantras.
One should place Brahmā, conjoined with the Gāyatrī, upon the forehead;
one should place Viṣṇu, conjoined with the Sāvitrī, upon the right skull.
One should place Maheśvara, joined with Vāgīśvarī, on the left cheek;
furthermore, one should place Śrī and Dhanapati on the tip of the left ear.
Having placed Smara upon the face with Rati, one should install Gaṇapati with Puṣṭi;
Sadyojāta is placed above the ear, and [Vāmadeva] in the space between the ear and the cheek.
One should place the root mantra on the face; then, one should again place it within the body:
at the base of the throat, on the pair of breasts, on the left shoulder, and in the lotus of the heart.
The preceptor [should place them] on the left side, on both flanks, and at the region of the navel;
[and others] on the forehead, the sides of the head, the abdomen, the sides, and in the heart.
Then, the characteristics of the other [mudrās], beginning with Brahmāṇī, are declared according to the rule;
one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) upon the body with the root mantra and meditate upon the Goddess.

I worship Bhuvaneśī, whose crown is the moon with the radiance of the rising sun, who has lofty breasts and three eyes, whose face is smiling, and who holds the gestures of granting boons, the *kuśa* grass, the noose, and protection in her hands.
The knower of mantras should recite the mantra thirty-two lakhs of times;
he should then perform oblations ten times that number (three million two hundred thousand) with eight substances consecrated with the *svāhā* mantra.
One should offer the *arghya* to the Lord of Day (the Sun), having meditated there upon Pārvatī;
[one should draw] an eight-petaled lotus on the outside, surrounded by a circle of sixteen petals.
One should draw a very beautiful hexagon in the center of the pericarp;
then, one should worship the pedestal (pīṭha) endowed with the nine powers (nava-śakti).
Jayā, Vijayā, then Ajitā, Aparājitā,
Dityavilāsinī, Dogdhrī, Aghorā, and Maṅgalā— these are the nine.
Having provided a seat enriched with seed-syllables (bīja), one should fashion the form [of the deity] by means of that very [seed-syllable];
upon it, one should worship the Goddess after having invoked her along with the enclosures (āvaraṇas) in due order.
In the center, the east, the south, the north, and the west, respectively,
Hṛllekhā and the others, who possess a radiance equal to the five elements, should be worshipped.
Holding a boon-granting gesture, a noose, a goad, and the gesture of fearlessness, and adorned with moderate ornaments,
one should worship the deities of the limbs in the previously mentioned locations.
In the six corners, one should worship the King’s Mantra and subsequently the deities of the pairs;
in the corner [of Indra], Indra, holding a shining staff, a goad, a rosary, and the gesture of granting fearlessness.
The practitioner of mantras should worship Gāyatrī, who resembles Brahmā;
in the southwest corner, one should worship her holding a discus, a conch, a mace, and a lotus.

One should worship Sāvitrī, clad in yellow garments, and Viṣṇu likewise; in the northwest corner [one should worship her] holding a parasol, a rosary, and displaying the gestures of protection and boon-granting.
One should worship Sarasvatī and Rudra with similar characteristics;
in the southeast corner, one should worship a jewel-pitcher and a jeweled casket.
[She] embraces with her right hand the yellow-clad, pot-bellied Lord of Wealth, who holds [a mongoose] in his two hands;
with her left hand she holds a water-lily.
One should worship Mahālakṣmī, who is mounted upon the emblem of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada),
and [worship] Madana, the deity of the western quarter, holding a bow, arrows, a noose, and a goad.
One should worship the protector Jālapāla, adorned with jewel ornaments,
who embraces the image with his right hand while holding a blue lotus with his left.
One should properly worship Rati, who rests upon the lap of her lover, with one's hand;
and in the northeast (aiśāna), one should properly worship Vighnarāja together with his beloved.
[She saw] the beloved of Varāṅga holding a goad and a noose, with cruel fingers,
richly endowed with a skull filled with honey-wine— the naked King of Obstacles (Vighnarāja).
In Puṣkala, she who wore a shimmering sword from which jewels were falling,
whose form resembled vermilion, and who was possessed of the playful grace of intense intoxication.
With his other hand, he touched the red lotus held by the goddess Dhvajā; she was embraced by her beloved, was crimson, full-bodied, and naked.
In the pericarp, the two Nidhis are to be worshipped; on both sides of the hexagon are the limbs (aṅgas);
these [deities] are in the filaments, and afterwards one should worship them on the petals.
After Anaṅgakusumā came Anaṅgakusumāturā,
then Bhuvanapālā, Gaganavegā, and after her, [Vidyutprabhā].
Śaktirekhā, Gaṇārekhā, and the eight Śuktis hold nooses, goads, boons, and gestures of fearlessness, and possess ruddy complexions.
Then, on the sixteen petals, [one should place] Karālī,
Vikarālī, Umā, Sarasvatī, Śrī, Durgā, Lakṣmī, Śruti, Smṛti, and Dhṛti.
Śraddhā, Medhā, Mati, and Kānti— these sixteen Śaktis,
dark-complexioned and bearing swords and shields, should be worshipped as the Mothers.
Outside the lotus, the attendant Śaktis are to be worshipped in order:
first Anaṅgarūpā, then Anaṅgamadanā.
Madanāturā, Bhuvanavegā, as well as Bhuvanapālikā,
Sarvaśaśirā, Anaṅgavedanā, and Anaṅgamekhalā.
Holding in their lotus-like hands a wine-cup, a palm-leaf fan, betel, a radiant parasol, two chowries, a goad, and a flower.
One should worship the World-Protectors (Lokapālas), adorned with all ornaments, outside; and the [deities] beginning with Vajra outside of them. In this manner, one should worship the Goddess.
Now, the hymn of praise to Bhuvaneśvarī.
Then [he worshipped] Ambikā, the cause of the universe, who is composed of bliss, who is the manifest embodiment of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman), and who bestows all perfections.
Having heard of you, O Ambikā— the primordial mother of the lotus-born Brahmā, the source of the bodies of Viṣṇu and Śiva,
and the cause of the creation, maintenance, and destruction of the three worlds— I purify myself with a stainless mind.

O Daughter of the Mountain King, you alone are indeed the cause of the possession of power for the God who is the enemy of Manmatha— He who assumes the forms of earth through water, of fire through the wind, and of the moon through the sun.
O Mother, you who are worshipped by the entire world in its three streams, it is for this very reason that you understand the cause of excellence:
because the matted locks of Śiva constantly revolve in the pure waters purified by the pollen of your lotus feet.

The Lord of the digits (the Moon) delights the night-lily, but no other [sun] delights the day-lotus; indeed, only one has the power to bring joy to each. Thus, by means of your excellent vision, you alone possess sovereignty over the manifestation of the entire universe.
Even now, you remain in the fresh youth of all the worlds; though your body is that of the King of Mountains, you are exceedingly tender.
You have not been scrutinized by these [sages] as the mother of these [beings], nor have you been envisioned in their minds as Gaurī, nor have you stood upon their path.
O Mother of the worlds, those who, having attained a human birth— so difficult to obtain after a long time— and having further acquired the full proficiency of their own senses,
do not worship you, fall back down again even after having ascended to the highest pinnacle of ultimate liberation.
O Himavat, those who are eager worship you with camphor powder stirred in cool water, and with well-born sandalwood and fragrant flowers; indeed, they become renowned throughout the entire world.
Having entered the central path of the first lotus and moved through the universe like a queen of sleepers,
she appears here in these five lotuses, manifesting the playful grace of a circle of lightning-streaks while shedding profuse tears.
Emerging from that [moon], they drenched their limbs with the essence of nectar and once again attained dissolution by way of that same path;
O Mother Maheśvarī, those in whose hearts You never manifest shall never possess the interior of a jasmine flower.

Today, with my mind, I turn over in meditation your fair form—possessing long, curly, and dark hair, a face enchanting with its curved brow, a beautiful neck-slope, and a slender, rounded waist; and whose hands are depicted today holding a rosary, a water-pot, and a lotus.
Having established themselves in yoga, conquered the sixfold group of enemies, and subdued the collection of senses within a tranquil mind,
the yogis behold you, O Bhuvaneśvarī— the beautiful-faced one whose form is enriched with the noose, goad, protection, and boon.
Being consecrated by four jars of nectar turned by elephants resembling molten gold,
and holding two beautiful lotuses in her two hands— even she, Padmā, O worthy one, has become nothing other than your supreme consort.

O Goddess Bhavānī, you are Durgā, who, having mounted the king of beasts with eight fierce armies bearing various weapons— those divine women whose luster is like the blade of durvā grass— overwhelm the hosts of the enemies of the immortals.

I remember again and again that first Pulinda maiden, whose face is radiant with droplets of perspiration like summer spray, who wears a necklace fashioned from clusters of *guñjā* berries, who possesses the luster of white moonbeams, and who is the immeasurable splendor of the God of Love’s bowstring.

O Consort of Śrīkaṇṭha, may you place your feet upon my head— feet that are followed by swans moving with black anklets held far away, as if by embodied words; and which, like lotuses, bear upward-pointing stalks resembling well-formed hair.
Having generated pride in his mind through two [verses] and, with a gaze full of arrogance, having produced a third eye on his forehead by means of the bull-bannered god [Śiva],
I have now bowed to both your shanks as they are being gazed upon by him, trembling with intense passion.
Your thighs, which surpass the elephant's trunk in their lack of leprosy, their girth, and their softness, have surpassed the pride of others;
they are capable of supporting the weight of your hips, and thus your waist alone has become the object of praise for its slender curvature.
May the form of the Middle One— whose essence is thrilled by the early onset of youth as she simultaneously expands her hips and breasts,
and who is made manifest by the play of the line of hair— shine within the center of my heart.

O Goddess, may I never forget you— the one who, through fresh youth, has provided an unassailable offering of fresh sprouts in the form of the waters of beauty for the fire of Śiva’s eye, which fears the friend of Smara (Kāma).
O two lotuses, though you possess the smile of Śambhu embraced by Īśā and the saffron of Kashmir, you do not equal the two temples of an elephant rising from a bath—
those two who, for a moment, resemble a million froths and are reddened with vermilion, reminding one of a pair of rutting elephants in love.
The two jars.

O Mother, why do these two arms of yours, which bear an overflowing and radiant luster, and which were fashioned by the fish-bannered god (Kāmadeva) as long nooses for seizing the necks of his enemies, never pass beyond the range of my hearing?

O Daughter of the Mountain King, having contemplated your neck— neither too long, stealing the beauty of the water-lily, resplendent with various ornaments, and possessing enchanting qualities— I shall never attain satisfaction; nor shall I ever find enough, O fair one,
contemplating your eyes that are exceedingly long, your noble forehead-plate, and the lines of your cheeks blossoming with a gentle smile.
When one repeatedly recollects a Vidyadhara with a face and a long, prominent nose, he is born again with that very same body.

O Goddess, for him whose mind perceives your mass of hair— marked by streaks of moonlight, indistinguishable from swarms of bees hovering over abundant fragrant flowers— the noose of past curses falls away of its own accord.
That mortal who, with a heart ever moist with devotion, recites here this hymn of praise to the wise one whose noose is the sacred revelation and virtuous conduct—
he becomes a high station for prosperity, bowing at the feet [of the Lord].
The fortune of the crest-jewels of kings has long resided in Lakṣmaṇācārya.
Thus ends the Śrī Bhuvaneśvarī Stotra.
Now, the armor of Bhuvaneśvarī.
The Goddess said:
And as for the Goddess of the World (Bhuvaneśī), whose knowledge has been revealed—having studied all these [vidyās], they have departed; now I wish to hear [of her].
The armor known as Trailokyamaṅgala, which was previously described—
The Lord said:
O Pārvatī, listen; I shall speak—attend with careful attention—to the armor known as Trailokyamaṅgala, which is the embodiment of mantra.
O Goddess, this mantra consists of perfected vidyās and bestows all sovereignty;
by reciting and retaining it, a mortal shall become a possessor of sovereignty over the three worlds.
The seer (ṛṣi) of this Trailokyamaṅgala-kavaca is Śiva;
the meter (chaṃdas) is Virāṭ; and the deity (devatā) is Bhuvaneśvarī, the sustainer of the world.
The application [of the mantra] is proclaimed for the sake of dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.
May the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* protect my head, and may Bhuvaneśī protect my forehead.
Aiṃ may protect my right eye; Hrīṃ may protect my left eye; Śrīṃ may protect my right ear—may Maheśvarī, whose nature consists of these three syllables, protect me.
May Aiṃ always protect my left ear; may Hrīṃ always protect my nose;
may the Goddess Aiṃ protect my face, and may Aiṃ protect my tongue.
May Vāk, who is threefold and consists of three syllables, protect the throat, O Supreme Mother;
may Śrīṃ constantly protect the shoulders, and Hrīṃ always protect the arms.

Klīṃ: May the Mistress of the Triple-Peaked [Abode], the bestower of the sovereignty of the Triple-Peaked, protect my two hands. Āṃ: May she protect my heart; Hrīṃ: may she always protect the region of my middle.
May Kroṃ, that three-syllabled Bhuvaneśvarī, protect the region of the navel;
may she who brings all under her control always protect the back as the seed of all.
Hrīṃ! May she protect my secret place; homage to the Blessed Lady, may she protect my hips.
May Māheśvarī always protect [me], and Śaktinī protect the pair of my knees.
May Annapūrṇā always protect [me], Svāhā! May she protect the two feet;
may the ten-syllable mantra protect me, and may Annapūrṇā protect my entire body.
Tāra, Māyā, Rasā, Kāma, and then the sixteen-syllable [mantra];
may she who dwells upon the head protect me from all sides with joy, she whose food consists of twenty bones.
"Tāradurge yugaṃ rakṣa svāhā"—this ten-syllable mantra [is used].
May Jaya Durgā, dark as a rain-cloud, protect me from all sides with joy.
This [mantra] begins with the seed-syllable *māyā* (hrl-lekha) and consists of ten syllables;
thereafter follows another [syllable], which, with the luster of molten gold, is like the face of the victorious Durgā.
The supreme [goddess] consists of eight syllables: *tāraṃ hrīṃ duṃ durgāyai namaḥ*.
Holding a conch, a discus, a bow, and arrows, she is like my own right hand.
May Mahiṣamardinī Svāhā, the supreme one whose essence is the Vasu-gold,
who destroys the demon Mahiṣāsura, protect [me] forever in the southwest.
Māyā Padmāvatī Svāhā is proclaimed as the seven-syllabled mantra;
may Padmāvatī, seated upon a lotus, always protect me in the west.
Oṃ Pāśāṅkuśapuṭāmāyai Hi Parameśvari Svāhā.
This mantra consists of thirteen syllables, begins with the Tāra (Oṃ), and is indeed the face of her who is mounted upon a horse.
Sarasvatī, Pañcaśara, Nityaklinnā, Madadravā, Svāhā, and Ṛkṣarī— may these always protect me from the north.
*Tāraṃ*, *māyā*, *kavaca*, *khecara*, *kṣataḥ*, *vadhūḥ*,
*krūṃ*, *kṣe*, *hrīṃ*, *phaṭ*— this twelve-syllable *mahāvidyā* bestows all things.
May Śivā, beginning with Ariṣṭā and the others, always protect me in the corner;
then may Bālā—[invoked] with Aiṃ Klīṃ Sauḥ—protect me from the upper region.
May the youthful Bhairavī, who possesses the bindu, protect me always upon the earth.
Thus is your meritorious armor, the supreme auspiciousness for the three worlds.
The merit of this, which embodies the flood of great vidyās, is more meritorious than the most essential;
by its recitation alone, even Kubera immediately becomes a lord of wealth.
By means of this dhāraṇā and recitation, all the gods beginning with Indra,
having become lords of all siddhis, attained complete sovereignty.
One should offer eight handfuls of flowers with the root mantra itself, separately at each [time];
one shall obtain the fruit of worship performed for a hundred years.
Having established mutual affection, Lakṣmī shall dwell unshakably in his home, and Vāṇī shall reside in his mouth; this is the truth, the truth—of this there is no doubt.
That meritorious soul who wears this supreme and holy armor named *Trailokyamaṅgala* is indeed the foremost among the virtuous.
Having become endowed with all sovereignty, a person— whether a man or a woman among human beings— shall become a conqueror of the three worlds by [placing it] on the right arm.
Having become possessed of many sons, even a barren woman obtains a son;
weapons such as the Brahmāstra do not bite that person at all.
