He who worships Bhuvaneśvarī without knowing this armor-mantra (kavaca) shall incur extreme poverty and, after a long time, meet his death.
Thus ends the *Trailokyamaṅgala* armor (*kavaca*), from the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord in the glorious *Rudrayāmala*. Now follows [the armor] of Śiva.
The mantra "Namaḥ Śivāya," preceded by the syllable Om (Tārā), consists of five syllables;
when preceded by Om, it becomes six-syllabled, and it is the means for attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation for the Brahmins.
The sage is Vāmadeva, the meter is Paṅkti, and the deity is Sadāśiva;
the best of practitioners should assign the six limbs by means of the six syllables.
Then one should meditate [on him] as having a luster equal to cow’s milk and a silver mountain,
adorned with a crown of matted hair graced by the beautiful king of the moon's crescent.
Śambhu, who possesses five faces, has five faces and three eyes;
he is clothed in a tiger skin and adorned with jewel ornaments.
With his upper right hands he holds a chisel and the gesture of granting boons;
with his upper left hand he holds a deer, and the other [lower left] displays the gesture of fearlessness.
His lotus-face was exceedingly serene as he sat upon a seat of goads,
while Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa, and the other gods praised him with devotion.
To Bhava, who is the primordial source of all, whose body is the universe, and who removes the fear of worldly existence.
And this sequence of Bhuvaneśvarī is completed.
Now follows the sequence of Dhūmāvatī.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the supreme mantra of Dhūmāvatī;
Pippalāda is the sage, Nivṛt is the meter, and Jyeṣṭhā is its deity.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the letter *dh* joined with the six long vowels and the *bindu*;
this should be done using the six syllables situated upon the first two seed-syllables.
One should again contemplate the Goddess in the six limbs, beginning with the thumb;
she is discolored, flickering, black, tall, and clad in soiled garments.
Her earrings were fallen off, her hair was long, she was a widow with sparse teeth;
mounted upon a chariot whose banner bore the sign of a crow, her breasts were sagging.
With hands like suns, with harsh eyes, shaking her hands and filled with haste,
she was a fierce mother, matted-haired and with crooked glances.
One should always meditate upon her as being constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst and perpetually intent on quarreling; having done so, one should then perform the ritual action.
One should worship Jyeṣṭhā upon the previously mentioned pedestal for the removal of enemies;
the six limbs are in the filaments, and the eight Śaktis reside in the petals.
Hunger, thirst, passion, sleep, destruction, misfortune, the ocean, anger, and intolerance—
therefore, the gods, led by Indra, equipped with their weapons, [confronted them].
Thus, by propitiating Jyeṣṭhā, one becomes accomplished in mantra.
Now follows the armor-mantra (kavaca) of Dhūmāvatī.
Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who bestow grace upon your devotees;
O ocean of compassion, please tell me the armor-mantra (kavaca) of Dhūmāvatī.
Mahādeva said:
O Goddess, there exists in the world a most secret armor that subdues enemies and bestows all desired objects; out of affection for you, it is now revealed.
Having heard which, Rāmacandra slew Rāvaṇa in battle;
and having heard which, Bhārgava also conquered the entire world of moving and unmoving beings.
I shall speak that very armor; listen with careful attention.
O Great Goddess, Pippalāda is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi) of this armor.
O Dear One, the meter is Virāṭ and the deity is the illustrious Dhūmāvatī;
the application (viniyoga) of the Goddess is proclaimed for the slaying of enemies.
Oṃ! May Dhūmāvatī, the crusher of enemies, always protect my head;
may the great goddess Caṇḍarūpā always protect me on the forehead.
May Kṣutkāmā protect my eyes; may Bhīmā protect my ears;
may Kākadhvajā, the destroyer of all enemies, protect my nose.
May Pralaṃboṣṭhī, who wears a garland of severed heads, always protect my face;
may Vikṛtāsyā, the destroyer of enemies, always protect my throat.
May she known by the seed-syllable Dhūṃ, the destroyer of misfortune, always protect my throat;
may Kaṅkālinī, adorned with a garland of human skulls, protect my shoulders.
May Śuṣkamāṃsā, who is ever terrifying, protect my two arms;
may Lamvastanī, who is smoke-colored, always protect my two breasts.
May Sūryahastā, the primordial Bhairavī, protect my heart;
may Śatrumāṃsapriyā protect my back, and may Rudhirapriyā protect me.
May Madirā, whose eyes roll with intoxication and who wears a crown, protect my side;
may Karālinī, who carries corpses, always protect my belly.
May Vajratuṇḍā, the beloved of Śiva, protect the region of the waist forever;
may Karālavadanā, who is naked, protect the secret region.
May Ghorāṭṭahāsinī protect my knees; may Virāladvijā always protect my feet, she who is eternally accompanied by hunger and thirst.
May Ghoraghaṇṭā, the beloved of Śaṅkara, always protect [me] in every limb.
Thus has this armor (kavaca) of the Goddess been told to you, which subdues enemies.
For one who recites this, the Goddess remains present as the bestower of all accomplishments;
for such a person there shall be no affliction from enemies, nor ever any affliction from evil beings.
O beautiful lady of the family, by worshipping Dhūmāvatī with black flowers, the practitioner shall not suffer from afflictions caused by planets or afflictions caused by spirits.
Having worshipped the Goddess with fish and meat offerings according to the prescribed rite,
the knower of mantras should then fumigate her with the incense of *mahāmāṃsa*.
O Dear One, O Mistress of the Gods, if one recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times with a single-minded focus for only half a month, one shall slay the enemy; of this there is no doubt.
O Great Goddess, one should employ all of this in rites of slaying;
O Goddess, by the mere recollection of the armor-mantra, the enemy goes to the abode of Yama.
Thus ends the Dhūmāvatī-kavaca from the Dhūmāvatī-kalpa of the Śrī Rudrayāmala.
Now, [the ritual] for Aghora.
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the mantra for the command of the Ghorāstra:
one should utter Māyā (Hrīṃ), followed by two *sphurat*s, and then two *prasphurat*s.
Afterwards, one should utter *turuturu-rūpām*, then two *caṭas*,
then two *pracaṭas*, followed by two *kahas* and two *vamas*.
"Vaṃdhadvayaṃ ghātaya dvi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ"—this mantra consists of eleven syllables;
Ghoramuni is its seer, the Triṣṭubh is its metre, and it has [the aforementioned deity] as its presiding divinity.
The seed-syllable *vaṃ* is proclaimed as the non-terrible form (*aghora-rūpa*), and *hrīṃ* is celebrated as its power (*śakti*).
One should mentally pierce the ten directions with arrows numbering as many as the suns.
One should perform the six-limbed assignment (ṣaḍaṅga) with the [seed] syllables; next, the placement of the steps (padanyāsa) will be described:
[it is performed] on the hips, face, throat, heart, navel, and on the thumbs and knees.
In this manner, one should place eleven steps on the shanks and feet; [the remaining spaces] are measured by five, two, eight, six, four, and four [units].
O Umā, with syllables numbering sixty-six (rasa-netra), the words "mṛt-padāni" (the foot of clay) arise;
one should then meditate upon [the deity] who is dark as a cloud, possessing terrible fangs and three eyes.
Adorned with serpents, wearing red garments, and beautified by unguents,
he holds an axe, a sword, an arrow, and a trident.
She holds [these] with her right hands, and with the others, starting from the top,
she carries a hand-drum (ḍamaru), a shield (kheṭaka), a bow, and a human skull-cup (nṛkapāla).
And this sequence of Dhūmāvatī is completed.
Now follows the ritual sequence of Vagalāmukhī.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the paralyzing Vagalāmukhī:
Nārāyaṇa is the sage, Triṣṭubh is the meter, and Vagalāmukhī is the deity.
The seed-syllable (bīja) of the Goddess is Hṛllekhā, and Svāhā is declared to be her power (śakti).
Its application (viniyoga) is renowned as being for the attainment of the four aims of human life (puruṣārtha).
Hṛllekhā is declared to be the heart; Śiva and Vagalāmukhī are the crest-lock (śikhā) for the sake of all wicked ones; then "vācaṃ mukhaṃ" is the foot.
"Paralyze!"—thus the armor-mantra is spoken; "Pillar the tongue," "Pillar the eyes," and "Destroy the intellect"—this is declared to be the six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) ritual placement (nyāsa).
On the crown of the head, the forehead, between the eyebrows, the two eyes, the two ears,
the two nostrils, the two cheeks, as well as on the lips, the chin, and the jaw.
Likewise, on the neck, at the root of the right arm, in its middle, at the wrist,
at the base of the fingers, and indeed at the tip of the hand.
On another day, [one should worship] on the left arm and so forth, then at the root of the right thigh,
on the right knee, the ankle, the base of the fingers, and the tips of the feet.
Profound and intoxicated with passion, resembling molten gold,
she has four arms and three eyes, and is seated upon a lotus throne.
She holds a mallet in her right hand and a noose, a tongue, and a vajra in her left;
she wears yellow garments and possesses full, round, yellow breasts.
Adorned with golden earrings, wearing a crest of the yellow crescent moon,
decorated with yellow ornaments, and seated upon a golden throne.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess of the Gods, who paralyzes enemies,
in a beautiful region of the earth well-perfumed with the fragrance of flowers;
Then, having smeared the pavilion with cow dung, one should prepare a seat made of gold,
silver, copper, or birch bark.
One should carefully smear the yantra with camphor, agallochum, musk, sandalwood, and saffron, using a pen made of gold or silver.
Having drawn the *yoni* in the center, one should draw a six-cornered figure outside of it;
outside of that, an eight-petalled lotus, and outside of that, a sixteen-petaled one.
Outside, there are three squares adorned with four gates;
therein are the seats (pīṭhas) and the powers of the seats (pīṭha-śaktis) for the deities whose [specific] seats have not been mentioned.
Therein, Māyā is known as the sacred seat (pīṭha), and these very [five] are its powers (śaktis).
One should worship that seat with its seed-syllable, or else with Māyā and this [seed-syllable].
Having invoked the Goddess there, one should worship her with well-prepared yellow offerings;
one should worship the six limbs in the hexagon, in sequence starting from the eastern door.
One should worship Gaṇeśa, Vaṭuka, the Yoginīs, and Kṣetrapālaka,
and then honor the lineage of gurus from Īśāna to Nirṛti.
Vagalā is on the first leaf, and after that is Staṃbhinī;
likewise Jambhinī, Mohinī, Valyā, Acalā, and Cañcalā.
The [five winds] are Durddharṣā, Akalmaṣā, Dhīrā, Kalpanā, and Kālakarṣiṇī; they are also known as Bhrāmikā, Mandagāmanā, Bhogākhyā, and Yogikā.
One should worship these [deities] upon the sixteen petals with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (akṣata),
conjoined with the sixteen vowels according to the tradition of the Kula scripture.
And one should worship the eight [goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī in the middle of the petals of the imagined eight-petaled lotus, starting from the east, accompanied by their vehicles and weapons.
One should likewise worship the Lords of the World and their weapons outside;
one should worship the Root Goddess in the center of the *yoni* with three handfuls of flowers.

Having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) according to the rules with incense, lamps, food offerings (naivedya), perfumes, betel leaves, and lights, one should thereafter report the number of recitations (japa) performed.
p. 216a) Now follows the Vagalāmukhī Stotra.
Oṃ, one should remember Vagalāmukhī, who is clad in yellow garments, possesses beautiful eyes, has two arms, blazes with the brilliance of fire, and holds a stone and a mountain in her hands.

In the center of a jeweled pavilion with a gem-studded altar, I bow to the Goddess who sits upon a lion-throne, possessing a deep yellow complexion, her limbs adorned with yellow garments, ornaments, and garlands, holding a mallet that has seized the tongues of her enemies.
I bow to the goddess who holds the tip of her tongue with her left hand, who torments her enemies with her left [other] hand,
and who, adorned with yellow garments, possesses two arms, one of which strikes with a mace.
Having meditated upon the Goddess, who holds a trident, who bestows all prosperity, and who is richly adorned with every graceful ornament and attire, one should worship her.
I meditate upon Vagalāmukhī, whose beautiful cheeks are radiant with swinging golden earrings, whose moon-like face shines with the luster of a blossoming golden campaka flower,
who strikes down her enemies with her mace, and whose flickering tongue is ever-moving.
She who causes those facing away and those facing toward her to become motionless.

He who beholds you— seated upon the corpse-throne of his enemies, split open at the crown by that lion-throne in a pavilion radiant with shimmering jewels amidst milk and curds; whose navel is golden, whose tongue torments the hosts of foes, and whose playful movements cause the earth to whirl— [attains liberation].
All calamities go to their immediate dissolution for him.
The practitioner, having placed his left hand in the *mudrā* with a handful of yellow flowers upon Your lotus feet, O Goddess, and reciting the pleasing syllables of the mantra,

should— while absorbed in yellow meditation— contemplate the earthly seed-syllable (*bīja*) through the power of breath-retention (*kumbhaka*). This is for one who desires the friendship of that [deity].
Stupor shall arise in the heart of the speaker at that very moment.
The mantra is your petal for crushing adversaries, and your hymn is pure; the yantra is yours, the purifier of disputants and practitioners of mantras throughout the three worlds.
O Mother Śrī Vagalamukhi, he whose mouth utters your beautiful name attains prosperity by the mere taking up of that name.
There shall be a paralysis of the mouths of one's enemies.
The king becomes speechless with fear; fire becomes cool; the lord of anger becomes tranquil; the wicked man becomes a virtuous person; and his mouth quickly becomes lame.
Obeisance to you, O auspicious Śrī Nityā Vagalāmukhī, by whom all those who are arrogant in this world are humbled, being restrained by your yantra; salutations to you every day.

O you who are filled with compassion, grant me for a moment the sight of that [Lord] who is the paralyzer of the wicked, the pacifier of obstacles, the destroyer of poverty, the bringer of union with kings, the magnet that draws the hearts of fawn-eyed women, and the sole abode of good fortune.
O Mother, may your form, which brings death even to Death itself, manifest before me.

You are the supreme knowledge, the mother of the three worlds, the destroyer of the flood of obstacles, and the performer of yogic attraction; you are the sole eradicator of the great multitude of sins,
the performer of the expulsion of the wicked, the one who infuses delusion into the minds of people, and the sovereign power that paralyzes the tongue.
But the supreme knowledge, the Brahmāstra, is victorious.
O Mother, paralyze the faces of my adversaries; nail down their flickering tongues; seal them with the Brahmī-mudrā; and arrest the movement of the fire within their intellects!
O fair-limbed one clad in yellow garments, crush, crush the enemies with your swift mace; O Vagala, whose eyes are filled with compassion, destroy the flood of obstacles every day!
O Mother Bhairavī, Bhadrakālī, Vijayā, Vārāhī, refuge of the universe, Śrī Nityā, Samayā, Maheśī, Vagalāmukhī, Kāmeśī, Vāmā, Ramā,
Mātaṅgī, Tripurā, higher than the highest, bestower of heaven and liberation— I am your servant; out of compassion, protect me who has come for refuge.
O Sovereign of the Universe, protect me!
In times of fear, amidst a band of thieves, at the moment of striking a blow, in captivity, in the midst of water,

in fire, in debate or dispute, when the king is enraged, during the time of divine ordeals, or in the night; for the purpose of recitation, for immobilization, at the time of slaying an enemy, or in battle free from calamity— whether going or standing still— [one should proceed].
This recitation of yours at the time of night brings about the attainment of success.
If a person, having always maintained this hymn of the Goddess as a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*),
wears this *yantra* on his arm, hand, or neck at the proper time,
then kings, excellent women, crocodiles, serpents, lions, and the wicked will be paralyzed when he merely utters it.
Just as the fortune residing within the enemy is brought to fulfillment.
The practitioner who recites this daily at the three times of day becomes a lord of the three worlds and is worshipped by the hosts of gods;
every rite of his succeeds upon being seen, and likewise, O Mother of the World, he attains supreme perfection.
Thus ends the hymn to Pītā Vagalā composed by the venerable Nārada.
Now follows the Armor of Vagalāmukhī.
The illustrious Mahogratārā said:
O Mahādeva, that king [ruled] over Maṇḍalaka and others who were crawling about like snakes, their minds corrupted by wealth and pride.
O Śaṅkara, tell me of the worship of elephants, serpents, and enemies, as well as of living beings.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
O Goddess, formerly in the Kṛtayuga, when the agitation of Vātaka arose,
the gods went to the undisturbed state where the seven oceans become one.
All the gods, including Indra and Viṣṇu, have approached me with fear.
The gods said:
O Śiva, Śaṅkara, Rudreśa, protect us who have come to you for refuge from the agitation of great winds and the like, and from this great ocean of hunger.
Having heard that, O Queen of the Gods, I gave to all the deities this armor fashioned of old, which cuts asunder all great fears.
This great armor of Vagalāmukhī bestows the life-force of Śiva;
formerly, it was he himself who was terrified and put to flight by the fear of the demon Bhasmāsura.
O Supreme Goddess, may you protect my life-breaths as I recite this;
therefore, it is renowned as the supreme protector that bestows the life-force of Śiva.
May Vagalā, whose supreme head emerges from the thirty-six [channels] on the right and left, protect me;
and may the Guru, blazing with supreme power, protect me in the thousand-petaled lotus.
The supreme power, whose nature is consciousness, is the consort of Śiva on my forehead;
Mahākālī is the pair of my arms, and the Supreme Sovereign is the pair of my eyes.
May the pair of ears, beloved of yellow flowers, protect me; may she on the cheeks be the supreme Śakti, and on the chin and the two breasts, the supreme Kalās.
May she whose nature is the Supreme Brahman protect the face;
may she who is worshipped with yellow flowers protect the throat; and may she who grants the breast of Skanda protect the shoulders.

Clad in yellow garments, she holds the right arm and the left [arm] with her left hand; she steals the beauty of her left limb, while her single face, like the orb of the sun, bears both her heart and her pair of breasts.
The one who assumes form, having touched the waist, should worship the moon-bearing [Śiva] who has been questioned;
she herself is the power (śakti) in the heart-lotus, pure and in the form of the individual soul (jīva).
The wheel of command (ājñā-cakra) is in the form of the bindu, the consort of the Supreme Brahman;
it is the thousand-petaled lotus known as the Brahma-randhra, which bears its own essential nature.
Pātumā, Paramāśakti, Cāmarī, Kuṭilālakā, the thirty-six-syllable Vidyā, and Pītāpītavapuḥ; these are the names.
Worshipped with yellow flowers, fond of yellow offerings and oblations,
may she who paralyzes enemies protect my entire body with auspiciousness.
May the Great Goddess, who carries one across the supreme ocean of saṃsāra and grants the desires of the mind, deliver me through the apertures of Brahmā.
May the Guru’s form at the Ājñā-cakra, who destroys great fear and is the most excellent of all vidyās, protect my tongue, which bears the body of the scriptures.
May she who dwells in the throat, bearing the body of the Lord of Life within the sixteen-petaled lotus of purity, and known as the embodiment of the thirty-six principles, protect me always.
May she who is the supreme self, whose form is both manifest and unmanifest as Bhavānī and Īśa within the lotus of the heart,
the formidable one, tear asunder the great enemies such as the senses and the rest.
In Maṇipūra, on the ten petals, Mahāviṣṇu assumes his own form;
tearing asunder all delusions, may that Māyā protect me.
May this Parā-vidyā, who is Prajāpati herself in her own form within the six-petalled Svādhiṣṭhāna,
protect me from delusion as she abides in the act of creation.
May he who assumes the form of Gaṇeśa protect me in the four-petalled [lotus] at the base;
may this supreme Kalā, whose nature consists of the sixteen vowels, protect me.
Ka, kha, ga, gha, and likewise ṅa; ca, cha, ja, jha, and likewise ña—let it be so.
Ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, and likewise ṇa; ta, tha, da, and likewise dha—let it be so.
May *dha*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, and *tu* protect me, who am intent on meditation, from enemies;
may *va*, *bha*, *ma*, and *ya*, in the form of speech, drive away my enemies for the sake of knowledge.
*Raṃ laṃ vaṃ śaṃ tathā ṣaṃ saṃ*: having thus torn asunder the tongue of the enemy, may the consort of Śaṅkara always protect my speech, my mouth, and my tongue.
Haṃ Laṃ Kṣaṃ—may these protect the whole [of my being], guarding my supreme glory;
likewise, the Praṇava, the firm Māyā, and the third, this triad as well.
The third vowel, the first of the *yā* group, the fifth vowel, the second *kā*,
and the right eye— this is remembered as the destroyer of all evil.
Likewise, with the vocative ending in the sixth case, one should paralyze speech by means of the tongue;
with the second case, one should summon [the enemy], and likewise destroy the intellect.
O Dear One, [the mantra] consists of the syllable *sthi*, followed by *māyā* (hrīṃ), then *tāraṃ* (oṃ), and finally *vahni-vadhū* (svāhā).
This great vidyā is the paralyzer of enemies.
Having recited the mantra three times, perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) upon all limbs;
one will surely conquer even heroic enemies in a great battle— of this there is no doubt.
Taking clay from a potter’s workshop with his left hand,
having made a lamp and ignited it with oil, he should place it on his left side and recite the mantra.
Having worshipped with devotion a young girl of fair complexion with yellow flowers, one certainly paralyzes the enemy army for three nights in a great battle.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon his body, the yogi worships while reciting the mantra,
satisfying that Śakti along with her retinue with yellow-colored offerings.
She surely brings even the Lord of the World under her control, how much more so a mere mortal;
she who causes the paralysis of speech possesses heroic power and a beautiful countenance.
O Dear One, having adorned a beautiful sixteen-year-old girl with gold ornaments, one should worship her;
and having recited the root mantra a thousand times, even Vācaspati [would be surpassed].
It certainly paralyzes even the supreme speech; what need be said of a mere mortal?
One desiring subjugation should therefore gird one's loins firmly.
Having placed the śakti upon the liṅga, one should recite the mantra three thousand times;
one certainly brings even Indrāṇī under control, let alone an ordinary human woman.
The lord of the mandala, facing north, stands subduing [the disciple];
he [should gaze upon] a beautiful sixteen-year-old woman with a face turned to the right and a pure smile.
Having grasped her breasts with his hands, he kisses her smiling face;
placing her upon his organ, he drinks from her mouth while muttering the mantra.
O Great King, one who is devoted to the worship of Vagalā will surely bring the triple-thousandfold world system under control by whatever means possible; it cannot be otherwise.
The power of Śaṅkara can paralyze all the worlds,
bring them under control, slay hosts of enemies, and even cause mountains to be uprooted.
Even Candra, the architect of the gods, would be unable to cover the supreme person; O Pārvatī, how could the majesty of this armor ever be fully described?
O Goddess, when the great, terrible end— the onset of the dissolution—
has arrived, the host of winds is then paralyzed by a single recitation.
Thus, this supreme knowledge, which rends asunder the great enemy [of ignorance],
is not for the atheist, the thief, the wicked, the fool, or the one who fancies himself a scholar.
This heart-vidyā should not be given; by giving it, one incurs blindness.
[It should be given] to one of virtuous conduct, well-subdued, and devoted to the service of the guru.
This supreme [teaching] should be given to one who is pure and recites the great mantra;
having first performed the excellent armor-rite (kavaca), he should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind.
It is certain that the *staṃbhinī* vidyā will not be accomplished in any other way.
Thus ends the Vagalāmukhī-kavaca, in the dialogue between Mahogratārā and [the Lord], within the Śrī-Ekavīrā-tantra.
Now, [the ritual] of Mṛtyuñjaya Bhairava.
The mantra "Oṃ Jūṃ Saḥ" is declared to be named Mṛtyuñjaya;
its seer (ṛṣi) is Kalāha Daitya, and its meter (chandas) is said to be Gāyatrī.
Mahādeva, the conqueror of death, is proclaimed as the presiding deity;
the ritual for the six limbs is declared to consist of the six long vowels joined with the three qualities.
Seated upon two lotuses, smiling, with eyes like the moon, sun, and fire,
he holds in his hands the gesture of wisdom (jñānamudrā), a noose, a rosary, and a garland of beads.
Resembling camphor, with the moon upon his head, he pours a stream of nectar from his left hand;
his body is half-formed, enriched with many ornaments, and he captivates the entire universe with his splendor.
And thus, this sequence of Vagalāmukhī is completed.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Propitiation of Tripurabhairavī, Mahālakṣmī, Mātaṅgī, and Bagalāmukhī," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*.

Now, having determined the daily individual worship (*nityārcana*), he first describes the worship of the *cakra*, because it is necessary for all eight types of spiritual accomplishments (*sādhana*).
I shall now proclaim the worship of the wheel (cakrapūjā), which is concealed in all the tantras;
there exists nothing else that bestows the desired accomplishment more than this.
The goddess Śrī, who grants all desired objects as proclaimed by all the gods,
should be propitiated even by those following the Vedic path through a priest for the attainment of their goals.
But having performed the Kaulika rite, O Goddess, their heart's desires shall be fulfilled.
In rites for pacification, nourishment, subjugation, attraction, paralysis, and killing;
in rites for causing hatred, expulsion, and the defeat of enemy armies.
For the attainment of mastery and for the sake of liberation, for the purpose of accomplishing spiritual powers,
for the destruction of obstacles, and for the warding off of defects caused by spirits.
It is for the loss of sovereignty of kings, for the seizure of their fortune,
for the acquisition of undesirable offspring, and for the warding off of calamities and diseases.
The people were pacified during a forest drought, when the circle of mothers was established;
and at the time of initiation, during the festival of Madana, on a sacred day of the Guru.
In times of misfortune for the lords of the land, or during a marriage alliance between clans,
upon setting out on a journey or while traveling abroad, as well as during festivals and the attainment of prosperity— these are the occasions [for such rites].
At that time, men should perform the worship of the discus, which is dear to all the gods and must be kept secret; I shall now describe its ritual procedure.
The commitment of the wheel-worship is proclaimed to be eightfold:
at the moment of sudden arising, during an activity, or when an activity has reached completion.
On a festival day dedicated to the deity, or upon the arrival of a weaver,
during the Umāmāheśvara conjunction, or during the union with Śakti.
On the day of Kāma, the worship of the discus (Cakrapūjā) in the kingdom of Bali bestows joy;
it may be performed at twilight, under the Abhijit asterism, or at midnight on the eighth lunar day.
If this yoga named Umāmāheśvara should occur on the ninth lunar day,
and this yoga Śaktisaṃgama occurs on the eighth or the fourteenth lunar day of Mars (Bhauma), [it is highly auspicious].
In the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvina, the five days beginning from the thirteenth are declared to be the sovereignty of Bali, for his enjoyment as he pleases.
They call that day "Kāmādi" (the beginning of desires); on the thirteenth lunar day falling on a Monday, having bathed on the preceding day and worshipped the Goddess for the sake of one's desire—
Having performed this, one should intend the worship of the wheel and offer the sacrificial oblation (bali) of the animal victim.
The specific manner of offering the bali-oblation, however, must be explained according to the source.
Having thus properly offered the bali-oblation and performed the daily rites,
one should invite the women and men for the sake of the purpose during the third watch of the night.
For the pleasure of the Goddess Amuktī, for the fulfillment of my heart’s desire,
and for the sake of the complete purpose of this worship of the Discus (Cakrapūjā), you indeed have been invited by me along with Umā.
Now, he describes the manner of the invitation:
Then one should invite all the yoginīs as well as the yogins;
having placed a flower in their right hand, one should likewise offer the invitation for conversation.
"O Ādya, please accept this invitation for the sake of worship; I now extend the invitation to you.
Then, having washed his feet with his hand, he should proceed to come.
O Goddess, one should invite the preceptor for his comfort with the mantra itself.
If there are eight or more women invited, men should be fewer than that number;
if men are fewer than the women, they bring about loss.
Whether they all abide by the Kaula vow or have previously abandoned the practice of the Dakṣas,
those who are devoted to initiation should be invited for the worship of the Cakra.
On that night, one should personally worship the deity without weariness;
the word "kula" is said to be twofold: "kulajā" and "piśācinī."
One should recite one thousand and eight times at night the thirteen-syllable mantra ending in *svāhā*; thereafter, one shall perceive obstacles as well as auspiciousness within the *cakra*.
When an obstacle is perceived, one should not perform the rite; rather, it should be preceded by pacification (śānti).
Pacification consists of Gaṇeśvara, fire-oblations (homa), and offerings to the planets and Bhairava.
Then, one should offer an external oblation (bali) while reciting this mantra:
Oṃ, salutation! Having uttered "Ca" three times, [one calls] such-and-such Kṣetrapālaka:
"Come, come, O Blessed One! Accept this worship, the pair, and likewise the bali offering."
"Bhakṣa-yugmaṃ cakra vighnakarān staṃbhaya yugmakam hūṃ phaṭ svāhā"— this mantra is proclaimed as having thirty-four syllables.
Having completed the duties of the day, one should fulfill the evening rite.
The Goddess said:
Now I wish to hear the definitive conclusion regarding the assembly:
in which places should one perform the Kulacakra that has arisen?
O Maheśvara, tell me by whom the wheel is to be fashioned.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
I shall speak, O lady of excellent hips; listen to the supreme location of the wheel:
in a cremation ground, at a solitary tree, on a mountain, or in the house of a mother-goddess.
In a palace, in empty dwellings, on a riverbank, or in a forest—
having swept one of these places and smeared it with cow dung.
Husks, hair, and so forth are to be purified by a servant or a servant-maid;
likewise, the cremation ground, the ritual application, the Varaṇā river, and the solitary tree.
On the mountain peak there is Aṭṭahāsaka, the size of Kollagṛha;
and there is the palace Jayantī, as well as Carita and Śūnyaveśma.
O auspicious lady, the places have been described—Sragāhyaka, the riverbank, the forest, and Devikoṭaka; now I shall tell you of their origin.

The *avarga* is indicated in the east, situated in the south-eastern corner of the *kavarga*; the *cavarga* is in the southern part, and the *ṭhavarga* is traditionally taught to be in the south-west.
The *va* group is in the west, O auspicious one; the *pa* group is in the northwest;
the *ya* group is in the northern part; and the *śa* group is situated in the northeast.
O lady of beautiful hips, having come to these places where the wheel originates,
one should perform the yoga of the hero by rising up once.
I shall describe the livelihood and the characteristics of the preceptor:
those who are learned in many scriptures, steadfast, and followers of the ten perfections.
Those who possess knowledge of the successive lineage, who have attained perfection through their gurus,
who are fully endowed with the complete initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka), and who abide in the practice of non-duality;
Having properly obtained the permission of the guru, one should remain in the company of the virtuous;
possessing compassion for all sentient beings, one should be free from hypocrisy and envy.
Forgiving, self-controlled, pure, and constant, protecting his disciples like his own sons—
one endowed with these qualities is a teacher worthy of Sthāṇu’s Sundarī.
Now he speaks of the mandala.
O beloved, one should have it well-measured with a fine thread made of linen;
for the sake of the gods, one should cause it to fall upon the ground as an eight-cornered lotus with eight petals.
The filaments should be six finger-breadths, the pericarp eight finger-breadths,
the petals twelve finger-breadths, and the joints between the petals two finger-breadths.
The moon-shaped mandalas are four finger-breadths [in diameter] and circular in form;
outside of those, the door-sections measure twelve finger-breadths.
It has four doors and four corners, marked with lotuses at the corners;
the pericarp is yellow in color, and the filaments are indeed red.
O auspicious one, the leaf is made white; O Goddess, the junction of its petals is yellow like a harītakī fruit; it possesses a black opening, and its white orb is like that of the moon.
For the sake of pacifying and bringing peace to disease, one should draw the Bhadra-maṇḍala.
I shall speak that which was uttered by Śiva; listen, O lady of excellent complexion!
O beloved of beautiful hips, one should have it measured accurately with a yellow thread.
One should drop the marks for the Āhūṃ-ṭhānas and the hands onto the ground using a thread;
the pericarp is six finger-breadths, and the filaments are four finger-breadths.
The petals are twelve finger-breadths long, beautiful with a lunar disc; the petals are auspiciously yellow, O auspicious one, while the joints of the petals are black.
One should make the moon white and the door red;
thus it shall be beautiful, with excellent lines and perfectly symmetrical.
In the east is a skull-cup, white; in the south, a sword, black;
in the west, a beautiful hand-drum (ḍamaru), green, O auspicious one.
In the north, with white and yellow [pigments], there is the trident of Varasundarī;
O Goddess, it is for the seizing of the crest-lock and for the rite of attracting the lips.
This [mantra] is pungent as poison everywhere; one should draw the maṇḍalas.
O lady of excellent complexion, I shall now describe the Lord of the Gaṇas:
a mandala measuring three cubits in length, well-measured with a red thread.
One should extend one cubit for the pericarp, the filaments, and the petals;
one should likewise describe one cubit for the sun, the moon, and the place of water.
Having drawn a very beautiful square door-frame measuring one cubit,
the pericarp is said to be green and the filaments yellow.
One should not draw the sun in white water-paint; rather, one should draw it with red.
The moon should be drawn with white, and the leaf should be very beautiful and red.
The eastern gate is white, richly endowed with great beauty; in the east is a black lion;
in the south is a white man; and in the west is a black trident.
In the north, Maheśvarī holds a beautiful hand-drum (ḍamaru) with a green appearance; she is the one who effects subjugation, attraction, and piercing through the mandala.
I shall now describe the *pratānaka* rite for the mother of a hero:
one should cause [the victim] to fall upon the ground with a cord made of cowhide that has been thoroughly tightened.
Beginning from a measure of two cubits, it is adorned with four gates;
the pericarp is five finger-breadths [in width] and the filaments are four finger-breadths.
The leaf [of the temple] should be sixteen finger-breadths wide and two cubits from the water-level;
the head [of the roof] should be four finger-breadths, and one should cause all the doors to be aligned with these measurements.
O auspicious one, the pericarp should be green, the filaments red, and one should make the petals black;
likewise, the joints of the petals and the water [should be made so].
With blood, one should make them very beautiful, and with incense, one should clear the doors;
[one should worship] the fourfold set: the sword, the skull-bowl, the axe, and the trident.
O Dear One, one should draw four doors so that they attain beauty,
especially at the time of the Great Accomplishment (mahāsādhana) and during the rite of slaying (māraṇa).

O auspicious one, O beautiful-eyed one, one should draw the Pretānaka mandala, which bestows all accomplishments (siddhis), including pacification (śāntika), enrichment (pauṣṭika), subjugation (vaśya), and the rite of destruction (māraṇa).
Having understood the specific maṇḍala by means of which one should undertake the ritual action.
I shall explain its meaning specifically according to its various modes:
they say that through the gross [form] it is the Kali age, and through the black [form] death occurs.
If there are crooked lines, there will be terrible suffering; if the lines are severed, there is fear of kings.
If the leaf is made uneven, the accomplishment of mantras does not arise.
Therefore, one should exert effort if one desires supreme accomplishment;
having thus understood the divisions of action, one should undertake action.
O Queen, what else do you wish to ask? The method for descending by means of a rope has been explained.
Now, he speaks of the substances for worship.
O lady of beautiful hips, having prepared all kinds of food and drink as well as whatever materials are available according to one's wealth, one should ask forgiveness for all those materials.
One should arrange, in due order, sandalwood, the sacred vessel, perfumes and garlands, the enchanting [image], the seat, incense, and vermilion.
Various kinds of meats, many species of fish,
the four types of foods, and side dishes and condiments.
One should here arrange all the aforementioned materials in their entirety.
Now, he states the eightfold group of eight in sequence.
In that regard, first he states the substances for washing the feet of the heroes (vīra) and others.
O Goddess, I shall now describe to you the washing of the feet:
fragrant priyaṅgu, uśīra, and likewise sandalwood.
One should take equal parts of hair, meat, and poison;
having ground them finely with water in the proper manner, one should prepare the mixture.
One should place a jar of warm water in the middle of the outer area and wash each of the hero's feet with that water.
Aṭṭahāsa arose in Caritrā,
Priyaṅgu in Kolāpurī, Surabhi in Jayantī, and Uśīraka as well.
O auspicious lady, *vadana* is in Ujjayinī, *bāla* at Prayāga,
*māṃsī* in Vārāṇasī, and *cauraka* in Karṇamoḍya.
These eight are declared to be the eight characteristics of the field.
O lady of excellent complexion, listen as I describe the procedure for the offering:
sandalwood, the sacred thread, and fragrant garlands, O enchanting one.
One should cause the seat, incense, vermilion, sandalwood, viraja, bhadra, pavitra, and likewise meruka to be offered in their proper sequence, O auspicious lady.
Hādrāpura is fragrance; Mālyamelāpura is known [as such];
Kāśmīra is to be known as Mohanī; likewise, Meruka is the seat (āsana).
They say that *tagara* is incense and *sindūra* is the *puṇḍravardhana*;
these eight are the ornaments and the characteristics of the secondary field (*upakṣetra*).
The wise one should offer [the oblations] to the preceptor and the others in their proper sequence;
thus, the ritual procedure for the offerings has been briefly described by me.
O auspicious lady, I shall now describe the installation of the image:
[it should be placed] in a large wooden vessel filled with cooked rice.
One should have a five-colored Vaijayantī banner raised;
it should be made without gaps and provided with garlands inside the offering vessel.
O beloved, just as a splendor is achieved through various flower garlands,
so too should one make the temple of the deity beautiful with that [garland].
O auspicious lady, [offer] fish and meat, incenses, sesame flour,
sweetmeats, vṛkṣāmla, blood, and likewise the red-dyed cloth.
(220b) These eight have been described by me for the rite of the *saṃdoha* offering:
on the opposite bank there should be meat and fish, as well as *pṛṣṭāpura*.
O auspicious lady, the incense should consist of *kudgaṇḍi*, along with sugar, sesame, and flour; likewise, there should be milk, sweetmeats (*modaka*), and fermented sour gruel (*puryāmla*).
In the Āmrātaka [mandala] there would be blood; in the Gṛharāja, lac;
in the Samudra, a wooden vessel; and in the Meru, cooked rice.
The serpent-king, the garland, the gift of a wreath, and the red flower-garland;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
The five-colored banner is pure, clothed in the five [elements];
O auspicious one, the ocean is the belly, and Meru is proclaimed to be the navel.
For indeed, O King, the one called Kuṇḍalā is the hair of the eyes and all over the body,
as well as prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
O auspicious lady, the five deities reside upon the pure seat;
the upward breath and the downward breath are proclaimed to be the moon and the sun.
Thirty-three crores of gods reside within each pore of his skin;
O auspicious lady, he is the establisher of the folds [of the body], both external and internal.
All the scriptures have been expounded here, extracted like clarified butter from burnt fuel.
Alcohol is said to be of eight kinds, and likewise the great meats are eight;
and there are eight Bhairavas, for whom heroes are proclaimed as the presiding deities in their respective places.
Likewise, Bhairavī has been proclaimed, as well as the eight Mothers;
in their place there are Śaktis, and that indeed is the group of eight eights.
Now, he describes the worship.
One should place the circle of the image of one's own vidyā in the center,
and there, having placed a jar filled with wine, one should invoke the Goddess and perform worship.
Various kinds of meats, many species of fish, the four types of foods, and various side dishes and condiments.
Having properly worshipped these deities along with their limbs and retinues,
the Śaktis and likewise the Vīras should be worshipped with flowers, unbroken rice grains, and other offerings.
Alternatively:
One should worship the Goddess Śakti directly as her own essential form;
one should employ the Vīra in the form of Bhairava among men.
To whatever extent the yoginīs have been fully worshipped within one's own circle,
O Queen of Gods, to that same extent are the gurus, Bhairava and the others.
O Maheśānī, the men situated within the center of the yantra extend as far as the guardians of the directions (dikpālas); O Queen of the Gods, the women and the men are of that same measure.
One should establish each of those according to one's understanding through the divisions of the locations of the wheels;
in the center, within the *bindu*, one should indeed worship you as a couple together with me.
Having discerned everything according to the rules, one should worship with all the ritual services (upacāra) using the previously mentioned mantra-forms proclaimed in the *Pūjākalpa*.
One should present as manifest the number of deities, their names, the ritual offerings (argha), the seats, the vessels, and the full jars.
With various kinds of ornaments and pairs of garments, each distinct,
as well as with flowers, incense, unbroken grains of rice, and delightful fragrances.
With ointments of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and musk,
as well as with ritual gestures (mudrās), prostrations, songs, and instrumental music.
One should satisfy the Great Goddess, one’s chosen deity, with discipline;
having gratified her, one should perform all rites such as recitation and fire-offerings as previously described.
Now, he describes the specific meditations for rites performed for desired results and so forth.

For rites of pacification (śāntika), one should visualize [the deities] as bestowing boons with hands held in the gesture of protection, possessing serene countenances, auspicious, white in color, and clad in excellent white garments.
For the rite of subjugation, one should visualize the two goddesses wearing red garments and bearing as weapons a noose, a goad, a great bow, and flower-arrows.
They were dark-complexioned, clad in black garments, fierce, and equipped with terrible weapons;
they bore fearsome skeletons and held excellent garlands of mantras in their hands.
One should contemplate the Mārīs as follows: holding skull-bowls and knives in their hands, they drink blood-wine, chew bones, and devour [flesh].
Clad in yellow garments, holding vajras in their hands, and possessed of great strength,
they should be meditated upon by Śrī Kulāmbikā as standing upon the frontal globes of elephants used for immobilization.
For the rite of eradication (uccāṭana), the great goddesses are mounted upon deer, holding banners in their hands, extremely restless, smoke-colored, and even performing austerities on mountains.
In the rite of delusion they are blue in form; in attraction, tawny and reddish;
in inciting enmity, pigeon-colored; and in increasing various diseases, variegated.
Thus, in accordance with one's karma, this sacred tradition (āmnāya) will become beloved, effective for sacrifice, and truly bestowing its fruit; it shall not be otherwise.
Worship, recitation, as well as fire-offerings (homa), the mantras and vidyās of the Gaṇa,
and meditation according to the path described for the wheels— all should be performed according to the rules prescribed for rites of pacification and the like.
Now, the offering of the bali-oblation.
To the north of the house, within a triangular enclosure in the ground,
one should worship Ucchiṣṭabhairava there with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
During the great festival of the Cakra-pūjā, the fault of impurity (ucchiṣṭa) occurs;
for the sake of avoiding that fault, I worship Bhairava.
*Tālatrayam*, *tathocchiṣṭabhairave*, *hi*, *dvayam*, *tathā*,
*valim gṛhṇa-yugam*, *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*— this mantra consists of twenty-two syllables.
With this, one should perform the offering of bali and the worship to her;
having entered the hall of worship, one should prostrate before her who is seated upon the wheel.
O auspicious lady, one who has well-cultivated a single-pointed state of mind should recite this hymn:
"Homage to you, O Universal Monarch; homage to you, the bestower of knowledge."
Salutations to you who are the form of Śiva; salutations to you, the savior from worldly existence!
May the sixty-four Yoginīs and likewise the Kṣetrapālas [be propitious].
"I bow to this Bhairava-cakra, which is of a single form.
Having thus recited this primordial hymn of praise, one should seat oneself upon the throne.
They should be seated upon their seats according to the prescribed rule, in order of seniority;
the women should occupy one place and the men another, separately.
Alternatively, having formed pairs, one should seat them in order,
either in the form of a row or again in the form of a circle.
One should worship all those whose minds are fixed on Śiva and Śakti in the center of the wheel.
Taking the Guru’s vessel filled with the nectar of wine in his hand,
he himself should recite the ritual procedure for peace and sprinkle [the assembly].
Victorious is the lotus-foot of the Goddess Hara, which bestows grace, the left-hand path, nectar, and liberation;
it awakens the intellect to the infinite Siddhānta. I bow to the host of Yoginīs, numbering sixty-four.
I bow my head to the Lord Bhairava, who dwells in the center of the circle of Yoginīs, surrounded by the mandala of Mothers, and to his beloved Bhairavī.
To the one who destroys the darkness of the beginningless and terrible saṃsāra.
Homage to the venerable Lord-Physician, the ordainer of the medicine of the Kula;
[may he remove] misfortune, evil, and diseases resulting from transgressing the conduct of the observance (samaya).
By the removal of all these [obstacles] through the conjunction of the divine wheel,
there shall be long life, health, sovereignty, fame, gain, auspiciousness, and victory.
May there be splendor and the fulfillment of desires; may all the deities protect [you].

May the Blessed One, the Lord of the Family, grant peace to those who worship and protect, to the lords of ascetics, the lords of yogis, and those whose wealth is penance, as well as to the universe, the kingdom, the city, and the king.
But Nanda, having been created by the Great Being for the sake of the assembly of practitioners and the spectators, is called Aghora and is four-faced; however,
Nanda is devoted to all families and Kaulas, while others are supreme, distinguished by the differentiation of their specific stations within the Śāmbhava [tradition].

May the Siddhas, Gurus, and those born of the lineages of the six Yoginīs and the foremost Vīras— those who are elders, juniors, observers of the rules (samayins), young men, and maidens— along with kings, gods, the twice-born, and virtuous people, rejoice in that succession of the flood [of grace]. May they indeed rejoice!
But Nanda’s teachers were skilled in policy, established in faultless conduct, free from envy, incomparable, and free from affliction;
they were eternally devoted to the stainless, unconditioned, tranquil yet fierce in their peaceful minds, having cast off sorrow and fear.
But those who delight in yoga, joined with the family-yoga (kula-yoga)—the teachers, those bound by the samaya, the practitioners, and the spiritual sons;
the twice-born, young women, ascetics, and maidens; and those devoted to the Dharma, joined as teacher and disciple—let them rejoice.
May the desired powers such as *aṇimā* delight the families of practitioners; may the curses of the Yoginīs descend upon those who violate the observances (*samaya*).
May that indescribable state of Śambhu manifest within me, in which there is only the lotus-feet of the Guru.
It is obtainable.
Those which are the dwellings on the stages of the sequential movement of the wheels, those which are situated within the channels,
and those which reside in the pores of the tree of the body, are established within the elements.
May those goddesses, who dwell upon the waves of the wind of exhalation and whose abode is the breath of inhalation, and who are intent on devouring the faction of enemies,
be satisfied when worshipped by the Kaulas.

Those who are born of the divine lineage, who have descended to the earth as deities, who are ever-singing near [the Lord], whose splendor is eternally renowned, who reside upon the crest [of the flame], who are the mothers worthy of their own praise;
those who are composed of the nectar of the orb of immortality, who are all-pervading, who are givers at all times— all of them [protect] me.
May those devoted to preserving the family path grant me peace.
Whether they are situated above in the cosmic egg or in the expanse of the sky, on the surface of the earth, in the partless realm, in the netherworld, in fire, in water, in wind, or wherever else;
whether they have taken their place in sacred fields, seats, and secondary seats, these goddesses are pleased by incense, lamps, and other offerings, as well as by meat.
May the beloved consorts of the lords of sages protect us, having always performed the ritual of offerings.
Brahmā, Śrī, Śeṣa, Durgā, Guha, the Gaṇas, the Bhairavas, the Kṣetrapālas, Vetālas, Ādityas, Rudras, the Planets (Grahas), Vasus, Sages (Munis), Siddhas, Guhyakas and others;
Bhūtas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Ṛṣis, Pitṛs, Kinnaras, Yakṣas, Nāgas, the Lords of Yogins, and the Cāraṇas.
May all those who move upon the wheel—the sages among men and the gods—protect us.
May all the deities residing in the body, the elephant-faced ones, the lords of the fields, the Bhairavas, the Yoginīs, the Vaṭukas, the Yakṣas, the Pitṛs, the Bhūtas, the Piśācas,
the Grahas, and others— the earth-dwellers, the directional guardians, the sky-goers, the Vetālas, and the Ceṭakas— be satisfied by this son of noble family.
As you drink my beverage, it is delicious.

If truth is [the goal], and if the gurus, sacrificial fees, gods, and ancestors, the Vedas and Agamas, and the Yoginīs are dear; if the Supreme Deity exists, and if the Vedas are indeed authoritative;
if the Śākta philosophy is held, and if the command of the Veda is unfailing—then let there be the True Fivefold [Path].
And if there should be a Kulikā, my victory shall always be mine.
All the practitioners, together with their mudrās and lords of the gaṇas, as well as the yoginīs and the guardians of the fields, are satisfied; they are all established within my body.
May the universe— from Śiva down to the forest-dweller (vaniparyeta), from Brahmā down to a blade of grass (stambha),
and from the beginning of time to Śiva— be satisfied by this sacrifice.
Having recited [the mantras] and performed the worship, the Guru should then dismiss the vessel;
he should then give the water from the jar to the disciple and separately to each of the Yoginīs.
In the same manner, he should drink from the vessel himself for both the heroes and the others.
You shall explain the Kaulika conduct, which bestows the fruits of both worlds;
the union of worthy vessels (pātra-melāpaka) is called the "skin" that brings about [liberation].
Neither a brother, nor a father, nor a friend is [fit] except as a recipient for the vessel,
provided they are not uninitiated, of improper conduct, ignorant of the mantras, or devoid of devotion to the deity.

By those who have violated their commitments, by the wicked, by those who observe vows for the sake of worldly deception, by those who hate women, by those who have offended their gurus, by those devoid of devotion, and by the evil-minded;
Not by means of food, drinks, animals, or minor rites;
but by those who know the words, sentences, and means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and who understand the meaning of the Śrutis and Smṛtis.
By those who hate women, by those hostile to their gurus, by those devoid of devotion, by evil-minded ones, by the ignorant, by those using improper vehicles, by beasts, and by those of mean conduct.

By those who know the words, sentences, and means of valid cognition; by those who understand the meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti; and by those who perform the Vaiṣṇava vows, even if they are devoid of noble lineage or traditional instruction.
One should never perform the joining of vessels with those who possess Brahmanic luster,
provided they are devoted to your worship, tranquil, and averse to the wealth of others.
They were skilled in family traditions, promoters of the ancestral path,
fond of women, praising women, steadfast, handsome, and speakers of gentle words.

It is maintained by those of noble lineage, by the guarded, by the learned, by the handsome, by those who have achieved success in their practices, by those possessing wealth and other resources, by the fortunate, and by the lustful.
When those devoted to Brahman and honored by kings meet by the power of destiny, one should effect a union with a worthy recipient; thus, happiness and prosperity shall accrue to both.
One should not use a single vessel even if it belongs directly to the Lord of the Family;
otherwise, the mantras turn away and obstacles arise at every step.
One should not offer liquor contained in one's own vessel even to Bhairava;
if one should offer it out of delusion, one would incur the curse of the deity.
One should never cause Śaṅkara to use a seat, food, a vessel, a sacred thread, a bed, or similar items that are provided by those who are ignorant or unworthy.
Or, according to the division of the currents (śrota), one should perform the union of vessels (pātramelana) with the Kaulikas:
the unification of the East and South, and likewise of the North and West.
Then, one should drink the full vessel offered by the yogis and yoginis, over which their own mantras, the pādukā-mantra, and the root mantra have been recited.
If, by chance, one obtains a vessel of wine, one should take it with devotion as before, offer it, drink it, and remember the Guru.
One may eat the remnants of those who are devoted to the guru, as well as those of one's own elder and younger brothers, but never those of anyone else.
The elder should bestow [the initiation] upon the younger, but should not cause him to receive it again thereafter.
One should drink the wine that is the leavings of the Śakti, and chew the food that is the leavings of the Vīra.
One should not give what is left over from one's own meal, nor should one eat what belongs to another. One may eat the leavings of women, but one should not offer one's own leavings to them.
One should also place a vessel for one's own gathering within a single maṇḍala;
then, one should worship the Goddess and perform the libations and other rites.
Having raised them, one should place each other's vessels into the hands of the other;
remembering the unity of the two, this is the "merging of the vessels."
Even a child who was initiated earlier [is senior] to an elder in the family lineage; likewise,
even a twice-born who was initiated later [is junior] to one who was initiated earlier, even if that latter is an outcaste.
The twice-born who is younger is the elder; such is the settled conclusion of the scriptures.
[One should worship] one's own power and the power of the hero, who is initiated and embodies the form of the Guru.
"Having caused [the consort] to drink, one should drink the wine; such is the firm conclusion of the scripture.
Therefore, [one should worship] the Śakti of auspicious marks with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings."
Having worshipped the deity with a focused mind, one should offer the vessel of enjoyments.

I salute this very nectar of the three sections (trikhaṇḍāmṛta), which is flooded by the nectar of the beautiful moon that is the remainder of the glorious Bhairava; it is worshipped by the hosts of Siddhas, Yoginīs, and the assembly of people who are lords of the sacred fields (kṣetrādhīśvara); it is an ocean of bliss, and not something to be abandoned.
The first [mudrā] is Śrī, joined with the lotus-like hands, which bestows purity.
It is filled with the clamor of all traditional doctrines, illuminating all wonders, and served by Candra, Upendra, Mahendra, Śambhu, Varuṇa, Brahmā, and others;
it is always meditated upon by hosts of gods and groups of sages seeking liberation.
Salutations to the second [Buddha], who increases the welfare of the worlds and is a vessel that brings happiness.

May the *pañcamakāra*—consisting of liquor, meat, fish, the seal (*mudrā*), and sexual union; filled with Hari, Hara, Brahmā, and the other gods; providing the bliss of the ritual of dharma; resting upon the salty, sour, and bitter [flavors]; honored by the Master, and purified through the placement of the digits (*kalā*) of the eight Bhairavas—protect you.
This third vessel is joined; obeisance!

Manifested is that bliss-bestowing Golakuṇḍa, worshipped by Brahmā and Rudra; it is the primordial kingdom, possessing the first-born elephant-flower, the supreme peak of divine power, and the most excellent essence beyond all others.
Having repeatedly partaken of that divine nectar, which is pure and stainless, one attains the fivefold state.
This fourth vessel, which grants liberation and desire, is for the sake of joy.
Upon the base which is the coil of the king of serpents, the vessel is the circle of the earth; the wine is the water of the seven oceans, and the flesh is the eight elephants of the quarters.
Worshipping Bhairava daily—He who is marked by the hosts of stars and headed by the Sun—I, [the sacrificer], offer this sacrifice.
By the hosts of gods and asuras, who were obedient servants acting according to his command.
The parasol, the fly-whisk, and the auspicious throne— then even that which bestows supreme bliss, enchanting to Queen Rāmā, bringing happiness, granting the sovereignty of union (sāyujya),
dispelling the darkness of various diseases, and destroying rebirth.
One should worship the glorious Suṃdaritarpaṇa, Indravarada, and the sixth, Pātra.

The pure consciousness that directly bestows the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the Fourth (turya) is described through the metaphors of lightning, the sun, fire, Indra’s bow (the rainbow), and light; it is the upward-moving Kuṇḍalinī, situated between the Iḍā and Piṅgalā and encircled by three coils, which serves as the vessel for the filling of the seventh [chakra].
May He, who possesses even greater bliss than that of the youthful [Kumāra], protect me.

The sword, the sandals, the collyrium, the pill, the Sārasvata [mantra] which bestows truth, the deception of death, the accomplishment of fierce deeds, the seizing [of powers], and the cause for the stability of the body.
May [He]— who brings about accomplishment, stabilizes the mind, subdues the world-renowned, is a vessel for the eight siddhis, and is ever mature and gracious— protect [us].

O Navanātha Śakti, you are the bestower of all bliss, the state of Sadāśiva, the singular devotion that transcends duality, the sovereign empire that grants happiness, the fulfiller of desires, the destroyer of ignorance, the increaser of longevity, fame, and glory, and the cutter of the delusion of saṃsāra; you are worthy of this vessel.
The youthful [sun] is risen with mature majesty.
One may drink from three vessels, five vessels, or even seven vessels;
one may drink from nine vessels, but one should certainly not drink from sixteen or half of that.
As long as the gaze does not waver and the mind does not waver, so long one should perform the drinking; beyond that is considered the path of the beast.
O Goddess, the name of those who are endowed with the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) is proclaimed;
lifting the vessel with both hands while recollecting the root mantra and the pādukā.
One should drink liquor until one is unconscious; he is liberated from this, there is no doubt.
Having drunk again and again, and drinking yet more, he continues until he falls upon the ground.
Having risen and drunk again, rebirth no longer exists;
the Goddess is satisfied by bliss, and Bhairava himself by the state of fainting (mūrchā).
Since all the gods are satisfied by this rinsing, one should therefore perform this triad.
If one ignorant of Brahman forcibly drinks wine repeatedly during the Kula practice, he falls to the ground; if the dust of that place should then cling to his limbs, [he is purified].
For that duration of time measured in *reṇu*s, he rejoices in the world of Brahmā;
having drunk again and again and having performed recitation, he is liberated together with ten million lineages.
O Goddess, she shall dwell in the world of Brahmā; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
There alone she attains pervasion and shall not fall back into this world again.
Having drunk and worshipped these, one certainly attains lordship;
one attains dissolution right there and does not return again.
In that state, among those heroes who are intoxicated, there is no distinction between what should be done and what should not be done;
whatever action is performed therein, whether auspicious or inauspicious, [is as it is].
All that arises for the pleasure of the deity; of this there is no doubt.
Idle chatter is the fruit of recitation (japa), and drowsiness is declared to be meditative absorption (samādhi).
Transformation is declared to be worship; what is vomited is the offering (bali) to Bhairava;
fainting is union with Śakti; and the hymn is speech uttered at that very moment.
Touching the limbs during the ritual placement (nyāsa) is declared to be eating;
the act of offering oblations is meditation; looking [at the deity] is gazing; and lying down is salutation.
And whatever action is performed through the manifestation of that [consciousness] is a virtuous deed;
however, he who undergoes the transformation of what should and should not be done is a sinner.
Those heroes situated within this wheel should be known as supreme yogis;
those men who do not [otherwise] speak are the very embodiment of Bhairava himself.
Socializing, the quelling of anger, falling and rising, dancing,
playing instruments such as the flute and lute, and the composition of poetry and the like.
Weeping, speaking, falling down, rising up, yawning, walking, and transformation— O Goddess, this is called Yoga.
When, having abandoned the modifications of the mind, the inner radiance proceeds,
then those preeminent yogis partake in the state of the deity.
Whosoever of deluded intellect reviles the Kaulikas who are possessed by Bhairava, the Yoginīs will undoubtedly destroy him; there is no doubt in this matter.
Just as a goldsmith, through the intense possession of devotion, is considered to have cast [the metal],
so too does that [work] become, without doubt, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious.
*Tāra*, *namas*! O Blessed Lady who dwells upon wine and meat, O beloved of Rati, O Goddess of the Cakra, speak, O you who are dear to the Kaulikas!
It is true that one should consume liquor mixed with meat after reflecting upon the state of the mind; one should offer it to the Kaulikas, for they, being intoxicated by it, speak the truth.
In that regard, if someone is not a Kaula, the Goddess of Speech does not manifest for them.
One should not revile, laugh at, or be proud toward the families intoxicated by the honey [of the wheel];
nor should one ever disclose to outsiders news concerning those who have entered this wheel.
One should not commit treachery against them, nor should one act for their harm;
with devotion one should protect them and guard them with great effort.
And having seen a beautiful woman, he should regard her with the thought that she is a deity;
he who rejoices in her and honors her with devotion shall go to the state of the Yoginī.
When the wheel of Bhairavī is set in motion, all castes become of mixed origin;
when the wheel of Bhairavī has ceased, all castes are distinct once more.
Whether it be a woman, a man, an animal, an outcaste, or the most excellent of the twice-born—within the center of the Cakra there is no distinction; all are remembered as equal to the gods.
All men situated within the center of the wheel are of the nature of Śiva, and all women are Pārvatī; therefore, one should not conceive of any distinction between them.
A lustful man should not approach a woman who has been consecrated by me if she does not desire it;
however, he may approach her if she has been immediately purified by the sacramental rite, for that is what is ordained.
By performing worship with a thousand wheels, one who has fallen from his kingdom shall become a king;
by fifty, one obtains a son; and by ten, one becomes free from disease.
If a woman falters while delighting in the worship of this wheel,
she will certainly become a sovereign ruler within a year.
For the sake of attaining one's desired beloved, one should perform the fivefold worship.
Now follows the worship of the Kaulika.
Having beheld Maheśvara, one should worship him according to the prescribed ritual,
with the five tattvas that are faultless, in accordance with one's available means.
The goddess shall always be pleased and she shall grant all desires;
otherwise, there will be no accomplishment, for the Yoginī becomes angry.
Whatever fruit a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas obtains by giving away the entire earth,
that same fruit is obtained through the worship of the Kaulika.
Whatever fruit one obtains by performing thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices,
that same fruit is obtained in the worship of the Kaulika.
Whatever fruit one obtains by giving gold equal to Mount Meru to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas, that same fruit is obtained from the worship of the Kaulika.
Whatever fruit one might obtain by constructing ponds, wells, and tanks,
that fruit is multiplied a hundred-thousandfold by the worship of the Kaulikas.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by giving a tawny cow (kapilā),
that fruit is multiplied ten millionfold by worshipping the Kaulikas.
Now follows the sacrifice to the female messenger (dūtī).
Nothing whatsoever is produced by primordial nature (prakṛti) without a person (puruṣa);
likewise, O God, without power (śakti), one is not capable of bestowing fruit.
Therefore, having united with the power of the male (*puṃśakti*), one should accomplish the mantra;
for in the Kaulika and Vāma paths, a man alone does not attain success.
One should meditate upon oneself as Śiva and the deity in the form of Śakti;
by means of the syllables "krī," "lā," "i," and "tyaṃ," the deity becomes well-pleased with him.
For one who possesses a firm conviction toward his mother on the path of Dakṣa, and toward women on the Kaulika path,
the deities are pleased with him.
This secret has been declared; it must be guarded like a lover's affair with one's mother.
O Pārvatī, those who follow Śiva, the Smārtas, and the hundreds of ritualists do not perform it; nor do the Kaulas, those who know the Āgamas, and those who abide by the Tantric conduct.
Among those who provide substitutes and likewise among those who remain neutral,
there are women for whom the notion that she is a goddess exists, yet whose intellect is extremely fickle.
O Goddess, for those who are always devoted to Kālī with a resolute mind,
the worship of Śakti and the worship of the Pīṭha are mandatory.
She should be worshipped with the understanding that she is Kālī alone, and not with a mind agitated by desire;
for those in the fourth stage of life who are intent on the worship of Kālī seek liberation.
Whether they are Kaulikas or Kaulas who follow this doctrine in the Left-hand path,
to them the Enemy of the Cities (Śiva) declared that the worship of the Nityā Śakti is indeed eternal.
That power (śakti) should be known as twofold: one's own and the wife of another. O beloved, the one of one's own kind is for procreation, while the married woman is for [enjoyment].
That which is one's own is thus designated; likewise, this is praised as the "to-be-led" (āneyā). I shall now describe, in order, the five types of those belonging to others (parakīyā).
One whose husband is living, one whose beloved is dead,
a female slave, a courtesan, and likewise an unmarried woman— each subsequent one is more highly esteemed than the preceding.
A young woman who has not yet given birth is praised for her very youthfulness;
even when she has borne a child, she is still considered equal to all others.
In the absence of each preceding one, the subsequent [form] is indeed to be grasped by the practitioners;
this applies to the Kaula woman who possesses the power, and for the man as well, it is exactly the same.
O Goddess of the Gods, mantras do not attain accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of kalpas without a male practitioner, nor without a female practitioner.
Sexual union with another's wife, the consumption of intoxicants, or the killing of animals—
if done for one's own sake, leads surely to hell; but if for the sake of the Goddess, it indeed leads to merit.
I do not understand the reason why these things bring such pleasure to the queen,
just as the slaughter of animals for the sake of a sacrifice does not produce sin.
In the same way, acts such as sexual union with another's wife do not produce sin.
Now, the specific classification of the powers (śakti).
An actress, a tavern-keeper, a courtesan, a washerwoman, a barber’s wife,
a Brāhmaṇa woman who has married a Śūdra, and likewise the daughter of a cowherd;
The daughter of a garland-maker is not proclaimed to be a maiden.
Neither deficient-limbed nor having extra limbs, neither too stout nor excessively thin;
neither with a severed nose or finger, nor tall, nor short.
There were none who were leprous, nor hunchbacked; none who were mute, blind, or deaf;
none who were squint-eyed, nor lame, nor of mixed birth, nor with drooping breasts.
These powers (śaktis) should not be performed daily for those with young children;
rather, I shall describe the appropriate and superior [powers] by which one becomes satisfied at all times.
A fair-limbed young woman, beautiful, with a smiling face and a lovely form,
possessing large, tremulous eyes and full, elevated breasts.
Her expansive forehead was adorned with three lines of whorls; she had beautiful sides, a slender waist, a melodious voice, and curled locks of hair.
She possesses diverse garments and ornaments, wears various excellent raiment,
is strewn with wonderful garlands, and bestows manifold delights.
Always possessing a serene countenance, she was devoted to the Goddess,
knowledgeable in the Kaulika practices, and intent on devotion toward the practitioner.
Free from fear, with a smiling face, always speaking kindly,
perfected in the conduct of the samaya, knowing the mantras, and devoid of dread.
One who is wise, yet not having given birth, and endowed with fortitude and independence—
one should honor all women who are possessed of such qualities.
Now, he states the specific power associated with a specific knowledge.
The great vidyās are proclaimed according to the distinctions of their classes and forms;
O Goddess of the gods, listen now with diligence to that sequence.
Maheśvarī should assign names in the order of form and fragrance;
Pārvatī should do so with effort, without abandoning the names given by her mother and father.
One should indeed bestow the name oneself, according to the proper method, just as Pārvatī did.
She who is black with a dark-blue luster, with eyes tawny like honey,
whose heart desires the practitioner, and who possesses an odorous scent that is beyond reproach.
Kālī should be joined within that; she is proclaimed as Kālī.
That woman who has the scent of liquor, whose eyes are red, and who is very harsh,
is called Mahogratārā; she is the destroyer of great sins.
Always unable to eat, yet eating much and fickle;
possessing a form that deludes the three worlds—these are proclaimed as the severed Vidyās.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, filled with various fragrances,
beautiful, with lovely hair, long eyes, and captivating.
Skilled in various amorous graces, conversant with the family scriptures, she rests upon the chest of her teacher; being of middle age, she gazes with a steady, piercing look.
That beautiful woman shall become Gaurī, the promoter of all undertakings.
She who is that third fair-limbed goddess, anointed with the fragrance of honey,
is the goddess named Tripurā, the accomplisher of the sequence of her own flowers.
With beautiful limbs and lovely eyes, seated upon a lotus throne,
her body adorned with golden ornaments— she is celebrated as Kamalā.

Adorned with a necklace of *guñjā* berries and other ornaments, dark-complexioned and with tremulous eyes, the goddess Mātaṅgī possesses a beautiful smile; she is known as the Great Goddess (*Maheśvarī*) of the Vidyā-mantra.
Divine in complexion, slender-limbed, and anointed with divine perfumes and unguents, she is adorned with various ornaments; she is called Bhuvaneśī by me.
With tawny eyes and tawny hair, laughing with a slightly mocking smile, she is called Dhūmāvatī; O beloved, listen to this perfected vidyā.
O Maheśānī, O lady of excellent vows, she who has a long face, long lips, and a yellow complexion, and who is motionless— that is celebrated as Bagalā for you.
O Maheśānī, these ten vidyās are said to be Pārvatī in the form of Śakti;
they are the Mother, the Wife, and the Sister, in successive order.
O Goddess, the Vidyās alone constantly sport; of this there is no doubt.
O Maheśānī, the ten-fold sequence consists of the ten Vidyās through diligent effort.
O Goddess, one should perform it in every way; otherwise, even in tens of millions of ages, O Mistress of the Gods, they will certainly not attain success by means of ten padmas of recitation.
Therefore, with every effort, one should practice the sequence of one's own respective knowledge;
for both one's own and that of others, O Maheśvarī, is merely Śakti.
The presiding deities of the mantras should be worshipped with all ritual offerings,
including various fruits, betel leaves, garments, ornaments, and gold.
Having worshipped according to the rules with devotion, one should cause many offerings to be presented;
yet he who performs the worship of Śakti while maintaining the latent desire for sensual enjoyment [is flawed].
He incurs poverty and will certainly become a denizen of hell.
What is the use of many nets of words? Listen to the rule in brief:
the worship of Śakti is prescribed by the Kaulikas day after day.
O Goddess, for those devoted to the Kula path, the daily taking of liquor and its daily acceptance are likewise declared to be obligatory.
O beloved, even the discrimination between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted is rare among those possessed of power;
for indeed, even for those who offer only secondary rites, there is certainly the state of permanence.
Indeed, only that power which is free from censure and is appropriate is accepted;
for others, there is the occasional worship of power performed out of desire.
For those whose minds are established in samādhi, there is the rejection of all else;
now Pārvatī shall prescribe the ritual procedures and the mantras as well.
She was bathed, divine, wearing excellent garments, adorned with various ornaments,
a young woman with full breasts, and likewise one who had not yet eaten.
Taking the supreme Śakti by the hand, one should place her upon the left thigh; if one is unable to carry her, she should be placed on the left seat of the Goddess.
On the left side, having drawn a triangle, a lotus, and a circle—
[the lotus] joined with white and red [colors], its stalk smeared with vermilion.
The practitioner, facing east, should worship the Goddess facing west;
he should worship Uḍḍiyāna in the Tretā age, and Pūrṇagiri in the Kṛta age.
Jālandhara in the Dvāpara ages and Kāmapīṭha in the Kali age—
I shall describe those four, which are more secret than the secret.
