First, one should perform the rite beginning with the Ṛṣi, and thereafter, one should perform the purification.
Now listen, O goddess worshipped by the gods, to the seer and other details of this worship of Śrī-Śakti: Gonarda is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi) of this [hymn].
The meter is called Vikṛti; when it follows [the syllable] 'ya', its form is Śakti. Mahākālī is the deity, and Kāma is declared to be the seed-syllable (bīja).
Śakti is the bride, Bhuvaneśī is declared to be the *kīlaka*;
the application (*viniyoga*) is in the light of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of Śiva and Śakti.

Having performed the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) upon oneself using the seed-syllables of the bride (vadhū-bīja) along with the five long vowels and so forth, one should then perform the assignment (nyāsa) of the powers (śakti) and limbs (aṅga).
In the place of the word "strīcchakti," one should utter the word "bhairava";
in the place of the word "yoṣidyoni," the arrangement of the word "liṅga" should be made.
O Goddess of the Suras, whether through the instruction of a guru or by one's own intellect,
one should perform the *druha* rite everywhere, specifically upon the *liṅga*, for each respective state.
It is the same, however, as that which measures the Gāyatrī on both sides;
now, listen attentively to this placement and extraction.
Trayākāśa, Ramārāva, Yoginī, Roṣayoṣitā, Ḍākinī, Pralayohāra, Phetkārī, and Karṇikā as well.
The letter *pra* is Nṛsiṃha, and the letter *ci* is Kulika; these two reside at the end of all [mantras].
O Goddess worshipped by the gods, one should place the seed-syllable after each individual name.
These also, at the beginning, are Kaulikī, followed by Bhagamālinī,
Ratipriyā, Anaṅgā, Akulā, and Samayapālinī.
Then Madanonmādinī, who causes the onset of passion; after that, Vittonmāthinī, who destroys wealth; and likewise Mohanī and Ākarṣiṇī.

O Goddess worshipped by the thirty gods, you are first Smarāturā (afflicted with passion), then Anaṅgarūpā (formless), then Anaṅgahṛtpramodinī (delighting the hearts of the bodiless ones), then Saṃtāpinī (the inflamer), and thereafter Saṃkṣobhiṇī (the agitator).
At the end of all [the others], she who consists of the nature of equanimity (sāmarasya) is to be fully known.
These sixteen [vowels] are the modifications (vaikārya), ending in the dative case and joined with the preceding consonants.
Since the female gender is used for the act of worshipping Bhairava, [the mantras] ending in "namaḥ" are all masculine; now, designate the locations.
The head, the two cheeks, the throat, the two shoulders,
the chest, the two arms, as well as the sides, the belly, the navel, the bladder, and the groin.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the vital breaths (jīva-nyāsa) upon her thighs, knees, shanks, feet, and the generative organ along with the two ears; then one should practice the state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya).
"O Goddess, this is declared to be the purification of Śakti;
having performed it, O Sovereign, one should then place the hands upon the heart and the chest."
Or else, the Goddess should be worshipped at the seat of desire (the genitals) or at the navel,
while reciting the mantra to be described hereafter either once or three times.
One should perform this purification of power (śakti-śodhana), which consists of the placement of the vital breath (jīva-nyāsa);
by this, the power is purified, and not otherwise, even by ten million mantras.
One should first contemplate the eight seed-syllables: Māyā, Kāma, Vadhū, Lakṣmī, Kūrca, Prāsāda, Śākinī, and also Ḍākinī.
The enjoyer, bliss, the digit (kalā), power (śakti), the individual self (jīvātman), the supreme self (paramātman),
reflection, non-duality (advaita), the designation of identity (ātmya), and the name "merger" (laya)— these are [the aspects].
Having sequentially uttered the ten peaks (kūṭas), one should utter Brahmā and its reverse;
these two are to be pronounced at the end of the ten, thus measured by half-and-half.
Then, having said "May he place [it] in my heart," one should say "in your heart";
having said "may he place it in my speech," one should utter the speech.
Thereafter, O lotus-faced one, speak to my senses;
having addressed those senses, attend to my words.
Then, let him enjoin you to me as "Siddhikarālī," and let him say: "As you are, so am I; as I am, so are you."
Having joined that very state through the *saṃdhi*, one should proclaim both of them;
immediately thereafter, [one should perform] the union of Śiva and Śakti.
Then, having proclaimed "one," one should say, "let us two accomplish [it]";
O beautiful one, that is the *saṃdhi* (junction), and thereafter follow the *tāra*, *hṛdaya*, and *śiras* mantras.
This mantra has been prescribed for the rite of purifying the Śakti;
it consists of one hundred and eight syllables, neither fewer nor more.
O limb, one should meditate upon the meditation previously described by me to you regarding the Bhagavatī,
and likewise upon her power, observing the accumulation of her limbs in that form.
One should contemplate oneself as being identical to the meditation on Bhairava;
then, one should invoke the Goddess into the limb of Śakti, which is like a sacred seat (pīṭha).
With the mantra to be recited hereafter, the practitioner, using the añjali mudrā,
[should invoke] Māyā, Kāmavadhū, Rāvā, Kamalā, Yoginī, and Ruṣā.
The Ḍākinī and Phetkārī are not located on the Vaitāḍhya mountains and so forth;
having said "Come, come, O Blessed One," one should invoke Mahākālī.
One should cause the presence [of the deity] to enter the Śaktipīṭha and then extract it; thereafter, having delineated you, I invoke you and proclaim your name.
Having meditated upon her as possessing all powers, one should then speak to her who is the embodiment of that nature:
"Oṃ, be established! [Then] hear the root mantra of Śakti, beginning with the head [syllable].
Māyā, Rāva, Smara, Nārī, and Śakti—
this is declared to be the nine-syllable mantra for the rite of worshiping Śakti.
There is no seer (ṛṣi) and so forth, nor consciousness, nor meter, nor the powers of the seed-syllables;
rather, it is caused by the offering of all services, beginning with water for the feet.
Indeed, this [mantra] should not be recited according to the words of Tripura;
rather, one should offer all the ritual services (upacāras) according to one's capacity.

O Goddess of the Universe, in my view, there is no other mantra distinct from this for whatever rites are desired, beginning with the offering of water for the feet and ending with the offering of food.
Let this tuft of hair be considered as belonging to the head; let that which is rootless be understood as the worship of Śakti, consisting of the remaining flowers, garlands, and unguents.
Whatever is given to oneself becomes the worship of equanimity (sāmarasya);
that should be performed without mantras—such is the teaching of Īśāna.
Then, having offered the fee (kara), the practitioner should perform recitation (japa) at the seat of the Yoni (yonipīṭha) with the Śakti-gāyatrī mantra,
one hundred times, or fifty, or even twenty-five times.
Nowhere is there a recitation equal to that performed at the Yonipīṭha;
this supreme seat (pīṭha) generates the immediate power of mantras.
For mantras that are devoid of power, whose application is performed by those with exhausted minds,
which have not been extracted from their curses, and which possess either a deficiency or an excess of syllables;

And likewise for those who have transgressed against the guru, for those who give away their vigor and strength, and for those who perform worship according to ignorance, as well as for those who offer [gifts] to unworthy recipients and those who share with their sisters.
Both [the external and internal forms] were proclaimed by the Enemy of Tripura for the purpose of rekindling those [virtues] that have been abandoned, forgotten, or likewise rendered powerless.
Having encapsulated the single syllable *nirvāṇa* with the mantra, one should perform its recitation;
there is no other practice of recitation than this on the Kaula seat, the sacred site of the Yoni.
The Kaula seat is at the sacred site of the womb; the recitation is the favoring of women.
The Guru’s wife is the Śakti, and having united, the two should perform the recitation together.
The kindling with other mantras is supreme for increasing the power of the seed-syllable.
p.

227b) Now, therefore, O Goddess, hear the Śakti-gāyatrī, which yields great fruit. One should first utter the Goddess following the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja), ending in the feminine nominative suffix -ī.
Then, having recited "vidmahe yonimālinyai dhīmahi," and thereafter saying "tannaḥ śaktiḥ," one should conclude with "pracodayāt" at the crest of all mantras.
For this Śakti-Gāyatrī is well-guarded by all the Āgamas;
without this, neither the worship of Nīlā nor the worship of Śakti, nor even penance consisting of its limbs, is possible.
Having recited this according to one's capacity and having offered it to Śakti,
O beloved, one should seat her upon the left lap and perform the recitation of the root mantra.
One should worship her in the abode of Madana, which is smeared with red sandalwood;
there, in her bhaga, the three channels (nāḍīs) that carry the flow [of fluids] are to be known.
The practitioner should worship Ekottarāhikā, Cāṇḍī, Saurī, and another Vāhikā, as well as Āgneyī and Aparājñeyā.
The Aindri [direction] flows with water, the Bhānavī with flowers, and the Āgneyī with seed; one should worship them by these names.
With a well-pleased mind, one should worship using the [syllables] beginning with Vāgbhava, joined with "namaḥ";
O Maheśānī, one should perform meditation upon the crocodile-faced goddess in the cavern.

One should contemplate that place where the Goddess, the Vidyā who deludes the world, resides— having the form of a copper-colored cock’s crest and possessing a splendor equal to the face of an elephant.
The mantra of Bhagamālā, however, is as follows:
One should write the Vāgbhava syllable at the end of the word "bhaga," followed by "bhage," "bhagini," "bhagodari," "bhagānte," "bhagamāle," and "bhagāvahe."
In the secret place of the vulva, at the edge of the vulva, at the edge of the womb, and at the end of the vulva;
she who causes everything to fall at the very end, and thereafter she who brings the vulva under control.
Then, within the form of the *bhaga*, two eyes free from dust should be drawn;
one should draw everything according to its true nature, including the eternally moist extremities of the *bhaga*.
One should write "bhagāni me hyā" at the end of the word *namaḥ*, followed by "varade tha.
Then, one should write "rete svarete bhagavat klinna klinna drave."
O Mistress of the Bhaga, moisten and dissolve all sentient beings;
O Amoghe, O Bhagavīcche, cause agitation and universal trembling.
O Bhageśvarī, one should address sentient beings with the Vāgbhava mantra *vrūṃ*; from this recitation, [one gains power]. Then follow *bhaṃ*, *plūṃ*, *māṃ*, *vlūṃ*, and thereafter *haiṃ klinne*.
And at the end of all the *bhagas*, one should utter "meva śaṃ cānaya";
and at the end of *hara*, the seed-syllable of the woman (*strīvīja*) and the syllable consisting of *vala*.
Having drawn Bhuvaneśī, this Vidyā is Bhagamālinī;
one should worship the Goddess ending with the dative case and cast a flower upon the vulva (bhaga).
Having washed [the vessel] with the family substance (kuladravya), one should worship it with perfumes and flowers;
having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should thereafter worship the enclosure (āvaraṇa).
Even here, there is no invocation; the Great Goddess is present through the placement of the vital breaths (jīvanyāsa).
Then, by this procedure, she [is worshipped] with the sixteen types of offerings (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
Then, having worshipped one's chosen deity, one shall become the sovereign lord of all supernatural powers (siddhis).
Immediately thereafter, one should worship one's own Śiva with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Next, I shall explain the ritual placement (nyāsa); one should contemplate [the deity] as being identical with Śiva.
One should sequentially assign the five-faced Mahādeva together with his digits (kalās):
"Īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām" is the first digit, Śaśinī.
"Īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānām," then "aṅgadā," followed by the word "brahmādhipati," and again "brahmaṇo'dhipatiḥ."
May Śivā, the bestower of the desires of Brahmā, be present; one should place the Marīci-sampuṭa.
Having uttered "Sadāśiva," then follows Aṃśumālinī, the supreme.
"Let us know that Tatpuruṣa"—thus is Kalā-śānti declared;
"we meditate upon Mahādeva"—and likewise Kalā-vidyā.
After reciting "tanno rudraḥ," the "pada" is said; then the "kalā" is "pratiṣṭhā. Having uttered "pracodayāt," there shall then follow "nivṛtti."
One should sequentially place the goddesses in the east, west, south, north, and above; [the mantra] "Aghorebhyaḥ" is the *stamaḥ* (darkness) digit in the heart.
Then, one should place "ghorebhyaḥ" and "mohaṃ" on the neck;
thereafter, following "ghorānte," one should place "kriyā" on the right shoulder.
"Salutation to you"—after [this], one should place "to Hunger" (kṣudhām) and then "to the Parts" (kalām) in sequence;
at the end, [the mantras] ending in "namas" begin with "to the forms of Rudra" (rudrarūpebhyaḥ) and conclude with "to Thirst" (tṛṣāntāra).
Having placed "Vāmadevāya namaḥ" at the end of the private parts and "Rajāsyāt" on the secret region,
one should place "Jyeṣṭhāyai vai namaḥ" on the right side of the face for protection.
"Salutation to Rudra; behind [him] is Rati, this digit with her beautiful face. At the end, 'Salutation to Kāla'; Pālinī is on the right thigh."
O Queen of the Gods, having uttered the word "namaḥ" for Kalakāma on the left and for Vikaraṇa at the right knee of Saṃyaminī;
The ritual of purification (valakriyā) is prescribed for the purpose of dispelling obstacles on the left side;
having uttered "Vṛddhi" at the end of the salutation (namas), one should place it upon the right hip.
"Salutation to the Subduer of Strengths"—one should place this on the left [hand];
"salutation to the Tamer of All Beings," ending with *namaḥ*, is the Brāhmaṇī-kalā.
Having placed the *mohinī* digit upon the region of the waist, and having placed the radiant *unmanā* digit on the right side, one should bow to it with the mantra: "Obeisance to Unmanā."
The practitioner should properly place the eight kalās arising from Sadyojāta on the feet, the breasts, the nose, the head, and the two arms, in their respective order.
"I take refuge in Sadyojāta; may there be success, the first digit (kalā).
Again, obeisance to Sadyojāta; this is declared to be prosperity (ṛddhi)."
The third [stage] would be *yuti*;
thereafter, the fourth is said to be *lakṣmī*, and from that follows the state of *nāti*.
The fifth digit is declared to be named Medhā; furthermore, Prajñā is said to be the sixth, and at the end of existence (bhavānte) there is the digit Prabhā.
After that, one should install [the mantra] "udbhavāya namaḥ," which is the eighth digit (kalā) beginning with nectar (sudhā).
These [mantras] should be arranged beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ), ending in the dative case, and concluding with *namaḥ*.
Having thus performed the ritual procedure, he himself should meditate upon Śiva,
placing the five-syllabled mantra before him and remaining intent on the meditation of Rudra.
Having established the state of aesthetic fusion (sāmarasya), one should recite the armor-mantra (kavaca) for the sake of protection;
then, having formed the agitating mudrā (kṣobhiṇī-mudrā), one should cast it into the center of the yantra.

Having recited all the principles (tattvas)— namely the vulva (bhaga), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the ladle (śruva), the primordial phallus (liṅga), and the semen (vīryaka)— one should perform a thousand recitations (japa).
With the mind as the sacrificial ladle, I perpetually offer the oblations of dharma and adharma into the blazing fire of the Self, by way of the path of the *suṣumṇā*, with the senses as the fuel.
The syllable *svāhā* and water are proclaimed at the beginning of the great mantra;
it is indeed the union of Śiva and Śakti, there is no doubt that this is Yoga itself.
The sound "śītkāra" is the form of the mantra; its speech becomes praise and its state becomes the divine abode.
Embracing is the musk, and kissing is the camphor;
the marks of nails and teeth and so forth are the various flowers.
Know that churning is *tarpaṇa*, and the falling of the seed is *visarjana*.
Embracing, kissing, and likewise the massaging of the breasts;
gazing upon, touching, the arousal of the female organ, and the rubbing of the male organ.
One should worship the entry, the establishment, and the nine flowers of the Śakti;
he who does not offer a kiss will certainly become poor.
O Goddess Pārvatī, without embracing, one becomes afflicted with leprosy;
O Goddess, without tooth-marks, one becomes censured in the world.
Through embracing, one removes diseases; through kissing, one gains wealth, grain, and so forth;
and by means of nail-marks, tooth-marks, and the like, liberation is then produced.
In union with that [state] upon meeting, there is indeed truth; of this there is no doubt.
Having grasped the Unmanifest (unmanī) with the ladle of light and space by means of the hands.
"I offer into the fire the smallest portion of merit and demerter, filled with affection;
svāhā. This great mantra is proclaimed for use at the time of emission.
One should perform the churning with pure mantras and medicinal herbs, and not with vehicles;
for when it is churned, the supreme reality is born from it.
One should diligently take that auspicious substance produced from the *kuṇḍa*;
with that divine nectar, one should always satisfy Kālī.
Through her presence, or even at that very moment, she, being pleased, bestows accomplishment;
and there is the constant satiation of all the deities with nectars.
One should perform the libation for all the gurus and practitioners;
by that divine nectar, they all indeed become satisfied.
Whatever desire the practitioner of mantra performs, it is accomplished at that very moment.
Having taken up the nectar of the family (kulāmṛta), the wise practitioner should pour it into the arghya vessel;
thereafter, the stainless digits of the moon (somakalā) should be worshipped by the practitioners whose minds are pure.
O Goddess, she would not be satisfied even by thousands of jars of honey or hundreds of loads of meat, except for the nectar of the *bhaga* and *liṅga*.
O beloved, having purified the family substance (kuladravya) which consists of Śiva and Śakti,
O beautiful one, one should pour in the nectar of life (jīvāmṛta), which is the form of the Supreme Brahman.
Having worshipped with the nectars from the arghya vessel, the ever-sinless one, free from conceptual construction,
O Goddess of gods, should worship the Goddess in the yoni with the arghya substances.
Without the worship of the *yoni*, even a performed worship becomes as if unperformed;
however, when the *dūtī-yāga* is performed, the practitioner certainly attains omniscience.
There is no returning for him again, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas;
by those who have performed the sacrifice of the messenger (Dūtī), all sacrificial rites have been accomplished.
He is said to embody all sacred fords and to consist of all the gods;
by him, every rite such as the preliminary service (puraścaryā) has been performed—of this there is no doubt.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices,
as well as the earth extending to the oceans, were given by him as the sacrificial fee.
O beloved, the merit that arises from the gift of ten million cows is indeed produced by offering gold equal in weight to Mount Meru.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the sacrifice to the messenger (dūtī);
O auspicious lady, this worship is complete and is the destroyer of all misfortunes.
When performed with the worship of the source (yonipūjā), this worship becomes inexhaustible even for those who have already offered it;
a person obtains immeasurable longevity, health, and prosperity.
By this very method, one afflicted by poison becomes free from poison;
one desiring a son obtains a son, and one desiring wealth obtains wealth.
Having worshipped the Śakti Mātaṅgī, one should worship her together with [the deity] for the sake of attaining all desires and goals— Mātaṅgī accompanied by Manmatha.
The mantra-deity Mātaṅgī should always be worshipped together with Śakti;
for that goddess, when devoid of Śakti, does not grant one's heart's desire.
The man who attempts to purify his power (śakti) without having received the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) is base, fallen, and diseased; he will certainly meet his death.
Because the senses are difficult to restrain and because lust, gain, and the like arise,
this Kaulika path generally leads to hell in the Kali age.
The daily worship is said to be the best; the worship on festival days is middling;
the monthly worship is declared to be the lowest; beyond a month, one becomes a beast.
Every month, or every three months, or every six months, or even once a year,
one should worship the venerable Guru with devotion, having first honored his wife, sons, and other dependents.
In his absence, one should satisfy a member of his family, his disciple, or another yogin with the substances of the kula,
preceded by the worship of the cakra.
Now, he describes the specific ritual procedure for the wheel.
One who is impure from eating should not touch the cakra, the kula-substances, or the guru;
having washed both hands outside, one should cause the kula-substances to be offered.
Having lifted up the vessel of liquor, one should not fill another vessel;
one should never cast away the vessel for enjoyment or the jar of wine.
That foolish-minded person who performs the ritual purification of the hands and so forth within the center of the *cakra* shall indeed become the very abode of misfortune.
He who should discharge spittle, impurity, urine, or downward wind into the center of the Śrīcakra shall become a beast for the Yoginīs.

If the jar in the center of the maṇḍala is broken, or if the vessel slips, or likewise if the lamp goes out, there will be suffering for the kingdom; for its pacification, the worship of the maṇḍala should be performed.
One should avoid jesting, idle chatter, mockery, excessive talking,
indifference, fear, and anger while in the midst of the assembly.
Holding the vessel in his hand, he should move around the center of the mandala with the full vessel;
he should not keep it in his hand for long, nor should he speak while his hands are occupied with the vessel.
One should never touch the bowl with one's feet, nor should one ever break it;
one should not give anything with only one hand, nor should one let even a drop fall to the ground.
One should not move the vessel from its place, nor drink without the mudrā;
one should not drink the liquor noisily, nor cause a mixing of vessels.
Two parts of the vessel should be filled with wine and one part [left as] the fourth;
one should not strike one vessel against another, nor should one strike a vessel downward.
One should not lift a vessel that has no base, nor should one set it down on something that lacks a base. One should not leave a vessel empty, nor should one step over a vessel.
Having washed the vessel, he should conceal it; then, ending with "namas," he should look upon the Brahmin.
If one gives the *kuladravya* (substance belonging to the Kula) situated within the *śrīcakra* to someone other than a member of the Kula,
his fruits [of merit] perish and the deity becomes angry.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Worship of the Cakras Common to All," in the *Śrī Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Now, he speaks regarding the construction and consecration of the yantra.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the determination regarding the installation of the yantra;
for it is said that the yantra is the house, and the yantra is proclaimed to be the pedestal (pīṭha).
In the case of a stationary yantra or an image, there is no invocation or dismissal;
having installed the great yantra, one should then dismiss that particular yantra.
Having established the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) in the yantra, one should meditate upon the Vidyā there;
then, having performed the placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa), one should meditate upon the Vidyā there.
Having first performed the consecration of the yantra, one should then install the deity therein;
in that case, there is neither dismissal nor invocation.
Therefore, due to the reversal of time, one should install the yantra alone;
having meditated upon the form residing within one's own heart there, one should worship it and then dismiss it.
O Dear One, one should have a yantra made of crystal and the like, or of gold and silver.
O beloved, for as long as one lives [the merit] would be in gold; twenty-two years in silver;
twelve years in copper; and in the [highest] color, the fruit is infinite.
What shall I say?
O beloved, [one may place it] in a yantra fashioned from coral, or from ruby,
or indeed from sapphire, cat's-eye, crystal, or even emerald.
O son, one certainly obtains wealth, as well as wives and fame;
and kings, along with those who rule the earth, [attain these] upon a throne fashioned of gold.
A yantra fashioned from silver bestows longevity and health;
a yantra crafted from copper is considered to grant all forms of sovereignty.
A yantra made of clear crystal bestows the objects desired by the mind;
a yantra fashioned from rubies grants sovereignty as well as worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The yantra fashioned on a monkey is the destroyer of all enemies;
the yantra produced from the three metals is considered to be the bestower of all accomplishments.
Śrīkhaṇḍa (white sandalwood) should be known as bestowing peace, while red sandalwood (raktacandana) is nourishing.
Śrīparṇī is prescribed as the pedestal for worship, which bestows wealth and sovereignty.
A coral [image] brings abundant prosperity; a four-line [verse] on birch bark [brings success];
a Gaṇḍakī stone [is auspicious]; and enjoyment and liberation are not far off.
A yantra fashioned with vermilion powder on the ground grants all desires;
however, one made in lead, bell-metal, or similar materials will continuously take away one's prosperity.
One should never place it on a wooden plank or against a wall;
if, out of delusion, it is so placed, it will destroy that wealth and the lineage.
Among those, however, the crystal one shall be the bestower of all accomplishments.
Now, he states the enumeration of the three metals.
The tenth part of gold, the twelfth part of copper,
and likewise the sixteenth part of silver— this is known as the triad of metals.
Now he states the measurement.
For an oblation of silver, it should be half a finger-breadth;
for copper, it should be of the same measure as previously stated; and for rubies and the like, it may be according to one's desire.
The worship altar and the beautiful pedestal should be made the measure of a *pala*.
Then, one should construct a square measuring one finger-breadth in width, extending east-west and south-north, with its upper side reaching the parārdha.
A pedestal made of rubies and the like that is smaller than the prescribed measurement does not cause any defect;
nor does one made of śrīparṇī, sandalwood, and so forth, cause a defect even if it is larger.
In the case of a large conch shell and a stone slab, there is no application of mechanical contrivances.
Alternatively:
One tola, two tolas, three tolas, or five tolas;
likewise one tola of mercury, four tolas, or seven and eight tolas.
Ten *tolas* for the sun,
sixteen *tolas* according to the number of digits (*kalās*), thirty-two *tolas*, sixty-four *tolas*, and one hundred *tolas*.
The yantra is pleasing, bestowing happiness, beautifully drawn, and an excellent pedestal.
Now he explains the *prastāra*.
For there are indeed fourfold types of arrays for the *cakra*:
the *bhū-prastāra*, the *kūrma-prastāra*, the *padma-prastāra*, and likewise the *meru-prastāra*.
The intersection of horizontal lines in the ground-plan described by me is the *kūrmapadmaka* grid;
the vertical lines therein have been described by me.
O Goddess, the layout on the ground (bhūprastāra) is twofold, according to the division of the upper [worlds] and the netherworlds (pātāla).
It may be elevated by three [units] in successive order, or likewise in reverse order.
Even if it is elevated by two or three steps, or alternatively by two or two [steps],
the interval between the *yava* marks should be half a *yava*, or joined with a sesame seed (*tila*) according to the rule.
That may be half a grain of rice, or it may be twice that, according to the difference in the sequence.
Meru is proclaimed to be in heaven and on Kailāśa in the mortal world;
the terrestrial expanse is in Pātāla—this triad has been described by me.
The lotus, the tortoise, and the jewel-wombed [earth] are auspicious in all forms of worship;
O Great Goddess, they are auspicious in every way and bestowers of all accomplishments.
The line designated as "upward" (ūrdhvarekhā) is for the purpose of worship and pertains to the domain of death;
however, in some traditions, the "subterranean" line (pātālarekhā) is considered to be for the purpose of installation.
Now, he states the locations for drawing the pericarp and other parts of the yantra.
Having drawn five concentric circles, the wise one should draw the yantra therein;
the first shall be the place for the pericarp (karṇikā), and the second for the filaments (keśara).

The third [circle] is for the middle of the petals, the fourth for the tips of the petals, and the fifth is to be drawn as the city of waters (būpura); thus it is prescribed in the ritual procedure for the yantra.
O Maheśvarī, the petal is said to be joined with two filaments;
O Maheśvarī, that which is shaped like a staff and has a dot at its tip is also said to be of that [same] nature.
O Goddess, in the grid of the layout, the downward line is considered the primary *bindu* at the filament;
in the moon [the upper part], the line is regarded as being of the nature of a filament.
In the Śrīvidyā and in Kālikā, the filaments may sometimes be present;
however, O Great Goddess, in the Śrīvidyā one should not fashion filaments at all.
Just as a petal is devoid of filaments when it is deprived of karma,
so too, O Goddess of Gods, the triangle becomes devoid of the bindu when it is deprived of it.
If the yantra should be devoid of the bindu,
one should likewise carefully fashion a circle above the eight petals.
Without a circular boundary, there should be an eight-petaled lotus devoid of central ornaments;
a straight line brings prosperity, while a curved line leads to poverty.
The practitioner should never cause the yantra to be marked at night;
if it is marked through negligence, he shall incur the curse of the deity.
O Maheśānī, I have explained the determination regarding the mere yantra,
as well as the mental visualization (ādhi), the worship of the orb (viṃva), and especially the specific ritual worship.
And through the practitioner’s faith, the deity desires to be present.
Now, he describes the meditation on the yantras.
The Goddess said:
O Lord, O Master, you previously indicated the meditation on the yantra;
how is it to be meditated upon, what is its specific nature, and what indeed is that which is both to be meditated upon and not to be meditated upon?
Is it to be meditated upon as circular, or as having the form of a physical image, or as having the nature of a girdle,
or as consisting of lines, or indeed as having the nature of the earth itself?
Or one may meditate upon the universal form; let all of that also be told.
Īśvara said:
O Maheśvarī, meditation is said to be threefold even in the case of a mere yantra:
first, that which has the form of Virāṭ Viśva; second, that which has the form of Caṇḍa; and [the third].
O Goddess, one should honor the yantra; this has been taught everywhere.
O Great Goddess, in the Śrīcakra and other such forms, there is equality with the form of Virāj.
And tell me, O Maheśvarī, how is the second [form] to be meditated upon—
that line resembling a mass of radiance, which is the embodiment of all consciousness?

One should contemplate all of this— from the *viṃdu* up to the *bhūpura*— as consciousness (*caitanya*), which is to be meditated upon like a mirror, self-luminous, and possessing its own essential nature.
O Dear One, one should meditate upon [the deity] as non-different from the light of the root-energetic power (mūlatejas).
O Goddess of the Gods, hear now of the third [form], the eternal form of Meru.
One should contemplate it as becoming increasingly higher, starting from the point of the *viṃdu*;
O Goddess, O Śivā, one should contemplate the *viṃdu* as increasing by one unit at each successive stage.
Or, O Maheśvarī, one should meditate upon the nine-fold sequence;
O Goddess, in the ritual of the Kālī-vidyā, one should contemplate the Nine Jewels as her very form.
O Goddess, one should honor the line like Mount Meru or like a grid-pattern.
O Supreme Goddess, the Śrīcakra joined with seed-syllables (bījas) is fruitless;
indeed, a cakra devoid of seed-syllables is "seedless" and does not bestow accomplishment (siddhi).
The wheel of emanation (sṛṣṭicakra) comes first, and the wheel of persistence (sthiticakra) is the second;
O Goddess, the extraction of the seed-syllables (bījasaṃlekha) has thus been described by me in three ways.
Without the seed-syllable (bīja), that yantra is "seedless" (nirvīja) yet still bestows accomplishment;
in the Kali age, it should be worshipped in the form of petals, for otherwise, O Śivā, it does not grant success.
O Goddess, there is the consciousness of the mantra, likewise the consciousness of the yantra, and the consciousness of the guru, O Goddess; one should contemplate these three within oneself.
Therein, there is no form of meditative absorption, nor fire, nor machine, nor mental visualization;
yet in that auspicious state, within the phenomenal world of saṃsāra, nectar is difficult to restrain.
Indeed, meditation alone has been fully proclaimed; meditation is considered the bestower of accomplishment.
Now, he describes the consecration of the yantra common to all.
The Goddess said:
O Great God, through your grace I have heard about the schism of the wheel;
now I wish to hear the definitive rule for the rite of consecration.
The venerable Śaṅkara said:
Listen, O Goddess, the creator of the universe, for I shall explain the concluding rite (udyāpana) of Kaulinī,
which includes the determination of all castes as part of its ritual procedure.
When the ascendant is endowed with benefic planets, favorable, and possessed of auspicious qualities,
one should perform the consecration of these [images] at a moment characterized by suitable constellations, lunar days, and so forth.
Having bathed, the practitioner of mantras should make a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and perform the worship of the Guru;
the Guru, with the mantra, should draw the yantra with a golden stylus.
Then, having prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) consecrated with the Śiva-mantra,
the practitioner, composed in mind, should cast the wheel there while reciting the Praṇava.
Having extracted that wheel from there, one should place it upon a golden lotus,
[anointing it] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), milk, and cool water.
And one should bathe [the deity] with sandalwood paste, musk, and saffron,
O Goddess, using eight golden jars filled with water.
One should bathe [the image] with water enriched by decoctions while reciting the mantra;
having lifted that [image], one should place it upon a golden vessel.
We know the King of Yantras; we meditate upon the Great Mantra.
At the end of that, one should utter: "May that Yantra inspire us."

Having touched the yantra with the tip of a blade of kusha grass, one should consecrate it with the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times, O Goddess, for the sake of accomplishing the state of the deity.
Then, having performed the purification of oneself, one should worship the deity with the six limbs;
having invoked the Goddess there, one should perform the ritual placement of the life-force (jīvanyāsa).
One should always worship the Goddess there with the sixteen services, beginning with the Mahāmudrā, as well as with fruits, betel, and food offerings.
O Maheśvarī, one should offer a thread and so forth, as well as garments and ornaments, a mirror, a fly-whisk, and a bell, according to what is appropriate.
One who is intent on their own welfare should offer all of that with great effort;
furthermore, one should worship the Goddess three times a day for three nights, again and again.
Then, for the sake of attaining all desired goals, one should perform a thousand recitations;
thereafter, having offered the bali-oblation, one should prostrate before the King of Yantras.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations, he should pour the remaining clarified butter (saṃpātājya) [into the fire];
if he is unable to perform the rite of homa, he should instead perform the recitation of the mantra (japa).

Having taken a single cow adorned with golden horns and other ornaments, one should give it as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor; thereafter follows the dismissal (visarjana) of the Goddess.
Then the goddess Kaulikā spoke the remainder.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the most secret of secrets:
the ritual purification of the yantra and the rites for both the Vāmins and the Kaulas.
Śiva said:
Now, the consecration of the great yantra, which bestows all accomplishments, is described:
having performed ritual bathing on an auspicious day, at an auspicious lunar mansion and at an auspicious moment.
Having performed his daily rites, the practitioner should face either the east or the north.

Having caused a beautiful and highly enchanting yantra to be drawn according to the prescribed ritual, using the previously mentioned medicinal substances, upon a fine line that bestows auspiciousness;
Then one should perform the consecration according to the authority of the scriptures,
at an auspicious moment and during a meritorious time, in a location such as a mountain or other prescribed site.
According to the ritual manual (kalpa), the minister (maṃtrī) should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) on the preceding day,
in the evening, following the rules for the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) and preceded by the installation of the bell (ghaṇṭā).
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa and the others, one should fully satisfy the guardians of the directions (dikpālas). [The five makāras are:
liquor, meat, fish, parched grain, and sexual union.
In rituals such as the consecration of a yantra, this substance has been prescribed by me;
one should worship the root deity with offerings and services according to one's capacity.
One should perfume it with substances such as fragrant oils and scents,
preceded by the chanting of the mantra beginning with "caṃdra" and so forth.
Having thus performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*), with his senses fully restrained,
he should first perform the daily morning rites and then enter the sacrificial ground.
It was crowded with banners and flags, adorned with divine mandalas,
and graced by canopies, yak-tail whisks, parasols, and flower garlands.
In the Sarvatobhadra [mandala], which is adorned on all sides with jars containing auspicious sprouts, leaves, and other offerings,
there is a mandala joined with a thousand lines.
O Goddess, one should draw a general auspicious [symbol] or a lotus around the perimeter of the altar.
Alternatively, I shall describe the Varuṇa-maṇḍala on the right or the left;
one should arrange the knowledge [mantra] within a square consisting of sixty-four compartments.
One should erase the squares in the directions within the last two rows;
the four central eyes are likewise designated as the gates, as previously described.
One should fill [the squares] with yellow, dark blue, white, and yellowish-green dusts, excluding the corner compartments; thus, forty-nine [squares] are connected.
One should fill the pedestal with white, red, yellow, and black [colors].
In the southeast corner, the square cells should be filled with yellow, red, green, and black.
One should cause four circles to be made in the center with white color;
then one should fill them and fix a canopy above them as is appropriate.
The first circle, with a diameter of thirty-six parts, is yellow;
it has the form of a pericarp and is surrounded by a white line.
The second [lotus] has double the width and is endowed with filaments in the form of *rūpaka*;
its filaments at the base, middle, and tip are yellow, red, and white in color respectively.
In front of that, draw a white line measuring seventy-two parts;
then, at the third part, there shall be a circle with an equal diameter.
Therein, the lotus has eight white petals, with the space between the petals being red;
the exterior is white, while the interior of those petals is black and red-limbed.
Outside [the central area], make a black line and then a white line as before;
outside that, one should fashion sixteen spokes joined to a circle.
Alternatively, one who is skillful may paint it with black, yellow, red, and white;
or the five lines may be white, yellow, red, black, and green.
One should fashion five very beautiful [weapons] and fill them in this manner within the center;
one should draw the thunderbolt (vajra), the spear (śakti), the staff (daṇḍa), the sword (khaḍga), the noose (pāśa), the banner (dhvaja), and the mace (gadā).
To the east and likewise in the northeast, it is provided with a trident,
a wheel, and a lotus; this mandala on the left and right is called Vāruṇa.
Facing the east and remaining silent, having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the attainment of his desired goal,
and having performed the fivefold purification, he should proceed while holding unbroken grains (akṣata).
Having established [the deities] there in the maṇḍala, beginning with Ādhāraśakti,
the wise practitioner should spread the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra) and place the water-pot (kalaśa).

Then, according to the procedure prescribed in the sequence of initiation (dīkṣākrama), one should likewise prepare the consecration jar (abhiṣekakalaśa) and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), both empowered by the recitation of the Śiva-mantra.
The mantra-practitioner should thoroughly bathe the yantra while reciting the Praṇava,
using the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), clarified butter, curd, and milk in succession.
Then, having performed the ritual rubbing of the body (udvartana), one should place it in water;
having brought the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should, with a concentrated mind, place the yantra therein.
The knower of mantras, preceded by the Veda-mūla mantra, should cast [the materials] into gold and so forth;
then, having extracted them, he should place the vessel of gold and so forth [therein].
With the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), with holy water, and with cool water,
preceded by the root mantra and the Sahasraśīrṣā mantra.
Having bathed [the deity] with great care using water infused with camphor and agallochum,
along with water containing all medicinal herbs and fragrant waters, one should perform the ritual cleansing.
Then, having pushed back the water with a pure silk cloth, the practitioner,
having put on two silk garments, [should sit] upon a swing made of gold.
Having brought him to the mandala with dances, songs, and shouts of victory,
he should then be anointed with saffron and other substances, and worshipped with all ritual offerings.
Then one should perform the worship of the *pīṭha* according to the measurements prescribed in its own respective ritual manual (*kalpa*).
O Goddess, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times with *kuśa* grass or with *kulīna* [grass].
Having recited the previously mentioned Yaṃtra-Gāyatrī, one shall attain divinity;
then, having meditated upon the desired deity, one should invoke them with a mudrā.
Then one should perform the *jīvanyāsa* (infusion of life) and worship the chosen deity,
preceded by the fivefold sounds of dance, song, and musical instruments.
Then the practitioner of mantra should recite the desired mantra one thousand and eight times over the fire in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
on the altar (sthaṇḍila), or over the consecrated fuel-sticks (nala) with clarified butter (havis).
The knower of mantras should perform the oblation with the *śruc* ladle according to the prescribed rules and ritual procedure,
drawing out the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) in mouthful-sized portions by means of the root mantra.
Then, having offered a ladle of clarified butter, one should make oblations before the fire;
one should perform the libation with the twenty-five principles according to their true nature.
One should offer the previously mentioned bali-oblation to Indra and the other guardians of the directions;
thereafter, one should perform oblations with clarified butter for the deities of the surrounding circle.
At the conclusion of that, O Goddess, one should perform one hundred and eight oblations with the mantra;
indeed, one should recite the mantra joined with the Mātṛkās amidst shouts of "Victory! Victory! and "Be Victorious!"
Having gone near the fire-offering (homa) and then offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti),
one should satisfy [the officiant] with gold, garments, and other gifts, and also bestow a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
With the five letters beginning with *kṣa*, the Goddess should perform the worship of the heroes;
she should worship the Śakti, the Kumārikā, and the Bālā as the fivefold pentad.
Or one should perform the tenfold or eightfold rite with all the substances belonging to the Kula;
through the practice of worshipping the yantra, one becomes the Lord of the Three Worlds.
Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and other rites, one should carry out the practice according to the method taught in the *Kalpa*.
At night, the Kaulikas perform the worship of the Śakti and the sacrifice to the female messenger (*dūtīyāga*).
Endowed with the five *makāras*, they should perform the worship of Vāminī;
having done so for three days, they should thereafter follow the daily ritual sequence.
The worship of the Sundarī-yantra is performed by way of creation, maintenance, and dissolution;
the worship of the Kālikā-yantra is performed by way of creation and withdrawal.
By way of the path of emanation and withdrawal, Tārā and Chinnā possess yellow luster;
thus, in the rite of installation, this sequence brings about the presence of the Goddess.
This is the rule for women, Śūdras, sinners, and Kaulikas;
it should be performed according to the prescribed injunctions, and one must not cause it to be done devoid of the injunctions.
I shall describe to you those obstacles that arise for one who is devoid of the prescribed rites:
quarrels, agitation, duality, as well as disease, piercing pain, and fever.
There will be trouble from the king, loss of wealth, as well as disease;
furthermore, there will be ominous signs such as the cries of crows and jackals, and the terrible howling of jackals.
Pigeons alight upon his house and enter it;
remaining hidden, they indeed create obstacles for his ritual procedure.
The yoginīs find his weak points and afflict him with various obstacles;
there are serpents, scorpions, spiders, and indeed dreadful insects.
And those exceedingly fierce ones, impelled by the rays [of the sun],
devour [all beings] along with the bulls, horses, lordly elephants, clouds, and likewise the wielder of the thunderbolt upon his throne.
The wicked, as well as fevers, spirits, and the like, cause affliction;
spiders, donkeys, and epilepsy likewise overcome [the person], and not otherwise.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Installation Rite Preceded by the Ritual of the Yantra," in the *Śrī Tantracintāmaṇi*.
Now, I shall explain the rosary; it is of two kinds: fixed (*sthirā*) and mobile (*calā*).
But it is stable for those of steady mind, and flickering for those of unsteady intellect.
That means of accomplishment is said to be threefold: the first is the garland of letters,
the second is the rosary for recitation, and the third is the finger-garland.
Now he speaks of the Acalamālā:
By means of the garland of letters fashioned from the phonemes of the Mātṛkā— beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', accompanied by the nasal bindu, and arranged both in direct and reverse order.
Uttering each syllable one by one, with the mantra interspersed between the syllables, the wise man should thus bring it to the end of the letter *la* and then to the end of the letter *āṃ*.
One should never overstep the letter *kṣa*, which has the form of Mount Meru;
one should utter it only once, and at its conclusion, one should not utter the mantra again.
Any garland that is devoid of the *meru* bead, and any garland that would be devoid of the *meru* bead, shall be impure in this context; such a garland will be fruitless.
That variegated channel, which has the appearance of a spider's web and extends into the Brahma-nāḍī,
should be meditated upon as strung together by it, bestowing the fruits of all desires.
Having first recited the neuter [seed-syllable] one hundred and eight times, one should then perform the recitation.
The four phonemes ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ are declared to be neuter;
or else, they are the eighth among the vowels according to the sequence of the division of desired [sounds].
Or rather, the eight groups [of consonants] are thus: a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, and va.
Alternatively, having uttered the three "mṛtas" at the end of the Praṇava,
the Mātṛkā [mantra] repeated in both direct and reverse order becomes one of one hundred and eight [syllables].

Through the union of Māyā, Vāk, Kāma, and Śrī, and through the application of the letters of the Mātṛkā in both direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) order, there arises the one hundred and eight [syllables].
O Goddess, three [prostrations] are prescribed for the Guru, and three for the Gaṇapa;
two are prescribed when there is deficiency or excess; one should conquer the remainder through the attainment of one's desired goal.
This rosary of one hundred and eight beads bestows success in all undertakings and purposes;
because it consists of the forms of the letters of the alphabet, it is declared to be a stable garland.
From the letter 'a' to the letter 'kṣa', this very [alphabet] is the rosary;
it is declared to be a fifty-fold garland, whose thread is Śakti and whose essence is Śiva.
The stringing together is the Kuṇḍalinī power; at the end of the short vowel, it is situated upon Meru.
One should perform this most secret rite, which consists of the beads and is of the nature of Śiva.
One must never act openly, nor should one ever leap over Meru;
this is due to the yoga of the sleeping, the pinned-down, the sealed, the severed, and the scattered.
Even those who are impoverished, devoid of valor, or afflicted by such disabilities as blindness or lameness,
certainly become accomplished masters through the power of the Sthiramālā.
Now follows its meditation.

I bow to the Goddess Śrīmātṛkā, who shines like coral within, who is resplendent with the colors of a sleeping serpent, who ascends and descends in a hundred-fold manner through the eighty-eight classes of letters,
who is the manifest embodiment of Brahman, who is the crest-jewel of the earth and Mount Meru, and who is the power of the syllables of the alphabet.
I bow to the mother of all mantras, the sprout of the single lamp of wisdom.
Now, regarding the different deities and the different types of garlands, I shall speak:
for Śrī Kālī there is a rosary of teeth, and for Tārā it is made of human bone or conch shell.
In the ritual of Chinnamastā, a beautiful rosary made of human bones is recommended;
for the ritual of Tripurā, there should be a rosary made of red sandalwood seeds.
Svayaṃbhūmālikā is in Bhairavī, Bālikā in the rite [of Vārāhī],
Bhujāmālā in Mātaṅgī, and Kharadaṃtajā in Dhūmrā.
The *haridrākṣā* is prescribed for the *brahmāstra*, the *kapālākṣā* for the *māyā-vidhi*,
and the *sphāṭikī* is proclaimed for the *vālā-bhuvaneśvarī*.
O Maheśvarī, the white guñjā is prescribed for the rite of Siddhividya;
the conch-shell rosary for the Vaiṣṇava, and the indrākṣa for the Śākta alone.
The Bhadrākṣa is prescribed for Śarabha; for Gaṇeśa, those made from elephant tusks;
for Tripuṭā, the Putrajīva; and for Govinda, Tulasī is considered appropriate.
O Śivā, [the image] may be made of jewels, gold, silver, or likewise copper;
it may also be made of udumbara wood, seeds, or the seeds of the vaṭa tree.
A rosary made of betel nuts as well as one made of jasmine fruits is for the purpose of attracting Madhumatī,
even in the ritual procedure of the Vīra-vidyā.
O Goddess, the Eastern Tradition is characterized by crystals; the Southern by Rudrākṣas born from the eye of Rudra;
the Western Tradition, O Goddess, by corals and pearls.
The rosary known as Mahāśaṅkha belongs to the deities of the Uttarāmnāya;
it is self-arisen in the Ūrdhvāmnāya and originates from jewels in the netherworld (Pātāla).
A rosary composed of Śiva and Śakti may consist of coral with the Sūrya-mantra,
pearls for the Śakti-mantra alone, or be joined with Rudrākṣas and crystal.
A rosary composed of Rudrākṣas joined with gold has Hari and Hara as its essence;
a rosary composed of Rudrākṣas joined with silver has Śiva as its essence according to the prescribed rite.
Rudrākṣas are used in all mantras, but not by day in the case of Śakti mantras.
And so it is said:
Due to the separation of Śiva and Śakti, there is no recitation with Rudrākṣa beads during the day;
when they are separated, Kālī, though worshipped, does not suddenly become propitious.
O Dear One, he who recites a Śakti mantra during the day using Rudrākṣa beads falls into a miserable state; his recitation is fruitless.
Thus, listen as the story of that curse previously given is told. Once upon a time, O Goddess, Dakṣa’s sacrifice was in full progress.
All the sages, gods, yakṣas, vidyādharas,
and nāgas were invited to the house through their connections as sons and sons-in-law.
Mahādeva was not invited by Satyavatī to that sacrifice; however,
Satī, having approached her husband there, spoke to him.
Śiva said:
"O beloved of my life, he did not do that because of me alone;
how is it that you feel no shame, that you go there yourself?"
The Lord is dear, life itself is dear, and even your ornament is indeed dear;
O Queen, how can you go there leaving me behind?
Where is this devotion to a husband, since it is devoid of a rival?
Nevertheless, if you have the desire to go, please show me your grace.
Having received his master’s command, he set out for the sacrificial pavilion;
in an instant, that lion carried him to the sacrificial pavilion of Brahmā.
Disregarded by him, Pārvatī stood there dejected in mind and sorrowful, her face cast downward, bearing her beautiful form.
"All the gods are present here, yet my husband is not to be seen;
therefore, a great sorrow remains seated within my heart."
In the meantime, O Goddess, Dakṣa Prajāpati himself,
having become intent on reviling Śiva, was once again prepared to utter insults.
Though forbidden by Viṣṇu, he remained ill-behaved;
becoming intent on constant censure, Bhaṅgī was mounted upon the bull as his vehicle.
Dwelling in cremation grounds, a meat-eater, naked, most steadfast, and sovereign;
bearing a skull-bowl and a trident, he is adorned with a garland of severed heads.
With his entire body smeared with ashes and seated upon a tiger skin,
he becomes one who is greedy and lustful, intent on much censure.
Indeed, distressed by reproach, you have come outside the pavilion;
having gone a distance of two eye-breadths away, you have prepared a fire-pit.
Having said "So be it," Satī abandoned her body there and attained the form of fire;
I, Śiva, in the form of wrath, became a blazing orb of flames.
O Maheśānī, by his wrath the three worlds were reduced to ashes; from his flame arose the all-pervading Vīrabhadra.
The unbearable conflagration at the end of millions of eons,
which was prepared for the purpose of destroying the sacrifice of Dakṣa Prajāpati, [was directed] toward all living beings.
Holding a trident in his hand, cruel and the destroyer of sacrifices, he made it his ultimate refuge; O Goddess, he took the auspicious Śavarddhapā upon his shoulder.
Therefore, they both wept, and drops of tears fell;
from those drops of tears there arose the great rudrākṣa trees.
Having attained a state of immobility for the sake of bestowing grace upon mortals,
they indeed bear fruit at all times, granting their fruits without interruption.
It is heard that the rudrākṣa is renowned throughout the three worlds;
it is proclaimed to have originated from the three eyes and to bestow wealth and fortune.
Born from the left eye, Moraṅgīya is proclaimed;
Dhanāśrī, Koṣṭhadaśa, and Pārvatīya shall be the Manus.
Up to twenty-one faces, he is proclaimed as Malākī;
thus were the faces produced from the weeping of Rudra.
O Lord, for one born with a clear face and a mountain-like (broad) forehead, there is clearly established prosperity;
and when the lines possess the splendor of wealth, fortune, and the mane of a lion, it arises.
When the destruction by fire occurs, at that time [the soul] comes from the midst of the water;
it arrives upon the water, and that is proclaimed as *malākī*.
Whatever action is performed by means of that [mantra], its fruit shall be infinite;
however, the power in the form of accomplishment found in other mantras does not exist in the Śakti-mantra during the day.
Thus, O Goddess, for this reason, recitation is prescribed specifically at night;
for the night is the form of union, and you, O Maheśvarī, are the Vidyā.
The Lord of Gods, whose form is knowledge, is proclaimed by the mantra scriptures.
Now I shall describe the greatness of the rudrākṣa in brief:
one who desires liberation through the rudrākṣa should regard the rudrākṣa as the means for attaining the highest good.
The rudrākṣa removes suffering; the rudrākṣa is the destroyer of sin. It causes the destruction of all evils for those who recite [its name] or even for those who hear it.
Whether one is a non-devotee or a devotee, whether low-born or even very lowly,
whoever wears a rudrākṣa is liberated from all sins.
With what could the merit of wearing rudrākṣas be compared?
Those sages who perceive the truth declare this to be a great vow.
He who, firm in his vows, wears a thousand rudrākṣas, is saluted by all the gods; he is indeed just like Rudra himself.
A garland for the head consists of thirty-six [skulls], while the necklace for the neck consists of thirty-two;
sixteen are prescribed for the elbows, and thirty-two for the two wrists.
A sacred thread (upavīta) consisting of one hundred and eight [strands] is prescribed;
above that, a garland of divine flowers is said to be worn on the crest-lock (śikhā).
The sequence for holding six [mudrās] on the two ears has also been described;
one should not perform it with fewer than that number, though having more does not cause any fault.
One who wears rudrākṣas shall indeed become Śiva at the end of the body;
he acquires abundant merit and is born here as a fortunate person.
During bathing, giving gifts, recitation, burnt offerings, the Vaiśvadeva rite, worship of the gods, penance, as well as at a śrāddha ceremony, and especially at the time of initiation;
And whatever Vedic rite a Brahmin may constantly perform while being a bearer of the Rudra-mantra, that rite shall become fruitful.
Even while eating meat, drinking liquor, or consorting with those of the lowest castes,
one whose soul is instantly purified by wearing a rudrākṣa on the head.
Those who worship the gods and Pūṣan, as well as those Vedic animal-sacrificers,
and those in the Kaula tradition who cause them to fall— Śiva himself is their punisher.
For the sake of protecting them, there is nothing else on earth superior to the rudrākṣa;
rudrākṣas bring about the attainment of mantras for all the gods.
If even a dog dies with a rudrākṣa resting upon its neck, it attains the state of Rudra; how much more so for humans and others?
Whether one is impure from remnants of food, engaged in forbidden acts, or joined with all manner of sins,
a man is liberated from all evils by wearing rudrākṣa beads.
Even one who performs sinful deeds, if he constantly wears a rosary of rudrākṣas around his neck— even if devoid of devotion— is honored in the world of Rudra.
He who bears [this] is himself of the nature of Rudra; he too is worshipped like Rudra, with pearls, coral, crystal, silver, lapis lazuli, and gold.
He who wears a complete set of rudrākṣas shall become Śiva himself;
even if one wears rudrākṣas alone due to laziness [in obtaining a full set], he likewise attains that state.
Sins do not touch him, just as darkness does not touch the fire;
a mantra recited with a rosary of rudrākṣa beads bestows infinite fruit.
For men who recite prayers without a Rudrākṣa on their body, even the recitation yields only that much fruit; however, for one who has even a single Rudrākṣa on their person, it bestows great merit.
The birth of one who is devoid of the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) would be in vain;
so too for him who, having placed a rudrākṣa on his head, performs a ritual bath of the head.
The fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā arises for him; there is no doubt in this matter—namely, for one who worships a rudrākṣa even without the sprinkling of water.
One certainly attains that fruit which results from the worship of a *liṅga*,
by constantly worshipping with devotion the rudrākṣa, which is of the very nature of Śaṃkara.
It makes even a poor man equal in fortune to the king of kings;
one obtains from the sight of it a merit equal to bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Whether it be thousands of lakṣakoṭis or hundreds of lakṣakoṭis [of merits], they are obtained simply by wearing rudrākṣa; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Śiva, who has one face, removes sins such as the killing of a Brahmin from one who recites with his garland; likewise, he grants the fulfillment of desires for sovereignty and other goals.
O Pārvatī, he who possesses a rudrākṣa endowed with one face truly attains universal sovereignty; this is indeed the truth of the wise.
This deity named Umāśaṅkara removes sins such as the killing of cows and bestows the happiness of domestic life and other blessings.
The three-faced [form] is indeed of the nature of fire; it destroys sins such as the killing of women.
Through its retention, its recitation, and so forth, dharma, artha, and kāma are accomplished.
One becomes four-faced Brahmā, the destroyer of sins such as the murder of a preceptor;
all branches of knowledge flash forth, and mastery over speech is also attained.
The five-faced Śiva is manifestly Kālāgni by name;
through the recitation of that [mantra], there is swift accomplishment for the devotees of Śiva, Gaṇeśa, and Śakti.
By wearing the five-faced [liṅga], one is released from the terrible sin of approaching those who should not be approached and even from eating that which should not be eaten.
By the six-faced Kārttikeyas, the vow slips away and destroys sin;
one is liberated from sins such as the killing of a fetus—of this there is no doubt.
By wearing [this mantra] on the right arm according to the prescribed rite, one attains victory in battle; furthermore,
through its recitation, one becomes the seven-faced great serpent named Ananta.
Infinite accomplishments arise for all, and no fear occurs;
one becomes fortunate through gold, and even a poor person becomes a lord.
Even after committing numerous sins such as violating the preceptor’s bed, one is liberated from them by wearing a rudrākṣa; of this there is no doubt.
The eight-faced one is Gaṇeśa, the remover of all obstacles;
by the recitation of his mantra, all enemies such as desire, anger, and the like, are destroyed.
One should not touch the wife of one's guru even with the back of the hand or the belly;
such acts and others like them are sins, indeed the gravest of sins in every respect.
His obstacles perish, and being liberated, he goes to the supreme goal;
he shall live for more than a hundred years, for he becomes like the wielder of the trident, unto whom death does not come.
Indeed, all these qualities arise from the wearing of these [amulets] of Aṣṭavaktra;
Bhairava with nine faces is remembered as bestowing liberation, being tawny in color.
Through recitation, the deities situated on the left-hand path become propitious;
if one holds [the mantra] in the left hand, one shall become a boon-granter equal to me.
Whoever commits thousands of millions of crores of killings of Brahmins—
by the recitation of the Navavaktra [mantra], all of that is swiftly consumed.
The ten-faced god Janārdana [is there],
as well as thousands of piśācas, vetālas, and brahmarākṣasas.
The ḍākinīs, the mothers, as well as the leaders of the pretas and the serpents,
are destroyed by the wearing of the ten-faced [mantra].
An eleven-faced rudrākṣa is known as the eleven Rudras;
listen now to the meritorious fruit of one who constantly wears it on the crest-lock.
The fruit that belongs to a thousand horse-sacrifices, hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices,
and a hundred thousand cows properly given as a gift— [that fruit is attained].
One obtains that fruit by wearing eleven Rudrākṣas;
the twelve-faced Rudrākṣa is the Sun, consisting of twelve aspects.
One should wear it around the neck or recite it with a concentrated mind;
thus one becomes radiant, powerful, and like unto the sun.
One is not afflicted by the nine planets, beginning with the Sun, even when they are most terrible;
the unfortunate become fortunate, and the diseased is liberated from illness.
It bestows the fruits of all sacrifices, such as the Gomedha and Naramedha;
[it yields] elephants, horses, deer, cats, buffaloes, boars, and so forth.
Even if one has killed many dogs, jackals, or crows,
one is liberated from that— of this there is no doubt— by the practice of the Dhāraṇā of the Twelve Suns.
O child, if one attains the thirteenth face through its retention,
one is constantly worshipped by the gods and obtains supreme merit.
One obtains every fruit, and supreme good fortune shall arise;
[one masters] mercury, elixirs, the sword, and various methods of alchemy.
The wish-fulfilling cow and the rudrākṣa bring about the fulfillment of one's desires;
by means of that rudrākṣa, even one who is devoid of fortune attains success.
One is burned even more than by a mother, a father, a kinsman, or a teacher.
One is liberated from terrible sins as well as other secondary transgressions if a fourteen-faced Rudrākṣa, which is meritorious, is obtained.
One should diligently maintain that crest-lock and sacred thread;
for, O child, Cāmuṇḍā herself is the mass of power (śaktipiṇḍa) belonging to Śiva.
Having worshipped it and worn it around the neck, one is indeed not born again;
it is perfected—of this there is no doubt, O Six-faced One, this is the truth, the absolute truth.
Just as that palace may wander anywhere in the world of mortals, so too the yogi should move everywhere; thus he shall become beloved by all.
Both the animal and the human, as well as the impure city,
[are transformed by] the elixir of mercury, which destroys old age and death.
He shall obtain the Vetāla-sword and the eight most wonderful siddhis;
for him there is neither merit nor sin, and he is not afflicted by disease.
He shall live for thousands of years; when dead, he becomes a bearer of the trident (Śiva).
He obtains wealth without asking, and there shall be no depletion of his riches.
The wise one is liberated from all sins; this becomes the fruit of sacrifice.
When recited with fourteen faces, it leads to infinity.
O Lord, he who is honored by gods and men attains an imperishable state;
like Hari among the gods, his body remains secure and free from death.
Just as the sun is among the planets, as Kaśyapa is among the sages,
as the Gaṅgā is among rivers, and as the ocean is among sacred fords;
As the bow is among weapons, as the fourteenth day is among sacrificial offerings,
as Skanda is among the Kumāras, so is Maheśvara among the gods.
Among goddesses, Umā-devī is foremost; among lordly elephants, Airāvata;
among cows, Sunandā indeed; and likewise, among horses, Harita.
Thus, among all those to be counted, the rudrākṣa is preeminent.
It is taught that one should bear a six-faced [image] upon the head, a three-faced one on the neck,
a five-faced one on the arm, and a four-faced one on the hand for auspiciousness.
One should wear a two-faced rudrākṣa at the waist, a single-faced one on the head,
and a nine-faced rudrākṣa on the left arm.
A wise man should wear a fourteen-faced Rudrākṣa on his crest-lock,
O Brahmin, and he should wear Rudrākṣas during the Sandhyā prayers and other ritual acts.
All that is declared to be fruitful, certainly multiplied a hundred thousand-fold or ten million-fold;
the merit from seeing a rudrākṣa is equal to the merit from seeing a liṅga.
A person obtains a hundred million-fold merit from wearing it;
by wearing it on the head one gains ten million, and on the ears, one hundred million.
Having tied a hundred crores around the neck, a thousand crores on the head,
ten thousand as the sacred thread, and a lakh of crores upon the two arms;
One who wears rudrākṣas shall have an immeasurable fruit in his hand.
Rudrākṣas that are flawless and well-ripened are prescribed for wearing;
O Six-faced One, an examination of the Rudrākṣa must therefore be performed.
It is traditionally held that [the sacrificial post] should be well-baked, very firm, well-pierced, and perfectly symmetrical;
it must be without holes or blemishes, and it bestows the fruits described in the Kalpas.
The white should be known as inferior, the black-colored as middling,
while the red-colored is superior and bestows all accomplishments.
O child, if the mouth [of the vessel] is broken, or especially if it has holes, the fruit will be somewhat diminished; it is destroyed by such defects.
Listen now to the fruit of each of these, O Goddess, along with the *madhuna* [rosary]:
by means of the rosary called *daṃtā*, one becomes a master of sixty siddhis.
Desired success is achieved instantaneously by means of a rosary known as the "Great Conch," fashioned from bone-jewels that destroy all enemies.
A garland made of red sandalwood is said to bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
O Goddess, by means of self-arisen flowers, one becomes a lord of all vidyās.
Enchantment is said to be achieved with *guñjā* seeds; the destruction of enemies with *kharadanta*;
immobilization (*stambhana*) is accomplished with turmeric; and excellent nourishment (*puṣṭi*) is obtained with lotus seeds (*padmākṣa*).
The accomplishment of speech (*vāksiddhi*) arises from crystal and bestows the fruit of all desires;
for the sake of wealth, it is achieved through white *guñjā*, while fame and prosperity are considered to arise from the conch.
With Indrākṣa beads, it is said that sovereignty is granted; with Bhadrākṣa beads, there is the attainment of enjoyments and prosperity;
and with Gajadanta beads, the accomplishment of all goals occurs at all times.
Through *putrajīvaka* seeds, one obtains wealth, grain, sons, and acquisitions;
through *tulasī*, one attains liberation; and through gems, it bestows enjoyments.
If it is made of gold, there shall be royal fortune; if made of silver, all happiness. Through the joints of the finger, one attains all perfections and sovereignty.

With *audumbara* fruits one destroys malevolent spirits; with *plakṣa* fruits, poverty is destroyed; by means of *vaṭa* seeds, one gains a yakṣiṇī; and by means of cowrie shells, great prosperity is attained.
The accomplishment of subjugation (*vaśya*) occurs through coral; likewise, it is achieved with pearls and emeralds. A knot made of *kuśa* grass destroys the multitude of sins.
For subjugation (*mohana*), a rosary made of coral is essential; for copper is considered best for attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*).
For enchantment (*vidveṣa*), it is with red sandalwood, and for killing (*māraṇa*), with a garland of *ariṣṭa* seeds.
By means of mirages, laughter, garlands, and the crushing of lotuses, there is destruction; likewise,
the sun is used for expulsion, and iron is prescribed for killing.
The *jvalahartrī* [mantra] is for lac; that which originates from the father [of weapons] brings satisfaction to the ancestors;
that arising from sandalwood is for crossing over poison; and likewise, the eightfold [mantra] is for pacifying hardships.
Rituals performed with flowers produced from Padmaka wood or those originating from Devadāru are radiant;
however, Tāmasa action is accomplished with those arising from Kṛṣṇa wood.
Born from the paralysis of spirits, and joined with the paralysis of people,
this great *ḍākinī* named Mahānīlā effects the paralysis of diseases through the paralysis of the earth.

If a wound or paralysis occurs from a tree, or if there is malevolent sorcery involving a human bone, or if one is situated among bears, there will be success with wild animals; the deity presiding over that is Śārdūlā.

Through human bone, one becomes subject to the Rākṣasas; through the bone of a hero, one becomes subject to the Vīras; through horse bone, one gains mastery over the Kṣudra-siddhis; and through serpent bone, one attains honor.
A rosary made of beads baked in clay bestows the siddhi of Śāvara;
through bilva fruits one attains knowledge, and with rudrākṣa beads it grants all siddhis.
Now I shall describe the practice of stringing the rosaries; therein, the consecration [of the beads] is performed.
On the fourth lunar day, one should string the rosary with the mantras of Gaṇanātha.
On the seventh lunar day or on a Sunday at midday, it should be strung with the mantras of that [deity];
on the twelfth lunar day, the Vaiṣṇava garland should be strung with the Viṣṇu mantra.
O son of the Earth, on the thirteenth day at twilight, or on the eighth, fourteenth, or ninth day, one should fashion a garland of *śiva* [seeds] with those mantras.
The Śaktis also must be worshipped according to the prescribed rule after eating at night;
with whichever mantra a rosary was made, one should recite the mantra with that very rosary.
From the recitation of another mantra, a curse from the deity arises.
Alternatively, O Dear One, one should have it strung together with the Mātṛkās;
the beads of the rosary consist of fifty gems, and there is one called Meru.
The rosary should consist of one hundred beads in both forward and reverse order;
then, having arranged the eight groups, the rosary becomes one hundred and eight.
Recitation with a rosary made of *mātṛkā* beads is praised for all mantras;
this supreme rosary, consisting of all accomplishments, brings about swift success.
Having meditated at that moment upon the Goddess who consists of that very mantra, one should perform the recitation with diligence; no hesitation should be entertained in this matter.
The supreme garland bestows all accomplishments and performs every task.
First, one should perform the rite for each individual jar in sequence with the *dhruva* mantra;
this supreme rosary, consisting of all mantras, bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhis*).
Having meditated upon the form of the deity of that mantra,
one should recite all the mantras within the rosary for the sake of accomplishing every purpose.

O Śivā, having strung together the Śakti-mantra with the Śiva-mantra, one should recite the Śiva-mantra; O Śivā, having strung together the Śiva-mantra with the Śakti-mantra, one should recite the Śakti-mantra.
Through the non-duality of Śiva and Śakti, she is the supreme [power] who effects the work of the garland.
"O Goddess, one should recite that very mantra by which [the rosary] is strung"—this and more was said by you previously; have you forgotten it, O Lord?
Now, O Lord, another matter has been stated, for which I have a doubt:
how can the Mātṛkā be distinct from the Tāra while being devoid of Śiva and Śakti?
This has not been stated in the *Mātṛkā*; it is the opinion regarding other types of garland rites that one should not perform the stringing [of beads] in any manner other than the prescribed method.
O Śivā, reciting that very mantra, one should not recite it elsewhere;
even when using the Mātṛkā or other [syllables], O Śivā, the rosary itself is of the nature of that mantra.
A garland for the pleasure of the Goddess should be strung with silk thread;
a Vaiṣṇava garland may likewise be made of kārvya fibers or even lotus fibers.
The Śiva-rosary may be made from wool fibers or from bark; it may also be made from thread.
It should be used for rites of dharma and other activities, as it grants all accomplishments.
Now hear the procedure for the production of the thread for almost all the deities:
O best of the twice-born, the thread should be spun by a virtuous woman and must be free of knots.
The thread spun by a beautiful woman who has a living child and is devoted to her husband, or else spun by a maiden;
White, red, golden-hued, and black—these are the colors starting from the twice-born (Brahmins) and so forth. Among all these castes, the red color grants everything desired.
Having tripled the three-fold [thread] and carefully washed it, one should take it;
here, a cord made of fine cotton is fashioned from a silk cloth with a thread.
It is fashioned from gold and silver; even one made of gold alone is considered auspicious.

One should always avoid yellow thread, as well as that produced from village-dwellers or from flax, when performing the work of stringing [the rosary]. One should also discard thread made from *caitra* (cotton) for this purpose.
A rosary strung by a Guru is the best; one prepared by oneself is inferior. One strung by a Śakti is excellent, O Īśvarī, but not one made by Śūdras and the like.
Among these, the Brāhmaṇa is the most excellent for the sake of the water-offering;
however, in the absence of twice-born men, even those of their own respective castes may perform it.
But in the Kali age, Brahmins are difficult to find—those Brahmins who abide in their own duty.
Now, O Supreme Goddess, I shall describe her purification in brief,
either according to the tradition of the Kula path or by the method prescribed in the Smṛtis.
Having performed his daily rites, being pure, and having gazed upon the desired object,
he should— free from sloth— observe either a fast, consume sacrificial food (haviṣya), or likewise eat only a single meal.
Having prepared the silk cloth, he should manufacture the thread by boiling it;
O Goddess, on the day of fasting, he should worship all of those [materials].
One should perform [the rite] twice, thrice, or even three times that amount,
using sandalwood paste, unbroken rice grains, incense and the like, flowers, offerings, and lamps.
The measurements should be made concise, neither too large nor too small;
having taken that thread in the morning, [the measurement] should be performed according to one's desire and the specific requirements of the task.
