One should likewise cause the colors white, blue, yellow, and red to be made.
Having diligently gathered rudrākṣas, crystal beads, and others—
whether they have one face, two faces, four faces, or five faces.
Alternatively, they may be made with six faces, but one should avoid mixing them with one another;
face should be joined to face, but one must avoid joining face to the base.
Joining face to face and back to back,
the elevated part of the rudrākṣa is said to be the face, while the depressed part is the tail.
The best [stone] is like the fruit of the *dhātṛ* tree; the middling is similar to a jujube (*badara*); and the inferior is not even like a *kābha*. Anything smaller than that causes misfortune.
A rudrākṣa that is excessively large, too fine, fragile, light, cracked,
previously worn, or decayed is not considered auspicious.
They should not be worn out, nor pierced by insects and the like, but should be new;
the first [type] is thick, and from that, each subsequent one is smaller and smaller.
A single Mount Meru, arising from the gross [element], is to be offered there for all;
one should bring it with its face turned upward and must not let it pass beyond that Meru.
Taking each individual gem, the wise one should string them together on a thread;
it should then be made in the shape of a serpent or likewise resembling a cow's tail.
One should visualize a Brahma-knot within each individual jewel;
this is done by three rotations through the center and then by half-rotations in that region.
A knot that spirals clockwise is called a Brahma-knot.
Alternatively, one should employ a firm thread that is free of knots and well-prepared,
just as a practitioner intent on recitation should perform his *japa*.
The wise have declared that with one hundred and eight [recitations], all perfections (*siddhi*) are attained;
with fifty, the fulfillment of desired aims (*kāmya-siddhi*) occurs; and likewise with four more [than that].
All goals are attained with twenty-seven [verses]; with fifteen, in the practice of sorcery;
with twenty-five, liberation; and with thirty, for the accomplishment of wealth.
Having thus fashioned the garland, the wise man should perform its consecration;
for that person who recites the mantra with unconsecrated garlands [reaps no fruit].
All that [effort] of yours should be known as fruitless, for the deity becomes angry.
Now, I shall proclaim the consecration of the general rosary.
Having recited either a Tantric or Vedic mantra known as "Sadyojāta," one should first bathe the rosary with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass—
this is declared to be the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), which destroys even the most heinous sins.
The milk should be from a cow of golden color, and the cow dung from a white one;
the cow urine should be from a copper-colored cow, and the curd from a blue-colored cow.
But ghee [is obtained] from a black cow alone, and the same applies to the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). Furthermore, cows of various colors are easily found in those regions.
In that regard, one should collect the five products of the cow according to their respective colors;
there is no fault if the colors are not obtained, but one should avoid using them if they are deficient in quantity.
Cow dung is said to be double the amount of urine, ghee four times,
milk eight times, and curd likewise [eight times] for the *pañcagavya*.
Alternatively, it is said that the portions of the five products of the cow are equal:
one should take cow urine with the *gāyatrī* mantra and cow dung with the *gandhadvārā* mantra.
One should offer milk with the mantra "āpyāyasva," curd with "dadhikrāvṇo," clarified butter (ājya) with "tejo 'si śukram," and water from *kuśa* grass with "devasya tvā."
One should wash it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other substances while reciting the "sadyojāta" mantra;
one should rub it with sandalwood, agallochum, and fragrant pastes while reciting the "vāmadeva" mantra.
One should also fumigate it with black aloe-wood, aguru, and guggulu using the Aghora mantra;
and one should smear it with sandalwood and other substances using the mantra known as Tatpuruṣa.
One should recite "Īśānaḥ sarvam" over each [item] a hundred times;
with that same mantra, one should consecrate Mount Meru, and one should also consecrate it with the Aghora mantra.
One should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of life-force) for it with its universal form;
having thus consecrated the garland, the preceptor should place it in the hand [of the disciple].
Having saluted the guru by touching his feet with one's head, one should personally grasp his hands;
prior to this, one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra five hundred times.
Then one should recite the root mantra; this is its specific rule.
Now I shall describe another method of consecrating a rosary using leaves of the *aśvattha* tree:
one should place nine [leaves] arranged in the shape of a lotus and install [the beads] therein.
Having washed the gem and the thread with perfumes and other substances, one should then consecrate them with mantras.

Oṃ Hrīṃ! Having sequentially placed one by one the letters of the primordial alphabet (mātṛkā) upon the jewel and the thread therein, and having worshipped them, one should then perform the fire oblation (homa).

With sesame and clarified butter, or with clarified butter alone, one should offer oblations separately with the five mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*, either one hundred times, eight times, or twenty-eight times each.

In the absence of fire-offerings (homa), recitation (japa) is prescribed as before, along with the ritual washing and other rites; however, in the Kaulika and other traditions, this specific distinction applies: the libation (tarpaṇa) is performed with wine.
Having thus consecrated the garland, O Goddess of Gods, the wise one should establish its vital breaths therein and worship it with devotion using the root mantra.
Having worshipped the Guru, one should receive the rosary from his hand;
for the sake of a Śūdra or a woman, the consecration of the rosary is prescribed.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Durgā with devotion,
one should then consecrate that rosary with the seed-syllable *hasauṃ*.
One should place it in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for three days, reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
then, on the fourth day, having extracted it, one should wash it with the Astra-mantra.
Having tied it with the heart-mantra, one should place it upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Then, having weighed the garland, one should place it in a golden vessel.
Having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and with cool water,
[one should anoint him] with fragrant sandalwood, musk, saffron, and so forth.
Then the practitioner should perform the consecration with the mantra "Oṃ";
he should worship the nine planets and also worship the guardians of the directions.
One should perform the fire-oblation according to one's capacity with sesame seeds mixed with nectar;
furthermore, one should give gold as a sacrificial fee to the guru, equal in number to the gems.
One should feed Brahmins who recite those mantras or those learned in the Vedas;
or, for one who possesses the mantra of "Oṃ Bhāve," a leaf of the Aśvattha tree may be accepted in place of a golden vessel.
Having stated that this is the consecration of the rosary, the recitation shall become a bestower of success.
Now I shall further explain the consecration of the rosary (mālā-saṃskāra).
It should be fashioned according to the prescribed measurements; one should immerse it in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) for three days.
Alternatively, on the fourth day, one should wash the thread with the Astra-mantras;
then, one should tie it with a thread of the same color while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
The most excellent practitioner should string it with qualities such as gold and so forth;
then he should apply either the Brahma-knot or the Naga-noose.
O Goddess, two and a half knots are proclaimed as the *nāgapāśa*;
O Goddess, three and a half knots are proclaimed as the *brahmagraṃthi*.
O Supreme Goddess, one should accomplish all rites by means of the Brahmā-granthi;
in the case of the Nāga-pāśa, two types of cruel rites are proclaimed.
One devoted to meditation should string the rosary with the *kavaca* mantra;
at the end of all [the beads], one should then place the *meru* bead joined by two threads.
The supreme practitioner should string them together using the *tāra* (OM) conjunction and bind them;
having thus completed this, O Goddess of the Gods, he should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Having prepared a sacrificial mound or a mandala according to the sequence of the rules for their respective portions,
one should worship the chosen deity in due order and according to the prescribed method.
Having first performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times;
and one should perform oblations (*homa*) with a tenth part of that number, using whatever is dear to whichever deity.
Then the wise one should place that garland in the center of the mandala;
having empowered it with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), he should contemplate it as a deity.
Having attained the nature of non-duality, one should likewise fashion a garland of that same essence;
then, together with those most excellent practitioners, one should offer the bali-oblation according to the prescribed rule.
Having thus established the deity within the garland, the mantra-practitioner should worship the chosen deity,
the preceptor, and the artisan according to the prescribed rite.
One should not recite another mantra there, if one desires success for oneself.
Now, O Pārvatī, listen as the method for making garlands for the Kaulikas and the Vāmins is described, beginning with the use of bones and other materials.
In that regard as well, within the *Kālikā-tārā-vidyā*,
many kinds of garlands are taught, distinguished by such varieties as the *mahāśaṅkha* (great conch) and others, which are produced from corpses.
The great rosary made of conch shells is the embodiment of all vidyās;
the goddess known as the tooth-rosary has Mount Meru as its central tooth.
O Goddess, the garland of the Śiva-universe, the series of bodies within bodies,
the rosary of the bones of the hands, and likewise the garland of its joints;
The shin bone serves as a peg and also brings success when used in a rosary.
Then there were those born from cows, horses, donkeys, deer, men, and boars;
and those born from bears, owls, tigers, leopards, elephants, and tusks.
Musk is produced from animals such as the *gavaya* and other deer species;
it arises from the bones of living beings and is found in the teeth of donkeys, camels, and horses.
An ivory substitute for a conch shell is excellent;
that which originates from Viśvāmitra is new and consists of all living beings.
O Maheśānī, a rosary made of conch shells, ivory, or coconut, as well as one made of bones, may be used by an elderly woman, provided it is without cow dung.
The rosary is said to be of three kinds: superior, inferior, and middling;
namely, one made of teeth, one made of ivory, and one with a central peak (meru).
The supreme Mālikā is proclaimed as the supreme Kālikā, the attractor;
that which resides between the ear and the eye is celebrated as the Great Conch (Mahāśaṅkha).
A garland made of fifty great conch shells is declared to be the medium-sized rosary; it is prescribed for the recitation of Tārā.
A rosary made of bones, or human skulls, or perhaps from human foreheads,
or from those situated on various parts of the body, is said to be the lowest (kaniṣṭhikā).
The goddess is severed in the ritual; thus, the goddess is considered to be threefold.
Those two teeth which face each other are proclaimed as the "royal teeth" (rājadaṃtau).
In ancient times, the Dānavas were devoured by Mahākālī, whose mouth was formidable;
her two fangs that reach throughout the three worlds are known as the *rājadaṃtau*.
"O beloved, the name 'Rājadaṃtā' was indeed previously given to the Goddess;
those two canine teeth of mine are both effectors of my purpose."
Therefore, with a joyful mind, they were appointed to the task of Meru.
The Goddess said:
O Śaṅkara, the general garland has been described; now describe it according to its specific varieties.
The illustrious Śiva said:
O Supreme Goddess, beginning from the lunar orb and extending to the ends of the ears on both the left and right pairs, the garland of Meru-maṇḍalas resides there.
O Parāmbikā, a rosary made from *meru* seeds grants all supernatural powers;
a second type, made from two and a half barley grains, is the "Enchanter of Sovereignty."
The skull is said to consist of a number of apertures in a single row;
that which is situated between the ear and the eye is proclaimed as the Mahāśaṅkha.
A garland made of great conch shells bestows all accomplishments;
O Supreme Goddess, it extends from the ears, eyes, and neck down to the tips of the teeth.
O Maheśānī, the "Muṇḍa" [mudrā] is prescribed for the ritual practice of worship;
O Parameśvarī, it begins from the crescent moon of the right eyebrow and extends to the ear.
O Śivā, beginning from the crescent moon of the left eyebrow and extending to the tip of the left ear,
one should apply the rosary-mark (mālā) and the triple-tilaka (tripuṇḍra) along the path of Śiva and Śakti.
Following the path of the half-tripundra, one should place the rosary below it like a garland of power (śakti);
the rosary arranged in an upward sequence is indeed the most excellent among all garlands.
O Goddess of gods, the garland should be placed above the skull in the sequence of the hair;
likewise, the jewels should be fashioned as Śiva alone and nothing else.
The second is a garland made of great conch-shells, the Dhruvamaṇḍala;
the third is proclaimed to be the goddess Unmanī-mālikā.
Merumāla shall be the fourth, and Merumaṇḍalā the fifth; O Maheśānī, Daṃtamālā is the sixth, followed by Merumaṇḍalamālikā.
By means of the "King's Tooth" (rājadaṃta), Meru is [attained], and by that, the entire circle of Meru;
this is the fivefold garland, the domain of the five subtle elements (tanmātras).
O Śivā, having joined the two central teeth (the "king-teeth") at Meru according to the path of the rows,
one should place the fangs above each other in successive order, O Śivā.
One should go toward the lower lip, which has a shining row of teeth as its central pearl;
the upper canine tooth is Mount Meru, while one should abandon the fourteen that are thin.
Thus, the garland, the great garland, consisting of fifty teeth as its range, is a garland composed of all accomplishments; it shines by means of that Meru made of silver.

The fifth rosary is known as the bestower of success (siddhi), yoga, and enjoyment, and it grants the three kingdoms; it is traditionally held to consist of sixty-four beads for those seeking spiritual perfection.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
these are the five great pretas in the ritual of the five garlands of Ambikā.
Tārāchinnā, as well as Kāmakalā, Kālī, and Kālikā;
even in Śrīvidyā and other [mantras], O Śivā, there is Mālikā, which consists of a garland.
O Supreme Goddess, regarding the nature of the previously mentioned gems,
these gems possess fragrance and form, resembling ivory and crystal.
Those desiring all accomplishments should diligently prepare [rosaries] made of jewels;
if one is unable to do so with a great conch-shell, one should perform the recitation with a crystal rosary.
Then he spoke to the officer in charge of the great garland.
A garland of all the bones is highly praised; now hear the sequence of authority:
one who is enriched by the ornament of the full and half-traditions (āmnāyas), and likewise initiated into the [divine] feet.
One who is unable to follow the sequence of the six lineages, yet is endowed with the glorious Medhā;
or one who is unable to follow the Mahācīna lineage, or is a follower of the Mahānīla lineage.
O Supreme Goddess, such a practitioner who is devoted to the recitation with a rosary is declared to be qualified for the use of the rosary in due order.
The secret garland of meanings and the ritual of giving [the skull] have been explained in the sections concerning common worship.
Now, the modes of emanation are described.
O Dear One, having first prepared the perfected severed head, one should have the garlands and other items made;
one should first worship the artisan with garments, perfumes, and ointments.
Highly delighted and drinking honey, he should cause a garland to be made purified by mantra;
the wise one should fashion the piercing-perfected garland according to what is appropriate.
O Goddess of gods, there is a rosary of teeth, a rosary of conch shells, one made from skulls of Viśvāmitra,
and a rosary of all bones fashioned from the bones of living beings.
From the big toe up to the crown of the head, [this practice] is auspicious in its progressive stages;
there the Goddess is always pleased, and there Pārvatī resides.
O Goddess, in this rite of knowledge and in the previously mentioned procedure, there is an excellent bone;
a rosary made of fifty gems [should be used], according to the sequence of the letters of the Mātṛkā.
If it consists of one hundred and eight [verses], then there is the arrangement into eight groups;
having made [the total] one hundred and eight, one should cast it into the vulva according to the lunar fortnight (ṛtu).
Having set it aside for one night, one should then wash it with appropriate substances;
thereafter, one should consecrate it with pure water and the juices of Vijayā while reciting the root mantra.
Having washed it, one should subsequently fumigate it and thread it with the desired cords.
O beloved, the threading of the needle should be performed with a red cloth, or with a cloth soaked in lac, or even with fibers; this is considered auspicious.
That channel spoken by the Self-Existent One is the most excellent of all channels;
there, the Heroine is worshipped with tūlaka flowers consecrated by the Self-Existent One.
The thread should be spun by a maiden or by a virtuous woman;
then, O best of the twice-born, that spun by a virtuous woman should be free of knots.
A thread produced from the hand of a courtesan, or even one born from the hand of a Mātaṅgī,
as well as one from the hand of a woman in her menses, is declared to be auspicious.
A thread smeared with kuṇḍa, smeared with cow dung, smeared with its own [dung], and likewise smeared with svayaṃbhū—
that thread is the most excellent of all.
One should recite the blue or black mantra of one's chosen deity for the rite of killing;
for enchantment, it is green; for paralyzing, it is smoke-colored, appearing like the touch of an enemy.
For pacification and nourishment, white [is used]; for hatred, it should be red;
for eradication, it should be yellow; and for subjugation, astringent [color] is considered appropriate for causing discord.
One should not tie the knots oneself, nor should one string the rosary.
Now, he speaks concerning the one authorized to string the garland.

O Goddess, regarding the rites for the Great Garland, the Tooth Garland, and the Garland of All Bones, the procedure and the qualified practitioners for stringing them shall now be described in due order.
O beloved, a mother, daughter, wife, and likewise eight daughters—
these women born of thirty-six lineages, or those born of one's own eight families— [are to be honored].
Whether it be Tārā, Kulākula, or those who are women possessing the ten vidyās;
or those born of the fifty pīṭhas, or even the seven classes of prostitutes—one should drink [from them].
O Goddess, listen to the auspicious and inauspicious omens regarding the stringing of a rosary:
curd, meat, liquor, flour, a conch shell, musical instruments, and the sound of three flutes.
The sounding of clay drums and trumpets, the sight of kettledrums and musical instruments, elephants, horses, chariots, courtesans, and other women, or a full water-pot;
O Supreme Goddess, the signs of success in recitation (japa) regarding the rosary are weeping,
singing, the wearing of a shaven head, and the sight of a corpse.
Quarreling, reviling one's teacher, disparaging the deities, reviling heroes,
the snapping of a thread, as well as the failure to obtain what has been reached, and likewise the bursting of a jewel.
If, at the time of stringing the rosary, a gem should break upon being touched, it is predicted that there will be grief for a son; he will certainly become a partaker of suffering.
If, at the time of stringing the garland, a jewel should fall to the ground, grief for that [person] is prescribed; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Taking the gem, one should string it with thread in the middle;
having thus fashioned the Brahma-knots, the Meru [bead] is joined with the knots.
Having first strung the garland, one should then begin the consecration ritual.
For the sake of accomplishment, I shall explain the consecration (saṃskāra) hidden in all tantras;
one who has performed the daily rites, who is pure, and who knows the mantras [should do so] during auspicious lunar mansions (śuddharkṣa).
Then, having performed the wheel-worship (cakrapūjā), the practitioner should offer one thousand and eight oblations of liquor and meat with the root mantra.
Then, one should cause the sacrificial offering (*bali*) of buffaloes and other animals to be presented according to the rule;
furthermore, one should feed the female practitioners (*śaktis*) and the male adepts (*sādhakas*), numbering as many as the [number of] jewels.
From this point forward, one who possesses a distinct form should perform the consecration of the rosary.
I shall now describe the ritual for the night of the rosary; listen attentively.
On an auspicious day, such as one with favorable constellations and other signs, on a pure and propitious day,
having taken up the great rosary, one should bring the vessel of the heroes.
Having approached the Vīra-yantra, one should purify the Vīramāla;
having worshipped the Goddess Maheśvarī together with her retinue and her enclosure.
Having offered twenty-one lamps and performed the bali offering,
one should thus fashion an auspicious garland and perform the great consecration.

At an auspicious moment and favorable conjunction, having invited [the deity] into either a garland or the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)— namely, the five products of the cow, cow urine, and cow dung— again...
Curd and ghee are proclaimed as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in their proper sequence;
having removed that [image], one should wash it thoroughly with pure waters while maintaining the consciousness of its divine nature.
Having cleansed it with the root mantra, one should place that substance there for a day;
on the third day, O Goddess, one should worship with yakṣa-clay.
One should worship with all perfumes, the eight perfumes, and the eightfold powers beginning with *aṇiman*; and with the eight waters for Tārā, in the jewel that shines like the star Tārā.
On the fourth day, O Goddess, having established the vital breaths, one should worship in due order;
the Seer (Ṛṣi) of this secret Mālā-mantra is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara).
The goddess Śrī Mahātāriṇī is proclaimed to have the Uṣṇik metre;
Krīṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Strīṃ is the power (śakti), and Hūṃ is remembered as the mantra-kīlaka.
The Mahāmālā and Daṃtamālā mantras are employed for purification;
one should perform the meditation on the six limbs with the Triśakti mantra according to the ritual procedure.
Having meditated with effort upon the mental resolve, O Pārvatī, [one should act] with this mantra:
the Praṇava, as well as Lajjā, Śrī, Lajjā, Kāma, and Kūrcaka.
With the mantra "phaṭ svāhā," one should cast two garlands of *vasaka* flowers;
there, with the invocation mantras and others, one should [worship] Kālikā, the bestower of the essence of time.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess along with her weapons and retinue,
reciting the root mantra and the third [mantra] while contemplating the dhenu-mudrā.
O Maheśvarī, having rendered [the object] nectar-like and having protected it with the armor-mantra (kavaca),
one should contemplate [it] as the form of the Goddess, completely enveloped by the Great Mudrā (mahāmudrā).
One should meditate there and cast the bindu; hear the mantras there, O beloved:
the Praṇava, the pair of Kūrca-s, Svāhā, and the Praṇava and Kūrca-s.
The consort of fire (svāhā) and the star (oṃ), the weapon (phaṭ), and likewise the poison (viṣam);
the star (oṃ), the consort of fire (svāhā), the star (oṃ), the modesty-gesture (hrīḥ), and those two with the beard-mantra (huṃ).
Then [utter] the wife of fire (svāhā), then the star (oṃ), then the modesty-goddess (hrīṃ), then *phaṭ* with the wife of fire;
[this is done] with a garland of mantras consisting of two or three chains, both in their separate and combined forms.
One should perform the casting of the *bindu* with the mantra repeated one hundred times,
using musk, saffron, sandalwood, agallochum, and incense.
Having removed the flower garland, one should consecrate it with the mantra:
"Oṃ, Hūṃ, Śrī Mahāvajriṇī."
Then one should utter the word "karkaśā" (the fierce one) in the form of the Great Terrible One;
having spoken [the phrase] "mahāsthimaṇḍale" (in the great circle of bones), one should likewise utter the word "praviśa" (enter).
"Grant all accomplishments," followed by the Praṇava (Oṃ), the Kūrca-bīja (Hūṃ),
the Māyā-bīja (Hrīṃ), the Vahni-jāyā (Svāhā), and the mantra "Mahākapālinī."
Then, with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and *māyā* (hrīṃ), followed by *mahāghorarūpe svāhā*,
and ending with *māyā-kūrca-tri-svāhā*, this is declared to be the *vidyā* for consecration (*abhimaṃtraṇa*).
Having worshipped with *durvā* grass and unhusked rice, one should perform the kindling (*uddīpana*) at the end;
having worshipped the Mātṛkā with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) and the ritual services (*upacāra*).
Then, having performed the kindling, one should encircle it with the syllable *kāra*;
one should offer the oblation (*bali*) with this very [mantra], uttering the *tāra* (oṃ) followed by the two *māyās* (hrīṃ hrīṃ).
One should utter Vāsudeva joined with the Bindu and enclosed by the Kūrca;
then the Kūrca, the Tārā, Phaṭ, the Kūrca again, and one should recite the two Praṇavas.
The seed-syllable *kūrca*, the wife of fire (*svāhā*), and the *praṇava* (oṃ), followed by the seed-syllables of *kūrca*;
then the word "Mahāyoginī," and thereafter "Tribhuvanatariṇī."
And a garland of great conch shells resides in the center;
it contains the word "Kuru," joined with "dehi" (give) and the term "surāpada."
O Pārvatī, with this mantra—"Accept [this] offering of flesh, O Yūkā, seize the two feet! Kullukā phaṭ! Svāhā!"—[one should perform the rite].
Having offered the bali-oblation according to the prescribed rite with appropriate materials,
one should place the rosary for five days using five substances, and on the fifth day, [perform the consecration].
One should perform the ritual for the rosary at night; by that, the rosary is perfected. One should place the rosary in a secluded spot; this is the secret ritual for the rosary.
O Goddess, listen to the further specific rule regarding the procedure for the tooth-brush:
one should utter the Praṇava, the Hṛdaya-mantra, the Bhagavatī-mantra, and the Mānarañjinī-mantra.
One should utter the word "vicce vicce valocceva haravicce," and likewise "mālāvicce mālādhāriṇī haralūṃ."
One should utter the words "I am Mahāśaṅkhāsthidhāriṇī," and one should utter the words "Karkaśāsthi-mahāmālāvāsinī."
When the *tāra*, *kālikā*, and at the end the *japamālikā* have been severed,
one should utter the word "kullukā phaṭ" in the midst of the *mahādaṃtamālā*.
O Indra among kings, then perform the dwelling for the couple and the garland;
having uttered the three *vāsinī* mantras, [recite] *krīṃ* three times and *hūṃ* twice.
The heart mantra is "māyādvayaṃ ca phaṭ svāhā" recited with the garland mantra (mālāmantra). I shall now declare the mantra for the offering of the bali; listen and be attentive.
One should utter the Praṇava, the word *karkaśapada*, the word *maṇḍala* followed by *ambike*,
and the words *mālinī* and *kaulinī*, ending with *gaurāṃ dhāri*.
O Girijā, O Mālāvatī, the word *padam*, then the word *kriyāvatī*; Gāyatrī, O beloved of the Gaṇas, O beloved of Śakra, and O Śāṅkarī.
In the Kālīkāpālika [tantra], one should extract the word "aśidhāriṇī" at the end of "jātavedase," followed by "kṛṣṇamuṇḍadhāriṇi."
"O Śrī Kālīkāli, O Mṛḍāṇī, and likewise Rudrāṇī;
accept this pair of offerings, and grant the perfection of the garland in the north."
Cause the pair [of hands] to offer the six wheels along with the dissolution-mantra (layāyuta);
one should present the oblation (bali) at the beginning, and at its conclusion, the practice of the waking state (jāgratī-kṛti).
O Pārvatī, know that the collyrium from the skull and the pair of collyriums from the feet of the thief constitute the collyrium named Viśvamohana.
O Mistress of the Gods, the supreme ash from his feet, produced in the month of Phalguna,
is renowned by the name Jagaddhūlī for the subjugation of enemies.
Having grasped this mantra, one should cast the dust known as *udbhrānti* upon the head and body of the enemy, as well as upon the bed of Gaṇeśa, Gaṇa, and water.
O Supreme Goddess, the dust that is cast forth causes delusion;
O Mistress of the Gods, by this deluding dust, the entire world is overcome with confusion.
Just as there are two eclipses, so too there are two lunar nodes (parvan);
one should not apply the distinction between purity and impurity regarding the asterism, zodiac sign, day of the week, and so forth.
One should utter the seed-syllable of desire *kṣūṃ*, as well as the seed-syllable *śrīṃ* three times, followed by *phaṭ*.
The mantra is considered to be: "O Siddhajagaddhūlisiddhi, grant success! Svāhā!"
Having gathered the finest dust from the whirlwind with this mantra, all accomplishments (siddhis) are attained through the mastery of the garland; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, the flower of one's own kind, as well as that produced from the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, and the scent of Anaṅga— O Queen of the Gods, these are proclaimed as the fourth.
Having prepared [herself] in this way, O Goddess of the Gods, while remaining awake, she should perform the ritual of adornment:
she should apply a tilaka of vermilion on her forehead and saffron on her face with *saṃvit*.
Seated in the hero’s posture (vīrāsana), dressed in the attire of a hero, and delighted by incense and lamps,
one should cast a garland into the essence of the milk of consciousness and then utter the word "Dugdha" (milk).
Then one should cast the garland into the red [fire] and thoroughly fumigate it with incense;
thereafter, O Śivā, one should indeed present the bali offering for the sake of the complete accomplishment of the garland.
Having worshipped the Śakti, the maiden, or the garland, one becomes a possessor of siddhis in the Kali age; O Goddess, having offered the bali according to the rule during the rite of bali-offering.
O Dear One, one should satisfy the rosary with blood from the neck of a goat,
as well as with streams of blood, marrow, and even menstrual blood.

O Goddess of the Gods, through libation (tarpaṇa), the [mantra] bestows success; it takes the form of the Mālā sacrifice and grants its fruit, either according to the previous sequence or by the sequence taught for the state of possession (āveśa).
O Goddess, in the Kali age, that very Mālikā, whose form is the body of the goddess, bestows boons.
Having thus fashioned this excellent garland, the practitioner shall attain accomplishment.
One who is impure must not touch her, nor should one ever reveal her;
[for she is protected from] spirits, rākṣasas, vetālas, siddhas, gandharvas, and cāraṇas.
Since they carry [the mantra] openly, one should therefore practice it in secret;
having re-strung a worn-out cord, one should recite the mantra one hundred times.
O Śivā, one should string the garland in two or three months, or in six months;
O Goddess, after six months have passed, the garland strung on the thread becomes worn out.
O Maheśānī, for one who should establish [the thread] otherwise, destruction will occur;
if the thread is severed, death will follow; therefore, one should be intent upon diligence.
A rosary made of great conch shells as well as one known as "tooth" (ivory) should not be given to just anyone; it must be kept secret like a mother's lover.
Alternatively, one may perform the recitation (*japa*) using the fingers as a rosary; that is described as follows:
beginning with the ring finger and the middle finger, one proceeds in sequence through the little finger.
The rosary is proclaimed to extend from the middle finger to the base [of the thumb].
One should arrange two joints between the middle finger and the ring finger.
Or else, on Mount Meru, starting from the base of the little finger and proceeding in order through the other fingers,
there are ten [tactile points], beginning from the tip of the index finger and ending at the base of the middle finger.
Alternatively, one may visualize Mount Meru with its central and other peaks,
extending from the middle joint of the ring finger to the base of the index finger.
The number ten is prescribed for *japa*, and likewise, it is considered to be of three kinds.
Among those, the threefold [classification] has been explained first; now hear about the one hundred and eight.
Starting from the base of the ring finger and proceeding in a clockwise direction up to the base of the index finger,
one should recite [the mantra] eight times on the joints.
The middle [finger] should grasp the triad, and the ring finger should likewise grasp the root. Making the ring finger and the middle finger into a single Meru, one must not cross over it.
This, when repeated twelve times, becomes one hundred and eight;
this is declared to be the "finger-counted" recitation (aṅgulījapa), performed with the hand neither bowed nor raised.
The thumb should be joined up to the tip of the little finger; this constitutes the ten [fingers].
By means of the lines upon the fingers, the counting of recitations (japa) becomes a written record of the recitation.
One should never separate the fingers while counting on the rosary;
by the separation of the fingers, the recitation flows away through the gaps.
One should not cross over the counting, nor should one contract the palm;
one should not show the hand, otherwise the Rākṣasas seize the fruit.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Installation of Different Types of Rosaries," in the venerable *Tantracintāmaṇi*. 30.
